en: The auspicious garland of rays of logic; the garland of rays of logic.
The First Pāda of the First Adhyāya.

May Hari, who has the face of a horse, protect you for a long time— he who, through the neighs of his horses that fill the ears with the sound of the Veda, reveals the very essence of the three Vedas as it existed in the past within the woman [Sarasvatī], manifesting her entire lineage of breaths.
This *Nayamayūkhamālikā* (Garland of Rays of Policy), which reveals the path dear and beneficial to those seeking the Lord of Fortune as if he were a treasure-house of excellence,
is composed following the noble heart of Lakṣmaṇa.

Beginning with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and ending with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), there is one single treatise consisting of twenty chapters (*lakṣaṇas*). Among these, the twelve chapters concerning the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) and the four chapters concerning the inquiry into the deities (*devatā*) have already been completed. Now, the four chapters concerning the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma*) are commenced. At the outset, [the author] examines the four reasons for not commencing [this inquiry]: the absence of prior knowledge regarding the subject matter (Brahman), the difficulty of its realization, its being established by other means of knowledge, and its lack of a fruit.

There are four sections (adhikaraṇas), beginning with the section on Concordance (samanvaya) and extending up to its conclusion, which serve as an introduction to the treatise for the purpose of establishing its commencement. Among these, this first section is intended to dispel the doubt regarding the absence of proficiency [in the subject matter].
Now, therefore, [begins] the inquiry into Brahman. 1.

The doubt is whether this treatise, consisting of an inquiry into Brahman, should be commenced or not. For that purpose, there is the doubt whether the Vedāntas are a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman. And for that purpose, there is the doubt whether linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is possible with respect to Brahman, which is an established entity (*siddharūpa*). If linguistic competency is impossible regarding an established entity, then the Vedāntas are not a valid means of knowledge concerning Brahman; consequently, the inquiry into Brahman—which is intended as a duty by means of the authority of the Vedāntas—should not be undertaken. For that reason, this treatise...

The relationship between the probandum (*phala*) and the proof (*sādhana*) regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: if it were possible for words to have their linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) established with respect to already accomplished entities (*siddha*), then the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman would be justified; consequently, this treatise, consisting of an inquiry into Brahman, ought to be commenced. This is the relationship between the probandum and the proof in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). In that regard, because a child acquires linguistic competency only with respect to what is to be done (*kārya*) through the usage of superior and intermediate elders, and because [the understanding of] those [Vedāntic texts] which depend upon it must follow the acquisition of competency regarding the "to-be-done" which they themselves depend upon—as in the case of the sentence "A son has been born to you"—[it follows that the Vedāntas do not refer to an accomplished entity].

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the word "action" (*kārya*) must necessarily be supplied in such subsequent usages as these, all words possess their linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) only with respect to action. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: although the initial apprehension of linguistic competency is restricted to the domain of action, one need not supply the word "action" in subsequent usages that concern established facts (*siddhārtha*). To explain: at the time of the initial apprehension of linguistic competency, is it understood that every single word in a sentence such as "Bring the cow" denotes an action? [No, it is not.]

Accordingly, in subsequent applications, even though all words are heard, once the general nature of the task (*kāryasāmānya*) has been understood, is it intended that there be an *adhyāhāra* (supplying) of a verbal root (*kriyāpada*) expressing a specific task due to a desire to know its particulars? Or is it [intended] merely because the first instance of linguistic usage was observed to consist of a verbal root? The first [alternative] is not tenable. For, just as the object-case-factor (*karmakāraka*) is understood from its co-occurrence with the word "cow" (*go*), the task (*kārya*) can be understood from its co-occurrence with a verbal root; thus, just as they [the words] relate to the object-case-factor, they [relate] to the task as well.

Because [the existence of] a capacity (śakti) is not to be postulated. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for just as in the case of hearing an instrument [denoted by the word] "with a staff" (*daṇḍena*) in the sentence "Bring the desired object with a staff" during the acquisition of primary linguistic competence (*avyutpatti-graha*), there is no supply (*adhyāhāra*) of an instrument in sentences such as "Look at the jar in front," so too the non-supply of the "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*) is logically consistent. Otherwise, if the sentence that first establishes linguistic competence were itself constituted by the task of bringing [the object], then in subsequent usages as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply that very same [sentence].

If the restriction to [words denoting] action (kārya) is abandoned because one hears sentences composed of other matters at the outset, then the restriction to action must also be abandoned, since there is an abundance of observations of words used for the description of established facts (siddhārtha)—that is, words devoid of terms expressive of action—such as those found in the beginning of stories and the like. Furthermore, the apprehension of the primary relation between word and meaning is observed even regarding established facts. For example, when parents and others teach the meaning of words to children, they point with their fingers to things such as the moon or a cow and employ the respective words that denote them; thus do the children [learn].

It is established by experience that people determine the relationship between word and meaning through the use of words accompanied by such pointing with the fingers. But one might object: how can a child, merely by seeing the use of a word accompanied by pointing at a finger, determine that "this is the meaning of this word"? For the child does not possess an acquisition of proficiency (vyutpatti) based on the idea that the use of a particular word together with a finger pointed toward a specific object is for the purpose of conveying the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) between those two; nor is there any such rule.

In a large assembly, when someone does not see Caitra and seeks him, the employment of the word "Caitra" accompanied by a pointing gesture with a finger directed toward him does not have the purpose of conveying the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). As for the claim that, when various objects are pointed out with the finger and the corresponding expressive words are used repeatedly, children develop a multitude of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from the observation of the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) of the pointing gesture directed at those objects and the employment of the specific words; [this is not the primary cause].

Immediately upon hearing each respective word, through the arising of one's own cognition regarding the object of that respective meaning, there would be a determination of the relationship between that word and its object in the form of denotative power (*vācakatva*), because the comprehension of an object from a word is impossible without a relationship and because no other relationship exists. This is not tenable; for if a child’s comprehension of an object from a word were dependent on another relationship—such as the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) consisting of the pointing with a finger toward that specific object while the word is being uttered—for what purpose...

Nor can another relationship, such as that of denotative power (*vācakatva*), be postulated, because the cognition of meaning is established through the relationship of concomitance (*sāhacarya*) alone. Indeed, once the cognition of meaning is established by means of one relationship, another relationship cannot be postulated as its explanatory basis; for even if it were postulated, it could not serve as the explanatory basis for a cognition of meaning already produced previously. This is because a relationship becomes a cause for the cognition of meaning only when it is itself known, and the knowledge of the relationship cannot be established prior to the cognition of meaning by means of a subsequent postulation of the relationship.

If it is argued that [the relationship exists], it is replied: It is observed that children, having repeatedly witnessed the employment of specific words accompanied by the pointing of fingers and other gestures made by their mothers, come to understand the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between those two; thus, upon hearing a word, they remember its meaning and act accordingly, and upon seeing an object, they remember the word that signifies it and employ it. Consequently, for those who have observed this, such a determination arises regarding those who are ignorant of the relationship between word and meaning.

The employment of words accompanied by specific gestures, such as pointing with a finger, is for the purpose of conveying the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). For this very reason, children, having acquired the knowledge of that relationship between signifier and signified, engage in linguistic usage accordingly. Thus, it is precisely those who possess such [latent] determinations who, upon entering childhood in another birth, are instructed by their mothers and others; therefore, through the persistence of impressions from previous births, there occurs the employment of specific words directed toward specific objects by the mothers and others.

There arises the recollection that the purpose [of language] is to convey the relationship between word and meaning; from that, there follows the ascertainment of the relationship in the form of the signifier-signified (vācya-vācaka) relation. Alternatively, in successive births, children acquire proficiency through the very force of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the grasp of proficiency resulting from the mother’s use of words accompanied by pointing with her fingers in previous lives. And this must necessarily be so, even in the case of grasping proficiency during worldly transactions such as "A son has been born to you."

It is necessary to rely upon the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births; for indeed, there is no room for the apprehension of initial linguistic usage (*ādyavyutpattigraha*) in that case. Even for a child who has heard the sentence "A son has been born to Caitra" and has subsequently seen Caitra performing bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, there is no cognition—either that "the newborn infant is Caitra's son" or [the reverse]—arising spontaneously. Therefore, when people perform bathing, giving gifts, and so on, being delighted upon hearing of the birth of a son, they do so only after remembering [the connection] through the awakening of impressions from previous births regarding that specific subject.

When a child is born as the son of Caitra, even the statement "O Caitra, a son has been born to you" has the birth of Caitra’s son as its meaning; for this very reason, it must be explained that one determines, "This person is performing the bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth, which are to be done immediately after hearing of the birth of a son not previously seen by me. Even when the sentence "A son has been born to you" is heard in the Lāṭa country preceded by the presentation of a cloth marked with the footprints of a son, [the meaning remains the same].

They say that there is indeed a dependence on the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births regarding this subject matter. Therefore, since the acquisition of the meaning of words (*vyutpatti*) exists, it is established that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman is fully justified. This is the meaning of the Sūtra: "Now" (*atha*) means after the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*), which constitutes the purpose of the first part of the Veda; "therefore" (*ataḥ*) means for the very reason that the inquiry into ritual action—the preliminary inquiry—has already taken place; thus, the inquiry into Brahman, which constitutes the purpose of the latter part of the Veda, ought to be undertaken. Although the word *jijñāsā*...

Although [the injunction] expresses knowledge and desire, nevertheless, because the duty (*kartavyatva*) thus supplied cannot be construed with a desire that is already self-evidently established, it is construed with the knowledge in the form of inquiry (*vicāra*), which is its qualifier. This is just as in the case of "He offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the injunction is construed not with the oblation—which is already obtained from the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*)—but with its qualifier, the curd. Even though inquiry might also be prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), nevertheless, for the sake of removing obstacles and strengthening that [inquiry] by way of dispelling the doubt regarding the absence of established proficiency (*vyutpatti*), [the injunction applies] there.

The connection with "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) is indeed appropriate. Now, one might ask: how can the investigation of ritual action (*karmavicāra*), which has already occurred, serve as a cause for the upcoming investigation of Brahman (*brahmavicāra*)? If it is argued that its causality consists in: (1) understanding the injunctions for the repetition of rituals; (2) realizing through that that the fruits of rituals are small and unstable; and (3) attaining knowledge of the nature of the rituals required for the meditations (*upāsanā*) aimed at attaining Brahman—then [we reply]: even so, the investigation of ritual action initiated by Jaimini would still be incompatible with the subject matter to be established by the treatise on the investigation of Brahman composed by Bādarāyaṇa.

If it is argued that [Jaimini's] status as an authority is not tenable because he rejects the renunciation of worldly life (*brahmasaṃnyāsa*) and so forth, and because he propounds meanings contrary to that [renunciation], as demonstrated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa himself in such sūtras as: "Jaimini [holds it to be] a statement of human purpose due to its being subsidiary, as in other cases," and "In the case of the reference [to ritual acts], Jaimini [says they are not enjoined], because there is no injunction and because he censures them"—then this is not so. In those sūtras, Jaimini’s position is stated as a *anvāruhyavāda* (a concessive argument); for this very reason, his acceptance of the renunciation of worldly life for the sake of Brahman is shown in the sūtra: "Jaimini [maintains] there is no contradiction even directly."

This has been demonstrated by such sūtras as, "But for one who has become that [state], there is no non-becoming of that state, according to Jaimini as well. Nevertheless, it might be argued that by accepting the denial and rejection of Brahman-sannyāsa and so forth, Jaimini was merely indicated to be subject to the same defects attributed to the Sāṃkhya and other schools in the sūtra, "And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. Even so, no defect arises regarding his reliance on the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) composed by Jaimini; for in the treatise on the inquiry into ritual action authored by him, there is no sūtra formulating a refutation of Brahman-sannyāsa and the like. Therefore, he is only at fault for propounding contradictory views outside of that [work].

If it is argued that this is not a fault, [we reply: even by those who reject the authority of the Veda, such as the author of the *Kāśikāvṛtti* and others, it must be stated—based on the sūtra "Speech that is joined with reason is to be accepted, not [accepted] out of respect for the person"—that the authority of the Veda exists solely because its purpose is action (*kriyārthatva*). Having raised the objection without distinction that those parts of the Veda which do not have action as their object lack authority, Jaimini established their authority by demonstrating that they serve that purpose through their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with injunctions (*vidhi*). That [argument] too was refuted by Bādarāyaṇa in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*.

The independent authority of Vedic statements concerning Brahman that do not have action as their purpose has already been refuted by establishing [the authority of] such statements through their own inherent validity. If it is asked how there can be a single system (*ekaśāstrya*) for these two contradictory positions, it is replied: Jaimini, in his own *Devatādhikaraṇa*, did not explicitly perform a refutation of the nature of the deity; nor is it appropriate to assume such a [refutation] was his underlying intention.

In the *Tīrthadhikaraṇa*, because he [Śabara] has established the existence of deities through the acceptance of the *Raya-sphujī* (the *Sphujī* of the *Raya*), there arises a contradiction with that [position]. For in that context, it is stated under the sūtra, "Not deities, because of the absence of another deity" (*na devatā, devatāntarābhāvāt*), that deities are not entitled to perform ritual acts (*karmasu nādhikriyante*). This is because for deities such as Indra, no other deity like Indra is observed to whom the sacrificial offering (*havis*) could be given; and since it is impossible to relinquish one's own ownership (*svatva-tyāga*) of a substance intended for oneself, the sacrifice and so forth cannot be accomplished. Now, even so, regarding the deities' entitlement to ritual acts by Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa...

The contradiction is unavoidable given the acceptance of both [the word's] being a quality (*guṇatva*) and its predominance (*prādhānya*). For instance, in Jaimini’s eighth chapter, in the section concerning the rule "in case of conflict, by the oblation" (*vipratipattau haviṣā*), it is stated: "In case of conflict, [the rule applies] by means of the oblation."

By the sūtra *niyamyeta karmaṇastadupākhyatvāt*, it is established that in the case of the *aindra-puroḍāśa* offerings, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *āgneya* sacrifice applies due to the commonality of the sacrificial material (*havis*) in the form of the *puroḍāśa* cake, and not the procedure of the *sānnāyya* sacrifice due to the commonality of the deity Indra. This is because the sacrificial act (*yāga-karman*), consisting of the abandonment of the offering material, is perceived and observed through the *havis*; for the sacrifice is seen being performed by means of the material being abandoned, and not by an imperceptible act consisting merely of the mental dedication (*uddeśya*). Having thus demonstrated the nature of the sacrifice...

Because it consists of the propitiation of a deity, the deity alone—being pleased—is the primary bestower of the fruit; thus, there might arise the doubt that the generality of the deity is stronger than the generality of the oblation. To refute this doubt, the Sūtra states: "The mention of the deity is subordinate" (*guṇatvena devatāśrutiḥ*). In that regard, in the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*), by means of the Sūtra—"Or rather, the deity should be the motivator, because, like a guest, the act of eating is for its sake"—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was stated that even sacrifice, consisting of the honoring of a guest, has the deity as its primary object since it is for the purpose of pleasing the deity.

By the sūtra, "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act would be primary; the mention of the deity is subordinate," the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated that the act of sacrifice does not have the deity as its primary object, but rather that very act produces the fruit through the medium of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), and not a deity gratified by the oblation; for the deity is mentioned in scripture merely as a subordinate element of the sacrifice, being the intended recipient of the substance. Then, by the sūtra, "In the case of a guest, there is primacy of that [gratification]; there would be an absence [of such primacy] in the ritual act, because that [the guest] consists in the injunction of gratification," the distinction from the case of a guest is shown.

*Ātithya*—the performance of hospitality for a guest—is ordained as something that must be done in such a way that the guest is pleased; thus, it is appropriately centered on the guest (*atithi-pradhāna*). However, in the case of ritual action (*karman*), there is no such ordainment of causing pleasure, nor is the sacrifice centered on the deity (*devatā-pradhāna*). But by Bādarāyaṇa, through the sūtra "The fruit [arises] from Him (the Lord), because that is logical," all ritual action is shown to be centered on the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-pradhāna*) insofar as it consists of the propitiation of the Supreme Lord; the fruit arises solely from the Supreme Lord who has been propitiated by those respective actions, and not from an intermediate operation (*apūrva*) produced by the action.

Having thus stated his own view, [the author] presents the position of Jaimini as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the sūtra, "Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the cause], for this very reason," asserting that action alone, by means of the *apūrva*, bestows the fruit. Then, with the sūtra, "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] the Supreme Lord [is the giver], because of the designation of Him as the cause," he establishes that the Supreme Lord alone is the giver of the fruits of all actions; for in the supplementary portions (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the injunctions regarding ritual acts—such as "He alone leads him to prosperity"—it is the Supreme Lord Himself, appearing in the form of Vāyu and others, who is designated as the cause of the fruit, since action itself is momentary and perishes.

By demonstrating the reasoning that refutes the view of Jaimini—namely, that when there is a requirement for a means (*dvāra*) to produce a result, it is improper to postulate another means while bypassing the satisfaction of the deity (*devatā-prīti*) provided by the supplementary portion of the Vedic text (*vākya-śeṣa*)—his own position has been established. [Objection: In this way, how can two texts with mutually contradictory meanings be justified as belonging to a single Śāstra? [Reply: It is said: This contradiction does not contradict the unity of the Śāstra, because there is no contradiction regarding ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And since there is no difference in that regard, there is merely a duality in the description of the meaning of the sentences.

Because even in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā), a division of chapters is observed; for instance, regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, among the four scriptural statements—"He spreads [the base], he pours [clarified butter] over it, he cuts off two portions of the oblation, and he offers the fourfold portion"—the injunction for the offering of the cut-off portion (*avattahoma*) is found in the statement concerning the fourfold portion (*caturavattavākya*). Then, having referred back (*anūdya*) the cutting off (*avadāna*) which is already established by implication, the statement concerning the two cuttings (*dvayavadānavākya*) contains the injunction that "two portions of the oblation are to be cut off. However, in the statement concerning the fourfold portion, the word "four" (*catuḥ*)...

That the number [four] taught in the sentence concerning the spreading (*upastaraṇa*), the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*), and the two-fold cutting (*dvayavadāna*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a cumulative number established by those [acts] was determined in the fifth book’s section [PMS 5.1.20]: "But when connected, it should be a subsidiary because of the commencement" (*saṃyukte tu prakramāttadaṅgaṃ syāt*). An alternative view holds that in the sentence regarding the two-fold cutting, there is an injunction for the cutting of the oblation characterized by duality; whereas, having restated the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*) obtained from the injunctions for the spreading, the pouring over, and the two-fold cutting, there is an injunction for the mere act of offering (*homa*). This is stated in the tenth book’s section [PMS 10.1.3]: "Because of its purpose at the time of origin, the four-fold portion belongs to the primary [offering]" (*utpattitādarthyāt caturavattaṃ pradhānasya*).

This has been explained. In that regard, having raised the objection regarding the mutual contradiction between the two authorities, it was established in the *Tantraratna* that there is no fault of contradiction because there is no difference in the performance [of the rite] in either case. Nor should it be argued that the meditation on the deity prescribed by the rule—"One should meditate in the mind upon whichever deity one is about to offer the *vaṣaṭ*-call"—is to be performed at the place of sacrifice according to the view of Bādarāyaṇa, whereas the injunction for meditating on the deity cited by Jaimini refers to the meditation on the words denoting those respective deities; for...

In the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vṛtti has cited the statement, "This [work] is a compendium with the sixteen-chapter treatise of Jaimini," thereby establishing the unity of the system through the twelve-chapter work for the investigation of ritual action (*karma*) and the four-chapter work for the investigation of the deity (*devatā*). Among these, in the section concerning the investigation of ritual action, the differentiation of the meanings of the twelve chapters—concerning the means of knowledge of Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*), its divisions, and the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) and so forth—is easily established. Regarding the section concerning the investigation of the deity, they state the differentiation of the meanings of the four chapters as follows:

"The essential nature [of the deities], their divisions, their worship preceded by that [nature], and the fruit thereof are described in the Devatākāṇḍa (the section on deities). Since ritual action (*karman*) and the worship of deities function as auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*) for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), they share a single unity with the inquiry into Brahman; and since the subject matter—the Veda to be explained—is one and the same, it is established that the earlier and later portions of Mīmāṃsā constitute a single treatise (*ekaśāstrya*). For this very reason, it is said: "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are the seats of the Vedas, and of knowledge and dharma."

There are fourteen [branches of knowledge]: the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra. Indeed, these are the fourteen branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*), according to such enumerations in the Smṛtis. Since Mīmāṃsā is enumerated as a single branch of learning—comprising both Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā—there would otherwise be an excess in the number of distinct categories; so, enough of this elaboration. Here follow the summary verses (*saṅgrahakārikā*).
The Vedāntas are not capable of establishing Brahman as an accomplished entity (siddha),
for in the world, the primary acquisition of the meaning of words occurs only with respect to that which is to be accomplished (kārya).

Therefore, when it is argued that the investigation of Brahman (brahmamīmāṃsana) is useless— either because one relies on the Vedas as they are, consisting mostly of mere syllables, or else not at all— it is replied as follows:
Pointing to objects with their fingers, the elders employ words;
from that, the children learn, and those words become fixed for them.

Thus, even though the acquisition of linguistic proficiency— which is established by the common experience of the world— is accomplished in this manner, why is it restricted to the capacity for action alone?
The activity regarding the finger of the aforementioned form was performed in order to make [the child] grasp the capacity [to understand];
however, the understanding of children arises from the latent impressions (vāsanā) of previous births.
For even animals in this world,
through the latent impressions (vāsanā) of their previous births, understand that specific male and female behaviors are intended for those respective purposes.
Alternatively, due to the concomitance between the pointing with a finger and the employment of the respective word,
the firmness of the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by the observation of that [object] [arises].

When the cognition of a specific meaning arises upon hearing a specific word, the world perceives a power (*śakti*) whose nature consists in the connection between that word and that meaning. Thus ends the section concerning the desire to know (*jijñāsādhikaraṇa*). ||1||
[The Brahman is that] from which there is the origin, etc., of this [world]. (Sūtra 1.1.2)

It is heard in scripture: "Bhṛgu Vāruṇi approached his father Varuṇa and said, 'Venerable sir, teach me Brahman,' beginning with [the inquiry] and concluding: 'That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at death—desire to know that; that is Brahman. Is this passage capable of establishing Brahman through its definition (lakṣaṇa), or not? A doubt arises based on whether the three—creation and so forth—are possible or impossible as definitions, depending on whether they function as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) or as indicators (upalakṣaṇa).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): On the position that [the attributes] are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the oneness of Brahman is not established, because the difference of the qualifiers would entail a difference of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). For a qualifier is that which differentiates, and the qualified is that which is differentiated; therefore, as in the cases of "the humped one, the shaven-headed one, the full-horned one, the cow, the horse, the buffalo," and so forth, a difference of the qualified is unavoidable. However, in the case of "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, and red-eyed," there is no multiplicity of the qualified because the oneness of Devadatta is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this is not the case when such establishment by other means of knowledge is absent.

However, even in that case, there must indeed be a plurality [of Brahmas] due to the difference among the qualifiers. Therefore, since the identity of Brahman—which is intended to be defined here by this very definition—with any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not apprehended, a plurality resulting from the difference of qualifiers is unavoidable. Furthermore, because the multiplicity of the qualificand is perceived through the difference of qualifiers such as "oneness" and so forth, it follows accordingly that terms like "one" refer to a common genus (*sājātya*), just as in the expression "one grain of rice. Nor can unity be established here on the basis of the singular number in the phrase "That Brahman," for that [singular number] refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

For one who desires to know [the meaning], in the sentence "The cow is spotted, hornless, and full-horned," it is logical that the singular number inherent in the word "cow" (go) has the universal (jāti) as its object. Indeed, a single cow cannot be both spotted, hornless, and full-horned, because being spotted and so forth are mutually contradictory properties. If, in that case, the singular number refers to the universal, then here too—since the natures of being the creator and so forth are distinct and mutually contradictory—the singular number must be said to have the single universal as its object.

It is the same. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the functions of creator and protector on the one hand and destroyer on the other; for a father who, having procreated a son, diligently protects him, does not also become his destroyer. By this, the position that [the attributes] are merely indicatory marks (*upalakṣaṇa*) is also refuted, because it is impossible for contradictory properties to have a single common indicator. Moreover, since no other form is apprehended, the status of being an indicatory mark is untenable; for when the indicated object is understood through an indicatory mark, that indicatory mark...

Three aspects are required: the indicator (*upalakṣaka*), the indicated aspect (*upalakṣyākāra*) which is the form already apprehended, and the indicated object itself. For example, in the phrase "the field where this *śarāri* bird [sits]," the connection with the *śarāri* is the indicator; ownership by Mitra is the indicated aspect; and the nature of being a field is the previously apprehended aspect. In the expression "the moon at the tip of the branch," the tip of the branch is the indicator; the connection with the upward space at the branch-tip at a particular time is the indicated aspect; and the true nature of the moon is the indicated object.

The previously apprehended form (*pūrvapratipannākāra*): In the inquiry "Which is the moon in this circle of light?"—an inquiry to be accomplished by a prior cognition—the answer "The moon is at the tip of the branch" descends [upon the mind], whereby the moon, or its excellence of light and so forth, is perceived through direct perception; this is the previously apprehended form. Now, one might object: "In this case as well, there exists a previously apprehended form characterized by the words 'Being, Knowledge,' and so forth, as established by the scriptural statement. If this is said, we reply: No. For even there, because the qualifiers such as "Being," "Knowledge," and so forth are distinct, it would follow that the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is also divided.

Because it is impossible for [the cause] to be a qualifier, and because the position of it being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is also untenable due to the non-apprehension of any other form, and because if one were to resort to another form as understood from such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these [beings arise]," there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence; therefore—

Since both the positions—that [the attributes] are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) or that they are mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*)—are untenable, Brahman cannot be apprehended. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Brahman can indeed be apprehended by means of its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Nor does the perception of a difference in the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) based on a difference in the qualifiers—which might seem to contradict the apprehension of [Brahman’s] non-duality—constitute a sublation of that apprehension; for, as in the case of "dark-complexioned" and "tall," the non-difference of the qualified object is logically consistent even when there is a difference in the qualifiers. Now, one might argue that a difference in the qualified object is the natural rule (*autsargika*) when there is a difference in the qualifiers, as in the case of "the broken-horned" and "the shaven-headed."

If it is argued that this is seen in such cases, and that in instances like "the dark-complexioned [man] is tall," the cognition of the identity of the qualificand—established by other means of knowledge—is what sublates [the difference], then that is indeed true as stated. However, it is poorly stated; for even when the qualifiers differ, the identity of the qualificand is the default rule (*autsargika*). In cases such as "the broken one, the shaven one," it is simply the contradiction between the qualifiers that acts as the sublater; thus, it is more appropriate to postulate a system based on the distinction between the default rule and its exception. If it is asked what the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) here is, [the answer is] the parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating identity as the default rule, rather than difference.

The argument that postulating a general rule (autsargikatva) involves unnecessary complexity (gaurava) serves as the decisive factor; for in cases such as "He is dark and tall," qualities like darkness are established as qualifiers by virtue of differentiating [the subject] from those who are fair-skinned and so forth. Likewise, the oneness of the substantive (viśeṣya) understood through the singular number in the phrase "That Brahman" is also [established in this manner].

The sublation of the distinction between the qualified (viśeṣya) dependent upon the distinction between the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) occurs because the singular number has, as its natural rule (autsargika), the identity of the individual (vyakti) as its object. In cases such as "the broken one, the shaven one," however, that [natural rule] is set aside due to the contradiction among the qualifiers; even there, the capacity of qualifiers to differentiate the qualified is the natural rule in instances like "the broken one, the shaven one," whereas in cases like "this dark-complexioned young man," that [differentiation] is set aside because the identity of the qualified is understood through another means of knowledge. Thus, the attempt to establish a contrary system of natural rules and exceptions is rejected.

One should consider this as the decisive factor: that there is parsimony (lāghava) in postulating that the universal has as its object the identity with the individual, whereas otherwise there would be prolixity (gaurava). Thus, this is a decisive factor common to worldly usage; for, in the case of the sentence beginning with "from which," because of its connection with the word "that" (yat), it is understood—as established by another scriptural passage such as "All these creatures, O dear one, have Being as their root, Being as their support, Being as their foundation"—to be a restatement of the cause of creation and so forth already established by other scriptures, in accordance with the promise of the knowledge of all things.

Since it is necessary that the subject matter possesses a single cause, one must state that the subject matter of the preceding statement (purovāda) possesses a single cause; thus, there must be another determining factor (*vinigamaka*). And so, just as in the case of the passage, "If the Soma sacrifice has the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, one should take the cups beginning with the *Aindravāyava*; if it has the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*, [one should take] those beginning with the *Śukra*," the qualifiers "having the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*" and "having the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*"—though recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma—do not serve to exclude other *sāmans* such as the *Gāyatra* or *Mahīyava* mentioned in that same context, so it is here as well.

We consider it logical that the state of being the cause of creation does not exclude the state of being the cause of maintenance and dissolution, as established by the preceding discourse. Nor should it be suspected that the Lord’s role as destroyer is contradictory to his having created and protected; for, just as with creation and protection, there is no contradiction in destruction when it occurs at a different time. This is seen, for example, in the reaping at a later time of crops that were themselves produced and protected; likewise, there is no contradiction in the Lord—who acts in accordance with the specific karma of each created being—performing their respective destructions.

This is because the faults of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) will be shown [later] not to apply. Thus, even in the view that [the attributes] are merely indicatory (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no defect. Just as in the example, the nature of being a friend’s field is the indicatory mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), while the specific form previously perceived is the field-ness-in-general; so too here, the causality of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world is the indicatory mark, and the form indicated by it is the state of being the Lord of Lakṣmī. This is with respect to the causality of creation and so forth, which serves as the indicatory mark and is being restated (*anūdyamāna*).

This is because [the term] culminates in the Lord of Lakṣmī, as established by the mantra therein—"Hrīḥ and Lakṣmī are your two wives"—in accordance with the preceding statement (*purovāda*) which is the *Puruṣasūkta*. Indeed, it is not only the Chāndogya Śruti passage, "Having Being as its root," that serves as the preceding statement; for, in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), passages such as the *Puruṣasūkta*, which present the causal reality, cannot be excluded from being the preceding statement. The nature of Brahman is the form previously apprehended; for that [nature], like the state of being a field (*kedāratva*), is common to many fields as perceived through direct perception.

Through the etymological derivation of the root *bṛh*, as understood from the Śruti passage, "Because it expands (*bṛhati*) and causes one to expand in Brahman (*brahmayati*), therefore it is called the Supreme Brahman," and from the Smṛti passage, "On account of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and its being Brahman (*brahmaṇatva*), that is designated as Brahman," this [nature] is apprehended in the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). This is established not as something common to various deities such as Brahmā and others who possess diverse glories known from mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), but because the definition culminates in Brahman-hood residing in the Supreme Person alone.

The Śruti passage beginning with “Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman” [is the authority]. Now, an objection is raised: since the word *bṛhat* (great) takes the suffix *-manin*, its meaning is merely greatness (*bṛhattva*); how then can the state of being Brahman (*brahmaṇatva*) also be described as its meaning? It is said in reply: the state of being Brahman consists in being the cause of the gross transformation of sentient and insentient beings through one's own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*). This too is indeed encompassed by the word *brahman*, which denotes greatness in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*), attributes (*guṇa*), and manifestations (*vibhūti*). Now, regarding the definition, there are two positions: that it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

How can that which is accepted by others be mutually contradictory? They say there is a distinction: a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) is that which, while being connected to the object to be known (*jñāpya*), excludes what is not so connected; whereas an *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator) excludes what is not so connected without itself being connected [to the object]. This is true. Here too, due to the difference in meditation (*upāsanā*), both positions regarding the causality of origination and so forth are possible through connection with others or non-connection with others, just as in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā: "All this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes"—in this, [Brahman] is connected within the scope of the object of meditation and is thus a *viśeṣaṇa*; whereas in the meditation on the Person residing in the solar orb, who has the *vyāhṛtis* as his body... [the attributes are not so connected].

It is an *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator) because it reveals the essential nature of the Brahman to be meditated upon. If the statement from the *Arthavaśikhā*, "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," is taken as applying to all meditations, then the quality of being the "Cause" is a *viśeṣaṇa* (direct attribute) common to all meditations; whereas those qualities that reside only in certain specific meditations are *upalakṣaṇas* for those other meditations. For the purpose of instructing the disciple, the Commentator has presented these two alternatives by taking his stand on the quality of being the cause of birth and so forth. Even though...

Each individual characteristic, such as being the cause of birth and so forth, cannot serve as a definition because it is not over-pervasive; nevertheless, in order to dispel the doubt arising from the ancient tradition that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are distinct causal persons who are each individually causes of birth and the rest, the recourse is taken to the combined definition. Thus, everything is faultless. The utility of another definition of Brahman stated in the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," etc., and its purpose, will be shown in the section titled "Bliss and the others [belong] to the Principal."
The summary verses.
The definition "Brahman is that from which [the world] originates, etc. is not tenable;
for if that [originating cause] were a qualifying attribute, Brahman itself would become differentiated.
The qualifier is the general rule for the entire class of non-specific properties;
because it is that which distinguishes, there is a difference in the qualified when there is a difference in that [qualifier].
Indication does not occur due to the absence of the form of that which is to be indicated;
for it indeed makes known another form in a thing whose some form has already been apprehended.
When the locus is perceived as being a field, by means of the statement of one who knows it,
the subject— just like the śarāri bird— is made to understand its own friend’s state of being in the field.
Therefore,
the doubt that "Brahman cannot be known even by means of its defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa)" is dispelled by accepting both positions.
When it is said, "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young,
and red-eyed," although there is a distinction among the qualifiers, there is no cognition of distinction in the qualified object itself.
In the case of "the cow is broken-horned, hornless, full-horned," there is indeed a cognition of difference due to the contradiction between the states of being broken-horned and so forth;
however, in this [present] case, there is no such contradiction.
Or let it be a case of secondary indication (upalakṣaṇatā) based on its being understood as "great" (bṛhattayā);
for that [quality] is indeed understood there by virtue of the mantras, arthavādas, and so forth.
Since many entities such as Brahmā and others are proposed as being "Great," this definition is stated in the Śruti in order to determine which among them is Brahman.
Just as, when a field is determined by its commonality as a "field," the notion that it is specifically "Mitra’s field" arises through the distinction of individuals among those who possess bodies.
Thus, when the Lord of Śrī has been determined to be the cause by virtue of His universal greatness as Brahmā and the rest, the cognition of His greatness becomes unimpeded.
Due to the force of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine regarding all causal statements,
the ultimate rest indeed lies in that very [pradhāna], following the logic of the goat and the animal.
Thus ends the section concerning "origination and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa). ||2||
Because it has the scripture as its source. (Sūtra 3)

The previously stated position—that the passage beginning with "That from which... establishes Brahman as the cause of the world along with its antecedent context—is untenable; for since Brahman is accessible through inference, the authority of scripture (*śāstra*) regarding it is impossible. This constitutes the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) by way of an objection. Regarding the doubt—whether or not the authority of scripture is possible with respect to Brahman, arising from the alternatives of its being accessible through inference or not—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: its authority there is not possible, because the earth, mountains, and so forth possess a creator.

Because the inference stated by the Naiyāyikas—namely, that [the world] possesses parts because it is an effect, like a jar—is fully operative, with "being an effect" as the mark (liṅga) inferred from "having parts. The mark of being an effect is not merely "having constituents" (sāṃśatvamātra), for if it were so, there would be an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) regarding time, space, and so forth, according to those who maintain that these possess constituents. What is intended here is that something is "possessing parts" when its constituent parts are capable of being separated from one another through human effort; therefore, there is no suspicion of inconsistency anywhere. Thus, regarding an object already established by other means of knowledge, the authority of scripture...

Validity [of the scripture] is not possible. If it is objected: "But surely, since the inference that establishes God as the mere efficient cause does not establish the scriptural meaning consisting of His being the non-different efficient and material cause, [the scripture lacks validity]," we say: no. For the scripture would lack validity regarding that meaning due to its contradiction with inference. If it is further objected: "Since there is a contradiction with the stronger authority of the scripture, the inference itself is invalid," we say: no. For it is impossible to establish the validity of the scripture without depending upon the inference for God.

The author of the Nyāyasūtras established the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*) solely on the basis of its being composed by God, stating: "Its authority is like that of mantras and Ayurveda, due to the authority of the trustworthy person. However, that proof depends upon the prior establishment of God through inference for the sake of proving the authority of the scripture; thus, it contradicts its own premise (*upajīvyavirodha*). Furthermore, regarding the aspect of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), the scripture merely repeats what has already been obtained from the premise; and regarding the aspect of being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*), the scripture is not authoritative. Nor can the authority of the scripture be established merely through acceptance by great people (*mahājanaparigraha*) without depending on its being composed by God.

It must be stated that its validity is established; for, in order to dispel doubts regarding other lineages, the acceptance by great men requires the firmness consisting in having a virtuous author. Thus, precisely because the scripture functions in dependence upon inference, the authorship described in such passages as "He created fire," which consists in being a creator preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*), is intended to reveal that it is rooted in inference—just as [the Upaniṣad says]: "By this sprout, my dear, seek the root, water; by the sprout of water, my dear, seek the root, fire."

Having demonstrated the inference of a cause by saying, "O gentle one, seek the root of Being through the sprout of splendor," it was stated, "O gentle one, these creatures have Being as their root," and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: since the Lord is perceived to be both the agent and the material cause—just as in the case of a potter—it cannot be that [the inference] refers solely to agency. This is not so; for the Lord is to be established by inference only as the substratum of such agency as is observed in potters and the like with respect to jars and other objects. In the case of potters and others...

Since agency is observed to consist precisely in being the presiding supervisor over all perceived causes, such as a lump of clay and so forth, an inference of God as an agent of that nature—based on conformity to what is observed—would necessarily involve a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). How, then, could this [inference] not reject the authority of the scripture regarding the aspect of His being the material cause? Therefore, since the purpose is not fulfilled by the mere statement of a definition, one must assert the authority [of the scripture] both with respect to the subject of the definition and its possession of the defining characteristics. And here, in the case of the definition consisting in being the non-different efficient and material cause—

"Since the authority of the Vedāntas is impossible, the inquiry into Brahman—which is intended as a duty by means of the Vedāntas—is not to be undertaken; therefore, this Śāstra should not be commenced. This being the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: There is no proof for the claim that the earth, mountains, great oceans, and so forth must have a creator solely because they were created by a single agent simultaneously. For their status as having a creator is equally established even if they were created by many agents in succession, just as it is in the case of a great temple complex consisting of a palace, pavilions, gate-towers, and walls. On the contrary—

The earth, mountains, and so forth have multiple creators, because they are great effects, like pots and other objects whose single creator is universally accepted; furthermore, it is possible to infer that there are indeed many creators, as in the case of city gates and ramparts. Nor can the oneness of the creator be established through the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), for we do not postulate many creators distinct from the well-known transmigrating beings; rather, among those very beings, certain individuals—whose specific merits have been accumulated through particular actions and meditations—act as creators of the earth and other things at various specific times.

[Such powers] are postulated. For the capacity of Agastya, Viśvāmitra, and others to arrest the Vindhya mountains, to reduce the great ocean to a handful, and to create other heavens, is well known. Even among contemporary people, such as those who produce sprouts and the like, there exist those possessing knowledge of subtle, hidden, and distant objects; thus, it is possible for yogins to be the agents in those cases. Therefore, it is more reasonable to postulate some agent distinct from transmigrating beings, who possesses direct knowledge, will, and other qualities regarding the material cause of the entire world, beginning with the earth.

There is the burden of postulating a substratum (*dharmikalpanā-gaurava*). And thus, by the example of a jar and so forth, the proof that the earth, sprouts, and so on are produced by a body is also rendered unavoidable. Furthermore, what is the meaning when it is said that a single agent, established through parsimony (*lāghava*), is established as distinct from the well-known transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*)? Does this mean that an agent is established as being one in reality, or that [an agent] is established as qualified by oneness? Not the first; for if oneness is not the object [of the inference], then does "an agent is established as one in reality" mean... or [what else]?

[The opponent argues: "It is established as qualified by oneness. [Reply: Not the first [alternative], because if oneness is not the object [of the inference], it is impossible to determine that the object is in fact a single agent. Not the second either; for if oneness is of the nature of a number, then since each [agent] possesses that qualification individually, its establishment would not contradict the existence of multiple agents. If it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is "agency qualified by the absence of having multiple agents," we say no, because this would lead to a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of temple gate-towers (*gopura*) and the like. Furthermore, there is no such thing as "lightness" (*lāghava*) as you intend it, which could serve to present a simpler object [of cognition].

Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that [the auxiliary] would bring about a multiplicity of objects. Indeed, there is no such accepted auxiliary of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which, for the sake of establishing the parsimony (*lāghava*) of the object later on, would impose a complexity of objects upon its own supported means of valid cognition. If that were the case, then the parsimony-based reasoning (*lāghavatarka*), which is an auxiliary of the means of valid cognition grasping the causal efficacy of the cognition of the desired object present before one, would—by not postulating a cognition with a non-corresponding qualifier in cases of error—for the sake of establishing the parsimony of the object later on...

One might as well posit the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) itself as the delimiting factor of causality, rather than the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) presented as being cognizable by the cognition of the knowledge; therefore, the claim that the identity of the agent is established due to parsimony (*lāghava*) is entirely untenable. By this, the following argument is also refuted: that since the agent being proved [as one] is not established as a single entity for each of the direct knowledge, desire to act, and volition—which are required for agency—due to parsimony, the identity of the agent who is their substratum is thereby established. This is because the objections raised against the position of establishing the identity of the agent, concerning the various alternatives, apply here as well.

Furthermore, in order to prevent the establishment of a difference in substrata—such as that one [person] has knowledge, another has the desire to act, and another has the actual action—it would follow that their identity of substratum must also be proven. For, in your own view, there is no relationship of producer and produced among the eternal cognitions and so forth of God; otherwise, since such a relationship is observed only between things residing in the same substratum, their identity of substratum would be established. Thus, their eternity would not be established on the grounds of their being unitary. The same applies to the immediate cognitions and so forth of yogis.

The proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is unavoidable. Nor should it be said that their presence in various locations at the moment preceding the production of the earth, sprouts, and so forth is unestablished; for according to the maxim, "It is better to postulate a property than a substratum," it is appropriate to postulate their presence here, as they are established by means of valid cognition such as the Yoga scriptures. If it is argued that once a mere agent is established through inference, the oneness of that agent may be established from Vedic texts such as "The one God, generating heaven and earth," then [we reply]: by inference...

Since it cannot be denied that the Lord’s infinite auspicious qualities—such as unsurpassed bliss—which are not subject to rejection, His eternal form, and His impermanent volitions for various acts of creation and so forth (established by such scriptural texts as *tadaikṣata*), are thereby proven, there is no establishment of an Īśvara as conceived by the Naiyāyikas—one who is devoid of a perpetually accompanying body and possesses only the three specific qualities of eternal immediate cognition and so forth; nor does this entail the lack of authority of the scripture on the grounds that it merely restates an Īśvara established through inference. Thus, by means of the scripture which is itself a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)...

Thus it is established that the proof of the Supreme Brahman—designated as Puruṣottama and the substratum of infinite auspicious qualities such as being the cause of the universe and possessing true resolve—is free from all opposition.
In the summary verses.
Brahman as the cause of the world is indeed established through inference;
therefore, the Vedāntas need not be investigated, as they merely restate what has already been proven.
This is not correct; for through inference, the identity of the agent and other such points are not established.
Therefore, Brahman, which is their cause, has the Upanishads (Vedānta) alone as its means of valid cognition.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Scripture being the source [of knowledge].

Thus, the doubt regarding the non-commencement of the scripture, caused by the suspicion of invalidity rooted in the establishment of other means of knowledge, has been dispelled. Now, for the purpose of removing the doubt concerning its non-commencement based on its fruitlessness, the fourth section begins:
"But that [Brahman is known] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (1.1.4).

Even though the Vedāntas do not function as a means of knowledge regarding Brahman in its established nature (*siddharūpa*) because other means of knowledge do not apply there, their validity is nonetheless untenable. This is because a sentence whose primary purport is an established entity—unlike a sentence whose purport is engagement (*pravṛtti*) or avoidance (*nivṛtti*)—cannot culminate in human purpose; consequently, no desire to know (*bubhutsā*) arises in the listeners toward it. Since no valid cognition (*pramiti*) arises in the listeners regarding that which they do not desire to know, the assertion of their validity is without foundation. Nor is it the case that, just as for someone who has fallen into a street by some cause and is being harassed by hunters...
To the prince who was conceiving the thought, "I am the son of a Kirāta," [the deity said]: "You are not the son of a Kirāta, but rather a prince; yours..."

Just as joy arises upon hearing Siddhārtha’s words, "The father, the great king, remains ruling his kingdom, youthful and endowed with unsurpassed enjoyments," so too here, upon hearing the words, "In this matter as well, there exists for you and others the Blessed One, who stands in the place of a father, possessing infinite auspicious qualities such as omniscience—the opposite of all that is to be abandoned—truthful resolve, compassion, courtesy, and magnanimity"—great joy arises in the hearer, and having sought the means to attain Him, he attains Him. Thus it is said.

It might be argued that even the statement of Siddhārtha culminates in a human goal (puruṣārtha) by virtue of its being a cause for joy; however, this must be rejected because that joy, like the joy of a prince, is merely temporary, and thus liberation would fail to be a stable human goal. Nor can it be argued that for one who has attained [liberation], the experience of that unsurpassed bliss of his always remains present, and thus it would be a stable human goal; for the objection is that the knowledge of another's bliss cannot constitute a human goal for that other person. This is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: there is indeed immediate joy for the time being. But the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the direct realization of unsurpassed bliss in Brahman, accompanied by equality in enjoyment with Brahman; it is not necessary that this realization be one's own. For if the qualification "being a direct realization" were applied [to the experience itself], then even the recollection of one's own past happiness and so forth would result in being a human goal, just like a direct realization of happiness. By applying that [qualification of "unsurpassed bliss"] alone, the over-extension is prevented, and thus the qualification "one's own" is unnecessary—so says the *Saṃgraha-kārikā*. Nevertheless, the Vedāntas have authority regarding this which is of the nature of an already established reality.
Because those who possess no fruit lack the intent toward engagement and so forth.
It is not so; for like a statement informing one of a treasure located within one's own house, these [scriptures] possess their fruit inherently by virtue of making that Brahman known.
Thus ends the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa). ||4||

Thus, this chapter serves the purpose of refuting the fourfold doubt regarding the reason for not commencing the treatise (*śāstra*). Among these, the demonstration that [the word *brahman*] possesses the capacity for linguistic usage with respect to Brahman as an established entity (*siddharūpa*) is useful for the Chapter on Concordance (*Samanvaya-adhyāya*). The demonstration that there is no contradiction among the qualifying attributes is useful for the Chapter on Non-contradiction (*Avirodha-adhyāya*). The refutation of establishment through inference (*anumāna*) is useful for the Chapter on Means (*Sādhana-adhyāya*); for if establishment were achieved through inference, then the meditation upon Brahman would be established by way of possessing the triad of knowledge and so forth as proven by inference, as well as by way of possessing the fivefold group beginning with number.

It is quite evident that the description of the culmination in the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) is for the purpose of the *Phalādhyāya* (the fourth chapter), by virtue of [Brahman] possessing qualities such as bliss and so forth. Thus, once the commencement of the treatise has been established through the four introductory sections (*upoddhātādhikaraṇa*), the treatise is expanded starting from the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.

The connections between the treatise (*śāstra*), the sections (*kāṇḍa*), the chapters (*adhyāya*), and the quarters (*pāda*) are clear. Now, the connection between the sub-sections (*peṭikā*) and the internal connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) must be stated. Because it is an inquiry into the meaning of the Veda, there is a connection with the Section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*); because its subject matter is the Cause (*kāraṇa*), there is a connection with the [first] two sections; and because its subject matter is the harmonization (*samanvaya*) of the scriptural passages concerning the Cause, there is a connection with this chapter.

The connection with the first quarter (*pāda*) is established because this section deals with sentences containing clearer indicative marks (*liṅga*) of *pradhāna* and the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, the five types of connections are clear. Now, the connection with the section (*peṭikā-saṅgati*) and the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*), which are to be stated, are explained: The connection with the section is as follows: by refuting the doubt that Brahman alone is not the cause of the world, but rather *pradhāna*, the individual soul, ether, and so forth, there is the exclusion of the possibility that Brahman is not the cause. This constitutes the meaning of the section, which serves as a supplement to the first quarter immediately following the four introductory topics (*upoddhāta-adhikaraṇa*). This is the connection with the section.

The qualities of Brahman, such as omniscience and the power of true resolve, which are implied by its being the cause, are the qualities to be attained by the liberated according to the *tatkratu-nyāya*; the quality of possessing great enjoyment belongs to Him alone, for the liberated one attains "the stainless supreme equality."

The statement in the *Samanvaya* section—that even according to the Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as "because of the mark of equality in enjoyment alone," the attribute to be attained by the liberated is [the Lord], and while the unsurpassed bliss of Brahman is not itself attained by the liberated one, it is nevertheless eternally tasted by him; thus, the exposition of the Supreme Brahman, who is a mine of infinite auspicious qualities and possesses unsurpassed great bliss, indeed culminates in the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—this is incorrect, because all the causal texts...

The intermediate connection is based on the objection that [the subject matter] concerns the Pradhāna. Indeed, the Sadvijñāna (Knowledge of Being) heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—beginning with the words "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—is the essence among the causal texts; it is that.

That [text] does not establish Brahman; rather, it restates the *pradhāna* established by Sāṃkhya inference. This is because the Śruti itself clarifies that it does not restate an object established by inference, through the presentation of the proposition, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and the citation of the illustration, "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known.

Nor should it be argued that the hearing of the phrase "it thought" (*tadaikṣata*) would be untenable because thinking is impossible for the insentient *pradhāna*; for there is the expression, "Rice expects rain."

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since we observe figurative usage (*upacāra*) of even insentient things as if they were sentient in common expressions such as "the rice plants rejoice at the rain" and "they sprout," and just as in the expression "the bank wishes to fall" there is a figurative usage regarding the bank's inclination toward the effect of falling, so too the figurative usage of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is possible for *Sat* (Being) regarding its inclination toward the effect of creating fire; furthermore, because the "seeing" of *Sat* is determined to be figurative by its inclusion in a context primarily consisting of figurative "sees"—as in "That fire saw" and "Those waters saw. The term *vṛṣṭyā modamānāḥ* means "rejoicing at the rain"; *kandalanti* means "they sprout"; *pipatiṣati* means "wishes to fall"; *gauṇa* means "secondary" or "figurative"; *prāyapāṭhena* means "by being read in a section primarily consisting of [figurative instances]. The final position (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Because the word "seeing" is used here in its primary sense, it is understood that the power of intelligence (*caitanya-śakti*) exists in the cause. Just as in the case of the sentence "Devadatta’s intellect sees," where the term "sees" is applied to Devadatta’s intellect in its primary sense, so too here, since the term "seeing" is applied to *Sat*, it is understood that the power of intelligence exists in *Sat*. Furthermore, the primary sense of the word "seeing" is established by the fact that it is not contradicted by anything else. Moreover, the scriptural statement "He thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (*tadaikṣata bahu syām prajāyeyeti*) establishes that the creator is possessed of intelligence. Therefore, it is concluded that the cause is indeed Brahman. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: First, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is common to both the communication of an object already known through perception and other means, and the citation of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is likewise common to both, since it serves the purpose of facilitating the mental apprehension of the matter stated in the proposition; otherwise, the proposition of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—expressed in the words, "By which the unheard becomes heard"—would not have been firmly established in the mind. Furthermore, the mere statement of the reason (*hetu*), which is unique to inference, is not heard here.

"Is it not the case that in such statements as 'Seek water, my dear, by means of food as its sprout; seek fire, my dear, by means of water as its sprout; seek Being, my dear, by means of fire as its sprout,' an inference of the cause is presented through the mark (liṅga) of the effects such as food? True—[but] the beginning, the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit," [and so forth].

"Explanatory praise (arthavāda) and logical consistency (upapatti) are marks for determining the intended meaning (tātparya). Thus, this mark in the form of logical consistency is enumerated among the marks that determine the intent of the scripture; however, there is no mention here of any mark intended by the Sāṃkhyas as a proof for the Pradhāna. For the inference intended by the Sāṃkhyas to prove the Pradhāna is as follows: "All effects have the Pradhāna as their material cause, because they are permeated by it, like a jar and other such things"—this being based on a general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti).

Nor is [Brahman] seen here even by a glance from Śruti; for a *prāyapāṭha* (contextual proximity) consisting mostly of secondary (*gauṇa*) instances of seeing does not necessitate that this seeing be secondary, since the fifth means of proof—*prāyapāṭha* characterized as proximity (*sannidhi*)—cannot sublate the Śruti of "seeing" and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of seeing expressed by it. Furthermore, the statement that "all this is of the nature of That" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*), that "That is Truth, That is the Self" (*tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā*), which declares the entire phenomenal world to have Being (*sat*) as its essence, and the declaration of Being as the Self with reference to that world, would not be possible if [the subject] were the insentient *pradhāna*.

And thus, since *sat*—which is the very self of all phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) and has fire and the other elements as its body—is intended as the "seer" in such passages as "That *sat* saw," there is not even a suspicion that the reading refers to a secondary or figurative seeing. Furthermore, having instructed the seeker of liberation, Śvetaketu, on the contemplation of his identity with *sat* through the words "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the text teaches that liberation follows the fall of the body as the fruit of that realization: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

Furthermore, it is not even accepted by the Sāṃkhyas that liberation belongs to one who rests in the Pradhāna; for they too regard that [Pradhāna] as something to be abandoned by those seeking liberation. Therefore, because there is no mention of its being something to be abandoned, the Pradhāna is not "Being" (sat).

Furthermore, *sat-pradhāna* (the Primal Nature as Being) is not [the object of the Upanishadic teaching], because it lacks the knowledge of all things. For even if the entire group of effects beginning with *mahat*—which are non-different from it—could be known through the knowledge of the Pradhāna as its effect, the knowledge of the group of conscious beings (*cetana-varga*) would not thereby be established. Moreover, having taught the "attainment of Being" (*satsampatti*) for a sleeping person in the passage, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being," the text declares that this attainment consists in deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) in the words, "He merges into his own Self. This "Being" (*sat*) is Brahman.

This is consistent with our position: prior to deep sleep, the Puruṣa is the effect-form of the Supreme Self, characterized by a gross body consisting of the individual soul (jīva) which is distinguished by a gross form such as the expansion of knowledge; during deep sleep, having abandoned that form, He becomes merged into His own causal form, which consists of the individual soul characterized by a subtle form consisting of the contraction of knowledge.

Because the root *i* preceded by *api* has the sense of dissolution (*laya*), as seen in other Vedic texts such as "For [Brahman] is the origin and the dissolution of all beings," and in statements of the Gītā such as "For [He is] the origin and the dissolution of beings"; and because it was shown in the *Lakṣaṇa-sūtra* that the word *sat*, which here refers to the causal reality, denotes the Supreme Self who has the subtle entity consisting of consciousness and non-consciousness as His body.

On the view that the *pradhāna* is the primary subject, the mention of "sleeping" (*svāpyaya*) is not tenable; for even if the word "own" (*sva*) could be justified as referring to its own [the *pradhāna*'s] nature, it is impossible for the dissolution (*laya*) of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (who has that *jīva* as His body) to occur in that [pradhāna], since it is not the cause of those two. Furthermore: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."

The same course of reasoning applies to the *Sadvidyā*—namely, the passage beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)—as it does to other scriptural passages such as "From the Self, space was produced," which establish that at the time of creation and so forth, the Supreme Self alone exists and is the creator of space and the rest. This commonality of application is what is intended.

Therefore, for us, "Sat" (Being) is not the Pradhāna; for in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, after introducing the Blessed Lord—who is the subject of the Puruṣasūkta mantras such as "The Person has a thousand heads" and "The Person alone is all this"—by stating that He is the cause along with His instruments, saying, "He is the lord of the lords of the organs, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him," the text directly establishes His status as the cause of the universe. Consequently, the Sat-vidyā must necessarily have the same meaning as that [text]. Thus, "Sat" is the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Brahman itself.
