If it is to be stated that "seeing" is used in its primary sense, then, since the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses consciousness and is thus worthy of primary seeing, let the *jīva* alone be the cause of the world; such is the objection that gives rise to the immediate connection [of this section]. To this, the followers of the *Taittirīya* school respond in the *Ānandavallī*: having begun with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," when the inquiry arises—"What is that? Of what nature is it? What is the fruit of knowing it?"—it is said: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. He who knows It as ordained in the secret cave, in the highest heaven..."

"He attains all desires together with the omniscient Brahman"—by this mantra, the nature of Brahman, the manner of its realization, and the nature of the fruit of that attainment are described. Then, by the passage beginning "From that very Self, space was produced," the origin of the entire universe, beginning with space, from that very Brahman is stated. For the sake of easy comprehension, following the maxim of the gross star Arundhatī, the mind is gradually directed toward food, vital breath, mind, and intellect; and from that [Self]...

Having introduced the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) with the words, "Different from this [self] consisting of consciousness is another inner self, consisting of bliss," the intellect is brought to rest upon that very [self] as the Brahman which is the cause of the world under discussion; for there is no subsequent instruction of another self following the statement, "Different indeed from this self consisting of bliss is another inner self. That...

In the doubt as to whether the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: this is indeed the individual soul, because of the scriptural mention of it as "the embodied self" (*eṣa eva śārīra ātmā*); for its pleasure is the head, joy is the right wing, rapture is the left wing, and bliss is the self.

"Brahman is the tail, the support"—this is because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the connection with the pleasure of satisfaction that follows immediately after the happiness produced by seeing, obtaining, and utilizing desired objects, which are designated as "dear," "joy," "delight," and "bliss. For while one might suspect such specific pleasures arising from the acquisition of desired objects for a *jīva* who must still strive to obtain what is to be enjoyed, such a suspicion has no place regarding the Lord (*Īśvara*), who has eternally attained all desires. Therefore, in the passage "From Him, indeed, from this Self, ether was produced," the word "from Him" (*tasmāt*)— [...continues...]

This is because, for the purpose of establishing that the Brahman under discussion—which has been grasped [as the source]—is identical with the individual soul (jīva), the text clarifies its being currently experienced through the reference "from this," and its being denotable by the word "Self" (ātman) as well-known in the Vedas through the reference "the Self. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, the text introduces [Brahman] as a substitute for the worldly notions of the "I" and "mine" by means of the maxim of the "large Arundhatī" (where one first points to a nearby star to lead one to the true Arundhatī). Thus, since worldly people lack the cognition of Brahman regarding food, vital breaths, and so forth, [the text proceeds] toward those [notions].

This is because the logic of the "thick Arundhatī" [being seen only after the stars are seen] does not apply here, as Brahman is not an object of the senses. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the creation of other things to be created—which would be rooted in the Creator's resolve—is impossible due to the impossibility of the individual soul (jīva) forming a creative resolve at the time of the beginning of creation, since there is no body prior to the creation of its own body and thus no means to achieve such a resolve. For even then, the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) exists from time immemorial; therefore, both the resolve for creation and the emanation of the world rooted in that resolve are logically established. This is stated in the section of the *Brahmasūtra* beginning with "Bādari says [the soul is non-existent], for so [the scripture] says. (BS 2.3.13).

Because the capacity of liberated souls to create fathers and other beings through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) in the state where they lack a body will be established from that very source [the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*]. Now, one might object: "But immediately after the description of the 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*), another Brahman is heard of in the words, 'Brahman is the tail, the support' (*brahmapucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*). This is not so; for by the passage beginning with "Joy is indeed the head," the limbs of the individual soul's bliss are described, and the word "Brahman" is used there to denote the indivisible bliss of that soul which was concealed during the state of transmigratory existence. And it is precisely that indivisible bliss...

The manifestation [of Brahman] at the time of liberation is indicated by the word "Brahman" because it is understood by Brahman as the fruit of that realization; for in this context, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes association with the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), since it is impossible to designate the enjoyment of the enjoyer or the agent as being within the category of the fruit of the meditation on the *ānandamaya*. Nor should it be argued that if the tail-Brahman were not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), the statement regarding the knowledge of the existence or non-existence of Brahman—"If one knows 'Brahman exists,' then by that he becomes [itself] existent"—would be illogical, because the existence of the soul is so well-established that any doubt regarding its non-existence would be unwarranted.

Since the worlds beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) are treated as the tails (*puccha*) of their respective subjects, it is likewise logical that the world mentioned in the section concerning the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) should have the "consisting of bliss" itself as its subject. Furthermore, although the "consisting of bliss" is well-known to possess joy, delight, and so forth, it lacks the renown of possessing the indivisible bliss denoted by the word *brahman*; therefore, it is appropriate for both the cognition of existence and non-existence to have that [bliss] as their object. Consequently, in the *Ānandavallī*, it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that is presented as the cause of the universe, and not anything distinct from it.

O Brahman, and thus, in accordance with that, other causal statements also ultimately refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. For this very reason, in the *Sadvidyā*, the reality that is the cause of the world, introduced by the word "Being" (*sat*), is concluded as being of the nature of the individual soul in the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "From which speech returns, along with the mind, having failed to reach it..."

"Knowing Brahman as bliss, one fears nothing at all. Since this great bliss, which is being cultivated as culminating in a state of unsurpassed excellence, is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) who possesses only a small measure of pleasure, it finds its fulfillment only by resorting to another—the Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), who partakes in such great bliss, is the Lord alone, not the individual soul. If it is argued that it has been stated that even the individual soul is accepted as possessing such bliss, that is true as far as it goes, but what was said there was poorly expressed. [As it is said: "He should be young and virtuous..."

"The young student who is most learned, most steadfast, and strongest—should this entire earth be full of wealth for him, that is one human bliss. Having thus described the range of bliss beginning from human bliss up to the bliss of Prajāpati, [the text continues] by stating that it is superior to the totality of the bliss experienced by all classes of living beings: "A hundredfold the blisses of Prajāpati..."

This is because it is impossible for the bliss of the *ānandamaya*, which is celebrated as "the bliss of Brahman alone," to be attributed to the class of individual souls (*jīva*) mentioned in the preceding passages—souls whose bliss is described as being exceedingly small in comparison to it. Furthermore, how could there be any suspicion that the *ānandamaya* is an individual soul, given that it was introduced as something distinct from the individual soul denoted by the term *vijñānamaya* in the passage: "Different from this *vijñānamaya* is another inner self, the *ānandamaya*"?

Nor should it be suspected that the term *vijñānamaya* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), because in other scriptural passages such as, "This one who consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) among the vital breaths, the light within the heart," it is used specifically for the individual soul (*jīva*). If it is argued that even in the section concerning *vijñānamaya*, the word "consciousness" alone is heard in the passage, "All the gods worship consciousness as the eldest Brahman"—we reply that this too refers to the individual soul, just as in other scriptural passages such as, "He who dwells in consciousness," and so on; for [the text continues]: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs the ritual acts."

Because its agency is heard of in sacrifices and other such acts, whereas the intellect (buddhi) lacks agency in them since it functions only as an instrument. Furthermore, by one who asserts that the living self consists of bliss (ānandamaya), it must be stated what the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ* is in that context; it cannot mean "modification" (*vikāra*), because according to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the common language (*bhāṣā*) in the sense of modification or constituent part," the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed only for those two meanings in the common language. How then is the Vedic usage in passages such as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood" explained? It is explained by the rule "in the Veda, [the suffix *mayaṭ* is used] after words ending in two syllables."

This is because of another rule [of grammar]. For this is a rule intended to provide for the application of the suffix *mayaṭ* where it would otherwise not have been obtained in Vedic usage. How then is the word "consisting of knowledge" (*vijñānamaya*) understood as Vedic? Since it is impossible for it to have the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), the suffix *mayaṭ* in "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) must also be stated to mean "abundance" (*prācurya*). And this sense of abundance takes the form of superiority relative to the entire class of living beings, from humans up to Prajāpati, as demonstrated by the manner shown in the supplementary passage of the "Investigation of Bliss" (*Ānandamīmāṃsā*) cited previously.

There is no room for the suspicion that any individual soul (jīva) possesses the nature of consisting of bliss (ānandamayatva). By this it is meant that the term *ānandamaya*, signifying an abundance of bliss, is applicable even to the individual soul; for in the case of a soul that possesses even a trace of worldly suffering yet is endowed with the great bliss manifested in liberation, there exists the possibility of the meaning of "abundance" as an excess of bliss relative to the smallness of its corresponding suffering.

When the word denoting abundance (*prācurya*) occurs as the subsequent member [of a compound], its meaning is necessarily abundance relative to a small number of dissimilar things within the same substratum; for it is impossible to conceive of abundance in any other manner when such abundance is being expressed, as in the case of the phrase "a village with many Brahmins" (*pracurabrāhmaṇo grāmaḥ*), where abundance is relative to a small number of similar things in a different substratum.

Furthermore, although there may be such usage when a noun-word consisting of many phonetic forms with an undetermined sequence of prior and posterior elements follows, there is no evidence to establish such usage when the suffix *mayaṭ*—which is prescribed by the rule "tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ" and possesses a fixed position as a subsequent element—follows. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed Brahman itself.

For this very reason, at the beginning [of the text], there is the instruction that He is to be meditated upon by the individual soul (*jīva*); there is the instruction regarding omniscience in the form of various powers of seeing, which are impossible for the *jīva*, in the words "He who knows Him hidden in the cave"; and in the supplementary passage, "Together with the wise Brahman," there is the designation of the state of being the one who causes bliss to the *jīva*, in the words "For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss did not exist in this space? For He alone bestows bliss"; and [the statement] "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

There is the designation of an independent desire for creation that does not depend on *pradhāna* and is impossible for individual souls (*jīva*) such as Hiraṇyagarbha; and there is the designation of being an object of enjoyment for the soul, in the passage: "He is indeed flavor; for having obtained flavor, this [soul] becomes blissful. By these reasons found in the opening and the conclusion, it is established that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not the individual soul, but Brahman alone; thus, it is proven that neither the individual soul nor *pradhāna* is the subject taught by the causal statements of the *sadvidyā*, the *ānandavallī*, and so forth.
The summary verses.
The one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed the individual soul (jīva), because of the mention of its being embodied;
it is the Self that was previously introduced as the creator of ether and the other elements.
Therefore, that very [Brahman] must also be the Self, because qualities such as "seeing" (īkṣati) are possible therein;
for this very reason, when it is said "That thou art," its nature as the individual self (jīvātmatā) is affirmed.

For if bliss were practiced in this manner, it would increase a hundredfold at each stage while one is still alive; since such [limitless] bliss is not possible for the individual soul (jīva), he is therefore none other than the Supreme Self (paramātman).
And because it is stated that [the Self] is other than the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the term "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya),
and because its distinguishing attributes are declared in the remainder of the passage.
There is the designation of the embodied self, and the instruction "That thou art."
One attains consistency throughout the entire body as well as in the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa). ||6||
The inner one [is Brahman], because of the teaching of its attributes. || 21 ||
And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the body]. || 22 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following objection: "Let it be granted that the cause of the world is not the *pradhāna* because of the scriptural mention of 'seeing' (*īkṣaṇa*), and let it also be granted that it is not the generic individual soul (*jīva-sāmānya*) because of the mention of its distinction [from Brahman] in the concluding statement 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*). Nevertheless, among those specific individual souls such as Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Sūrya, and sages like Viśvāmitra who have accumulated particular merits, some one specific soul might, by virtue of a difference in *kalpas*, be the cause; for in his case, all the majesties mentioned in the *Ānanda-vallī* would be possible. The translation of the provided text is as follows: The connection [of this section] arises from the following objection: "Let it be granted that the cause of the world is not the *pradhāna* because of the scriptural mention of 'seeing' (*īkṣaṇa*), and let it also be granted that it is not the generic individual soul (*jīva-sāmānya*) because of the mention of its distinction [from Brahman] in the concluding statement 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*). Nevertheless, among those specific individual souls such as Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Sūrya, and sages like Viśvāmitra who have accumulated particular merits, some one specific soul might, by virtue of a difference in *kalpas*, be the cause; for in his case, all the majesties mentioned in the *Ānanda-vallī* would be possible."

In this regard, according to the maxim of the grain from the cooking pot (*sthālīpulākanyāya*), a certain passage concerning a deity is cited from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, golden all over even to the nails, entirely like pure gold—just as the lotus flower is like the seat of a monkey (*kapyāsa*), so are his eyes; his name is 'Udit' (risen). He has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. Both the *Ṛg* and the *Sāman* are his *Gāyatrī*."

By the passage beginning with "vittyā," the Person to be meditated upon within the solar orb has been described; and by the passage beginning with "Now, that person who is seen within the eye, he is indeed the Ṛg, he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha, he is the Yajus, he is the Brahman; his form is the very same as that [solar] form, his two joints are the two joints of that, his name is the name of that," the Person to be meditated upon within the eye has been described.

Regarding these two branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), there arises a doubt: is the person to be meditated upon in both cases simply a particular individual soul (*jīva*) who has attained the status of the presiding deity of the solar orb by means of specific merit, and thus that very soul—possessing all the majesties described in the *Ānandavallī*—is the subject of all the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*); or is it something other than that, namely the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which alone is the subject of the causal statements?

In the Ānandavallī, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is shown to be distinct from that [Brahman] by being presented as the cause of fear for the sun, in the passage: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises. How, then, can there be room for the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) here that this very same [sun] is the one consisting of bliss? It is said in reply: according to the logic of the "sample grain" (sthālīpulāka-nyāya), it is stated here that the sun and the individual soul (jīva) are cited as examples.

Even Brahmā, Indra, and others are merely examples here; thus, the opponent's position—that they possess the status of the cause of the world due to differences in the kalpas—would be rendered purposeless by the scriptural declaration that they are causes of fear to even Āsādya and Sūrya. In this very same manner, the scriptural declaration that they are causes of fear to Indra and others is also to be understood as being logically consistent.

Although the logic established in the *adhikaraṇa* is common to [the cases of] Brahmā, Indra, and others, the author of the Sūtras—intending that both the conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Brahman (distinct from the individual soul presiding over the orb) is the cause of the world, and the conclusion that by the mark of having lotus-eyes it is indeed the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama, should be established with a single effort—has indicated in this Sūtra that the two meditations, namely the *antarāditya-vidyā* and the *antarakṣi-vidyā*, are the examples here by means of the word "within" (*antaḥ*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: the individual soul presiding over the orb is the one [subject], and not [Brahman].

Furthermore, there is another Brahman favored by the Siddhāntin; however, since a body is mentioned [in scripture], and a body is indeed caused by karma, how can that be possible for the Brahman accepted by the Siddhāntin, who is devoid of karma?

One should not raise the objection: "How can there be a body caused by karma for one who is declared in scripture to be free from all evil, on the grounds that 'he has risen above all evils'? For the body is of three kinds: that of the gods, which is begun solely by merit and is the exclusive abode of happiness; that of stationary beings and the like, which is begun solely by sin and is the exclusive abode of suffering; and that of humans and the like, which is begun by both merit and sin and is the abode of both pleasure and pain. And thus, according to the scriptural text, "Indeed, no evil reaches the gods," [the bodies of] the gods are of the first kind.

Even if [the body] is not a product of sin, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its being a body commenced solely by merit. If it is argued that even for Brahman, as intended by the Siddhāntin, corporeality—in the sense of abiding in the region of the heart within bodies caused by the karma of individual souls in the capacity of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin)—is indeed possible, let it be so, however that may be; yet, such corporeality is not what is meant here. Rather, it refers to that which, by virtue of its extreme loveliness, is a desirable abode of divine enjoyment for the Embodied One (Śarīrin).

Because that body has entered [the self] from the hair to the tips of the nails, it is said to possess a body by means of that body. Here, the scriptural passage beginning with "The golden person" and ending with "his eyes" is cited as having splendor (*sāśri*), describing his extreme loveliness; therefore, this body, which is obtainable only through the accumulation of extraordinary merit, is possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. Since such a description of a body is heard, this is indeed the *jīva*, and there is no evidence for a Brahman distinct from that.

That very [Self] is composed of bliss (ānandamaya). For this very reason, it is heard in the Ānandavallī: "He who is here in the person and he who is yonder in the sun, he is one. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the body mentioned here is not caused by karma, because of the scriptural statement regarding the embodied one's rising above all evils—that is, its state of having risen above all sins.

For the state of "having risen" (*uditatva*)—like that of a bird that has flown out from its nest—is figuratively understood as the absence of all connection with evil, since a literal act of rising from evil is impossible. Furthermore, for one who possesses the absolute non-existence of all evil, a body caused by karma is not possible; nor [is it possible] even in the absence of evil, because [the body] is common to both merit and demerit.

"Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds—indeed, all evils turn back from it. Since, in this section concerning Brahman, the word *pāpman* (evil) is heard to apply equally to good deeds (*sukṛta*), and since, according to the teaching of the venerable Parāśara—"O dear one, these indeed are hells for that place which is the Supreme Self"—good deeds are considered to have undesirable results for one seeking liberation just like evil deeds, it is appropriate that even such deeds be included under the term *pāpman*.

Furthermore, since the very fact of being the means to an undesirable, non-worldly result (*alaukikāniṣṭaphala*) is the ground for the application of the word "evil" (*pāpman*), even that [ignorance] cannot be excluded from the meaning of the word "evil" with respect to one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). Moreover, it might be argued: "In the Vedāntas, there is no fixed rule that the word 'evil' applies equally to old age, death, grief, merit, and demerit; for [the text says]: 'neither old age, nor death, nor grief, nor merit, nor...'"

Even though in the context of the Dahara-vidyā, after proclaiming the absence of evil in the passage, "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, and sorrowless," the absence of old age, death, and sorrow is established separately by saying, "May all evil deeds and all sins turn away from here," nevertheless, in the passage, "He has risen above all evils," the word *pāpman* must be understood as referring to both [evil deeds and] good deeds alike, as stated in: "Indeed, he rises above all evils who knows thus."

Because it is heard that the arising of all evils is the fruit of knowledge according to the principle of "that-which-is-willed" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), and because the cessation of even what has been done once is also stated to be the fruit of knowledge in the fourth chapter; therefore, this body heard of here is not caused by karma. Since possessing an exceedingly beautiful, divine, and auspicious form not caused by karma is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) in any context whatsoever, this Person heard of in the solar orb is none other than Brahman, distinct from the *jīva*. And that Brahman, by the mark of having lotus-like eyes, is indeed the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama.

Although Yāska and the author of the Vākya explain the passage, "His eyes are like a lotus on the lap of a monkey (kapyāsa-puṇḍarīka)," by stating that just as the solar orb (*kapyāsa*) and the heart-lotus (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*) are his places of worship, so too are his eyes his places of worship—and thus they offer an alternative interpretation that does not touch upon the mark of having lotus-like eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣatva*)—nevertheless, that description of an alternative meaning was provided for the sake of demonstrating the vastness of the subject.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it is well known that the person within this orb is the very same as the person in the right eye, and thus the right eye alone is established as the locus for its meditation. Furthermore, Śaṅkara accepts that the mark of having lotus-like eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣatva*) is indeed applicable here. Regarding that meaning, he explains the term *kapyāsa* in three ways: *ka* is water; that which drinks through its own apertures (*svarandhra*) is *kapi*—namely, the stalk. That which sits (*āsta*) upon that is *kapyāsa*. Thus, one meaning is "that which has an unbroken stalk [free from] insects and the like."

The word *kapā* is like the word *somapā*; in its grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), it is either the locative case form *kapi* (in the water) as a separate word, or it has another meaning: "that which is not drawn up from the water" (*ke jale pyāsta iti jalādanuddhṛtam*). When the root *ās* is preceded by *api*, and the vowel *a* is elided according to the rule "vaṣṭi vāgurirallopam avāpyoḥ upasargayoḥ," the form *pyāsta* is produced. Furthermore, the sun is called *kapi* because it drinks (*pibati*) the water (*kaṃ*) with its rays; thus, another meaning is "that which is not to be opened by the sun" (*tasyāsaṃ vikāsyaṃ*), meaning "not blossomed by the sun's rays."

Having adopted all three of these meanings, the author of the Commentary described the meaning of this sentence in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*: "O you whose long, pure eyes are like the petals of a white lotus blossoming on a well-polished stalk arisen from a deep pool of water."

If it is asked: "How can such a body be accepted as not having karma as its cause, given that in the world it is observed as a rule that bodies are produced by karma?"—it is replied: In this very context, since it has been stated that [the Self] possesses the absolute absence of evil (*pāpa*), it is impossible to say that the body is composed of both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*). Even if it were said to be composed of merit alone, the worldly-observed rule that [bodies] are composed of both merit and demerit remains; for [the scripture says]: "For one who is embodied, there is no cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant."

To override the Vedic scripture which is reinforced by the statement, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is indeed bodiless," is unavoidable. This being the case, in accordance with such corroborative texts as, "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of the union of elements," "His form is not material," and "It is not born of action for the sake of benefiting the worlds," it is proper for those learned in logic to accept that the Lord’s divine, auspicious form is non-material (aprākṛta) and not caused by karma.

Because the rule observed in the world is more powerful than the secondary explanatory passages (*upabrahmaṇa*). Now, it may be objected that the logic stated above can be applied only to the passage concerning "within the sun" (*antarāditya*), but not to those passages which establish the great majesty of Brahmā, Indra, and others; for indeed, in the worlds of Hiraṇyagarbha, Purandara, and so forth, the presence of the Lord’s divine, auspicious form is not found in the well-known scriptures in the same way as it is in the solar orb.

It is said: the statement in the Commentary—that "one among [the gods] beginning with Brahmā, having attained such sovereignty through a particular merit in a single kalpa, performs even the creation of the world and so forth"—is not intended to mean that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the Brahman distinct from it should be applied to other subject-passages (*viṣayavākya*) that establish the greatness of Brahmā, Indra, and others; rather, it is intended to show that, just as in this subject-passage, the individual soul who has attained the status of the deity Āditya is what is being propounded.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): In this very subject-vacuum (*viṣayavākya*), another prima facie position should also be advanced, namely that Śakra is the one to be propounded, and Hiraṇyagarbha is the one to be propounded. With this intention, [the author asks]: "How does that cohere? It coheres thus: from the wording of the mantra, "O Slayer of Vṛtra, whatever you have risen over today, O Sūrya—O Indra, all that is under your control," it is understood that Śakra is the presiding deity of the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*).

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent, it grew. It turned into an egg. It lay for the duration of a year. It split open. Those two halves of the eggshell became silver and gold. That which was silver is this earth; that which was gold is the sky. What was the outer membrane are the mountains; what was the inner membrane is the clouds and the mist. What were the veins are the rivers; what was the fluid within the womb is the ocean."

Furthermore, from the context of the *Chāndogya* passage—"Now, that which was born is this very Āditya; as he was being born, shouts and cries arose after him, as did all beings and all desires; therefore, at his rising and at his setting, shouts and cries arise after him, as do all beings and all desires"—it is also understood that Āditya is the individual soul (*jīva*), namely Hiraṇyagarbha.

Moreover, because it is heard that he rules over those worlds which are beyond this one and over the desires of the gods, and that he rules over those worlds which are below this one and over the desires of men—due to these scriptural statements regarding his lordship over all worlds and his power to bestow the fruits desired by both gods and humans—this person within the eye and the sun is not the individual soul (*jīva*). Although the lordship over the desires of the world of the gods and the lordship over the desires of the world of men are heard of as being divided according to the difference in their locations (the eye and the sun), nevertheless, the two locations are one.

In this very way, as that person attains [the state of Brahman], he presides over it, and his lordship over the desires of the two kinds of worlds culminates in the form of lordship over the desires of all worlds. Likewise, because of the scriptural mention of the *ṛk* and *sāman* being his "geṣṇas" (places of rest), this [being] is not the individual soul (*jīva*). The word *geṣṇa* denotes singing; singing is of two kinds: one has sound as its object, as in "he sings a verse," and one has meaning as its object, as in "he praises the king. Here, the intended sense is that the *ṛk* and *sāman* constitute singing with meaning as its object, and that [meaning] is manifested here by the act of singing in the form of the *sāman*.

The nature of praise, which consists in the expression of qualities residing in a subject established by the *ṛc*, is common to both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. Thus, in the praise of the Person in the Sun (*ādityapuruṣa*), the *ṛc* is the direct means, while the *sāman* is the means through the manifestation of the *ṛc*; for it is heard [in scripture] that "one should praise with the *sāman*," establishing the *sāman* also as a means of praise. Since both serve as sequential means of praise, they possess the character of being sung (*gāna*). Consequently, because the Person in the Sun is the object of the praise accomplished by the *ṛc* and *sāman* in the form of Agni, Indra, Soma, and so forth, his identity with all things (*sarvātmya*) is established.

Although for the Sāma-singers, the term *parvan* is well-known as referring specifically to the constituent parts of the Sāman hymns such as the *prastāva*, and the term *geṣṇa* is likewise well-known among them to refer to those [parts] when a Sāman is divided—this usage being established even in the *Auddhakyākhya* treatise defining the Sāma-parvans—nevertheless, because of the similarity in their being means for successive stotras (*stotra*), the two terms *ṛk* and *sāman* are metaphorically applied to the two *geṣṇas*. Therefore, since it is impossible for the Self to be identical with everything in the sense of having the *ṛk* and *sāman* as its *geṣṇas*, [the passage] "He who dwells in the sun" and so forth refers to the Antaryāmin (the Inner Controller) in the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa.
And because of the designation as "Bhaga," it must be accepted that the person within the sun is not the individual soul (jīva), but rather Brahman, which is distinct from it.
The summary verses.
Dwelling within the sun, he inhabits a body endowed with beard, hair, and so forth;
indeed, due to the persistence of such karma, that living being (jīva) becomes a body for that duration.
Thus, the living being alone is the cause of the world as proclaimed in the *Ānandavallī*.
By that very [fact], its distinction from that [other] would become even more manifest, as was established by him.
Indeed, no living being can escape the consequences of their good and evil deeds;
even if one were to become immortal by having shaken off all sin, they would still not transcend them.
The word *pāpman*, though sung of in the Upaniṣads as evil,
denotes merit as well, due to the difference in its causal basis, as being equal to evil.

From the observation of the signs arising from all those evils, it is known that the Supreme Person, the God who has entered the inner sun, possesses a form beyond the material world; and his manifestations, such as the primary emanations and incarnations, are likewise of such a nature.
The intermediate legal case.

Thus, the intermediate section of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) based on the supporting marks [of the individual soul] has concluded, namely that the reality which is the cause of the world—taught in the *Sadvidyā* and *Ānandavallī*—is the individual soul (jīva). Now, another intermediate section of the prima facie argument based on the authority of Śruti is introduced, asserting that this reality which is the cause of the world is indeed Ākāśa and so forth, and that there is no other reality called Brahman that is the cause of the world.
It is space, because of its characteristic marks. (2.3.23)

Previously, it was stated that the person within the sun possesses the status of being the cause of the world as known from the Vedānta, on the basis of specific indicative marks (*liṅga*). That [statement] is untenable; for, by means of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) which is stronger than an indicative mark, it is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone that is the cause of the world. This constitutes the intermediate connection (*antarasaṅgati*) arising from such an objection.

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having begun with the reply of Jaivali to Dālbhya—who had asked, "What is the goal of this world?"—saying, "It is space (ākāśa)," it is heard: "Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they merge into space; for space is indeed greater than these, and space is their ultimate resort."

Is this "space" (ākāśa) the elemental space (bhūtākāśa), or is it the Supreme Self (paramātman) which is distinct from that? There is doubt because of whether the elemental space is fit or unfit to be the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of all beings as heard in scripture. In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is as follows:

This [ether] is indeed the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), because the scriptural term "ether" is conventionally established in that sense; therefore, Brahman—the cause of the world characterized by such definitions as "from which these beings are born"—is simply the elemental ether. This is because the very definition stated there regarding its being the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of all beings is here described in the passage beginning with "All these beings indeed," which culminates in the elemental ether. Furthermore, that [definition] requires a specific locus of culmination.

[Objection: But has it not been stated in the Bhṛguvallī itself that the conclusion rests upon a specific entity whose nature is bliss, in such passages as, "Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born"? [Reply: Not so; for in that context, the word "bliss" is heard in grammatical apposition with the word "ether" (ākāśa) in the passage, "For who indeed would inhale, who would exhale, if this ether were not bliss? And since it is impossible for both of those terms, which have contradictory referents, to be in apposition in their primary sense, [the word "bliss"] must be taken in a secondary sense.

Since there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) available as to whether the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is secondary (*gauṇa*) or the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is, one might suspect that there is no final determination regarding where the definition of being the cause of the world culminates. Anticipating this doubt, it is concluded here that since the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone is determined to be the cause of the world by virtue of the scriptural mention of "ether," the word "bliss" must be secondary in this very context.

But how can it be doubted here that the insentient elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is the cause of the world? For it was established previously, on the strength of the marks (*liṅga*) of sentience found in the *Sadvijñāna* and *Ānandavallī* passages of the Śruti, that the reality denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), which is the cause of the world, is indeed a specific sentient being. True. The words "Being" (*sat*) and "Bliss" (*ānanda*) can indeed be applied to a sentient being, and they were so applied in accordance with those marks. However, in this case, it is not proper to apply the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), which is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) to the elemental ether, to something else merely in accordance with a mark.

The objection is that the marks such as being the "seer" (īkṣitṛtva) must be applied to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) according to the logic of the expression "the bank wishes to fall" (kūlaṃ pipatiṣati). Now, one might ask: how can the elemental ether, which is heard in scripture to possess an origin—as in "from the Self, space was produced"—be logically connected with the defining characteristic of being the cause of the abiding and dissolution of all beings? The answer is as follows: in that context, the word "from the Self" (ātmanaḥ) means that the gross state of the elemental ether was produced from its own subtle state in the form of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra).

The word *ātman* refers to consciousness itself when it is related to the body, because it is used in the sense of essential nature in such expressions as "the jar is of the nature of clay," and because lexicographers teach its multiple meanings in works such as: "The word *ātman* [denotes] the living being (*jīva*), support (*dhṛti*), the body, essential nature (*svabhāva*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."

Therefore, since it is determined that the definition of Brahman—consisting in being the cause of the world—applies specifically to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), the term *brahman* heard in the *Sadvidyā*, *Ānandavallī*, and *Bhṛguvallī* as referring to the reality that is the cause of the world must refer exclusively to the ether of all beings. For this very reason, in another scriptural passage, the term *brahman* is heard in reference to it: "That which is called 'ether' is indeed the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman."

This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: this "ether" (*ākāśa*) is other than the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*); it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone, because of the scriptural hearing of its being the cause of all beings—which is impossible for the elemental ether—since that causality of all categories of beings is identical in meaning with the definition-statement: "From which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live. Nor is it possible for the elemental ether, even if it were the cause of the insentient category, to be the cause of the sentient category.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the elemental ether—which is insentient, devoid of human purpose, and fit only to be discarded—to possess the quality of being the "goal" (pārāyaṇatva), which implies being the supreme object of attainment for sentient beings; nor can it possess the quality of being "greater than all" (sarvatojyāyastva), which denotes a state of unsurpassed excellence through its superior auspicious attributes. Nor should it be argued that, because the word "ether" provides a specific reference when there is an expectancy for a particular cause of the world, everything must somehow be explained as referring only to the elemental ether.

Indeed, by the sentence "All this, verily... (sarvāṇi ha vai...), causality is not being enjoined here; for the word *havai*, which signifies well-known fact, indicates that this is a restatement of a matter already established in another passage. Therefore, when there is an expectancy for a prior statement (*purovāda*), the sentence "All these creatures, O Somya, have Being as their root" (sanmūlāḥ somyemāḥ sarvāḥ prajāḥ) and so forth must stand as that prior statement. Consequently, it must be stated that what is referred to here by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is that very cause denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*), which is established as sentient by such qualities as being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*).

Regarding the statement, "From the Self (ātman), space (ākāśa) was produced," because the word *ātman*—due to its abundant conventional usage for the conscious principle associated with the body and because of the scriptural declaration that "this very one is the embodied self (*śarīra-ātman*)"—must necessarily refer to the conscious principle; and because the meaning "space was produced from itself" is untenable, as the elemental space is incapable of being construed as the cause of all beings; therefore, this is not the elemental space, but rather Brahman alone which is distinct from it, in which the word *ākāśa* [is used] in the sense of "shining forth on all sides" (*āsamantāt kāśate*).

In this manner, the application of the word through *yogavṛtti* (etymological derivation) should be accepted; for there is no fault in breaking a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in a restatement (*anuvāda*) that follows a preceding injunction (*purovāda*), and because the breaking of the conventional meaning of a word in favor of an unsuitable sense based on a *liṅga* (indicative mark) rooted in the hearing of a suitable meaning is observed in cases such as "the sound [of cows] at the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāghoṣa*).
The summary verses.
Even if the Unmanifest or the individual soul (jīva) were not the cause of this world, space (ākāśa) would certainly be so;
for it is thus recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The statement "From the Self, space [arose]" means "from one's own Self alone," indicating that it was not produced by anything else.
Following the first scriptural passage (Taittirīya), the mention of bliss there is secondary.
Do not say so; for the Chāndogya passage is indeed a restatement, as indicated by the particle *khalu* and the word *ha vai*.
He pursues only that which is beneficial, as before, with a pure heart.
Thus ends the section concerning space (ākāśādhikaraṇa). ||8||
For this very reason, it is the vital breath (prāṇa). ||24||

In the *Chāndogya*, when Uṣasti approached a certain king and asked about the deity of the *prastāva* section, the *prastotṛ* priest—who did not know it—asked, "Which deity is that? To this, Uṣasti began his reply with, "He said, 'The vital breath (*prāṇa*)'" (ChāU 1.11.4), and continued: "Indeed, all these beings merge into the vital breath alone and emerge from the vital breath; this very deity is dependent upon the *prastāva*" (ChāU 1.11.5). This section concerning the extension [of attributes] is similar to the preceding section.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (uttarapakṣa): Since there is a scriptural mention of "prāṇa," it follows that the vital air (prāṇavāyu) alone is the cause of the dissolution and origination of all beings—this being the initial position. However, because the words "ha vai" indicate that this is a restatement of what has been previously mentioned, and in accordance with both the preceding context and logical fitness, it is established that the Supreme Self (paramātman), distinct from the vital air, is indeed the "prāṇa" that serves as the cause of the dissolution and origination of all beings.

Since it is observed that the maintenance and activity of the entire class of beings depend upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is well-established that Vāyu alone deserves to be the cause of the dissolution and origination of all beings. Furthermore, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* explicitly states: "When a person sleeps, speech indeed merges into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, the ear into the vital breath, and the mind into the vital breath; when he awakens, they are born again from the vital breath alone. Thus, during both sleep and awakening, the vital breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*) is the locus of the dissolution and origination of all beings.

Furthermore, the purpose [of this section] is the removal of the additional doubt that arises from the scriptural mention [of the origin of the vital air]. This removal is necessary because it is impossible for the vital air (prāṇavāyu) to be the cause of the class of sentient beings; moreover, since in the Ānandavallī that [vital air] is heard to have originated from ether—which itself is produced from a specific sentient being—it is impossible for it to be the cause of all insentient things. Consequently, it is not fit to be designated as the locus of the dissolution and origin of all elements. For this very reason, even the "unmanifest" (aprāṇa) mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad is none other than the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Summary Verses.
Thus, since the statement regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) follows immediately after that concerning food, it is not the case that food alone is the cause;
rather, let it be seen that the mere body is dependent on the vital breath, for such a thing is not observed in living beings like goats and the like.
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).

Thus, having concluded the intermediate section concerning the prima facie view based solely on the Śruti, another intermediate section is now introduced, which relies on the Śruti as supported by indicative marks (liṅga) that imply [Brahman's] causality.
The light [is Brahman], because of the mention of its feet. || 25 ||

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the mention of the meters, we say no; for there is a scriptural teaching on the fixing of the mind [on the Self], and such is indeed seen [in other passages]. ||26||
And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "the elements" (bhūta) is thus appropriate. 27.
If it is argued that [the meditations] are not identical because of differences in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. ||28||

The Chandogas record: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest of the high worlds—that indeed is this light which is within a person here."

In this context, since there is no contradiction—just as in the passages concerning ether (*ākāśa*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*), where one hears that they are the cause of air, ether, and all beings, whereas here one does not hear that [the subject] is the cause of all effects including light (*jyotis*)—and since it is impossible to rely on scripture when a contradiction exists, the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) arises from the objection that "let the well-known sun and so forth be the light. Now, if the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is formulated as "the well-known sun and so forth are indeed the light here," what subversion of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is being suspected by that?

For light is not heard of here as the cause of the world, such that it might be suspected that the established doctrine—that the sun and so forth are indeed the cause of the world and that there is no other cause of the world than Brahman—is being subverted.

Now, it might be argued: the connection with unsurpassed radiance heard here is an indicative mark (liṅga) implying causality, because in the context of the passage, "The sun does not shine there; by its light all this shines," and subsequently, "From that Imperishable, all this world arises," the causality of a thing endowed with unsurpassed radiance is heard.

If the opponent maintains that the meaning of the word "light" (*jyotis*) here refers to the cause of the universe—a reality endowed with unsurpassed radiance—which is heard of in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* as a form of natural light that overpowers the sun, moon, and so forth, then how can it be argued that the sun and others are the "light" here? For it is not tenable that the sun and such are themselves the light that overpowers the sun and others.

It is said: The opponent’s intention is that the mantra “the sun does not shine there” does not state that [the light] overpowers the sun and so forth, but rather that it is not illumined by the sun and so forth; and since the statement in the *Gītā*, “neither the sun nor the moon nor fire illumines it,” shows that such non-illumination by the sun and others is possible even for the sun itself, this constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, given the doubt as to whether the light is the sun and so forth or whether it is Brahman distinct from those—based on both common usage and the mention of its feet—the prima facie view is established.

The light is indeed the sun and so forth, because it is improper to override what is well-known in common usage, and because of the teaching of identity with the physical light in the passage: "This indeed is that light which is within this person. For such a teaching of identity is appropriate only when referring to natural lights, intended to express their similarity to that [divine] light. Nor should it be argued that the quality of possessing a radiance spreading through the highest of all worlds—as heard in the text, "on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds beyond the highest"—is not possible for the sun and other such lights; for that is not the case.

Since the rays of the sun extend everywhere from the earthly world (*pṛthivīloka*), from all parts of the intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*), and even into the highest celestial worlds (*dyuloka*) above, it follows that the quality of being the cause of the universe—implied by the mark of unsurpassed luminosity—belongs to the light of the sun and so forth alone; therefore, there is no other cause of the universe called Brahman. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the "light" mentioned here is none other than Brahman, distinct from the well-known physical lights, because of the preceding passage: "A foot of Him are all beings... (*pādo'sya sarvā bhūtāni*).

Because the text, "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven," declares that He has all beings as His feet, and because such a state is impossible for the commonly known physical light; and because it is understood through the recognition of the connection with heaven (*dyusambandha-pratyabhijñāna*) that the very same entity previously described as having all beings as its feet is here referred to by the word "light"; furthermore, the instruction regarding the identity with the gastric fire is intended for the purpose of enjoining meditation on its nature for the sake of a specific fruit, since we see a similar injunction later on: "One should meditate upon this as seen and heard; he becomes beautiful to look at and famous. Thus, that does not establish its being the common physical light.

But is it not the case that in the preceding section, having begun with "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having stated its four-footed nature in the words "This very [Gāyatrī] is four-footed," the present mantra was cited as an authoritative source for that stated meaning—"That which has been declared by the Ṛgveda verse: 'Such is His greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than that; a quarter of Him are all beings, three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven'"; therefore, this mantra concerns the Gāyatrī, and thus it cannot be used here to establish the fact of being a quarter of all beings.

If it is argued that there is thus the establishment of the Supreme Self, let it not be so. The word *gāyatrī* does not here denote the mere meter, because it is impossible for a meter to have all beings as its foot; rather, the meditation on the similarity of *gāyatrī* to Brahman is taught here for the sake of a specific fruit. And there exists a similarity between Brahman—which is traditionally described as having four feet in the passage, "One foot of It are all beings, three feet of It are the immortal in heaven"—and the four-footed *gāyatrī*, for *gāyatrī* indeed has four feet, as in: "Indra, the lord of Śacī... [and so forth].

"He is oppressed by strength; he is the invincible bull; he is victorious in battles"—thus, elsewhere as well, a word denoting a meter is seen to be employed in a different sense due to its similarity to the *gāyatrī*.

Just as in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, beginning with the words, "These five and those other five make ten," and concluding with, "This is the Virāj," it is stated that among these ten—the five being wind, sun, moon, fire, and water, and the five being breath, speech, eye, ear, and mind—the nature of the Virāj metre is attributed due to the numerical correspondence, for the Virāj metre consists of ten syllables.

Furthermore, after specifying the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart, it is stated, "This very [Gāyatrī] has four feet"; because of this designation of having the fourfold set beginning with the elements as its feet, that which is denoted by the word Gāyatrī is indeed the Supreme Self alone. This is because it is impossible for a meter (chandas) to possess such a nature. Now, one might object: let it be something that has all beings as its foot.

If it is argued that although the *vastu* (the subject matter) was mentioned previously, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of it here because of the difference in designation—namely, the use of "in heaven" (*divi*) versus "from heaven" (*divaḥ*)—we say no. For even though there is a difference in designation, there is no contradiction in meaning; we observe, for instance, that when a hawk is perched at the top of a tree, one may still designate it as "the hawk beyond the tree. Therefore, [this refers to] that which is taught in the *Puruṣasūkta*, as recognized by the mantra "Such is his greatness."

In the verse, "O Thou of solar hue, beyond the darkness," that Supreme Brahman called the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa), which is understood there as possessing a divine and auspicious form endowed with unsurpassed radiance, is here designated as the "Light" endowed with unsurpassed radiance.

Now, an objection may be raised: since it is established by the Puruṣasūkta alone that the Supreme Person—the Supreme Brahman—is distinct from the entire complex of sentient and non-sentient beings and is the cause of all of them, what is the purpose of this fourth quarter [of the verse] which serves to exclude other possibilities?

It is said: since the causal reality is indicated in many other Vedic passages by such terms as Prāṇa, Kāśa, Jyotis, Indra, and so forth, this investigation—whose purpose is to exclude what is not [the cause] (ayogavyavaccheda)—is intended solely to firmly establish that the Supreme Person, who is the object of the Puruṣasūkta, is indeed Brahman, the cause of the universe.
Summary Verses.

The "supreme light" heard in the Sāma-veda is well-known here as being of the nature of the digestive fire within the stomach; its status as the supreme light is not established as residing in the [primordial] cause.
Therefore, let the sun be the cause of the worlds on the basis of this indicative mark (liṅga).
This suspicion may be dispelled by your clear statement regarding the man's conduct.
Thus ends the section concerning the light (jyotir-adhikaraṇa). ||10||
Likewise, the vital breath [is Brahman], because it is found to follow [through all states]. ||29||

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because of the instruction regarding the Self by the speaker, we say no; for in this [text], there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections. ||30||
But the instruction [is given] by means of the vision gained through the scriptures, as in the case of Vāmadeva. ||31||

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (prāṇa), we say no; for there is a threefoldness of meditation, and because that [threefoldness] is applicable here due to the fact that [the meditation on the Self] has been resorted to. 32.

In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, beginning with the passage, "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra," and after Indra had said, "Choose a boon," Pratardana replied, "You yourself choose the boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being. Indra’s response to Pratardana—who requested this, implying that Indra alone knows the boon most beneficial for him as a human and thus asks him to select and grant such a boon—is heard as follows: "He (Indra) said:"

"I am the vital breath (prāṇa), the self consisting of intelligence; meditate upon me as life and immortality. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the one indicated here by the words "Indra" and "prāṇa"—as the object of the meditation on that which is most beneficial—the well-known Indra or the individual soul (jīva), or is it the Supreme Self (paramātman) distinct from those?

Regarding this, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is as follows: "In the passages concerning Prāṇa and Ākāśa, just as there is the hearing of being the cause of all beings—which contradicts the specific mention of Prāṇa and Ākāśa within those respective passages—and just as in the passage concerning Jyotis there is the hearing of being the feet of all beings prior to that—which contradicts the specific mention of Jyotis—here, in the context of Indra, there is no such hearing either within his own passage or prior to it that contradicts the specific mention of Indra. On the contrary, at the very commencement of the Indra-passage, there is the hearing that Indra is the object of meditation as the means for attaining immortality, which is described by the term 'most beneficial'."

Furthermore, the state of being the object of worship for one who has become thus (i.e., a liberated soul) is a mark pervaded by the causality of the world; this is understood from the statement in the *Sadvidyā*: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body, then he shall be merged [in Brahman]. Therefore, it follows that a specific individual soul named Indra alone is the cause of the world, and there is no Supreme Self distinct from him.

This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: this one designated by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" is not merely the individual soul (jīva), but rather Brahman, which is an entity distinct from the soul; for, in the passage "He is this very Prāṇa, the conscious self, bliss, undecaying, and immortal," there is the mention of attributes belonging to the one introduced by the terms "Indra" and "Prāṇa" that are impossible for any individual soul.

But surely, at the beginning, Indra taught his own self alone as the object of worship through the restrictive statement, "Know me alone"; and for the sake of establishing that, he described his own great majesty by means of deeds such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, saying: "I gave the Arunmukha demons to the hyenas; having transgressed many leagues, I struck down the sons of Prahlāda in heaven, the Paulomas in the intermediate space, and the Kālakañjas on earth; not even a single hair of mine was harmed. Thus, [he taught this] because of his possession of such great power.

He praised his own self. Therefore, if it is argued that since the opening section determines that a specific individual soul (jīva) is the object of meditation, the subsequent mentions of bliss, agelessness, and immortality must be interpreted merely as commendatory statements in accordance with that conclusion—this is not so. For in this context, an abundance of internal characteristics is observed that are impossible for any ordinary living being.

For instance: first, in response to the question, "Choose for yourself that path which you consider most beneficial for humanity," it is stated regarding the one addressed by Indra—that the object of the meditation (*upāsana*), which is the means to liberation unique to the Supreme Self, is indicated by the terms *Indra* and *Prāṇa*: "Know Me alone; this indeed I consider most beneficial for humanity, that one should know Me. Furthermore, the fruit of being untouched by all sins, as understood from the "lotus-leaf" passage, is described as the justification for that: "He who knows Me thus... [and so on].

One should know that his world is not measured by any deed—not by the killing of a mother, nor by the killing of a father, nor by theft, nor by the destruction of an embryo. Furthermore, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is raised as follows: "Let there be such power in Indra alone to bestow fruits [of action]," based on such passages as: "Indra is the king who rules over the moving world; Indra is the king of the world and of men. Indra is the king of the stationary and the moving; no other than you is heavenly, nor earthly, none has been born, nor will ever be born," and so forth, which describe his great majesty.

It is heard [in scripture] regarding this: what is the inconsistency in that [Brahman] being the object of meditation (*upāsana*) as a means for attaining immortality? Nevertheless, after stating that those which are designated by the term "elements" (*bhūtamātrā*), being insentient, are established in those designated by the term "cognitions" (*prajñāmātrā*), which are sentient—"Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed to the spokes, and the spokes are fixed to the hub; even so, these elements are fixed to the cognitions, and the cognitions are fixed to the vital breath (*prāṇa*)"—that their establishment in the vital breath is further stated. This...

The passage beginning with "I am the vital breath" (prāṇo'smi) is not possible unless it refers to the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the well-known Indra. For, according to the principle established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, Indra—seeking liberation—could not have attained liberation for himself without first propitiating someone else through meditation. Therefore, Indra taught the meditation upon the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the well-known Indra, saying, "Meditate on me. Consequently, the non-adherence of all sins, which is a secondary fruit of the meditation he was performing for the sake of his own liberation, is presented in the passage beginning with "the three-headed one" (*triśīrṣāṇam*).

This is indeed more consistent. And thus, even those statements occurring in the middle—such as, "He does not become greater by good action nor smaller by evil action; for he alone causes him to perform good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds, and he alone causes him to perform evil action whom He wishes to lead down; He is the Lord of the world, He is the Protector of the world, He is the Ruler of the world"—are harmonized, as they describe the absence of increase or decrease resulting from the performance of good and evil actions, which is impossible for any living being.

Therefore, when [Indra] instructs, "Worship me," he teaches that the Supreme Self alone—distinct from Indra and the individual soul (jīva)—is the object of worship. How then was it instructed by Indra, "Worship me"? It was with the intention that his own inner controller (antaryāmin) is the object of worship, based on the vision of the scriptures such as: "He is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa. This is just as Vāmadeva, knowing that words such as "I" ultimately refer to the Supreme Self who dwells within those respective bodies, spoke of his own inner controller as being identical to himself, saying "I [am Manu...]."

The identity with all things, such as Manu, the Sun, and so forth, has been taught. For it is heard in scripture: "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun,'" and so on. If it be objected: "But how can there be an abundance of references to the internal self (adhyātma) here, given that there exist marks pertaining to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), such as: 'One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker'; 'He slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ'; and 'As long as the vital breath dwells in this body, so long is there life'? It is replied: It is precisely the Supreme Self that is intended here as the object of a threefold meditation.

In that regard, there is meditation on [Brahman] by way of its essential nature through the passage "Bliss, undecaying, immortal"; meditation on it as qualified by consciousness (cit) through passages containing the marks of the individual soul (jīva); and meditation on it as qualified by non-consciousness (acit) through the marks of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).

Elsewhere as well, a threefold mode of worship is observed; for instance, in the Ānandavallī: in passages such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," there is worship of [Brahman] in its essential nature (svarūpeṇa); and in passages such as "Having created that, He entered it; having entered it, He became the existent and the non-existent, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and unconsciousness," there is worship of the Conscious One as qualified by the sentient and as qualified by the insentient. Thus, here too, the recourse to a threefold worship of the Supreme Self is appropriate, and everything is faultless. [Summary Verse:]
One might argue that Indra here is the cause [of immortality] because his sole function is the meditation on the "Hita-tama" (the Most Beneficial);
but this is not correct, because [immortality] is preceded by the mention of agelessness, deathlessness, and so forth, which consist of that very [meditation].
For Indra, when viewed as the Lord within his own body, is the locus for the meditation "Māṃ" (Me).
Therefore, this explanation is consistent with the view that the supreme cause is distinct from both consciousness and unconsciousness.
Thus ends the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa.

In the first chapter, the existence of the cause of the universe—known as Śrī Puruṣottama, whose nature consists of the totality of the sentient and the insentient—as the object of knowledge of the Vedānta was established; nevertheless, the doubt that certain Vedāntic passages appear to teach specific entities included within the categories of the sentient and the insentient is now being dispelled.

Furthermore, in the *janmādi-sūtra*, the two exclusions—namely, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*)—are intended for the definition [of Brahman] in order to avoid the faults of impossibility and over-extension, respectively, by way of the statement "Brahman alone is the cause" and "Brahman is indeed the cause. In this regard, the division is such that the exclusion of non-connection is established by the first quarter [of the sūtra], while the commencement of the remaining three quarters is for the purpose of excluding connection with another.

In this regard, the general division of the subject matter of the chapters (pādas) is as follows: in the first chapter, those passages containing clearer marks of the individual soul (jīva) were examined; in the second, those with less clear marks of the soul are considered; in the third, those with clear marks of the soul; and in the fourth, those that follow the semblance of propounding the Pradhāna and other such principles. This is the general distribution of the contents of the chapters.
Because the teaching is established everywhere. ||1||
And because the intended qualities are possible [in that case]. ||2||
But because of the impossibility [of its being so], it is not the embodied soul. ||3||
And because of the designation of the action and the agent [as distinct]. ||4||
Because of the distinction of sound. ||5||
And because of the Smṛti. ||6||
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [all-pervading] because of its having the bowels as its abode and because of designations to that effect, we say no;
for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space. (7)
If it be argued that [the soul] attains hearing [of the Veda], we say no, because of the difference in nature. ||8||

The Chandogas record: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, as originating from, dissolving into, and breathing in That; one should meditate upon it with a calm mind. Now, a person consists of will (*kratu*); as is his will in this world, so does he become after departing from here. Let him form a will: [may I be] composed of mind, having breath for its body, consisting of light, with true resolve," and so forth.

In this context, by the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman; as that from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes—being tranquil, one should meditate upon it," it is enjoined that one should meditate upon Brahman, who is the Self of all, while remaining tranquil. The subsequent statement, "One should form a resolve," is a restatement (anuvāda) of that very meditation for the purpose of enjoining further attributes, such as its being composed of mind (manomaya) and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: how can other attributes such as being composed of mind be enjoined in a case where the object is already occupied by the attribute of being the Self of all, which is taught at the time of the original injunction?

Now, it might be argued: "The sentence ending with 'All this, indeed, is Brahman; from that, indeed, it is born, into that it dissolves, and in that it breathes' (tajjalān) is a distinct sentence, because the connection with the word 'all' in 'All this, indeed' precludes its being a single syntactical unit with 'one should meditate on the Peaceful'. This is not tenable.

Nevertheless, in the passage "One should meditate on it as Peace," just as Brahman—which is present for another purpose—is connected as the object of meditation, so too its universal selfhood (sārvātmya) cannot be excluded from being connected as a quality of the object of meditation. Furthermore, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa’s Agnirahasya section, within the injunction for the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā—"One should meditate on Brahman as Truth"—the object of meditation, Brahman, is heard to be qualified by "truth"; therefore, for the sake of consistency with that, it is appropriate here as well to enjoin the quality of identity (tādātmya).

Furthermore, the identity of purpose between the two is easily established by following the scripture, "That which is existent and that which is non-existent," wherein the word *satya* (the Real) refers to the nature of all things, both manifest and unmanifest. If it is asked how other qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) can be enjoined when [the Self] is already occupied by the quality of being the Self of all (*sārvātmya*), the answer is: a quality enjoined at the time of origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) cannot tolerate only that subsequent quality (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*) which is contradictory to itself, but not merely any other quality.

For the fact that the substance *soma* is enjoined as the primary material of origin does not exclude other qualities such as the deity, just as it does not exclude other substances. Now, one might object: even so, it is not logical to enjoin qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomayatva*) as attributes of the Brahman to be meditated upon; for, through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in passages such as "One should form a resolve: [he who is] consisting of mind, whose body is breath," these qualities are perceived as qualifiers of the meditator himself. To this, we reply: in the *Agnirahasya*, within the same context, it is stated: ... [text continues] ... Thus, since the qualities are understood to belong to the object of meditation, they are not merely figurative. Furthermore, the passage "He should form a resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*) indicates that the act of forming a resolve is directed toward the object of meditation, not toward the meditator. Therefore, the qualities like "consisting of mind" are indeed attributes of the Brahman to be meditated upon. Moreover, the statement "He should form a resolve" implies that the meditator should direct his mental resolve toward the aforementioned qualities of Brahman. Consequently, the qualities such as "consisting of mind" are established as belonging to the object of meditation. This is further confirmed by the subsequent passage: "He has true desires and true resolves" (*satyakāmaḥ satyasaṃkalpaḥ*). Since the quality of having true desires is an attribute of the object of meditation, the preceding qualities must likewise be understood as attributes of the object of meditation. Thus, it is concluded that qualities such as "consisting of mind" are indeed attributes of the Brahman to be meditated upon.
