Attributes such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) are recorded as qualifications of the object of meditation. For in that context—after prescribing the meditation on Brahman qualified by truth in the passage, "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; let one meditate with a calm mind," and then demonstrating the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) with the words, "Now, this person consists of resolve; whatever resolve he has when he departs from this world, with that resolve he reaches the next world after death"—it is taught: "He should meditate upon the Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body..."

"Brahman is of the nature of light, whose self is space, who can take any form at will, who is as swift as thought, whose resolve is truth, whose steadfastness is truth, who possesses all fragrances, who possesses all tastes, who has pervaded all quarters, who has swallowed this entire universe, who is without speech and without concern, and without interior or exterior"—thus it is clearly stated in scripture that qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) serve as attributes of the object of meditation.

Now, one might ask: even following that [scriptural passage], how can the words *manomaya* and so forth, which appear here in the nominative case, be construed as providing the qualities of the object of meditation in the phrase "one should form a resolve" (*kratuṃ kurvīta*)? They must be construed by transforming them from the nominative case into the genitive case.

Alternatively, the passage beginning with "consisting of mind, having vital breath for its body" and ending with "I shall attain Him after departing from here" serves to provide the method for the meditation on Brahman as the Self of all, which is restated in the injunction "one should form a resolve. This is because the syntactical connection is understood as "one should form a resolve in this manner," owing to the force of the particle *iti* following that section; and because such a connection is necessary to ensure the consistency of the statement, "This is my Self within the heart."

For, unless it is intended as an illustration of the method of worship, there is no consistency in the syntactical connection of the word "ma" if it were an independent scriptural statement; and only that being the case, the threefold repetition of the passages beginning with "This is my Self within the heart" and the twofold repetition of the passages beginning with "possessing all works, possessing all desires," become intelligible.

For if that were the case, then in such passages as, "The *prāyaṇīya* is the first day; the *caturviṃśa* is the second; four *abhiplava* six-day periods; one *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; [this] is the first set, the second, the third, the fourth, and the fifth; three *abhiplava* six-day periods; one *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period," and so forth—which constitute the injunctions for the arrangement of days within the *gavām ayana* sacrificial session—the repeated recitation of terms such as "*abhiplava-ṣaḍaha*" would have to be understood solely as intended to signify the repetition of the performance of the six-day periods and other rites at their respective locations.

The repeated recitation [of these passages] attains its fruitfulness for the purpose of practicing the contemplation that [the Self] resides within the heart in each respective location; otherwise, if those sentences were merely scriptural statements intended to inform one of the existence of various attributes in the object of worship, they would be redundant. Furthermore, by this, the objection that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the injunction of multiple qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) by way of restating an enjoined meditation is also refuted.

Because they are to be enjoined in a single form, expressed by the manner indicated by the word "iti," there is no contingency of sentence-split (*vākyabheda*) when the form that delimits the object of injunction (*vidheyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*) is one, even if there is a difference in other forms that constitute the objects of the injunction.

Therefore, in the injunction regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—"A cow, a horse, a mule, a donkey, goats, sheep, rice, barley, sesame, and beans; his sacrificial fee consists of these twelve hundred"—although there is a difference in the forms of the cows and other items, there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) because they are enjoined under the single form of being the sacrificial fee. Thus, by accepting the injunction of a single sacrificial fee consisting of cows and so forth, the fault of sentence-splitting is avoided.

Alternatively, the word "iti" in the Śruti indicates the manner consisting of sequence—that one should perform the sacrifice by means of the sequence of reflection upon the qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomayatva*). Thus, it is not the case that a single, extended sequence itself is what is enjoined here.

There is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); however, the injunction of the qualities of the object of meditation, such as "consisting of mind" (*manomayatva*) and so forth, is obtained by implication through the injunction of that [meditation], just as in the case of the statement "The Viśvajit is an Atirātra with all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]," where from the injunction of the "allness" pertaining to the *pṛṣṭhas*, the [use of] the *pṛṣṭha-sāmans* such as the *rathantara* and others is implied—enough of this elaboration. Thus, when it is established that in the sentence ending with "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) there is an injunction for the meditation on Brahman as the Self of all, while in the ritualistic (*kratu*) sentence there is an injunction of the qualities of the object of meditation such as "consisting of mind," a doubt arises.

Is the one indicated here by the word "Brahman" as the object of worship the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Brahman? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the individual soul; for it is the soul alone whose coordination with all the terms [of the passage] is logically possible. Indeed, the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is designated by those terms, and the various states of being—beginning with Brahmā—are possible for the individual soul alone through different births resulting from the ripening of the stream of beginningless karma. However, for the Supreme Brahman, who is the source of all auspicious qualities and is devoid of any connection with things to be discarded, such a state consisting of all that is utterly base is not possible.

Nor is the application of the term *brahman* inappropriate for the individual soul (*jīva*), because in another scriptural passage, "This *brahman* comes," that term is used even there; furthermore, we observe that in various places, the term "Supreme *Brahman*" (*parabrahman*) is used with a qualification in order to distinguish it from that [individual soul]. Moreover, since the individual soul—when freed from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of transmigratory existence—possesses "greatness" (*bṛhattva*) through the expansion of its attributes and knowledge during the state of liberation, the causal designation "from which [it] is born, into which [it] dissolves, and in which [it] breathes" (*tajjalān*) is also logically consistent, as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world are caused by its [past] karma.

Therefore, it follows that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the Brahman indicated here as the object of meditation. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: The Brahman enjoined as the self of the entire world indicated by the words "All this, indeed," is the Supreme Brahman alone, not the individual soul. This is because the identity [of the world] with the cause of the world's birth and so forth is taught as something well-known.

Because it is born from Brahman, because it dissolves into Brahman, and because its very existence is dependent upon Brahman—for these reasons, it is said that this entire world is indeed of the nature of Brahman. For when it is stated that the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the world are well-known in the Vedāntas, it is understood that "Brahman" here refers to that [source]. And that is none other than the Supreme Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as, "From which indeed these beings are born."

Furthermore, for the entire universe—which consists of gross sentient and insentient entities whose birth, subsistence, and dissolution are dependent upon Brahman—there exists identity (*tādātmya*) with Him, characterized by His being the Self of all through the fact that the world is non-different from Him and constitutes His body. This identity is not contradicted by the fact that He is a mine of auspicious qualities and is antagonistic to all that is to be discarded; for defects residing in the body, which serves as a mode (*prakāra*), do not necessarily extend to the Self, which is the possessor of that mode (*prakārī*). However, such a declaration of universal identity is not tenable in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because that [individual soul] is distinct in each body, it is impossible for there to be mutual identity between them; therefore, what is indicated here by the word *brahman* is indeed the Supreme Brahman. If it is objected: "In that case, how can the two attributes 'consisting of mind' (*manomaya*) and 'having vital breath as its body' (*prāṇaśarīra*) be connected to Brahman as qualities of the object of meditation, given that the connection of the mind and vital breath with the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is well-established through their relationship as instrument and agent? It is replied: The connection with the mundane mind and vital breath is not fit to be accepted here as the intended meaning, because of that [mundane nature].

Since that which is to be abandoned (*heyasya*) cannot possess the qualities of the object of meditation (*upāsyaguṇatva*)—because that would contradict the principle of "becoming as one wills" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) mentioned immediately above—it follows that their meaning must be understood exactly as stated in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*): namely, that "consisting of mind" (*manomayatva*) means being graspable by the pure mind whose attributes and knowledge have blossomed in the state of liberation; "having the vital breath as its body" (*prāṇaśarīratva*) means sustaining the life-breath of all living beings; and "having light as its form" (*bhārūpatva*) means possessing a divine, auspicious form endowed with unsurpassed radiance. Thus, these meanings are to be accepted.

Furthermore, qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth are not possible in the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. Likewise, there is the instruction that the aforementioned Brahman is to be attained by the worshiper after departing from this world—expressed as "I shall attain Him"—and the designation of that [Brahman] as distinct from the worshiper, who is indicated by the genitive case in the phrase "This is my Self within the heart," using the nominative case; as well as Smṛti texts such as "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna. These would be inconsistent with the position that the Brahman to be worshipped, residing in the region of the heart, is the individual soul.

It is not tenable. [Objection: Even if Brahman is the subject, the designation of having a small abode and being minute—found in the passage, "This is the Self within the heart, smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley"—is not tenable. [Reply: It is not so; minuteness is taught for the purpose of meditation, but its essential nature is not actually minute. This designation should be understood as being like that of space.

Therefore, its natural greatness is also heard in scripture: "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds. And thus, since its natural greatness is understood without mentioning any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it follows by logical propriety that the limitedness spoken of with reference to a stated adjunct must itself be adventitious (*aupādhika*).

In this context, since there is no scriptural mention of the attribute of being "greater" (jyāyastva) corresponding to the attribute of having the heart as its abode (hṛdayāyatana), which is limited by smallness, it is intended that the smallness is adventitious for the sake of meditation, while the greatness is natural; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. If it be argued that, in that case, just like the individual soul (jīva), the Supreme Being would also undergo the experience of pleasure and pain resulting from that [residence within the body], because there is no difference in His being a conscious entity residing within the body, we say: No.

Because of the distinction in cause; for it is not merely the state of being a conscious entity residing within a body that is the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain, but rather subjection to karma as well. This cannot be suspected of the Supreme Self, who is free from all evil. Therefore, it is established that the Brahman to be meditated upon here is indeed the Supreme Brahman.

This [universal nature] is appropriate for that [soul] which possesses beginningless impurity, but not for the Supreme.

Do not say so; for by means of a figurative application (khalu-prayoga), that which arises from being the cause of all is restated as if it were well-established, and that [universal nature] is renowned in the case of Brahman.
Those other qualities, such as consisting of mind and so forth, which are heard in the supplementary portion of the passage,
are all applicable to Brahman alone, and not to the enjoyer.

In the Kaṭhavallīs it is heard: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who indeed knows where He is? The meaning is: "Who knows that mode [of existence], characterized by which mode He resides? That is to say, who knows that specific manner?

In this context, because of the connection between the boiled rice (*odana*) and the condiment (*upasecana*), the one designated by the genitive case in the word *yasya* ("of whom") is understood to be the eater (*attṛ*). Since it has not been determined whether this state of being an eater consists in being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma or in being the withdrawer of the world, a doubt arises. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: due to the connection with the boiled rice and the condiment, the eater is indeed merely an enjoyer. Nor should it be argued that the eater is perceived as the withdrawer because death—which performs the withdrawal—is figuratively described as the "condiment."

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is eternal, it cannot be subject to death; therefore, with the intention that death is merely something to be prescribed for the soul, the doctrine of "death as a condiment" (*mṛtyūpasecana*) is justified. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: [the doctrine of] "death as a condiment" is indeed justified.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is not proper to maintain that the doctrine of death being a condiment (*upasecana*) intends to convey that death does not obstruct [the soul's enjoyment]; for even though the word "condiment" is used figuratively, since it is itself being eaten, it is possible for it to be figurative in its specific form as the cause of another’s eating, rather than figurative in the sense of non-obstruction. Indeed, in the expression "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" is not intended to be figurative in a general form such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), but rather in its specific form such as "bravery" and so forth.

For this very reason, even in the *Pūrvatantra*, in the section [sūtra 3.5.26] beginning with "The cup of the Udgātṛ belongs to one, because of its connection with the Vedic text," it is established that regarding the word *udgātṛ* occurring in the Adhvaryu’s injunction—"Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forth, the Brahman’s, the Udgātṛs’, and the Sacrificer’s"—when it must function by secondary indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) in the plural sense according to the plural suffix, its specific form of application is restricted solely to the group of Udgātṛs; it is not the general form common to all sixteen officiating priests (*ṣoḍaśartvig*).

And just as when rice is moistened with curds, milk, and so forth for the purpose of eating, those [curds and milk] also become edible; likewise, since that by which death—which stands in the place of the rice—is moistened is perceived as edible, death itself is perceived as being most edible through that [rice]. This is because the devouring of the world by death occurs only at the time of dissolution (pralaya), and at the time of dissolution, all things, both moving and unmoving, are withdrawn; thus, the entire multitude of moving and unmoving beings—

It is determined that [the term 'odana'] is indicated by the words *brahman* and *kṣatra*. Furthermore, since it is impossible for the entire world of moving and non-moving beings to be the primary "food" (*odana*), it is determined that the word *odana* possesses a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of being "destructible"; even though this quality of destructibility is a general characteristic when compared to the qualities of being edible or being an object of enjoyment.

Nevertheless, since everything—whether moving or unmoving, or even just the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas—is neither edible like rice for anyone, nor is it an object of enjoyment like a wife or a servant, one must accept the common characteristic of being destructible as the cause [of the term's application], as this is obtained through the force of the other co-occurring words and is established by logic.

Therefore, in the passage, "Having touched this, one should sing the Udgītha; for all beings subsist upon this," it is accepted that the word "this" (imām) refers to the Earth, as established by its association with being the sustainer of all beings, and not that it refers to the nearby Udumbara post. Likewise, since the characteristic mark of the Supreme Self—namely, being the destroyer of all moving and non-moving things—is thus established, the Eater is indeed the Supreme Self.

This is also determined from the fact that the Supreme Self under discussion is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "wherein [he]," following such passages as: "The wise man, having known the great, all-pervading Self, does not grieve. Now, it might be argued: "The two who drink the reward in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest, supreme place..."

If it is argued that—because the immediately following mantra, "The knowers of Brahman speak of shade and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and the three *nāciketa* sacrifices," declares the state of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action denoted by the term "drinking the *ṛta*"; and because that [state] has been established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*); and because one of these two is the individual soul who performs the drinking of the *ṛta*, while the second must be either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since they are related to the drinking of the *ṛta* as instruments for the enjoyment of the fruits of action; therefore, the "eater" (*attṛ*) previously introduced must also be understood as the individual soul alone due to belonging to the same context (*prakaraṇa*)—to this we reply: [The answer follows: ... [as provided in the source text].

Neither the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), are said to have "entered the cave" or to be "drinking the *ṛta*"; rather, it is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) that are so described. For in that context, it is seen that only the individual soul and the Supreme Self are designated as having entered the cave: "Him, difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret place, placed in the cave, dwelling in the abyss, the Ancient... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12).

The designation of the Supreme as entering the cave is seen in the passage: "Having known the God through the attainment of self-yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow"; and of the individual soul (jīva) in the passage: "Aditi, who is composed of the deities, who comes into being with the vital breath, having entered the cave, she abides and is born through all beings. Here, the word *aditi*—used in its etymological sense of "one who eats the fruits of karma"—denotes the individual soul, and not the Mother of the Gods or the Earth, because neither of those two can enter the cave of the heart of people like us.

"It arises with the vital breath" means it exists together with it. It consists of deities (*devatāmayī*). Since the word *devatā* here denotes the sense organs (*indriya*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own primary sense; thus, its experience is dependent upon the sense organs. Having entered the cave of the heart, they abide there. Together with the elements such as earth and so forth, they are born in various forms as gods and others.

And thus, the designation "the two drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) is to be applied by way of the "umbrella-bearer" logic (*chatrinyāya*) through a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). Alternatively, since the suffix *-śatṛ* (in *pibantau*) refers to the commonality of agency shared by both the independent instigator and the one being prompted, it can be applied primarily to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*). For otherwise, if the suffix were taken in its primary sense of "agent" with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*), which are merely instruments, one would have to justify this as a metaphorical attribution of agency, just as in the expression "the eye is the grasper of form" (*cakṣūrūpagrāhakam*). This is how it must be supported.

Nor is there any inconsistency in the phrase "the world of good deeds" within the view that the Supreme Self is accompanied by [the individual soul], on account of its being acquired for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma; for, just as the experience is attributed to the enjoyer, the presence of the one who causes the enjoyment must likewise be asserted at the place of enjoyment.

Nor is it untenable to designate the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) as shadow and heat, given that they are both of the nature of light; for this designation is justified by their distinction as ignorant and omniscient, according to the scriptural text: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord. It is therefore logical that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul have entered the cave of the heart, as stated: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself."

For in this very context, it is described that the individual soul (jīva) is the rider of the chariot and the intellect (buddhi) is the charioteer, as they are mounted upon the chariot in the form of the body—according to the passage: "Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind indeed to be the reins. To claim these two are the Supreme Self (para) and the individual soul (jīva) is not tenable, because of the designation of a relationship between the attainer and the attained in the verse: "He reaches the end of the journey, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. If it is asked: "If the object to be attained is already on the chariot itself, for whose attainment is the mounting of the chariot imagined? [the answer follows].

It is said: It is appropriate that the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) have entered the cave, according to the passage: "The wise man, having perceived through the attainment of the yoga of the self that ancient God—who is difficult to see, hidden, entered within, seated in the secret cave, and dwelling in the abyss—transcends both joy and sorrow."

This is because, in the preceding and following mantras such as "He abandons," it is those two alone who are specifically characterized by their relationship as the object of meditation and the meditator, and as that which is to be attained and the attainer. Furthermore, the metaphorical representation of the chariot, the charioteer, and the driver is for the purpose of mastering the body and other instruments necessary for meditation, as is known from another mantra: "But he who possesses discernment, with a disciplined mind, his senses are under control, like good horses under a charioteer."

But it is not for the sake of attaining the supreme state, because until that point there is no departure from the ordinary body, senses, objects, and so forth. All of this will be clarified in the section concerning the "knower of the field" (ānumānikādhikaraṇa). Therefore, it is established that the two who have entered the cave are the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para), and not the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul; and the Eater is indeed the Supreme Self alone.
The summary verses.
Because of its connection with the boiled rice, the one who eats would be the individual soul (jīva) alone;
for there is no introductory context concerning Brahman, and the mantra that follows refers to the intellect and the individual soul.
Because of the proximity of the description of death as the sprinkling [of the offering], the entire sacrificial procedure is understood here as being performed for the sake of consumption;
therefore, it is appropriate that "taking away" (haraṇa) refers to the food, and its eater—the Lord himself—is the individual soul (jīva) residing within the *ṛta* mantra.
Thus ends the section [1].
Because of the intermediate state [of existence]. ||13||
And because of the designation of place and so forth. ||14||
And precisely because of the designation [of the fruit] as being distinguished by pleasure. ||15||
And for this very reason, it is "with Brahman. ||16||
And because the path of one who has heard the Upaniṣads is described [in the scriptures]. ||17||
And because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other. ||18||

The Chandogas recite: "This person who is seen in the eye—this, he said, is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Even if one pours clarified butter or water into it, it flows away along the eyelashes. They call him 'the one in whom all blessings meet' (saṃyadvāma), for all blessings indeed meet in him. All blessings meet in him who knows this. He is indeed the 'leader of blessings' (vāmanī), for he leads all blessings. He is indeed the 'leader of light' (bhāmanī), for in all..."

"He shines in the worlds. In this context, the person within the eye could be the reflected image, because of the reference as something well-known in the words "this one which," and because of the expression of immediacy in the word "is seen. Or it could be the individual soul (jīvātman), since it has a special proximity to the eye; for when the eye is opened, people determine the soul's presence in the body by looking [into it]. This is also supported by the Māṇḍūkya Śruti: "The waking state is situated in the eye."

The opponent’s position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: It must be either the eye itself or a particular deity established within it, because of the Vedic well-known usage: "By means of rays, he is established in this. But it cannot be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because it is inappropriate to refer to that which was described as "difficult to see" by the words "hard to see" with the expression "this one who is seen. Thus ends the prima facie view.

Now, how is this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) tenable? For in the very passage under discussion (*viṣayavākya*), there are recorded the marks (*liṅga*) of immortality and fearlessness, as well as the scriptural terms *ātman* and *brahman*, along with the qualities of being the center of blessings (*saṃyadvāmatva*), being a leader (*vāmanītva*), and being a source of light (*bhāmanītva*). Furthermore, there is the recording that the location is untainted because the occupant is untainted, in the words: "Therefore, even though I am in this... and "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus."

This is because the two statements, "He is united" (*śliṣyate*) and "Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him or not, they indeed reach the light" (*arciṣam evābhisambhavanti*), establish the results of the knowledge of Brahman—namely, the cessation of all taints and the attainment of Brahman—and because the context of Brahman introduced at the beginning of the passage, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," continues throughout. Furthermore, this is so because, unlike in the case of the Supreme Self, there is not even a single instance of *śruti*, *liṅga*, or other such indicators in support of the views regarding a reflection and so forth.

If it is argued that the quality of residing in the eye—found in other scriptural passages such as "He who dwells in the eye" and "This person who is seen in the eye"—is common to both [the individual soul and] the Supreme Self, we reply: the fact of having the eye as a locus excludes the Supreme Self and indeed gives rise to the position that [the one in the eye] is a reflection or the like.

For that [Self], which is established in its own majesty, primary residence in the eye is first of all impossible; even if a figurative residence based on the limiting condition (upādhi) of being delimited by a particular form were possible, it should be accepted only if there were some scriptural statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), or other such evidence here among the means of knowledge that would establish the identity of the one residing in the eye with the Supreme Self. But this is not the case.

Because the hearing of qualities such as being the "center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*) in the scriptural passages concerning the Self (*ātman*) and Brahman lacks the particle *iti*, it is understood—as in the case of "the mind is Brahman"—that these passages intend to produce a cognition of those [qualities] as belonging to that [Self]. Furthermore, because the hearing of immortality and other attributes mentioned in proximity to those qualities is intended solely for their own sake, the cited fruits are possible even through meditation on what is not Brahman, by the force of the scriptural statement itself—just as prosperity results from seeing the bridegroom and bride at a wedding.

Furthermore, the continuity of the section on Brahman is unestablished, because passages such as "Prāṇa is Brahman" and so forth are intended to enjoin the meditation upon [the vital breath] as Brahman by virtue of their similarity to "Mind is Brahman" and other such texts; and even if that were an injunction for the worship of Brahman, this particular sentence concerning the fires is distinct from the teacher's previous discourse due to the difference in speakers, and because it is separated by the teachings regarding the fires (Agnividyās).

For it is related as follows: Upakosala approached Satyakāma as his teacher and remained for twelve years attending to his sacred fires. Even though the teacher had not yet imparted the instruction on Brahman to him, when the teacher had gone away on a journey, the three fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—perceived that he was still intent upon the service of the teacher's fires; and out of compassion, they gathered together and taught him the knowledge of Brahman, beginning with "Prāṇa is Brahman," and [the passage] "That person who is seen in the sun..."

Having taught each of them their respective knowledge of their own specific objects through such statements as "I am that," and having declared, "O dear one, this is our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self," [the teachers] reflected: "In accordance with the Vedic text, 'Knowledge truly reaches its most perfect state when learned from the teacher,' may the Brahma-vidyā taught by us attain its highest perfection through the instruction regarding the path provided by our teacher. With this in mind, they said, "But the teacher will tell you the way. Therefore, since it is the path alone that remains to be told...

Because it has been left over [as a remainder], even though that [section] is a supplement to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is no inconsistency in its having as its object a reflection and so forth, since passages such as "He who is in the eye" do not themselves constitute supplements to that [knowledge of Brahman]. As for the argument that the description of the non-sticking of ghee, water, and so on—caused by the greatness of the locus—is a mark (*liṅga*) indicating that the locus is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), we say no; for while there is indeed sticking in reality, the description of the non-sticking of ghee and water due to the greatness of the locus (the eye) is merely a figurative praise (*stuti*).

Therefore, one among the reflections and so forth is indeed the person in the eye. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: Where the intended meaning is a connection with the words of an authoritative teacher (āpta), there the word *iti* does not preclude the intention to convey that meaning. For example, in the phrase, "Thus, indeed, the teacher says," the word *iti* does not preclude the meaning because it conveys a connection with the teacher's speech. Therefore, here, since the connection with the teacher's words regarding immortality and other qualities is what is to be established, the word *iti* does not preclude the intention to convey that meaning.

The qualities of being "the most beloved" (*saṃyadvāma*) and so forth cannot belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) by its own nature, nor can they belong to a reflection in any way whatsoever. Since the status of the Person within the eye as the Supreme Self is determined by numerous marks—such as the scriptural declarations of it being the Self and Brahman, its immortality, fearlessness, being the "most beloved," being the "leader of the good" (*vāmanī*), and being the "leader of the noble" (*abhimanī*)—its location in the eye must be understood as a single figurative indication; for multiple subsequent authorities are more powerful than a single authority found at the beginning of a passage.

Furthermore, from the designation, "This person who is seen in the eye," it is understood that what is intended is the state of being present in the eye at the time of meditation; this, however, is not possible in the case of a reflection. To assume that the original object (the *bimba*) is brought into proximity with the eye at the time of meditation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Moreover, even if one assumes the presence of the original object while the gaze is fixed on the tip of the nose during meditation, the emergence of a reflection is not possible. Furthermore, it is not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to abide invariably in the eye during the waking state.

Since that [Self], which has an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), would reside only in the eye during every waking state, the cognition of sound and other objects would be impossible; therefore, one must accept that the statement in the Śruti, "situated in the eye," refers to its presiding over all the sense organs—indicated by the term "eye"—by means of the expansion of its attribute-like knowledge (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*), while it itself remains situated in the heart as the source of all the senses.

Even if one were to accept the specific deity presiding over the eye—since scripture states, "By its rays, it is established in this"—the fact that its being supported by the eye remains merely figurative does not change; therefore, it is improper to disregard the scriptural designations such as "Brahman" by accepting that [deity] alone.

Furthermore, because the passage "That person who is in the eye" is stated for the purpose of prescribing other qualities and the locus of meditation for the Supreme Self characterized by bliss—which was introduced in the text "What is Brahman? Kha is Brahman"—the person in the eye is indeed the Supreme Self. Now, one might object that because of the intervention of the knowledge of Agni, the Supreme Self introduced in "What is Brahman? does not remain present here.

It is said: Having returned from his journey, the teacher, seeing Upakośala with a serene countenance, asked, "My dear, your face indeed shines like that of one who knows Brahman; who has instructed you? When Upakośala became afraid, [the teacher] concluded that the fires had taught him, and having asked, "But what, my dear, did they say to you? and being told by him, "They said this much," [the teacher], perceiving that there was more to be said on that matter, spoke the words beginning with, "But I shall tell it to you, just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf."

Having promised his own teaching, he was requested by [Nārada] with the words, "May the Blessed One tell it to me. Thereafter, how can we possibly conceive that the person in the eye—endowed with qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*) and so forth—who was taught by him, refers to anything other than the Brahman characterized by bliss which is the subject under discussion? For indeed, when the knowledge of the Supreme Self is concluded with the statement, "This, my dear, is that knowledge of the Self and the knowledge of all," it has been taught in its entirety.

If it is argued that even if one assumes the Teacher taught [the path] himself after considering the existence of a remainder of what was yet to be said, the consequence would still follow that the Fires were either speakers of untruth or ignorant; this is not so. For in the statement of the Fires, "But the Teacher will tell you the way," the mention of the "way" (gati) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of everything that remains to be told by the Teacher hereafter; otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the subsequent words of the Ārya.

If it is argued that in the passage "Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman," there is no instruction regarding the knowledge of Brahman, but rather merely the injunction to view the well-known ether and worldly pleasure as Brahman—since the word "Brahman" is applied to each individually—it is replied: Upakosala, terrified by the fear of worldly existence, approached Satyakāma for refuge.

This is because of the censure expressed by the teacher’s wife when she said, "I am filled with diseases," thereby attributing a state of illness to Uṣas in regard to worldly objects; and also from this indicative mark: that while all the other students who had approached for the sake of study were taught and allowed to return home after completing their vows (*samāvartana*), Satyakāma did not allow him to return, but instead appointed him to the service of the sacred fires and departed himself.

Thus, how could they teach the rules for the sacrificial fires—which are useless for one who has approached them with the desire for liberation? Therefore, just as in the passage "Prāṇa is Brahman," there arises a question with the desire to determine the internal meaning: do the words "bliss" (sukha) and "ether" (ākāśa) refer to Brahman by virtue of being its body (as the prāṇa-body), or rather, do they intend to convey the nature of Brahman as unsurpassed bliss by means of mutually excluding each other?

Knowing this intention, the fires said, "That which is indeed *kaṃ* (bliss) is the same as *kha* (space), and that which is *kha* is the same as *kaṃ*"; the implication is that their second alternative alone was intended. For this very reason, the two terms for Brahman in the phrase "Brahman is *kaṃ*, Brahman is *kha*" are also justified: to convey that Brahman is, like space, unlimited (*anavacchinna*), and that very Brahman is also of the nature of bliss (*sukharūpa*).

And thus, the statement of the qualifier-qualified relationship in both ways—"That which is indeed *ka* is the same as *kha*, and that which is *kha* is the same as *ka*"—is for the sake of accomplishing meditation in both ways, namely, that Brahman is of the nature of unlimited bliss and that Brahman is the essential nature of the unlimited reality whose essence is bliss; therefore, everything is beyond reproach.

Furthermore, because the Teacher taught to Upakosala—who had heard the Upaniṣads and understood the true nature of the Supreme Person—that path beginning with light (arcis) and so forth, which leads to the attainment of the Supreme Person characterized by non-return, as stated in the passage from "They reach the light" up to "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool," therefore the Person in the eye is the Supreme Self, and not [the individual self].

But [the case of] the reflection and so forth is different; for it does not necessarily abide in the eye at the times of meditation, nor is it possible for it to possess such qualities as being "immortal" (amuta) in its unconditioned state.
The summary verse:
Since the introductory statement "this person who is seen in the eye" is well-known [to refer to] the soul (*ātman*),
it is inappropriate to claim that it refers to the bearer of the body or a mere reflection, as such an interpretation would be contradicted by many [scriptural] obstacles.
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate [state]. ||3||

The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is [the Supreme Self], because His attributes are designated in relation to the deities, the worlds, and so forth; nor is He the one mentioned in the Smṛti, because there is a description of attributes not belonging to him; nor is He the embodied soul.
For both [schools] indeed study this [text] with a distinction. ||20||

In the sūtra, "And because of the designation of abiding and so forth," it was established—on the basis of such statements as "He who dwells in the eye"—that abiding in the eye, controlling it, and so forth, are attributes of the Supreme Self; having thus proven that the Person in the eye is the Supreme Self, that very point is now being further supported, which constitutes the logical connection.

The Vājasaneyins record: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. In this same manner, they record Him as dwelling within water, fire, the intermediate space, air, the sun, the directions, the moon, the stars, and so forth—remaining within them, being unknown to them, having them as His body, and controlling each of them.

The Mādhyandinas, however, record other parallel passages as well, such as: "He who is in all worlds, in all Vedas, and in all sacrifices. Regarding this, when the doubt arises whether this Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (para), the initial position is that it must be the individual soul; for in the supplementary portion of the text, it is heard that he possesses knowledge dependent on the instruments of the eyes and so forth, in the words: "the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower."

It should not be argued that the words "seeing," "hearing," "thinking," and "cognizing" denote the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of form and so forth, nor do they denote visual and other sensory cognitions; for even the Supreme Lord possesses the direct perception of form and so forth, as attested by such scriptural passages as, "He sees without eyes, He hears without ears."

If that were the case, it would be impossible to negate other seers and so forth as heard in the scriptural passage: "There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this; there is no other thinker than this; there is no other knower than this. For if words such as "seeing" and so on referred merely to sensory cognitions like visual perception, then the negation—that there is no possessor of such [cognitions] other than the individual soul (jīva)—would be appropriate. However, if they denote the direct intuition of form and so forth, then since that [intuition] exists in the Supreme Self as well, its negation elsewhere would be inappropriate.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that even in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the singular number in the passage, "He who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within," as well as the statements regarding His abiding in the earth and so forth in "He who dwells in the earth," the statement regarding His being unknowable by the earth and so forth in "Whom the earth does not know," and the statement regarding His being the controller of the earth and so forth in "He who controls the earth from within," would be untenable [if He were the individual soul].

This is because [the scriptural statements] can be interpreted as follows: the singular number [of the term "Self"] is intended to refer to the collection of individual souls; the statement regarding its "abiding" is according to the manner of saying it is established in its own majesty; the statements regarding being "within that" and being its "controller" are according to the manner of saying it is the Self and the Lord; and the statement regarding its "unknowability" is intended to mean the absence of knowledge of its isolated essential nature. Therefore, this inner controller (antaryāmī) is indeed the individual soul.

This being the case, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Regarding Uddālaka’s question, "Tell me of that Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within," there exists a certain single Inner Controller who is the controller of all; for Yājñavalkya’s reply, "He who dwells in the earth," and so forth, is the answer to that. In this context, it is not appropriate to interpret the singular number [of the word *antaryāmin*] as referring to a genus or the like, because it must follow the question which was initially directed toward a single subject.

Because it must be stated that all subsequent statements have as their sole object the one Controller of all worlds and so forth; therefore, it is logical that in this context the Antaryāmin intended is none other than Puruṣottama, who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, as heard in the passage from the *Subāla Upaniṣad*: "He whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth, whom the earth does not know... whose body is water," and so on, followed by the reference: "This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa."

Furthermore, it is consistent with this very [Self] being designated as "this Self is the inner controller, immortal," that it is distinct from the individual soul (jīva) and possesses innate immortality. As for the argument that the statement "there is no seer other than this" and so forth is best understood as a negation of any other [seer] possessing knowledge dependent on an instrument, rather than a negation of another possessor of knowledge of form and so forth—thus establishing the individual soul as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)—the reply to that is: the passage beginning with "there is no seer other than this" does not merely intend to negate the existence of another seer and so forth.

Rather, it is intended to negate other perceivers of the form who are the controllers of all beings similar to Him, according to the grammatical maxim: "When a negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with 'iva' or 'yukta', it refers to something else similar [to the original], for such is the understanding of the meaning. Indeed, relying on that very maxim, in the sentence "The procedure is the same as that of the Śyena," which is recited after the mention of certain specific attributes of the sacrifice named *Iṣu*, the word "other" (*itarat*) serves to extend (*atideśa*) the specific attributes of the sacrifice named Śyena, and not [anything else].

It has been determined in the seventh chapter of the *Pūrvatantra* that [the text] is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ritual elements which are common to the hawk sacrifice (*śyena*) and are obtained through the rule of transfer (*codaka*). By this, [the meaning of] the words "should hear" (*śroṣyasi*) and so forth in the passage from the *Maitrī Upaniṣad*: "One should not see the seer of seeing; one should not hear the hearer of hearing; one should not think the thinker of thought; one should not know the knower of knowledge. Verily, the Self (*ātman*), my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," is established.

Since it is observed that [the scriptures] refer to the agent who performs hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it is appropriate here as well to state that they refer to such an agent; thus, the doubt that the negation of other agents for hearing and so forth is consistent only with the individual soul (*jīva*) and not with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is also dispelled. This is because, by relying on the maxim of the particle *nañ* joined with a relative pronoun (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), the meaning of that negation is established as being intended to exclude other controllers similar to Him—specifically, a negation that accords with the meaning well-known from other scriptural passages such as "He sees without eyes. Therefore, that very sense must be accepted as the intended meaning.

Although the negation of any other entity similar to visual perception and so forth is also possible in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), nevertheless, like the *pradhāna*, the individual soul cannot be the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*), because of the impossibility of its being the controller of all and possessing unconditioned immortality and other such attributes. Furthermore, both the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas study this individual soul as distinct from the inner ruler; for the Kāṇvas read: "He who dwells in consciousness, yet is within consciousness," and so forth.

In that very same passage, the Mādhyandinas read, "He who dwells in the self," and so forth; therefore, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is indeed the Supreme Self and not the individual soul (jīva).
Summary Verses.

It is incorrect to say that the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is the embodied one (śarīrī), on the grounds that he is the substratum for the various cognitions produced by the instruments denoted by words such as "seer" and "hearer," since the term "embodied" here merely figuratively denotes the act of self-governance.
For how could the status of being the controller of all that has been studied belong to anyone other than Brahman?
In that regard, the perception of objects such as form and the like, as well as non-perception and so forth, are possible.
Thus concludes the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). ||4||
That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes. ||22||
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is not the other. 23.
And because of the presentation of form. ||24||

The followers of the Atharva Veda recite: "Now, there is the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and undecaying; that which the wise perceive as the source of all beings. Immediately following this, they recite: "For divine is this formless Puruṣa, who is both within and without, unborn, without breath, without mind, radiant, and higher than the high Imperishable."

In this regard, is the Imperishable (akṣara) characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, while that which is "higher than the high" (parataḥ paraḥ) refers to both Nature (prakṛti) and the Person (puruṣa); or is both of these the Supreme Self? First, it might be argued that they are Nature and the Person, for in this Imperishable who is the inner ruler, [attributes] such as "the unseen seer" and so forth do not apply.

A certain attribute of consciousness, such as being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*), is indeed recorded in scripture. Furthermore, in the passage "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ*), that which is described as higher than the entire aggregate of modifications—the aforementioned Imperishable source of beings—is called the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the collective Person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*). Now, one might object: even if no attributes of consciousness are heard here, since qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*) are common to both [the Pradhāna and Brahman], how can the determination that the Imperishable is the Pradhāna be established?

It is said: Just as indeed words such as "this person is not a child" or "this person is not young," when applied to a particular person, refer to that very person by way of its proximity to other states; so too, the negations of being visible, being graspable, and being an object of the intellect, the sense organs, and the action organs—when there is a requirement for a specific substratum (dharmin)—it is logical that they reside in the class of insentient things alone, in their subtle state, just like visibility and graspability. For it is possible for that very [insentient matter] which has undergone a change of state to be the substratum.

Because it is impossible to conceive of [the subject] as being either the Dharma (the possessor of attributes) or its opposite. Now, one might argue: "In that case, since there is a set of negations—'without lineage, without caste, without eyes, without ears, without hands or feet'—well-known in relation to the individual soul (jīva), when there is a requirement for a substratum (dharmin) for these negations, it is logical that the soul itself, in its subtle state as distinguished from the body, should be the substratum; thus, the Imperishable which is the source of beings would be the soul alone. For even though the negation of the marks of Primordial Matter (prakṛti)—'unseen, ungraspable'—occurs at the beginning of the passage, the negations of the soul's marks, such as 'without lineage,' are more powerful due to their multiplicity."

If it is argued that the term *akṣara* (the Imperishable) applies to the individual soul (*jīva*) as well—since we see the word used for the soul in the passage, "The perishable is the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the immortal and imperishable is Hara"—because the term *akṣara* is appropriate for the soul in the sense that it does not perish nor undergo transformation in its essential nature; and because the designation of being the "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) is also applicable to that soul as the cause of the world through the medium of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)—we reply:

It is stated [in the scripture] immediately after the mention of the *akṣara* as the source of beings, in order to explain that very quality of being the source of beings: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread], as herbs arise upon the earth... [and so forth].

Just as hair and body hair arise from an existing man, so does this universe arise here from the Imperishable (akṣara). By means of the examples of the spider and the like, which serve as illustrations for the Imperishable as the material cause through the process of transformation, it is understood that the nature of the Imperishable as the source of beings consists in its being a material cause via transformation. Immediately following that, [the text continues]: "Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar form emerge, so do various states of being, O Soma, arise from the Imperishable."

Furthermore, by the statement, "And even there they go," which declares that the imperishable source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is the origin of its effects possessing form, its status as the source of beings is understood to consist in its being the material cause through transformation (*pariṇāma*). Therefore, since the status of the imperishable source of beings as the primal nature (*prakṛti*) is established by both the opening and the conclusion, the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) found in passages such as "that which is without lineage" must be interpreted in some way as referring to that very same [source].

But surely, according to the reasoning stated, let it be that the Imperishable (akṣara) which is the source of beings is the primary [subject]; however, it is incorrect to say that "the Person who is the aggregate (samaṣṭi-puruṣa) is higher than the highest Imperishable," because this contradicts the introductory passages and so forth. For instance, at the very beginning of the supreme [text], it says: "He taught the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son."

The designation "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) is recorded [in scripture]. Consequently, in the passage beginning, "But when, O Venerable One, all this is known, what is it that, being known, all this becomes known? the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing is stated. Furthermore, in the sentence concerning the Imperishable (akṣara), the designation of higher knowledge (paravidyā) is also seen. Moreover, for the purpose of refuting the view that the sentences concerning the Reality-knowledge (sadvidyā) have the Pradhāna as their primary subject, [the following is stated].

The arguments demonstrated in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* apply here as well. Indeed, there is the scriptural hearing of creation preceded by "seeing" (*īkṣā*) here too, in the passage: "By austerity (*tapas*), the Word (*brahman*) is built up. For the word *tapas* here is derived from the root *tap* meaning "to contemplate," and thus denotes knowledge in the form of contemplation upon that which is to be created, as is clarified later in the text: "Whose austerity consists of knowledge. Furthermore, the word *ātman* occurs in the phrase: "For this Self is established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether"; and there is also the instruction on liberation for one who is established in that [Self].

"When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality. Furthermore, its being something to be abandoned is not stated; it has also been said that there would be a contradiction with the initial proposition [if it were so]. Moreover, the agency and material causality of Brahman are directly heard in scripture: "the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman."

If the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that these authorities refer to the Person who is beyond the syllable (*akṣara*), then they are justified as having that as their respective objects. If, however, the prima facie view is that even He is the collective person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*), and while this may be tenable for some [authorities], what would be the status of the others? To this it is said: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge..."

Therefore, that which is known in all the Vedāntas as the Supreme Self—the knower of the whole in its general and particular aspects—is referred to by the word "Brahman" in the opening passage, "From that, this Brahman, name, form, and food are born," and "That is Brahman-knowledge. It is stated that "from that, this Brahman is born," referring to the Brahman named Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of all individual souls (kṣetrajña). The status of that knowledge as "higher knowledge" (paravidyā) is justified because its fruit is liberation, unlike the knowledge of the lower Brahman.

The opponent maintains that its status as having liberation as its fruit is consistent with the force of scriptural statements; furthermore, since by the knowledge of the universal person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*) other individual field-knowers (*kṣetrajña*) also become known, the statement regarding the "knowledge of all" is likewise tenable. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

The imperishable source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is indeed Brahman alone. This is because, in the mantra "as a spider [spins thread]," which serves to explain the nature of the source of beings, the word "universe" (*viśva*) in the phrase "from that Imperishable, this universe arises here" refers to the entire phenomenal world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities; and within the category of sentient beings, there is no quality of being an effect of *prakṛti* (primordial matter), as there is the quality of being an effect of Brahman. Nor should it be argued that, following the presentation of the spider and other examples as material causes (*upādāna*), the word "universe" must refer only to the insentient portion capable of undergoing transformation.

This is because it is logical that the presentation of an example pertains only to the aspect of being the material cause required by the proposition (*pratijñā*), since any other similarity residing in the example that is not required by the meaning of the proposition is useless. Likewise, the subsequent mantra, "By austerity Brahman is built up," also serves to explain—by means of demonstrating through the word "from that" (the ablative case) that the element of being the source of beings (*bhūtayonitva*) residing in the subject under discussion, the Imperishable (*akṣara*), consists in its being the cause of the subtle elements of sound and so forth, which are denoted by the words "food" and the rest.

By the mention of "Brahman" in that very passage, it is determined that the Imperishable (akṣara) is Brahman. Likewise, in the immediately following mantra, "He who is all-knowing," because the word "who" (yat) refers back to the subject under discussion, it is likewise determined [that the Imperishable is Brahman], since this mantra sets forth characteristics of Brahman such as omniscience. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the masculine gender of the word "akṣara," for that is justified by the intention of referring to the source of beings (bhūtayoni), given that the word "source" (yoni) possesses both genders. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the similarity between cause and effect mentioned in the mantra "As a well-kindled fire... indicates that the Imperishable is the material cause (prakṛti).

In this context, by the term "beings" (*bhāvāḥ*), only the class of sentient beings is understood, since the status of being their cause exists in Brahman alone. For here, by the qualification "well-kindled" (*sudīptāt*), it is understood that the intended similarity is the state of being luminous, and that belongs only to the class of sentient beings. Furthermore, this section distinguishes the Imperishable (*akṣara*)—the source of all beings—from both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, through such means as the statement regarding the knowledge of all.

Nor does the statement, "All this has been known," which speaks of the knowledge of the entire phenomenal world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, deserve to be construed with difficulty as referring to the state of being known through the knowledge of either the collective person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*) or the individual person (*vyaṣṭipuruṣa*). The distinction of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) under discussion from primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and from the collective person is declared: "For the divine, formless Person is both within and without, unborn, without breath, without mind, pure—higher than the high Imperishable."

The meaning is that this Person, who is the source of all beings and whose nature is the Imperishable (akṣara), is superior even to that collective Person (samaṣṭipuruṣa) who is beyond the undifferentiated Imperishable. Now, one might object: why not take the meaning to be that He is superior to that very Imperishable which was introduced as being beyond its own effects? And that [interpretation] would indeed be more appropriate, since the two ablative cases in the phrase "akṣarāt parataḥ" can be understood as being in grammatical apposition. To this we reply: in the verse "sabāhyābhyantaraḥ," the word *sa* is a separate term qualifying the Person, just as in the expression "sudīptāt."

The phrase refers to the syllable that is the source of all beings as manifested by the mantra, for the purpose of conveying its non-difference from the Puruṣa who is beyond the syllable; it is not, however, a single compound word "sabāhyāntarābhyantara," because that would be redundant. For by the very statement of its omnipresence in "sabāhyāntarābhyantara," its connection with all things is already established.

When the identity of the Imperishable (akṣara) as such—the source—and the Person (puruṣa) who is beyond the Imperishable is established through non-difference, the term "Imperishable" expressed by the word in the ablative case ultimately refers to the unmanifest (avyākṛta). This meaning is also determined by the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the words "Imperishable" and "Person" in the mantra preceding the verse "beyond the Imperishable is the Supreme," which states: "By which one knows the true Imperishable Person—he taught that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence."

Furthermore, in the mantra: "Fire is His head, the sun and moon His eyes, the quarters His ears, and the Vedas His uttered speech; the wind is His breath, the universe His heart, and from His feet the earth arose—for He is the inner Self of all beings," the Puruṣa who is the subject under discussion—the Imperishable (Akṣara) that is the source of beings—is referred to by the pronoun "His" (*asya*). Since the fact that the three worlds constitute His body is thus presented, the Akṣara cannot be the Pradhāna, nor can it be the Cosmic Person (Samaṣṭi-puruṣa), even though in the Purāṇas and other texts [it is said that] "He who is higher than the highest Akṣara... [is the Supreme].

Although it is well known that even Hiraṇyagarbha possesses a Vairāja body consisting of the three worlds, nevertheless, that [body] of his cannot be such that the entire world, including both the moving and the non-moving, is established within it like a gem in a casket. Even that which does exist [in him] is essentially of the nature of the Supreme Self, according to the statement: "O Prajāpati, having entered you, I shall bring about another creation."

Furthermore, the state of being the inner self of all beings, as declared in the mantra "Agni is the head," is not possible in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, the Imperishable (Akṣara) and that which is higher than the Imperishable must be the Supreme Self alone.
The summary verses.
Due to its lightness, it resorts to a subtle form among the objects of the senses; following after the inert world, there is the negation of visibility and so forth.
That which is thus described is the Pradhāna, the Imperishable (Akṣara) mentioned in the Atharvaṇa.
And above that is the one described as being intent upon that, the twenty-fifth.

Because it is described as possessing qualities such as omniscience, the Primordial Syllable is indeed the Supreme; other than that, it is unmanifest. That which is beyond the unmanifest is also the Supreme.
Thus ends the section concerning the one whose qualities are invisibility and so forth. ||5||
Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction of a common term. 25.
That which is being remembered would be an inference. ||26||

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the one referred to] because of its being mentioned along with sound and so forth, and because it is established within, we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [otherwise] there would be no hearing [of the truth], and they also study this as the Puruṣa. ||27||
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an element. ||28||
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. ||29||
"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. (30)
Bādari [maintains that the soul's departure] is according to its remembrance. ||31||
Jaimini [holds that the fruit is] attainment, for so the scripture shows. ||32||
And they record this [name] in it. ||33||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: because the presentation of the form of the three worlds is made, Vaiśvānara is determined to be the Supreme Self, just like the Imperishable (Akṣara). The Chandogas record in their subsequent passages the answer given by the King of Kekaya—when questioned by the sages with the words, "You indeed know this very Self as Vaiśvānara; tell us about Him"—to the effect: "But he who meditates upon this very Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading..."

In this regard, is it possible to determine whether this Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self (paramātman) or not? Because the word "Vaiśvānara" is common to multiple meanings, there is doubt; and regarding this doubt, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: the word Vaiśvānara is seen to apply to four different objects.

First, with respect to the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), it is said: "This is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, by whom this food is cooked which is eaten; his sound is this which one hears when one covers one's ears. With respect to the third of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is said: "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the universe for the sake of all beings. With respect to the deity, it is said: "May we abide in the good will of Vaiśvānara, for he is the king and the glory of all beings. And with respect to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it is said: "He is indeed this Vaiśvānara, whose form is the universe."

"The vital breath (prāṇa) arises as fire. Now, it may be argued that this word *vaiśvānara* refers to the sun and not to the Supreme Self, because immediately following [the passage], after beginning with "This very thing is declared by a Ṛg-verse," there is the citation of a solar mantra concerning Vaiśvānara: "This sun, the thousand-rayed one who revolves in a hundred ways, rises as the vital breath of all creatures. Furthermore, in that context, the two pronouns "this very one" (*sa eṣa*) refer to the previously mentioned sun, as seen in the phrase "The sun is indeed the vital breath" (*ādityo haiva prāṇaḥ*). To this, we reply:

The word *vaiśvānara* there does not refer solely to the sun; rather, it extends up to the Supreme Self residing within the sun, because it is heard further on: "Then, by means of austerity, faith, and knowledge, having sought the Self as food, they are born in the sun; for this is the abode of the vital breaths, the immortal, the fearless, the supreme goal; from this they do not return again. Now, one might argue that Vaiśvānara can be determined to be the Supreme Self by the scriptural mention of "Brahman" in the opening passage: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"

Nor should it be argued that the opening statement in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā—“Vaiśvānara, indeed, the venerable one knows well; tell us that”—serves as a non-determinative factor because of the use of the word *vaiśvānara* at the outset; for that common term *vaiśvānara*, following the scriptural mention of *brahman* in the opening of the Chāndogya, can appropriately be understood as referring to the Supreme Self. If this is said, we reply: not so.

For those, such as Prācīnaśāla and others, who were reflecting on the questions "What is the Self? and "What is Brahman?", the vision of Vaiśvānara as the Self was described with respect to the sky and so forth; accordingly, because the terms "Self" and "Brahman" occurring in their speech are used elsewhere only in a figurative sense, by way of being objects of the vision of the Self and Brahman.

For it is related as follows: the five great sages, beginning with Aupamanyava, having deliberated—"Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"—and failing to reach a certainty, went to Uddālaka, who was devoted to the meditation on Vaiśvānara. Since even he was not fully conversant with that [meditation], they said, "Aśvapati Kekaya meditates upon Vaiśvānara; let us go to him. Thus, with Uddālaka as the sixth, they approached him. He, having examined their knowledge and intending to explain what remained to be said, addressed Aupamanyava.

Having questioned those six sages one by one with the words, "Upon what self do you meditate? and so forth, and having been answered by them in order with "The heaven alone, O Venerable King," and so forth—wherein heaven and the others were described as being meditated upon by them as Vaiśvānara in their respective forms as sky, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth—the text refutes the meditation on these [elements] individually as being the head, eyes, breath, middle body, and feet of Vaiśvānara, rather than as Vaiśvānara himself; and [it then establishes] the object of meditation as the aggregate [of all].

The form of Vaiśvānara, characterized by having heaven as his head and so forth, which was previously introduced, was taught by unifying [the various parts] through the passage beginning with, "His head indeed is *sutejas*. Therefore, it cannot be determined that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: It can indeed be determined that he is the Supreme Self, because he was taught by the King when questioned by Prācīnaśāla and others—who, desiring to know the Supreme Self who is the very Self of all individual souls (*jīvātman*), had approached the King, an expert in that matter—asking, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.1).

Nor should it be suspected that they (the Chāndogyas) intend the terms *ātman* and *brahman* to be used figuratively; for the inquiry, "What is our *ātman*? What is *brahman*? concerns the actual reality (*vastutattva*)—namely, among the entities such as the sky (*dyu*) and so forth, which we meditate upon as *ātman* and *brahman* respectively despite their mutual contradictions, what is that which is truly such a *brahman*, and is it one of these or something else? It does not concern an object characterized by a superimposed form, such as whether one should meditate by superimposing the notion of such a *brahman* upon those [entities], as in "Food is *brahman*; mind is *brahman*."

Just as in those [other cases], since it is impossible for the vision of Brahman to apply simultaneously to multiple symbols, there is no contradiction; therefore, there is no need for a definitive selection among our objects of worship—such as the sky and so forth—as to which one should be worshipped with such a vision of Brahman.

Therefore, by such statements as "The divine King is indeed heaven," their own respective delusions are exposed; for even today, just as some may have the delusion that the moon, sun, and so forth are Brahman, it is possible for them to have that same delusion regarding heaven and the other [elements]. Consequently, Vaiśvānara can be determined to be the Supreme Self by means of the scriptural designations *ātman* and *brahman*, which leave no room for the suspicion of being used in a figurative sense.

Furthermore, by the statement, "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves," it is said that he experiences the Supreme Brahman—which exists everywhere—as an object of enjoyment consisting of unsurpassed and infinite bliss; it does not mean that he eats the food consumed by those selves who are subject to karma, for such food is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu). Moreover, the fruit of experiencing supreme bliss is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self.

As it is said, "Just as a tuft of cotton-wool thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so all his evils are consumed"—this result of the burning away of all sins is consistent only with that [the Vaiśvānara] being the Self. Furthermore, the body consisting of the three worlds, from heaven down to the earth, is taught here [in this context] in the Śruti: "Fire is the head, the eyes are the moon and sun," and "Whose head the wise call heaven, whose navel is the sky, and whose eyes are the moon and sun."

And in such Smṛti passages as, "Know the quarters to be his ears, and the earth his feet—he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings," the well-known form of the Supreme Self is made recognizable as Vaiśvānara.

It makes known the Supreme Self. This might be so; however, by the reasons stated, it cannot be determined that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self, because from the word and other factors, as well as from his being established within, he is also perceived to be the digestive fire (jāṭhara). To begin with, in the Vājasaneyaka, the word "Agni" is heard in grammatical apposition with Vaiśvānara in the passage, "This is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara. And in the Chāndogya, the arrangement of the three sacrificial fires is made for Vaiśvānara: "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya."

The fact that Vaiśvānara is the substratum for the oblation to the vital breaths is recorded in the text: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered; when he offers the first oblation, he should offer it with [the mantra] 'Svāhā to Prāṇa,'" and so forth. Furthermore, his being established within the person is recorded by the Vājasaneyins: "He who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara thus, as having the form of man and as being established within the person."

If it is argued that, by the reasons stated thus, Vaiśvānara is understood to be the digestive fire within the belly (*jāṭhara*), this is not a fault. For the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who has the three worlds as his body, is taught as the object of meditation insofar as he is qualified by having the digestive fire as his body. By means of words such as "fire" (*agni*), it is not the mere digestive fire that is presented, but rather the Supreme Self qualified by that [digestive fire], since it is impossible for the mere digestive fire to have the three worlds as its body. [As stated: "Becoming Vaiśvānara, I have entered the bodies of living beings."

Furthermore, in the *Gītā*, it is stated: "Joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the fourfold food"; this establishes that the Blessed One, by virtue of having the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) as his body, is the digester of the food that is eaten and drunk.
