For these very reasons, even the suspicion that the deity Agni or the third great element (fire) might be Vaiśvānara is refuted.

The teacher Jaimini, however, maintains the following: Just as the word *vaiśvānara*, though common to others, is determined to denote the Supreme Self because of the perception of attributes exclusive to the Supreme Self—whereby "Vaiśvānara" is one who leads all men (*viśveṣāṃ narāṇāṃ netā*), and by the addition of the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthika*) becomes *vaiśvānara*—so too the word *agni* is determined to denote the Supreme Self through its connection with the act of leading forward (*agranayana*) and so forth; for that connection exists more fully in the Supreme Self, the Inner Controller of all, than even in the blazing fire.

Regarding the phrase "because of being well-established": [an objection is raised]—how can it be consistent for the Supreme Self, which is unlimited, to be described as having a limited measure (*mātrā*) in relation to the space from heaven down to the earth, as heard in the scripture: "But he who knows this one as of the measure of a span (*prādeśamātra*)"? [The answer is: such a presentation of being of the measure of a span is for the purpose of facilitating its apprehension by the intellect of the meditator, and not with the intention of asserting actual limitation. For in that very same passage, it is stated to be "immeasurable" (*abhivimāna*), meaning that its measurement has departed on all sides.

Even so, it may be argued that possessing a head and other limbs like those of an ordinary being is not possible for the Supreme Self, whose form is non-material; if this is said, we reply: no, for such a conception of having the form of a person is appropriate for the purpose of meditation.

If Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Self, how can there be this instruction regarding the chest and other parts as being the altar and so forth—namely, "The chest is the altar, the hairs are the sacrificial grass, the heart is the Gārhapatya fire," and so on? For such an instruction is appropriate only if the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is accepted. To this it is replied: This instruction that the chest and other parts constitute the altar and so forth is intended to establish the nature of the Agnihotra for the oblation of the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti), which is performed daily by the practitioners as a means of worshipping that Vaiśvānara.

For this very reason, the Śruti demonstrates both the fulfillment of the Prāṇāgnihotra as a true Agnihotra and the fruit appropriate for the meditation on the Supreme Self: "He who, not knowing this, performs the Agnihotra—just as if one were to remove the live coals and pour the oblation into ashes, so would that be; but he who, knowing it thus, performs the Agnihotra—for him the offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is utterly consumed, even so are all his evils consumed."

"They are consumed. Now, it may be argued that it is improper for the Supreme Self to have heaven and so forth as its body, because the injunction for meditation prescribes that only the head and other limbs of the meditator are to be meditated upon as heaven and so forth; for the passage beginning with "Of this very one... establishes that the meditator has heaven as his head and so on, due to its syntactical connection with such statements as "The chest itself is the altar. This is true; however, the contemplation of the meditator’s having heaven as his head and so forth does not mean that the Supreme Self’s having heaven as His head and so forth is being stated—rather, it is [the meditator's] own [limbs] that are intended.

The state of having heaven as the head and so forth has been taught even for the worshipper; for in the passage, "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara," heaven-as-head and the rest are indeed described as belonging to the worshipper by being referred to as his own. Therefore, one who is intent on the contemplation in such forms as "I am heaven-headed through the head of the Supreme" and "I am sun-eyed through the eye of the Supreme" must perform the propitiation by means of the Prāṇāgnihotra. Consequently, it is established that the Vaiśvānara introduced here is the Supreme Self.
These are the summary verses.
Vaiśvānara cannot be determined as the Supreme Self because there exist reasons for doubt regarding four possible objects;
for the term "Vaiśvānara" is common to the digestive fire, the third element (fire), its deity, and the Supreme Self.
Not so; for from the question of one desiring liberation, from the hearing of the word "Brahman," and from the teaching of such a fruit, that [Self] is determined to be the Supreme Brahman.
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara.
Thus ends the second quarter.
Now begins the third quarter.
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. 1.1.20.
And because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated. ||2||
Nor is there inference [of a creator], because of the word "that" (tat) and because of the living being (prāṇabhṛt). ||3||
And because of the designation of difference. ||4||
On account of the context. ||5||
And because of abiding and eating. ||6||

The followers of the Atharvaveda recite: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; cast off other words; this is the bridge to immortality."

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (para). For the time being, it is argued that it must be the individual soul. This is because in the subsequent verse—“Therein the channels converge like the spokes in the nave of a wheel; he moves within, being born in many ways”—there are recorded characteristics of the individual soul, namely its dependence on the channels, its movement within the body, and its state of being subject to birth. Furthermore, in the initial mantra—"The mind is woven together with all the vital breaths (prāṇas)"—there is recorded the characteristic of the individual soul consisting in its being the substratum of the mind and the vital breaths. [And] "This subtle Self is to be known by the intellect..."

"In that [Self] wherein the vital breath (prāṇa) is fivefold, and wherein the mind (citta), pervaded by all beings, exists through the vital breaths; when that is purified, the Self indeed manifests"—for elsewhere it is heard that the mind and the vital breath are woven upon the individual soul (jīva).

When it is argued that the status of heaven, earth, and so forth as the abode of the individual soul (jīva) must be understood through the medium of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), we reply: the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self (paramātman). This is because of the scriptural hearing of its being the "bridge of immortality" (amṛtasetu), which is unique to Him. For "bridge of immortality" means the cause of attaining immortality; a bridge, indeed, is that which provides access to the further bank of a river and the like. Thus, the meaning is that He is the provider of access to immortality, which constitutes the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.

And here, the word *ātman* means "one's own" (*sva*). It is derived from the root *āp* (to pervade) with the suffix *man*, and through irregularity (*bāhulaka*), the letter *d* is added. Its primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) is indeed to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who possesses universal pervasion by virtue of being the controller. Furthermore, the state of being the support of the channels (*nāḍī*) is possible for the Supreme as well, because of the scriptural tradition which begins, "It hangs down continuous like a hollow gourd," and concludes, "In the middle of its tip, the Supreme Self is situated."

He also possesses the state of being born in many ways, as seen in such scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti) as: "Though unborn, He is born in many ways; though unborn and of immutable nature, though the Lord of all beings, yet presiding over My own material nature, I manifest by means of My own māyā. Furthermore: "When the seer beholds the golden-hued maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman..."

Furthermore, because it is heard that the liberated one attains [the Supreme], as stated: "Then the wise man, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains the supreme equality; just as rivers flowing toward the ocean disappear, casting off name and form, even so the wise man, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high," the abode consisting of heaven, earth, and so forth, is the Supreme Self.

Moreover, just as in this section the Pradhāna is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth because there is no word indicating the Pradhāna, so too the Jīva is not it, because there is likewise an absence of any word indicating the Jīva; indeed, both this illustration and the subject of the illustration have been stated.

To explain: first, regarding Pradhāna, the word "That" (tat) refers precisely to that which is described in the passage beginning with "In whom the heaven... For in the Akṣara-Brāhmaṇa, through the passage beginning with "That, O Gārgī, which is above the heaven and below the earth," it is established that Pradhāna is the support of all worlds, including heaven and earth; thus, by its connection with the word "in whom" (yasmin), the phrase "In whom the heaven... is understood to be a restatement (anuvāda) of that very thing. Nor is there any inconsistency in designating it as "the bridge of immortality" (amṛtasyaiṣa setuḥ).

In this context, the word *amṛta* refers to Brahman, not to liberation in the form of immortality. This is because the word *amṛta* is applied to Brahman in the mantra preceding "in which [rest] heaven," namely "this is the Truth, the Immortal," and also in "that which shines as the form of bliss, the Immortal"; thus, it is that very same [Brahman] which is recognized here by the word *amṛta*. Therefore, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) cannot be designated as "the bridge of the Immortal," since it is only through its dependence on Brahman that it possesses a relationship with Brahman. Furthermore, it can also be designated as a "bridge."

The word *setu* is derived from the verbal root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind") and thus denotes the cause of binding. Its meaning is neither merely the cause of binding in general, nor merely the cause of binding water; for it is not applied to beeswax or other substances that bind water escaping from the interior of a jar. Rather, its meaning is the state of being a cause for binding water, as qualified by the condition of being situated between two shores (*pārāvāra*). Therefore, in this context, it is appropriate for the word *setu*, used here figuratively (*lakṣaka*), to indicate "having a further shore" (*pāravattva*), because of its natural association with that quality.

Furthermore, because it is a part of the meaning of the word [pradhāna]. Limitation (pāravattva), however, belongs only to pradhāna and not to Brahman, according to the Śruti: "The Great Being, infinite, and boundless. The word *ātman* is also applicable to that [pradhāna] when referring to the body, based on traditional authority (smṛti) such as: "Ātman [is used] for the living being, for fortitude, and for the body. As for the statement, "Abandon other words," this means: "Know that pradhāna alone is the body; abandon those words concerning 'body' which refer to the gross body."

For the sake of knowing the Self as distinct from the body, those desiring liberation must know the body; yet that [body] is not the gross body, because the distinction from it is easily known due to its coming into being and passing away. Rather, the subtle body consists of the unevolved self (avyākṛtātman) having assumed the form of the internal organ and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that *pradhāna* is the support of heaven, earth, and so on. The position that it is the individual soul (*jīva*) is also tenable, since the instruments of the soul—those [elements]—have their origin and subsistence dependent upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the soul, and thus it is appropriate to designate them as resting upon it.

Just as everything is fastened to the nave, so too is everything fastened to this vital breath (*prāṇa*), according to the *Bhūmavidyā*; and likewise in the *Pratardana-vidyā*, it is stated: "In this same way, these elements of being are fastened to the element of consciousness (*prajñāmātra*). Furthermore, this is because the scriptural texts establish that the aggregate of non-sentient things rests upon the individual soul (*jīva*).

"This subtle Self is to be known by the mind, in which the vital breath has entered fivefold"; and "By the vital breaths, the mind of all creatures is pervaded; when that [mind] is purified, this Self manifests"—for in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* itself, it is established at the outset that the mind and the vital breaths are dependent upon the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, the word "Self" (*ātman*) is appropriately applied to that [individual soul].

For in that very same ancient mantra—"The *praṇava* is the bow, the self (*ātman*) is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target; one must pierce it with undistracted mind, and like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in That"—the word *ātman* is employed. Furthermore, the statement "Know Him alone as the Self" is also appropriate in reference to that [Brahman].

"For the mind-made [self], the leader of the body of vital breaths, is established in food, having fixed its seat in the heart. By the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth. Since this statement declares that the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva) is the cause for the vision of Brahman, it follows that the soul is required only as a subordinate means. Furthermore, the injunction "abandon other words" is also appropriate in reference to that [soul]. "One should take up the bow of the Upaniṣads, the great weapon; one should fix the arrow sharpened by meditation."

"Drawing it with a mind focused on that state, O gentle one, know that very syllable"—since this immediately preceding mantra speaks of "thinning" (tanūkaraṇa) the individual soul (jīva), which appears as characterized by bodily bulk and so forth, by means of meditation that brings about firmness in the discrimination between the body and the self; and because in the meditation upon the jīva, there must necessarily be a relinquishing of speech directed toward objects other than that [Self]. Furthermore, the designation "this is the bridge to immortality" is applicable to the jīva as well, in the same manner as was explained regarding the Pradhāna.

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no inconsistency in either the *pradhāna* or the *jīva* being the subject, we reply: It is first of all untenable for the passage beginning with "In whom the heaven... to be a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the *pradhāna*, which requires another substratum such as heaven and earth as mentioned in the Akṣara-Brāhmaṇa. This is because, when it is possible for it to be a restatement of Brahman—the independent substratum of all things as proclaimed in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad text, "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root"—it is improper to assume it is a restatement of a dependent substratum.

And thus, for the sake of establishing the statement that [Brahman] is the support of all things such as heaven and earth, the meaning of the word *ātman* must be taken as its essential sense of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), because it has been established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*) that a metaphorical meaning (*lākṣaṇikārtha*) is to be accepted only when it is capable of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with other words uttered in proximity. In this way, in accordance with the scriptural texts (*śruti*) regarding the self as the exclusive support of heaven, earth, and so forth, [it is said]: "Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless..."

Since the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* shows the designation of Brahman as "the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed," one should understand the meaning of the phrase "this is the bridge to immortality" accordingly: that it is the very means by which immortality itself is attained. Nevertheless, if it is argued that the mention of moving within the body found in the subsequent mantra is not applicable to all-pervading Brahman, we say no.

In the Subālopaniṣad, within the textual sequence beginning with "He whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth," we observe that because He is the pervader of all through His role as the universal controller, He is designated by the term "moving. Therefore, it is logical that He is likewise designated here [in this context] in that same manner. Furthermore, in this very section: "The person, immersed in the same tree, grieves while deluded, being powerless..."

The mantra is heard: "When he perceives the other, the Lord, and His glory, he becomes free from sorrow. Its meaning is as follows: Immersed in one and the same tree—that is, in a body whose nature is as worthy of being cut down as a tree—the individual soul (*puruṣa*, *jīva*), having attained identity with it like a drop of water submerged in a heap of dust, grieves while being deluded by *anīśā* (the non-Lord, i.e., *prakṛti*).

When he perceives the other than his own self—whom he honors, who is beloved, who is gracious, and who is the Lord of all—and when he perceives the glory of this Lord, which consists in the governance of the entire universe, then he becomes free from sorrow.

Although in this mantra the individual soul (jīva) is mentioned alongside Brahman, nevertheless, this scripture—by designating "being deluded" as co-located with the state of being the seer (draṣṭṛtva), and "lordship" (īśatva) as co-located with the state of being the object seen (dṛśyatva)—re-identifies the Lord alone as the support of heaven, earth, and so forth, who was previously pointed out as the object of knowledge in the words, "Know Him alone as one. Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated in the Akṣarādhikaraṇa that this context refers to the Supreme Self; therefore, this [Self] is indeed the Supreme Self.

Nor should it be suspected that since the status of the Supreme Self as the support of heaven, earth, and so forth is already established by the context of the syllable *akṣara* in the preceding section (*akṣarādhikaraṇa*), what is the purpose of this present section? This is because the suspicion arises that the context might be interrupted by various attributes pertaining solely to the individual soul (*jīva*), such as its connection with the channels (*nāḍīs*), its being born in many ways, and its being the support of the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*); this section is intended to dispel that doubt. Furthermore, in this very context [it is said]: "Two birds, inseparable companions, embrace the same tree."

Although one of these two eats the sweet fruit while the other, not eating, shines—the latter being established as the Supreme Self—nevertheless, it is logical that the support of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self alone; for by the mention of its "shining," there is a natural consistency in connecting the omniscience and other attributes mentioned in the context to that very [Self].

By this Sūtra, the doubt that the purport of the section lies in the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—arising from the introduction of the proposition that all is consciousness in the opening and the conclusion that "one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—is also refuted. For, by the designation of their difference accompanied by the reasoning of "eating" and "not eating," their very distinction is established.
In the summary verses.
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the individual soul (jīva), because of the scriptural connection with the mind and the vital breaths;
and because in the immediately following mantra, there is mention of its conjunction with the channels (nāḍīs).
The Supreme Lord alone must be the sustainer of all things,
because he is established as the foremost among those who bestow immortality and other such qualities.
Thus ends the section concerning heaven, earth, and so forth.
The Infinite [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (samprasāda). ||7||
And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine. ||8||

Since the status of the Supreme Self (paramātmatva) was established in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad through the non-interruption of the context of the Supreme Self, there arises a connection [to the present topic] by way of the objection: "In that case, the Bhūma-vidyā must refer to the individual soul (jīva), because it occurs within the non-interruption of the context of the individual soul. The Chandogas recite: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Bhūman."

"That wherein one sees another, hears another, and cognizes another—that is the finite (alpa). The word *bhūman* is derived from the word *bahu*, which is listed in the *pṛthv-ādi* group [of nominal stems] by the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā*; when the suffix *imanic* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the rule *bahoḷopo bhūca bahoriḥ* applies, whereby the *ikāra* of the suffix *imanic* following *bahu* is elided and the word *bahu* is replaced by *bhū*. Thus, it is established as denoting "abundance" (*bahutva*). Although "abundance" may signify either vastness or a specific numerical quantity, [in this context it refers to the latter].

Nevertheless, the meaning here is "vastness" (vaipulya), because we hear of its being the counter-correlative of "smallness" in the passage, "That wherein one sees something else—that is small"; and also because in the preceding passages such as, "Space, indeed, is vaster than fire," the word *bhūyas*—derived from the root *bahu*—is seen used for space and other things that possess vastness even when they lack the numerical quality of "many. This word *bhūman* refers to the substratum itself, not merely to a quality, precisely because it has as its counter-correlative the substratum indicated by the word *alpa*. Therefore, the meaning of *bhūman* is "the vast."

And the Self is distinguished by its extensiveness (*vaipulya*). For, having introduced the subject with "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and having taught the Infinite (*bhūman*), the text concludes with "All this is indeed the Self. Regarding this, when a doubt arises as to whether this Self characterized by extensiveness is the individual self (*pratyagātman*) or the supreme self (*paramātman*), the initial position is that it is the individual self.

To Nārada, who approached with a desire to know the Self, [the teacher] taught that which is to be meditated upon, beginning with Name and ending with Breath; yet, while there are questions and answers such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than Name? and "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than Speech?", the absence of a question like "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than Breath? and a corresponding answer like "That indeed is greater than Breath" leads to the understanding that the instruction regarding the Self terminates with Breath. Consequently, it is logical to interpret the word "Breath" as referring to the inner Self (pratyagātman), which is associated with the vital breath.

Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "father," "mother," "brother," and "sister"—which denote a father and so forth who are sentient beings—as in the passage, "Breath indeed is the father, breath is the mother, breath is the brother, breath is the sister," it is understood that this refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of a father and so on; therefore, it is not correct to say that this instruction concerning the Self has the Supreme Self as its object.

"If he should speak harshly to his father, or mother, or brother, or sister, or teacher, or a Brāhmaṇa, they say to him: 'Fie on you! You are indeed a patricide; you are indeed a matricide,'" and so forth—because there is mention of injury and reproachful speech directed at living beings such as the father and others when they are being reviled.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning, "Now, even if one were to thoroughly pierce and tear them apart with a spear while their vital breaths have not yet departed, they would not say of him, 'You are a slayer of a father,' nor 'You are a slayer of a mother,'" it is described that even when those [bodies] whose vital breaths have departed are being thoroughly pierced and torn apart on all sides with a spear, there is an absence of the conventional designation of "violence. For there is no state of being "to be slain" in another, nor is there any departure [of the self] from that [body].

Nor should it be suspected that, because the word *tu* ("but") indicates a break in the context immediately after the presentation of the individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the word *prāṇa*—with the statement, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly through Truth"—therefore, from that point onward, the section concerning the Supreme Self denoted by the word *satya* begins, and thus the *bhūman* (the Infinite) being taught in that section must be the Supreme Self alone.

Regarding the statement, "He who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus becomes an 'exceeding speaker' (ativādī)," since the exceeding-speaker-ship of the proponent of *prāṇa*—defined as speaking of the superiority of his own object of worship over others—is recognized in the sentence "But he indeed [is]," there is no interruption of the context.

When it is stated, "But he indeed is an Agnihotrī who speaks the truth," the speaking of truth is enjoined as an auxiliary (aṅga) for the one under discussion—the speaker of the breath's transcendence—just as it is for the well-known Agnihotrī; for the word "but" (tu) is appropriate only in the sense that, provided there is truthful speech, the status of being a speaker of the breath's transcendence becomes firmly established, just like the status of being an Agnihotrī. Therefore, the inner self alone is what is to be understood here. For this very reason, [it says]: "I am indeed below, I am above..."

Beginning with [the passage] "I alone am all this," the conclusion teaches the majesty of the inner self (pratyagātman) itself; and its vastness, expressed by the word *bhūman* through such statements as "I indeed am below," is established as being possible in liberation due to the expansion of virtue and knowledge. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

In the passage, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly by means of Truth," one understands from the words *tu* ("but") and *satya* ("Truth") that the speaker of Truth and so forth is distinct from the speaker who surpasses by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, in the passage, "Other animals are indeed inferior to cows and horses; cows and horses are the [true] animals," one understands that, just as cows and horses are superior to other animals, the speaker of Truth and so forth is more excellent than the aforementioned speaker who surpasses by means of the vital breath.

And thus, from that [preceding statement], it results that the excellence of this [Brahman] is due precisely to the superiority of the Truth (satya) which is the cause of that "speaking beyond" (ativadana), compared to the vital breath (prāṇa) which is the cause of that speaking beyond; by means of this sentence, the "Plenum" (bhūman) is taught as being superior to the individual self (jīva) under discussion.

Nor does the logic of the passage "Or rather, let this Agnihotrin... apply here; for in that case, since there is no other substance or deity, another Agnihotra is understood, which necessitates setting aside the natural force of the word *tu*. But here, since we perceive a different cause for transcending speech—namely, transcending by means of the Supreme Self denoted by the word *satya*, which is distinct from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that was the cause of transcending speech in the context under discussion—why should its natural force be set aside? Indeed, the word *satya* denotes the Supreme Self, as it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself: "The name of that Brahman is *satya*."

The word "satyena" is in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*), expressing the sense of an instrument (*karaṇatva*); it indicates that truth is the cause for the speaking of falsehood. Therefore, there is no room for the assumption that the particle "tu" (but) breaks the accent of the instrumental case-ending and refers instead to the subject under discussion—the proponents of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. And thus, because [the Self] is taught as being superior to the living self (*jīva*) denoted by the term "vital breath" which was the subject under discussion.

The term "Bhūman," which is expressed by the word "Truth," refers to the Supreme Self. Nor should it be argued that this reason is fallacious because of the body, which is taught in the scripture "Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest" as being superior to the individual soul (jīva); for the intention of that teaching is to show its superiority in terms of being the Self that transcends the individual soul. Likewise, the Bhūman is the Supreme Self because of the scriptural hearing of His unsurpassed bliss.

But is it not established in the Siddhānta that the one denoted by the word "Truth" (satya) is indeed the Supreme Self as the subject of the context, whereas the one denoted by the word "Prāṇa" is the individual soul (jīva), being an inferior stage [of manifestation] below it—this being demonstrated by the questions and answers beginning with, "Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than name? and "Speech, indeed, is greater than name"?

If it is argued that it is not logical for that which was commenced for a certain purpose not to be stated, it is replied: because "speaking beyond" (*ativāditva*), which was not mentioned in the preceding sections, is established in the section on the vital breath (*prāṇa*), Nārada—thinking that the instruction on the Self commenced [there] has been concluded with the vital breath alone—questions Sanatkumāra again. Sanatkumāra, however, [realizing] that even the knowledge of the vital breath does not have the commenced Self as its object, and that perfect "speaking beyond" is not attained through that, but rather through Truth (*satya*) which is the Supreme Self, himself introduced the knowledge of Truth. Thereafter...

To him who asked, "May I, O Blessed One, speak by means of the Truth? [the Teacher] taught that very Supreme Self—the plenitude (bhūman) denoted by the word 'Truth'—through a succession of means such as discernment, faith, and so forth; thus, the absence of further questions and answers is otherwise accounted for.

Now, one might object: since the passage beginning with "wherein there is nothing else" (*yatrānyat*) conveys the sense that in that locus one sees nothing else, it appears—given that everything within the range of seeing, hearing, and so forth is illusory with respect to Brahman—to be a statement concerning the *bhūman* whose subject matter is the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*). How, then, can it be described as teaching the Blessed Lord, who is a mine of infinite auspicious qualities? And how [can it be said that] "he does not see death, nor disease, nor even suffering"?

By the mantra, "For the seer sees all; he attains all in every way," which describes the seer of the Infinite (bhūman) as seeing everything, the non-perception of suffering is also established. It is said in reply: in that context, one must supply the word "being experienced" (*anubhūyamāne*) after the phrase "in which" (*yasmin*). For it is not from the mere existence of Brahman that there occurs the non-perception of anything else therein; otherwise, it would follow that even people like us would lack the perception of objects of sight and so forth.

And the meaning of the word "wherein" (*yatra*) is "distinguished by His own entire multitude of qualities and manifestations. Since the word *bhūman*—like the word *brahman*—signifies the state of being devoid of the three kinds of limitations (*pariccheda*), it is logical to speak of the non-perception of anything else as distinct or separate from Him who is thus distinguished by His own entire multitude of qualities and manifestations; for everything exists only within Him.

If, however, *vibhūti* (sovereignty) consists of the nature of controlling, then that [control] is dependent upon the cognition of the object to be controlled; thus, because it stands in a relationship of opposition (*pratiyogitā*) to the form of the controlled, the perception of everything—including suffering—is necessarily required. Let this be so; nevertheless, how can the non-perception of suffering be established? For, since all sufferings belonging to all transmigrating beings are included within the scope of such sovereign power, their perception cannot be avoided.

Furthermore, according to the method stated in the *Samanvaya* section, just as the mere direct perception of happiness is considered a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too must the mere direct perception of suffering be considered something to be abandoned (*heya*). Consequently, for one who has attained liberation and perceives the "plenum" (*bhūman*), there would be an experience of even greater suffering compared to the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Nor can it be argued that everything experienced as a manifestation of Brahman's glory (*vibhūti*) must necessarily be of the nature of happiness alone.

If it is argued that this is contradictory—because that which is experienced by transmigrating beings as something other than Brahman, taking the form of suffering or limited pleasure, would then, when experienced as a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Brahman, take the form of pure bliss, since it is impossible for a single thing to possess the nature of both pleasure and pain—it is replied: For those under the sway of karma, the world, experienced as distinct from Brahman, becomes of the nature of suffering or limited pleasure according to their respective karmas; however, for one who is liberated from the ignorance consisting of karma...

That very same world, when included within the experience of Brahman as distinguished by its powers and qualities, becomes nothing but happiness. Just as milk being drunk by one afflicted with bile becomes painful and only slightly pleasant according to the degree of that bile, yet that same milk, when drunk by one not afflicted by bile, becomes purely of the nature of happiness; for when whatever is experienced is favorable to a person, then it is happiness, and when it is unfavorable, then that very thing is suffering.

Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that cold, heat, and so forth take on the dual nature of pleasure and pain according to the different conditions of summer, winter, and the like. As for the passage beginning with "I myself am below" and ending with "He alone is all this," it is intended for meditation upon [Brahman] in its own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*); whereas the passage beginning with "The Self alone is below" and ending with "The Self alone is all this" is intended for meditation upon [Brahman] as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the knower. [And regarding the passage: "For him who sees thus... and so forth.

In the passage beginning with, “To him who thus reflects and understands, from the Self comes breath, from the Self comes hope, from the Self comes memory,” etc., the fact that the previously introduced Self is the Self of the knower is specifically stated during the demonstration of the origin of breath and the other principles from that very Self. Thus, this threefold instruction regarding its being the Self of all is for the purpose of accomplishing three types of meditation; therefore, one should discern that there is no pointlessness whatsoever in any of these statements.
The summary verses.
The "plenum" (bhūman) is the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, it is superior to name and so forth, such as speech, because it is introduced without any questions or answers.
And the *prāṇa* is clearly the individual soul (*jīva*) itself, because of the opening and concluding statements concerning the self,
because of the mention of motherhood and so forth, because of the statement that it is not to be killed, and because of the declaration of "I-ness."
It is true that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the individual soul (jīva), but it is not the "Full" (bhūman); rather, the Supreme Person alone is so.
This is because, in the passage "But he indeed speaks surpassingly," the word "but" (tu) serves to exclude what preceded it.

Furthermore, because the state of unsurpassed bliss is heard in passages such as "where there is nothing else," the realization of the "I" (aham-graha) is shown therein by the statement "I alone am below."
Thus ends the section concerning the "Fullness" (bhūman). ||2||
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports that which has the sky as its limit. ||9||
And that [is so] because of the command. ||10||
And because of the exclusion of other states. ||11||

Just as the "plenum" (bhūman) is not the individual soul (jīva) because it is taught as being superior to the soul, so too it is established that the "imperishable" (akṣara) is not the primal matter (pradhāna) because it is taught as being superior to the primal matter; this is the connection [of the topic]. The Vājasaneyins record: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare that this indeed is the imperishable—neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, without shadow," and so forth. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the imperishable is the primal matter or the Supreme Self; for now, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is the primal matter.

Because the word *akṣara* is used in such passages as "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*) to denote the *pradhāna*, and because, although that same word is used for the Supreme Self in passages such as "that Imperishable is attained," between the *pradhāna* and the Supreme Self—both of which are well-known from other sources of knowledge—the *pradhāna*, being established by other means of proof, enters the intellect more quickly and is thus apprehended first; therefore, inference requires only perception [as its immediate antecedent].

Since both [scripture and inference] are required for the acquisition of linguistic proficiency regarding scripture, the syllable (*akṣara*) established by inference is more swiftly cognized than the Supreme Self as understood through scripture; furthermore, among scripture, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, each preceding one is stronger than each succeeding one. Moreover, since attributes such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) can also apply to the Pradhāna, there is no exclusive mark for the Supreme Self in the passage concerning the syllable that is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*). This being the prima facie view, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: the syllable is the Supreme Self, not the unevolved Pradhāna.

For in this passage—"In this very Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, the ether (ākāśa) is woven to and fro"—the Imperishable is taught as the substratum of the unmanifested (avyākṛta). It might be argued: let this word "ether" refer to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), since it is improper to override its conventional meaning.

If it be argued that, prior to the Akṣarabrāhmaṇa, in the Gārgibrāhmaṇa, within the succession of questions and answers between Gārgī and Yājñavalkya—beginning with the passage, "Whatever is here, Gārgī, is woven to and fro upon the waters; upon what, then, are the waters woven to and fro? 'Upon the wind, Gārgī. 'Upon what, then, is the wind woven to and fro? 'Upon the worlds of the intermediate space, Gārgī,'" and continuing until the end of the section with, "'Upon the worlds of Brahman, Gārgī'"—[the self is taught].

After describing how each preceding world—earth, water, air, the intermediate space, the world of the Gandharvas, the world of the sun, the world of the moon, the world of the stars, the world of the gods, the world of Indra, the world of Prajāpati, and the world of Brahmā—is woven like warp and woof into each subsequent one, Yājñavalkya was asked again: "In what, indeed, are the worlds of Brahmā woven like warp and woof? To this, Yājñavalkya replied: "Gārgī, do not ask beyond; lest your head shatter! You are asking about a deity that should not be questioned beyond; do not ask beyond!"

Addressed with anger, Gārgī became afraid and desisted. By this, it is indicated that some great deity must be described as the support of all the worlds, ending with the world of Brahmā. Subsequently, while many Brāhmaṇas were engaged in successive turns of debate with Yājñavalkya out of a desire for victory, Gārgī entered the discussion; although she had then ceased out of fear, after her cessation, when Uddālaka—who was renowned as a knower of Brahman—had questioned [Yājñavalkya] regarding the Sūtra and the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) and had been defeated by Yājñavalkya...

Thinking, "Mastery arises only for all Brāhmaṇas; let it be equal," and desiring to ask Yājñavalkya while seeking to avoid being thwarted by his second question, he asked the Brāhmaṇas for permission, saying: "O Yājñavalkya, just as a Kāśya or a Videha, the son of a noble father, might rise up having strung a formidable bow and taken in hand two feathered arrows capable of piercing the enemy, even so have I risen up toward you with two questions; answer them for me."

Having simultaneously requested permission for two questions from Yājñavalkya, she asks, being granted that permission: "O Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what, then, is all that woven togetherness and crosswise? When this has been answered with the words beginning, "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky... and ending, "...in space alone is that woven togetherness and crosswise," she then asks: "In what, indeed, is space woven togetherness and crosswise?"

As the answer to the second question, the entire Akṣara-Brāhmaṇa, beginning with "This, indeed, is that syllable" and ending with "In this very syllable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof," has been set forth.

In that context, at the conclusion of the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa, the question which was angrily rejected by Yājñavalkya was indeed suggested by Gārgī—who was afraid that it would lead to the defeat of all the Brahmins—as a deity who ought to have been addressed first; it is indicated that this very deity is what is expressed here by the word "ākāśa. And if this is so, how could this word "ākāśa" refer to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*)? In that case, it could not even refer to the Pradhāna, because the Pradhāna also lacks the status of being a deity.

Therefore, one who maintains that the passage is intent upon the Pradhāna might offer this defense: "In the initial question concerning the support of all worlds up to the world of Brahmā, the subsequent answer was not intended to exclude that [Pradhāna] as its object; rather, with a far-reaching vision, the exclusion was made with the thought: 'This [Sañjayin] is audacious and will ask for the support of that [Pradhāna] as well, and thus his question will concern the Supreme Deity. If it is argued that the same defense can be applied even if the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa):

It is said: [In the passage] beginning with "That which is above the heaven, O Gārgī," and so forth, the word *ākāśa* can only be consistent if it refers to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), since even that is included within the category of effects. Therefore, in this context, the word *ākāśa* refers to the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). And the Imperishable (*akṣara*) taught as its substratum is none other than the Supreme Self; it is not the unmanifest. As for the argument that what is established by another means of knowledge (inference) is understood prior to what is established by scripture—that is not so, because the word *akṣara* [is derived] through its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) as "that which pervades" (*aśnoti vyāpnoti*).

Because it does not depend on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the communication of its own meaning, that by which the nature of the object was apprehended at the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) is of no use at the time of its communication. For it is said in the *Vārttika*: "Since there is no dependence upon the comprehension of the object, another means of valid cognition is not required; and that which served as the means for acquisition is [useful] only in that regard alone."

Furthermore, just as perception does not operate with respect to the Pradhāna—as it does with respect to individual entities possessing dewlaps and so forth, which are the objects of grasping the relationship between a word such as "cow" and its referent—so too, the inference favored by the Sāṃkhyas and others does not operate there; this will be explained in the *Sāṃkhya-adhikaraṇa*. Consequently, like Brahman, the Pradhāna is also to be known solely through Śruti; thus, there is no distinction between the two based on whether they are well-known or unknown. Therefore:

Since it is understood from the mark of being the substratum of all modifications that what is denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa) is the unmanifest (avyākṛta), and because the reason for identifying the unmanifest as that denoted by the word "syllable" (akṣara) is unestablished, the "syllable" spoken of as the substratum of the unmanifest denoted by the word "ether" must be the Supreme Self alone. Furthermore, because of the teaching of its being the seer and so forth in the passage, "Then, O Gārgī, this syllable is unseen but the seer, unheard but the hearer, unthought but the thinker, unknown but the knower," the syllable is the Supreme Self and not the unmanifest.

[Objection: "In that case, let the individual souls (jīvas) be the Imperishable (akṣara), for in their case both the state of not being an object of perception and the possession of perception and so forth are possible; moreover, its status as the substratum of the entire aggregate of conscious beings is established by the scriptural statement: 'Just as the spokes are fixed in the nave, so in this Prāṇa everything is fixed. [Reply: This is not so, because of the scriptural hearing that its support is dependent upon governance (praśāsana): "By the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart," and so forth.

Although it might be possible, in some way, to justify the rulership over heaven, earth, and so forth—even for a living being who undergoes successive births as gods, humans, and others—by means of attaining those specific births appropriate for such offices; nevertheless, supreme rulership in the form of independent sovereignty, as well as the sustaining of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies preceded by that [sovereignty], is simply impossible in such a being.

Furthermore, the fact that [the Imperishable] is the seer of all while itself unseen, as well as the negation of any other seer established in such passages as "There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this," is not possible in the case of the individual soul (jīva), but is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self (paramātman) according to the method explained in the Antaryāmi-adhikaraṇa. Therefore, the Imperishable is indeed the Supreme Self alone.
The Summary Verses.
Prakṛti is to be understood through inference from the syllable, while Brahman is not defined by the scriptures [alone];
for inference depends upon the syllable, whereas that [scriptural knowledge] depends upon both.
It is not so; for that which is held to be indeterminate is the Vedic Brahman, that Imperishable.
Scripture is required for the acquisition of linguistic proficiency, but not for the communication of the meaning [of what has already been learned].
For those whose primary characteristics are seeing, hearing, and so forth, do not perceive the Indeterminate;
nor is the individual soul (jīva) this Imperishable (akṣara), because of the incongruity of its being a ruler and other such attributes.
Thus ends the section concerning the syllable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). ||3||
He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. ||12||

In the *Praśnopaniṣad*, following Satyakāma’s question to Pippalāda—"O Venerable Sir, among men, he who meditates upon that [syllable] until the end of his life, which world indeed does he conquer by means of it?"—and beginning with the reply, "O Satyakāma, this *oṃkāra* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise man follows one or the other by means of this very support," it continues: "If he should meditate upon it as having only one *mātrā*, being made known by that alone, he very quickly..."

"He reaches the earth; the Ṛg-verses lead him to the world of men. There, endowed with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness. Then, he who merges into the mind by means of two measures is led up to the intermediate space by the Yajus-formulas to the world of Soma. Having experienced glory in the world of Soma, he returns again"—thus, for one who meditates on the Oṃkāra as having one measure, the fruit is the attainment of the world of men, which is brought about by the Ṛg-verses consisting of that first measure; [and] the two measures...

Having described the attainment of the *yajus* consisting of two measures for one who meditates upon that [first measure], as well as the fruit of reaching the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), the following is taught: "But he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable *om* consisting of three measures—he, having become united with the heat of the sun, is freed from evil just as a snake is freed from its skin; even so is he freed from evil. He is led up by the *sāmans* to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings, he reaches the One who dwells in the city, who is higher than the high."

"...one beholds the Puruṣa. Here, the Supreme Puruṣa alone is the object to be beheld. This is because of the rule that meditation (*dhyāna*) and beholding (*īkṣaṇa*)—the means and the end—must have the same object. Furthermore, although in the phrase "the Supreme Puruṣa," the term "Supreme" might be intended as having some limit of comparison (since it is possible for something to be superior to certain things), the designation "the Puruṣa dwelling in the city, higher than the high" does not imply a difference from that [Supreme Being]. Thus established, is the Puruṣa who is to be meditated upon and beheld the four-faced Brahmā, the aggregate of individual souls (*jīva-samaṣṭi*), or...?

Regarding the doubt as to whether [the one referred to] is the Lord of All (Sarveśvara) or the Four-faced One (Caturmukha), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it must be the Four-faced One. This is because he is being beheld by one who has reached the world of the Four-faced One, which is denoted by the term "Brahmaloka. Nor should it be argued that the word "Brahmaloka" refers to the world of the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat); for, due to its placement in a sequence alongside the worlds of humans and the intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*), it too refers to the natural world of the Four-faced One. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the word "jīva-gha" denotes the Four-faced One as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of individual souls (*jīva*), and therefore the Person beyond him must indeed be the Lord of All; for his...

This is because it is logical for [the term] to denote the aggregate of individual (vyaṣṭi) living beings; for the word *ghana* is recorded in the sense of an aggregate in the statement: "The *ghanas* are a solid aggregate, the density of clouds, and mallets. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the one beyond the aggregate of individual living beings must be the universal (samaṣṭi) living being, and therefore the Person (*puruṣa*) beyond that must be the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) alone; for it is logical that Caturmukha (Brahmā) is superior to the aggregate of individual living beings, which are themselves superior to the body, senses, and so forth.

Since it is impossible to assume a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "the Supreme" (*para*) and "the mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*) when such coordination is possible, one cannot resort to a lack of coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Nor can it be argued that, because immortality and other qualities mentioned in the immediately following verse—"By the *ṛg* verses this [world], by the *yajus* verses the intermediate space, and that which the seers know through the *sāman* verses—that the knower follows by means of the syllable *Oṃ*, which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme"—belong to the Lord of All alone, the "Supreme Person" must therefore be the Lord of All, as He alone is the object to be meditated upon and attained.

This must be stated: according to the introductory passage, the immortality and other attributes mentioned in the concluding portion can be appropriately construed as being merely relative immortality and so forth, pertaining specifically to the four-faced Brahmā (Caturmukha). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarma*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is because of the designation of immortality and other qualities found in the subsequent mantra, and because of the designation "higher than this mass of living beings (*jīvaghana*)," since Hiraṇyagarbha, despite his lack of distinction from other living beings, is included within the category of the "mass of living beings. Furthermore, the term "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) refers to the world of the Lord (*bhagavat*), because it is that which is to be attained by one who is liberated from all sins.

Regarding the passage, "What the seers (kavayaḥ) perceive," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, that it is to be seen by the seers (*sūri*) as established in other scriptural passages such as "The wise always behold that highest step of Viṣṇu"—and because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the meditation on the Supreme Being introduced by the words "This, O Satyakāma," the *prāyapāṭha* (the principle of general enumeration) is set aside by these *liṅga* and *prakaraṇa*, and thus it is of no consequence. If it is objected: "But since the meditation on the Lower [Self] is also heard of in the introduction alongside the meditation on the Supreme, should not that too be explained?"—it is true.

This has already been established previously. For earlier, having divided that meditation into two types—pertaining to this world and the next—it was set forth that meditation upon [the Self] by means of the one-measure *praṇava* results in attaining the world of men, while meditation upon it by means of the two-measure *praṇava* results in attaining heaven; subsequently, meditation upon the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) by means of the three-measure *praṇava* was commenced. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Person, who is the object of meditation and vision, is the Lord of All.
The summary verses.
For this Puruṣa, the Creator, who dwells within the city [of the heart], was indeed instructed regarding Satyakāma;

because he is seen as one who has attained that world of the person (puṃs), it is stated here that it is the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) and not the world of the Supreme Brahman (parabrahmaloka). For at that time, [the latter] does not exist [as a distinct realm].

It may be argued that for one who knows the *praṇava* as having one or two *mātrās*, there would be a sublation of the textual sequence which primarily concerns the fruit [of the three-mātrā recitation].
This is Viṣṇu, because of the mention of freedom from old age and immortality, and because of the designation of the supremacy over all living beings;
since the phrase "the world of Brahman" refers to his station, let there be a sublation of the immediate context by means of the indicative mark.
Thus ends the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa). ||4||
[The word "small" (dahara) is used] because of its being small [in size] and because it is superior [to all else]. ||13||
For it is seen thus from both movement and sound, as well as from the inferential mark. ||14||
And because this greatness of steadfastness is perceived in him. ||15||
And because of common renown. ||16||
If it is argued that he [is the enjoyer] because of the clinging to the vital breath, we say no, because of its impossibility. ||17||
If it be argued that [the soul] comes from the north, [we reply]: no, for its true nature has already been manifested. ||18||
And the reference has another purpose. ||19||
If it be argued that this is because [the scripture] has little to hear, that has already been answered. ||20||
And because of the imitation of that [world]. ||21||
It is also recorded in the Smṛti. ||22||

In the preceding section, it was established that the "dweller in the city" (puriśaya), described as "one who beholds the Person higher than the high," is the Supreme Self; here, likewise, the status of the dweller in the city as the Supreme Self is established—this is the connection.

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, and within that, the small ether (ākāśa)—that which is inside it is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. Here, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) mentioned in the Śruti as being situated within the heart-lotus inside the body referred to by the term "city of Brahman" is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa). And the Supreme Self (paramātman) is that which is heard in the text as "that which is within it," to be sought within that small ether. Alternatively, the small ether itself is the Supreme Self.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the collection of qualities such as "having one's evil removed" mentioned in the scriptural passage, "In that which is within it," refers to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) or something else—since the term "ether" has its conventional meaning (rūḍhi) there—the initial position is that it is the elemental ether. However, [the qualities] mentioned in the scriptural passage, "In that which is within it,"...

The Supreme Self is intended, and not the collection of its qualities. For if [the phrase] "that which is to be sought after" were connected only with "that which is within it," it would follow that only the qualities are to be meditated upon, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the possessor of the qualities (the Supreme Self) would not be an object of meditation. Thus, all the attributes of the Supreme Self heard in the supplementary portion of the passage find their connection in the Supreme Self indicated by the words "that which is within it"; therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding them either. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion is: the "small ether" is the Supreme Self.

It is not the elemental ether, because of the reasons found in the supplementary portion of the passage. For in that supplementary portion—"As far as this [outer] ether extends, so far extends this ether within the heart"—there is a requirement for the distinction of the small ether from the elemental ether; by means of that, the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is established. Immediately after that: "Within this [ether], heaven and earth are contained, as well as both fire and wind, and both the sun and the moon..."

Having pointed out the aforementioned small ether (*daharākāśa*) by saying "lightning and stars are within it," its status as the substratum of the entire universe is declared. Then, by the statement, "Whatever exists here of his and whatever does not exist—all that is contained within this," it is shown that all the objects of enjoyment existing in this world for the worshiper, as well as everything that exists here only as an object of mental longing and does not have physical form—all those objects of enjoyment are contained within this small ether. Thus, by virtue of being the unsurpassed object of enjoyment, its nature as unsurpassed bliss is established.

It is demonstrated as follows: by referring back to that very same "small ether" (daharākāśa) with the word "this" in the passage, "This is that true city of Brahman," its nature as a city consisting of the true Brahman is stated. This is because, in the term "city of Brahman" (brahmapura), grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is appropriate according to the maxim of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (niṣādasthapati).

Then, by referring to that very same small ether (daharākāśa) with the word "in this," and by referring to the desirable qualities with the word "desires" (*kāmāḥ*), it is stated that these qualities reside within the small ether; and thus, that very small ether—characterized by such desirable and auspicious qualities—is described as the Self (*ātman*) itself, with the words: "This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger or thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true."

Thereupon, the fruit is shown for those who, having understood the Self and these true desires here, depart, by means of the passage: "For them there is freedom of movement in all worlds," where the word "Self" (ātman) refers [to Brahman] and one contemplates both that which resides within it and the desirable qualities such as being untouched by evil.

Likewise, in the passage: "Just as people walking back and forth over a hidden treasure of gold might not find it because they do not know its location, even so all these creatures, though going there day after day, do not find this world of Brahman, for they are held back by untruth," we see that the term "this" (*etam*) refers to the previously mentioned small ether (*daharākāśa*), and that the daily departure of all beings to that place is indicated by the designation "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*).

Indeed, it is observed that the daily going of all beings to the Supreme Self during the time of deep sleep is described elsewhere: "In this very way, my dear, all these creatures, having reached Being (sat), do not know 'we are reaching Being'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2). Furthermore, the term "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka) is seen used for that [Self]: "This, O Emperor, is the Brahma-world," he said (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.3).

Likewise, in the passage, "Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded," the small ether under discussion is designated as "the Self," and its quality of supporting the universe is established. And this is the majesty of the Supreme Self, according to another scriptural text: "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded. For these reasons, derived from the supplementary portions of the text, the small ether is the Supreme Self.

For the term *ākāśa* (ether/space) indeed possesses Vedic renown even for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as seen in other scriptural passages such as, "He said, 'It is Ākāśa,'" and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: if the phrase "that which is within it" were intended to refer primarily to the multitude of qualities residing in the Supreme Self, rather than to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) itself, then the status of that [small ether] as the primary object of meditation must also be established. This is because of the concluding portion of the passage: "But he who, having discovered the Self here, and these true desires, departs... and so on. If this is argued, [the response follows].

This is true; such is the justification for that. Regarding the statement, "That is to be sought after," the word "that" (*tat*) does not refer only to what was mentioned in the nominative case (the internal space), but rather also to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) mentioned in the locative case. This is because, according to the grammatical rules—"pronouns such as *tyad* and others are always [retained] with all [genders and numbers]," and "when combined with a non-neuter [word], the neuter remains, and optionally takes the singular"—the formation of a neuter singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is justified. Thus it has been stated in the Bhāṣya and other works.

In this regard, the following is considered: the neuter gender for the remainder in the form *tat* must indeed be stated by the subsequent rule itself, namely, "The words beginning with *tyad* [are always used] with all [other pronouns]. In that context, there is no recurrence of the rule regarding singular concord (*ekavadbhāva*). This is because [the singular concord] occurs only in the rule "And optionally, it [the group of pronouns] is treated as a singular."

This is because this rule for singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) applies specifically to that very *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) which was established by the sūtra on neuter nouns. Nor should it be argued that, for the sake of establishing the retention of the neuter (*napuṃsakaśeṣa*) among the *tyadādi* pronouns when both neuter and non-neuter forms occur—such as in the case of "he and she" (*sa ca sā ca*) resulting in *tau*, or "she and he" (*sā ca sa ca*) resulting in *tau*—the subsequent application of the sūtra "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.69) must also be intended there. [For in those cases, the retention of the masculine is required.]

Furthermore, because the author of the Vārttika exerted a separate effort by stating, "In the case of *tyad* and the rest, when one remains, the gender and number are those of the masculine or neuter," for the purpose of establishing the remainder as neuter when it follows both a neuter and a non-neuter; and likewise, because a separate effort is observed in the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika, and other works for the purpose of establishing the singular collective expression (*ekavadbhāva*).

How, then, in the case of the *tantra* form, is it established that in the injunction for the *citreṣṭi* sacrifice—"Curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice; these mixed together constitute the *prājāpatya* [offering]"—there is a group of sacrifices (*yāgagaṇa*) each consisting of individual substances such as curd and so forth, rather than a single sacrifice consisting of one mixed substance? To this end, it is stated that the word *tat* (in the compound *tatsaṃsṛṣṭam*) does not refer to a single mixed substance denoted by the word "mixed," but rather refers to the multiple substances beginning with curd. This is then resolved through the application of the neuter gender and the singular collective remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) to the words *tat* and *dadhyādi*.

Thus, another interpretation was formulated for the sake of excellence; for it is by the very nature of pronouns that they refer to what has already been introduced, and since referring to what is yet to be introduced is a resort of last resort, and because a specific substance alone can satisfy the expectancy—since a mere conglomeration is unfit to have a connection with Prajāpati—it follows logically that the word "tat" (that) must necessarily refer to multiple substances such as curds and the rest.

The singularity conveyed by the singular number in the word *tat* is not intended to be significant—just as the plurality of the *pāśas* [is not intended]—according to the maxim "but when a secondary quality is involved, an improper assumption [of its literal meaning] is made. Alternatively, it is appropriate that the neuter singular form is used even though it refers to multiple items, both neuter and non-neuter, because of the grammatical rule: "A neuter [word] combined with a non-neuter [word] becomes neuter and optionally singular. This is because it has been stated that the same should be understood for the *prājāpatya* [animal] as well.

In this regard, the following is the resolution: when the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) consisting of both neuter and non-neuter terms is made for the word "anveṣṭavyam," a singular grammatical operation occurs there, just as it does for a single referent. Consequently, that [singular] function applies even to its qualifier, despite the impossibility of a single referent for the pronoun; just as by the rule "asmado dvayośca," the plural number is used for the referent of *asmad* when it denotes singularity or duality, and this plural form occurs even in the verbal form residing in the sense of *asmad*, as in "vayaṃ brūmaḥ" (we say). Here too, [in the case of] "śuklaśca śuklā ca... (the white male and the white female... [the same principle applies].

Just as the singular number is observed even in the verbal form "śuklaṃ ca śuklaṃ vartate," so too it ought to occur in the case of a pronoun. For this very reason, in the Mahābhāṣya—wherein two types of examples for the neuter rule are given, namely: "śuklaśca kambalaḥ śuklā ca bṛhatikā śuklaṃ ca vastraṃ taditaṃ śuklaṃ tānīmāni śuklāni"—the word *tad* (that) is employed as an attribute of the first example specifically in its collective (ekavadbhāva) form. Similarly, in the sentence regarding the *citreṣṭi* sacrifice, when the word *prājāpatya* functions according to the neuter rule, [it follows the same logic].

The *Tantraratna* maintains that even when the word *tat* occurs within a compound, it takes the neuter singular; thus, here too, in the phrase "to be sought" (*anveṣṭavyam*), once the singular collective form has been applied by the rule for neuters, it is entirely appropriate that the word *tat* occurring within that compound also takes the neuter gender and singular number. Therefore, it is established that the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone, who is to be meditated upon together with the collection of attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) residing within Him, and not the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).

[Objection: Granted that this [space] may not be the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), let it be the individual soul (*jīva*), because in the context of the Dahara-vidyā, there is a reference to it in the passage: "Now, that serene being (*saṃprasāda*), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form. [Reply: No, because in that case, qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are impossible [for the individual soul]. [Objection: But in the Prajāpati-vākya, which follows the Dahara-vākya, the individual soul is indeed recorded as possessing freedom from sin and other such qualities.

In that context, having heard as a traditional report the words of Prajāpati: "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that Self is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known; he who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," Prajāpati spoke to Maghavan, who had approached him with the desire to know the Self that was to be sought, saying: "This person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self. "Who..."

It is true that in the passage, "This one who is being honored in sleep, this one who is enjoying pleasure—this is the Self," it is taught that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, which possesses the three states beginning with waking, is the Self characterized by qualities such as freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) that are sought to be known. However, during the state of transmigratory existence, the *jīva* has its qualities such as freedom from evil obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*). Later, when its bondage of ignorance in the form of karma is liberated, having risen out of the body and attained the Supreme Light, it is described in Prajāpati’s discourse as being distinguished by qualities such as freedom from evil.

Having stated that the individual soul (jīva), upon rising from this body and attaining the supreme light (paraṃjyotis), manifests in its own true nature characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin, and having established that the supreme light to be attained is the "Supreme Person" (puruṣottama) by the words "He is the highest person," [the text continues] with "He moves about there, laughing, playing, rejoicing, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen," etc., [describing] the state of the soul that has attained Him.

Because of the mention of great fruits and renown to be experienced by the worlds therein; however, in the passage concerning the small [space], the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is understood to be precisely that whose qualities—such as being eternally manifest and free from sin—are already established. For when it is possible to accept such qualities as freedom from sin as being eternally present, it is improper to accept that which has its manifestation dependent upon causes. Therefore, one should not entertain the suspicion that the small ether is the individual soul (*jīva*).

If this is so, then for what purpose is the reference to the individual soul (jīva) in the context of the Dahara-vidyā through the passage beginning with "having risen up from this body"? It is for the purpose of demonstrating a specific greatness of the individual soul—namely, its attainment of the manifestation of its true nature—which is analogous to the Dahara-ākāśa’s sustaining of the universe; it is a restatement of a matter already established in the Prajāpati-vākya.

Now, if it be objected: "If the *dahara* (the small one) is not the individual soul (*jīva*), then how is the scriptural mention of its small dimension to be explained?"—to this the answer must be stated: it has already been said previously in the section beginning with "On account of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere" (*Sarvatraprasiddhopadeśāt*) and continuing with "Because it is to be meditated upon as such, like the ether" (*Nicāyyatvādevaṃ vyomavacca*). Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that, apart from the attributes of freedom from sin and so forth belonging to the individual soul—which are concealed during the state of transmigratory existence—there exists another set of attributes such as freedom from sin that is eternally manifest.

In the context of the Dahara-vidyā, it is logical that the hearing of qualities such as "freedom from sin" (apahatapāpmatva) refers to the very same freedom from sin and so forth belonging to the individual soul (jīva), which is established and agreed upon in the Prajāpati-vākya. Therefore, the claim that the "small" one (dahara) is not the individual soul because its freedom from sin and other qualities are eternally manifest is incorrect. Rather, on the basis of the mark of subtlety (sūkṣmatva), it is more reasonable to hold that the "small" one is indeed the individual soul—if this is argued, it is replied: liberation is indeed the attainment of equality with Him, consisting in the imitation of the Supreme Self.

This is because of the Śruti passage beginning with, "When the seer sees the golden-colored [Self]," and the Smṛti passage: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, nor are they disturbed at the time of dissolution. Thus, the manifestation of qualities such as freedom from sin in the liberated soul is not possible without the Supreme Self possessing those same qualities—freedom from sin and so forth—manifest eternally. Otherwise, it would be impossible for the soul to attain equality with Him upon liberation.

Therefore, just as the state of liberation manifests for the individual soul (jīva), it is established by the force of Prajāpati’s statement—which does not teach [this] of the jīva—that the Supreme Self possesses eternally manifested qualities such as being free from sin; consequently, it is appropriate that the passage heard in the context of the Dahara-vidyā, beginning with "That Self which is free from sin," has the Supreme Self as its object. Thus, it is proven that the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is indeed the Supreme Self, and not the individual soul.
The summary verses.
The small ether is the elemental ether because it is well-known;
however, qualities such as being free from evil and so forth are connected to that which is contained within it.
Or rather, this [self] is the individual soul (jīva), because it is heard [in scripture] as being of the nature of that [Prājāpati];
for this is the traditional teaching, and the qualities mentioned there are present in the statement concerning Prājāpati.
"It is not so; it is appropriate that this Supreme Self is designated by the qualities mentioned in the word 'Lord' (svāmin).
Therefore, because of the mention of qualities in the word 'yat', that [word] refers to the qualities. This is the meaning of the verse.
Those qualities are not present in the individual soul (jīva) as eternally manifest;
however, they do exist in the Supreme, because liberation consists in attaining supreme identity with Him through the subtle body (liṅga).
Thus ends the section concerning the "Small" (dahara). ||5||
He is known from the word alone. ||23||
But with regard to that [other case], however, it is because human beings are the qualified subjects. ||24||

In the preceding section, the nature of being minute—that is, having a small dimension—was established with respect to the Supreme [Self]. Now, even the form of being the size of a thumb is established as having a small dimension with respect to that same [Self]; this is the connection. In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad it is heard: "The Person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the body; he is the Lord of what has been and what is to be; one should not shrink away from Him," and so forth. When the doubt arises whether this person measured by a thumb is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme [Self], the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is the individual soul.
