"He, the creator of all forms, whose path consists of the three qualities, the lord of the vital breaths, moves about according to his own actions; he is the size of a thumb, endowed with the sun-like form, volition, and egoism"—because of this scriptural statement regarding his being the size of a thumb, it refers to the individual soul (jīva) and not the Supreme Self, for there is no scriptural mention of the latter being such anywhere. Thus, in accordance with the initial description of the size of a thumb, the scriptural mention of his being the lord of the past and the future must be interpreted as referring to the individual soul alone, insofar as he is the controller of the body, senses, and so forth.

But is it not the case that the *Śvetāśvatara* states: "The Person of the size of a thumb, the inner self, is always seated in the hearts of men; he who knows him as fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind, becomes immortal"? And the *Taittirīyaka* states: "The Person of the size of a thumb, resting upon the thumb, is the Lord of the entire world, the Master; he, the All-pervading, is pleased"? Thus, the supreme Self is indeed heard in scripture to be of the size of a thumb. True.

This section should be considered on the grounds that there is no scriptural statement whatsoever regarding the other [the Supreme Self] being the size of a thumb. Alternatively, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that even those two mantras—"thumb-sized and having a form like the sun"—refer to the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self respectively, in accordance with another mantra. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The Supreme Self is measured by the size of a thumb. This is because of the scriptural hearing that He is the Lord of the entire universe consisting of the past and the future; for it is impossible to restrict Him to the domain of being merely the controller of the body, senses, and so forth. [Objection: But since the state of being thumb-sized is heard first, the latter statement [of His lordship] should be interpreted in accordance with it as referring to the domain of being the controller of the body, senses, and so forth. [The text continues: "One should draw Him out from one's own body with firmness, like a stalk from a reed."

One should know that because the mantra, "That one should know as the bright, the immortal," mentions its being situated within the heart, it must be said that the Supreme Self’s state of being the size of a thumb is possible by virtue of having the heart as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). In the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, it is heard that the Supreme Self's minuteness is indeed due to the heart as an adjunct: "This is my Self within the heart, more minute than a grain of rice. Furthermore, in the Dahara-vidyā of the Taittirīya, it says: "In the middle of it stands a flame of fire, more minute than the tip of an awl."

If it is argued that—since the statement, "The Supreme Self is situated within the middle of its flame," indicates that the Supreme Self is extremely subtle by virtue of residing within the center of a minute flame, it follows that its being the size of a thumb cannot possibly be due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the heart—it is indeed possible.

In the Dahara-vidyā and the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Supreme Self is to be meditated upon as residing within the cavity at the top of the heart-lotus; thus, its minuteness is conditioned by that specific limitation. Here, however, the intention is to meditate upon the Self as pervading the entire heart; therefore, its being "the size of a thumb" is conditioned by that [different] limitation. This distinction is logically consistent. Nor should it be argued that this definition of being "thumb-sized" as conditioned by the heart is non-pervasive, because donkeys, horses, serpents, and so forth lack thumbs.

Since the qualification for worship belongs to human beings, and since their hearts are measured by the size of their respective thumbs, it might be argued that it is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*), which is only the size of the tip of an awn (*ārāgra-mātra*), to be "thumb-sized" even when limited by the heart as its adjunct (*upādhi*). To this, the following must be said: being thumb-sized is merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the individual soul. For by the word "thumb-sized," there is an exclusion of any dimension greater than a thumb; however, the actual measurement of a thumb is not being enjoined. This is because it is impossible for a single word to have two distinct intended meanings simultaneously.

For this very reason, in the *adhrigu-praiṣa* for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, there is the mantra—"He has twenty-six ribs"—which reveals the number of the bones located on both sides of the goat, denoted by the word *vaṅkri*; and [likewise] in the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), for the horse, there is the mantra obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*).

When the occasion for an exception arises due to the specific mantra recited in that context—"The thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the divine kinsman, meet with the axe"—then, for the purpose of setting aside that exception, the original (prakṛta) mantra itself must be employed as it stands, containing the word "twenty-six": "Twenty-six are their ribs. It is not the case that an *ūha* (modification)—consisting of a collective statement of the ribs of the horse, the hornless goat (*tūpara*), and the *gomṛga*, as prescribed by the injunction "The horse, the hornless goat, and the *gomṛga* belong to Prajāpati"—should be performed; such being the position reached in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding the sentence, "One should say 'twenty-six' only," the particle *eva* (only) indicates that the intention is to understand that any other mantra obtained—such as the alternative mantra "thirty-four"—is not to be performed. This is because if one were to assume an intention even when the word "twenty-six" is used [to exclude other things], it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Thus, it was established in the ninth chapter of the *Pūrvatantra* that there is no sublation of the *ūha* (modification)—in the form of a collective statement regarding the limbs of the horse, the hornless goat, and the spotted deer—which is obtained through logical necessity.

For this very reason, the commentators have raised an objection here in this section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the statement, "As far as this space [is]," which describes the small space (*daharākāśa*), identified as the Supreme Self, as being equal in dimension to the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). They argue that such a description is improper, because in other passages such as "Greater than heaven," its dimension is heard to be greater than that. Anticipating this, they state that the passage beginning with "As far as this" is intended merely to negate the smallness of dimension resulting from its confinement within the heart, and does not intend to describe it as having a dimension equal to that of the elemental space.

If it is argued that, just as being the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭha-mātra*) consists in the exclusion of any dimension greater than a thumb, so too being the size of the point of an awl (*ārāgra-mātra*) would consist in the exclusion of any dimension greater than the point of an awl—and thus the soul (*jīva*) could not even possess the dimension of the point of an awl—[we reply: in reality, it does not even possess the dimension of the point of an awl. For this very reason, immediately after the statement, "Even one who is inferior is seen to be the size of the point of an awl," [the text continues]: "Of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts..."

By the mantra, "The portion of the living soul (jīva) which is to be known is fit for infinity," another measure—extremely minute and as small as the point of an awl—is established. Therefore, since the exclusion of a measure larger than a thumb is impossible in the case of the Supreme Self, whereas it is possible in the case of the individual soul (jīva), it is determined that the jīva alone is "thumb-sized. Following this conclusion, the quality of being the lord of the past and the future—which is heard last in the text—must be restricted to that very [jīva] when interpreted in accordance with the former; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) to be described.

Regarding the term "thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātra*), one should not assume that the word *mātra* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) to exclude any measurement larger than the thumb; rather, it is more appropriate to assume that the word functions as the suffix *mātra* prescribed in the sense of measure (*pramāṇa*) according to the rule "the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, and *mātraC* [are added] after a word denoting measure," and thus it signifies having a measurement equal to that of a thumb.

Since it is possible to accept a meaning that is both existent and easily established, it is improper to postulate a cumbersome meaning involving two absences. Furthermore, the state of being the size of a thumb is possible only for the Supreme Self; for while a larger dimension can appear small in things like space due to the limiting condition (upādhi) of a smaller dimension, such a thumb-sized measure cannot belong to the individual soul (jīva), whose dimension is traditionally held to be one ten-thousandth part of the tip of a hair, even when conditioned by the heart.

For nowhere is it observed that a thing of small dimension is designated as having a larger dimension simply because it exists within a substance of larger dimension. As for the hearing of the phrase "the size of a thumb" in passages concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), this must be explained as referring to the exclusion of any dimension exceeding that of a thumb, since even a single word can have different appropriate meanings in various contexts.

Alternatively—the size of a thumb and the size of the tip of an arrow, which reside in *dharma* and *jñāna* respectively within those [channels] by virtue of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being delimited by the hundredth heart-channel—have a mediated connection (*sadvārakānvaya*) with that [Supreme Self]. However, in this statement concerning the thumb, a mediated connection should not be assumed; rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) should be described as follows: because a direct connection with that [Supreme Self] is possible in the case of the Supreme Self.

If this is so, since the conclusion that it is the Supreme Self could be reached by the very first heard mark of being the size of a thumb alone, why did the author of the Sūtras rely on the scriptural word *īśāna* for the sake of that determination? It is because he intended a swift determination based on the fact that the word is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of the Lord of All. For this very reason, the word "only" (*eva*) is used in the Sūtra: "From the word alone" (*śabdādeva*).

Let alone the determination [of the identity] through the indicative mark (liṅga) which is understood from an investigation into its etymological meaning; rather, the intention is that such a determination is possible from the word "Īśāna" itself, by virtue of its conventional usage as a designation. Therefore, it is established that the one measured by the thumb is the Supreme Self.
The Summary Verses.
The embodied person is the size of a thumb, as it is well-known from another Vedic scripture;
however, his lordship is mentioned later in the text and is dependent upon the existence of the objects of enjoyment and the experience thereof.
Brought by the natural force of the word *Īśāna*, this Supreme Person is the leader of all;
let the state of being "thumb-sized" apply to the atom as well as the omnipresent one, provided it is understood in relation to the heart, for otherwise its natural sense would be lost.
Out of fear of this [destruction], the activity of the world toward its own functions has been described;
and the light that favors all is seen to be eternal for this [world].
By these two indicative marks— namely, "whatever this is" in the *manas* [passage] and "the sun does not shine there" in the mantra—
it is established that the Supreme Self is indeed the size of a thumb.

The topical section (adhikaraṇa) established by the [sūtra] "But on account of the expectation of the heart" (Hṛdyapekṣayātvi) will be concluded later by the two sūtras "On account of trembling" (Kampanāt) and "On account of the vision of light" (Jyotirdarśanāt). In the interim, three incidental topical sections have proceeded as incidental to the main topic, like the section concerning the drinking of soma by Indra and others in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā system. However, for the sake of ease of understanding, the meaning of the subsequent two sūtras has also been summarized here within the summary verses (saṃgrahaśloka).
Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that] it is possible even beyond that, because of the possibility. ||25||
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [results]. ||26||
If it be argued that [the world] is sound, we say no; because [the world] originates from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference. (27)
And for this very reason, there is eternality. ||28||
And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of re-entry [into the world], on account of both scriptural vision and Smṛti.

In connection with the discussion regarding the eligibility of human beings, it is now examined whether gods and others possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) or not. On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: they have no eligibility because those who are devoid of bodies lack the capacity to practice the knowledge of Brahman. Nor is there any means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) to prove that they possess bodies. Furthermore, mantra-passages and explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "the thunderbolt-handed Purandara" and "Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vṛtra" do not constitute proof in this regard.

This is because those [passages] intended for the praise of what is to be remembered regarding the meaning of what is to be performed lack any *tātparya* (intentional focus) directed toward that [existence of the object]. Nor can its establishment [be claimed] by way of being a door to such remembrance; for since praise is observed to occur both with respect to what exists and what does not exist, praise does not depend upon the actual existence of the object serving as a door. Furthermore, its establishment cannot be based merely on its being perceived for the sake of praise, because in the absence of *tātparya*, such establishment fails, given that the authority of verbal testimony is dependent upon *tātparya*. Moreover, there is no *tātparya* even in that case, due to the absence of any grounds for inferring it.

For that postulation [of a body for the deities] is intended solely to establish the validity [of the scriptures]. Indeed, the fulfillment of the purpose of the words of the *karmakāṇḍa* is already secured through the engagement in action and desisting from it based on injunctions and prohibitions; likewise, the fulfillment of the purpose of the words of the *brahmakāṇḍa* is secured by the presentation of Brahman, which is in itself the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Nor should it be argued that only the injunctive sentences concerning sacrifices—which consist of the relinquishment of a substance dedicated to a deity—require a deity, because even for one devoid of a body, dedication (*uddeśa*) is possible; therefore, the necessity of a body for them is not established.

Nor can it be argued that, because actions which perish in a moment require a medium to ensure the production of a fruit occurring at a later time, the fivefold attributes such as having a physical form must be accepted for those [deities]—on the grounds that the grace of the deity, understood from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Being himself satisfied, he thus satisfies Indra with offspring and cattle"—is to be taken as that medium; for since the *apūrva* exists as a medium, there is no need for another medium. Nor...

It should not be said that because the grace of the deity is established through the cognition of the *arthavāda*, no *apūrva* (unseen potency) need be postulated; for in acts such as giving (*dāna*) which lack a deity, the postulation of an *apūrva* is inevitable, and even in sacrifices and oblations (*yāga-homa*), whether they involve a deity acknowledged as insentient or some that involve a sentient deity, the postulation of it is likewise inevitable.

For instance, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, when oblations are being performed with mantras such as "Svāhā to the black one, Svāhā to the white one, Svāhā to that which you urinate, Svāhā to that which you excrete dung, Svāhā to the teeth, Svāhā to the jaws," directed toward the qualities, actions, and limbs of the sacrificial horse, there is no conscious deity present. Nor, in the Śrāddha rites performed for ancestors who have entered animal births, are those ancestors existing as animals capable of bestowing the fruits [of the rite].

Furthermore, even Indra and the other deities, once their offices have ceased at the end of a kalpa, are no longer capable of bestowing the fruits of sacrifices and other rites performed during that kalpa—fruits intended to be enjoyed in a future kalpa. By this, the following objection is also refuted: namely, that because the Smṛti states "yaj (to sacrifice) means worship of a deity," a sacrifice is essentially the propitiation of a deity; and since such propitiations, like those directed toward a king, must necessarily result in the granting of the fruit by the deity who is the object of the propitiation once pleased, the corporeal form of the deity is established by the force of the injunction for sacrifice.

The king’s children, his sandals, and so forth are honored by the king’s servants with appropriate rites of service; in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Soma creeper is honored by the offering of milk and rice; and fathers, mothers, teachers, husbands, guests, those advanced in learning, and others are honored through service and the like. Yet none of these possess the capacity to bestow fruits [of action].

If it were argued that the service rendered to princes and others is in fact worship of kings and such, and that they possess the power to bestow the fruits [of that worship], then [we reply]: worship of the deities is in fact worship of the Lord of All (Sarveśvara) alone, who is the originator of the conduct pertaining to the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama); since He alone possesses the power to bestow the fruits, the sacrifice is established as worship of a deity precisely on that basis, and not from that [fact] the corporeal form (vigraha) of deities such as Indra is established.

By this, even the suspicion that Indra and others possess physical bodies—based on the narratives found in the Brahma-kāṇḍa such as "Indra indeed went forth against the gods, and Virocana against the Asuras"—is refuted. This is because, according to the principle established in the *Pāriplava-adhikaraṇa*, even the narratives occurring in the Karma-kāṇḍa serve as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) to the injunctions for specific meditations (*vidyā-vidhi*); thus, like the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the Karma-kāṇḍa, those in the Brahma-kāṇḍa do not establish the reality of their subject matter, but function merely as praise. Therefore, since deities and others lack the capacity due to being devoid of physical bodies, they have no qualification (*adhikāra*) for the knowledge of Brahman. Such being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) follows: [The Siddhāntin replies: It is not so. Just as in the case of the *arthavādas* in the Karma-kāṇḍa, the narratives in the Brahma-kāṇḍa are intended to praise the meditations; however, they do not thereby prove the non-existence of the entities described. For the purpose of praising the meditation is accomplished even if the object of praise is unreal, whereas the purpose of the *arthavāda* in the Karma-kāṇḍa is not accomplished unless the object is real. Furthermore, the existence of Indra and others is established by Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, which are based on the Vedas. Moreover, the fact that Indra and others possess bodies is proven by the very fact that they are addressed and respond in the Upaniṣads. Nor can it be argued that these texts are mere figurative descriptions (*upacāra*), for there is no reason to assume figurative usage when the primary sense is possible. Furthermore, the Smṛtis and Itihāsas are not independent means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apart from the Vedas. Thus, since Indra and others do possess bodies, they are capable of performing actions and attaining results; therefore, they are qualified for the knowledge of Brahman. This is the established conclusion.

The worship of Brahman is indeed possible even for those who are above humans, such as the gods and others. Nor can it be argued that they lack the capacity due to the absence of a physical body, because in all the Upaniṣads, within the sections on creation, the birth of the gods and others is established through statements such as: "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born; from Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born; Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, and Rudra [are born]. Furthermore, in all the Śrutis, the status of Indra and the other deities is established as the fruit of specific ritual actions.

For instance, in the *Sāmavidhānabrāhmaṇa* of the Sāma-singers, it is heard: "One who employs [the chant] for four years according to the ritual procedure beginning with 'In me, splendor' (*mayi varca*) attains sovereignty over the three worlds. Sovereignty over the three worlds is indeed the state of Indra. Likewise, in the *Upaniṣad* of the Chandogas: "Becoming one of the Vasus themselves, by means of Agni alone..."

Through such statements as, "Having seen this very nectar with his mouth, he is satisfied," the attainment of the status of the classes of deities known as Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas is presented as the fruit of the Madhu-vidyā. Likewise, their possession of embodied forms (vigraha) is established by the scriptural hearing that the subjugation of deities is the fruit of specific ritual acts (*karma*). For instance, it is heard in the *Sāmavidhāna-brāhmaṇa*: "He who desires, 'May I cause [them] to turn back,' should stand for one night with a razor [in hand]; [then recite] the section beginning with 'The most honey-sweet of these [waters]'."

Employing one, several, or all of these, he brings under his control a householder in one night, a royal dependant in two nights, a king in three nights, a village in four nights, a city in five nights, a district in six nights, the Asuras and Rakṣasas in seven nights, the Pitṛs and Piśācas in eight nights, the Yakṣas in nine nights, the Gandharvas and Apsarases in ten nights, Vaiśravaṇa in half a month, Indra in a month, and Prajāpati in four months.

"In a year, whatever exists in this entire world becomes subordinate. Thus, once the general possession of bodies by the deities is established, the specific nature of their bodies—such as having a thousand eyes and seven hands—is established through mantras such as: "May the thousand-eyed Indra, the breaker of the mountain, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the god who is our kinsman, bestow wealth upon us; he has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands. Nor should it be suspected that these [mantras] do not depend on the presentation of such specific bodies.

One should meditate in the mind upon whichever deity one is about to consecrate with the *vaṣaṭ* call, because [the literal sense] is impossible; likewise, even by means of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), the existence of a physical body characterized by such features as "having a thunderbolt in hand" is established. For this very reason, in the *Śābarabhāṣya*, it is shown that even in the case of statements such as the digging up of Prajāpati, the reality of the meaning—even though it serves merely as a means—is maintained by adopting a figurative sense. Furthermore, in the case of statements such as "Indra [fought] against Vṛtra," the words "Indra," "Vṛtra," and so forth must first be admitted to possess meaning, in order for case-endings to be produced from them.

In the absence of that [word], there would be no production of case-endings due to the lack of nominal stem status (*prātipadikatva*). Therefore, the required meaning—which is supplied by the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)—culminates precisely in the form of "having a thunderbolt in hand" (*vajrahastatva*) and so forth. Since the specific required meaning is already provided, it is impossible to abandon it and adopt another meaning for the sake of fulfilling that requirement.

Now, one might object: do not such mantras as "O Indra, there is none higher than you; O slayer of Vṛtra, there is none greater; there is no one else like you," "May the Soma drops enter into you as rivers flow into the ocean," "Nothing surpasses you, O Indra," and "All songs have magnified Indra, who is as vast as the ocean," reveal only Indra? Yet they also praise him with attributes that are unreal, such as being supreme over all, being the vessel for all Soma-libations, and being the object of all Vedic hymns.

If it is argued that, for this reason, the existence of an object is not determined by way of praise, [we reply: where there is a contradiction, we observe—as in the case of "the pressing-stone hears," and so forth—that the statement may even rely upon a non-existent object. However, where there is no contradiction, the existence of the object must be accepted on account of the general rule of intrinsic validity (*autsargika-svataḥ-prāmāṇya*); how much more so when that [intrinsic validity] is taken into consideration!

Therefore, since the possession of bodies by the gods and others is established through injunctions (*vidhi*), mantras, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and because they possess the requisite capacity, they have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman which has liberation as its fruit. Now, if one accepts that the gods possess bodies on the basis of mantras, explanatory passages, and so forth—such as: "O Agni, bring Agni hither; O Indra, come, O possessor of bay horses (*harivat*), come; O Adhvaryu, let the Soma flow, for Indra thirsts; he has yoked the two vigorous bay horses; the slayer of Vṛtra has arrived"—then [one must ask]: "Whose sacrifice do the gods come to? Whose [sacrifice]?"

Since we observe numerous mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "or [the sacrifice] of many sacrificers," it must be accepted that the gods do indeed come to the place of sacrifice. How, one might ask, can a single Indra arrive simultaneously at many places of sacrifice? We reply: because, like yogins who have mastery over the elements, it is possible for them to assume many bodies simultaneously.

In such scriptural passages as, "Agni had three elder brothers; while carrying the oblation to the gods, they perished, having made the offerings fragrant," the mention of Agni as the "carrier of oblations" (*havyavāhana*) refers to those *darvihoma* and other sacrifices in which the invocation of the deity or the arrival of the deity is not heard.

Alternatively, there is no contradiction between the scriptural statements regarding the arrival at the place of sacrifice and the carrying of the oblation—namely, that the gods who have come to the sacrificial site take the *havis*, and that "whatever small offering the gods enjoy, even a single oblation, increases to the size of a mountain. Let there be no contradiction regarding ritual action (*karman*) due to Indra and the others possessing bodies; however, there would be a contradiction regarding the word (*śabda*), because since bodies are necessarily non-eternal, the words "Indra" and so forth, which denote those [bodies], would inevitably be devoid of referents both before and after the production of those bodies.

If it is argued that, like conventional words such as *Ḍittha* and so forth, these words possess meaningfulness through some occasional referent, even then, it cannot be avoided that words such as "Indra, come! are devoid of meaning during the times preceding and following Indra; this is not so, because since Indra and others originate from the word "Indra," words like "Indra"—just like words such as "jar"—denote a genus (*jāti*) produced by a continuous succession of individual manifestations (*vyakti*).

For just as an artisan, having recalled the form of Indra or others as understood from the treatises on the arts, fashions a statue with that very form, so too Prajāpati, having recalled the forms of the successive Indras and others as understood from the Vedas, creates Indras and others distinguished by those respective forms. Indeed, this is heard in such scriptural passages as: "By means of the Veda, Prajāpati differentiated the two forms; he uttered 'Sat' (Being) and 'Asat' (Non-being), and created the earth; he uttered 'Bhūḥ', and created the atmosphere; he uttered 'Bhuvaḥ', and created the sky," and so forth.

And it is likewise recorded in the Smṛti: "In the beginning, he fashioned the names and forms of beings, as well as the expansion of their activities and so forth, for the gods and others, solely from the words of the Veda. Now, one might object: let there be no contradiction regarding the meaning in the case of Vedic words; however, there may be a contradiction regarding the words themselves. For it has been established that the authority of mantras, arthavādas, and the like resides in the very meanings they manifest.

And if it is argued that the Veda must necessarily be of human origin on the basis of such authoritative statements as, "He chooses the composers of mantras," and "There is a hymn (*sūkta*) of Viśvāmitra, [as well as those] of the authors of the *Saṃhitā*, the author of the *Pada-pāṭha*, the author of the *Sūtra*, and the author of the *Brāhmaṇa*," this objection is not valid.

From Vedic words such as "There is a hymn of Viśvāmitra," Prajāpati—having considered the specific names and forms, as well as the particular functions (such as the vision of specific hymns) of Viśvāmitra and others, and by virtue of the merit performed in previous cycles (*kalpas*)—is capable of making Viśvāmitra and others able to see the hymns and so forth even without having studied them.

Having created them, He establishes them in positions such as that of Viśvāmitra and others; moreover, the capacity to see those respective hymns (*sūkta*s) and so forth constitutes their status as "makers of mantras" (*mantrakṛt*). Therefore, there is no consequence of the Vedas being non-eternal. Now, it might be argued: since the four-faced Brahmā lives for two *parārdha*s by his own measure, at the end of an intermediate kalpa—which consists of a single day made up of a thousand cycles of the four ages—there occurs a periodic dissolution (*naimittikapralaya*) consisting of a night of equal duration, wherein only the three worlds (*trailokya*), namely Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, are destroyed. Since the Vedas persist through this, let it be granted that the subsequent creation is preceded by the word "Veda."

If it is asked: "At the conclusion of his hundred-year period, there occurs a dissolution of the primary nature (*prākṛta-pralaya*) of that same magnitude; since at that time there is the total destruction of everything, including the manifest (*vyākṛta*), the Vedas must necessarily perish. How then can creation at the beginning of the subsequent great cycle (*mahākalpa*) be preceded by the word of the Vedas? Furthermore, how can the Vedas be eternal if they perish during the dissolution of the primary nature? It is replied: The destruction of the Vedas at that time is not a defect, because the scriptures state their creation at the beginning of the great cycle, as in the Vedic text: "From Him the meters (*chandāṃsi*) were born. Thus, even the Vedas are created at the start of each great cycle.

However, there is no contradiction in [the world's] being eternal in the sense of having an identical sequential order; for even upon the recurrence of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), the created things possess names and forms identical [to those of the previous cycle]. Nor is that [identity] unestablished.

Regarding the mantra, "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him," the fact that the bestowal of the Vedas to him is heard [to occur] after the creation of Brahmā at the beginning of a *mahākalpa* is for the purpose of [showing that] Brahmā—according to the analogy of the artisan (*śilpin*)—should create Indras and others with names and forms identical to those of the previous *kalpa*, having understood them from the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). [As it is said: "From the navel of that sleeping God, a lotus was born."

Furthermore, from such traditional texts (smṛti) as: "In that lotus, O one of great being, was born Brahmā, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; by Him [Brahmā] was told: 'O you of great intellect, create the subjects. Therefore, it is established that gods and others who possess embodied forms have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, owing to their possession of desire and capability.
The summary verses.
Deities and others have no entitlement to the Vidyā;
for them, being devoid of physical form, there is not even the slightest capacity.
Nor is it appropriate to seek the establishment of that [self] from the mantras and arthavādas,
because of their different purport and because of the unavoidable contradiction between the words *ka* and *garmam*.
It is not so; for the mantras and arthavādas possess authority even with respect to their secondary meaning (dvārārtha).
There is no contradiction regarding the ritual action, since multiple grammatical analyses (vigraha) are possible.
It is not in sound, because it is a generic term for sound, and because name and form are of the nature of existence.
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). ||7||
Jaimini [holds that] there is no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those such as the Madhukas, because [the means of knowledge] are impossible for them. (Sūtra 30)
And because of the state [of the soul] being in the light. ||31||
But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] that there is indeed an existence [of the soul after death]. ||32||

In the preceding section, it was stated in a general sense that the gods possess the qualification for the worship of others as desired by them. Now, the connection [of this section] is as follows: it is considered whether or not specific deities have the qualification for specific forms of worship. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, there is the Madhu-vidyā (the Science of Honey). In that [science], the Vasus and other deities are heard of as both the objects of worship and the goals to be attained.

For it has been described there that the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), consisting of the five forms beginning with red and dependent upon the sun, are to be meditated upon as objects of enjoyment for the groups of Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas; and the fruit of those meditations is the attainment of the status of the Vasus and others, according to the passage beginning: "The Vasus satisfy themselves with that first nectar; he who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus, satisfies himself by seeing this very nectar through Agni as his mouth," and so forth. In that [meditation], the Vasus and others have no qualification (*adhikāra*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is impossible for one to be an object of worship for oneself, and because the attainment of one's own state is itself the fruit [of the practice]. If it is argued: "This prima facie view is not tenable; for in this *kalpa*, those who are Vasus and so forth will possess the status of Vasus and so on even in another *kalpa*. Just as there is a desire such as 'May I remain a Brāhmaṇa in a future birth, having been a Brāhmaṇa in this life,' such a desire is logically possible. Furthermore, within the Prāṇa-vidyā situated in the midst of the Bhūma-vidyā, there is an agreement that one may indeed be an object of worship for oneself. To this, the proponent of the prima facie view replies: It is thus that the opponent thinks.

The fruit of the Madhu-vidyā is not the attainment of the state of being a Vasu or other such deities; rather, it is the equality of enjoyment with them, preceded by the attainment of their respective abodes. This is just as when one says, "You are one among our brothers," implying equality of enjoyment with those brothers. Otherwise, if those devoted to the Madhu-vidyā were to attain the state of being Vasus and so forth immediately after death, there would be the undesirable consequence of exceeding the number established by scriptural texts such as "the eight Vasus."

And it is observed that in the case of the injunction, "One who is competing should sacrifice a dwarf animal dedicated to Viṣṇu," its supplementary explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds," has as its sole purport the mere fact of being a conqueror like Viṣṇu. Therefore, the statement that the Vasus and others have not attained the fruit [of their office] is indeed appropriate; likewise, the statement regarding the impossibility of their own worship is also appropriate.

Because through the worship of those [deities], one attains equality in their enjoyment, and since being a means for their pleasure is the general rule, there is a contradiction regarding the relationship of agent and object—namely, the state of being the one who pleases and the one who is pleased—among the Vasus and others. For it is not possible that one, by pleasing oneself, should obtain a fruit from oneself once one is pleased. In the case of the Prāṇa-vidyā, however, the attainment of the fruit occurs solely through the grace of the Lord; for there is no scriptural statement there that the fruit of one's own worship is the attainment of an enjoyment equal to one's own.

Furthermore, the scriptural passage, "The gods meditate upon that as the light of lights, as life, as immortality," does not intend to establish the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of the gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). This is because their eligibility is established by itself, given that they possess the requisite desire for liberation (*arthitva*) and other necessary conditions, just like human beings. However, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this [passage] establishes their eligibility specifically for the Madhu-vidyā. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

The Vasus and others also certainly possess the qualification for this [meditation], because it is possible for them as well to meditate upon Brahman through its own nature as their inner ruler (antaryāmin); because in the concluding passage, "He who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus," it is heard that this is a knowledge of Brahman; and because it is possible for them to desire to attain Brahman after first attaining the state of being the Vasus and so forth. By this, every objection raised by the opponent—rooted in the fallacy of identifying the one who pleases with the one who is pleased—is refuted.

Because the Lord of All alone—who is to be meditated upon as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) by the Vasus and others—is the one to be propitiated; therefore, since it is possible for the Vasus and others also to have the desire for the fruit of the meditation on Him whom they themselves must propitiate, they possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the Madhu-vidyā. In the same way, the qualification of Vāyu and others for the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other such meditations is also to be understood. Now, an objection is raised: it is not possible for Indra and others, who reside above Agni and the rest, to be remembered as traveling along the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

And that [recollection] is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of knowledge; the author of the Sūtras himself will clarify this in the sūtra "The upward flaming of the abode at that time" (*tadokograjvalanam*) by means of the portion of the sūtra: "Because of the connection with the recollection of the path which is its remainder" (*taccheṣagatyanusmṛtiyogāt*). [Objection: If it is asked how the gods—who are incapable of performing the performance of the limbs—can have eligibility for knowledge (*vidyādhikāra*), [the answer is: if the recollection of the path were for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then the deities of the path beginning with Light (*arcis*) would likewise remember that the path beginning with Light is the path for humans who are being liberated.

If, however, one should perform daily recollection (smaraṇa) thus: "The supreme state is to be attained by me through this path and through knowledge," then, in that worship where there is a rule for the officiating priests (ṛtvij) to consume the remnants of the oblation (haviḥ-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa) for the sake of generating enthusiasm for their own continuous series of rites to be performed, Agni and the other deities will—setting aside those parts not required by themselves—remember from their own positions the portion of the movement (gatyaṃśa) that is required and situated above them.

Just as the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha consume only the required portion from among the vast quantities of sacrificial remnants produced by many animals, so there is no difficulty whatsoever. [Objection: But of what use is this inquiry into the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman? It is of no use for the activity of people like us, nor for the gods themselves; for they possess their own embodied forms and the powers resulting therefrom, and thus they already have direct realization of these matters on their own.

It is said in reply: If deities do not exist, then the attainment of the status of the Vasus and others could not be the fruit of the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations. For, just as in the case of liberation from Varuṇa’s grasp, that which is heard in scripture as a fruit—even if it is sublated—cannot logically be the fruit of the enjoined action; therefore, some other fruit would have to be postulated for it. Furthermore, in the Antarāditya-vidyā and others, the meditation on Brahman as the inner controller of the solar deity would not be established. And in the recollection of the path, the insentient stages such as light (arciḥ) and so forth would themselves have to be meditated upon as the mountains of the path.

According to the logic stated in such sūtras as "Or [the enjoyment of results] is figurative, because they do not know the Self," detachment (*vairāgya*) cannot be established for those who, while enjoying the fruits of sacrifices and other rites, constantly perceive themselves as performers of the duties of *ājāna*-born gods. Such failure to achieve their desired goal for human beings is the very proof of the existence of deities.

Since explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) do not lose their authority regarding the meaning they convey when there is neither contradiction with what is established nor impossibility, the logical arguments supporting the proof of the embodied form of the deities are likewise valid. [However, this does not override the following: "Frail indeed are these boats in the form of sacrifice—those eighteen in which the inferior ritual is taught. Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good, fall again and again into old age and death."

"Be born and die"—this is the third station; by that means, this world is not filled. Therefore, one should feel aversion [to it]. By ascertaining the authority of such mantra-explanations (arthavāda), the result is the attainment of discrimination, dispassion, and so forth; this is to be inferred from the beginning.
The summary verses.
Nevertheless, the Vasus and others have no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā,
because of contradiction and because that fruit has already been attained by them.
Let it not be so; for that [knowledge] has been described in the remainder of the passage as the knowledge of Brahman, with the attainment of that as its fruit.
Therefore, the word "Vasu" and the others possess a power extending up to the fully expanded Supreme Brahman.
In the injunctions for meditating on Brahman according to its own states, there is no room for the suspicion of identity between the object of action and the agent.
Even the future attainment of wealth and so forth is possible as a fruit that serves as a gateway prior to liberation.
Thus ends the section concerning honey (Madhu-adhikaraṇa). ||8||
For it is indicated by the hearing of that contempt for Śuka and by his rushing toward him. ||33||
And because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya. ||34||
And because of the indicative mark [found] later in the case of Caitraratha. ||35||
Because of the misapprehension of formative forces and because of the denial of their existence. ||36||
And because it occurs in the sense of specifying eight [of them]. ||37||
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda]. (38)
And [the same applies] to those mentioned in the Smṛtis. ||39||

It has been stated that because the Vasus and others possess both the desire for liberation and the requisite capacity, they have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the meditation on Brahman. Now, there arises a connection [to the next topic] based on the following doubt: "In that case, since Śūdras also possess those two qualities, they too should have the qualification. Thus, regarding the doubt as to whether Śūdras have the qualification or not—based on the presence or absence of their capacity to undertake such meditations—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: They do indeed have the qualification. For it was established in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* of the previous Mīmāṃsā system that while Śūdras lack qualification for ritual acts due to the absence of the injunction for maintaining the sacred fires (*agnividhi*), this does not apply to meditations (*upāsana*).

Since they consist merely of mental modifications, there is a dependence on that [mental state]; therefore, they indeed possess eligibility just like women. Nor is it the case that for them there is an impossibility of performing actions that assist the injunctions.

Because the duties pertaining to their own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) are possible for them, and because there is no impossibility of their possessing knowledge of the nature of Brahman and the means of attaining It—since the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* exist [to attest this]—it is for this very reason that Vidura and others were established in Brahman. Furthermore, there is evidence in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* regarding their eligibility for the performance of ritual injunctions (*vidhi-adhikāra*). For in that context, within the section on the "Doctrine of the Absorber" (*saṃvarga-vidyā*), we observe the addressing of those eligible for the injunction as "O Śūdra": "Bring these, O Śūdra; by this very mouth you will make me speak"—thus is it narrated therein.

A king named Jānaśruti, a protector of his kingdom who gave abundantly out of faith, caused dwellings to be constructed in all directions—in villages, cities, market towns, hermitages, holy fords, and other places—fully supplied with food, water, bedding, clothing, and all varieties of enjoyments for travelers. When that most eminent of the righteous had exhausted his sins through his deeds, certain great sages, desiring to arouse in him the desire to know Brahman, assumed the form of swans and, forming a row, flew over his palace at night while he was lying in bed.

A certain swan, addressing the leader of those [swans] with the words "O Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa!"—using the term *bhallākṣa* ironically (*viparītalakṣaṇayā*) to mean "O dull-eyed one"—called out twice in agitation. To him who said, "The light produced by the power of Jānaśruti’s gift of food and other virtues pervades as far as the heavenly world; do not burn yourself there," the swan who was moving ahead replied.

"What kind of greatness does this wretched Jānaśruti possess, accompanied as he is by a cart, that you compare him to Raikva? Having heard this, the swan following behind him asked again, "Who is this Raikva? and he replied: "Raikva is one in whom all the collection of good deeds and knowledge belonging to everyone else is contained within his own superior good deeds and knowledge."

Having heard these words of Haṃsa—which contained both self-reproach and praise of Raikva—Jānaśruti somehow passed the night; then, rising from his bed, he summoned the charioteer, instructed him to find Raikva by the sign of the cart, and sent him forth in search. Upon returning after seeing Raikva scratching an itch beneath a cart in a certain place, the charioteer informed him; thereupon Jānaśruti approached Raikva in person, bringing six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot yoked with mules.

Having brought a chariot, he requested, "Please instruct me in the deity you worship. Then Raikva said to him: "Ah! Let this necklace along with the chariot remain yours alone, O Śūdra, together with the cows. *Aha* is an indeclinable particle. Its meaning is: "Let the chariot, accompanied by the necklace (*hāra*), remain yours alone together with the cows."

Janasruti, realizing that Raikva was not satisfied with this much alone, brought back the previously mentioned thousand cows, the necklace and other gifts, and his own daughter for the sake of marriage; then, requesting him for the purpose of receiving instruction in knowledge, he addressed Raikva with these words: "O Śūdra, you have brought these [gifts]," and so forth. The meaning is: "You have brought these sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās); by this very means—by this method of acquiring knowledge—you shall converse with me; you shall make me your instructor of knowledge."

Although there is an address of "O Śūdra" even in the preceding sentence, "Ahaha! Bring this, O Śūdra," nevertheless, it can be explained away as being otherwise established—that the Kṣatriya himself was addressed as "Śūdra" out of anger because he brought only a small sacrificial fee, like a Śūdra, without recognizing the dignity of the knowledge of Brahman. However, with the intention that this is not the case in the second sentence, this statement of satisfaction is cited in the Bhāṣya. Thus, when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been reached that even a Śūdra has the qualification for knowledge, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

For Śūdras, there exists no means for the thorough knowledge of the nature of Brahman and the methods of its worship. Nor is the Purāṇas and similar texts such a means, for they are employed for the purpose of determining the intent of the Vedas, according to the injunction: "One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Furthermore, the argument that the hearing of Purāṇas and other texts by Śūdras is futile—based on the permission: "One should cause the four castes to hear them, having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront"—is not tenable, as it is logically established that this is for the purpose of destroying sins.

In the case of Vidura, the Dharmavyādha, and others, however, their steadfastness in Brahman was not due to the Purāṇas and such texts, but rather through the persistence of impressions from previous births. Furthermore, the address "O Śūdra" is not an indicative mark (liṅga) for the eligibility of Śūdras to acquire knowledge.

In this context, because the word *śūdra* does not denote the *jāti* (birth-class) by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it is derived through etymological application (*yoga*) as follows: from the root *śuc* meaning "to grieve" (*śuca śoka*), according to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* "śucerdaśca"; with the suffix *ap* following the rule "sphāyitañcivañciśakikṣipikṣudisṛpī-"; with the lengthening of the vowel following the subsequent rule "amitamyordīrghaśca"; and with the substitution of the letter *d* for the letter *c* of the root. Thus, the word is established as signifying "one who grieves."

Nor should it be suspected here that the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger; for the word *śūdra* applied to Jānaśruti is etymological (*yaugika*), since his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from the context. This is because the conventional sense is superseded by the etymological sense, which is present in the mind due to the grief indicated by the fact that he immediately approached Raikva upon hearing the words of the swans, and by the subsequent action. Furthermore, because Jānaśruti is known to be a Kṣatriya, the word *śūdra* used in reference to him must be taken in its derivative sense. Indeed, at the beginning of this narrative: "Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, being full of faith, generous, a great giver, and possessing many chariots, had hundreds of thousands of dwellings constructed."

It is stated that Jānaśruti was a patron of all and a giver of cooked food to everyone, as indicated by the phrase, "He thought, 'Let me not appear inferior to anyone. In the middle of the passage, the dispatching of the charioteer is mentioned: "As he was rising, he said to the charioteer, 'This is my wife, this is the village in which I dwell. Furthermore, the giving of his daughter to Raikva and the gift of the very village where Raikva resided at that time are described. And at the end, it is said: "These are the Raikvaparṇas among the Mahāvṛṣas, where we dwelt."

Thus, it is stated that he granted many villages located in the country known as Mahāvṛṣa. From these signs, Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya is understood. Although even Śūdras who follow improper conduct may protect a kingdom and perform tasks such as guarding the royal harem—since it is said, "From a Vaiśya, on a Brāhmaṇa maiden, a son called a Kṣattṛ is born; his livelihood is the protection of kings’ inner apartments"—nevertheless, because those duties are not enjoined by the Veda, it cannot be claimed that [Jānaśruti] was of such a [Śūdra] class.

In the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), that which is righteous (*dharmya*)—as understood through Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*)—must alone be accepted. Otherwise, since it could be argued that the Śūdra’s acquisition of knowledge, as understood from the address "O Śūdra," is unrighteous and thus prohibited by the Veda, the Vedic indicative marks cited for the Śūdra's eligibility for knowledge would fail to be established; consequently, there would be no need to even present arguments against such eligibility. Therefore, it is entirely reasonable that Jānaśruti is understood to be a Kṣatriya.

Furthermore, in this very Saṃvarga-vidyā, later on, because Caitraratha is a Kṣatriya, it is understood that Raikva also was a Kṣatriya. For later on, in the passage beginning, "Then a religious student begged from Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni while they were being served," since Śaunaka is a Brāhmaṇa, his companion Abhipratārin is a Kṣatriya; by analogy with that group, Jānaśruti, who is the companion of the Brāhmaṇa Raikva, must also be a Kṣatriya.

Thus it is understood. It might be argued: the determination of Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya here depends on the presence of his inclusion in a group of similar castes (prāyapāṭha); that [inclusion] depends on the determination of Abhipratārin’s status as a Kṣatriya; that [determination] in turn depends on the determination of his being a Caitraratha; and that depends on the determination of his being a descendant of Kāpeya and a conqueror—so how is that determined? For that is not heard of either here or elsewhere in the scripture.

Nor should it be argued that because of the mention of Kāpeya in the same recension (*sahapāṭha*), a relationship with him—specifically the status of being his sacrificial priest—is established somewhere. For such "mention in the same recension" merely means they sat together for the purpose of eating. A family relationship is not established by that alone, due to the inconsistency seen between guests and householders, and also due to the inconsistency found in designations such as the Prācīnaśālas. If their connection were simply the fact of belonging to the same Vedic school (*ekavidyatva*), then that very same thing would constitute the relationship here as well.

Because both [the Chāndogya and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka] are students of the *asaṃvarga-vidyā* (the science of the non-encompassing). Now, in the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa, after stating the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the fruit for the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*) prescribed as follows—"Now, for him whose first day is the Jyotir-ukthya and whose second day is the Āyus"—namely, "He makes this very performer of the two-night sacrifice the sole lord over food among his circle of kinsmen and others," another explanatory passage is recorded to support that: [The text continues: "Just as one who has entered a village sees a man standing alone on the road, and thinks, 'This man is surely a thief, or a highwayman, or a spy,' and seizes him; and when he asks, 'What have you done? he replies, 'I did nothing at all'; and they beat him with sticks or throw him into a pit; even so, O Gārgya, does this person become the lord of food, yet he is not the lord of food. In this context, the doubt arises whether the term "lord of food" (*annāda*) refers to the mere eating of food or to the mastery over food. If it were the former, the objection would be: "How can there be a distinction between the two texts, since both teach the same meditation? To resolve this, the author states: "Because both are students of the *asaṃvarga-vidyā*. If it is argued that the *Śruti* states that the Kāpeyas officiated for Citraratha—"The Kāpeyas indeed caused Citraratha to perform sacrifice; they made him the sole overseer (*adhyakṣa*) of food; therefore, among the Caitrarathas, one is born as a lord of the *kṣatra* (a king)"—and thus the fact that the descendants of Citraratha were to be officiated for by the Kāpeyas is heard in scripture, what of it? For Abhipratārin was certainly not Citraratha, since their difference is understood from the difference in their names. Nor was he a descendant of Citraratha, because there is no such scriptural statement.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the reading of the Śruti text, "These Kāpeyas officiated for Citraratha," is cited. Even there, the doubt regarding the non-establishment of Abhipratārin’s being a patron for whom the Kāpeyas officiated remains equal, precisely because his status as a descendant of Citraratha (caitrarathatva) is not heard [stated] therein.

If it is argued that, for this reason, it is impossible to understand both Abhipratārin’s status as a patron of the Kāpeyas and his descent from the lineage of Citraratha, we reply: first, it is beyond dispute that the Kāpeya is recognized as the priest of Citraratha on the strength of another Vedic text (*śruti*). Consequently, the natural inference (*autsargikī buddhiḥ*) is that Abhipratārin, who was seated together with him, was the patron of the Kāpeya and a descendant of Citraratha; for there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) to the contrary.

It is indeed so; for example, when a man previously known as an elephant-keeper is seen near an elephant, once he is recognized as "this is the king's elephant-keeper," there arises the cognition: "This elephant is the one to be trained by this elephant-keeper, and it belongs to the king. [Objection: Granted that Abhipratārin’s status as a sacrificer for Kāpeya may be established, yet his descent from the lineage of Citraratha is not thereby established, because it is possible for someone else to have been his sacrificer as well. [Response: This is true. However, the fact that Abhipratārin was a sacrificer for Kāpeya—who himself was a descendant of Citraratha—establishes that Abhipratārin too must belong to the same lineage as Citraratha. For it is impossible for a person who does not belong to the lineage of a particular individual to be the sacrificer for that person. Therefore, since Abhipratārin was a sacrificer for Kāpeya, he must belong to the lineage of Citraratha. Furthermore, the fact that Abhipratārin was a sacrificer for Kāpeya—who was a descendant of Citraratha—is established by the statement: "The son of Kāpeya, the son of Citraratha, performed the sacrifice for Abhipratārin, the son of Kāśirāja. Thus, the descent of Abhipratārin from Citraratha is established. And since Abhipratārin was a descendant of Citraratha, it follows that Citraratha himself was a descendant of Aṅgiras. Consequently, the fact that the *Bhāllaveyas* and *Śāṭyāyanins* are descendants of Aṅgiras is established. And since they are descendants of Aṅgiras, they are *brahmabandhus*. And since they are *brahmabandhus*, their recitation of the *Veda* is not authoritative. Thus, the entire argument is consistent. Therefore, the *Veda* is not eternal. Q.E.D. Indeed, there are three kinds of officiating priests (*yājaka*): those who have come down through the lineage of father, grandfather, and so forth by family succession are "father-like" (*pitṛbhūta*) priests; in their absence, those who act as priests in all rites beginning with the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) are "human-like" (*manuṣyabhūta*) priests; and in their absence, those who happen to arrive there by chance and perform the priestly office for that rite are "god-like" (*devabhūta*) priests.

Since the relationship of priest and patron (*yājyayājakabhāva*) among those of similar lineage is primary and thus the general rule, and since we observe in the accounts of former kings a frequent establishment of priestly and patronal lineages—and specifically because it is determined that the Kāpeyas had as their priest one who was their father—it is established that [Citra] belonged to the lineage of Citraratha by virtue of his connection with a priest of the Kāpeya clan. Therefore, of the two who are connected to the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the second is a Brāhmaṇa.

Because of the subsequent mention of "Kṣatriya" and because of the predominance of that term in the context, Janaśruti, who is paired with Raikva, is a Kṣatriya. But how is it known that Raikva is a Brāhmaṇa, such that Janaśruti, as his counterpart, would be a Kṣatriya like Śaunaka is the counterpart [of Raikva]?

When the steward (kṣattṛ) was sent out to search for him and returned without having found him, [Naciketas] said, "O man, go where the search for a Brāhmaṇa is being conducted; seek him there. Since this statement—which means "go to that place where it is appropriate to search for a Brāhmaṇa, namely the dwelling places of Brāhmaṇas such as the Tāpana forest"—makes clear his Brāhmaṇahood, it follows that because he is understood to be a Kṣatriya when addressed here, he is not a Śūdra on account of being addressed as "O man. Thus, his eligibility for knowledge and so forth is established.

Because the *upanayana* sacrament is referred to in the contexts of instruction regarding knowledge (*vidyā*), and because the absence of that sacrament is declared for the *śūdra*, the *śūdra* has no entitlement to knowledge. For it is related thus in the *Chāndogya*: Satyakāma, whose father had died while he was still a child, approached a teacher for the sake of knowledge and asked his mother, "I shall practice the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*); what is my lineage (*gotra*)? When she replied, "Having remained here solely in attendance upon your father, I do not know your lineage," he approached Gautama.
Having said, "I shall practice celibacy; I will approach the Blessed One," he was asked, "What is your lineage? and he replied, "I do not know my lineage, nor did my mother know it."

"My mother is Jabālā; I am Satyakāma," he said. Then Gautama, having determined through his truthful speech that "this man is not a non-Brahmin," said, "My dear, bring fuel; I shall initiate you. Now, one might object: initiation (*upanayana*), whether as a constituent part of knowledge (*vidyā*) or as a constituent part of Vedic study (*adhyayana*), is not established in either case [as being necessary here]. For, in an initiation that is a constituent of knowledge, there is no requirement for the thorough knowledge of one's lineage (*gotra*); therefore, the question regarding the lineage is inappropriate.

Since there is a distinction in types based on the difference of *gotra* specifically in the initiation (*upanayana*) which is a constituent part of Vedic study, the inquiry regarding *gotra* is purposeful; for if it were the initiation for the purpose of Vedic study, the application [of the mantra] "Bring the fuel, my dear" would be untenable.

It is precisely at the initiation (*upāyanam*) for the sake of knowledge that [the scripture] states: "For the purpose of knowing That, he should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman"; for the state of "having fuel in hand" is thus enjoined there. Furthermore, later on, we see only the instruction of the sixteen-part knowledge of Brahman to Satyakāma, and no mention of the teaching of the Veda. To this it is replied: This initiation is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to Vedic study, in accordance with the question regarding his lineage (*gotra*) found at the beginning [of the Upaniṣad]. As for the study itself, it is already encompassed by the very word "having initiated" (*upanīya*).

Because that [reference] is intent upon the initiation (*upanayana*) which marks the conclusion of Vedic study; for in the *Pūrvatantra*, it was determined in the section on the definition of sequence (*krama-lakṣaṇa*) that in the passage, "Therefore, one who has built the fire-altar (*agnicit*) should not run when it rains," the phrase "one who has built the fire-altar" refers to the ritual act (*kratu*) that possesses the fire-piling as its constituent part—extending up to the purpose for which the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire-altar is performed—and not merely to the state of having undergone the consecration of the fire-piling itself. Thus, in the section on knowledge (*vidyā-pradeśa*), there is a reference to the initiation which is a constituent part of Vedic study.

There is also a dependence on that [initiation] for the sake of knowledge; therefore, one who is devoid of it has no qualification for knowledge—this is the meaning intended to exclude [the Śūdra]. As for the injunction regarding the fetching of fuel, however, the intention should be described as follows: "Out of compassion toward him, I shall also instruct him in knowledge. If it is argued that initiation (upanayana) may also exist for a Śūdra, we say no, because immediately after the statement, "In a Śūdra there is no sin, nor does he deserve any sacrament," it continues: "But those seeking dharma, knowing dharma, and following the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur fault even when acting without mantras, and they attain praise."

If it is argued that the permission for righteous Śūdras to undergo sacraments—excluding the recitation of mantras—has been granted, that is true; however, it refers only to rites such as the *jātakarman* (birth ceremony) and so forth, and not even to the *upanayana*. This is because the *Gautama-smṛti* states, "The Śūdra is the fourth caste, having only one birth," thereby explicitly declaring the absence of the *upanayana*, which constitutes a second birth. Furthermore, even in this context, the discussion regarding the engagement in the *upanayana* as a prerequisite for Vedic study occurs only after the absence of Śūdra-status has been determined. Moreover, regarding the Śūdra...

The hearing of Vedic statements, their study, the investigation of their meaning, the knowledge [derived therefrom], and their performance [of the prescribed rites]—[these are prohibited for a Śūdra], as it is said: "A Śūdra is indeed a cremation ground; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."

By the prohibition of study in the presence of a Śūdra in the Gautama-smṛti—"Now, for one who overhears the Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with lead and lac; in the case of reciting it, the tongue shall be cut out; in the case of retaining it, the body shall be split"—and by the prescription of punishment for a Śūdra regarding the hearing of the Veda and so forth, [such acts] are effectively prohibited. For how could he hear it, when the Vedic text must not be studied even in his presence, and when there is great punishment for merely hearing it? Since there is no hearing, how could there be study or performance? Therefore, it is established that a Śūdra has no eligibility for knowledge (vidyā).
The summary verses.
The entitlement to knowledge and the benediction (svasti) belongs to Śūdras as well, because they also desire the fruits [of dharma],
because [the dharma] is to be known through Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and because it is observed [to be so].
They [Vidura and others] attained knowledge for the sake of learning through the expansion of the Vedas, but not independently;
whereas King Jānaśruti had knowledge that arose within him spontaneously.
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). ||9||
Because of trembling. ||40||

Thus, when the three incidental topics have been concluded, that which was stated to remain at the end of the section on the thumb and to be completed later is now concluded by means of two sūtras: between these two mantras, "The person of the size of a thumb resides in the middle of the self" and "The person of the size of a thumb is the inner self," [the following occurs]: "Whatever this entire world is, it moves, having issued forth from Prāṇa."

The mantra is recited: "Great is the fear, the raised thunderbolt; those who know this become immortal. Its meaning is as follows: In this Person (puruṣa) the size of a thumb, designated by the word *prāṇa*, upon whom all this world depends, there exists a great fear comparable to a raised thunderbolt. Because of that fear—that a transgression against His command will result in misfortune—the world trembles and quakes; the meaning is that it engages in its respective duties out of fear. "Out of fear of Him the fire burns, out of fear the sun shines."

Immediately following this, in the subsequent mantra—"From fear of Him, Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run along"—the engagement of Agni and the others in their respective functions is presented as being caused by fear of that which is the size of a thumb. Observing that here too, in the mantra "A great fear, a raised thunderbolt," the nominative case has the sense of the ablative (fifth case), and that the word "trembles" (kampate) signifies the engagement in one's own respective function, it has been explained in this way. Thus, from such trembling as well, the one measured by a thumb is the Supreme Self.
Because of the perception of light. ||41||
Between those two mantras, which have as their object that [space] the size of a thumb, [it is said]: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine there."

From where does this fire come? "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. Here, the light of the person the size of a thumb is seen as the unique attribute of the Supreme Self—obscuring all other splendors, being their cause, and their sustainer. For in this passage, by stating the sequence of shining through the phrase "everything shines after Him who shines," its causality with respect to all splendors is declared. By the first half-verse, its quality of obscuring all splendors is declared.

By the fourth quarter (of the verse), the quality of being the favorer of all light is stated. This is unique to the Supreme Self, as seen from other scriptural passages such as, "The gods know Him as the light of lights, by whose light the sun shines," and because the mantra of the Atharva Veda, "There the sun does not shine," is recited [in that context]. From the perception of such a light, it follows that the person the size of a thumb is the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the section concerning what has been measured (pramitādhikaraṇa). ||10||

Previously, in order to establish that the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Brahman, the objection regarding its being "small" was refuted; in connection with that, it was proven that the one "measured by a thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamātra*) is the Supreme Self. Following that sequence, there are three further topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Now, since the Dahara-vidyā under discussion remains present in the mind, the subsequent passage concerning "ether" (*ākāśa*) is examined to determine that it refers to the Supreme Self; this constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*).

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, immediately following the Dahara-vidyā, it is heard: "Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self. In this context, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the term "ether" refers to the liberated self (muktātmā) introduced in the preceding mantra: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes off its hair, and freeing myself as the moon frees itself from Rāhu's mouth, I, having perfected my self, shall attain the uncreated world of Brahman, shaking off the body. Thus, it is that liberated self.

By the statement, "That which is between them," there is a description of being untouched by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) because of its situatedness in the midst of name-and-form. However, the phrase "he brings forth name-and-form" is appropriate when referring to the liberated self with respect to its prior state. For that [self], while in the bound state, was indeed the bearer of name-and-form; it remained as the bearer of manifold names and forms through the succession of births as gods, humans, and so forth. To this [objection], it is replied:

This "Space" (ākāśa) is the Supreme Self (paramātman), not the liberated self (muktātman). This is because scripture declares it to be the sustainer of name and form, which establishes the distinction between the liberated self and others. For "sustainer-ship" (nirvoḍhṛtva) primarily denotes agency (kartṛtva) by conventional usage (rūḍhi), rather than the secondary sense of "one who carries completely" (nitarāṃ voḍhṛtva) through etymological derivation (yoga), since conventional usage is more powerful. Furthermore, the agency regarding name and form is not possible for the individual soul (jīva) in either the state of bondage or liberation, due to the prohibition of its involvement in the cosmic operations (jagadvyāpāra). That quality, however, belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self.

This is because of such scriptural passages as: "I shall manifest name and form; therefore, from this Brahman, name, form, and food are born. Thus, although in the preceding mantra the liberated self was the subject as the one who attains [Brahman], nevertheless, since the Supreme Self is also the subject as that which is to be attained, this word "ether" (ākāśa) refers specifically to Him. Furthermore, because of the recognition of the previously mentioned "small ether" (daharākāśa) by means of the word "ether," this [word] has that very [Supreme Self] as its object.

Nor should it be suspected that there is no recognition of that [Self] because of the intervention of the Prajāpati passage; for that passage also serves as a supplement to the Dahara passage by means of explaining the true nature of the worshiper. The distinction is this: what was introduced in the Dahara passage as the object of worship—the subtle ether (daharākāśa)—is here concluded as the goal to be attained. Now, it might be argued that there is no other Self at all distinct from the individual self (jīvātman).

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) under discussion as "this one consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths," there is the instruction on its identity with the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the passage, "This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman"; furthermore, there is the negation of difference in the statement, "There is not even the slightest diversity here. Thus, even the status of being the creator of names and forms is compatible with the liberated soul, since that very soul is the Supreme Self. Therefore, if it is argued that the conclusion—that this "ether" (*ākāśa*) is not the liberated soul but rather the Supreme Self distinct from it—is untenable, we say: do not think so.

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, with reference to the individual soul (jīva) among the vital breaths (prāṇas), it is said, "Mounted by the conscious self (prājña-ātman), he departs," and thus there is a designation of distinction even at the time of departure. Furthermore, because of words such as "Lord of all," "Ruler of beings," and "Protector of beings" heard in scriptural passages like "He is the Lord of all, He is the Ruler of beings, He is the Protector of beings," it is impossible to deny the Supreme Self who is distinct from the individual soul. As for the teaching of identity and the prohibition of difference, these are based on the identity of the substratum (prakārin), as will be explained in the immediately following section (pāda).
Therefore, it is entirely logical that the "ether" (ākāśa) here is the Supreme Self and not the liberated soul.
