In this section (pāda), the reconciliation of those statements that bear the appearance of propounding the Sāṃkhya system with Brahman—by means of refuting the meanings favored by the Sāṃkhyas—is set forth. Thus, both the subject matter of the section and its logical connection have already been shown in the first section itself. It is heard in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self; higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa."

"There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the term "Unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the Pradhāna established in the Sāṃkhya system, or to the body. This doubt results from the recognition of the Sāṃkhya's own philosophical framework and from the process of elimination based on the body being the subject under discussion. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that this Unmanifest is the Pradhāna favored by the Sāṃkhyas.

This is because of the recognition of that specific system in the statement, "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great; the Puruṣa is beyond the Unmanifest," and because of the negation of any reality beyond the twenty-fifth Puruṣa in the statement, "There is nothing whatsoever beyond the Puruṣa. However, the body is not the Unmanifest, for there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "Unmanifest" applied to that which is manifest; rather, the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the term for the Pradhāna is stronger than its figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*).

If it is argued that this conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) imagined by the Sāṃkhyas—just like the usage of terms such as *pakṣa* (the subject), *sapakṣa* (the similar instance), and so forth, imagined by the Naiyāyikas—is useless for determining the meaning of words elsewhere, we say no. This is a restatement of principles established in the Sāṃkhya system; since the system's own methodology is recognized here, its established usage must be accepted. [As the Sāṃkhya says: "It exists neither in the *pakṣa*, nor in the *sapakṣa*, but only in the *vipakṣa*."

For even in the verse from the *Kāvya* (the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*), "The smoke rising at night is a wonderful indicator of fire against which one moves," we see the utility of this established convention among Naiyāyikas. Now, if it is asked: "In the statement 'There is nothing higher than Puruṣa,' how is it understood that Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth [tattva], such that this would be a negation of anything beyond the twenty-five?"—it is as follows.

The ten organs of cognition and action are included under the term "organs" (indriya); the ten objects are designated by the term "objects" (artha), comprising the gross elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras). The internal organ consists of the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the Great Self (mahān ātmā), which is the principle of Mahat; and there is the Unmanifest (avyakta), also called Pradhāna. These twenty-four principles are those accepted by the Sāṃkhya school as previously indicated. Therefore, the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.

Although among the Sāṃkhyas the term *buddhi* refers only to the principle of *mahat*, and the term *ātman* refers only to the conscious [Self], nevertheless, in accordance with the abundance of indicative marks (*pratyabhijñāpaka*), the term *buddhi* is applied to the *ahaṅkāra* through metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect, and the term *ātman* is applied to the principle of *mahat* by virtue of its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*). This is because in the subsequent mantra, "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that in the knowing Self," the term *ātman* is seen to be used even for the faculty of cognition (*jñāna*). Now, one might object: in the preceding passage it says, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot."

Know the intellect (*buddhi*) as the charioteer and the mind (*manas*) as the reins; they say the senses (*indriya*) are the horses, and their objects are the paths. If it is argued that—among the chariot, the charioteer, and so forth, which are metaphorically described in relation to the eternal Self, the body, and other entities—the passage concerning the mastery over the senses (*indriyādiparatva-vākya*) employs terms such as "senses" to denote those things distinct from the body, while the body alone is not mentioned by its own specific term, and since the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is additionally present, it is therefore appropriate to conclude by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the word "unmanifest" refers to the body through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—we say no. For even in the passage concerning mastery over the senses, the very same entities described in the form of the chariot, the charioteer, and so forth are mentioned without deficiency or excess.

There is no reason for a restrictive rule that [only the former] should be grasped. For if such a restriction were applied, there would be no cause for the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the sentence concerning the chariot and so forth; that sentence—intended to demonstrate that the soul, when unrestrained by the senses and other faculties, repeatedly undergoes transmigratory existence, whereas when restrained, it attains liberation—has fulfilled its purpose by assuming the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) in the form of the charioteer, the chariot, and so on, and is thus devoid of further expectancy. Nor is there any expectancy of the sentence concerning the supremacy of the senses and so forth to serve as a cause [for such a restriction]; for that too has fulfilled its purpose by assuming the status of a subordinate member in the demonstration of the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*), and is thus devoid of further expectancy.

Therefore, since it is illogical that the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) should, by process of elimination, denote the body, it is more appropriate that it signifies the Pradhāna as established in the Sāṃkhya system, following the recognition of the system's own methodology. This being the prima facie view, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

It is logical that among those things previously metaphorically represented as the chariot, the charioteer, and so forth, that which was assigned the form of the chariot—the body—is here understood by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) because it remains as the only one not yet identified. For in that context, six entities—the self, the body, the intellect, the mind, the senses, and their objects—were metaphorically represented as the chariot, the owner of the chariot, the charioteer, the objects being grasped, the horses, and the reins, respectively. That these were so represented for the purpose of meditation leading to liberation and because they are to be brought under control is beyond dispute.

For it is heard in that very same place: "But he who is without discernment and possesses an uncontrolled mind, his senses are unsubdued, like the vicious horses of a charioteer. But he who possesses discernment and possesses a controlled mind, his senses are subdued, like the good horses of a charioteer. In that context, a discrimination between what is primary and what is secondary among those things to be brought under control is required, so that an extraordinary effort may be achieved toward the subduing of that which is primary.

Even the statement regarding the superiority of the senses and so forth finds no other scope than the relationship of higher and lower—consisting of predominance and subordination—within the context of their being subject to mastery (*vaśīkāryatā*). For it is said: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten *manvantaras*; those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred; those who contemplate the ego (*ābhimānika*) remain for a thousand; the followers of the Buddha (*bauddha*) remain for ten thousand, free from feverish distress; and those who contemplate the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) remain for a full hundred thousand."

It might be argued that the distinction between higher and lower—consisting in the greater or lesser abundance of the fruits of various meditations as conceived by the Sāṃkhya—is established by the statement: "Having attained the Person devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), no calculation of time exists. However, in that case, since the mind is not enumerated separately from the senses, it would fall into a state of inferiority relative to the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the gross elements; consequently, it would be untenable to state that the mind is superior to the objects denoted by the word "artha," as in the passage: "The mind is higher than the objects."

Nor can it be said that [the relationship] consists of the nature of cause and effect. For, according to the Sāṃkhya system, since the senses are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), the statement "the objects are higher than the senses" would be untenable, as it would imply that the subtle elements (tanmātras) of the material elements are higher than the senses—which they are not. Furthermore, if those [objects] were admitted to be material, the statement "the mind is higher than the objects" would be untenable, as it would imply that the mind is higher than the material elements. Therefore, in terms of being subject to mastery, the objects of the senses are superior to the senses themselves.

Even for one whose senses are under control, the mind is superior to them because the senses expand [into activity] when objects are present. When the mind is engaged in the contemplation of objects, passion expands even in the absence of those objects; therefore, the intellect (*buddhi*) is superior to that as well, because without the function of determination (*adhyavasāya*), the mind is ineffective. Even more superior than that is the Self (*ātman*), because every mental activity regarding objects is dependent upon the will of the Self. For this very reason, the Self—though atomic—is qualified as "great. Even more superior than that is the body.

Because all human activities are dependent upon Him, for that reason also, He who is the inner controller of all, the impeller of all, and the perfect Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is declared to be superior to each subsequent one among the senses and so forth in terms of being subject to mastery. Its meaning should be explained as follows: the mastery over the Blessed Lord, the inner controller of all, is nothing other than taking refuge in Him, according to such scriptural statements as, "Go to Him alone for refuge."

The scripture itself demonstrates later on that among these factors, beginning with the senses and ending with the Supreme Person, each succeeding one is superior in terms of being subject to mastery: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self of knowledge; he should restrain the knowledge in the Great Self; he should restrain that in the Peaceful Self. The meaning of this mantra is as follows: one should restrain the entire collection of organs of knowledge and action—exemplified by speech—within the mind. Having abandoned the activity of the external organs, one should abide in the mind alone.

That mind, which is directed toward the conceptualization of sense objects, one should restrain within the intellect (buddhi) that abides in the self and consists of the ascertainment of the defects of those objects. One should restrain that intellect within the Great Self (mahat), the innermost self (pratyagātman), and should make it inclined toward and intent upon that [Self] as its object of attainment. And one should restrain that innermost self within the unafflicted Supreme Self (paramātman), making it realize its state of being subordinate to that [Supreme Self].

Therefore, because the subtle unmanifested (*sūkṣmavyākṛta*) is worthy of the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), that causal body (*śarīra*), which exists in a different state [from the gross], is metaphorically called "unmanifest. If it is admitted that the subtle unmanifested exists, then one might ask: "Does this not result in the acceptance of the Sāṃkhya doctrine? How, then, can that be refuted? The Sāṃkhya doctrine to be refuted is the claim that the unmanifested is independent and brings about its effects by itself.

The distinction is this: our position is that because [the unmanifest] is dependent on the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), it brings about the collection of effects such as the Mahat and so forth only while being impelled by Him. Furthermore, if the Śruti had intended here the Unmanifest (avyakta) as conceived by the Sāṃkhyas, then it would have declared that both that [Unmanifest] and its manifest effects are objects of knowledge; for the proclamation of the Sāṃkhyas is that "liberation results from the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower."

If it be argued: "Does not that very scripture immediately following [the passage in question] speak of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)? Since it is logical that the negations of manifest attributes such as sound and so forth should culminate in the unmanifest, and because of the mention of being 'beyond the Great' (*mahataḥ paraṃ*), and because even the general reference 'that which' is appropriately directed toward the unmanifest—then this is not so. [The response: This is not correct.

"The man who has consciousness as his charioteer and restrains the mind reaches the end of the path—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. This is because the context concerns the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). Indeed, it is He alone who is presented elsewhere as the object to be perceived. Therefore, the doubt arises that the statement, "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa," is a negation of any reality beyond the twenty-fifth principle (the individual soul).

[The objection] is refuted by the context, because in that passage the word *puruṣa* refers to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). Furthermore, the description beginning with "without sound, without touch" is applicable to Him as well, just like the description beginning with "that which is invisible and ungraspable. The phrase "higher than the Great" indicates His superiority over the individual soul (*jīva*), who was introduced as "the Great Self, higher than the intellect" (*buddher ātmā mahān paraḥ*). Moreover, in this context, we observe that only three things—the Supreme Person to be attained, the meditation which is the means of attainment, and the meditator who attains—are presented as objects of knowledge and are the subject of inquiry. Among these, [it says]: "Him, difficult to see..."

"The wise man, having realized the Ancient One—who has entered the hidden, who is placed in the cave, who dwells in the abyss, the Divine—through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self, abandons both joy and sorrow. Thus, by the phrase "the wise man, having realized the Divine," there is a sequential presentation of the object of meditation, the meditation, and the meditator. [This refers to the inquiry: "When a person has died, there is this doubt: some say 'He exists,' and others say 'He does not exist.'"

"Instructed by you in this knowledge, this is the third of my boons. By means of this question regarding the nature of liberation, there is an inquiry into all three: the means (upāya), the goal (upeya), and the attainer (upetṛ). [The opponent claims: "The deceased (preta) has gone forth (itaḥ) excellently—that is, he has attained liberation without returning"—this is the misconception of the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) who maintain that "liberation is the annihilation of the self," as introduced in the verse, "And some say, 'This [self] does not exist. However, in this context, the word *preta* does not mean "dead."

Furthermore, since Naciketas had heard the words of Vaivasvata—such as, "The world beyond does not reveal itself to the fool who is heedless, deluded by the infatuation for wealth; thinking 'this world exists, there is no other,' he falls again and again into my power"—and since he had thereby ascertained that the deceased exists apart from the body, it would be impossible for him to raise a doubt regarding non-existence.

Therefore, since only these three are presented here as objects of knowledge and are the subject of the inquiry, there is no possibility of referring back to the *avyakta* (the Unmanifest) as established in the Sāṃkhya system. Furthermore, in the passage "The Great Self is beyond the intellect," the principle of *mahat-tattva* (the Great Principle) is not to be understood [as the referent], because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self" (*ātman*), which is conventionally used for the conscious entity. In the passage "One should restrain that in the knowing Self," however, the two locative endings were previously explained as being in a state of non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). For these reasons as well, it is logical that the *avyakta* mentioned here—being spoken of as referring to the individual self (*jīvātman*)—is not the *pradhāna* (Primary Matter) established in the Sāṃkhya system; this is because it is not stated to be the *mahat-tattva*.

In the previous section, it was stated that because a body (*śarīra*) is mentioned in the passage concerning the metaphor (*rūpaka*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*) cannot be the *prakṛti* established by the Sāṅkhya system (*tantra*). Now, the connection [of this section] arises from the objection that since a body is not mentioned there, the unmanifest might indeed be the *prakṛti* established by the Sāṅkhya system. The *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* is recited as follows: "There is one unborn female (*ajā*), red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; one unborn male lies beside her, enjoying her, while another unborn male abandons her after he has enjoyed his pleasure."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the word *ajā* (the unborn) refer to the independent *prakṛti* established by the Tantras, or to the *prakṛti* dependent on Brahman as accepted in our own system (*siddhānta*)? This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). It refers only to that which is established by the Tantras; for we hear of its being "unborn," which implies freedom from birth, and we hear of it as "creating," which implies independence. It cannot, however, be of the nature of Brahman; because according to our system, it is admitted that Brahman is its cause, and thus it lacks freedom from birth, and because it is admitted that in the act of creation it is impelled by Brahman, and thus it lacks independence. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Furthermore, the absence of birth will be established even for that which has Brahman as its cause. Likewise, because the meaning derived from the etymology of the word *ajā*—namely, the state of being devoid of birth—is common [to other things], no specific distinction is perceived therein by means of it alone. As it is said: "The ladle is downward-facing and upward-vented; in it is placed glory of every form."

In the mantra, "Of that non-existent one, the sages [are] the heated banks," by means of the word *camasa*, which is etymologically derived as "that by which one tastes (*camyate*) or consumes (*bhakṣyate*)," only the instrument of tasting is perceived. No specific meaning is determined, because the determination of the meaning of etymological words is impossible without the context of the subject matter, the supplementary portion of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), and so forth. In this regard, there exists a supplementary passage—"Just as this head is a cup with its opening downward and its base upward"—which determines that the head is the cup here. That which is placed within it is glory, the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*). Its...

Regarding the phrase "the seven seers standing on the bank," there is a supplementary statement that determines [their identity] as "the pair of ears, eyes, two nostrils, and the tongue. However, in this case, there is nothing whatsoever to determine that the "Unborn One" (ajā) refers to the *prakṛti* established in the [Sāṅkhya] system. Furthermore, independence in creation—consisting in being the agent of its own activity—is compatible even with being impelled by another; for even a chariot, though impelled by a driver, is conventionally referred to with independence as in "the chariot goes. Therefore, the "Unborn One" established in that system should not be accepted here.

However, it must be understood as having Brahman alone as its essence, because scripture declares that Brahman is the cause. For, in the Taittirīya tradition, beginning with the mantra "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great," and starting from "From Him the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) arise," up to the end of the passage "From whom, once born, they do not go back and nothing else exists," those [scriptures] teach the origin of the entire phenomenal world—including the vital breaths, the oceans, and the mountains—from Brahman; and right in the midst of those mantras, [it says] "the one unborn..."

They recite: "The one unborn, rejoicing, lies beside her who produces many offspring of similar form—red, white, and black; yet another unborn leaves her after she has been enjoyed. Therefore, because it is read here in the midst of the section concerning the effects of Brahman, it is determined that the *ajā* (the unborn) is also intended to have Brahman as its cause. Now, an objection is raised: this *ajā* mantra concerns the story of a living being (*jīva*) who is liberated from bondage in the form of the abandonment of enjoyment [of Prakṛti]; how then can the word "ajā," ending in the accusative case, be construed with the verb "proceed forth" (*prabhavanti*) which recurs from the phrase "seven vital breaths proceed forth"?

If it is argued that, for this reason, Brahman is not understood to be the cause of this [creation] in the same way as the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, it is replied: Just as the sentence, "To those two, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma at the full moon," although appearing to concern merely a past event involving Indra, becomes—in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—a prescription for the sacrifice consisting of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is said to have been given by Indra to Agni and Soma; so too, although this [text] appears to concern merely a past event, [it functions as a prescription].

It must be accepted, based on the consideration of the preceding and following context, that the mantra establishes that Prakṛti, the progenitor of all effects, is created by the Supreme Lord. [Objection: But how can Prakṛti have the Supreme Lord as its cause while simultaneously being devoid of birth? [Response: This is not contradictory, owing to the distinction between the gross and the subtle.

Just as in the Madhu-vidyā, the sun—being the substratum for the essences to be enjoyed by various deities such as Vāyu—is described as having rising, setting, and so forth; yet it is subsequently stated, "Then, rising from there, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the midst," which refers to abiding in oneness through the abandonment of all distinctions. This abiding in oneness is not contradictory to the distinctions of states consisting of cause and effect, or the distinctions of gross and subtle states. The insertion of the letter 'l' in the word *ekala* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage; the meaning is "he alone.
Therefore, it is established that this "Unborn One" (*ajā*) is indeed dependent upon Brahman, as proven by scriptural authority.
The summary verses.
That which is heard in scripture as "the unborn one who creates while being devoid of independent birth" is the *prakṛti* spoken of by the Sāṃkhyas; it is not the Supreme Self.

Do not say so; for even in the case of the category of Brahman, if it were unproduced by its causal state, it would possess the status of being the locus of its own activity, just as a chariot does here when it is impelled by another.
Therefore, this is not a distinction; rather, there is a distinction in the process of creation by another.
From this [exegesis], the purport of this mantra—which is without beginning—becomes exceedingly clear.
Thus ends the section concerning the cups (Camasādhikaraṇa). 2.
Nor [is the number] established by the inclusion [of the senses], because of their diversity and because of the excess [of organs]. ||11||
The vital breaths and so forth [are meant here], because of the remainder of the passage. ||12||
For some, when food is unavailable, [the offering] consists of light. ||13||

The objection is raised as follows: "If the word *ajā* (the Unborn) were an independent primary noun (*prakṛti*), then in the absence of any specific qualifier, its nature as Brahman was established based on the requirements of other scriptural passages. That [interpretation] does not apply here. Because there is an excess of number if Brahman were the subject, it is possible to determine that the primary noun is non-Brahman even without completing the number [with Brahman]. This is the connection [of the objection]. The Vājasaneyins record: "In whom the five groups of five people and space are established..."

"The knower, knowing that very Self as Brahman, becomes immortal—immortal. Regarding this mantra, there arises a doubt: does it refer to the principles established in the Sāṃkhya system, or does it refer to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it refers to the Sāṃkhya principles, because of the perception of a number exceeding twenty-five, and because that [number] is perceived from the word "five" being qualified by another "five" in the term *pañcajana*. For the word *pañcajana* is not a term denoting humans and the like.

Since the second word "five" is also determined to refer to a number through its co-utterance with the first word "five," this compound must therefore have a collective sense (samāhāra), meaning "a collection of five people. Once this is established, the absence of the suffix *ī* (as in *pañcapūlī*) and the change of gender must be explained as Vedic (*chāndasa*). This is because, in the absence of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or a subsequent member of the compound, a compound necessarily has a collective sense.

When there is an expectation as to how many such groups there are, they are further specified by the number five, as in the expression "five bunches of flowers. Now, why resort to assuming a compound and justifying the form on the grounds of Vedic usage (*chāndasatva*), when even without a compound, the meaning could be conveyed by two instances of the word *pañca*?

This is because the attainment of the number twenty-five is logically established. In this way, the attainment of a specific number through multiplication is also well-accepted elsewhere. For example, in the passage "fifty-three fivefold years," the number two hundred and fifty is obtained by multiplying the number fifty by five. Or likewise, in the passage "of each age, he gives seven times seventeen," the number two hundred and eighty-nine is obtained by multiplying the number seventeen by seventeen.

If it is argued that, as in the passage, "The Creator ordained this by five; he produced five from each of those sisters; these approach them in succession, twenty-five in number, assuming various forms through their ritual powers; thirty sisters approach the appointed place," the number twenty-five is obtained by multiplying the number five by five—this is not so. For since the word *pañcajana* is a compound (*samāsa*), the rule [of multiplication] does not apply there.

Furthermore, the fact that this mantra, as recited in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, is a compound word is determined by its final *anudātta* accent; for this final *anudātta* accent takes the form of an acute (*udātta*) substitute based on the reason that it is a mantra recited in a Brāhmaṇa text, as prescribed by the treatise known as the Bhāṣika, which governs the accents of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, because of the rule of grammar—"of that which has its place [in a compound], the accent is on the final syllable"—and because a compound is observed in another mantra, "Of you, the five peoples," there must also be a compound here. Consequently, it is logical to conclude that this is a collective compound (samāhāra-samāsa), and its grammatical form is established by virtue of being Vedic (chāndasa). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of an excess of principles (tattvas).

The statement that the twenty-four principles are established in the Self is figurative (bhākta), because they are dependent upon the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) of that Self; for it is logical that the statement regarding the Self is likewise figurative, like the statement that the Self is established in its own majesty.

[This objection is raised] on the grounds that if the Sāṅkhya principles were not accepted, the connection with the number twenty-five mentioned in scripture could not be maintained. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (siddhānta) follows.

Even by including the number twenty-five, there is no realization of the Sāṃkhya principles, because they exist separately from those [five groups] and because they are distinct from them. This is because, in the passage "In whom the five groups of five people," their nature as being identical with Brahman—indicated by the word *yat*—is perceived; furthermore, the number would exceed [twenty-five] due to the inclusion of both the Self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*). Nor should one resort to the strained interpretation mentioned at the conclusion of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) merely to force the application of the number twenty-five.

In the Kaṭhavallīs, because it is possible to include—by means of the word *ākāśa* in passages such as "that eternal ākāśa"—both the non-material world of the Lord (which is well-known from the sequence beginning with "higher than the senses are the objects") and the gross and subtle bodies (along with the organs of knowledge, organs of action, the elements, the subtle elements, mind, intellect, and the enjoyer), which are described as being lower than the Puruṣa, it is logical that the term *avyakta* in the Kaṭhavallīs refers to these two types of bodies, the gross and the subtle.

Thus, since it is possible to include the number of categories seen in other internal branches without any affliction, it is improper to include the non-authoritative Sāṃkhya principles through a forced, external method. In reality, there is no perception of the number twenty-five here at all.

In a collective compound (*samāhāra-samāsa*), the absence of feminine suffixes and the masculine gender may be justified by their being Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, by accepting that the word *pañcajana* is a proper name (*saṃjñā-śabda*), its description as a compound formed according to the rule "when direction and number [are compounded] in the sense of a name" (*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*) is appropriate. If it is objected, "In that case, certain beings designated as *pañcajana* must be described here," the answer is: "True."

The vital breaths and so forth are indeed heard as the remainder of the sentence in the passage: "They who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind. For in this remainder of the sentence, the well-known vital breaths and so forth are heard through words such as "breath" ending in the genitive case. Now, one might object: the reading of "food" (anna) occurs only in the Mādhyandina recension of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, not in that of the Kāṇvas.

If it is argued that, for this reason, the five groups of beings (*pañcapañcajanāḥ*) cannot be the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, it is replied: In the mantra preceding "in whom the five five-people [dwell]," namely, "The gods worship Him as the light of lights, as the immortal life," while Brahman is being designated as the "light of lights," the word "lights" (*jyotiḥ*) ending in the genitive case—which denotes certain lights whose effects are dependent on Brahman—refers to the organs of perception (*jñānendriya*), which are the illuminators; thus, by means of this term which conveys specific sense-organs...

This is determined by the supplementary passage beginning with "the life of life. In that context, by the word "of life" (*prāṇasya*), there is the inclusion of the sense organ of touch associated with air (*vāyu*). It is because it is impossible to indicate the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) by means of the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the genitive case. By the words "of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaḥ*) and "of the ear" (*śrotrasya*), there is the inclusion of the sense organs of sight and hearing. By the word "of food" (*annasya*), there is the inclusion of the sense organ of smell, which is connected to the earth denoted by the word "food."

By the etymological derivation "that by which food is eaten," the sense organ of taste is also included through a double entendre (*tantra*). The term "of the mind" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*). Thus, for the sake of establishing the inclusion of all the aforementioned sense organs, this [term] must also be supplied in the Kaṇva recension.

Since the introduction of the senses by means of the word *jyotis* ending in the genitive case, as well as the subsequent mention of specific senses in the remainder of the passage, are identical in both cases, it is thus established that there is no room for the suspicion that this is a restatement of the twenty-five principles established in the Sāṃkhya system—which are independent of Brahman—because the text demonstrates that all principles have Brahman as their substratum, stating: "In whom the five groups of five and the ether are established," wherein the senses are indicated by the term *pañcajana* and the elements are indicated by the term *ākāśa*, and all these are established in Brahman.
The Summary Verses.
In that [text] called the Pañcaśikha-mantra, the five aggregates of persons (pañcajana) are mentioned;
these are the twenty-five principles (tattva) declared by Kapila.

Let it not be so; for there is no difference in their having Brahman as their substratum, nor in their being described by those [terms], because they exceed the number mentioned in relation to the locus and space.
By the designation "five people" (pañcajanāḥ), the five sense organs are meant;
those which are observed to have their respective functions dependent upon Brahman.
The word "food" (anna) must also be understood by the Kāṇvas as referring to the nose and the tongue,
because of the equality of the concluding statements found at the beginning of the section concerning the sense organs introduced by the word "light" (jyotis).
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number [of elements]. ||3||
And because space and the other [elements] are mentioned as causes in accordance with how they were previously designated. 14.
Because of the drawing together. ||15||

Even if the five groups of five (the twenty-five principles of Sāṃkhya) do not exist, nevertheless, the Siddhāntin’s intended position—that Brahman is the cause—is not established. This is because the causal statements, being mutually contradictory, lack any firm foundation anywhere; thus, setting those aside, one must assert that Pradhāna alone is the cause in accordance with Smṛti. It is on account of this objection that the connection [of the present section] is established.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doubt—whether it is possible to determine that Brahman is the cause by means of the causal statements, or whether, due to their mutual contradictions, nothing can be determined by them and one must instead determine that Pradhāna is the cause by relying on the Smṛtis of Kapila and others—is as follows: In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the creation preceded by Being is recorded in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second."

In that very same [text], having introduced the doctrine of non-being as the cause with the words, "Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-being alone, one only, without a second,'" it refutes the doctrine of non-being as the cause with the words, "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? How could being be born from non-being?"

In the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the creation preceded by Being is established. However, in the Taittirīyaka, having adopted the theory of non-being as the cause—which had been refuted in the Chāndogya—the creation preceded by non-being is recorded: "Non-being indeed was this in the beginning; from that, Being was born. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka as well, it is recorded in the same manner: "In the beginning, this was Being alone; that Being existed; that became compacted."

In that very context, a creation preceded by the unmanifest is also recorded in scripture: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it was then manifested through name and form. For the unmanifest is indeed the unevolved *pradhāna*.

Thus, since no definitive conclusion can be reached as to whether Brahman or Pradhāna alone is the independent cause due to the mutual contradictions among the causal statements, it must be determined—on the basis of the Smṛtis composed by the most authoritative teachers such as Kapila—that Pradhāna is the cause; all the causal statements should be interpreted accordingly, and even the acts of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and so forth should be understood in a figurative sense. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

It can be determined that the world originates from Brahman alone. For in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 1.1.2), Brahman is defined as characterized by omniscience, the fulfillment of true volitions, and other such attributes; and it is precisely this single Being, as thus described, who is established by scriptural passages such as "From this very Self, space was produced" and "He created fire," as the cause of space and the rest. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is such an establishment, how are the contradictions among the cited sets of causal texts to be reconciled?"

It is said: In the Ānandavallī, having referred back to the previously mentioned *ānandamaya* by means of the words "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and having stated His resolve for the creation of the world, [the text] declares His status as the creator of all, His entry into all, and His being the Self of all through the passage beginning with "He created all this, whatever exists here. Then, after stating "Regarding this there is also this verse," the verse beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asad*)" is cited as a witness to the entire matter.

Therefore, because of its attraction to that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the word "non-existent" (*asat*) must be understood as intending the state of having name and form unmanifested in that very [Brahman]. This same interpretation applies to the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad evedam agre āsīt*); for what is denoted by the word "non-existent" is drawn back toward the word "existent" (*sat*) in the statement, "That became existent" (*tat sad āsīt*), since it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to attain the nature of existence according to the principle: "Because what is non-existent has never been seen [to become existent]. Likewise, in the passage, "In the beginning, this was undifferentiated" (*tad dhedam tarhy avyākṛtam āsīt*), the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) refers to the Supreme Person whose body is the undifferentiated [state].

In the immediately following passage, "This very one has entered here up to the tips of the nails, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind," the term "this very one" (*sa eṣa*) draws back the subject previously mentioned as unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), thereby designating it as the Puruṣa who has entered within as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. Regarding the statement, "It was differentiated by name and form," the verb is used in the reflexive-passive sense (the agent is also the object). The meaning is that Brahman, whose body was then unmanifest and in which name and form were undivided, made itself its own self possessed of divided name and form.

This is because it must have the same meaning as other scriptural passages such as, "He made Himself by Himself. Thus, since the causal statements refer to Brahman, the scriptural mentions of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and "Brahman-Self" (brahmātman) are also upheld. Therefore, it is established that the world has Brahman alone as its cause.
In the Saṃgrahakārikā.
Because of the contradictions among the causal statements, that which was spoken by the most authoritative [teacher] must be the primary cause;
therefore, the causal statements regarding the entire world should be interpreted in accordance with that.

Let it not be so, for since the "drawing forth" (samākarṣa) of Brahman exists everywhere, there is no contradiction among those [scriptural passages]; therefore, Brahman alone is the cause of the world.
Thus ends the section concerning the nature of being the cause. ||4||
Because it denotes the world. ||16||
If it be argued that this is so because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), that has already been explained. ||17||
Jaimini, however, [holds that the mantra] has another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus some [teachers] also [maintain].

In this regard, the purification of the subject matter (*viṣayaśuddhi*) is as follows: King Ajātaśatru of Kāśī, having approached Bālāki Gārgya who said, "I shall tell you about Brahman," praised him, saying, "We give a thousand [cows] for such a speech; indeed, people run after Janaka, [saying], 'Janaka!'"; and then [the king] rejected as non-Brahman those persons residing in the sun, the moon, lightning, thunder, and so forth, whom Bālāki had taught as being Brahman through such statements as, "I meditate upon that very person who is here in the sun."

Immediately after each of those persons was mentioned, [Bālāki] rejected them and remained silent. Then [Ajātaśatru], having asked, "Is your knowledge limited to this much?", and when Bālāki assented that it was indeed so much, [Ajātaśatru] set him aside with the words, "In truth, you have spoken falsely to me; I shall tell you of Brahman," and instructed him himself, saying, "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, and whose work this is—he is indeed the one to be known."

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is the person who is taught here as one to be known the *puruṣa* established in the Sāṅkhya system, or is it Puruṣottama? This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This person is indeed the *puruṣa* established in that system, because of the scriptural hearing of his connection with merit and demerit in the passage, "He whose karma is that. Nor is it impossible for him to be the creator of the sun and other things, since scripture declares, "He is the maker of these persons."

Because those things useful for its enjoyment—such as light and so forth—are produced by that unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), it is its agent through the medium of that *adṛṣṭa*. As stated in the supplementary passage: "Just as a chief enjoys [the wealth] by means of his own [subordinates], or as his subordinates enjoy [the benefits] through the chief, even so this wise Self (*prājña ātmā*) enjoys by means of these selves; even so these selves enjoy this Self. Just as [in this analogy].

Just as a sovereign enjoys pleasures provided by his own servants who bring him the means of enjoyment, and just as those servants protect the sovereign while providing those means of enjoyment, so too it should be understood that the Self, taught as the object to be known, enjoys through the elemental beings such as the Sun and others, and they in turn protect Him; for this has been stated. Now, even so, what is the determining factor that the person possessing merit and demerit is the one to be known and accepted?

If it is argued: "Since the word *karman* possesses both a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) as 'merit and demerit' (*puṇya-pāpa*) and an etymological application (*vyutpatti*) as 'that which is done'—thereby signifying any effect whatsoever—it is appropriate even in the case of the Supreme Person (Brahman) that He be described as 'He whose work this is. Furthermore, if one relies on the predominance of conventional meaning, since the convention for 'action' (*calana*) also exists, there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*) for choosing between the two. Thus, when the two conventions are at conflict, it can be said that here the etymological sense (*yoga*) has gained its opportunity and is therefore stronger. This is not so.

The term *karman* is employed here because it possesses a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for "the unseen potency" (*apūrva*), which serves to convey the intended sense that the agency of the Person (Puruṣa) as Āditya and others is mediated by the *apūrva*; furthermore, since no other conventional meaning is applicable, this conventional sense is more powerful. Moreover, the conventional meaning of "motion" (*calana*) is irrelevant to the doctrine of the Supreme Person, as He is all-pervading; it is also irrelevant to the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the Person, as they accept Him to be all-pervading; and even in the doctrine of the atomic nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), there is no purpose in speaking of motion.

Furthermore, there is no room for the suspicion that another [meaning] might be established by conventional usage (rūḍhi). Therefore, since Brahman—which was introduced as the subject to be explained—is none other than the Puruṣa established by the system [of Sāṃkhya], there is no proof of an Īśvara distinct from that.

And thus, although in the preceding sections it was stated that the Pradhāna possesses the nature of being the material cause of the world by having Brahman—well-known throughout all the Vedāntas—as its substrate, nevertheless, since it is understood here through the introduction of the definition of Brahman and the definition of the Sāṃkhya Puruṣa that such a Brahman is indeed the Sāṃkhya Puruṣa, one must conclude that all the Vedāntas find their final rest in that alone. This prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is advanced by challenging all the previous sections. For this very reason, it also maintains formal connection (*saṅgati*) with those preceding sections. Such being the position, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

In the phrase “yasya vaitatkarma,” the word *etat* (this) refers to the entire universe as presented through perception and other means of knowledge, because there is no restrictive factor such as the context (*prakaraṇa*) or a qualifying term (*upapada*). Therefore, it must be accepted that the word *karman* (action/work), being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it, also refers to the entire universe by virtue of its connection with the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*). This is because, through its apposition with the word *etat* which denotes the entire universe, even the weaker conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is set aside, allowing the etymological sense (*yoga*) to emerge.

If it is argued that the term "apūrva" (the unprecedented) is present in the mind as the means of accomplishment (*nirvāhakatva*) for the agency attributed to the Sun and other deities mentioned in the preceding sentence, we say no. For by the mention of the Sun and others, who constitute a single part of the world, it is equally possible to state that the world—the whole of which they are parts—is present in the mind. And when both [the whole and the part] can be present in the mind, it is more logical that the term denotes the world itself through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with this word. If it is argued that denoting the "unprecedented" is useful in the present context as the means of accomplishing the agency of the Sun and other deities, we say no.

To the inquiry, "How can one [being] be the creator of so many persons such as Āditya and the rest?", the answer is that he is not the creator of these alone, but rather the creator of this entire world. Thus, when for him this whole world is the effect, what doubt could there be regarding his being the creator of the persons such as Āditya? By the logic of the "how much more" (kaimutika-nyāya), since even the possession of the general quality of being an effect serves to establish his authorship of the persons such as Āditya, it is equally applicable to the subject at hand; and when that equality is established—

Because, by the force of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with this word, one must accept that the term [jagat] denotes the world precisely through the manifestation of its connection to being an effect (*kāryatva*); for, having referred back to the agent under discussion—the creator of these persons—by means of the word "whose" (*yasya*), the word "effect" (*karman*) functions as a designation of that which is related to him. Thus, even in the case of the word "effect" used in coordination with the agent, there is a manifestation of its connection to being an effect, consisting in being the object of the agent's operation. Consequently, since it is possible for the word to apply even to the *apūrva* (unseen potential) by way of the general property of being an effect—which is common to all effects—it applies there as well.

Furthermore, it is because it is impossible to assume a conventional meaning (rūḍhi) for that [word] in an exclusive sense. For in the *Pūrvatantra*, in the section concerning *barhis* and *ājya*, it was stated that although the word *barhis* is used by the learned in a universal sense for *darbha* grasses consecrated by rites such as cutting, and the word *ājya* is used for ghee (*ghṛta*) consecrated by rites such as purifying (*utpavana*), one should rely on their occasional usage for the mere genus (*jāti*) of *darbha* and ghee respectively. Since the application of those words is thereby established through that very [usage], no other ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the form of a consecration need be postulated for them.

"Even when a word is observed in only one instance, it is based upon a genus (jāti); since that [genus] is not abandoned, there is no room for postulating another cause [for its application]. Therefore, according to the maxim that "an established etymological derivation (yoga) subverts a postulated conventional usage (rūḍhi)," there is no occasion for postulating a new conventional meaning. Consequently, the teaching "He whose work this is" refers to His being the creator of the entire universe.

In this way, the word *etad* (this), which brings to mind the entire world presented through perception and other means of knowledge, and the word *vā* (or), which serves to exclude the mere agency of only a single portion such as the Sun-person (*ādityapuruṣa*), both become meaningful. Furthermore, the introduction to the definition of Brahman, the presentation of the agency of the Sun-person and others as attributes of the Supreme Brahman known from such scriptural passages as "I am the eye... who is born," and the instruction regarding the Person unknown to Bālāki—who is distinct from the individual soul well-known to all the world—all become appropriately explained.

Thus, the description of the fruit of knowing Brahman found in the concluding passage—"Having struck down all evils, he attains the preeminence and sovereign rule over all beings, he who knows thus"—is also established as being consistent.

If it be objected that two marks of the individual soul (jīva) are heard in the supplementary portion of the text—namely, the state of being an enjoyer in the phrase "he enjoys through these selves," and the connection with the chief vital breath (prāṇa) residing in the person to be known, as indicated by the locative case in "then he becomes one in this very breath"—and that these two lead to the conclusion that the person to be known is the individual soul, the resolution of that objection has already been stated in the context of the Pratardana-vidyā.

Since the passage is determined to have Brahman as its primary subject by the force of its opening and concluding sections, those other indicative marks found within it must be interpreted in conformity with that. If it is asked how they are so interpreted, it is as follows: the mention of the individual soul (jīva) is for the purpose of awakening one to the true nature of Brahman as distinct from the jīva; this is understood through the question and the subsequent explanation. First, the question posed by the King to Gārgya is: "Where was this person sleeping? Where did he then become? Whence did he come back?"

When Gārgya, not knowing the locus of the soul during deep sleep, was thus questioned by the King, the King himself provided an explanation of the matter he had asked about, beginning with "The veins of the heart are called hitāḥ" and ending with "then [the soul] is in those [veins] when, being asleep, one does not see any dream whatsoever. Having stated that the soul's movement through the veins—which serve as the path for reaching Brahman, which is delimited by the heart, is the locus of deep sleep—he concluded, "Then [the soul] becomes one with this very breath (prāṇa). Thus, the King explained the meaning of his own question.
This is its explanation, establishing the absorption of the individual soul (jīva) into Brahman during deep sleep: "Then, my dear, one has become united with Being (sat)."

This is because it is consistent with the *Chāndogya* Śruti, and because it is consistent with the question and answer found in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru as recorded in the Vājasaneyi branch: "When this person who consists of consciousness was thus asleep, where was he then, and from whence did he return? and the reply: "When this person who consists of consciousness was thus asleep, then, having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness, he lay in that space which is within the heart."

Therefore, it is established that the Person taught as "that which is to be known," who is described as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) in deep sleep by virtue of being its substratum, is indeed the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person.
The summary verses.
That which is cherished as "Brahman" in all the scriptures is none other than the Puruṣa proclaimed by the Sāṃkhya;
for the discussion concerning Brahman, when engaged with King Ajātaśatru, was brought to its conclusion therein [in the context of ritual action].
It is not so; here the word *karman* refers to "effect" (*kārya*) and certainly not to "merit and demerit" (*puṇya-pāpa*),
because it is grasped through its co-occurrence with this term [the world] which is used in its natural sense for the entire universe,
and because it enters into the sentence that teaches the Person unknown to Bālāki.
And because of the conformity with such scriptural statements as "The sun is the eye."
Thus ends the section concerning the term "world" (jagat). ||5||
Because of the connection with the sentence. ||19||
Āśmarathya [holds that] the mark [of inference] exists because the thesis is established. ||20||
"Audulomi [holds that the soul] will thus become [of such a nature] precisely when it is about to depart. (21)
"On account of abiding," says Kāśakṛtsna. ||22||

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Yājñavalkya, desiring to renounce the world himself, wished to divide his wealth between his two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. When questioned by Maitreyī as to whether it was possible to attain immortality through wealth, he replied: "As is the life of those who possess worldly means, so shall be your life; there is no hope for immortality through wealth. He then said: "What should I do with that by which I cannot become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows."

Furthermore, when he was asked by her for the means to attain immortality, [Yājñavalkya] began with the passage: "Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self that the husband is dear," and so on, ending with: "Verily, it is not for the sake of all that all is dear, but for the sake of the Self that all is dear. Having thus introduced the Self as the enjoyer of everything—such as husband, wife, children, and wealth—which is dear only because it serves the purpose of enjoyment, he said: "Verily, the Self, my dear..."

Having taught that the vision of the Self is the means to immortality—stating, "It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"—and having further instructed on its means, such as hearing and so forth, [the text] declares that through the knowledge of the Self everything is known: "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and realized, all this is known. Then, after explaining how all things proceed from the Self, it says: "Just as from a fire of wet fuel, when kindled, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, this Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda... and so on.

Having demonstrated that He is the cause of the entire phenomenal world consisting of names and forms—stating: "The Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, verses, aphorisms, explanatory treatises, commentaries; what is sacrificed, what is offered, what is eaten, what is drunk; this world and the next world, and all beings—all these are His very breaths"—the text further declares: "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements and having dissolved back into them, there is no consciousness after death."

Having stated that there is an absence of specific knowledge regarding its origin and destruction, the scripture concludes by declaring that the means to immortality for that Self is its realization, saying: "Verily, my dear, so much alone is immortality. Here, it is understood that the collection of passages concerning the husband, wife, and so forth, as well as the passage concerning origin and destruction, have the Supreme Self as their object. All these passages proceed with a single subject matter, as they are introduced by subsequent sentences using the word *ātman* and various pronouns that refer back to the subject under discussion.

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter, attributes unique to the Supreme Self—such as "the great being, infinite, and boundless"—are indicated through grammatical coordination with marks of the individual soul (jīva), such as birth and destruction, mentioned in the passage beginning with "a mass of consciousness alone. Thus, although there is the appearance that sentences containing marks of both the individual soul and the Lord refer to a single subject, it is not reasonable to accept that the non-difference between the two is the intended meaning of the scripture.

Because the experience expressed in such statements as "I am not omniscient" sublates the existence of the Lord—characterized by omniscience and other attributes—in the individual soul (jīva), the assumption that these two are being presented here as distinct entities contradicts the perception that they share a single subject matter. Therefore, either the individual soul or the Lord alone must be the subject taught here. Since it is established that the characteristics of the untaught entity are to be applied to the taught entity, the final conclusion (siddhānta) will be reached by applying the attributes of the individual soul to the Lord.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: by the application of the marks of the Lord (*īśvara-liṅga*) to the individual soul (*jīva*), it is the *puruṣa* established in the Sāṃkhya system that is being propounded here. For instance, the relationship between husband, wife, and so forth is an unchanging mark of the individual soul; this is indicated in the passage, "Nor indeed for the sake of the husband's desire," by the word "indeed" (*vai*), which signifies what is well-known.

For this is well known even to you, Maitreyī: that husbands and the others are not dear to wives and the others for the sake of the husbands and so forth, but rather for their own sake alone; such is the understanding of the meaning. Therefore, it is consistent that the passage beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen" is stated to mean that one should set aside husbands and the like, and instead accomplish the vision of one's own Self—which is the means to immortality—through hearing and other such practices. Now, one might object: having stated that husbands and the others are dear for the sake of one's own enjoyment, the subsequent statement that the nature of the Self alone should be sought is inconsistent.

If it is argued that one must seek only what is dear, and not the essential nature which is devoid of the dear, it is replied: for everyone, one's own self is dear by its very nature; whereas husband, wife, and others are not dear by virtue of being a husband or wife, because affection is not observed toward them when they bring about what is undesirable, just as it is absent when they fail to accomplish what is desired.

Therefore, having reflected upon the reality of one's own self and of [objects] such as a husband—determined or undetermined in terms of being human goals according to experience—one should abandon the husband and others, which constitute undetermined, secondary human goals, and take refuge in the primary goal alone; thus, the injunction for the vision of the Self liberated from primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as the hearing, reflection, and meditation directed toward that end, is indeed consistent.

By such statements as, "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten Manvantaras," the Sāṃkhyas establish that meditation on the Puruṣa as perfected in the Tantras results in liberation. Consequently, the scriptural declaration of "all-knowledge" (*sarvavijñāna*) is also consistent with that view; for when the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is to be meditated upon for the sake of liberation and is distinct from *prakṛti*, is realized within oneself as being uniform due to the absence of any internal difference, it becomes possible to know that "all souls have this same form."

However, the statement regarding [Prakṛti] being the material cause of everything is consistent when understood as referring to the Pradhāna presided over by the Jīva; for in that context, fire qualified by wet fuel is cited as the illustrative example of the material cause of smoke. It is not fire alone that is the material cause of smoke, but rather the wet fuel itself, since an increase in smoke is observed to result from an increase in that [fuel].

Likewise, even in the case of the subject under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*), the description of the conscious [Self], which is like fire and distinguished by a dull nature comparable to wet fuel, as the material cause (*upādāna*) follows from the analogy; this is like the injunction "one offers with curds," where the qualification is transferred [to the act]. Thus, here, because the attributes of Brahman can be applied to the individual soul (*jīva*), and because the attributes of the individual soul—such as the relationship with husband, wife, and so forth, birth, destruction, and the absence of specific knowledge—can be applied to Brahman.

Since the two Maitreyī-brāhmaṇas recited in the fourth and sixth chapters of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad culminate in the Puruṣa established by that [Puruṣasūkta] tradition, all causal statements (kāraṇavākya) are similar to them and thus refer to the Pradhāna presided over by the Puruṣa as the cause. Therefore, the Pradhāna alone is the cause of the world; there is no such thing as an Īśvara. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The treatise begins with the knowledge that is the means to immortality (*amṛtatva*), and it concludes with that same theme; furthermore, the hearing, reflection, meditation, and glorification of the vision of the Self as the means to immortality are only logically consistent if the subject matter of this section is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and not the *puruṣa* established in the Tantras. This is because the scriptural statement, "There is no other path," renders nugatory any Tantric assertion—such as "having reached the qualityless *puruṣa*"—which contradicts the Śruti. How, then, can verses concerning husband, wife, and so forth be applicable to Brahman?

Thus—husband, wife, children, wealth, and so forth, do not become dear by virtue of their own volition, thinking, "I shall be dear to him for his sake"; rather, they become dear for the fulfillment of the Supreme Self’s desire to obtain those who are dear to His worshippers. For when the Supreme Self is propitiated through ritual acts, He brings about a state of dearness toward various objects—each determined by its specific place, time, nature, and measure—in accordance with those very acts, within the infinite range of each respective worshipper. As the scripture states: "For He alone causes one to rejoice."

But no object whatsoever is inherently pleasant or unpleasant. As the venerable Paraśara has said: "That very same thing, having become a source of joy, later arises as a source of sorrow; that very same thing again becomes a source of anger and then a source of serenity. Therefore, nothing exists that is essentially sorrowful, nor does anything exist that is essentially joyful. Now, one might object: in this way, statements concerning the husband, wife, and so forth, would indeed have to refer to the Supreme Self.

If it is asked how the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in passages such as "they perish after it perishes" can have the Supreme Lord as its object, the answer is as follows: First, the individual soul is produced from the Lord, according to scriptural texts such as "as sparks fly forth from a well-blazing fire.

Therefore, between these two, which stand in the relation of cause and effect, there exists a primary identity, just as between a jar and a lump of clay. This identity must be made known here for the sake of fulfilling the promise of "knowing all" stated in the preceding passage, "But when the Self is seen... It is the teacher Āśmarathya who maintains that the Lord is designated by the word "individual soul" for the purpose of making this identity known.

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that although there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) during the state of saṃsāra, upon the attainment of liberation, non-difference is reached according to the analogy of rivers and the ocean stated in the mantra, "As rivers flowing [merge] into the ocean... Therefore, he holds that the term "jīva" denotes the Lord. The teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that because the Lord dwells within the individual soul as its inner ruler (antaryāmin), the soul is His instrument of control; thus, since words denoting a body refer to the embodied one as well, the term "jīva" denotes the Lord.

This very view is the one intended by the author of the Sūtras. This is because the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) will be refuted at the point where it is stated, "The Self [is not produced], on account of the absence of scriptural statement" (*na-ātmā-śruter*); because the manifestation of an adventitious form in liberation will be refuted at the point where it is stated, "Having attained [the Self], there is manifestation" (*saṃpadyāvirbhāva*); and because the fact that all words ultimately refer to the embodied Supreme Self will be established by the Sūtra, "But [the word 'Self'] may depend on the moving and the non-moving" (*carācara-vyapāśrayas-tu syāt*). Therefore, based on the consideration of its beginning, middle, and end, the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa refers to the Supreme Self.
Thus, it is established that all causal statements have as their ultimate purport the Supreme Self, rather than merely a person perfected through the Tantras.
The summary verses.

It is well known in the Tantras that the twenty-fifth principle, as described in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa through its connection with husband, son, wife, and so forth, attains liberation through knowledge when it is divested of Prakṛti. By this same logic, let all words found throughout the entirety of the Vedas that denote exclusively conscious entities find their application there alone; and let that Pradhāna be understood as having that [conscious principle] as its presiding controller.
Even when there is mention of a wife, son, and so forth, the word "Self" (ātman) does not touch one who remains within the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti).
Since, in this case, through the examination of the opening statement and other criteria, it refers to the Supreme Object, what possible occasion is there for its application to anything else?
Therefore, in this context, the Self is said to be the Supreme Person; the attainment of happiness by the worshiper is desired for His sake.
To accomplish that, sons and other dear ones may be useful, but not for their own sake; thus, one should desire them only for His purpose.
This reference to the "living being" (jīva) extends up to the embodied soul and the Supreme Self;
for in that [state], the absence of knowledge regarding birth and destruction has indeed been declared for Him.
Thus concludes the section on the syntactical connection of sentences (vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). ||6||
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because that would not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. 23.
And because of the teaching regarding covetousness. ||24||
And because both [the Self and the Brahman] are directly mentioned [in the text]. 25.
Because of the creation of a self. ||26||
From transformation. ||27||
For it is indeed sung as the source (yoni). ||28||

Thus, once the atheistic Sāṃkhya has been refuted, there follows the connection [of the present topic]: the refutation of the theistic Sāṃkhya view, which asserts that while Īśvara is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*) alone is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) of the world. Is Brahman merely the efficient cause of the world, or is it also the material cause? Regarding its status as the material cause, a doubt arises due to the conflict between scripture and reasoning on one hand, and their conformity on the other; thus, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: Īśvara is merely the efficient cause, while *pradhāna* alone is the material cause.

This is because of the observation in Śruti and Smṛti such as, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara; by me, as the supervisor, Prakṛti brings forth the moving and the unmoving," and because in the world we observe a distinction between the instrumental cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna), such as the potter and the lump of clay respectively; furthermore, it is impossible for the Supreme Self to be the material cause. For being a material cause consists in undergoing transformation into the form of the effect, and not merely in being the substratum of that which undergoes transformation. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even the ground, which is the substratum of the clay while it transforms into the form of a jar, would also be the material cause.

Nor should it be argued that Brahman must be accepted as the material cause because of the scriptural hearing of its resolve to become manifold in the form of fire and the rest about to be created, expressed as, "May I be many, may I procreate. For even if it were not the material cause and even if there were a difference from those effects, such a statement would be possible through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference based on the fact that they belong to Him.

"May we multiply through offspring, O Rudra; O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that for me," he says; by this he means, "Whatever is deficient in my offspring and cattle, fill that for me. Indeed, such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras declare his own generation in the form of offspring and cattle, as well as his own nature as consisting of offspring and cattle. Nor should it be argued that its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) must also be accepted in accordance with the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Even when there is knowledge of Brahman, and even when there is knowledge of clay-lumps and the like regarding jars, bowls, and so forth, doubt is observed; therefore, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) must be understood in a figurative sense. This is because passages such as "He made Himself His own self" can be interpreted in the same manner as passages like: "Whenever there is a decline of Dharma, O Bhārata, and an uprising of Adharma, then I manifest Myself. Such being the case, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, not merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*). For it is only if Brahman is the material cause that the promise of "knowing all" and the analogies of the lump of clay, the pot, the bowl, and so forth, would not be contradicted. Nor should these two [the promise and the analogies] be considered figurative, since their primary (literal) sense can be established as consistent.

To explain: in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," the word "Being" (sat) refers to the reality characterized by the subtle sentient and insentient [principles]. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) because the class of individual souls and the unmanifest, which are distinct from Brahman, would still exist; for such a restriction must be understood as excluding any other entity separate from that [Being]. Furthermore, when that [Being] is known, everything that is its effect also becomes an object of knowledge, because the effect-substance is non-different from its cause.

The gross state of the effect (*kāryagatasthūlāvasthā*) alone is not the [primary] object; therefore, doubt regarding that form is appropriate. Whatever else is required here shall be explained through the expansion of the statements of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and will be investigated in the section on "Origin" (*ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*). Nor should one suspect a difference between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) based on the analogy of the potter and the lump of clay; for in that case, their difference exists because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) grasping their non-difference, whereas here, since such a means of valid knowledge is manifest, how could there not be non-difference?

Nor should it be said that the statement regarding Brahman being the material cause (*upādāna*)—as the substratum of the transforming material cause—is without foundation, like the case of the ground. For the nature of being a material cause consists in being the locus of an effect that is non-different from it; this [definition] applies primarily even to Brahman. Furthermore, "directness" need not be included in the definition of being the locus of the effect, which would otherwise result in *prakṛti* alone being the material cause as its direct locus. This is because such a qualification would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Moreover, the fact that Brahman is the material cause is established by both the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

This is also determined from the instruction of the desire, "May I be many, may I procreate. Furthermore, since its primary sense is possible, one should not resort to a strained interpretation as was done for the mantra and arthavāda cited by the opponent. Likewise, its nature as both the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) is directly declared in scripture: "Brahman was the forest, Brahman was the tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth; O wise ones, declare it with your mind—I proclaim—that Brahman stood above, upholding all worlds."

For here, by the word "tree," its status as the material cause (*upādāna*)—produced through the act of carving—is stated; by "Brahmā presided over [it]," its status as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is stated; and likewise, by "He made himself by himself," [its status as the cause] in creation is stated.

Furthermore, because that very [Brahman] is heard of as being both agent and object, its nature as both the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) is understood. If it is argued that this is established as appropriate by the statement, "Then I manifest myself," we say no; for even there, the establishment of the status of being both efficient and material cause is no different. This, however, is the distinction: in that case, the creation of one's own self is said to occur in the form of an incarnate body, whereas here it occurs in the form of the phenomenal world (prapañca).

Although its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established by many scriptural passages, it must be understood in a way that does not contradict other numerous scriptures concerning its changelessness, such as "partless, actionless, and tranquil. Furthermore, since such an interpretation is possible even without intending [the Self] to be the direct substratum (*sākṣāt-āśrayatva*) according to the aforementioned definition of a material cause, one should not insist on its being the direct substratum. Nor should it be suspected that there can be no indirect substratum—just as there is no indirect cause—such that it would be merely the substratum of a substratum.

Furthermore, when a person is lying on a couch covered with cloth, even though the couch—which is separated from the person because it is not capable of being the direct substratum for that person who possesses only the cloth—is unfit to be the substratum, it nonetheless serves as the substratum through the medium of the cloth; this is also seen in common usage, such as the expression "he sleeps in the palace" regarding a man sleeping on a couch situated within a palace.
