By this, the objection is also refuted which claims that the definition of material cause (*upādāna*) is "being the substratum of an effect-state non-different from itself," and thus, since there is no identity between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) despite their non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*), Brahman cannot be the material cause of the world.

Because a definition that includes inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*) must be stated in order to establish the status of being the material cause as taught in scripture—and because it is appropriate to postulate what is not explicitly stated in accordance with the justification of what is stated—therefore, when the aforementioned kind of transformability (*pariṇāmitva*) is accepted, the status of being the material cause is indeed faultless; for it establishes the scriptural status of being the material cause and does not contradict the scriptural teaching of being changeless (*nirvikāra*). This very nature of transformability is celebrated even by terms such as "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) found in the passage concerning the Imperishable (*akṣara*), for the word "source" (*yoni*) is a synonym for "material cause."

In the section on the syllable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa), because there is also the scriptural hearing of agency in the passage, "The agent, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman," it is established from that as well that [Brahman] possesses the dual nature of being both the efficient cause and the material cause. Therefore, it is proven that Brahman is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world.
The summary verses.
Although Īśvara exists, he is nevertheless not the material cause because he is formless;
rather, the Pradhāna presided over by him is the material cause, according to both Śruti and Smṛti.

The Leader of the Universe, being inherently faultless and changeless, does not admit association with defects or transformations through his own body, which consists of both consciousness and matter. Therefore, in this case, there can be no state of being a substratum for future conditions, as that would entail a loss of the defining characteristic of being the material cause.
For it is by resorting to the movement of his body that he appears as if seated upon a couch strewn with a rug.
Thus ends the section concerning the primordial nature (prakṛti). ||7||
By this, all [objections] have been explained; they have been explained. ||29||

The connection [of this section] is established because it consists of the principles and methods of the twenty-five previous sections. Regarding the doubt—whether those specific causal statements not cited in the previous sections refer to Brahmina as defined above or not—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from the possibility or impossibility of those statements falling within the scope of the aforementioned principles. The prima facie position is that all those specific causal statements not cited previously do not exclusively refer to the Supreme Person.

"In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed. Because in such other causal statements, another cause denoted by terms such as Brahmā and Śiva is perceived. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

By the very same principles stated in the previous section, those [terms] referring to the Supreme Person are also established. The manner of their establishment, however, should be seen as elaborated in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* and other works; it is not written out here for fear of excessive prolixity. If it is argued that words such as "Śiva" are also heard in the scriptures with reference to the causal reality, then by the aforementioned principles, they too must be applied to Nārāyaṇa, who is Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the interpretation of all [scriptural passages]. ||8||

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the second section of the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, a work on the essence of the four systems composed by Appayadīkṣita, the son of the eminent Raṅgarājādhvarin— the performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and the preceptor of the non-dualistic Advaita-vidyā, who was a Kaustubha-jewel in the ocean of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage.
The first chapter is completed.
Prosperity!
The second chapter.
"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other [Vedic] Smṛtis."
And because the others are not perceived.

In the first chapter, it was established through reasoning that the Supreme Brahman known as the illustrious Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the entire universe, by demonstrating the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedāntas. Now, the second chapter is commenced to further consolidate that very conclusion by resolving all possible contradictions. Therein, in the first topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), the suspicion that the Vedāntas might have another purpose due to conflict with the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is refuted.

Now, one might object: how can there be a suspicion that the Śruti has another meaning when it contradicts Smṛti? For it was established in a previous section of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtras—"In case of conflict, however, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded, for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference"—that in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Smṛti alone lacks authority.

For in that case, it has been stated that the Smṛti rule, "The Audumbarī post is to be entirely covered," is to be disregarded because it contradicts the direct Vedic revelation (śruti), "Having touched the Audumbarī, one should sing"; and it has also been stated that when there is no contradiction with a direct Vedic revelation, the Smṛti possesses authority by virtue of its capacity to lead to the inference of a foundational Vedic text (mūla-śruti). This is true; such is indeed the case when the meaning of the direct Vedic revelation is clear.

The Vedānta texts concerning the cause of the world, however, do not have their meaning made explicit like the Śruti on touch; rather, they are extremely profound and diverse in nature. As it has been said: "Even if one knows the meaning of the Veda by oneself, there may still be ignorance regarding it; but when it has been determined by the great-souled sages (ṛṣis), what doubt could there be? Thus, for the purpose of providing certainty through such corroboration (upabṛṃhaṇa), there arises a suspicion that these [Vedānta texts] might have another purport in accordance with the Sāṃkhya Smṛti composed by great sages such as Kapila. It is for the purpose of refuting this that the present section (adhikaraṇa) is undertaken.

Here, a doubt arises as to whether the Brahman’s status as the cause of the world—established in the first chapter—is untenable or tenable. Because of conflicting views among the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas, Manu, and others, it remains undetermined whether the Vedānta texts are to be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti and thus intend Pradhāna as the cause, or whether they are to be supplemented by the Smṛtis of Manu and others and thus intend Brahman as the cause. In this state of doubt, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is that the Vedānta texts are to be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, because that [Smṛti] is otherwise without scope (niravakāśa).

This is because the *smṛtis* of Manu and others have their scope (*sāvakāśatva*) within the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), as well as in rituals such as the *agnihotra*. Nor should it be argued that the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti* must be assumed to be based on error due to its contradiction with the many *smṛtis* of Manu, Vyāsa, and others; for in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, it is heard that the author of Sāṃkhya, Kapila, was perfected in knowledge, as stated in the verse: "He who in the beginning supported with his knowledges the sage Kapila, who had been brought forth, and beheld him as he was being born. Thus, such an assumption [of error] is untenable.

If it is argued that the authority of Manu’s utterances is established in its entirety by the Vedic text, "Whatever Manu said was indeed medicine," we say no; for that [authority] is not proven, since the word "medicine" (bheṣaja) does not signify "authoritative validity."

In the Yajurveda, after prescribing a sacrifice for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) with the injunction, "He who desires spiritual luster should offer this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra," and following the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the fruit—"As much as there is spiritual luster, he makes all of that"—there occurs the statement: "They say that by performing this [sacrifice], excessive spiritual luster is produced; therefore, the sacrificer is liable to become afflicted with skin disease. Thus, through the performance of this sacrifice, the very same result [of spiritual luster] is [described].

Having again proclaimed that [the condition] results in a defect, for the purpose of its removal, there is the injunction: "One should employ two verses seen by Manu as *dhāyyā*s. Regarding the expectation—how the removal of leucoderma (*śvitra*) is effected by the two verses seen by Manu, namely "I praise Agni, your ancient one, the Aṅgiras, the god of the Vasus," and so forth, which are to be placed in the form of *dhāyyā*s within the *sāmidhenī* verses—the following explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) provides the connection: "Whatever Manu said is indeed a remedy; he thus provides a remedy for him. However, it does not...

This establishes the authoritative validity of the meanings of the *ṛg* verses of Manu, such as "Agni is the first among the Vasus," as well as the meanings of the statements in the *Manusmṛti*. If it is argued that the meaning of Manu’s words is contradicted because they serve as a remedy for leprosy or some other disease, then let them be considered merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) based on an unreal subject matter. For it is not appropriate to adopt another meaning that does not cohere with the primary context in order to establish that an explanatory passage must be based on a real subject matter.

Therefore, since it is unestablished that the passage beginning with "Whatever [is here]" and so forth is intended to demonstrate the authority of all *anuvākyās* regarding their respective objects in every respect, it is more appropriate to assume that the statements of the *Manusmṛti* find their scope only within the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), setting aside the portion concerning Brahman as the cause. Consequently, because the Vedāntas must be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti—which has no other scope—they should be interpreted according to the method set forth in the *Kapila-sūtras*, the *Hari-hara-vārtika*, and other such works.

Those [scriptural passages] that intend the Pradhāna as the cause must be interpreted otherwise. Among them, those which explicitly state that the Puruṣa alone is the cause should be understood as attributing the primary function of the Pradhāna to the Puruṣa, just as one might attribute the king’s own victory to his minister; thus they are to be interpreted in accordance with the Smṛtis of Manu and others. This is because those many Smṛtis, composed by the most authoritative sages, cannot be rendered inconsistent.

Nor do those [scriptures] concerning ritual actions possess any independent scope, for even those texts that enjoin rituals—which constitute the worship of the Supreme Person—have their ultimate purport (tātparya) solely upon Brahman, the cause of the universe and the Supreme Person who is to be worshipped and who subsists as the substratum of those rituals. For this very reason, when Manu was questioned by the sages regarding the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma), he first taught the Supreme Person who is to be worshipped through them, and only thereafter did he instruct those duties themselves: "This [universe] existed as darkness, unperceived, without defining marks..."

Inconceivable and indescribable, as if entirely asleep, thereupon the Lord Svayambhū—the unmanifest one who dispels darkness and whose power resides in the great elements and other principles—appeared, making this world manifest. Desiring to create various beings from his own body, he meditated and first created the waters; into them, he cast his seed. That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun. Within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.

It is clearly evident from such passages as, "The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*; since they are declared to be his *ayana* (abode), he is therefore remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*," and from statements in the Purāṇas such as, "Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, is to be worshipped; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction," which demonstrate that the teaching of ritual action is solely for the purpose of worshipping Him and subservience to Him.

Likewise, Yājñavalkya also, having introduced the Lord with the statement, "The supreme purification of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is held to arise from the knowledge of the Lord," establishes His status as the cause of the universe through the method of the Puruṣasūkta, just like Manu, stating: "The social classes (varṇas) would be born from His mouth, feet, thighs, and flanks, respectively."

The ultimate intent is revealed to be Nārāyaṇa alone—the Lord of Śrī, who is praised in the Puruṣasūkta and who is to be propitiated by those whose duties regarding caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) have been well-described by themselves. Likewise, Āpastamba also introduces Nārāyaṇa in the form set forth in the Subālopaniṣad—beginning with "All living beings are indeed the city of Him who dwells in the cave, who is unslain and stainless," and "This one inner self of all beings, the divine, singular God Nārāyaṇa, free from sin"—and continues: "From that body, everything originates along with its root."

By stating that [Brahman] is "eternal and imperishable," it is revealed that its intent is to show that He alone is the object of worship for the duties of the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) described by Himself, as He is the sole fundamental cause of everything. In this manner, the statements of other Smṛti-authors may also be cited as examples. Nor should it be asked: "Since the lack of scope [for other means] is equal [in all cases], how is the determination made that [the Veda] is to be supplemented specifically by the Smṛtis of Manu and others? For Manu and the others are the most authoritative among trustworthy persons (āpta).

The supreme authority of Manu is established by the scriptural statement that his words possess the quality of being medicine (*bheṣaja*). To explain: here, the term "medicine" is intended merely to signify the removal of faults common to both the pacification of disease and the pacification of sin; it does not mean exclusively the pacification of disease. Otherwise, the statement "whatever [Manu has spoken]" would result in the absurdity of being entirely purposeless. Indeed, among the utterances of the *Manusmṛti*, there is no single statement that, like medical science, teaches medicine for the purpose of curing disease.

However, there certainly exists a collection of Manu’s statements concerning the duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) which serve to establish the pacification of sins, because the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties of the classes and stages of life are causes for the destruction of evil. One might object: "Even so, not all the statements in the *Manusmṛti* are applicable to the destruction of sin, since the *Manusmṛti* also contains matters pertaining to royal policy (*rājanīti*) and the adjudication of legal disputes (*vyavahāra-pada*), which have visible worldly purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, the use of the word 'whatever' (*yat kiñcit*) in its distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is inconsistent. To this it must be said: [this objection does not hold].

For even those [other duties] possess an indirect purposefulness (*tādarthya*) insofar as they assist in the performance of rites intended for the destruction of evil; and because, even in their absence, it is logical that the word "all" (*sarva*), when its primary sense of totality is precluded, should be restricted to refer to the collection of injunctions concerning the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), rather than being impossible to apply to all things without restriction—it is therefore appropriate that "all" here refers to a restricted "all."

Therefore, regarding the scriptural statement within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, "All indeed desire to obtain the Hāriyojana [cup]," since it is impossible for the word "all" (sarva) to refer to an unrestricted totality, and since its reference to a totality must be specified by some delimitation, it is logical that it refers to the totality delimited by the priests belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Thus, it was concluded in the Pūrvatantra that this sentence prescribes the consumption of the Hāriyojana specifically for the officiating priests.

And thus, since it has been stated that for the words of Manu—which have attained authority by being described as "medicine"—it is impossible for their ultimate purport to terminate merely in the act of propitiating him, setting aside the object of propitiation which is the ultimate purport; and since it has been stated in that very same context that for all the words of Manu in the form of Dharmaśāstra, it is impossible for their ultimate purport to terminate merely in the act of propitiating him, setting aside the object of propitiation which is the ultimate purport.

In that very context, the authority of all the verses in the form of Dharmaśāstra is obtained; thus, he possesses the status of being the most trustworthy (āptatama). Likewise, by the Śruti statement, "Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, said," the gravity [of his words] is demonstrated through the fact that they were spoken by Vyāsa regarding the subject matter he himself propounded; thus, the authority of everything taught by Vyāsa is obtained, and therefore he possesses the status of being the most trustworthy.

In this way, Yājñavalkya and others also possess the status of being most authoritative (*āptatamatva*) through the stylistic expressions found in such passages as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Janaka, indeed, performed the sacrifice with many sacrificial fees. However, Kapila possesses merely the status of being authoritative (*āptatvamātra*). This is because statements such as "the seer was impelled" (*ṛṣiṃ prasūtam*) are satisfied even by referring merely to his possession of knowledge regarding a few Vedic texts and the meaning of the Vedas that pertains to his status as a seer (*ṛṣitva*).

Likewise, it is well known that those who expounded the Sāṃkhya treatise—such as Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and others—are only three or four, whereas those who expounded the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas—such as Manu and others—are exceedingly numerous. Furthermore, it is quite evident that the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas are far more voluminous than the Sāṃkhya treatise, which consists of only a few sūtras composed by Kapila and others.

Therefore, because it contradicts the many treatises composed by Manu and others who are most authoritative, the Sāṃkhya system lacks any scope of validity and is ineffective; thus, the Vedāntas are to be supplemented precisely by the Smṛtis of Manu and others, which possess no such lack of scope. Consequently, due to their consistent harmony (samanvaya), the status of Brahman as the cause of the world remains unshakable.
The summary verses.

For the sake of ascertaining the true meaning of the flood of Vedānta and the exceedingly profound Sāṃkhya-smṛti, it is appropriate that the Smṛti— which finds its scope through corroboration (upabṛhmaṇa) by no other subject— should be employed;
for no other [Smṛti] is renowned for its focus on the comprehension of Dharma, nor does it possess such scope.
Therefore, that Brahman is not the cause of the world, as it is known through the Vedanta.
Do not think thus; for even the Smṛtis originating from the mouth of Manu are recognized as having no scope [for contradiction].
Indeed, those [Smṛtis] intend their application toward Nārāyaṇa when he is to be propitiated by their respective rites.
Therefore, those [teachings] composed by the most authoritative sages are indeed what they follow;
that Sāṃkhya Smṛti which is seen to have meanings contrary to them is based on delusion.
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti.
By this, Yoga is refuted. (Sūtra 3)

Here too, the subject matter, doubt, prima facie argument, established conclusion, and reasons are to be understood as before; for since error is impossible for Hiraṇyagarbha, [it cannot be] that which was produced by him.

Since this Śāstra accepts the existence of Īśvara, describes the practice of Yoga as taught in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and other texts, and differs from the Smṛtis of Kapila and others, it is an integral part of the Vedānta; therefore, the Vedāntas are to be supplemented by it. Consequently, the objection that "Brahman cannot be the cause because one must accept the causality of Pradhāna presided over by Īśvara according to the method stated therein" constitutes the specific doubt of this *Atideśādhikaraṇa*.

The rebuttal of that [objection] is as follows: since even Hiraṇyagarbha is a *kṣetrajña* (an individual soul), it is possible that the scripture composed by him is rooted in error; furthermore, because he accepts the non-Brahman *pradhāna* as the cause, because he admits that God is merely the efficient cause, because there is a discrepancy with the object of meditation intended by the Vedāntas, and because he prescribes a distinct form of meditation defined differently from that [Vedāntic view], the Vedāntas cannot be supplemented by such a contradictory work. This is the refutation.
The Summary Verses.

[The opponent argues: "In that case, let Yoga be the means of nourishment [for the self], for the Lord (Īśvara) fashioned by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] is accepted therein, and Yoga is known from the Śruti and has Him as its object.

[The author replies: "Do not say so. For those two [Yoga and Sāṃkhya] possess characteristics distinct from the Lord declared in the Śruti and from the Yoga declared therefrom; indeed, who here would not have delusion regarding them?"
Thus ends the section concerning the refutation of Yoga.
Not so, because this [scripture] possesses a different characteristic; and its being such is known from the word itself.
But the designation [of the Self] as the presiding deity is due to distinction and following after.
But it is indeed seen.
If it be argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because of the recognition of the material cause and because of the attainment [of the effect].
On account of the same contingency applying to the dissolution, [the theory] is inconsistent.
But it is not [the case] because of the existence of an example.
And because of the faults in one's own position.
Also because reasoning is not firmly established.
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

The previously stated position—that the [Vedānta] should be supplemented by the Smṛtis of Manu and others—is incorrect, because those [Smṛtis] contradict reasoning (tarka). Therefore, the connection [of this section] arises from the counter-argument that the supplementation should instead be performed solely by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, which is supported by reasoning.

If it be asked whether Brahman’s status as the cause is logical or illogical, there arises a doubt based on whether the production of a non-conscious universe from a conscious Brahman—which is of a different nature—is possible or impossible. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the production of a non-conscious universe from a conscious Brahman is not possible because they are of different natures. For the relationship of cause and effect is observed only when there is similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) by way of the unique form residing in the cause, such as "clay-ness" or "gold-ness," in the cases of jars, earrings, clay, gold, and so forth.

Furthermore, the unique characteristic of consciousness—namely, being conscious—is not perceived in its effects; nor can it be postulated that consciousness, though never unperceived, remains unmanifest in objects such as jars (as it does in living beings during deep sleep), on the grounds that the doctrine of Brahman as the cause would otherwise be inexplicable. For if consciousness were present, its manifestation would necessarily occur at some time, making such a postulation untenable.

Otherwise, by the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of explaining otherwise), one would have to assume that even the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) possesses a non-manifest solar nature, as it is heard [in scripture] to be the Sun; furthermore, there would arise a contradiction with scriptural texts that distinguish between the conscious and the unconscious, such as "Consciousness and the unconscious," and if one accepts a causal relationship between the dissimilar and the non-dissimilar, then since difference is necessarily entailed by dissimilarity, there would arise a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the identity of cause and effect. As for the established doctrine:

If it is argued that, despite the difference between worms and honey and so forth, a causal relationship is observed there because the insentient portion of the worm is of the same nature as honey, and thus there is a similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*), we say no. For if some kind of similarity were the cause of a causal relationship, then everything could arise from anything.

The objection that [the effect] would follow as being identical [to the cause] is based on your intended notion of similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) by way of the unique, specific form residing in the cause. However, that cannot be established here, because the nature of being a honeybee (*mākṣikatva*) is absent in a worm. Thus, the relationship of cause and effect is established even between the world and Brahman, despite their having different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*). Nor does this entail the admission of difference; for even when similarity is denied, non-difference remains possible, just as in the case of a bracelet and gold.

Furthermore, if there were no difference between the world and Brahman, then since the creation and so forth of the world exist, the states of the world—which are to be abandoned—would exist in Brahman as well, just as they do in the world. Consequently, there would arise the predicament of inconsistency: that within the one Brahman alone, there would be both qualities to be abandoned and their opposites, such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, which are established by other scriptural passages.

Since the non-difference between cause and effect—which is accepted as the established doctrine (siddhānta)—is of the nature that Brahman having the subtle sentient and insentient entities as its body is the cause, while Brahman having the gross sentient and insentient entities as its body is the effect, the [alleged] consequence does not arise; for there exists the supporting example of the non-connection of childhood, youth, old age, and so forth with the Self, given that the attributes residing in the body do not extend to the embodied one.

And thus, although it can be said that there is a similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) between the cause and the effect insofar as their respective qualifying aspects—the gross and subtle bodies—are insentient, while their substantive aspects are sentient; nevertheless, by accepting that the substantive aspect of the cause must also be admitted as the cause for the qualifying aspect of the effect, a dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is established. In this regard, there is an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

This has been proposed: for even when a thing in its state of childhood undergoes a transition to another state such as youth, the specific aspect residing in the cause remains a causal factor even with respect to the qualifying aspect residing in the effect; this is because a body devoid of a self cannot attain youth and so forth. Thus, it is shown that here too, despite the difference in nature, the relationship of cause and effect is logically established.
The summary verses.

"How could the insentient universe arise from that which possesses sentience? This objection is too crude; for if there were a cause-and-effect relationship between two distinct entities, this objection would indeed find no footing."
Nevertheless, it is said that there is a counter-argument to the argument; absolute similarity is not observed anywhere.
In some way or another, this applies even to the case under discussion, but especially so in the case of worms, bees, and the like.
Thus concludes the section concerning the difference in characteristics.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.

This section is intended to extend the previous reasoning in order to dispel a further doubt: namely, that even if there is no subversion of the doctrine of coordination (*samanvaya*) by the logic of the Sāṃkhyas alone—who maintain primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause—there might still be such a subversion by the logic favored by the many followers of the three systems, such as Kaṇāda (the eater of atoms), Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama), and the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas), who maintain atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the cause.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from doubt regarding whether the refutation of the doctrine of homogeneity (*samanvaya-bhaṅga*) occurs through the reasoning of those who maintain that atoms are the cause, despite the existence of mutual contradictions among them; this doubt concerns whether they possess the capacity for such a refutation or not. Such capacity for refutation is indeed possible, just as when dogs, though mutually antagonistic, act with a common purpose out of a desire to devour a boar, resulting in the death of the boar even if they do not all succeed in catching it.

Thus, although there exist internal disputes among those who maintain that atoms are real, empty, of the nature of consciousness, momentary, fourfold, or singlefold, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: since it is observed that only things of small dimension, such as threads and the like, can be the originators (*ārambhaka*) of large-dimensional effects such as cloth, the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) between Brahman and the world—which possess dimensions contrary to one another—is impossible. Therefore, the refutation of that [atomistic theory] is established by means of the logic accepted by all proponents of atomism. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Just as the single sun dispels even a vast mass of darkness scattered in various directions, so too does the Veda itself remain awake, refuting the aforementioned and other such webs of reasoning by means of counter-examples—such as the clay-lump and others—starting with the passage, "O dear one, as by a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay [is known]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4). Therefore, no further effort need be exerted here.
The summary verses.
The doctrine of atoms as the cause, though established here through reasoning according to the views of many disputants, is in vain;
for one who is exhausted by the quarrels over its internal subdivisions will have no power at the boundary of the revealed scripture.

"The view of those who argue that 'from the small comes the great' and 'the great does not come from the small' has been cast aside by the Śruti through the description of the dog and the boar as examples."
Thus concludes the section concerning that which is not accepted by the learned.
If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the identity with the enjoyer, [we reply] that it may be so, as in the case of the world.

Since the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*) serves as a basis for extension (*atideśa*), this present section is connected to it by way of its foundational source rather than by directly following it. For in that [preceding] section, by means of the sūtra, "But not so, because of the existence of the analogy" (*na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt*), it was stated—using as an analogy the fact that childhood, youth, and so forth residing in the body do not apply to the embodied soul—that defects residing in Brahman, whose body consists of the sentient and insentient (*cid-acit*), do not attach to Brahman itself. That [conclusion] is challenged as being untenable; for if Brahman were the embodied soul like the individual self (*jīva*), there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain produced by that [body]. Thus the objection is raised.

In the first chapter, by the sūtra “If it be argued that there would be the attainment of experience [of pleasure and pain], no, because of the difference [in nature],” the possibility of the Supreme Being undergoing the experience of pleasure and pain resulting from entering bodies such as our own was refuted. Just as the owner of a house does not partake of joy or dejection caused by the completeness or deficiency of a house entered by another, so it is with the Supreme Being. Here, however, that [experience] resulting from being the master of the body is refuted.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because of the scriptural statement, "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant," it is impossible to prevent the experience of pleasure and pain caused by that [body] as long as one holds ownership of the body. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Just as one who has built a prison to afflict an offender in accordance with his crime, and having entered it himself for that purpose, does not incur the suffering caused by that act because he is independent, so it is for the Supreme Lord as well. Furthermore, scriptural texts such as "Not indeed for one who possesses a body" (*na ha vai saśarīrasya*) refer to a body acquired through one's own karma, and not merely to the state of being a master of a body.

This is evident from the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, which, after stating the Supreme Lord’s mastery over the bodies of earth and other elements in passages such as "whose body is the earth," [proceeds to describe His transcendence].

Just as in the case of the presiding deities of those respective things, the statement of immortality in every instance—"This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal"—is intended precisely to dispel the suspicion that [the Inner Controller] might be subject to the pleasure and pain produced by them.
The summary verses.
If Brahman, whose body consists of consciousness and unconsciousness, were described as the cause,
then this embodied being would necessarily be the experiencer of pleasure and pain.

Let it not be so; that [agency] is produced by karma and is not produced by the body, therefore it would not belong to the body, just as the power to bestow favor or inflict punishment belongs to the king.
Thus ends the section concerning the identity of the enjoyer.
The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning "origination" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.
And because [the self] is perceived when there is a mental state.
And because there is existence of another.

If it be argued that [the soul] does not [exist] because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for [its existence] is established by means of another attribute, on account of the supplementary passage, logical reasoning, and other scriptural texts.
And like a cloth.
And as in the case of the vital breath and so forth.

In the section concerning difference in characteristics (*vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*), it was established against the Sāṃkhya that even though the effect—the world—is different in character from its cause—Brahman—it is nonetheless non-different from it, as stated in the *Guṇasūtra*: "If it be said 'no,' because [the word] 'non-existent' is a mere negation," and this was demonstrated by the analogy of the earring and gold. Now, however, it is argued that non-difference is untenable when there is a difference in characteristics, since difference in characteristics is pervaded by (i.e., implies) actual difference; for this very reason, the non-difference between the earring and the gold is also unestablished.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having adopted the view of the Vaiśeṣika—who asserts that "in all cases, a distinction between cause and effect must necessarily exist on account of differences in cognition, distinct words, and so forth"—the non-difference [of the world from Brahman] is challenged and then resolved. In this regard, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: if there were non-difference [between them], it would be impossible for Brahman to be the cause of the world. This is because, in the world, we determine through differences in cognition, distinct words, and so forth, that the causal relationship between things such as a jar and a lump of clay is pervaded by their difference.

For neither does the word "clay-lump" arise in the pot, nor does the cognition of the form of a lump arise in the pot; nor is the word "pot" applied to the clay-lump, nor is the word "lump" applied to the pot; nor does the form of a lump exist in the pot, nor does the broad-based and bulbous form exist in the clay-lump; nor is water-carrying performed by the clay-lump, nor is wall-construction performed by the pot; nor is there multiplicity in the pot as there is in the threads, nor is there unity in the threads as there is in the pot.

Furthermore, the staff, the wheel, and so forth do not constitute the cause of the jar in the same way that the lump of clay does; nor does the kneading preceded by the addition of water constitute the cause of the jar in the same way that the lump of clay does. Moreover, the lump of clay does not exist at the time when the jar exists, nor does the jar exist at the time when the lump of clay exists. Furthermore, there is no perception of the jar and so forth at the earlier time, nor is there a perception of the lump of clay at the later time. Therefore, due to the difference in cognition, verbal designation, and so forth, a distinction between cause and effect must be admitted.

If it is argued that, just as the distinctions between states such as childhood and youth occur within a single body, or as the distinctions between states such as a lump of clay and a jar occur within a single material substance like clay, so too do differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth arise—[we reply: no, because if these states were impermanent, it would result in the fallacy of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause), since it is impossible for impermanent states to be non-different from their cause, which must exist prior [to them].

Furthermore, this would result in the collapse of the established doctrine that the cause and its effect are non-different. For if those [states] were also eternal, it would be impossible to establish the distinctions between cognition, different words, and so forth, and it would entail the absurdity of the entire collection of causes—such as the staff and the wheel—being useless. [Objection: But surely, while clay is in the state of a lump, the state of being a jar is unmanifest; it is only when that state becomes manifest that it becomes the locus for different cognitions, words, and so on. And the collection of causes, such as the staff and the wheel, serves the purpose of bringing about that manifestation.

And this being the case, it does not follow that by the operation of the staff, wheel, and so forth—which serves to manifest the state of a jar residing in a lump of clay—one would also have to manifest the states of the handle, the rim, the neck, the bowl, and so on, just as a lamp brought in to manifest a jar in a room might be said to manifest the handle and other parts within it. For although both blueness and the nature of a blue lotus are present, the light of the lamp manifests only the nature of the lotus.

If it is argued that—just as we observe a fixed rule such that when the water of one well remains within another well, there is the manifestation of "water-ness" alone among the properties of water and whiteness, and thus a variety of relationships between the manifested and the manifestor is possible here as well according to observation—it is not so.

Even regarding manifestation (*abhivyakti*), the previously mentioned faults would not fail to apply to the alternatives of its being either eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, what is this manifestation? If it is cognition (*jñāna*), then since the conjunction of the staff, wheel, and so forth would result in being the cause of the cognition of the jar, in the absence of that [conjunction], the arising of the cognition of the jar would never occur anywhere. If it is the suppression of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), then what is that obscuration suppressed by it? If you say it is the state of the lump (*piṇḍāvasthā*) previously residing in the clay—no.

If that were the case, it would follow that even after the blow of a mallet that destroys a jar, the state of the jar would still be perceived; for its veil, namely the state of the lump [of clay], would have been concealed at that time. [Objection: But surely, at that moment, the state of the shards manifested by the blow of the mallet is the veil; for it is accepted that any effect-state manifested by its own cause serves as a veil for all other effect-states residing within it.

And this being the case, there is no unwanted consequence that the state of a jar would manifest at some time when the causes of the jar are assembled within the shards; for such an outcome is accepted. Furthermore, by pulverizing the shards and applying operations such as mixing with water and clay, and kneading, softness [is produced].

If it is argued that this is because the manifestation of a jar is observed when the collection of causes such as the staff and the wheel is brought together; and that one should not suspect that the state of being a cloth is never seen again in the case of the causes of a burnt cloth—since the ashes of that cloth, having fallen upon the surface of the earth, eventually manifest as cloth through the gradual transformation of the fruit of a cotton tree grown from that soil—we say: not so.

Likewise, regarding the existence of states such as that of a jar within states such as a lump of clay, since there is no basis for postulation (*kalpakābhāva*)—both for the claim that they are not perceived at that time and for the claim that the currently perceived states of the lump and so forth act as their concealers—it is logically consistent to establish these states as adventitious (*āgantuka*) according to actual experience. Otherwise, the distinction between what is experienced and what is not experienced would be untenable; for one might then have to explain why only a particular state is ever experienced at a given time, while other states are never experienced at all.

For manifestation is not something obtained by the self-choice of experience, whereby one could establish a fixed rule such that there is the experience of the state of the lump alone prior to the conjunction of the staff, wheel, and so forth; then the experience of the state of the jar alone immediately thereafter; and then the experience of the state of the shards alone after the fall of the mallet, and so on.

Nor can the establishment [of the distinction between states] be maintained by asserting that the conjunction with water, the softening of the clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth, as well as the striking with a mallet, are the instruments for the experiences of the states of the lump, the jar, and the shards—whether those various other states are experienced or not. This is because even after the aforementioned respective causes have ceased, there persists the experience of the states such as the lump and the non-experience of their respective opposites.

Therefore, it is reasonable to accept the established order according to experience: first the state of the lump alone, then in the middle the state of the jar alone, and finally the state of the shards alone. If it is argued that since this is so, the states are adventitious and thus the theory of non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) would follow, and that this [theory] is postulated to avoid that consequence—[we reply: does that [consequence] not follow when the manifestations (*abhivyakti*) are adventitious? Furthermore, if the manifestations themselves are eternal, how can the established order you described be established in any way?

Thus, since the states or their respective manifestations are adventitious, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) remains beyond refutation; consequently, the acceptance of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be purposeless if it were restricted merely to the substance (*dravya*).

Just as one observes the uncontradicted linguistic usage of distinction between the agent and the action in such cases as "the pot was made by the potter" (*kulālena ghaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) and "the earring was made by Kalāda" (*kalādena kuṇḍalaṃ kṛtam*), so too does one observe the uncontradicted linguistic usage of distinction between the inherent cause and the effect inhering in it in such cases as "the pot was made from a lump of clay" (*mṛtpiṇḍena ghaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) and "the earring was made from gold" (*suvarṇena kuṇḍalaṃ kṛtam*). Therefore, it is logical to accept a difference in substance between cause and effect, just as there is a difference in their states. If it is argued that the linguistic usage of distinction is sublated by the linguistic usage of non-distinction—as in "the pot is clay" (*mṛdghaṭaḥ*) or "the earring is gold" (*suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalam*)—we say no.

Since the properties of "earth-ness" (*mṛttva*) and "gold-ness" (*suvarṇatva*) are universals (*jāti*) residing in both parts and the whole, such conventional usage is logically consistent; therefore, it is impossible for that [usage] to subvert the conventional usage of difference. For this very reason, where a universal such as "thread-ness" (*tantutva*) resides in the parts but not in the whole cloth, there is no such conventional usage as "the threads are the cloth."

Therefore, because it is logical that there is indeed a difference between the substance of cause and effect due to their co-existence—and because in the world one observes a fixed rule regarding the distinction between cause and effect—it is impossible for Brahman to be the cause of the world if the world were non-different from Brahman; thus, the claim that there is a "harmonious convergence" (*samanvaya*) upon Brahman as the cause of the world does not hold. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

The non-difference from that means the very non-difference of the world from Brahman, the supreme cause; this is established by the scriptural passages beginning with the word *ārambhaṇa*. Thus, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having introduced the subject with "There was once Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi; his father said to him," and then instructing him, "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student; for, my dear, no one in our family has ever returned without having studied the Vedas—he would be like a kinsman of a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied," [the text describes] his departure to the teacher’s house and his return after staying there for twelve years.

Having said, "He shall return when he is twenty-four years old," the father—perceiving his son's pride rooted in his study of the Vedas, desiring to remove that pride, and wishing to arouse in him the desire to know Brahman (brahmajijñāsā)—questioned him as follows: "Are you so conceited? Ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. This means: by which [instruction] being heard, thought, and understood; for another Śruti says: "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and understood, all this becomes known."

Thus, having kept in mind that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause and that the effect is non-different from its cause, and once the proposition had been stated that by the knowledge of Brahman there is the knowledge of everything, the son—failing to understand the intended meaning and thinking, "How can the knowledge of one thing result in the knowledge of another?"—asked, "How, indeed, O Venerable One, is the instruction given? To this, the father spoke a worldly illustration regarding the non-difference of the effect from the cause in order to establish his own proposition; so it has been described.

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay might be known"—the meaning is that just as jars, bowls, and so forth, which are produced from a single lump of clay, are known through the knowledge of that [clay] because they do not possess a substance distinct from it.

In this context, having raised the objection—based on the Vaiśeṣika method—that the effect is a distinct substance from the cause due to differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth, the remainder of the passage, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," is intended to establish the non-difference of the effect from the cause through common worldly experience. Its meaning is as follows: *ārambhaṇam* means that which is commenced, grasped, or touched. The letter *ra* is used for *la*, as in the phrase "He beheld the middle of the stream," because *ra* and *la* are not distinct. Here, *ālambha* refers to touching.

The authors of the *Kośa* state that the root *ālabh* means "to touch" or "to injure. Here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The word "by speech" (*vācā*) means by the cause of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), such as fetching water preceded by a sentence like "fetch water with a jar. By the term "speech," practical activity itself is also included through the figure of speech known as *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication). The instrumental case in "by speech" (*vācā*) denotes the cause, as in the expression "he dwells for the purpose of study" (*adhyayanena hetunā vasati*), where the purpose is intended to function as the cause.

For the sake of establishing conventional usage preceded by speech, a specific configuration—a modification such as having a broad base and a bulbous belly—is touched upon by means of the material clay itself, and the name "pot" (ghaṭa) is applied to it on that account. According to the rule "The neuter [remains] with the non-neuter, and optionally singular," the word *ārambhaṇa*, which refers to both the modification and the name, takes the neuter gender and the singular number.

For the sake of accomplishing specific worldly transactions such as fetching water, the substance of clay itself undergoes different states and receives different names. Therefore, even a jar and the like are real and authoritative only as clay, and not as a different substance. By the phrase "from the word *ārambhaṇa* and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought, 'May I be many, may I grow forth,'" which establish the non-difference between the effect and the cause, namely the world and Brahman.
And thus, although according to the perspective of a child and an elder...

Differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth, are accounted for by differences in state (*avasthābheda*), just as objects like a jar or a golden ornament are accounted for by differences in substance (*dravyabheda*). Indeed, a difference in substance would provide the ultimate consistency. Nevertheless, since the scripture—citing examples such as clay and a jar—teaches the non-difference of cause and effect, it demonstrates that there is only a difference in state; therefore, one must accept that differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth, are caused solely by differences in state. Nor is it a fault to claim that states are adventitious (*āgantuka*), as this does not entail the fallacy of the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*).

Indeed, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the arising of a substance that already exists; it does not mean, however, that even its various states (*avasthā*) are non-accidental. Nor is there any logical impossibility in the arising of a substance that already exists previously. For we do not accept that "arising" means coming into being after having been non-existent. Rather, arising is the production of a different state, while destruction is the relinquishing of the previous state. In this way, when jars, bowls, and so forth are produced from a single lump of clay, there is the attainment of a state of multiplicity through the relinquishing of the state of oneness.

In a cloth woven from densely packed threads, there occurs the attainment of the state of unity through the abandonment of the state of multiplicity. Therefore, in a cloth woven from loosely spaced threads, even when the state of unity belonging to the cloth is attained, there is no abandonment of multiplicity—just as the nature of being a thread (*tantutva*) persists; rather, multiplicity continues to exist as delimited by the nature of being a thread (*tantutvāvacchedena*), while unity is attained as delimited by the nature of being a cloth (*paṭatvāvacchedena*). Such specific distinctions should also be understood in accordance with what is observed.

Now, it has been explained that by the scriptural text, "It is clay alone that is real," which means that for a jar, a bowl, and so forth, only the clay is authoritative and not their status as separate substances, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has also been shown regarding the non-difference of the substance of the effect from its cause. If one asks what that other means of knowledge is, we reply: it is the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*). For even while the state of the lump of clay persists, the existence of the substance of the jar, bowl, and so forth is perceived through the perception of recognition.

Regarding this, we observe the recognition that "all these things, such as the jar and the bowl, existed earlier in the morning as nothing but a lump of clay," meaning that the single mound of clay situated in the morning was of this very extent—namely, the form of the jar, the bowl, and so forth. Now, one might object that in common worldly usage it is also observed that "all these things, such as the jar and the bowl, did not exist in the morning. Likewise, in the Śruti it is stated, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asat*)," thereby designating the prior non-existence of the world.

If it is asked how the establishment of the non-difference between cause and effect in both the world and the Veda is proven by direct perception and scripture, it is said in reply: this designation of "non-existent" refers to that other property of subtlety which is opposed to the grossness of the broad base, belly, and so forth; it does not mean that the effect was absolutely non-existent prior [to its production].

Why? Because of the remainder of the scriptural statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). For in the passage, "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing whatsoever," there is heard a remainder of the statement that conveys the mental volition (*mānasa-saṅkalpa*) called "mentalizing" (*manaskāra*) regarding the non-existent, namely: "That [non-existent] made itself, thinking, 'May I be. Even in common worldly usage, it is understood through reasoning that the designation "non-existent" (*asad-vyapadeśa*) arises for that very reason. Indeed, everywhere, there is no such thing as "absence" (*abhāva*) apart from the exclusion of those specific properties that are its opposites.

Since it is sufficient for the conventional usage of "non-existence" (abhāva) to have as its objective support simply another established positive entity (*dharma*) that is opposed to the object of conceptualization—just as [the absence of a jar is understood through the presence of its opposite]—it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate non-existence. Furthermore, because there is another word in both common parlance (*loka*) and the Veda that is the antonym of the term "non-existent" (*asat*), such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), and "This [world], consisting of jars, bowls, and so forth, in the forenoon... [is perceived].

It is understood from such statements as "the clay alone existed" that the designation of non-existence is weaker than the designation of existence—which culminates in the non-difference between cause and effect—due to its lack of supporting reasoning. Indeed, the reasoning previously set forth was that no other entity called "non-existence" (abhāva) should be postulated apart from the absence of contradictory positive attributes. For example, the threads themselves do not exist as a separate composite substance called "cloth" apart from the interwoven threads.

For if it were devoid of color and so forth, it would follow that it lacks visibility and other such qualities; and if it possessed a different color and so forth, it would follow that a distinct color would be perceived in the whole apart from the colors of its parts, as well as a doubling of its weight.

Thus, just as there is the state of a cloth in threads that are interwoven, and just as there is the state of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth in the single element of air through its various modes of functioning within the body, so too the existence of the world in its diverse forms of moving and non-moving beings is possible from Brahman alone; therefore, one should conclude that the designation of "Being" (sat) is more powerful than the designation of distinct entities, based on this reasoning as well. And in this way, even common usage such as "a ring was made from gold" is to be explained solely through the relation of cause and effect produced by a difference in states.

Otherwise, if gold were weighed and given to a goldsmith to be made into an earring, and after he had fashioned the earring, it would have to be returned by him upon weighing again as being twice as heavy; therefore, because there is non-difference between the lump of clay and the jar, bowl, and so forth, by that example, there is likewise non-difference between Brahman and the world, which stand in the relation of material cause and effect.
Summary Verses.

The diversity of effects from their causes—due to distinctions such as intellect (*buddhi*), word (*śabda*), form (*ākṛti*), fruit (*phala*), enumeration (*gaṇanā*), cause (*hetu*), time (*kāla*), and so forth—is not permanent; that diversity does not arise from a difference in the states (*daśā*) of the cause. For it is a single [cause] alone that manifests various states through different times, appearing in forms such as existence and non-existence; thus, this entire world is indeed non-different from Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the originative material cause (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa).
On account of the designation of [the Self] as something else, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. (21)
Furthermore, [the self is] distinct, because of the teaching of its differentiation. ||22||
And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is untenable. ||23||

The introductory connection (*saṅgati*) is by way of an objection: if Brahman were the creator of the world without being distinct from it, defects such as His failure to act for the benefit [of the world] would follow; and this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Nor can Brahman’s causality—with respect to the subtle aggregate of sentient and insentient phenomena—be established by the cited examples of a lump of clay and its products like a jar or a bowl, nor can His state of being the effect—with respect to the gross aggregate of sentient and insentient phenomena—be established thereby."

It should not be said that non-difference is stated only between Brahman and its effects and causes, and not between Brahman and the world; for since Brahman is the cause of all, its causality must necessarily be affirmed even with respect to the world—which is its own effect—consisting of the sentient and insentient as its specific attributes.

Consequently, since non-difference from that [Brahman] must also be asserted for the individual soul (jīva), it would follow that Brahman—which is omniscient and omnipotent—though perceiving the jīva as non-different from itself, creates a world that is not beneficial to it, but rather creates a world that is indeed harmful; thus, defects such as the failure to act for its own benefit would accrue to Brahman itself. Therefore, the claim that Brahman creates a world that is non-different from itself is untenable. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

Brahman is superior to the individual soul (jīva) and is indeed distinct from it. This is because of scriptural indications of difference, such as: "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true"; "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord"; "He who is with cause, the lord of the lords of the senses"; and "The Illusionist creates this universe, while another, bound by illusion, is confined within Him. However, the scriptural texts concerning non-difference refer to the state of being non-separate. For the phenomenal world, consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, exists as a mode of Brahman that is not separate from It.

In the scriptural passage beginning with "sadeva," the subsequent statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—"All this was Being alone"—indicates that in its subtle state, the world possesses the status of being a qualifier of Brahman, who is denoted by the word "Being. Furthermore, this is supported by the description of Brahman’s resolve to become manifold, expressed as: "It thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate.'"

By demonstrating that [the world] possesses the status of being a qualification of That (Brahman) during its state of grossness, it is understood that the world never exists as something separate from Brahman; thus, even the clay, the jar, the bowl, and so forth, serve as examples for non-difference insofar as they consist in non-separateness, because it is impossible for anything to ever exist separately from itself when it is non-different from itself.

Nor should it be argued that the scriptural texts concerning non-difference, such as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "That thou art," have as their primary object the essential identity [of the self and Brahman], whereas the scriptural texts concerning difference refer only to a figurative difference based on the distinction between various attributes; for if that were so, one would fail to avoid the very defects already entailed, such as the failure to perform what is beneficial, and because it is impossible for individual souls—whose qualities are utterly to be abandoned like stone, wood, or clods of earth—to be identical with Brahman, who consists solely of faultless, auspicious qualities.

Therefore, it is logical that the scriptural passages concerning non-difference, such as those stated in the sūtra beginning with "Because of the subsistence [of the world in Brahman], thus [says] Kāśakṛtsna," have as their object the relationship between a substrate and its mode in which they are not separate.
The Summary Verses.
In this way, since individual souls (*jīvas*) are necessarily non-different from Brahman according to such statements as "That thou art," one should not perform creation devoid of Him.

This is not so; for the statement does not intend to express identity, since difference is observed [in scripture]. Rather, it is taught that [the soul] exists within Him; such is the position of Kāśakṛtsna.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the other.
If it be argued that [the soul does not pervade the body] because we observe its withdrawal, we say no; for it is like milk. 24.
And also like the gods and others in the world. ||25||

Because of the mention of distinctions such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpa*), the scriptural texts concerning non-difference (*ananya*) refer merely to the state of being non-separate. It is not the case, however, that even if Brahman possesses true resolve and omnipotence, the scriptural texts regarding Brahman’s being the material cause (*upādāna*) and the creator (*sraṣṭṛ*) of the world can be justified [if it were entirely independent]. For even one who is capable cannot produce an effect if devoid of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). This constitutes the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) arising from this objection.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: By the restrictive statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," Brahman is indeed heard in scripture to be devoid of all auxiliary causes prior to creation. How then could it attain the status of being the cause of the world? Nor can any distinction be made on the basis of its possessing all powers; for even a potter, who possesses the power to produce jars and the like, produces them only by depending upon auxiliary factors.

In this way, if Brahman also possesses the power to produce all effects, it must produce those various effects only by depending upon auxiliary causes (sahakārī) appropriate for each respective effect. For a potter, though he has the power to produce a jar, does not produce it without depending on auxiliary causes. One who lacks power does not produce it even when auxiliaries are present; this indeed is the distinction between the powerful and the powerless. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that Brahman, being devoid of auxiliaries, cannot be the cause. However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows:

Even in the absence of auxiliary causes, Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe and its creatorship are both established, just as milk attains the state of curd, or as gods, sages, and others create the means for their respective enjoyments. Furthermore, in the transformation of milk into curd, neither heating nor churning serve as auxiliary causes; likewise, there is no auxiliary cause whatsoever for Brahman’s role as the material cause of the universe.

Furthermore, for gods and others who have attained sovereignty through the power of yoga and thus possess mastery over the elements (*bhūta-vaśin*), the status of creator is established by means of elements drawn forth by their own volition. If it is argued that the Lord, being eternally perfected, does not possess such a power of yoga that brings about mastery over the elements—this is not so. Even without heating or churning, milk certainly becomes curd after a long time; however, there is a need for those two [processes] to bring about the state of curd quickly and to produce a specific flavor.

The attainment of lordly power (*aiśvarya*) through the practice of yoga is to be understood from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts. Furthermore, there is no distinction [between the yogin and the Lord] insofar as even Brahman is a creator by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), for there are scriptural mantras and explanatory passages to that effect. Moreover, it is observed that everyone causes their own body to function by mere volition; since the entire world is the body of Brahman, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in His presiding over the operations of the world.
Summary Verses.
How could that which exists as a single unity at the beginning, devoid of auxiliary causes, serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world?
And how could it create [the world] by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), like a deity or the like, through milk and so forth? Understand this thus.
Thus ends the section concerning the observation of reabsorption (*upasaṃhāradarśana*).
Either there would be the consequence of the whole [cause] being consumed, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding its partlessness. (26)
But [the authority of the Smṛti] rests on Śruti, because it has its root in the Word [of the Veda]. ||27||
And likewise within the self, for they are indeed manifold. ||28||
And because of the defect in one's own position. ||29||
And by seeing that, one becomes endowed with everything. ||30||
If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered. ||31||

If, by the analogy of milk, Brahman undergoes a transformation into the state of the world, then—just as milk entirely becomes curd—it would follow that Brahman too must undergo a transformation into the state of the world in its entirety; this constitutes the objection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Does Brahman transform into the form of the world in its entirety, like milk transforming into the form of curd?

Or does it transform only in certain parts used for various effects, like a lump of clay joined with fire transforming only in one part used for a ring or similar object? It cannot be the first, because if the whole were to become the world, it would follow that no Brahman remains.

Nor can it be argued that there is no contingency of the defect of leaving nothing remaining of Brahman in the position where Brahman qualified by the subtle *cit* and *acit* manifold is the cause, and Brahman qualified by the gross *cit* and *acit* manifold is the effect, because Brahman exists as the effect; for it must now be stated that Brahman exists even in its causal form. Otherwise, there would follow the futility of those scriptural passages which teach the eternal existence of Brahman as the cause and which enjoin the knowledge (*vidyā*) that is the means to its direct realization.

Furthermore, since Brahman, as the material cause of everything, must be declared to be the cause even with respect to its specific attributes consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness, the objection remains as unassailable as a diamond coating (*vajralepa*): that if the entire Brahman were to transform into the nature of one effect, there could be no transformation into the nature of other effects, nor could there be any remaining portion of the causal Brahman. Therefore, the first position is not tenable. Nor is the second position tenable. If it is argued that because a partless entity cannot undergo transformation through a single part, it must therefore be admitted to have parts, we say: no.

This is because it would entail a contradiction with scriptural texts such as "partless, actionless, and tranquil," which declare that [Brahman] is devoid of parts. Therefore, the view that Brahman is the material cause of the world is incorrect. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

There is no room for such doubt, because the Śruti itself explicitly teaches that Brahman, though partless, transforms into the form of the world while remaining as before, perfectly complete in itself. An object established by the Śruti cannot be subverted by fallacious reasoning; for the Śruti declares: "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning. If it is argued that even the Śruti is unable to teach what is contradicted by other means of valid cognition—just as in the case of stones floating on water—the answer is: no.

Because Brahman is understood solely through the word (śabda), it is distinct from that [empirical reality]. For even the Śruti does not convey anything contradictory regarding an object that is accessible to perception and other means of knowledge; however, an object that is knowable only through the Śruti is established precisely as the Śruti presents it. It cannot be sublated by another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that is incapable of having that as its object. Indeed, the ear, which is incapable of apprehending color, cannot sublate it. Furthermore, in the case of the individual self (jīvātman), agency, enjoyership, and so forth—which are distinct from the attributes of insentience—are accepted.

In this way, why should there not be attributes in the Supreme Self that are distinct from the attributes of consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit)? In the world, even fire, water, and so forth, are seen to be diverse by virtue of their heat, cold, and other qualities; indeed, they are not accepted as being devoid of mutually distinct attributes merely on the basis of mutual analogy. Nor is it the case that "a genus (jāti) exists in an individual (vyakti) neither partially—because it is partless—nor by being fully contained."

"Because it would follow that [the universal] is absent in other individuals"—thus, by means of the dilemma of whether it subsists in its entirety or in part, the subsistence of the universal (*jāti*) in the individual (*vyakti*) is refuted. And this same objection applies equally to the Sāṃkhya’s own position: how can the partless *pradhāna* be the originator of diverse effects such as the *mahat* and so forth? If it is argued that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are its parts, we say no.

If one were to admit that those parts of [Prakṛti] exist apart from Pradhāna itself, it would contradict the established number of twenty-four principles (*tattva*); furthermore, those parts too could not serve as the originators of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and so forth, due to the dilemma of whether they originate them as a whole or by their parts. This same logic applies to proponents of atomism (*paramāṇu-vāda*) and other theories of causal origins, for whom the production of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and subsequent entities is likewise untenable due to the dilemmas of conjunction as a whole or by parts.

Therefore, for one who considers even the postulated *pradhāna* to be beyond the scope of the dilemma regarding whether it exists as a whole or in part, what hope can there be that Brahman—established by scripture—is within such a scope? Furthermore, because Brahman is endowed with all powers, its transformation into the form of the diverse world is possible even though it is without parts; for Brahman is indeed endowed with all powers, as seen in such scriptural passages as, "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold."

Even among those possessing limited power—the sentient and insentient entities within the phenomenal world—an inconceivable and manifold diversity is observed. How then could this not belong to Him who possesses all powers? Now, it may be argued that even for those with power, the manifestation of that power is seen to depend upon instruments and bodies; therefore, [how can He manifest power] independently of such things? Even though [He is independent],...

If it is argued that possessing all powers (*sarvaśaktimattva*) is irrelevant to the study [of the Vedas], just as possessing intellectual power is irrelevant [to worldly action]—the answer to this has already been stated: an entity whose sole authority is the Word (*śabda*) must be accepted exactly as the Word describes it. It cannot be rejected on the grounds of an absence of causes observed in the world. And thus says the Śruti: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes and hears without ears. No activity or instrument is found in Him; neither anyone equal to Him nor anyone superior to Him is seen."

"His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are innate. Therefore, it is entirely logical that Brahman, though partless, transforms itself into the form of the universe and remains fully complete in that very state, as established by scripture and supported by the reasoning shown therein.
The summary verses.

If Brahman were to undergo transformation in its entirety, then nothing would remain; nor could it do so partially, because it is partless. This same objection applies even to the specific position [of partial transformation].
Such defects would apply to the Pradhāna and to atoms and the like,
but not to Brahman, who is endowed with manifold powers as established by hundreds of scriptural texts.
Thus concludes the section concerning the consequence of the whole [of Brahman] being affected.
Not so, because it possesses a purpose. ||32||
But as in the world, [the Lord's action] is mere sport. ||33||
There is no inequality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He takes account of [other factors]; for thus Scripture shows. 34.

If it be argued that [the distinction between soul and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of action, we say no; for it is established by the beginninglessness [of the series], and it is both logically justified and observed. ||35||
And because all phenomena arise [from it]. ||36||

Even though the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been established by refuting defects such as the over-extension of the principle to everything through scripture supported by reasoning, it is not possible to establish its status as the creator (*sraṣṭṛtva*). This is because the activity of an intelligent being is necessarily governed by the rule that it must have a purpose; this constitutes the connection based on the arising of a doubt. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): Is the creation of the world by Brahman for its own sake or for the sake of others? It cannot be the first, because one who has attained all desires lacks any purpose to be sought.

Nor should it be suspected that even for discerning persons, the perception of games such as ball-play is seen to be purposeless; for even in those intent on play, there exists a temporary joy arising from it. Furthermore, one should not postulate a similar motive for Brahman in the creation of the universe, because that would contradict the scriptural testimony that [Brahman] has attained all desires. If it is argued that even kings who have attained all their desires are seen to engage in games like ball-play—the answer is no.

For even those who have attained all desires through the enjoyment of various objects still engage in that [creation] solely for the sake of obtaining the joy of playful sport (*krīḍānanda*), which they have not yet obtained.
