But such a thing cannot be said of Brahman. Furthermore, if Brahman were to immerse living beings in the suffering of *saṃsāra* for its own sake, it would follow that Brahman is partial (*vaiṣamya*) and cruel (*nairghṛṇya*). Moreover, its play (*līlā*) would be comparable to the play of Aśmaka and Sagara’s sons. By this, the second position—that creation is for the sake of others—is also refuted.

For if creation were for the sake of another, He would surely create all beings as happy alone; He would not create some happy and others miserable through partiality and inequality. Furthermore, it would follow that there is cruelty in one who creates miserable beings. Nor should it be argued that Brahman brings suffering upon sinners merely to protect them by exhausting their karma—just as a physician inflicts the pain of cauterizing or cutting a wound merely to protect the patient from it.

For while it is possible for a physician who is unable to effect the healing of a wound without first causing burning and other such pains to inflict suffering such as burning upon the patient, it is impossible for Brahman—who possesses all powers and is capable of protecting beings even without inflicting suffering—to cause them to experience it. Nor should it be argued that the faults of partiality and cruelty do not attach to the Creator of an unequal world when He is dependent upon the respective karmas [of those beings].

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," thus it is heard that in the primordial creation, there remains only Brahman. Since there is an absence of karma at that time, the objection that the unequal creation of that period would entail partiality and cruelty cannot be avoided. Therefore, it is argued that Brahman’s status as the creator of the world is not tenable. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

True. The activity of a discerning person is indeed for the sake of a purpose. Here too, there exists a purpose in the form of sport (*līlā*) for Brahman through creation, just as it does for a king or a child through dice-games and the like. This is because of the words of the venerable Parāśara: "All this is the sport of Hari; let it be understood that it is perishable. Behold His activity, like that of a playing child. And this being so, there is no contradiction with Brahman’s state of having attained all desires.

The capacity to obtain whatever one desires is indeed the attainment of all desires; however, this is common even to universal monarchs (*sārvabhauma*) and others, and does not imply the fulfillment of every desire at all times. Otherwise, there would arise the defects of partiality and cruelty due to the unequal creation of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, according to differences in time such as cold and heat, because of the scriptural statement: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action. The inequality of the world is rooted in specific actions (*karma*); God is merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta-mātra*) in its production, serving as the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*), just as rain is the common cause for the growth of crops.

This disparity—such as the greater or lesser quantity, or the nature of rice, barley, and so forth—is accepted as being produced by the specific differences of the field, the seed, and other factors. As stated by the venerable Parāśara: "He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating those things to be created, since the powers of the objects to be created are indeed the primary causes. Here, "the powers of the objects to be created" refers to the actions of those things to be created.

And thus, when Brahmā observes the worldly dealings of his subjects and bestows specific favors according to their appropriate or inappropriate speech—just as a king does—there is no loss of his faultlessness; on the contrary, it would be a loss for the observer of dealings if he were to grant uniform favor to those who speak appropriately and inappropriately regarding a creation that is otherwise uniform despite its diverse actions. Nor should it be argued that because unity was established prior to creation, there could be no doubt about the non-existence of individual souls and their actions at that time.

Because both the individual souls (*jīvas*) and the streams of their karma are beginningless (*anādi*), the determination of their oneness is intended to signify the absence of gross forms characterized by distinct names and forms that would warrant separate designations. Therefore, although the souls and their karmas exist as beginningless entities, their state of non-division (*avibhāga*) is logically established. This beginninglessness of the souls and the continuous flow of their creation is found in such scriptural passages as: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and "The Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before."

Since the stream of diverse creation is beginningless, it is likewise determined that the stream of the diverse karmas which serve as its causes is also beginningless. Therefore, because all attributes necessary for Brahman’s being the material cause and the creator of the world are logically consistent with Brahman, whereas they are inconsistent with Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth—according to the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated—it is established that it is entirely reasonable to hold that Brahman is the fundamental cause of the world.
The Summary Verses.

There is no fruit whatsoever to be attained by one whose desires are fulfilled; thus does the creative play proceed in the world, for there is nothing improper among those who have reached their goal.
If He were for the sake of others, how could He ever create suffering for anyone?
Furthermore, the avoidance of dependence on karma would entail the absence of a pervasive first creation.
Just as gambling is a mere sport for a king, so too is this creation of the world by Brahman;
due to the necessity of depending upon karma, there is neither inequality nor cruelty.
And that [consciousness] exists even during the cosmic dissolutions (pralaya), because the enjoyers of saṃsāra are beginningless;
for in the Śrutis, the determination "Being alone" (sadeva) refers to that state when [names and forms] are not yet differentiated.
All those factors which can successfully fulfill the requirements of causality are applicable to Brahman;
their deficiency, however, exists in Pradhāna and other such principles.
Thus concludes the section concerning the possession of purpose.

Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled *Caturmatasāra*, composed by Appayadīkṣita, the son of the venerable Raṅgarājādhvarin— the Kaustubha-jewel of the ocean of the noble Bharadvāja family and the preeminent teacher of the non-dualistic Vedānta (*Advaitavidyā*).
The first quarter.
Salutations to the glorious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.
And because the production [of the world] is not logically possible, inference is not valid; and because of the activity [of the Lord]. (1)
If it is argued that [the soul's movement] is like that of milk or water, [we reply] that this is also the case there.
And because there is no stability in the absence [of the cause], since [the effect] is independent [of it]. ||3||
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the self] is not like grass and so forth. ||4||
If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the objection remains]. ||5||
And because the status of being a constituent part (aṅgin) is untenable. ||6||
And otherwise, in the case of inference, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge. ||7||
Even if it were admitted [that there is a cause], it would be because of the absence of an object. ||8||
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. ||9||

In the first chapter, the objections raised by the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others—who maintain that the cause of the world is primordial matter (pradhāna) or atoms (paramāṇu)—by relying solely on mere logic against the doctrine that Brahman is the cause of the world, were refuted in the first pāda. Furthermore, the suspicion that those arguments might be acceptable due to the venerability of their authors was refuted in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* and the *Yogādhikaraṇa*. Finally, the suspicion that they might be acceptable upon closer examination of the nature of those specific arguments was refuted at the commencement of the *Avilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*.

Thus, although there is a difference in the intermediate subject matter between the first two sections and the eight subsequent sections beginning with the third, they possess a single purpose insofar as they aim to refute the arguments that seek to reject the doctrine of Brahman; for in this section, the positions of the Sāṃkhya and others who rely on dry logic are refuted by means of precisely such logical arguments.

Otherwise, for those of dull intellect who establish the causality of *pradhāna* and other such principles, and who recognize that the opposing views are rooted in a mere semblance of reason, their faith in the doctrine of Brahman might falter due to the suspicion that those [opposing views] possess authority. Thus, this first quarter (*pāda*) is for the purpose of establishing one's own position; this [second] quarter is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others. Since the establishment of one's own position is more important, it was performed first; therefore, this follows immediately after it.

Although the establishment of one's own position is carried out in the third and fourth quarters as well by resolving contradictions with the Śruti regarding the scope of the effects, nevertheless, there is an intermediate connection between the first and second quarters because they share a single purpose concerning the cause. Among them, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is refuted first, because it presents a greater ground for the possibility of being adopted due to its acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) and other views sanctioned by the Vedas.

The Sāṃkhyas establish their own doctrine through independent reasoning and interpret Vedic statements in accordance with that doctrine. The interpretation provided by them has been refuted in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* and other sections. Now, their independent reasonings themselves are being refuted; thus, there is no tautology.

This is the system of the Sāṃkhyas: "Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and modification; the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. In this context, root-nature is the state of equilibrium of the substances whose forms are the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas. It is one, non-conscious in itself, intended for the enjoyment and liberation of all conscious beings, eternal, and omnipresent; it is nature alone and is not a modification of anything.

From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from the Great One comes the ego (ahaṅkāra); and from the ego come the five subtle elements (tanmātras), consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. These seven are "evolvents" (prakṛtis) with respect to their own respective effects, and "evolutes" (vikṛtis) with respect to their own respective causes.

The sixteenfold group of qualities—consisting of the five great elements beginning with space, the five organs of cognition beginning with the ear, and the five organs of action beginning with speech—is exclusively a modification (*vikṛti*) and not the primal nature (*prakṛti*) of anything else. The *puruṣa*, however, because it is unchanging, is not the primal nature of anything; because it is eternal, it is not a modification of anything. It is devoid of attributes, its form is pure consciousness, it is all-pervading, and it is distinct in each individual body. Because it is free from transformation, it is neither an agent nor an enjoyer.

Even though reality is such as this, the deluded, through the mere proximity of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, superimpose consciousness upon *puruṣa*. Consequently, due to the association with consciousness and the possession of the power of agency, there arises the state of being a knower. They further superimpose the agency of *prakṛti*—which has assumed the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—upon that *puruṣa*. Thus, through mutual superimposition, there occurs experience consisting of the conceit "I am the agent" and "I am the enjoyer. Liberation results from the knowledge of reality. Such are the twenty-five principles.

In that system, it is held that liberation results from the knowledge of the reality of that which is considered the universal root cause; thus, there are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). Since the entire doctrine of that school is refuted by the rejection of the inference for an independent *pradhāna* (primordial matter) considered to be the universal root cause, that [inference] is here being refuted. Their inference here is as follows: "Every effect has as its material cause a substance whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because it is permeated by them, like a jar and so forth. This is the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*).

In the first inference, substances consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion are established as the causes of effects; they resolve precisely into *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, because they possess that very nature. As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "They consist of joy, displeasure, and despondency, and have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes. The meaning of this is as follows: the qualities (*guṇas*)—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—consist respectively of joy, displeasure, and despondency, which are themselves the natures of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and they have, respectively, illumination, activity, and restraint as their functions.

Sattva manifests clarity; the quality of rajas impels sattva toward the activity of manifestation. Since it follows that the light quality of sattva would cause movement everywhere due to its inherent nature of motion, the heavy quality of tamas restrains it according to the specific effect required. Nor is the first reason unestablished, for it is well-known in the world that effects are invariably associated with pleasure, pain, and delusion. To illustrate: when a jar is obtained by someone, for that person the jar becomes pleasant in nature due to the emergence of the quality of sattva.

When an object belonging to one person is taken away by another, it becomes sorrowful in relation to that person due to the emergence of the quality of *rajas*. When, toward that same object, there arises not even the perception of indifference, it becomes delusive in relation to that person due to the emergence of the quality of *tamas*—the verbal root being *muha*, meaning "to be bewildered. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor for the emergence of these qualities based on the specific distinctions between individual *puruṣas*; for their emergence is established by virtue of the purpose consisting of the experience of this or that particular *puruṣa*.

For example—just as *sattva* occasionally overcomes *rajas* and *tamas* with respect to something and attains its own peaceful state, so too *rajas* overcomes *sattva* and *tamas* and attains its own terrible state, and *tamas* overcomes *sattva* and *rajas* and attains its own deluded state. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) in the second inference by taking atoms and the like as the cause, because parsimony (*lāghava*) establishes that there is a single cause.

Nor, even so, does there arise the fallacy of proving something else (an arthāntara), namely that the collection of effects—which is insentient and consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion—is caused by Brahman as its material cause; for it is impossible to establish that something which is not of such a nature [as the effect] can be its cause. Thus, the following inference is stated as a refutation of the Sāṃkhya inference of this kind: "Pradhāna is not capable of the construction of the world, because, while being insentient, it is not presided over by a conscious being; whatever is thus [insentient and unguided] is so [incapable], just like clay, wood, and the like, which, when not presided over by a conscious being, are incapable of such construction."

Nor is there a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it is logically impossible for that which is not presided over by a conscious being (*cetana*) to initiate an effect, and because it is observed everywhere that only that which is presided over by a conscious being engages in the commencement of an effect. Now, one might object: "In your final position (*siddhānta*), the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished. It should not be argued that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) established by the scripture, "The Lord of *pradhāna* and *kṣetrajña*, the Master of the *guṇas*," exists even in our system; for since that [scriptural *pradhāna*] cannot be apprehended through inference, it is improper to designate it by the term "inference" (*anumāna*) as used in the *Sūtra* in its etymological sense of "that which is to be inferred."

If it is argued that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the probandum (*sādhya*), because even in the [Sāṅkhya] final doctrine (*siddhānta*) the capacity for the construction of the world is admitted for the Pradhāna; and that there is a non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason (*hetu*), because in that final doctrine the existence of superintendence by a conscious being (*cetana*) is accepted—[we reply: True. However, since one must refute an opponent by means of their own method of operation, this inference was stated while adopting the subject (*pakṣa*) and other elements established by the opponent. Alternatively, this is an inferential refutation in the form of a counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) against the opponent’s inference: if the Pradhāna were insentient and not superintended by a conscious being, it would be incapable of the construction of the world.

Alternatively, the qualificand portion of the reason (hetu) is construed as a qualifier of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) within the probandum (sādhya). Consequently, the formal structure of the inference is as follows: "The Pradhāna is not a producer of effects without being presided over by a conscious entity, because it is insentient, like clay, wood, and so forth, which produce jars, houses, and the like. Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi), since the Pradhāna is not accepted as a subject known through inference.

In our final position (siddhānta), it is possible to accept the inference—"the Great One (mahat) and the rest, together with primordial nature (prakṛti), are effects because they are produced, like a jar"—since there is no contradiction [with scripture]. This is because independence is not included in the probandum (sādhya); for regarding that [dependence], we rely on scripture only to establish that [the world] is dependent upon God. Now, one might object: "It is not an absolute rule that the activity of the insentient occurs only when presided over by a sentient being, since we observe that the milk contained in a cow flows out of its own accord for the sake of the growth of the calf."

If it is argued that just as water released from a cloud flows out of its own accord for the sake of increasing crops, so too the activity of *pradhāna*—though devoid of consciousness—is possible for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of the soul (*puruṣa*), we say no. This is because milk and water are also insentient; since their activity is impossible in the absence of a conscious controller, there is no deviation [from the rule] even when the case is equal to the subject, as the two cases are identical. By this, [the argument is refuted].

The transformation of grass and other substances consumed by a cow and the like into milk and so forth has also been explained. In that case as well, because there is a necessary dependence on the superintendence of a conscious being, the two cases are equal. Otherwise, in the absence of the regulating volition of a specific conscious being, it would follow that even grass and other substances consumed by an ox or similar animal would likewise turn into milk. Furthermore, there is no difference in the cooking [of the food] when it occurs in the stomach of a cow versus that of an ox; for the mere contact with fire is the cause of cooking, and that contact is no different whether it occurs in the stomach of an ox or elsewhere.

In the world, it is observed that a specific result of cooking arises from a specific intention of the cook. Now, if it is argued that this inference for a conscious controller is not the cause [of the activity], because—just as a blind man endowed with the power of movement proceeds through proximity to a lame man endowed with the power of sight, and just as iron moves through proximity to the magnet-stone—so too the activity of *pradhāna* is possible through the mere proximity of the *puruṣa*, whose nature is consciousness; even if such examples are adduced, [the same applies] to *pradhāna*.

The defect consisting in the impossibility of activity remains as it was. For instance, there is the case of a lame man who lacks the power of locomotion but is being carried by a blind man; there is his own observation of the path and his instruction regarding that path to the blind carrier. But for the Puruṣa, who is devoid of action, no such activity exists. Even if there were activity [in the case of the body], there would still be no deviation [from the rule] because the necessity of a conscious presiding principle (adhiṣṭhāna) must exist. Therefore, the inference of the defect is faultless.

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya inference itself is refuted by counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*). If the *pradhāna* undergoes transformation merely through the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of the *puruṣa*, then there would never be a dissolution (*pralaya*) distinct from creation, because the proximity of the eternal *puruṣa* remains unchanged at all times. Therefore, it must be accepted that the specific volitions (*saṅkalpa-viśeṣa*) of the presiding Lord (*adhiṣṭhātṛ īśvara*) alone are the regulators of creation and dissolution. Nor should it be argued that merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) themselves are the regulators of those two.

For *dharma* and *adharma*, as established by all the scriptures, consist precisely in the propitiation of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*) and its opposite; thus, if those are not accepted, they lack any means of attaining their own existence. Furthermore, if one were to admit that the *guṇas* sometimes abide in a state of equilibrium, then—since there would be no basis for the predominance of the *guṇas* and consequently no relationship of primary and subordinate factors (*aṅga-aṅgin*)—there would be no production of the world caused by that [predominance]. Therefore, in the state of dissolution, when the *guṇas* abide in equilibrium, they must themselves enter a state of disequilibrium through the activity of a person (*puruṣa*) who acts as their agitator.

Since the relationship of part and whole (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is impossible for those [qualities] that cannot attain such a state, the creation of the world would never occur at any time. If, on the other hand, one infers the three qualities (triguṇa) as existing in a state of inequality according to their effects upon seeing the world in its state of inequality consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, then—given that the state of inequality established by the means of cognition apprehending the subject (dharmigrāhakapramāṇa) exists eternally—there would necessarily be eternal creation.

If it were argued that the three qualities (*triguṇa*) are inferred neither to be in a state of imbalance nor in a state of equilibrium—lest there be perpetual creation or dissolution—but rather that, due to the existence of a continuous succession of two kinds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the root of the beginningless flow of creation and dissolution, it is inferred to possess a dual nature consisting of both equilibrium and imbalance according to the predominance of the awakening of this or that particular impression; even this is not tenable.

Just as one who is blind becomes a knower of the path through the presence of an eminent guide who points out the way, it has been stated that it is impossible for the *pradhāna* to become a knower through the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyāpatti*) due to the presence of the inactive *puruṣa*. Furthermore, since such knowing is impossible, an insentient entity cannot function without being presided over by a conscious being. Moreover, if there were some purpose in postulating the *pradhāna*, we might somehow accept it; however, there is no purpose whatsoever.

It is maintained that the purpose of the *puruṣa* is indeed experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). Experience consists in the perception of pleasure and pain, which is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), itself a transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*). For the *puruṣa*, however, experience is the witnessing of that [intellectual state] through the falling of its reflection upon it, as if it had attained identity with it. Because of its failure to discern the difference from that [intellect], the *puruṣa* possesses a superimposed status of being an enjoyer; the cessation of this superimposition of being an enjoyer through the discriminative knowledge of the difference between them is what is intended by the Sāṃkhyas as liberation.

Furthermore, for the Puruṣa, whose nature consists solely of changeless consciousness, neither the false identification with the intellect (buddhi) which undergoes modifications, nor the perception of its experiences, nor even the non-perception of that distinction, is possible. But surely the Sāṃkhyas themselves have established the existence of a Puruṣa distinct from the intellect and other such factors—both as an experiencer and as one who engages in hearing and so forth, which serve as the means to liberation—on the grounds that such activities are impossible for insentient things like the intellect; as it is said: "The Puruṣa exists because there must be an experiencer, and because of the engagement in activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya)."

The fact that Nature exists for the sake of the Spirit’s experience, and that the Spirit’s liberation occurs at the very moment that Nature’s true nature is perceived—both of these points have been explained in great detail. "By various means, Nature, who is beneficent, acts for the sake of the Spirit, who is non-beneficent; she, who possesses qualities, acts for the sake of him who is devoid of qualities, yet her efforts are ultimately fruitless. Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after showing herself to the audience, so does Nature cease from her activity after revealing herself to the Spirit."

"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti), which, having been seen by the person (puruṣa), ceases to appear to him again. Therefore, according to that system, the person indeed possesses the state of being an enjoyer of primordial nature, as well as the agency for performing hearing and other acts for the sake of perceiving its true nature. If it is asked how, then, there could be an impossibility of purpose in that system, [the answer is: because it merely states mutually contradictory things.

That doctrine is inconsistent. For in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, it is elaborated at length that bondage and liberation belong to *prakṛti* alone, through such statements as: "Prakṛti, having various substrates, is bound and liberated. Furthermore, by those very people who assert that when the cause of the world is established, it is established as one—namely *prakṛti*—on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), they have themselves admitted that *prakṛti* is merely a collection of the three *guṇas*, and that there is no such thing as *prakṛti* existing apart from them; for this reason as well, their doctrine is self-contradictory.

Having stated that there are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), it was further asserted that the qualities (*guṇas*) are mutually distinct; this too is contradictory. For if the qualities were distinct, there would be twenty-seven principles. Furthermore, this is shown to be a contradiction in meaning: it is not logical to imagine that pleasure, pain, and delusion inhere in objects simply because they possess qualities such as color and texture. Otherwise, one would have to admit that objects themselves possess those qualities, since desire, aversion, and so forth arise in those who perceive silver, snakes, and the like [in mother-of-pearl or similar substrates].

Furthermore, since objects are invariably associated with pleasure, pain, and so forth, from what source is their cause established? If you argue that it is established as being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*), we say no; for whiteness, cowness, and the like do not become causes by being associated with an object in the manner that clay is the cause of a jar. This is because *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* cannot be established as substances (*dravya*). Indeed, *sattva* and the others are merely the qualities (*guṇa*) residing in substances such as earth, acting as the causes of lightness, illumination, and so on. For this very reason, they are well-known simply as "qualities. Therefore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent both through mutual contradiction and through contradiction with the nature of its objects.
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world].
Or [the relationship between cause and effect] is like that of the large and the long in relation to the short and the circular. ||10||
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] does not exist. ||11||
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being on the same footing [as the related entities]. ||12||
And because it exists eternally. ||13||
And because it possesses form and so forth, there is a reversal [of the argument], as seen from observation. (14)
And because there would be a fault in either case. ||15||
And from non-possessiveness follows absolute lack of concern. 16.

The logical connection of the example is that, just like the theory of the Pradhāna as the cause based on inference, the theory of atoms (paramāṇu) as the cause based on inference is also not tenable. Since the Lord is not admitted [in the Vaiśeṣika system], there is no lack of a conscious supervisor; thus, unlike the theory of the Pradhāna as the cause where the impossibility of formation (*racanānupapatti*) exists, such a defect does not exist in the theory of atoms as the cause. Furthermore, because the Lord is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas, the fault of the impossibility of dissolution (*pralayānupapatti*) also does not apply.

Furthermore, there is a connection by way of a counter-example, because it is possible to assert that at that time the Lord’s will—in the form of a desire to create—is absent, since it is conditioned by the specific karma of living beings that brings about creation. This is the process here according to the proponents of atoms (paramāṇuvādins): when the world has dissolved and the Lord’s will in the form of a desire to create arises due to the influence of the particular awakening of the karma of living beings, the first motion arises in the immobile, partless atoms. By that motion, two atoms conjoin.

A dyad (dvyaṇuka) is initiated by two conjoined atoms; a triad (tryaṇuka) by three dyads, and so on, in this sequence the entire world arises. In that regard, first of all, the partlessness of atoms is untenable.

Just as two fingers, each delimited by ten spatial points (pradeśa) connected to the ten directions, when joined together, are conjoined with three points each by one great direction (mahādiś) and two intermediate directions (vidiś), thus becoming united on six sides; in the same way, the threads that constitute a cloth, while being joined, are conjoined on six sides, and being thus possessed of seven sides—six conjoined and one unconjoined—they possess a magnitude greater than their own.

It is observed that one begins a cloth [from threads]. In the same way, atoms also, when conjoined on six sides, cannot account for the magnitude of a dyad (dvyaṇuka)—which possesses a dimension greater than its own spherical dimension—and of a triad (tryaṇuka), which is larger and longer than the dyad. Nor should it be argued: "Let there be no magnitude for the dyad from the atoms; however, the magnitude of the triad will arise from the plurality of its causes (the dyads). This is not so.

If that were the case, there would follow the consequence of an absence of distinction between the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) as the size of an atom and the minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) as the sizes of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Furthermore, if the conjunction of two atoms were all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), it would entail that the dyad itself is also spherical; for one who accepts the conjunction of two atoms as the producer of a dyad must thereby admit the existence of spatial parts (*pradeśa*) in those two atoms. Indeed, when two atoms conjoin, they cannot both occupy the same location, for [otherwise] their spatial parts would not be established.

For two atoms, even when in conjunction, do not join while occupying the same location, because it is a contradiction for corporeal entities to occupy the same space. Therefore, it must be said that they join while situated in different locations—by way of being in front and behind, or south and north, or above and below.

That being the case, consider this yourself: when an atom situated in a certain location is conjoined with another atom, is it possible for it to be conjoined with that [other atom] as well by means of a location distinct from that [first] location? Or, if it is not possible for it to be so conjoined, how could there not be a distinction of locations within that [atom]? Reflect upon this.

[Objection: "But even if atoms are partless, it is possible to speak of a distinction of spatial locations (pradeśabheda) obtained through their delimitation by various directions; from that alone, the localized nature (prādeśikatva) of the conjunction of two atoms and the increase in magnitude (parimāṇotkarṣa) in the dyad (dvyaṇuka) will occur. [Reply: No—for even the conjunction with a specific direction would necessarily be all-pervasive (vyāpyavṛtti) within the atom, since there is no part to establish its non-pervasive occurrence (avyāpyavṛttitva); and thus, it would be impossible for that [conjunction] to establish the non-pervasive occurrence of the atom's conjunction with another atom.

For it is not the case that, merely by the existence of some kind of distinction in the delimiting factor—even in the absence of a fixed spatial delimiting factor such as the root or the top of a tree which delimits conjunction with a monkey and its absence—[the two could be established as distinct].

It may be argued that the conjunction of two atoms occurs as non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). However, since all spatial conjunctions are equally pervasive, there is no determining factor here to establish that a particular spatial conjunction delimits the conjunction with another atom. Consequently, all spatial conjunctions would likewise result in being such delimiters; and in the absence of a distinction between delimiters, or even if some distinction were somehow obtained, the lack of a fixed location would render it impossible to establish that those two conjunctions are non-pervasive.

Otherwise, since earth possesses number, "substantiality" (dravyatva) would be the delimiting property for that, and since it possesses odor, "earthness" (pṛthivītva) would be the delimiting property; because of the existence of such distinct delimiting properties, there would follow the undesirable consequence of treating number and other qualities as non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). Therefore, in order to account for the conjunction that produces a dyad (dyaṇuka), one must necessarily admit a distinction of parts in the form of spatial divisions within atoms. Likewise, that [distinction] must also be admitted in order to account for the conjunctions of three dyads that produce a triad (tryaṇuka).

For that conjunction between the body and the book must be accomplished by means of the conjunction between the hands and the book, just as the conjunction of a dyad with another atom that initiates a subsequent dyad is accomplished; this is because you yourself have accepted the principle that "from the conjunction of cause and non-cause arises the conjunction of effect and non-effect."

And likewise, when the conjunction of another atom that initiates it has already been established and persists in the atom that initiates a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), how could there also be a conjunction with another dyad at the time of the production of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) without a distinction of spatial location? This is because of the contradiction of corporeal things occupying the same location. If, however, despite their corporeality, one does not accept the limit of the contradiction regarding the occupation of the same location by atoms, then a triad in the form of a mass composed of six atoms would be no larger than a single atom.

Regarding this, they say: "Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts; if the six were in the same location, the aggregate would be no more than a single atom. The meaning is as follows: when a central atom is connected with six surrounding atoms situated in the directions of east, west, south, north, below, and above, that central atom must possess six parts, because the points of contact are distinct. Alternatively, if all these connections occupy the same location, then the entire aggregate of them would result in a mass no larger than a single atom.

This same refutation applies equally to the production of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) from dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Therefore, even those proponents of atoms who do not wish to admit that atoms have six parts must nevertheless accept it for the sake of establishing the production of dyads, triads, and so forth, as well as the increase in their dimensions. [Objection: But if that is accepted, then by the aforementioned reasoning, those respective parts would also possess parts, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And thus, since there would be no difference in being composed of infinite constituent parts, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be equal in dimension.

If you argue that having parts (*sāṃśatva*) is therefore not worthy of acceptance, then abandon this addiction to the theory of atoms as the cause—which falls into the same fault in both positions: namely, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if they have parts, and the impossibility of the production of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth if they are partless (*niraṃśatva*). Be happy! Furthermore, there is no fault in atoms having parts; for even though Mount Meru and a mustard seed are both composed of infinite constituent parts, a difference in their dimensions is logically established due to a specific difference in those infinities.

Indeed, there is no gradation between the infinite individual instances that serve as the substrata for universals such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*), which are delimited by the regions above Pātāla and below the solar orb—specifically those occurring prior to the Padma-kalpa and subsequent to the Vārāha-kalpa—and likewise between the infinite atoms contained within Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.

If, however, the possession of parts by the atom is not accepted—on the grounds that it would entail impermanence and thus result in the failure to establish its status as the fundamental cause (mūlakāraṇa) as you yourself admit—then the impossibility of the production of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth, as well as their magnitude, becomes unavoidable. Therefore, there is an infinite regress (anavasthā). Consequently, the theory of atoms as the cause, being beset by one or another of these refutations—namely, the impermanence of the atom, the impossibility of producing dyads and so forth, or the impossibility of their magnitude—is simply to be rejected.

Furthermore, it must be accepted that during the dissolution (pralaya), when atoms are motionless, a conjunction cannot occur because action—which would produce the conjunction initiating the dyad (dvyaṇuka) at the beginning of creation—is impossible. Now, one might object: "It is accepted that 'the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial action of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)'; therefore, a conjunction is possible through action produced by the power of the unseen force. To this we say: no.

If that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is inherent either in living beings or in atoms, in either case it cannot be the cause of action. For if it were the cause of such action, then since that force acquired in a previous cycle would still exist even during the dissolution (*pralaya*), actions would arise from it at that time as well, leading to the undesirable consequence of the world being constantly in a state of formation.

Now, regarding the commentary by the author of the *Vārttika* on the group of *Ākṣapāda* (Gautama) sūtras beginning with "The Lord is the cause, because we see the fruitfulness of human action" (*īśvaraḥ kāraṇaṃ puruṣakarmasāphalyadarśanāt*), which aims to establish that the Lord is the cause of the world in both its aspects—as the cause of the ripening of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and as the cause of action itself—the following is stated: "We do not say that the Lord is the cause independently of action; rather, the Lord favors the action of the person. What is the meaning of this favor? It is that he ensures that whatever [action] is of such a nature, for whom it belongs, and at whatever time it is due to ripen, that it occurs in that manner and at that very time."

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because [the scripture] teaches that [the soul] is "appointed" [to experience results], we say no; for just like the substance of the *harītakī* fruit, there can be no ripening (*vipāka*) of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which is a quality of the self. Ripening is the arrival of the time for the fruit, and if it is claimed that this occurs only at the arrival of the time of creation, we say no; for it is not the case that the time for the fruit of the various unseen merits produced by the non-simultaneous performance of ritual acts by infinite living beings is only at the time of creation. This is because the assumption that there is not even a single moment prior to that during the dissolution (*pralaya*)—which lasts for two *parārdhas*—is devoid of authoritative proof (*aprāmāṇika*).

Indeed, on the day that is the period of creation, the Lord—desiring to cause those living beings who have been incessantly engaged in coming and going to rest by making a period of time equal in measure to that [day] into the form of night, and having induced them into a profound sleep (mahāsuṣupti)—renders even those karmas whose results have arrived during the interval of dissolution as having their power obstructed.

If it is argued that for this very reason, the fruit prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin—namely, the experience of torment for the duration of a *kalpa* immediately after the fall of that body, followed by the persistence of those marks such as consumption and leprosy for seven subsequent births—does not apply to a person who committed the murder of a Brahmin at a time immediately preceding the dissolution (*pralaya*), [we reply: no, because in your own view, the eternal will of the Lord exists even during the dissolution.

Even though at the time of dissolution there exist the previously established unseen merits and demerits (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings and other volitions of the Lord, there is an absence of creation because of the absence of those future volitions of the Lord which take the form of the creative resolve for that specific time, such as: "May I become many, may I procreate; let me make each of these [elements] threefold; let me unfold name and form."

If it is argued: "In that case, at whatever time you maintain that the will of the Lord in the form of such a volition occurs, my desire to produce the motion of the atoms will be that very same eternal divine will as conditioned by that time," it is replied: I do not accept some such time for volition imagined by my own fancy; rather, [I rely on scripture] such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

The period consisting of a great night (*mahāśarvarī*) of two *parārdhas*—which is established by the authority of the Vedas, their exegeses (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth—is accepted here. And for one who desires to postulate the Lord and His activities of creation and so forth through reason alone, it is not possible [to maintain] such things as: the resolve to become manifold during this period; the subsequent gradual creation of the elements; the resolve to perform the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the tripartition itself; and the resolve to differentiate names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) and that differentiation itself.

It enters the path of reason. For the life of Rāma and so forth, as established in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts, cannot be constructed by means of [mere] logical arguments. If scripture must be sought as a refuge regarding the Lord’s activities such as creation, which are delimited by specific times, then it is likewise proper to seek that very same scripture as a refuge regarding the Lord himself. Thus, the Lord should be accepted as a mine of infinite auspicious qualities according to scripture, performing the sport of the world’s activity through various volitions arising at their respective times; however, one should not [ignore] those portions in the scriptures that are not favored by oneself.

One must accept [the Lord] as being devoid of constant knowledge, will, and effort, and as a mere agent of the activity of creation according to His own whims. Furthermore, the God inferred through logic has been refuted in the section on "The Scripture Being the Source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa). By that [section], His status as a creator—according to your intended view—through the process of producing motion in atoms is already effectively discarded. Therefore, because it accepts the doctrine of atoms as the cause of things despite their lack of intelligence, the Vaiśeṣika system is inconsistent. Likewise, it is inconsistent because it accepts the category of inherence (samavāya).

Inherence (samavāya) is indeed postulated for the purpose of establishing inseparable connection (*ayutasiddhi*) among parts, qualities, actions, and universals that are themselves inseparably established; however, in that case, inherence itself would require another relation, since it is equally characterized by inseparable connection. Thus, for each subsequent relation that establishes inseparable connection, yet another relation would be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that inherence is accepted as having an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), like non-existence (*abhāva*) and so forth, then let that same [essential relation] suffice for the whole (*avayavin*) and the rest as well.

[Objection: But surely, since the wholes and so forth are infinite, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), one single inherence (*samavāya*) common to all is postulated? [Reply: No. For while it is true that when both one and many are to be postulated, the postulation of one is favored by parsimony, in this case, since many [inherences] are already established, why postulate even one more? [Objection: Even if many are established, their status as relations must still be postulated; and that cannot be postulated as a single entity.

Because it is impossible to define a single relation that conforms to the nature of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth; therefore, rather than postulating an infinite number of relations, one might argue that it is simpler to postulate a single *samavāya* (inherence) and a single relatedness residing therein. But this is not possible to establish as a single entity, because it is impossible to define a single relation that conforms to the nature of the whole and so forth. Thus, against the argument that—rather than postulating an infinite number of relations—it is simpler to postulate a single *samavāya* and a single relatedness residing therein, we reply: no.

If it is argued that since the status of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) is already established for things such as wholes (*avayavin*) with respect to their respective absences (*tattadabhāva*), and there is no established relationhood defined by parts (*avayava*) and so forth in those [absences], therefore those [relations] must be postulated as infinite—this is not so. For if the relationhood differs according to the difference in the relatum (*nirūpaka*), then even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), those [relations] would have to be postulated as infinite due to that difference, and inherence itself would also have to be postulated; thus, in the theory of inherence alone, the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) arises.

If it is argued that, by encompassing the parts, qualities, actions, and universals—along with their possessors—through the relation of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*), one may postulate for inherence (*samavāya*) only a single relationship defined by this inseparability, we say no. For, while such an approach might justify postulating a single relationship among those entities by encompassing them, it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a distinct category of inherence itself. Furthermore, even if inherence were accepted for the relation between parts and wholes and so forth, the acceptance of a relationship consisting of their own essential natures (*svarūpa-sambandha*) would still be indispensable.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the relationship between container and contained could not be established among parts and wholes and so forth, even through a specific type of inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" and similar instances must be accounted for by means of two distinct relations of essential nature (*svarūpasambandha*): one being the nature of being a container as defined with respect to the parts and so forth in relation to the whole and so forth, and the other being the nature of being a contained as defined with respect to the whole and so forth in relation to the parts and so forth. It is by means of these two relations of essential nature, serving as the objects of cognition, that such a cognition is sustained.

If that [inherence] were to effect [the relation] by way of inherence itself, then since the inherence of color exists in air, the cognition "color in air" would result. Therefore, since an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha) is necessary even in cases of inherence, and since the cognition of the locus-and-located relationship can be accounted for by that alone, what is the use of inherence? By this, the statement in the Kaṇāda-sūtra—"Inherence is that from which [the notion] 'here' arises with respect to cause and effect"—is refuted.

For the cognition "here" (ihapratyaya) necessarily has as its object two types of relations—namely, the relation of locus and located and the relation of essential nature—and since the specific cognition [of inherence] is fully accounted for by those alone, [inherence is not required]. It might be argued: "It is true that in this sūtra it was stated that the existence of inherence (*samavāya*) is established by its being the means of accounting for the aforementioned cognition; however, its being the means of accounting for that was not intended in the sense of being its object, because in that [Vaiśeṣika] system, inherence is not perceptible."

"But that which is established as the common cause for cognitions qualified by the action of parts and so forth, in its capacity as a cause, is *samavāya* (inherence). This is not so; for since cognitions qualified by parts and so forth are themselves non-uniform, they have no requirement for a uniform cause, and [if such a cause were postulated], it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the concept of inherence to all qualified cognitions.

If it is argued that there is a unifying factor (anugama) consisting in being a qualified perception whose object is a pair of related things lacking very distinct discrimination—and which is thus not over-extensive—then let the causality in that case belong to the parts and the whole themselves, as they are unified by their lack of very distinct discrimination; what is the use of postulating *samavāya*? Furthermore, this aforementioned nature of being a qualified cognition is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), as it applies to the qualified cognition of an absence and its locus, and even to the qualified cognition of the two supporting substances in the case of "the gold is yellow."

[Objection: Surely, when a single, common cause is postulated for all specific cognitions of perception—by virtue of its being present in every cognition qualified by a staff or the like—it is established as *samavāya* (inherence) alone, because it is eternal and unitary, and thus possible everywhere; for its status as a cause in all those [cognitions] is possible even without its being an object (*viṣayabhāva*). [Reply: This is not so, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible as the common cause. For in the case of visual and other specific perceptions, the respective conjunctions of the substance and the sense organ are already established as the causes.

Even in the case of the perception of sound, there exists a conjunction between the ear and the mind. Let it be that these very conjunctions possess the status of being the cause by virtue of their nature as conjunctions. Furthermore, since "being a qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭajñānatva*) is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the effectness of the cognition of a qualifier, and "perceptuality" (*pratyakṣatva*) is the delimiting property of the effectness of the sense organ, [the former]—because it subsists in an effectness that already possesses another delimiting property—is like "blue-pot-ness" and is thus established by the force of the object itself; therefore, "qualified perceptuality" is not the delimiting property of the effectness. Consequently, there is no requirement for a common cause delimited by that [qualified perceptuality].

If it is argued that—by this [argument]—when the thread and so forth are destroyed, those qualities and parts residing therein which perish, cannot be subsumed under the property of "being the destruction of the whole (avayavin) residing therein," because the property of "being the destruction of what is related to that" would over-extend to the destruction of grass and such things conjoined with it; therefore, the relation established as being thus pervasive must result in being *samavāya* (inherence)—we say no. For even if *samavāya* is accepted, when the thread is destroyed...

This is because the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of the threads—which possess the inherence [of the cloth]—cannot be avoided. Nor can "being inherent" (samavatatva), defined as the state of being a superstratum while possessing inherence, be introduced as the delimiting property (avacchedaka); for even so, the aforementioned consequence of the destruction of grass and other objects resting on the threads would remain as it was, since inherence is one and thus the inherence of the threads exists in the grass as well. Furthermore, it is more appropriate to introduce the unburdensome and already established notion of "being a superstratum that is not separately established" (ayutasiddha-ādheyatva) itself into the delimiting property of the effect.

And this being the case, it does not follow that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of the cloth's destruction and so forth—which are inseparably established (ayutasiddha) with the cloth—since the same consequence of the destruction of universals (jāti) and other properties inhering in the threads applies equally to the opponent's position as well. If you maintain the rule that "upon the destruction of the threads, the effect inhering in them is destroyed," then let there be the rule that "upon the destruction of that [effect], that which is inseparably established with it and is subject to destruction is also destroyed. Nor does anything undesirable result from the destruction of a destruction; for just as a pot is the destruction of its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), the destruction of that [destruction] is likewise logically possible.

For, by accepting that both the destruction of the jar and [the subsequent destructions] possess the nature of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destruction (pradhvaṃsa), one can establish the non-reemergence of the prior non-existence; and likewise, by accepting that the series of the jar's destructions possesses the nature of the jar's destruction, it is logically consistent to establish the non-reemergence of the jar.

Thus, since inherence (samavāya) is unestablished, its constituent property—being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva)—is also unestablished; consequently, the inference of dyads and atoms as the inherent causes of triads and dyads cannot proceed. For this reason as well, the doctrine of atoms as the cause [of the world] is inconsistent. Furthermore, because inherence is admitted to be eternal, it must be admitted that its substrata are also eternal; otherwise, upon the destruction of the related entities, inherence would necessarily perish, just like conjunction (saṃyoga).

Furthermore, since you would have to assert that even a triad (tryaṇuka) is eternal by virtue of its being the substratum of inherence (samavāya), the inference of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth as its cause is likewise unestablished. If it were argued that "the property of being a conjunction" (saṃyogatva) is the determinant for destruction through the destruction of the related relata, on the grounds of parsimony (lāghava);

It is not the case that "relatedness" is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) [for proving the existence of atoms], because [if it were,] one who follows this principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) must also follow the parsimony of unity in the inference for the root cause of the universe. Thus, since either Brahman or Pradhāna is established by that [inference], atoms are not established by it. Nor should it be argued that parsimony is irrelevant here on the grounds that the rule—that an effect-substance is invariably produced by the conjunction of parts—is observed in the case of cloth and the like, and therefore the production of a substance from a single [cause] is impossible.

If one assumes that curd is produced from milk in the form of a single composite whole, this would violate the rule [of causal efficiency]; furthermore, there is no evidence for the hypothesis that the constituent parts of the milk, having conjoined with one another and subsequently attained further conjunctions, initiate the production of curd. Just as the cause of the destruction of the milk is not perceived, so too is the production of curd established; for the sūtras of Akṣapāda, such as "The transformation of milk is not [the case], because other qualities appear," lack a foundation in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, even while the substance persists, it is like the case of the earth-atoms.

Because the manifestation of a different quality is logically possible; and because, given the identity of the causal complex—consisting of the conjunction of threads and the weaver’s activity and so forth—the cloth and the conjunction of the threads are produced at the same time, it is not accepted that the cloth is originated by the conjunction of the threads. Nor should it be argued that since the destruction of the cloth is observed upon the destruction of the conjunction of the threads, and since the destruction of a non-cause cannot entail the destruction of its effect, one must assert a cause-and-effect relationship between the cloth and the conjunction of the threads; for even in the case of these two destructions, their simultaneity is established through the identity of their respective causal complexes.

Furthermore, if the root cause of the world were possessed of color and other qualities, then its permanence and partlessness would be subverted; for it is observed that things possessing color and other qualities are impermanent and composite. Thus, because this [position] is refuted by the inference—supported by reasoning—that the root cause of the triad (tryaṇuka) is devoid of color and other qualities due to its permanence and partlessness, the existence of atoms as a causal substance possessing color and other qualities is not established.

If it is argued that this reasoning has a loose foundation because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then what subverting argument against the counter-example is observed for the two inferences establishing the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*)—namely, "the triad (*tryaṇuka*) is originated by an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it is the originator of something large"—by which my inference would be weak and yours would be strong? Surely, there is a subverting argument against the counter-example for the inference establishing the triad.

For instance, if magnitude (*mahattva*) is produced, the only operative factor is the mere inferiority (*apakarṣa*) consisting of a sub-class of magnitude; it is not two distinct sub-classes consisting of superiority (*utkarṣa*) and inferiority, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

And likewise, since the largeness of a triad (tryaṇuka) is produced by virtue of its being a form of diminished largeness, it requires a cause; and since, regarding largeness, only specific numbers, dimensions, and conjunctions residing in the inherent causes of its own substrate are the causes, the inherent causality of the triad must necessarily be admitted. Thus, in this very manner, there exists a reductio ad absurdum (tarka) against the contrary [of the] pervasion rooted in reasoning: if color and so forth were produced, then "color-ness" (rūpatva) and the like would be the efficient cause, because they are inclusive and parsimonious.

But [the property] such as "being a color residing in an effect" is not [the cause], because it does not inhere in the color and so forth of the earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*), and because of its heaviness. Furthermore, if you accept that color exists in atoms, then according to your own view—that colors and so forth which are not produced by contact with fire are produced by the color and so forth residing in the causes of their own substratum—it follows that the atoms must be established as having parts (*avayava*). This is because, in the production of the color and so forth residing in water-atoms and the blackness of earth-atoms, those very atoms would have to serve as the substrata for the required colors and so forth. Thus, they cannot be prevented from having parts.

Furthermore, since having parts entails impermanence, you must necessarily accept that when color and other qualities are produced, the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth are the determining causes; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that color and other qualities could not be established in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), which are inferred to be the causes of triads (*tryaṇuka*). For in inferring the possession of color and other qualities in those [dyads], one must indeed rely on a reductio ad absurdum (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) based on the rule that qualities are preceded by the qualities of their causes.

Furthermore, if magnitude (*mahattva*) were produced, it would be logical that a diminution of dimension (*parimāṇāpakarṣa*) is its efficient cause; for this reason alone, the exclusion of the "supremely great" (*paramamahat*) magnitude found in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth is established. However, a diminution of "greatness" (*mahatvāpakarṣa*) is not the cause, because it is a specific form and because length (*dairghya*) is not invariably concomitant with it. Thus, if one were to admit a diminished dimension in the primary cause of a triad (*tryaṇuka*), then, since that [triad] is produced, it would follow that the primary cause possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*) in relation to the dimensions of its own causes. To avoid this consequence, one must admit that the primary cause possesses supremely great magnitude itself.

Furthermore, there is no rule that an effect-substance must be produced by a substance of smaller dimension; for we observe that a thread of lesser length is produced from long threads twisted more tightly together, and a thread of lesser width is produced from wide cloths twisted together. Therefore, the inference regarding the primal cause of the world is set aside by a stronger counter-argument, just like the inference regarding [the existence of] color and other qualities.

Likewise, if, in order to avoid [the charge of] impermanence and so forth, it is asserted that atoms are devoid of color and other qualities, then the rule that the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their cause would be unestablished. And if, for the sake of establishing that rule, one accepts that they possess color and other qualities, [then...]

Since it results in the fallacy of impermanence and other defects, the theory of atoms as the cause is flawed in both ways; thus, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is inconsistent. Therefore, although the Sāṃkhya position contradicts both scripture and logic, there is partial acceptance of it by the Vedists in certain respects, such as the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). However, because no part of the Vaiśeṣika position is accepted, it must be regarded as entirely unworthy of consideration.
The summary verses.
In the world, the production of something vast from the conjunction of minute things is observed;
therefore, atoms are the cause, being partless, for the sake of ending the infinite regress.

Since their conjunction occurs through the division of their parts, where would it ever find rest? If not, then let there be even a non-conjunction of the atoms; how then could there be magnitude in the effect?
And the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the triad (trasareṇu) is inferred by that very [triad] itself;
for there exist many subverting arguments, and because inherence itself lacks any means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, because being the fundamental cause of that [earth] would entail impermanence in respect of its possessing form and so forth;
for in the world, it is observed that things possessing form and the like are impermanent due to their having parts and other such qualities.
Thus ends the section concerning the "large" and the "long."
Even when based on a collection [of causes] as the cause, there is no attainment of that [result]. ||17||
If it is argued that [the formation of the world] is established because of mutual causality, we say no, because this is not the cause for the state of being a composite. ||18||
And because of the cessation of the preceding [moment] upon the arising of the succeeding one. ||19||
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction of one's own thesis and the simultaneous occurrence [of cause and effect]. (20)
The non-attainment of cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation [is established] because there is no interruption. ||21||
Because there is no fault in either case. ||22||
Because there is no distinction from space. ||23||
And because of mindfulness. ||24||
Because it is not seen to exist [independently]. ||25||
And thus, there is the attainment of even those who are indifferent. ||26||

The Buddhists are of four types, designated as Mādhyamika, Yogācāra, Sautrāntika, and Vaibhāṣika. All of them are disciples of the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*), who respectively propound the doctrine of universal emptiness, the emptiness of external objects, the inferability of external objects, and the perceptibility of external objects. Regarding this, it is said: "When things are analyzed by the intellect, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is apprehended. Therefore, they are shown to be inexpressible and devoid of intrinsic nature."

By such principles as "the more they are investigated, the more [they are found to be empty]," when the disciples have been taught the total emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) by the Guru, those who accept what the Guru has said exactly as it is and do not raise further objections are the "superior" because they accept the Guru’s teaching with faith; yet, because they fail to go beyond that and raise objections, they are the "inferior. Thus, due to this combination of being both superior and inferior, they abide in the state of the "middling."

The Mādhyamikas are those who, while accepting the emptiness of external objects, raised the objection: "How can consciousness itself be empty? For that would result in the world being blind. They are called Yogācāras because they possess both the practice (*ācāra*) of accepting what was taught by the Guru, as defined in their own system, and the yoga (*yoga*) of further inquiry beyond that, as defined in their own system.

The Guru informed them: "In reality, there exists only consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). That very [consciousness] appears in the form of blue and so forth; however, there is no external blue or the like apart from it. This is because the non-difference between blue and its cognitions is established by the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*); for if they were different, it would follow that this rule would not exist, as in the case of a cow and a horse. Thus, that very blue and so forth, which consists of the forms of consciousness, appears as if external due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). When this was explained, [the question arose]: "How can there be the emptiness of external objects in every respect? For [there is the appearance of] the external..."

Regarding those who have raised the following objection: "Since blue and so forth appear [externally], while consciousness appears as internal through the imprint of 'I' and blue and so forth appear as external through the imprint of 'this,' when such a distinction is manifest, the mere rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*)—being an insufficient reason—is incapable of proving non-difference; moreover, by the very mention of simultaneity, difference is admitted. To them, we reply: It is true that there is an external blue and so forth, but it is not perceived (*pratyakṣa*). For that which has not yet arisen or does not exist cannot be perceived, and that which has already arisen is momentary and lacks duration.

However, when it is explained that an object, such as blue, perishes while arising by imparting its own form to the cognition, and that the past blue and so forth are thus inferred by means of the form residing in the cognition—then, when those [students] ask at the end of the treatise how far the thread of instruction will extend in response to their inquiries, the Teacher replies:

Because they asked for the end (*anta*) of the Sūtra, they are the Sautrāntikas; thus, they are called Sautrāntikas. Consequently, the claim that the external world is to be inferred through consciousness is a contradictory statement. For that very consciousness is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of its own object, and in the absence of any object whatsoever being perceived, there would be no locus for the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus inference could not function. Those who have been questioned in this manner are the Vaibhāṣikas. To them, the direct perceptibility of the external world has also been taught.

Thus, having faith in the meaning of the answers to their respective questions exactly as they had heard them, they maintained their various differing views. In that context, there are four formal investigations (*adhikaraṇas*) intended to refute, in sequence, the four types of Buddhists beginning with the Vaibhāṣikas. Following that, this present investigation is for the purpose of refuting the Kṣapaṇakas.

Following the refutation of the Vaidika, Kāpila, and Kaṇabhuj [schools], those non-Vaidikas are now being rejected; thus, following the refutation of the partial nihilists (*ardhavaināśika*), the total nihilists (*sarvavaināśika*) are being refuted. This constitutes the structural connection (*peṭikā-saṅgati*) with the preceding section. Among the three sections concerning the Vaibhāṣikas and others, certain logicians who accept momentariness are the partial nihilists.

For, due to the imbalance of constant increase and decrease among the components of the food and drink consumed—which are being digested by the digestive fire—the composite body itself also becomes something new every moment through that constant process of increase and decrease.

Although there is no perception of the body's increase or decrease at every moment, nevertheless—just as one perceives the water in a pond due to the falling of rain showers, or the water in a well due to the drawing of a water-wheel—at the end, such a perception occurs; thus, it is logical that there is indeed a knowledge of some slight increase or decrease occurring at every instant. This is because, through the assimilation of the components of food into the components of the body, the decrease or increase of the body necessarily follows from the decrease or increase of those [components].

For just as they accept that there is a logical inference of the moon, stars, and so forth reaching slightly different locations every moment—based on the observation of their arrival at many distant places after intervals of time such as a muhūrta—so too do all the Nihilists (Sarvavaināśikas) accept the momentariness of the earth-globe due to its increase and decrease caused by inevitable processes such as digging and filling every moment, and the momentariness of the ocean due to its increase and decrease caused by the contact with river waters and the rising of spray.

The Buddhists, however, accepting the momentariness of the entire phenomenal world, are thoroughgoing nihilists (*sarvavaināśika*). The Buddhists, however, accepting the momentariness of the entire phenomenal world, are thoroughgoing nihilists.

Even among the Buddhists, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas are proponents of atomism (*paramāṇuvāda*); thus, in the first section, both are refuted by means of arguments common to both—due to their proximity to the followers of Kaṇāda—as well as by arguments unique to the Sautrāntikas. In the second section, the Yogācāras are refuted due to their similarity to [the Sautrāntikas] in their doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*). Following that, the Mādhyamikas are refuted due to their shared status as Buddhists, and subsequently, the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas) are refuted due to their shared non-Vedic character; such is the distinction.

Although the Jainas (*kṣapaṇakas*) are also proponents of the theory of atoms (*paramāṇuvādins*), nevertheless, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas accept four kinds of atoms characterized by the natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. Logicians (*tārkikas*) accept the absolute momentariness of atoms just as they accept their absolute stability; however, the Jainas maintain that atoms are of a single kind and argue against the variability of stability and other qualities. Thus, one should observe a particular affinity between the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas due to their superior proximity to the logicians.

In this regard, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, who maintain the theory of atoms (paramāṇu), say as follows: Earth-atoms have the nature of visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility; water-atoms have the nature of visible form, taste, and tangibility; fire-atoms have the nature of visible form and tangibility; and air-atoms have the nature of tangibility. These combine in the form of the primary elements (bhūta) consisting of the earth, mountains, oceans, the submarine fire (vaḍabānala), and great winds. And from these [elements], such as earth and the rest, there arise material aggregates (bhautika-saṃghāta) in the form of bodies, sense organs, jars, and other objects.

In every case, a composite (*saṃghāta*) is merely a collection of parts; there is no production of a distinct substance possessing parts (*avayavidravya*) apart from those [parts]. For if such a [distinct] production were to occur, one would have to admit that it possesses its own separate color and other qualities (*rūpādi*) in order for it to be visible and so forth. Furthermore, no color or other quality belonging to the whole is perceived as distinct from the color and other qualities of the parts. Indeed, when a cloth is produced from threads of various colors, no other color exists in the cloth apart from the various colors residing in the threads; nor is there any other taste in a mango fruit apart from the sweet or sour tastes located in the different parts of the fruit—whether it be very ripe or slightly underripe.

We do not perceive any distinct odor in the betel leaf other than the odors of the fragrant and putrid substances established in its various parts; nor do we perceive any distinct touch in the plantain petal other than the hard and soft touches established in its various parts; nor do we perceive any distinct dimension in the tree other than the large, small, and very small dimensions established in its root, middle, and top parts.

If it is argued that some accept a distinct color called "variegation" (*citra*) in cloths produced from threads of various colors, this has already been refuted by others: "If it is variegated, there can be no unity; if it is one, how can there be variegation? That it should be both one and variegated—this is truly most strange! Furthermore, no one accepts that taste and the other qualities exist as non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

Therefore, the external object consists solely of two types of aggregates: an aggregate of primary elements caused by atoms, and an aggregate of derivative matter caused by the primary elements.
