This theory is untenable; for if these two types of aggregates caused by atoms and primary elements are accepted, the existence of the world as a single aggregate and the conscious being's practical engagement with it would not be possible. Why?

If atoms and elements were causes without an activity directed toward the purpose of their conjunction, it would follow that the effect would be produced at all times. Therefore, it must be stated that atoms and elements possess causality for the production of the gross elements and their derivatives only when they are qualified by an activity that serves as the cause of conjunction. However, this is not possible if they are momentary; for those [atoms] in whom the activity resides have perished by the time of the conjunction, and those [atoms] that do conjoin have not yet arisen at the time of the activity.

Because that which lacks consciousness ceases to exist at the time when cognition arises for it, and that for which cognition arises ceases to exist at the time of activities such as avoidance; and because if one were to admit the conjunction of some [atoms] through the operation of a cause of conjunction while admitting the sensation of another through the contact of a sense organ with one, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor can it be argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because those atoms which possess activity and conjoin belong to a single continuum, and because the conscious being who possesses sense-contact and sensation belongs to a single continuum; for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness do not admit a stable continuum distinct from the momentary continuum. [Objection: Even among unstable things, there exists ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of the delusion of stability, and this is the cause of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; furthermore, subjection to passion and the like is the cause of ignorance. Thus, [there is a reciprocal causality] between ignorance, passion, and the rest...

The stream [of existence] is indeed established by experience; since it would be untenable in the absence of the collective state consisting of the body, sense organs, objects, and so forth, the establishment of that collective state implied by it cannot be rejected. If this is argued, we say no. For when the impossibility of the collective state has been stated due to the absence of a cause, its possibility must be supported by stating such a cause. And ignorance, attachment, and the like are not the cause of the collective state independently of the operation of atoms and so forth.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that through the avidyā in the form of the error of silver regarding mother-of-pearl, the mother-of-pearl—by abandoning its collection of mother-of-pearl characteristics—would attain the state of being a collection of silver characteristics due to the attachment to silver and so forth. Moreover, if one thing were to produce attachment and so forth in another through avidyā, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby the continuity of the stream of avidyā, attachment, and so forth would be untenable. It might be argued that the fault of over-extension—namely, that the action of one thing produces conjunction in another—is not applicable to the Buddhist system; for they do not admit of action or conjunction in momentary entities such as atoms.

However, the production of one thing situated in another place by something situated in a different place is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that which possesses an action-condition; and the production of something in a proximate location by something in a remote location is [the condition] for that which possesses a conjunction-condition (*saṃyoga-pratyaya*). Consequently, just as in the Nyāya system, when many sounds are combined through a sequence of sound-productions originating from various directions, there arises the cognition of a "clamor" (*kolāhala*), so too, when many atoms are thus aggregated, there arises the cognition of "earth," "mountains," and so forth.

For it is observed that although a single hair is not visible from a distance, when many hairs are gathered together in the form of a braid or the like, that collection becomes visible. Nor is there a rule that a collection of invisible things must itself be invisible, because such a reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

Just as a collection of threads possesses the power to attract a shuttle even though each individual thread lacks that power, and just as a collection of atoms possesses the power to attract [an object] even though each individual atom is invisible, it is logically established that a collection of atoms can be visible even though each individual atom is invisible. As they say: "Even if atoms are individually unfit for perception, visibility may arise when they are joined, just as threads possess the power to pull a boat and the like."

If it is argued that, therefore, the impossibility of a cause does not entail the impossibility of the existence of a composite whole, even so, the relationship of cause and effect is untenable. This is because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment of the jar, the preceding moment of the jar has already perished; thus, it is impossible for that [preceding moment] to function as the cause of the subsequent moment of the jar. In the Buddhist view, time does not exist in reality. A jar or similar object, being inherently fragile and perishing as soon as it arises, serves merely as the basis for the conceptual construction of "moments."

And that [entity], such as a jar, is metaphorically designated as "momentary" because it possesses moments (kṣaṇa) as conceptually constructed through its own arising and destruction—just as one says "the stone statue has a body"—such is their system. Therefore, according to the limits of that doctrine, the convention found in the treatises, expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that "the jar is a moment," is actually "the jar itself is the moment. Now, an objection: it is impossible for what has perished to be a cause; for it is said by them in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "The causality of entities is neither through having perished nor through remaining present."

Moreover, [it acts] by way of being real (*bhūtatayā*). And that which is real may be either persisting or destroyed; provided there is the completeness of other auxiliary causes, it produces its own effect without delay. For it is observed that the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced in a seed by watering (*dohada*) is the cause of specific colors and tastes found in the flowers, fruits, and so forth that arise at a later time. Therefore, since causality is not undermined by the fact of having been destroyed, [the objection is invalid]. If this is argued, we say: not so.

If, even when non-existent at the time of its effect, a cause were to produce it merely by virtue of having existed previously at some point, then everything would arise everywhere at all times. Even at the moment of the production of a jar, a sprout and so forth would also have to be produced, because the seed and other such things, though destroyed, possess existence in the beginningless flow of time. Nor should one suspect the absence of auxiliary factors such as the field or its cultivation; for those too, being destroyed, are no different in terms of their prior existence.

Indeed, it is well-known from the treatises on *dohada* (pregnant cravings) and *vṛkṣāyurveda* (the science of trees) that the substances of a craving continue to persist in a subtle form until the production of the effect.

It might be argued: "Let there be no causality for that which has long since perished and is devoid of activity; however, causality may belong to that which exists in the preceding moment, whether in its own nature or through its own operation. Furthermore, the priority (*pūrvavṛttitva*) of the cause must necessarily be asserted. Since the status of being a cause is established by that alone, what is the use of its existing at the time of the effect? In common experience, the causality of a seed that has perished with respect to a sprout, of milk with respect to curd, and of a lump of clay with respect to a jar is observed."

If, however, it were required that a cause exist at the time of its effect, then one might argue: "Let it be that the destruction of seeds and so forth is the cause of sprouts and so forth, and the destruction of the preceding moment of a jar is the cause of the subsequent moment of the jar. If this is the case, and you maintain that causality belongs to that which does not exist at the time of the effect, then you contradict the Buddhist tenet: "The four conditions—the dominant, the co-operative, the objective, and the immediate—are the causes of mind and mental factors."

For it is said in the *Buddhasūtra*: "Mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes. The dominant cause (*adhipati*) is the sense faculty (*indriya*). For that [faculty] is the regulator that restricts knowledge to each individual object among the five, such as form and so forth; and in the world, that which regulates is called the "dominant. The cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) is light and so forth. The objective support (*ālambana*) is the jar and so forth. The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the prior cognition.

The meaning of the proposition is that having obtained these four kinds of causes, consciousness, knowledge, mental factors (*caitasika*), and feelings such as pleasure—which are non-different from them—arise. This proposition would indeed be undermined, because if they do not exist in the preceding moment, they cannot function as causes; and if they do not exist in the subsequent moment, they cannot be objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends the present.

Otherwise, in order to establish that the cause possesses the status of being an object (*viṣayatā*), one would have to admit that it persists even at the moment the effect arises; in that case, there would be simultaneity between the contact and the cognition, which stand in the relation of cause and effect. By this, the view that the destruction in the preceding moment serves as the cause for the succeeding moment is also refuted. For if that were so, it would contradict the established doctrine regarding [the six kinds of] causes such as the dominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*) and others. Furthermore, the very destruction called "cessation" (*nirodha*) as conceived by the opponent is impossible. For they imagine it in the following way:

In every case, that which is denoted by the term "cessation" (nirodha) is entirely without residue and without continuity; it is not otherwise. It is of two kinds: gross and subtle. The gross destruction of a jar, perceived by everyone immediately after the falling of a mallet, is "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "Deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to the worldly cognition that is contrary to the apprehension of an object's existence and instead grasps its non-existence. Opposed to this is "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is subtle, incapable of being perceived by worldly means, and established through reasoning as the momentary destruction occurring at every instant.

This twofold non-sequential destruction is also impossible because there is no interruption. For a substance that persists at all times through an uninterrupted continuity, the conventional usage of "destruction" and "origination" occurs solely through the relinquishing of a prior state and the assuming of a subsequent state; however, as established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, there is never any non-sequential destruction of a substance. Therefore, it is impossible for destruction to function as a cause. As it is said: "Space and the two types of cessation—these three are eternal and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); everything else, which is cognizable by the intellect and distinct from these three, is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and momentary."

Furthermore, for the Buddhists, it is untenable for the two types of cessation (*nirodha*)—which they accept as eternal, asserting that "the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), being an effect, is impermanent, while the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such as the triad beginning with space, being non-entities, is eternal"—to function as causes; for if that which persists without interruption were a cause, it would follow that all effects would arise everywhere at all times, since even those factors intended to act as its auxiliaries would be eternal due to the eternity of the two cessations.

Furthermore, the Buddhists maintain that the triad consisting of the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*) is non-substantial (*tuccha*). In that case, how can the world arise from what is non-substantial? If it were to arise from the non-substantial, then because the non-substantial is devoid of any distinctions, it would be impossible to establish a fixed order of specific effects produced by specific causes; consequently, the entire world might arise immediately after the moment of a single jar. Moreover, an effect produced from the non-substantial would itself have to be non-substantial, and its perception as having the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) would be impossible.

Because the effect conforms to its cause, according to the analogy of gold and its ornaments such as bracelets (*rucaka*) and the like. Furthermore, the Buddhists assert that even space (*ākāśa*) is insubstantial (*tuccha*). How is this tenable? For space is clearly perceived as the locus of the flight of hawks and other birds, as in the cognition, "A hawk flies here; a vulture [flies] there. Now, it might be argued that this perception is accounted for by having the light of the moon or the sun as its object. Or, in thick darkness, the perception that "a firefly falls here" is accounted for by having the light of the firefly as its object.

The cognition, "The moon is here; the sun is here," is also explained by taking each respective light as the object. Furthermore, the cognition of the light—which itself rests upon that [surface]—as being the locus of those [objects] is also explained by means of a specific relation of identity-in-difference (*svarūpa-sambandha-viśeṣa*). This is because we observe that in the expression "the *tilaka* tree in the forest," the forest, which consists of a collection of trees, is perceived as the locus of the *tilaka* tree through such a specific relation of identity-in-difference. Indeed, even the fact that the sky is the locus of a hawk must be established through a specific relation of identity-in-difference alone.

For it is impossible for that [space] to be primarily the locus of a heavy substance, just as the surface of the earth and the like are loci for dense, material objects. Furthermore, the two cognitions of being a locus and not being a locus—expressed as "the bird is here" and "the bird is not here"—can be accounted for in the case of light by means of the delimitation of different parts; however, this is not possible in the case of space, because it is partless (*niravayava*). Nor should it be argued that even in the case of space, the very distinction between various downward portions of the earth serves as the differentiating delimiter (*avacchedaka-bheda*).

If it is argued that [the notion of space] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding space because the cognitions "there is a bird here" and "there is no bird here" with respect to upper and lower locations lack [a real object], since the perception of a hawk’s flight and so forth could possibly have light as its object—then it is replied: There certainly exists the cognition, "The hawk flies in the eastern part; the vulture in the western part," and so on. In that cognition, a locus such as the eastern direction is perceived. That very [locus] is space (*ākāśa*), because directions are not admitted apart from that.

For it is possible for that very [space] to assume the form of the eastern direction and so forth through its various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor should it be argued that by connection with those respective adjuncts, light itself takes on the form of the eastern part and so on; for even in cognitions such as "the moonlight is in the eastern part" or "darkness is in the western part," the location in the east and so forth is perceived as the locus (*ādhāra*) of the light and other objects. If it is then argued that, by the common usage "there is space in the eastern part," there must be a location distinct from space—which consists of mere vacuity—that serves as the locus for it, we say no.

In this context, the word "space" (*avakāśa*) refers to the absence of obstruction by another corporeal substance, which is the opposite of the state of being occupied by a dense corporeal substance. For this very reason:

In some places, even the prohibition of space is observed, such as: "There is room in the eastern part, but not in the western part, for it is crowded with those eating. For a prohibition of *ākāśa* (space) itself is not possible there, because it is all-pervading (*sarvagata*). If it were not all-pervading, it would follow that there would be no room even when obstructions are removed; for *ākāśa* was not non-existent previously. Thus, the objection—that "room" is merely the absence of corporeal substances (*mūrtadravyābhāva*), which, being delimited by various adjuncts (*upādhi*), serves as the basis for designations such as "east" and so forth—is also refuted.

This is because that [space] is perceived as being contained within a location; furthermore, even when there is a negation of space in the form of an absence of obstruction—as in the statement, "There is no room in the eastern part; the birds sit there packed closely together"—there is still the conventional usage of the existence of a location such as the "eastern part. Nor is there, in this way, a conventional usage of a location in the form of the eastern part and so on as being contained within another location, in the same manner as space in the form of the absence of obstruction; for if there were, a location distinct from that would be established. Indeed, the conventional usage is simply "this is the eastern location," and so forth.

It is not, however, in the form "in this place" or "in that place," and so forth. If it is argued that because of the common worldly cognition "here is space," there must be a place distinct from space itself, we say no. This is because the worldly cognition of space is established by scripture as being fixed upon a blue substance—specifically the radiance of jewels on the peak of Mount Meru—which appears like a great sapphire bowl turned downward all around and above; thus, there is no contradiction in its being perceived as contained within a particular direction.

Since spatial ether (*deśarūpam ākāśam*) does not appear independently in any worldly cognition—unlike time, which appears as an object of a category (*padārtha*) in cognitions such as "now here is a jar"—its independence is not admitted. Therefore, because ether is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), the claim that "ether and the two types of cessation (*nirodhadvaya*) are the three kinds of non-existence (*tuccha*) that are eternal, while everything else, being of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), is momentary" is incorrect. [Objection: But how can momentariness, which is established by valid means of knowledge, be rejected?

If it is argued that perception, having the present object as its domain, makes known its own object as distinguished from what is non-present—namely, from the past (the preceding moment) and the future (the succeeding moment)—just as the perception of a blue jar makes known the jar as distinguished from red ones and so forth; we reply: while the aforementioned cognition of direct recognition (*abhijñā*) grasps the jar's connection with the present time, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) expressed as "this is that same jar" also takes as its object its connection with a non-present time.

Therefore, since the connection of a single entity with both the present and non-present times is established in accordance with that [perception], and since the non-contradiction of these two times is possible through their sequential occurrence, the cognition whose object is the connection with the present time should be understood as excluding non-conjunction (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not as excluding conjunction with another (*anyayogavyavacchedaka*), nor as excluding conjunction with another by means of its own delimitation (*svāvaccheda*). It does not, however, exclude it in its entirety. For this very reason, the cognition of blue in a multicolored cloth does not lead to the exclusion of the non-blue; rather, it leads to that exclusion only as delimited by a specific location.

Indeed, the non-contradiction between two properties need not be established solely by means of a difference in their substrata; rather, it may also be established through the failure of a cognition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) to arise. However, once such a cognition does arise, a contradiction imagined merely through one's own subjective fancy does not appeal to the hearts of those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). If it is objected: "Since memory and perception have distinct, well-established causes, there ought to be two separate cognitions—one of the nature of memory in the form 'that,' and one of the nature of experience in the form 'this jar'—rather than a single cognition in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)," we reply: no.

Since those seeking that [silver] are observed to act toward this object upon hearing "this very silver has been deposited by me," the identity of the cognition is established; and since that is so, it is logically consistent to postulate—on the strength of the resulting action—that the cause there is the sense organ conjoined with the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as its proximate relation (*pratyāsatti*). But even so, is not recognition merely of the nature of an error?

If it is argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is nowhere a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is seen to be a false witness even in cases such as trees, shrubs, and creepers—which undergo a continuous succession of the increase and decrease of parts—or in mountains and oceans, which are entirely distinct [at different times], or even in bodies that have passed through childhood and old age; we say no. For the recognition cited as an example is established as valid, since its object is the identity of the substance (*dravya*) possessing those states, despite the difference between the states themselves.

For the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not the identity of the state (*avasthā*), by which it would be invalid; rather, it is the identity of the substance (*dravya*) that possesses those states. Nor should it be said that there is no substance at all persisting through multiple states apart from the states that appear and disappear, for it is impossible to reject that [substance] since the validity of the very recognitions cited above is established therein. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to imagine that the mere recognition of a flame, or of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again, is an error based on similarity.

If one were to postulate the invalidity of even those cognitions that are not sublated by using as an example a cognition that is sublated, it would follow that the very establishment of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be lost. By this [argument], the following Buddhist claim is refuted: "Memory is a cognition of an object previously experienced, while perception is a cognition of a present object. Since these two are absolutely distinct, by what could their identity be perceived? Due to differences in form, capacity, and so forth, an old man is vastly different from a child; not even a trace of the former's nature is perceived in the latter."

Even for another [opponent], how could that [entity] be one in the preceding [moment]? "If this distinction belongs to the states (*avasthā*) and not to the possessor of the states (*avasthāvat*), then only the states are perceived, and nothing beyond them, even in a dream. Now, this entire web of arguments for refuting momentariness does not apply to the Sautrāntika system as it does to the Vaibhāṣika position. Specifically, the objection regarding the contradiction with recognition—that the object of perception could not be the cause of that [recognition]—does not apply there at all.

For that proposition belongs only to those who maintain the perceptibility of external objects; and as for the statement that the conceptualization of momentariness is sublated by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), that too does not apply, because the perception of recognition regarding external objects is unestablished. Thus, even the Buddhists' inference of momentariness—namely, "a jar and so forth are momentary because they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), like the body and so forth"—is free from disturbance, since the sublation by recognition remains unestablished.

And here there is a counter-argument that subverts the opposing view: the consequence of the destruction of existence (*sattva*). For existence is nothing other than the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); it does not consist of a separate form such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because there is no evidence for such. Furthermore, that [capacity] is not possible in the case of a permanent entity. To explain: would a permanent entity perform its own causal efficiency sequentially or simultaneously? In the first case, with respect to an effect occurring at a later time, is it currently capable or not?

First of all, one should perform [the action] right now; for it is not the case that what is incapable at this time becomes capable at another time. However, according to the view that [all things] exist simultaneously (*yugapat*), since everything that is to be done has already been performed right now, it would be capable at another time. But in the view of simultaneity, because everything to be done has already been completed right now, its non-existence would follow at another time. Now, is there not a powerful counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) against this inference of momentariness?

For if things were momentary, even the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) you have stated to refute the contrary position would not function; this is because the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the determination of the absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and so forth—which require the observation of numerous concomitances between the probandum and the probans suitable for that purpose—are restricted to a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). Do not say so. For proponents of momentariness do not admit such a restriction to a single substratum regarding these matters. Furthermore, any suspicion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be warded off by the fact that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) itself acts as the regulator.

For Caitra, Maitra, and others consist each of a collection of moments of *ālayavijñāna* that arise in an uninterrupted succession, having entered into a state of cause and effect. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in the Sautrāntika position; such is the view of the Sautrāntikas who argue against [the opponent] with further reasoning: "The external objects are inferred by means of the forms (*ākāra*) such as blue and so forth residing in the cognition. For the cognition produced by an external object such as blue, which is in contact with the sense organ, itself assumes the form of blue and so forth, just like the object."

That cognition, by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*), takes itself as its object; however, the outward activity of one desiring an object such as blue does not arise from that immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*). Rather, it arises from the inferential cognition (*ānumānikajñāna*) that follows immediately after it. This is just as one who desires to catch the wind, upon seeing the movement of a branch, directs his activity toward the base of a tree. This activity does not result from the visual cognition of the branch's movement, but rather from the inferential cognition whose object is the movement of the wind, which is inferred from that mark (*liṅga*).

In this regard, the following is the refutation: cognition arises in the moment immediately following the moment of an object that is in contact with the sense organ. In that case, it is not tenable for that objective moment to be the cause of the transference of its own attributes [to the cognition]. This is because one does not observe non-existent things, such as flowers and the like, acting as causes for the transference of their own attributes onto objects such as crystals. Even if the transference of blue and other qualities were admitted, would properties residing in that object—such as being present before one, proximity, distance, or insentience—also be transferred, or not?

If [the object] were to transfer [its qualities], then there would be no appearance of its internal nature, such as its being consciousness, which is contrary to that [external form], just as when redness transfers to a crystal, its whiteness does not appear. Or, if it does not transfer—as in the case of the face's facing forward or its proximity appearing in a mirror—then, due to the absence of a probans (*liṅga*), there would be no appearance of it. Therefore, since in the doctrine of momentariness the inference of an external object is impossible just like its direct perception, permanence must indeed be accepted by them for the sake of establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Since all entities are momentary, the agent of those worldly and prescribed actions performed for the sake of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired would not be the enjoyer of their fruit; rather, it would be someone else entirely. Consequently, even those who are indifferent would achieve results [without effort], and no one at all would engage in actions. If it is argued that engagement occurs due to the delusion of identity with a future enjoyer, we say no; for one who possesses the certain knowledge of momentariness would not engage in action. If it is again argued that engagement occurs due to the delusion of identity with a future enjoyer, we say no.

Because for one who possesses the certainty of momentariness, purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is untenable. [Objection: But surely, even when there is a perception of difference, we observe activity toward ritual acts due to a desire for a fruit to be experienced by a succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth; likewise, activity might occur here as well. If you say that this is because the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established as the regulating factor, then the fruit of all actions performed by a father would accrue to the lineage of sons and grandsons, and there would be such things as the memory of the fruit of the father's experience and so on.

Because the relation of cause and effect exists in that [stream of consciousness] just as it does in one's own stream of cognition (*vijñānasantāna*), the relation of cause and effect is therefore not a restrictive factor. Consequently, for the sake of establishing the order of effects and so forth, and for the sake of maintaining the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), one must accept the stability of the self and other things. Furthermore, no counter-argument (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) can be advanced against the inference of momentariness, since even a capable [cause] can produce an orderly sequence of effects through the gradual arrival of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). The detailed refutation of momentariness, beginning with these points, is to be found elsewhere.
Summary Verses.

When the Vaibhāṣika has stated that the two— the momentary existence and the collection— do not account for the arising of contact, cognition, grasping, abandoning, destruction, water, fire, and so forth,

then the one called Sautrāntika says that these [objects], though non-existent, are inferred from the forms of cognition; he must be instructed by the dull-witted opponent through the argument that the transfer of the form of a perished object is untenable.
Thus concludes the section concerning the collective whole.
Not non-existence, because [the world] is perceived. ||27||
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and so forth. (28)
Non-existence [is established] because of non-apprehension. ||29||

The objection stated against the Vaiśeṣika and Sautrāntika positions—that if objects such as blue are momentary, their status as either perceptible or inferable is untenable—does not apply to the Yogācāra position. This is because, since objects such as blue are of the nature of internal consciousness and are self-luminous, it is possible for them to be perceived by that very [consciousness]; thus, the rebuttal is consistent. Now, here in this context, regarding the Yogācāra position, the specific correspondence of cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth to their respective objects cannot exist without the similarity (sārūpya) of those cognitions to those respective objects.

Since [external objects] cannot possibly exist [as perceived], one must necessarily admit that cognition possesses a form identical to the object; for by this alone, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is established. Apart from the blue and other forms within cognition, there is no postulation of an external object. Furthermore, regarding the blue and other forms being aspects of cognition, there is the following inference: "Blue and so forth are non-different from cognition, because they are manifest, because they are invariably perceived simultaneously with cognition, and because they are cognition. Nor should it be argued that the second reason is contradictory, on the grounds that simultaneity implies difference.

This is because the meaning of that [term] is "being the object of a perception that is pervaded by the perception of knowledge," and because pervasion—in the form of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—exists even when there is non-difference. Nor does non-difference contradict the appearance of difference in the form of the relation between action and its object (agent and patient) in the cognition "I know this"; for that [appearance] is an error, like the cognition of two moons. As they say: "Because of the rule of simultaneous perception, there is non-difference between difference and the cognition thereof; difference, however, is seen through erroneous cognitions, like the [dual] moon in the case of the non-dual."

If it is asked how the appearance of external objects such as blue as distinct from internal cognition is an error, [we reply that] the appearance of externality is also indeed an error, like the appearance of stars and other celestial bodies situated above as being on the ground when they are rising. By this, the appearance of duality in the form of the relationship between agent and object—as in "I know"—is also explained. As they say: "Though the nature of consciousness is undivided, it is perceived by those with perverted vision as if it possessed the distinction of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness."

If it is asked: "How is it that a single cognition, in reality, manifests as if divided into the forms of agent, object, and action—as in 'I know this'?"—the answer is: "Due to the force of preceding latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And the reason why a cognition of the form of potsherds does not arise immediately after the production of a cognition of the form of a pot is: "Because of the diversity of latent impressions. This is incorrect; for while the perception of external objects such as blue and so forth occurs during the waking state—with the agent appearing as the object of the action—it is impossible for an inference of their non-difference from cognition to arise.

Nor should it be argued: "Even for those who accept external blue and so forth, the fact that cognitions possess the form of blue and so on must be admitted as established by experience; since all worldly transactions are accounted for by that alone, what is the use of postulating an external object? For two forms—of the cognition and of the object—are not perceived. This is because the "form of blue and so on" of a cognition is simply its conformity to the activity of desire and the like directed toward specific objects such as blue; it does not possess a primary form of blue and so on in the same way that an external object does.

For [otherwise] there would result the contradiction of multiple mutually exclusive forms within a single synthetic cognition (samūhālambana) of blue, cold, heat, and so forth. Furthermore, the postulation that cognitions are devoid of external objects on the analogy of dreams is not tenable; for by means of sublation and non-sublation, even dream-cognitions possess objects existing at that very time. Nor is it tenable to justify the arising of diverse cognitions based on the diversity of latent impressions (vāsanā), since in the doctrine of momentary destruction without residue (niranvaya-vināśavāda), the very implantation of a latent impression is impossible.
The Summary Verses.
For the Yogācāra who asserts that consciousness alone consists of the threefold circle [of subject, object, and act of cognition],
the denial of the cognized and the cognizer is refuted by the very fact of apprehension.
Thus concludes the section on apprehension.
And because it is impossible in every respect.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: immediately after the refutation of the Yogācāra school, which asserts the existence of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*), the doctrine of the Mādhyamikas—who deny even that [consciousness]—is now being refuted. They indeed say: "That consciousness is not accepted by the wise as ultimately real, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky. Even for cognitions, there is no ultimate reality because of the difficulty of the conceptual alternatives regarding whether they possess a nature that is one or many, such as blue, yellow, cold, or heat; therefore, their very emptiness is the truth. This is incorrect.

For one who asserts that [the world] is void, the intended meaning of that voidness must be either its nature as existence, its nature as non-existence, or some other mode; yet in any case, this is not possible in the world.

Since it has been established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*) are merely specific states of a substance that persists eternally, it is impossible to demonstrate that [the effect] is either non-existent, existent alone, or something other than these two; for in all effects, only that which is existent can be the cause, since an effect cannot arise from what is purely non-existent, nor from what is non-existent having merely assumed another form. By this, it is shown that "insubstantiality" (*tucchatva*) consists either in being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), or in being devoid of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭivinirmukta*).

This is refuted by the statement: "The Madhyamikas do not know reality, which is neither non-existent nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is liberated from the four extremes. For, since they do not admit an absence (abhāva) distinct from an entity (bhāva), their assertion that absence is the cause results ultimately in a doctrine of real causality (satkāraṇavāda). Furthermore, just like the cognition and term for "existence," the cognitions and terms for the negation of existence and so forth also have as their object things delimited by space and time; therefore, unreality (tucchatva) is not established on that basis.

Since it is well known in the world that even the cognition and the word "existent" (sattva) have as their object only existence delimited by space, time, and substance—such that one says, "this exists now," or "this is of such a form"—a negation of existence without any limiting conditions (nirupādhika) cannot be established anywhere.
The Summary Verses.
The doctrine of universal emptiness, however, is not tenable in any way,
because the expressions "existent" and "non-existent" refer to a thing and its states, which are themselves dependent upon that thing.
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility [of the world] in every respect.
Not [in one], because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes]. 31.
And thus, the self would be non-omnipresent. (32)
And even by way of figurative interpretation there is no absence of contradiction, because of [the necessity of] modification and so forth. (33)
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both are eternal, there is no distinction. ||34||

The followers of the Sugata have been refuted; now the Jains are being refuted. They indeed maintain that the world consists of six substances (ṣaḍdravya) known as soul (jīva), merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), matter (pudgala), time (kāla), and space (ākāśa), and is devoid of a Lord (nirīśvara). Among these, souls are of three kinds: bound, those who have attained yoga-perfection, and the liberated. Merit is a pervasive, distinct substance that is the cause of motion for things possessing movement. Demerit is a pervasive, distinct substance that is the cause of stability. Matter consists of atoms, mountains, oceans, and so forth. Time is a distinct substance consisting of atoms that serves as the basis for the conventional usage [of expressions] such as "it was," "it is," and "it will be."

Space (*ākāśa*) is also one; however, it consists of infinite points (*ananta-pradeśa*). Furthermore, they provide another summary: "Soul (*jīva*), non-soul (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), shedding (*nirjarā*), restraint (*saṃvara*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). The souls have been described. Non-soul is the entire collection of things that are objects of experience for the soul. Influx is the aggregate of the sense organs, because by means of this, the soul flows toward [objects] in the form of cognitions of jars and so forth. Some, however, say that influx is the bondage of karma, because while the soul flows, it follows after [the object] everywhere.

Thus Jinadatta said: "Influx (āsrava) is bondage through karma; liberation (nirjarā) is release from that. Bondage is of eight kinds, distinguished by the four destructive (ghāti) karmas and the four non-destructive (aghāti) karmas. Among these, the first group of four consists of an evil nature beginningless in its continuity, which obstructs the qualities of knowledge, vision, bliss, and vigor of the soul that are destined to manifest in the state of liberation.

The second group of four consists of the body, its configuration, the ego-identification with it, and the sustenance thereof; these are of the nature of merit (*puṇya*) because they are mixed with merit that serves as the cause for pleasure and so forth. Austerity (*tapas*) is defined etymologically as that by which desire, anger, and other passions are worn away (*niśśeṣaṃ jīryati*) without remainder; it takes the form of practices such as plucking out the hair and climbing heated stones. Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the suppression of the senses. Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the manifestation of the soul’s own innate nature. Some, however, maintain that liberation is the continuous upward movement, for it is the inherent nature of one freed from bondage to move upward.

Just as for a parrot released from a cage, or as for a fully ripened castor seed that has burst open, or as for a dried gourd whose coating of thick mud has been washed away by immersion in water; so too, due to the cessation of bondage that has persisted since beginningless time, there is a constant upward movement. They say that the infinite *alokākāśa* (space beyond the world), situated above all the worlds, provides the space for this constant upward movement.

Thus they recite: "The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again; yet those traveling on the path of the *aloka-ākāśa* (the space beyond the world) do not return even today. Others, however, say that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding in a higher region for one whose qualities such as knowledge have become manifest. They apply all this collection of entities according to the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī-naya*).

"It may be that it exists, it may be that it does not exist, it may be that it both exists and does not exist, it may be inexpressible, it may be that it exists and is inexpressible, it may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible, and it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible. Herein, there are four modes concerning existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and the inexpressibility consisting in being distinct from both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, by combining existence, non-existence, and both existence and non-existence with indeterminability, three modes are produced; thus, seven modes can be conceived by those who propound them. All these modes are described by the Jains regarding every category of reality that they have accepted even in the slightest degree. Some hold that the word *syāt* means "in some small measure" (*īṣadartha*). Others hold that it means "non-exclusive" (*anaikāntya*). In either case, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

The method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*), demonstrated regarding existence—taking the form "it may be eternal," "it may be non-eternal," and so forth—is equally applicable to properties such as eternity and its opposite. Therefore, this Jaina doctrine is also not tenable; for it is impossible for contradictory multiple attributes to coexist in a single entity without a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). [Objection: But is it not accepted that even in a single entity, there is a coexistence of contradictory attributes through a distinction of limiting conditions such as place and time?

But surely, even in a single entity, the coexistence of contradictory attributes is admitted through the distinction of limiting conditions such as place and time? [We reply: That is not accepted merely on the grounds that a distinction of limiting conditions is impossible there; rather, it is accepted because there is valid evidence for it.

For this very reason, even though the Siddhāntin accepts the coexistence of "lump-ness" (piṇḍatva) and "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) through the distinction of temporal adjuncts (kālopādhi), he does not accept the coexistence of "jiva-hood" (jīvatva), "Lord-hood" (īśvaratva), and so forth, on the grounds that there is no evidence for such coexistence. Thus, it being established that the coexistence of attributes depends solely upon evidence and not upon the mere possibility of adjuncts, [the status of] reality (satyatva) and so forth—

If it is argued that since those various disputants have established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and so forth, why should there not be a convergence of them all? We say no; for while it is possible for all the [criteria] imagined by those various disputants to be valid, because they are mutually contradictory, it is necessarily the case that some among them must be fallacious (*ābhāsa*).

Otherwise, because the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is accepted by disputants, even defects such as its unreality would be established as objects of cognition; consequently, since those [defects] would also have to be superimposed, it would follow that even the proponent of non-contradiction (*anaikāntya-vādin*) would be subject to the very defects asserted by each respective opponent. By this, the statement in the *Syādvādamañjarī*—“Just as other sectarian doctrines are envious due to their mutual status as thesis and counter-thesis, so too is not the system [of the Jains], which desires all vehicles without distinction and is thus free from partiality”—is refuted.

If one were not impartial, there would be the undesirable consequence of including even those defects such as non-existence that have been stated by various [opposing] systems, along with the inclusion of existence and so forth as taught by all [systems]. [Objection: In that case, we shall establish the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) precisely without contradicting worldly convention. For there is indeed universal agreement regarding both existence and non-existence of a single thing at different times. Therefore, based on the desire to express each of these in its own respective time, there are two propositions—“it exists” and “it does not exist”—when expressed sequentially.

The third limb is "this is both existent and non-existent," intended by the desire to express existence and non-existence simultaneously. The fourth limb is "it is indescribable" (anirvacanīya), for it is indeed impossible to describe the simultaneous existence and non-existence of a single thing. When existence and non-existence are combined with their indescribability, and when existence, non-existence, and their two successive states are combined, the remaining three limbs arise. As Anantavīrya has said: "When there is no desire to express those [specific] modes, the understanding would be 'it exists' (syād asti)."

"If one intends to negate [existence], the formulation 'it does not exist' (syān nāsti) should be used. When there is a desire to express both [existence and non-existence] sequentially, the formulation involves their combination. When there is a desire to express them simultaneously, it is 'inexpressible' (avācya) due to incapacity. When there is a desire to express the first [existence] as inexpressible, the fifth proposition (bhaṅga) is accepted. When there is a desire to express the last [non-existence] as inexpressible, the sixth proposition arises. And when joined with a conjunction [of the two inexpressibles], the seventh proposition is stated."

If it is argued that, therefore, the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) is established without contradiction, [we reply: if this *saptabhaṅgīnaya* is merely conventional (*pāribhāṣika*), then it is indeed accepted. For there is no disagreement among common people or investigators regarding the coexistence of existence and non-existence through the distinction of place, time, and counter-correlate—such as a jar existing in its own place but not in another place, existing at its own time but not at another time, and existing in its own nature but not in another nature. However, this does not establish the manifoldness (*anaikāntya*) of the object as intended by the Jainas.

This is because there is no loss of the restrictive rule that [a thing] exists only at its own time and does not exist at other times, and so forth. One might object: "For those who maintain the non-exclusivity (anaikāntya) of all phenomena, even unity is not established; therefore, by adopting 'multiplicity' (*anekatva*) as a synonym for 'might be many' (*syādanekam*), the coexistence of existence, non-existence, and so on, is logically possible. This is not so, because it is impossible to establish—even without contradiction—the very coexistence of unity and multiplicity that was required in the first place.

Furthermore, if one does not accept the absolute certainty (*ekānta*) regarding number, it would be impossible to present one's own established doctrine that there are six substances, such as the soul, merit, demerit, and so forth. What more need be said? For those who maintain the doctrine of universal non-absolutism (*anaikāntavāda*), even the social order—such as "this is her son," "this is her husband," or "this is her father"—could not be established; consequently, the appropriate conventional designations of motherhood and so forth for the son and others would likewise fail to be fixed. Therefore, this doctrine of non-absolutism must be entirely rejected.

Furthermore, the Jains maintain that the self (ātman) has the same dimensions as the body; this too is incorrect. For if the self, which occupies the entire body of an elephant, were to enter the body of a mosquito, it would follow that it suffers mutilation. Moreover, when entering the body of an elephant from the body of a mosquito, because it lacks the necessary transformation to pervade that [larger] body, it would follow that it could not experience pleasure throughout all its limbs.

If it is argued that there is no fault because it is accepted that the self undergoes contraction and expansion, attaining successive states of contraction or expansion according to each respective body, we say: no. For if that were so, the self would be subject to modification, which would entail the consequence of impermanence and other such defects. Therefore, even the Jainas must maintain that the final dimension of the self in the state of liberation remains exactly as it is; for thereafter, in the absence of another body, there is no possibility of a dimension appropriate to one.

Therefore, since its dimension likewise possesses the same quality of eternity as the nature of the Self abiding in the state of liberation, it is logical to accept that very [dimension] as the innate dimension of the Self; however, it is not characterized by contraction and expansion.
Summary Verses.
The Digambaras should not place their hopes in the system of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī),
for it is impossible for existence, non-existence, and so forth to occur simultaneously in a single thing.
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] existing in one [substratum].
On account of the inconsistency regarding the Lord [as the cause]. (35)

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is established that the doctrine of the Śaivas is also inconsistent, due to internal contradictions—such as those between "existent" and "non-existent"—similar to the Jaina view, and because it contradicts the Vedas. Among the fourfold Śaiva systems known as Kāpāla, Kālāmukha, Pāśupata, and Siddhānta-Śaiva, the doctrines of the Kāpālas and Kālāmukhas have been presented in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the Pāśupatas, they say: "The five categories—effect, cause, yoga, rite, and the end of suffering—must be understood for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its bonds (pāśa)."

In this context, the effects (*kārya*) consist of ten types: the five elements beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*), and the five qualities (*guṇa*) beginning with form (*rūpa*). The instruments (*karaṇa*) are thirteenfold: the five organs of perception (*jñānendriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Sacrifice (*yajña*) consists of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Ritual injunction (*vidhi*) is the activity directed toward merit (*dharma*) and wealth (*artha*); it is twofold by way of vows (*vrata*) and gates (*dvāra*). Vows include the ritual bathing in ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), sleeping on ashes (*bhasmaśayana*), and offerings (*upahāra*). Ritual bathing in ashes is of two kinds: one is the daily (*nitya*) practice to be performed at the three junctions of the day as a substitute for water-bathing.

In cases such as the voiding of feces and urine, sneezing, or spitting, one should perform another occasional rite called *anusnāna* (subsequent bathing), which serves as a substitute for ritual purification with water; furthermore, there is the *bhasmasnāna* (ash-bath). Sleeping on ashes should be performed using ashes obtained by begging, just like food, from the houses of householders. The offering (*upahāra*) is of six kinds, distinguished as laughter, song, dance, the *huḍukkāra* sound, prostration, and recitation (*japa*). Among these, *hasita* is loud laughter. *Gīta* and *nṛtta* are to be performed according to one's inclination, without regard for the rules of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*).
*Huḍukkāra* is a sound resembling the bellowing of a bull, produced by the contact of the tongue with the palate. Regarding this, worldly people...

In that context, these four [practices] do not exist; they must be applied secretly. The recitation (*japa*) consists of the five Brahma-mantras; the salutation (*namaskāra*) is well known. The doors are sixfold, distinguished by: bodily movement (*kāyanam*), trembling (*spandanam*), slow walking (*mandayānam*), amorous gestures (*śṛṅgāraṇā*), acting like another (*itatkaraṇā*), and speaking like another (*itadbhāṣaṇa*). Bodily movement (*kāyanam*) is the display of the characteristics of sleep while one is not actually asleep. Trembling (*spandanam*) is the shaking of the limbs of the body like one overcome by a wind-disease (*vātavyādhi*). Slow walking (*mandayānam*) is moving like one whose faculty of the feet is impaired.

*Śṛṅgāraṇa* (amorosity) consists of those playful gestures by which one displays oneself as if desirous upon seeing a woman endowed with beauty and youth; it also includes performing actions censured by the world like one devoid of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done, and speaking words that are contradictory, meaningless, and so forth. *Duḥkhānta* (the end of suffering) is of two kinds: non-substantial (*anātmaka*) and substantial (*sātmaka*). The non-substantial is the absolute cessation of all sufferings. The substantial, however, is sovereignty characterized by the power of the faculties of vision and action.

In that regard, although the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) is one, it is figuratively designated as fivefold according to the distinction of its objects: seeing, hearing, thinking, discerning, and omniscience. Knowledge whose objects include all visual and tactile things—whether subtle, concealed, or distant—is "seeing. Knowledge whose objects include all sounds is "hearing. Knowledge whose objects include all scriptures without exception is "thinking. Knowledge that is free from doubt regarding both the letter and the meaning is "discerning. Omniscience is well known.

The power of action (kriyā-śakti), though single, is treated as threefold: swiftness like thought (manojava-tva), the state of assuming any form at will (kāmarūpa-tva), and the quality of being free from the limitations of instruments (vikaraṇa-dharmitva). Swiftness like thought is the capacity for movement exceeding even the mind in speed. The state of assuming any form at will is the ability to preside over infinite bodies and sense organs by one's own will, independent of karma. The quality of being free from instruments is the possession of unsurpassed sovereignty even when the body and senses have been withdrawn. Furthermore, Paśupati, the Supreme Lord, is the instrumental cause in every effect.

For the animals, He bestows fruits by His own will alone, independent of their karma, because He possesses unsurpassed sovereignty. Nor is karma rendered useless in this way; for karma that is favored by the Lord’s will is fruitful, while karma not so favored is fruitless—just as agricultural labor is fruitless when not favored by rain—but even in such cases there is no fault, since engagement in actions is justified by the possibility of receiving His favor. Furthermore, the sequence of creation is dependent upon the Lord’s will at that particular time, but it is not necessarily fixed as "ether" and so forth.

The contradiction between such a Pāśupata doctrine and the Kāpālika and Kālāmukha doctrines is evident. Even though there is agreement regarding practices such as bathing in ashes, there is a contradiction concerning the nature of the ash to be accepted—specifically, that it should not be ash from a corpse. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the Veda; for practices such as making the *huḍukka* sound are not clearly found in the Vedas or their auxiliary texts (*upabṛhmaṇa*).

The practice of sexual dalliance (*śṛṅgāraṇa*), the substitution of bathing in ashes for ritual bathing with water, the abandonment of water purification, and the disregard for the sequential order of rites prescribed for living beings are all utterly contrary to the path of the Vedas. Thus, it is established that the three Śaiva systems beginning with Kāpāla are incoherent due to their mutual contradictions and their opposition to the Vedas. Although Siddhānta Śaivism does not possess such extreme contradiction with the Vedas, [it is still subject to critique].

And since there is no contradiction with the Vedas, any mutual contradictions among the twenty-eight forms of Tantras, beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula, along with their sub-divisions—such as those consisting of the Āgama-siddhānta, Divya-siddhānta, Tantra-siddhānta, and Antaratantra-siddhānta varieties of the Pāñcarātra—can be reconciled by means of the distinction between the specific qualified aspirants (adhikārins) intended for each respective Tantra, just as the internal contradictions among the various sub-Tantras of the Pāñcarātra are resolved.

The statement regarding the superiority of the Śiva-āgamas over the Veda found in the *Kāmika* and other texts can be reconciled in the same manner as the statement regarding the superiority of the *Pāñcarātra* over them. Nevertheless, even while accepting the authority of the Veda, the Siddhānta Śaiva Tantras conceal the Veda and establish the existence of God through inference alone. This is surely because, if one were to accept God in accordance with the Veda, the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*) would almost invariably designate the causal substance by the name "Nārāyaṇa," which is unique to Puruṣottama; thus, He alone is the cause of the universe and the Supreme Brahman.

It is concluded that the term "distinction" (*bheda*) is used for the purpose of concealing that [non-distinction]. Therefore, we point out the inconsistency in their attempt to establish God through inference alone. For, by observing distinctions such as the potter and the lump of clay in the world, they establish God as a mere efficient cause through inference, disregarding the non-difference between the efficient cause and the material cause established by scripture. If that is so, then on the basis of worldly observation alone, He must also be admitted to possess a body; for it is observed that only embodied beings, such as potters, function as agents.

Nor should it be argued that his body must consist solely of things like illusory power (*māyā*) and the like, because he does not require a body other than the one governed by his own bodily functions; for we do not posit a mere body, but rather a body that serves as the locus of experience. Indeed, it is observed that for one who presides over such a body for the sake of experience—whether for the sake of pleasure or for the avoidance of pain—there is a localized nature [of that experience].

Furthermore, if one accepts a body as the locus of experience for the sake of accounting for agency, then there would necessarily follow possession of merit and demerit rooted in that [body], finitude due to the rule that a body is impermanent, and non-omniscience because those subject to the cycle of birth and death are observed to possess only limited knowledge. Therefore, for those who seek to establish the existence of God through inference, God would not be established in the form they intend.

As for the objection raised in the section on "The Scripture Being the Source" (*Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*)—namely, that if God were established through inference, then the multiplicity of Gods and so forth would also be established—that too is simply an objection belonging to this very context. For it is here alone that we see the author of the Sūtras explicitly stating his refutation of inference. In that [previous] section, however, the author of the Sūtras established the fact that the Supreme Lord has scripture as His source precisely through an investigation into the purport of such scriptural passages as "He is to be known through the Upaniṣads" (*Tattvaupaniṣadam*). Therefore, there is no tautology between the two.

Regarding the Sāṃkhya section [of the *Brahmasūtra*] beginning with "On account of the impossibility of the arrangement" (*racanānupapatti*), the Sāṃkhya—who infers that the world, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, must have a cause of the same nature as itself according to the analogy of clay and pots—is met with the following: by that very same example, it is merely established that there must be a presiding intelligence (*adhiṣṭhāna*). However, an independent inference for God (*īśvara*) is not thereby proven to be faultless; thus, while God was established therein [in the Sāṃkhya context], He is refuted here. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that the inference for God was accepted there but criticized here. (Summary Verse)

The husband's opinion is certainly not to be respected, because it is contradicted by each other even according to scripture; for if God is conceived as a mere instrumental cause, then even the notion of divine supervision becomes inconsistent.
Thus concludes the section concerning Paśupati.
Because origination is impossible. (39)
And there is no instrument for the agent. 40.
Or, if consciousness and the other [aggregates] exist, there is no negation of that [self]. ||41||
And because of contradiction. ||42||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that the *Pāñcarātra* is unauthoritative because it is a *tantra*, like the *Pāśupata*, that doubt is now being refuted. The *Pāñcarātrikas*, who are known as *Bhāgavatas*, maintain that the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, abides in the form of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) beginning with Vāsudeva. Among these, Vāsudeva possesses the six complete attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). These six attributes are knowledge, strength, sovereignty, power, and splendor.

In this context, His knowledge (*jñāna*) is said to be that which has all things as its object, because it is free from all distinctions whatsoever arising from the entire manifold (*prapañca*) consisting of both sentient and insentient beings. His power (*śakti*) is the state of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the world. His strength (*bala*) is the absence of fatigue for Him while creating the world, and the effortless sustaining of the entire universe He has created, like a mole on the skin. His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the state of having unimpeded will. His valor (*vīrya*) is the absence of transformation despite being the material cause of the world, just as milk remains itself even when becoming curd.

*Tejas* (splendor) is the independence from auxiliary causes in the creation of the world and the capacity for the subjugation of others. From that, through the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñāna*), he appears in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa. Then, through the manifestation of the power of valor and sovereignty (*vīryaiśvarya*), he appears in the form of Pradyumna. Then, through the simultaneous manifestation of power and splendor (*śakti-tejas*), he appears in the form of Aniruddha. And Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others have the forms of the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

Thus, by propitiating the Blessed One in his fourfold manifestation every day through the fivefold practice beginning with approach (*abhigamana*), as well as through vows lasting a hundred years and so forth, a person is liberated from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Among these, "approach" (*abhigamana*) consists of the recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, prostrations, and so on, dedicated to the Blessed One in the morning. Thereafter, "procurement" (*upādāna*) is the gathering of flowers and other materials for worship. Thereafter, "worship" (*ijyā*) is the act of offering. Thereafter, "self-study" (*svādhyāya*) consists of listening to the scriptures of the Blessed One, the Purāṇas, and the Āgamas that are consistent with them.

"Therefore, Yoga is the concentration of the mind upon the Blessed Lord following the evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā). This is the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument, which is as follows: In the Pāñcarātra, the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is traditionally taught: "From Vāsudeva, the individual soul named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born; from Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind named Pradyumna is born; from that, the ego (ahaṅkāra) named Aniruddha is born. And it is not possible for the individual soul, being beginningless (anādi), to have a birth.

Nor should it be said that this passage asserts that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others possess the conceit (abhimāna) of being the individual soul (jīva) and so forth; for if that were the case, statements such as "Saṅkarṣaṇa is the name of the individual soul" would be untenable. For by this [passage], the names Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are prescribed—according to the technical terminology of the Pāñcarātra—for the well-known [entities] of the individual soul, the mind, and the ego-sense respectively.

Furthermore, when the *Saṅkarṣaṇa* and others are mentioned by name and their forms, weapons, and so forth are prescribed in that scripture, it is established that this is for the purpose of meditation upon those very [entities], just as specific colors are prescribed for the letters beginning with 'ka'. It does not mean that there are deities presiding over the mind who possess such distinct forms, weapons, and so on. Moreover, just as the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) is impossible, the production of the instruments such as the mind from the individual soul as their creator is likewise impossible.

Because it is heard in scripture that the mind and all the senses are born from the Supreme Brahman alone—according to the text, "From Him is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses"—therefore, the Pāñcarātra system also lacks authority due to its contradiction with the Veda.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: in the Pāñcarātra, the production of the individual soul from Vāsudeva, or of the mind and other faculties from the individual soul and so forth, is not stated. Rather, what is taught is the manifestation of the emanations (vyūhas) such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others, who are the presiding deities over the individual soul and the rest; this manifestation is established by the Śruti text: "Being unborn, he is born in many ways."

Furthermore, the verbal root is *janī-prādurbhāve* (to appear or be manifested). However, the names Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others have not been stated as referring to the well-known individual souls (*jīva*) and so forth. This is because it will be established in the second chapter that words such as *jīva*, which denote those who are governed, actually refer to specific manifestations (*vyūha*) of their respective governors; that words denoting bodies extend to the embodied soul; and that words expressing inseparable modes extend to the substratum of those modes. Moreover, in the Pāñcarātra itself, concerning the individual soul, it is said: "For he is indeed beginningless and endless in the ultimate sense..."
Furthermore, because its [the opponent's] origination is denied by the statement "it is determined," the Pāñcarātra composed by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is indeed the preeminent authority.
The Summary Verses.
If it is argued that the Pāñcarātra is not to be accepted because it teaches the origination of the individual soul (jīva), we say no;
for it speaks of the manifestation of the Vyūhas and explicitly denies the birth of the soul therein.
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility of origination.

Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled the Essence of the Four Systems (*Caturmatasāra*), composed by Appaya Dīkṣita— the son of the illustrious Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and a Kaustubha-jewel in the ocean of the venerable Bharadvāja lineage, and a teacher of the illustrious Advaita-vidyā.
The Third Quarter of the Second Chapter.

It has been stated that the systems such as Sāṃkhya and others are inconsistent because they are rooted in fallacious reasoning and involve internal contradictions. Now, with the counter-argument (pratibandī) revolving in the mind—that even our own position suffers from the defect of conflicting scriptural statements regarding whether the ether is produced or unproduced—we shall, in the first two quarters [of this chapter], clarify the manner in which the phenomenal world, as an effect of Brahman, is produced, in order to demonstrate the absence of such defects in our view.

If this were the case, then, because it serves to avoid the objections raised by others regarding the proof that ether and so forth are effects, it would follow that [the section on the effect] must immediately follow the first quarter (pāda). If you argue that the two quarters concerning the effect begin only after the two quarters concerning the cause, then this pair of quarters concerning the effect would have no connection whatsoever to the chapter as a whole.

If it is argued that the purpose of the second chapter is indeed the resolution of contradictions that obstruct the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with Brahman as the cause of the world—concordance which was established in the first chapter—it is replied: The concordance of the scriptural texts concerning the cause with respect to Brahman depends upon the concordance of the texts concerning the origination of ether (*viyat*) and the other elements with their own literal meaning. Otherwise, if ether were eternal and if air and the other elements were not produced from ether and so forth, how could Brahman be the cause of ether and the rest?

And how could Brahman be the cause of every effect? Therefore, there follows an inquiry into the concordance of the scriptural texts regarding the origination of ether and the other elements; and, as a consequence thereof, an inquiry into the eternity of the individual soul, its nature as a knower, its atomicity, and so forth.

Alternatively, after it has been established by such sūtras as "And because of contradiction, [the Sāṃkhya and other systems] are inconsistent" that the systems of the Sāṃkhyas and others lack authority due to their mutual contradictions, one might suspect that the Vedāntas also lack authority because of internal contradictions—such as between the scriptural texts regarding the origin and non-origination of ether and the soul, and those concerning the soul's nature as a knower or its being of the nature of knowledge—and thus, due to this doubt regarding their lack of authority even in respect to their cause (Brahman), their authoritative status could not be established beyond doubt.

One should also consider that the inquiry into the nature of the knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth is directly relevant, as it raises an objection regarding the harmony of the scriptural texts concerning the cause established in the first chapter. Here, first of all, the non-origination of ether (*viyat*) is demonstrated: "Ether does not originate, because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]. (Sūtra 1.1.2).
It exists. ||2||
Because figurative application is impossible and because of the scriptural statement. (Sūtra 3)
And it may belong to one [thing] alone, as in the case of the word "Brahman. (Sūtra 4)
There is a loss of the proposition because there is no distinction. ||5||
From words. ||6||
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world. ||7||
By this, Mātariśvan is explained. ||8||
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable. 9.

Regarding the doubt as to whether space (*ākāśa*) is produced or not—based on the presence or absence of scriptural passages capable of demonstrating its production—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Space is not produced, because there is no scriptural passage capable of demonstrating its production. In the *Chāndogya*, for instance, there is no such scriptural passage at all regarding it. Even though such a passage exists in the *Taittirīyaka*, the *Atharvaṇa*, and other texts, it is not capable of demonstrating its production; for space is understood to be eternal due to its being partless and all-pervading. Nor is the second reason unestablished.

Because it is impossible for its non-existence to be apprehended anywhere; for the negation "space does not exist here" is contradictory, since that very place where it is negated is itself of the nature of space. Therefore, the term *saṃbhūta* ("come into being") heard in reference to space in the Taittirīya Śruti—"From this [Being] are born breath, mind, and all the senses, as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports all"—and the term *jāyate* ("is born") applied to space in the Atharvaṇa, must both be understood in a figurative sense. Nor...

There is no fault whatsoever in the difference of meaning between the two words *sambhūta* and *jāyate*, which are used in connection with what has been heard [in scripture]. Indeed, in the Atharva Veda itself it is said: "Brahman is built up by austerity; from that, food is produced."

Therefore, since we observe that even in the two scriptural passages—"From that, this Brahman is born as name, form, and food"—the word *brahman* is used both in its primary and secondary senses, the proponent of the origination of ether (*viyat*) must likewise accept that in the scripture stating, "And it is all-pervading and eternal like space," the words "eternal" and "all-pervading," though mentioned once, have a primary sense in one instance and a secondary sense in the other. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Where the primacy of fire (*tejas*) is heard, it is precisely there—in the *Chāndogya*—that the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, which was promised by means of the analogies of the lump of clay and so forth, remains unimpaired; for this occurs simply because space (*ākāśa*) also does not differ from Brahman, being its effect. Therefore, it is determined that the fact of space being the effect of Brahman is also approved by the *Chāndogya* scripture.

This is understood from such statements as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," which establishes unity prior to creation, and "All this has that as its self," which demonstrates that everything has Brahman as its self.
