Thus, when it is determined by these words that even ether is a modification of Brahman in a general sense, its specific production in the form of a separation from Brahman is already stated.

Just as in the world, having stated generally that "all these are the sons of Devadatta," one then specifies for some of them their origin from him, whereby it is already implied that all of them are born from him; so too, if this is the case, how is it that the *Chāndogya* mentions the priority of the creation of fire? It is certainly not heard in scripture that fire was created first by Brahman, such that its priority would be established by scriptural authority.

However, since the creation of fire is mentioned first, its priority is established by the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*). Nor does the authority of position override the scriptural statement of origination in the phrase "space was produced" (*ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*). The reason—that space is eternal because it is partless—is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), for even that which is partless can be shown to be non-eternal within the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), according to the logic of pots, bowls, and the like being fashioned from a single lump of clay cited in the scripture.

Nor is the all-pervasiveness of space established here by the contradiction of the negation "space does not exist," because in that context, it is logical for "space" to refer to the absence of dense, material substances as understood through the cognition of "here. This is because even in common usages such as "one must stay here in this space," that [absence] is also cognized through the notion of "here. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the scriptural statement regarding the immortality of space, namely, 'The wind and the intermediate space—these are immortal'? the answer is: it has the same status as the scriptural statement regarding the immortality of the wind.

For even wind, which has a manifest origin, is heard in scripture to be immortal. What need is there for more? Whatever exists apart from Brahman—whether it be the unmanifest (avyakta), the great principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), fire, and so forth—all that, like space and wind, possesses an origin, in accordance with the promise of the knowledge of all and other such statements.
The summary verses.
Space is eternal because it is partless and because of the scriptural declaration of its immortality;
furthermore, since light is mentioned first in the account of creation, the scriptural statement regarding the "birth" of space is figurative.
The indivisibility [of the self] is non-probative, as is its immortality like that of the immortals;
the primacy of fire is not heard [in scripture], and the contradiction is established by the textual order.
Therefore, space and air possess birth along with the Mahat and the other principles;
for in this way, the proposition that all things are cognizable and so forth is established.
Thus concludes the section concerning ether.
Therefore, [the self] consists of light, for thus it says. ||10||
The waters. ||11||
The earth. 12.
[The word "self" denotes the Self] because of its specific authority, its form, and other words [in the same context]. ||13||
But he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation, on account of its characteristic mark. 14.
But by way of the reverse order, the sequence as well as rebirth is established. ||15||
If it is argued that the intermediate consciousness and the mind arise sequentially because their respective signs appear in succession, we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. 16.
But the designation [of the Self] as dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative, because it exists only when those [bodies] exist. 17.

It has been established that everything other than Brahman is the effect of Brahman. Here, this is considered: does the production of fire and the other elements arise from each preceding element, such as air, their status as effects of Brahman being only through a succession; or rather, do they arise from the Supreme Self, who possesses each preceding element as His body? On this point, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is as follows: their production arises from each preceding element alone. For scripture declares: "From air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth."

But is it not the case that the scripture declares the creatorship of fire and the other elements to be preceded by reflection, stating: "It [the Self] thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and it emitted heat; that heat thought, and it emitted water; that water thought, and it emitted food"? And reflection is not possible for insentient things. Therefore, on the basis of the mark of reflection, the words "heat" and so forth must refer to the Supreme Self as possessing those respective bodies; thus, it is appropriate to say that water arises from the Supreme Self whose body is heat, and earth arises from that [Self] whose body is water.

Nor should it be asked how the earth is denoted by the word "food" (*anna*) in the passage, "They created food. This is because the context concerns the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). In the section describing the forms of the great elements as they have been made tripartite—stating, "That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food"—the form of food is mentioned. Furthermore, in the same context, another word denoting the earth is heard: "From water, the earth."

If it is argued that, therefore, words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth must be understood as referring to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) who has those respective things as His body—since in the *Antaryāmi-adhikaraṇa* it was stated that all things have the Supreme Self as their body—we say: not so. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of abandoning the direct meaning of the scripture (*śruti-hāni*) by resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for words like "fire" to denote the Supreme Self within those bodies. Nor is it proper to subvert the scripture on the basis of the mark of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*). Rather, in accordance with the scripture, it is proper to maintain that "seeing" itself is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). [As it is said: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the senses."

The Atharvaṇa mantra, "Space, air, light, water, and earth, the supporter of all," is also appropriately explained as having for its purport the fact that [all things] are effects of Brahman, whether directly or through a lineage such as son, grandson, and great-grandson. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The world originates from the Supreme Self (paramātman) who possesses those respective bodies, as indicated by the mark of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa). Nor is there any contradiction with scripture (śruti), because all words denoting the manifold universe of moving and non-moving beings have their primary meaning in the Supreme Self who possesses those respective bodies. This is because, in worldly usage such as "the Brāhmaṇa studies" or "the Brāhmaṇa is learned," and in Vedic usage such as "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa" or "a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," it is established through linguistic convention (vyutpatti) that words denoting the body extend to the embodied being.

This is because it is understood from the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa that all things, both moving and non-moving, constitute the body of the Supreme Self, and from the scriptural statement regarding the differentiation of names and forms—"Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"—which describes the manifestation of names and forms preceded by the entry into fire and the other elements. Nor should it be argued that the scriptural hearing of the state of being the body of all is merely figurative; for the scripture speaks of entry specifically for the purpose of manifesting names and forms after the creation of fire and the rest, as seen in another scriptural passage: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing. Thus, it must not be said [that the bodyhood is figurative].

Since it is impossible for the omnipresent Lord—who was previously non-existent in any particular place—to enter [the egg] later, the scriptural texts concerning "entry" are intended to establish His eternal existence as the Controller. Therefore, because words such as "light" (*tejas*) and so forth have their primary meaning in the Supreme Self, it is determined through passages such as "That light thought" (*tatteja aikṣata*) that the Supreme Self alone is the direct creator of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This is likewise determined by the Atharvaṇa mantra beginning with "From this [Self] is born" (*etasmāj jāyate*).

For this mantra—according to the principle of son and grandson, wherein each subsequent effect among the unmanifest, mahat, ahaṃkāra, and so forth, arises from each preceding one—is naturally intended to convey the sequence in which everything arises directly from the Supreme Self alone; that is, the sequence consisting of the immediate succession of everything from the Supreme Self.

And that [creation] is established as proceeding directly from Brahman as the source of those respective bodies, because in the passage "from this [Brahman] is born," directness is the primary and natural sense. If it is argued: "But this mantra has as its purport the sequence in which the eyes and other senses, as well as the mind, arise among the vital breath (prāṇa) and the elements, based on the evidence of the sequential enumeration starting from ether (kha) and ending with earth; it does not intend to teach the origination of everything, including the vital breath and so forth, from the Supreme Self"—we reply: No.

The sense organs, the mind, and the ether (kha) are also included among those created directly by the Supreme Self, as indicated by the phrase "from this [Self] it is born," since they are not distinct from the vital breath (prāṇa) which is explicitly stated to be so created. For there is no scriptural statement of distinction suggesting that the vital breath alone is born directly, while others—such as the ether—are born from Brahman only through a succession, according to the analogy of a grandson and so forth. Furthermore, this mantra is not intended to establish a sequence; rather, the sequence regarding the ether and the others is merely restated as established in other scriptural passages. A sequence contradicted elsewhere in scripture is not accepted, because the sequence is clearly taught in the Subāla Upaniṣad. Therefore, the entire world [is created directly].
Thus it is established that [the world] arises directly from the Supreme Self alone.
The summary verses.
Fire, water, and earth arise from air, fire, and water respectively, in accordance with the Vedic revelation; however, Brahman alone is the ultimate source, like the immutable Puruṣa.
From the scriptural teaching beginning with "That heat meditated," it follows that the direct cause of those [bodies] is Brahman, which possesses each of those as its body.
Thus, the statement, "From Him [Brahman] this is born," and so forth, is logically established;
for, since there is no distinction [among these], it teaches that they are immediately preceded by Brahman alone.
Although words such as "splendor" (tejas) and others are well-known in the world in other senses,
through the study of grammar and the Vedas, they are understood to extend up to Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning light.
The Self is not [the body], because it is taught [in scripture] and because of its eternity, as shown by those [scriptural passages]. (18)

It is now considered whether the individual soul (jīva) is produced like ether and the other elements, or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is produced. This is because of scriptural statements such as, "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; Prajāpati created the creatures," and because of the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one, as well as the determination of oneness prior to creation. Nor is the production of the soul untenable simply because of the scriptural hearing of its non-difference from Brahman in the statement, "That thou art."

For, by the scriptural hearing that "all this, indeed, is Brahman," there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the ether and other elements are unproduced. Nor should one suspect that the denial of the soul's birth is intended by the passage, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," because that would lead to the denial of the birth of air and space as well—since they are spoken of as immortal—and because that [text] actually refers to the absence of birth and death associated with the production and destruction of a body.

Furthermore, because this [text] is understood to have the same intention as other scriptural passages that deny death as something inherent to the soul—such as, "Verily, it is when devoid of the living self (jīva) that this body dies; the living self does not die"—there is no fault of the loss of what was done (kṛtahāna) or the acquisition of what was not done (akṛtābhyāgama). This is because, according to the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) accepted by the Siddhāntin, wherein the substance is eternal and its destruction is the abandonment of a previous state while its origination is the attainment of another state, there is no such contingency for the soul, which is eternal in its nature as a substance.

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, it would follow that the individual soul (jīva) must be admitted to undergo origination in the form of coming into being after not having existed, just like jars and other such objects. Therefore, the soul is produced just like the ether and other elements. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The individual soul (jīva) is not produced, unlike ether and other elements; for its non-production is heard in such passages as, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," and from such scriptural texts as, "Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain," and "He is the eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among conscious beings," by which its eternity and consequent lack of production are understood.

Nor should it be argued that the Śruti statement, "It is neither born nor does it die," is intended merely to negate birth and death associated with the body's production and destruction; for in that very context, by the statement, "It is not slain when the body is slain," which speaks of the absence of slaughter associated with the body's slaughter, there is no need to state that [negation] separately, as its meaning is already established.

Furthermore, if one were to admit that the non-sentient (ajīva) transforms into the form of the sentient (jīva) prior [to creation]—just as space was previously admitted to exist in the form of ether—it would follow that merit and demerit, which are necessarily the products of a sentient agent, could not reside in the non-sentient; thus, the faults of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) could not be avoided. Moreover, the proposition that all things are consciousness and the determination of their oneness are both consistent with the view that the sentient being existed in a subtle state prior to creation and attained the state of gross effects during creation. How, then, is this different from the doctrine of the Vedas and other scriptures?

Thus, for ether and the other elements, there is a change in their essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*); therefore, they possess the status of being effects (*kāryatva*) by virtue of that [change]. However, for the soul (*jīva*), which is immutable, there is no change in its essential nature. Rather, there is merely a change in its attributes (*dharma-anyathābhāva*), characterized by the contraction and expansion of the quality known as knowledge (*jñāna*). It is by that much alone that the soul possesses the status of being an effect. This will become clear in the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The Summary Verses.
It may be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is also subject to birth because of scriptural testimony; but this is not so, because there is scriptural testimony regarding its lack of birth.
The scriptural mention of its "birth" refers to a change in its attributes, such as dharma and knowledge.
Thus ends the section concerning the self (ātman). 3.
For this very reason, he is a knower. ||19||
Because of the departure, the going, and the returning. ||20||
And by its own nature, [it is the cause] of the two subsequent ones. (21)
If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural statement "not so," we say no, because of the context. ||22||
And because of its own word and its measure. (23)
And there is no contradiction, as in the case of a chariot. 24.
If it be argued that [the soul's size] varies according to its state of existence, we say no, because it is admitted [to be atomic] in the heart. ||25||
Or [the Lord is all-pervading] because of His qualities, like light. ||26||
There is exclusion [of the property] from that which lacks it, just as in the case of possessing odor; and thus he shows. ||27||
Because of the separate instruction. ||28||
The designation [of the Self] by that [name] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, just as in the case of the Wise One (the individual soul). ||29||
And because it has been cultivated as long as the self exists, there is no fault in seeing it. ||30||
But because there is a connection with the manifestation of that which already exists, just like virility and so forth. ||31||
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other. (32)

In the context of investigating the origin of the individual soul (jīva), its attributes such as being a knower (jñātṛtva) are examined by resolving contradictions with scriptural passages concerning its nature as pure consciousness; this is for the purpose of establishing the unimpeded authority of those scriptural texts regarding Brahman, the cause of the universe. Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that the modification of the soul consists in a change of its attributes rather than a change in its essential nature (svarūpa), because there exists no attribute called "knowledge" apart from the essential nature itself.

Since knowledge alone is its very nature, the introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṃgati*) should also be understood as arising from this point. When the doubt arises—whether the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of knowledge, or whether it is indeed insentient (*jaḍa*) with knowledge being adventitious (*āgantuka*), or whether it is eternally a knower by virtue of being the substratum of the quality of knowledge—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts."

One prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the self is indeed of the nature of knowledge, based on such scriptural and traditional texts as: "He who, dwelling in consciousness, is within consciousness," and "Its nature is knowledge, which is ultimately and utterly pure. However, another [prima facie] view holds that its being of the nature of knowledge is not tenable; for if the individual soul (jīva) were of the nature of knowledge, then since it is all-pervading, there would follow the consequence that it would always perceive all objects, and the consequence that the eyes and other sense organs would be useless, as well as the consequence that states such as deep sleep and fainting—characterized by a lack of cognition—would never occur. Thus, its nature as knowledge is not logical.

Therefore, even the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), as intended by the Siddhāntin on the grounds of being the substratum of eternal knowledge, is untenable. Rather, it must be accepted—according to the system of the Naiyāyikas and others—that [the Self] possesses knowledge dependent upon instruments such as the eyes. This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as, "Now, he who thinks, 'Let me smell this,' he is the Self; seeing these desires with the mind, he rejoices; the seer sees not death; this person indeed knows," and "For he is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster," it follows that this Self is indeed known. And even though this is so, there is no consequence of its perceiving all objects at all times, because of its atomicity (*aṇutva*), as established by such scriptural passages as, "He is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster."

And its atomicity follows from the scriptural mention of its departure, going, and returning. For its departure, going, and returning are heard in such passages as: "By that light this self departs; and all those who depart from this world go to the moon; from that world they return again to this world for the sake of action. These [processes] cannot be logically established if [the self] were omnipresent.

If it is argued that the self is not atomic because, after introducing the individual soul (jīva) as connected with the vital breaths in the passage, "This one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," the text declares it to be "this very great unborn Self" (*mahān aja ātmā*), and thus it is large—we say no. For in that context, it is Brahman, distinct from the individual soul, that is the subject of discourse. Although the introduction begins with the individual soul, the Supreme Self is established in the middle of the passage by the statement, "He whose Self is known and awakened," and the declaration of its greatness is also intrinsically connected to that [Supreme Self].

Furthermore, the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is directly heard in scripture: "This subtle self is to be known by the mind, into which the vital breath has entered fivefold. Also, its status as an extremely minute atom is heard in such passages as: "The soul is to be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold," and "A part of the hundredth part of the tip of an awl. If it is asked how the soul, residing in only one part of the body, can experience pleasure and so forth extending to all its limbs, we reply: "Like sandalwood paste."

Just as a drop of yellow sandalwood paste, though residing in only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation that pervades the entire body, so too the individual soul (jīva), though situated in one place, experiences happiness extending to all its limbs. This is because its residence in the region of the heart is accepted on the basis of such scriptural passages as: "This which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart," and "For this Self is in the heart."

In reality, however—the individual soul (jīva), although situated in the heart, pervades the entire body by means of its own quality, which is knowledge; just as a gem or the sun, though existing in one place, pervades many places by means of its own rays. Nor should it be suspected that the self is of the very nature of knowledge and does not possess knowledge as a quality; for just as fragrance, though perceived as a quality of the earth, is distinct from it, so too is this case.

This is because knowledge—which is experienced as an attribute of the self—is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, the scripture states, "This person indeed knows," thereby demonstrating that knowing is an attribute of the knower; and in the scripture, "For there is no loss of the knower's consciousness," the knower and knowledge are taught as distinct. How then is there the conventional usage of its being "knowledge" in passages such as "Knowledge performs the sacrifice"? It is because knowledge is its essential attribute (*sāra*); for knowledge is indeed its essential quality.

And therefore, just as for the wise Brahman, knowledge and bliss are its essential qualities—evidenced by the designations of knowledge and bliss in such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "Bliss is Brahman"—so too here is there a designation of knowledge. Now, one might object: in the phrase "truth, knowledge," the meaning appears to be "possessing knowledge" due to the force of the final udātta accent; for if it were merely a *lyuṭ*-derived noun denoting the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*), the final udātta accent would be untenable.

For instance: when the suffix *ana* (of the *lyuṭ* class) is applied, by the rule "ādyudāttaśca," the first vowel (*a*) of the suffix receives the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Then, by the rule "lit-svareṇa," since the suffix marker *lit* is present, the radical vowel (*a*) also becomes acute. Consequently, by the rule "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam," the remaining vowels are depressed (*nighāta*), so that both *a*s residing in the suffix become grave (*anudātta*). Finally, when the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the radical *a* and the initial *a* of the suffix occurs, it becomes acute by the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodātta"; thus, the final *a* of the suffix remains grave.

Furthermore, regarding the vowel *a* of the case-ending, by the rule "the *suP* and *tiṅ* suffixes are unaccented" (*anudāttau sup-tiṅau*), that *a* would be unaccented due to the accent of the *suP* suffix. When the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the rule "the preceding [vowel] becomes the same as the following" (*ami pūrvaḥ*) occurs, it would be unaccented according to the metarule "the substitute is the most similar to the original" (*sthānāntaratama*). Consequently, for that unaccented vowel, the substitution of a circumflex (*svarita*) by the rule "after an acute, an unaccented [vowel] becomes circumflex" (*udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*) would take place. For this very reason, the word *tat jñānam*, if formed solely with the *lyuṭ* suffix, would end in a circumflex accent, as in the Kaṭha recension: "saṃjñānaṃ vijñānaṃ prajñānam."

Therefore, in order to ensure that the word has an udātta accent on the final syllable, this word *jñāna* must be explained as being derived from a *lyuṭ* suffix (equivalent to *ana*), or else as ending in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). This is because the *arśas-* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). When this is the case, the udātta accent on the final syllable is logically established.

When the suffix *yaC* is applied to the word *arśas-* according to the rule *arśādyac*, the final vowel *a* of the base is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Then, by the rule *citaḥ*, the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) becomes udātta (acute-accented). Consequently, both that [acute accent of the suffix] and the single substitute for the case-ending *a*—by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*—become acute-accented as well. Thus, if one follows this derivation of the word *jñāna*, it would only establish that the self possesses knowledge (*jñānavattva*), not that its very nature is knowledge (*jñānarūpatva*).

If it is argued that, therefore, its nature as knowledge is not perceived by this [word], it is replied: by resorting to the fact that it ends in the *uṇādi* suffix *-na*, that too is manifested. Even though no suffix is prescribed directly for the verbal root *jñā*, because the term "variously" (*bahulam*) is included in the rule "the *uṇādi* suffixes occur variously," these suffixes occur elsewhere as well; thus, its establishment [as meaning knowledge] is achieved. Furthermore, when it ends in an *uṇādi* suffix, its status as having the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) is also justified.

Since the suffix *man* prescribed by the *Ary-ādi* sūtras would result in an udātta accent, and since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for that [suffix] and the vowel of the case-ending would also necessarily be udātta, it might be argued that even though both derivations of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are possible here, the view that it denotes the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*)—ending in the *uṇādi* suffix *na*—is more appropriate due to its brevity in grammatical derivation. With this in mind, the author of the Bhāṣya cited this as a proof for [Brahman] being the very nature of knowledge. Furthermore, Brahman is designated by the term "knowledge" because knowledge persists as long as the self exists.

This is because we observe that words such as "cow" (gav-ādi), which denote properties like "cowness" (gotva) that persist as long as the substance itself exists, are used to designate things such as curds (khaṇḍa). Furthermore, the designation of the individual soul (jīva) as "knowledge" is justified by its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva). This self-luminosity is relative to itself alone and not dependent on another; even this self-relation consists merely in its being characterized by "I-ness" (aham-pratyaktva) and unity. However, the quality of illuminating both itself and others belongs specifically to the knowledge of attributes (dharma-jñāna). This is the analogy of light and its source regarding the relationship between the attribute (dharma) and the substratum of attributes (dharmin) in the case of knowledge.

As they say: "A lamp is the illuminator of itself, while its radiance is [the illuminator] of itself and of another; thus there is a distinction between the two cognitions, even though they are equal in their nature as property and property-bearer. Now, one might object: since cognition is absent during states such as deep sleep, how can it be a property inherent to the very essence of the self, like the property of being a cow?

We say that it is manifested like virility and so forth: just as in a body composed of the seven constituents (*dhātu*), the seventh constituent—the essence of virility—though always present, is not manifested in childhood or even in youth; likewise, the attribute of knowledge, though always present, is not manifested in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) as it is in the waking state. Even then, there is no loss of self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), which consists in the fitness for being self-manifesting. Indeed, the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) continues to be manifest even in deep sleep.

This is because of the retrospective reflection (parāmarśa): "I slept happily. As they say: "When the self-luminous, eternal, and blissful Person is established [as the witness], in such instances as 'I slept happily,' there is an inferential establishment regarding the temporal element and so forth. In cases such as 'I sang sweetly' or 'I drank wine,' just as sweetness and the like [are perceived in the past], here too, the happiness shines forth as belonging to that very time. Therefore, in our position—that the quality of knowledge possesses contraction and expansion, while its substratum, the individual soul (jīva), is atomic—there is no defect whatsoever.

However, regarding the position that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of consciousness and is all-pervading," there would necessarily follow either the consequence of its being perceived or not perceived at all times, or else a restriction to one or the other. To explain: if the nature of the soul, which is all-pervading consciousness, were the cause of perception alone, then it would be perceived everywhere, just as it is in the region delimited by the body; if it were the cause of non-perception alone, then it would not be perceived even in the region delimited by the body. If it were the cause of both, [the same contradiction would apply].

In the third case, constant perception and non-perception would be mutually contradictory. This same defect applies even to the position of the Naiyāyikas and others, who hold that the soul is omnipresent but possesses knowledge that arises and moves depending on instruments such as the eyes. This point will become clear in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "A part [of Brahman], because of various designations" (Aṃśo nānā-vyapadeśāt).
[This is stated in] the summary verses (saṃgraha-kārikās):

Some have declared that the living self (jīva) is of the nature of consciousness, and it is heard that it is so; yet others have said that it possesses the state of being a knower through adventitious cognitions.
Others [hold] that it is an eternal knower; thus, here, the middle position of reasoning is established.
For this all-pervading soul would indeed know even what is situated at a great distance, otherwise, according to you [the opponent], it could not.

It is not the case that this [self] becomes omniscient merely by being of the nature of a knower as proclaimed in the Upaniṣads— such as "this one indeed knows"— since it is atomic according to the measures of its departure, movement, and so forth; rather,
its pervasion of the body is logical due to its quality of knowledge, which is like the light of a lamp.
The statement that it is "knowledge" is consistent with its being an essential quality; furthermore, it is self-luminous.
Thus ends the section concerning knowledge.
There is a creator, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. (Sūtra 33)
Because of the teaching on abiding through grasping. ||34||
And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the grammatical instruction. ||35||
There is no fixed rule, just as in the case of perception. ||36||
Because of the reversal of capacity. ||37||
And because of the absence of meditative concentration. ||38||
And as the carpenter [acts] in both ways. ||39||

Following the examination of the nature of the knower (*jñātṛtva*), the nature of the agent (*kartṛtva*) shall now be examined; since volitional action (*kṛti*) is dependent upon knowledge, there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) based on the relationship of cause and effect. Just as in the case where the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading and of the nature of pure consciousness, the established order of the restriction of perception and so forth would not be possible, so too, if Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) were the agent, it would be common to all [beings], and thus the established order of the restriction of agency would not be possible; this is what is stated here.

And there is a connection with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntasaṅgati*). When the doubt arises as to whether the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is due to the superimposition of agency upon it because Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) alone is the agent, or whether the soul is an agent by its very nature—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the Self is indeed a non-agent. This is because of the scriptural statement in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "If the slayer thinks to slay, or if the slain thinks himself slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. Here, "hantuṃ" means "to slay"; the suffix *-tu* (as in *jantu*, etc. is an *auṇādika* derivative.

This is because it has the same meaning as the statement in the *Gītā*: "He who thinks this [Self] is the slayer and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. Furthermore, the negation of being the agent of killing is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the negation of agency in general. For this very reason, there is a statement by the Blessed Lord in the *Gītā*: "Actions are performed in every way by the qualities of nature (*prakṛti*); the one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the agent. Nature is said to be the cause in the state of being the effect, the instrument, and the agent."

"The person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause for being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), superimposing upon itself either the agency residing in primordial nature (prakṛti) or the agency residing in the intellect (buddhi)—which is a specific modification of nature unique to each soul—is designated as the "agent. The scripture likewise proceeds by taking into account such agency, along with the practical conventions regarding the acquisition of materials and so forth. This being the prima facie position, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

If either the intellect (*buddhi*) or primordial nature (*prakṛti*) were the agent, then scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "one desiring liberation should meditate upon Brahman" would be enjoining only the enjoyer who desires results such as heaven and liberation; this is according to the maxim: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer. Furthermore, the scripture enjoins the agent by means of generating cognition. Since neither the insentient intellect nor primordial nature possesses the capacity to be made aware [of their duties], it is logical that the Self alone—by virtue of being the enjoyer and being capable of being made aware—is the one to be enjoined by the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions.

Nor can one's own doctrine—that the immutable Self is not the agent—successfully manage to superimpose agency upon the Self. Therefore, just as superimposition must be understood as a property of that [Self] by way of being a transformation of the knowledge of attributes which stand in the place of the Self’s own light, so too must action (kṛti) be brought to have that same status as its property. Why, then, even when no sublation is perceived, is it postulated that the manifestation "I am the agent" is of the nature of an error, and that the scripture has for its object an agency produced by error?

If the killer thinks, "I kill," this [notion] is consistent with the subject matter of the mantra, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," because of the preceding context in the statement, "It is not killed even when the body is killed," which establishes that the Self, being distinct from the body, is incapable of being slain. Furthermore, the mantras that negate agency are consistent with another statement by the same author: "In that case, he who, due to an unrefined intellect, perceives the isolated Self as the agent, does not see, O dull-witted one. Thus, they share a single intended meaning.

Furthermore, because we see the teaching regarding its abiding through appropriation in the passage, "Just as a great king, having taken hold of his subjects, moves about in his own kingdom according to his will, even so this [Self], having taken hold of these vital breaths, moves about in its own body according to its will," and because of the designation of agency in both worldly and Vedic activities in the statement, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts," the Self is indeed the agent. Nor does the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for if it were a reference to the internal organ...

Because in the Śrutis the instrumental case alone is observed; and here too, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of a reversal in that designation. For in other passages such as, "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of [his own] consciousness," the word *vijñāna*, referring to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is indeed seen to be designated in the instrumental case. Furthermore, if Prakṛti were the agent, then because it is common to all souls, the restriction of karma would likewise be impossible—following the same logic as the impossibility of the restriction of perception and so forth mentioned in the previous section—since Prakṛti is common to all persons.

And thus, all actions would result in the experience of everyone, because according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, since the selves are omnipresent, there is no distinction in their proximity to everything everywhere. Nor should it be argued that this fault does not apply to the view where the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the agent, on the grounds that internal organs are distinct for each body; for it is impossible to establish a restriction to individual selves when those organs and their substrates—the bodies—arise in the presence of all selves.

Furthermore, on the view that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent, since it is untenable for one who is the agent to be a different entity from the enjoyer, the intellect itself would have to be the enjoyer; consequently, the Self (*ātman*) would lack the power of being an enjoyer. Thus, there would be a contradiction with their own accepted doctrine that "the Puruṣa exists because there is the state of being an enjoyer. Moreover, if the intellect were the agent, then even the agency in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the means to liberation and consists in the realization "I am other than Prakṛti," would have to be attributed to that very intellect.

Furthermore, neither Prakṛti—whether in its own nature or in the form of the transformation of the intellect (buddhi)—is capable of concentrating with the thought, "I am the immutable one, distinct from Prakṛti. Moreover, if agency were admitted for the Self, it would act when there is a desire and not otherwise; this restriction is logically consistent, just as a carpenter, though equipped with tools such as an axe, acts only when there is a desire and not otherwise. However, if the insentient intellect were the agent, it would have to be an agent at all times, because there would be no cause for restricting its desire for experience and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that the Self alone is the agent by its very nature.
"He is not the agent of the qualities, for agency is attributed to the all-pervading Lord.
[Reply: "It is not so; because of the meaningfulness of the scriptures and other reasons, he is the agent through his connection with the qualities."
Thus concludes the section on the agent.
But [the self] is from another, because of scripture. ||33||
But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons. (34)

The connection [of this section] is that once agency has been considered, its specific nature is now being examined. A doubt arises from the scriptures on injunctions and prohibitions on the one hand, and the scripture concerning the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) on the other: does the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) belong to itself, or is it dependent upon the Supreme Self? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the agency of the soul is indeed self-dependent; otherwise, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would be utterly redundant.

Nor should one suspect that agency is dependent upon the Supreme Self on the basis of such scriptural texts concerning the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) as: "The Teacher has entered within, the Self of all beings; He indeed makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds, and He makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down."

If that were the case, it would follow that the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions—which function solely for the purpose of inciting or restraining human activity—would become utterly useless; furthermore, it would result in the inconsistency of the scriptures concerning the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī). For it is not reasonable to suppose that anyone, having himself caused another to perform some undesirable action, would then inflict punishment as its fruit. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

His agency is dependent upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because it is impossible to subvert that [agency] when there is no contradiction with the multitude of scriptures concerning the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). Furthermore, the non-futility of the scriptures prescribing injunctions and prohibitions can be established without contradicting that [dependence], since the Lord exists in three states: He is indifferent toward the first activity, but toward subsequent activities He is the permitter and the one who causes His own devotees and those who hate Him to perform their desired and undesired actions. Thus, the Lord possesses these three states.

For instance: in the beginning, having provided the soul with the instruments of the body and so forth, the Lord remains indifferent, observing, "What will this [soul] do? Whatever merit or demerit it performs, He permits the subsequent activity in the form of its fruit. Permission (*anumati*) is the authorization of one who has already begun to act.

As for the virtuous action of those seeking liberation, such as surrender (*prapatti*) and meditation (*upāsana*), and the non-virtuous action of the tamasic who hate the Lord, such as reviling Him—He Himself causes both of these to be performed; it is with reference to these two categories that the two scriptural passages beginning with "For He alone... are intended, not with reference to all beings. As it is said: "To those who are ever steadfast and worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me," and: "But these [others], hating Me, cruel, the lowest of men in this world..."

"And I constantly cast the inauspicious ones into the very wombs of the Asuras," according to these words of the Blessed One; therefore, some teachers maintain that there is scope for the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions elsewhere [than in this state], and thus they resolve that those scriptures are not entirely useless.

Others, however, say: "One should not conceive such a restriction of the scope of the scripture concerning the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). For there is no evidence for conceiving that the Blessed Lord is indifferent toward or merely a permissive witness regarding the specific actions of individual souls. Furthermore, there is no basis for conceiving the two cited verses from the Gītā as implying anything up to the point of His not being the instigator of other actions. Nor can such a conception be made on the grounds of avoiding the futility of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions."

Even though God is a cause in all prescribed and prohibited actions—just as time, unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), and the sense organs are causes—the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) remains unimpaired; for it is logical that God’s causality exists just like His will and other attributes. Nor is it the case that...

Thus, it cannot be said that the soul’s agency—characterized as "the agent is independent" with respect to enjoined and prohibited actions—would be absent, resulting in a loss of independence due to the Lord acting as the impeller by force, like a man being dragged by the current of a river. For we observe that even ministers and others who are subordinate agents appointed by a king as their employer act according to their own will in their respective duties, thereby possessing independence.

Therefore, since it is impossible to establish the non-futility of injunctions and prohibitions without restricting the *Antaryāmi-śāstra*, one should not assume such a restriction. The detailed exposition supporting both of these views is to be found in their respective treatises.
The summary verses.
If the agency of embodied beings is described as being dependent upon the Lord,
then the futility of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions can be countered by no one.
There is indeed the scriptural testimony that the lotus-eyed Lord is both the ruler and the controller;
it is now explained how he conducts himself so as not to permit the transgression of injunctions and prohibitions.
Having first given the instruments, the body, and so forth, the Lord remains indifferent while [the soul] perceives effort;
afterwards, He sanctions the fruit thereof as a second [act]. For some, He even becomes the instigator of their action.

Some have asserted that the scriptural texts concerning the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) must be restricted in scope, fearing otherwise that other [scriptural] passages would be rendered purposeless; this they claim applies specifically to those actions performed with aversion toward those seeking liberation.
Just as there is dependence on desire and so forth, there is likewise dependence on the Lord;
yet, by that much alone, the scriptures do not become useless—thus the opponents maintain that [the Lord's power] is unrestricted.
Thus ends the section concerning dependence on another.
He is a part [of Brahman], because of various designations; and otherwise also, some record that He possesses the nature of a servant, a fisherman, and so forth. (Sūtra 3.3.43)
On account of the wording of the mantra. ||36||
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti. ||37||
But the Supreme is not like this, as in the case of light and so forth. ||38||
And they remember. ||39||
Permission and avoidance [of ritual acts] result from the connection with a body, as in the case of light and so forth. 40.
And because there is no continuity [of the self], there is no confusion [between different transmigrations]. ||41||
And it is merely an appearance. ||42||
Because there is no restriction regarding what has not been seen. ||43||
And the same applies to cases involving intentional ambiguity and so forth. (44)
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to a difference in location, we say no, because [all such locations] are included within [the whole]. ||45||

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, if there were a relationship of the impelled and the impeller between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as in the case of a king and his servant, there would be an absolute difference between them; consequently, even the statement that the individual soul is a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman) would become merely figurative (aupacārika).

Is the individual soul (*jīva*) absolutely different from the Supreme? Or is it the Supreme Brahman itself in a state of ignorance? Or is it Brahman itself as delimited by adjuncts (*upādhi*)? Or is it a part of the qualified Brahman in the form of its qualification? Given these conflicting scriptural statements, a doubt arises. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: the individual soul is absolutely different [from Brahman], because of the mention of difference in such passages as "The two, the Knower and the ignorant. Alternatively, the individual soul is simply the ignorant Brahman, because of such scriptural declarations as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman."

Brahman itself, when delimited by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of being a sentient being, is the individual soul (jīva). This is established solely through the hearing of such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). It is not logical, however, to hold that the individual soul is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman. For "part-ness" does not consist in being a physical limb or member, as in the case of threads [in a cloth] and so forth; this is because Brahman, being partless, cannot be composed of constituent parts. For the same reason, it is not a part in the sense of a fragment of stone split by a chisel, since Brahman is incapable of being divided. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

The individual soul (jīva) is indeed a portion of Brahman. This is because both difference and non-difference are taught. For a great many designations of difference are observed, such as being the creator and the created, the controller and the controlled, omniscience and limited knowledge, self-dependence and dependence on another, lordship and subservience, and so forth. Likewise, designations of non-difference are also seen, such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). Furthermore, in the *Brahmasūkta*, the followers of the Atharva Veda study that Brahman possesses forms such as the gambler (dāśakitava) and others.

"Brahmadāśas, Brahmadāsas, and gamblers—these are mine; both male and female are born from Brahman; whether it be a woman or a man, they are Brahman. Therefore, one must accept that the individual soul (jīva) is a specific part (aṃśa) of the distinguished Brahman, acting as its qualifying attribute. Only when this is so are the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference, as well as the established order of bondage and liberation, logically consistent.

However, in the theories that define the Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) as being delimited by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of truth and falsehood respectively, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation becomes untenable, as does the consistency of all the scriptures; this has been elaborated elsewhere. Therefore, it is logical that the individual soul is indeed a part (*aṃśa*) whose nature consists of a specific portion of the Whole. This is understood precisely from the Vedic mantra: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three immortal feet are in heaven," and from the statement in the *Gītā*: "A part of My very self, existing as the eternal individual soul, is in the world of living beings."

And thus, just as light is a qualifying part (*viśeṣaṇa-aṃśa*) of luminous objects such as gems, or as the body of gods, humans, and so forth is [a qualifying part] of embodied beings, in the very same way, the individual soul (*jīva*) is a qualifying part of the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of being an inseparably established mode (*apṛthaksiddha-prakāra*) and being His body. Yet, it is not that [the soul] is identical to Him. Because of the difference in their qualifying attributes, the scriptural texts concerning difference are justified; and because of the identity of their qualified nature (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa*), the scriptural texts concerning non-difference are likewise justified.

The individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) and so forth, is not of the same nature as the Supreme (*para*), which is characterized by being the principal (*śeṣitva*) and so forth; thus, through the analogy of light and its source, and by way of the relationship between body and embodied, the established relationship of subordinate and principal between the *jīva* and the Lord is logically consistent. Furthermore, Parāśara and others record this analogy of light and its source, as well as the relationship of body and embodied, regarding the *jīva* and the Lord: "Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this entire universe the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Brahman."

"O twice-born one, whatever being is created by whomsoever, in the production of that which is created, all of that is indeed the body of Hari. Now, if it is asked: "Since there is no distinction in the fact that all are portions of the Lord, why is there permission for the twice-born to study the Vedas and so forth, while for the Śūdras there is its prohibition? We reply: It is due to the connection with a particular type of body.

Just as fire, water, and so forth are fit for ritual action when situated in the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), yet those very same elements become unfit for such action when they reach a cremation ground, so too the two states of permission and prohibition are logically established for selves (*ātman*) depending on the state of their residence in various bodies. Although all selves are uniform insofar as they are portions of Brahman (*brahmāṃśatva*), there will be no confusion of experiences because they are distinct from one another and, being atomic (*aṇu*), are separate in each individual body.

However, the doctrine of the identity of Brahman and the Self would necessarily entail the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Supreme (*para*), as well as among the individual souls themselves. Nor can this consequence be avoided by means of distinctions created by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); for there is no valid cause to establish the distinction of limiting adjuncts that could obscure the essential nature of Brahman, which is an undivided, single-flavored manifestation of pure light. Indeed, an adjunct, even when applied to Brahman like an axe falling upon a block of wood, does not divide Brahman as the axe divides the wood. If it is argued that the adjuncts themselves are distinct, [the response follows].

What follows from that? How could the confusion resulting from the identity of the substratum of experience—which arises because those [individuals] are distinct while their substrata of experience are one—be avoided? If it is argued that, in the theories of Brahman and the individual soul as conditioned by real and unreal adjuncts respectively, there will be a systematic distinction due to the power of beginningless *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) which is the cause of the adjuncts, we say: no.

Since even unseen limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot effect division and so forth in the indivisible Brahman, by this [argument] the objection that "the systematic order [of experience] is established through the specific determination of the body and so forth, which are the locus for the performance of volitions caused by the unseen merit" is also refuted; for there is no cause for the restriction of volitions and the like to each individual soul when they arise in the presence of all souls. If it is argued that "let the systematic order of experience be established by the distinction between the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) of the self," we say no; for the spatial parts of Brahman that are contained within bodies must be stated to be the very substrata of experience.

However, the spatial points contained within those [bodies] are not fixed, because almost all spatial points are included within all bodies as they move about. Therefore, just as in the view that the self is omnipresent, even in the view that there is a unity of the self conditioned by real limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the systematic allocation of experience (*bhoga-vyavasthā*) is not possible. Thus it is established that, like the atomicity of selves, their distinctness (*bheda*) must also be accepted.
The Summary Verses.

If the soul were absolutely different [from Brahman], its movement [into liberation] would be merely figurative; if there were absolute non-difference, however, the confusion resulting from the multitude of texts on difference would be unavoidable.
Therefore, it is appropriate here that the soul is a part of the Supreme; indeed, it must be a single portion of a single reality.
This well-known specific type is a particular aspect of the distinguished Blessed One.
Thus ends the section concerning the parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa). ||7||

Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled *Caturmatasāra*, composed by Appayya Dīkṣita— the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a jewel of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage and a teacher of the glorious Advaita-vidyā, and who performed the Viśvajit sacrifice.
The fourth quarter of the second chapter.
Likewise, the vital breaths. ||1||
Because figurative application is impossible and because it is understood prior to that. ||2||
Because speech is preceded by that [mind]. ||3||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: after the determination of the origin of the soul (*jīva*), its subsequent bondage, its nature as a knower (*jñātṛtva*), and so forth, the manner of the origin of the sense organs (*indriya*), which are the instruments of the soul, is now being clarified. A doubt arises due to conflicting scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*): is the origin of the sense organs, like that of ether (*viyat*) and the other elements, an origin consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpa*); or, like the soul, is it merely an origin consisting of a change in attributes (*dharma*)? Regarding this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: although it was established in the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*) that "everything other than Brahman is subject to origination," nevertheless, regarding the sense organs—

There is no origination in the form of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*), as in the case of space (*viyat*) and other elements. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the state of existence even at the time of the beginning of creation: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; they said, 'What existed then?'—'The *ṛṣis* indeed existed then.'—'Who are those *ṛṣis?'—'The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the *ṛṣis*. Since the plural form of the word *prāṇa* is used for the sense organs, as seen in the usage, "When the [chief] *prāṇa* departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it," and since the word *ṛṣi* is also applied to them in the passage, "Of that non-existent, the seven *ṛṣis were the shores."*

And because [the usage] is observed [in that sense]. Although the word *prāṇa* is indeed observed to be used for Brahman, and the word *ṛṣi* is applicable to it because of its possession of knowledge, nevertheless, the connection of these two words in the plural number with that [Brahman] is not possible. The plural number here cannot be construed as referring to a multiplicity of parts—as in the case of "the nooses of Aditi"—because Brahman is partless. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Because it is heard in many restrictive Śrutis that Brahman alone exists at the time of creation and so forth; because the word *prāṇa* has a conventional usage (*nirūḍhi*) for Him; and because the word *ṛṣi*, by its natural fitness, refers to one possessing knowledge in relation to the senses which are the means of knowledge—here, *prāṇas* refers to Brahman alone. As for the plural number, it is to be understood according to the maxim "when a secondary sense is involved, an improper [literal] conception is not to be adopted," just as in the case of the plurality of ropes (in the expression "the ropes are broken"). This is because, even in the absence of physical parts, there exists a basis for the plurality of qualifiers.

Nor should it be argued that even if oneness is established, the existence of the sense organs must likewise persist as it does for the individual soul (jīva). For, in order to avoid the fallacies of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), their existence at that time cannot be asserted, since they serve as the substrata for unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) just like the soul; furthermore, it has been shown that the cited scripture demonstrates the existence of the voice specifically in Brahman alone.

At the time of the beginning of creation, there is no activity of the organs such as speech, because no such activity is observed; for it is heard that the differentiation of names and forms occurs only after the creation of the elements, from which it is understood that prior to that, activities of the organs such as the utterance of names did not exist; and furthermore, in the mantra "From this [Self] it is born," their birth is heard to be a transformation into a different state, similar in nature to the birth of ether and the other elements.
Summary Verses.

If it is argued that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are eternal because they exist from the beginning, we say no, because they are created. The plural usage of the term *prāṇa* with respect to Brahman is to be understood as a metaphorical designation (*pāśava*).
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
And because the sevenfold course has been specifically distinguished. ||4||
But since hands and so forth exist [only] when [the body] exists, it is not thus. ||5||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having established that the sense organs possess an origin—just like ether and other elements—their specific number is now being considered. Regarding the doubt arising from conflicting scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*) as to whether the sense organs are seven or eleven, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: there are only seven. For it is heard in scripture that in both this world and the next, only seven [organs] proceed along with the individual soul (*jīva*).

"From that, the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) arise; seven are the flames, seven the fuels, and seven the tongues [of fire]. These seven worlds exist within which the vital breaths move—seven by seven, hidden in the secret cave. The repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended to refer to the distinction between different persons. And those moving vital breaths are further specified by a description of their essential nature: "When the five means of knowledge (*jñāna*), together with the mind, come to rest..."

"And when the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal. For here, the seven internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa)—namely, the five beginning with the eye, along with the mind and the intellect—are specified as the means of knowledge. "The supreme goal" means they call yoga the means to liberation, which is the supreme state.

Regarding the scriptural mentions of numbers exceeding eight—such as, "There are these eight graspers (grahas) and eight over-graspers (atigrahas)," "There are indeed seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in the head and two directed downwards," "There are nine vital breaths in a person, with the navel as the tenth," and "There are ten vital breaths in an animal, with the self (ātman) as the eleventh"—these are merely figurative designations of "sense organs" (indriya) because they assist the living being in some way, just like the navel. For the navel is not a cavity that is a sense organ; rather, the sense organs are only those seven which possess the capacity for movement.

Regarding the hearing of both fewer and more [organs], it is logical to accept the smaller number because of parsimony (*lāghava*). If it is argued that it is more logical to accept the larger number—since the smaller numbers are included within the larger and thus there is no contradiction with all [scriptural statements]—we say no. For if that were the case, since in some places fourteen organs are heard of, including speech and so forth along with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind (*citta*), there would be the consequence of accepting the number fourteen; consequently, the restrictive rule that there are "eleven" would be undermined. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: [The text continues: ...the elevenfold nature of the organs is established by the fact that the scriptural statement regarding the five [organs] is a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*) intended to exclude the possibility of more than eleven, while the mention of fourteen is merely a descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known from other sources. Furthermore, the mind (*manas*) is not distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); rather, the internal organ itself is threefold, consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*). Therefore, the organs are indeed eleven. Thus, the objection that the number of organs is indeterminate is refuted. This concludes the section on the organs. Now, the following doubt arises: if the organs are instruments for the Self, then who is the agent? Is it the body, or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the mind, or the intellect, or the self-nature (*svabhāva*), or the Lord (*īśvara*), or the transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti-pariṇāma*), or the soul (*puruṣa*)? Among these, the body cannot be the agent, because it is composed of the elements (*bhūta-maya*) and is insentient (*acetana*). Nor can the vital breath be the agent, because it is merely a modification of air (*vāyu-vikāra*) and is observed to function even in a corpse. Nor can the mind be the agent, because it is an instrument like the eye and other organs. Nor can the intellect be the agent, because it is an instrument for discerning objects. Nor can self-nature be the agent, because it is insentient. Nor can the Lord be the agent, because He is eternally free from desire and action. Nor can the transformation of primordial matter be the agent, because it is insentient. Therefore, the soul alone is the agent. How so? Because it is taught in scripture that "it sees through the eye, hears through the ear, and knows through the mind. Moreover, the agency of the soul is established by its being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Since enjoyment is impossible without an agent, the soul must be the agent. Furthermore, the soul's agency is proven by its being the substratum of effort (*prayatna*). Effort resides in the agent, and since effort is observed in the soul, it is the agent. Also, the soul is the agent because it is the locus of volition (*saṅkalpa*). Volition is an attribute of the agent, and since volition belongs to the soul, it is the agent. Finally, the soul is the agent because it is the substratum of desire (*icchā*). Desire resides in the agent, and since desire is found in the soul, it is the agent. Thus, the soul is the agent. This concludes the section on the agent. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul is the agent, does it act spontaneously or through the grace of the Lord? It acts through the grace of the Lord. How so? Because scripture teaches that "by the grace of the Lord, one attains supreme peace. Furthermore, the soul's dependence on the Lord is established by its being subject to bondage and liberation. Bondage and liberation are possible only if there is a controller. Therefore, the soul acts through the grace of the Lord. This concludes the section on the grace of the Lord. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul acts through the grace of the Lord, then what is the purpose of the soul's own effort? The purpose of the soul's effort is to serve as a means for the Lord's grace. Just as a king rewards those who perform service, so too the Lord bestows grace upon those who exert effort. Therefore, the soul's effort is not useless. This concludes the section on the soul's effort. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul is the agent, is it eternal or non-eternal? It is eternal. How so? Because scripture teaches that "the soul is eternal, pervasive, and unchanging. Furthermore, the eternity of the soul is established by its being the witness (*sākṣin*). A witness is eternal, and since the soul is the witness, it is eternal. Also, the eternity of the soul is proven by its being the substratum of consciousness (*caitanya*). Consciousness is eternal, and since the soul is the substratum of consciousness, it is eternal. Finally, the eternity of the soul is established by its being the object of the notion of "I" (*aham-pratyaya*). The notion of "I" refers to something eternal, and since the soul is the object of this notion, it is eternal. Thus, the soul is eternal. This concludes the section on the eternity of the soul. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul is eternal, is it one or many? It is many. How so? Because scripture teaches that "there are many souls. Furthermore, the plurality of souls is established by their having diverse experiences. If there were only one soul, then the experience of pleasure and pain in one body would result in the experience of pleasure and pain in all bodies. Since this is not the case, there must be many souls. Also, the plurality of souls is proven by their having different destinies. If there were only one soul, then the attainment of heaven or hell by one would result in the attainment of heaven or hell by all. Since this is not the case, there must be many souls. Finally, the plurality of souls is established by their being the objects of the notion of "mine" (*mama-pratyaya*). The notion of "mine" refers to something distinct from the "I," and since the soul is the object of this notion, there must be many souls. Thus, the souls are many. This concludes the section on the plurality of souls. Now, the following doubt arises: if the souls are many, are they all-pervasive (*vibhu*) or atomic (*aṇu*)? They are all-pervasive. How so? Because scripture teaches that "the soul is all-pervasive. Furthermore, the all-pervasiveness of the soul is established by its being the substratum of space (*dig-deśa*). Space is all-pervasive, and since the soul is the substratum of space, it is all-pervasiveness. Also, the all-pervasiveness of the soul is proven by its being the substratum of time (*kāla*). Time is all-pervasive, and since the soul is the substratum of time, it is all-pervasive. Finally, the all-pervasiveness of the soul is established by its being the substratum of the ether (*ākāśa*). The ether is all-pervasive, and since the soul is the substratum of the ether, it is all-pervasive. Thus, the soul is all-pervasive. This concludes the section on the all-pervasiveness of the soul. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul is all-pervasive, how is it perceived? It is perceived through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Just as the sun, though all-pervasive, is perceived through a lens, so too the soul, though all-pervasive, is perceived through the internal organ. Furthermore, the perception of the soul is established by its being the object of introspection (*pratisaṃvedana*). Introspection is a form of perception, and since the soul is the object of introspection, it is perceived. Also, the perception of the soul is proven by its being the substratum of reflection (*vimarśa*). Reflection is a form of perception, and since the soul is the substratum of reflection, it is perceived. Finally, the perception of the soul is established by its being the object of the notion of "I. The notion of "I" is a form of perception, and since the soul is the object of this notion, it is perceived. Thus, the soul is perceived. This concludes the section on the perception of the soul. Now, the following doubt arises: if the soul is all-pervasive and eternal, is it active or inactive? It is inactive. How so? Because scripture teaches that "the soul is inactive. Furthermore, the inactivity of the soul is established by its being the witness. A witness is inactive, and since the soul is the witness, it is inactive. Also, the inactivity of the soul is proven by its being the substratum of consciousness. Consciousness is inactive, and since the soul is the substratum of consciousness, it is inactive. Finally, the inactivity of the soul is established by its being the object of the notion of "I. The notion of

Since the hands and other limbs also serve as instruments for the experience [of the self] through their specific functions while the living being resides in the body, one should understand that there are eleven sense-faculties (*indriya*): five organs of cognition, five organs of action, and the mind (*manas*). Therefore, the number of sense-faculties established by such scriptural and traditional authorities as, "These ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the self as the eleventh," is indeed fixed. When various numbers are heard in the scriptures, it is logical to determine the number according to their functional roles.

It is like the restriction of what is to be expressed according to one's capacity when hearing various kinds of *avadāna* (edifying tales). As for the claims regarding a higher number [of faculties], they are intended to refer to the different modifications (*vṛtti*) of the mind: the mind assisted by the Great Principle (*mahat*) performs determination (*adhyavasāya*); the mind assisted by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) performs self-conceit (*abhimāna*); and the mind assisted by prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) performs reflection (*cintā*). Thus, it is the mind itself, when endowed with these distinct modifications such as determination and the rest, that is designated by the terms "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ego-sense" (*ahaṅkāra*), and "mind" (*citta*).

However, the mentions of fewer numbers in various places are intended with reference to specific functions, such as movement, which are intended to be expressed in those contexts. Regarding the state of yoga, there is a predominance of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) over the organs of action (karmendriyas) insofar as they must be brought under control through effort; it is with this intention that the Smṛti says, "When the five [organs] come to rest. Similarly, the statement "There are seven breaths in the head" indicates a predominance based on their location in the head, and it is with this intention that the Śruti speaks of "seven breaths," as well as the scriptural texts concerning movement.

The scriptural mention of eleven [faculties] indeed exists for all of them: "These ten are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the self (*ātman*) as the eleventh; when they depart from this mortal body," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that there are eleven sense-faculties (*indriya*). [This concludes the] summary verse.

"It is not so; there are seven vital breaths (prāṇas) joined together because only seven are mentioned as having movement, [but] they become eleven along with the hands and other organs due to the differentiation of their functions."
Thus concludes the section on the seven destinies.
And they are atomic. ||6||

Regarding the doubt as to whether those sense organs are all-pervading (*vibhu*) or limited (*paricchinna*), since there is the scriptural hearing of their infinity—namely, "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite"—and because no specific measurement such as "this is the dimension of this particular sense organ" is stated, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they must be all-pervading. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Because their movement is heard to be characterized by going upward and reaching the end, and because the hearing of their infinity—in the supplementary passage, "He who meditates upon these as infinite wins an infinite world"—is understood to be for the purpose of meditation, they are indeed limited. Furthermore, the perception of distant objects is possible through their possession of rapid speed and other such qualities.
The Summary Verses.
They are infinite because of the scriptural hearing of their infinity; it is not so by means of going, coming, and departing.
They are subtle, and for them, the fruit of worship is again the hearing of infinity.
And he is the most excellent. ||7||

Following the investigation into the origin of the sense organs, the origin of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is investigated; this constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*). For, in the dialogue concerning the village of the Chāndogyas, it is understood that the principal vital breath possesses a status equal in luster to the sense organs, precisely because it is described as engaging in a dispute with the sense organs after having attained preeminence through that very dispute. Thus, immediately after the inquiry into the origin of the sense organs, the origin of the principal vital breath is considered.
