Although the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—just like that of the sense organs—is established by the mantra itself, "From this [Being] is born the vital breath," nevertheless, the origin of the *prāṇa* is considered here for the following reasons: first, to determine its distinctness from both elemental air and the functions of the sense organs by resolving scriptural contradictions; second, to establish its relevance to the present discussion on the origin of things previously introduced; and third, to dispel certain further doubts.

Furthermore, there is this additional doubt: at the time of the beginning of creation, just as the activity of the individual soul (jīva) does not exist because it remains in an unmanifest state, so too the activities of the organs such as speech—the utterance of names and so forth—do not exist. Therefore, it has been stated that the words "prāṇa" and "ṛṣi," having been observed to be used for Brahman, refer to Brahman.

Regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), in the *Nāsadāsīya* hymn which begins with "There was neither non-existence nor existence then; there was only the Unmanifest (*tamas*) hidden by darkness in the beginning," it is heard that "It breathed, windless, by its own power (*svadhayā*), as the One" (*ānīd avātaṃ svadhayā tadekam*). Thus, the existence of a specific activity called "breathing" (*ānanākhya*) is established. Nor can it be argued that the word *ānīt* is never seen used for Brahman, or that because of the qualification "windless" (*avātam*), the word *ānīt* does not refer to the activity of the unmanifested breath but rather denotes the existence of Brahman. This cannot be said.

[Objection: In the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other passages, because Vāyu and Prāṇa are taught separately, it is possible for Prāṇa to exist even in the absence of Vāyu. [Reply: That objection is refuted as follows: Since there is no separate ontological principle (tattva) apart from Vāyu, Prāṇa is indeed a specific mode of Vāyu itself. Therefore, because the term "without wind" (avātam) negates Vāyu in its general sense, and because it is impossible for the word "āni" to denote the function of Prāṇa, it is proper to say that it refers exclusively to Brahman. Thus, by the etymology "that which is supported by or enjoyed by itself" (svena dhīyate upabhujyate), the word *svadhā* denotes Lakṣmī; [the passage thus refers to] the Blessed Lord as qualified by Lakṣmī.

Some say that since the subsistence of the Supreme Brahman at the time of creation and so forth has already been stated, the sūtra "And because He is the Best" (Śreṣṭhaśca) is merely a supplement to the preceding section, intended for the subsequent inquiry—just like the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā sūtra "The grinding of the Pūṣan-cake is understood to apply to the modified sacrifice"—and not a separate section. Thus ends the section on the minuteness of the Best.
Nor [are they] the functions of air, because of the separate teaching. ||8||
But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. (9)
And because it is not something to be performed, there is no fault; for [the scripture] shows this thus. ||10||
The fivefold activity is designated as being like that of the mind. ||11||

Is this principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) merely air, or is it the action consisting of inhalation and exhalation, or is it air that has attained a particular state? In the face of this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: it is merely air, or the action of inhalation and exhalation; for there is the scriptural statement, "That which is the prāṇa is air," and because the word *prāṇa* is applied to it in that context. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: it is not merely air, because in the mantra "From this [Self] it is born," it is taught as distinct [from air]; furthermore, the word *prāṇa* is not applied to mere air. For this very reason, it is also not the action of inhalation and so forth belonging to that air.

Just as in the case of the activity of fire, the activity of air also cannot be taught as having a separate origination in the mantra concerning the production of substances which states, "From this it is born"; for although that [air] is fit to be designated by the word *prāṇa* ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvārthapratyaya*), there is no usage of it with a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛarthapratyaya*) as in "it breathes" (*prāṇiti*), nor with a suffix denoting an instrument (*karaṇārthapratyaya*) as in "one lives by means of this" (*anena jīvati*).

Now, if prāṇa is merely air that has reached a certain particular state, then would prāṇa, like fire, abandon its nature as air? No, it is said in reply: this is not another element like fire; rather, without abandoning its nature as air, it is a specific instrument of the living self (jīva), like the eye and other organs, because it is distinguished by them.

For in the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is said: "Then indeed the vital breaths disputed among themselves for the sake of superiority, saying, 'I am superior,' 'I am superior,'" which indicates that they are determined to be of the same kind by the description of their quarrel with the eye and the other organs. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, the primacy of the vital breath is established by the words of the eye and the others: "You are not the best. Indeed, a mutual dispute over superiority arising from doubt regarding equal utility occurs only among things of the same class when they are mentioned together.

Furthermore, the determination of primacy occurs through the observation of a preponderance of benefit and so forth toward someone. Moreover, the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belongs to the same class as those well-known as the instruments of the living being (*jīva*) is established only if it too is an instrument for that being. If it is objected that no specific benefit to the living being is seen from the vital breath in the way it is seen from the eyes and other senses, we reply that this is not a fault; for scripture itself shows that the function consisting of the maintenance of the body and the senses constitutes its benefit to the living being.

Just as in the Dialogue on the Vital Breaths (Prāṇasaṃvāda), there is the statement of Prāṇa to the eyes and other organs: "Do not fall into delusion regarding me; it is I who, having divided myself fivefold and having taken hold of this arrow-like body, sustain it. Now, one might ask: when there is a fivefold division, are Vyāna and the others distinct principles from Prāṇa? To this, it is said: no.

Because of the scriptural statement, "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind," desire, resolve, and so forth are merely modifications (*vṛtti*) of the single vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), just as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and the others are. By this, the Sāṃkhya position—that *prāṇa* is the common function (*sādhāraṇī vṛtti*) of the sense organs—is refuted. For they [the Sāṃkhyas] imagine that it is like the movement of a cage causing all the parrots within it to move, or like [the movement of a single body affecting] all [the senses].

"The common function of all the sense organs located in the body—like the raising of a snare that has fallen upon a flock of pigeons—is *prāṇa*. This is not correct; for apart from the perception of objects, which is the specific function of the sense organs, we observe that the activities of inhalation and exhalation, as well as the activity of sustaining the body by dividing itself fivefold, are the independent functions of the *mukhya-prāṇa*.
These are the summary verses.

The chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is also merely air, as it is stated that it was produced from Brahman according to the same method described for the group of sense organs; nor is its activity within the body in the form of inhalation and exhalation [merely air], because it is taught that it arises together with the material elements.
The statement that it is "air" is consistent with the fact that this [element] is merely another state of air;
because its prior state persists, it does not constitute a separate element, unlike fire.
This [air], which serves as a constant instrument for those subject to transmigratory existence, remains distinct from the sense organs such as the eyes.
Renowned for its supreme service, it sustains this body composed of the subtle instruments and functions through five modes of activity.
Thus ends the section concerning the function of air.
And it is atomic. ||12||

The connection [of this section] is that, immediately after determining the essential nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), its dimension is now being defined. Since there is a conflict of scriptural statements regarding whether the vital breath is all-pervasive (vibhu) or limited (paricchinna), a doubt arises; the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is all-pervasive, because of the scriptural hearing: "He is equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe; everything is established in the vital breath, for all this is enveloped by the vital breath."

[Objection: Even though the infinity of the sense organs is heard in scripture, their finitude has been established by the evidence of their departure from the body and so forth; by that same logic, the finitude of the vital breath (prāṇa) would also be proven. What, then, is the purpose of this section? [Reply: It is said: The opponent maintains that while the infinity [of the senses] is included within the injunctions for meditation, this [infinity of the prāṇa] is not like that. Alternatively, the scriptural hearing of equality with all things—accompanied by the supporting argument that "all this is indeed enveloped by the prāṇa"—is more powerful than the evidence of departure and so forth.

Therefore, the opponent's intention is that the process of departure (*utkramaṇa*) and so forth, which is the means to that [attainment], must be described. Furthermore, the fact of being supplementary to an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi-śeṣatva*) is equally applicable even to the mark of universal similarity, because of the proximity to the injunction for meditation in the passage: "In this way, this similarity is found in the Veda. Moreover, the statement, "Everything is established in breath; for all this is enveloped by breath," speaks of the establishment of the entire body in breath and its being enveloped by breath, but not of the entire world being enveloped by breath.

The conclusion is that the pervasiveness of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established because the use of the word "hi" (for) indicates that it refers to a well-known fact; furthermore, the abiding of the vital breath within the body and its enveloping of the body are well known from common experience as well as from other scriptural passages.
Summary Verses.

Because of the scriptural tradition stating "equal to the three worlds," this [Self] is all-pervasive; however, its minuteness is established by the texts concerning its departure [from the body] and so forth, while the scriptural statement of total equality is merely a praise.
Thus concludes the section concerning the minuteness of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
But the presiding over fire and the other elements belongs to Him who possesses the vital breath, because of the scriptural statement and because of the comparison with the vital breath.
And its eternity. ||14||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: immediately after the investigation into the origin, dimension, and other attributes of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the specific manner in which they are presided over by deities such as Agni is now considered. Is the presiding authority of deities like Agni over the vital breaths that which was previously mentioned in the context of the sūtra, "But there is designation of the presiding deities because of distinction and following" (*abhimānivyapadeśastu viśeṣānugatibhyām*)?

Regarding the doubt as to whether that [presiding] is dependent on itself or dependent on God, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Although it was stated in the section beginning with "But from the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement" (*parāt tu tacchruteḥ*) that the agency of individual souls is dependent on God, nevertheless, since fire, the sun, and so forth—whose sovereignty has been granted by God—possess qualities such as being givers of boons and bestowers of fruits similar to God, they possess independence; therefore, let their presiding be dependent on them alone. This is because the scriptural statements regarding dependence can be restricted to human beings and others.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

The fact that light and the other elements—namely fire, the sun, and so forth—possess the status of presiding over the eyes and other senses is due solely to the volition of the Supreme Lord. Why? Because of the scriptural testimony that He is the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all. Therefore, just as it is logical that the individual soul’s (jīva) presiding over the senses is dependent on another, despite the hearing of its independence in such passages as, "In this very way, having taken these vital breaths (prāṇas), he moves about in his own body according to his will," so too is it logical for the presiding deities (abhimānidevatās) to be likewise dependent.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between deities and humans because the deities possess sovereignty granted by the Supreme Lord, this is not so; for all transmigrating beings are eternally subject to the Lord’s control, as it is heard without distinction in scripture: "He alone is the eternal Lord of this world.

Therefore, since they were subject to the Supreme Lord even prior to attaining their status as deities, that subjection to Him remains unavoidable even thereafter, just as ministers remain subject to the king even after their appointment.
The summary verses.

What harm is there if the presiding over the vital breaths (prāṇas) by deities such as Agni— who are themselves worthy of worship and bestowers of fruits— were to be under their own independent control?
Let it not be so; for these [qualities], such as Īśvara and the rest, possess a constant connection with those [entities] that have vital breath, namely, their state of being governed by them.
Thus ends the section concerning the presiding over light and the other elements.
These are the sense organs, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one. ||15||
Because of the scriptural statement of difference and because of their distinct characteristics. ||16||

Following the determination of the origin and other characteristics of the sense organs (*indriya*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is now investigated whether all those designated by the term "prāṇa" are sense organs, or whether they are distinct from the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of this investigation? If it is argued that the purpose of investigating the definition that distinguishes [the senses] from the principal vital breath is simply for the sake of specific conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we say: not so. Indeed, unlike in the Vaiśeṣika system, an investigation into definitions for the mere sake of conventional usage is not stated to be the purpose of this scripture.

This inquiry is indeed for the purpose of resolving contradictions in the scriptures. For instance, it is beyond dispute that the word *prāṇa* ending in the plural number is a synonym for the sense organs (*indriya*). Its usage in a sense distinct from the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is observed in such passages as: "When the *prāṇa* departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it. By this, it is understood that the sense organs are none other than the eyes and so forth, which are distinct from the best [vital breath].

Furthermore, because the term *mukhya-prāṇa* (the chief vital breath) is applied to that which is the principal *prāṇa* in the passage, "Now, they meditated upon him who is this principal *prāṇa* as the Udgītha," it is understood that this too is included among the sense organs (*indriya*). For by whatever basis of application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) the word *prāṇa* is applied to the eyes and so forth, by that very same basis it is applied to the chief one; thus, the chief *prāṇa* becomes the foremost among the *prāṇas*, just as a certain individual becomes the foremost Brāhmaṇa among the Brāhmaṇas.

Thus, given this conflict in scriptural statements, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: Prāṇa is indeed an organ (indriya), because it is established as being primary among those things denoted by the word "prāṇa. Nor should one suspect that there is a difference between prāṇa and the organs based on the statement of its separate origination in the mantra, "From this [Self] it is born"; for if that were the case, it would follow that the mind (manas) is also distinct from them.

Even if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were indeed a sense organ (*indriya*), the mutual rivalry and dispute observed in common worldly experience among those of the same class—such as that which is heard regarding the eyes and so forth on one hand and the vital breath on the other—is only consistent if it is understood thus. Furthermore, since homogeneity based on the internal factor of being a sense organ is possible, that [dispute] cannot be explained away by a more external homogeneity consisting in being an instrument of the individual soul (*jīva*). Consequently, scriptural statements such as "the ten and one sense organs" refer to the sense organs and so forth as distinct from the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*).

Just as the statement "there are seven vital breaths" refers only to the breaths located in the head, there is no contradiction with the mention of the number eleven; therefore, the meditation on the sense organs prescribed in the passage, "He who meditates upon these as infinite," must be performed together with the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The term *mukhya-prāṇa* (the chief vital breath) does not mean "the principal sense organ among those denoted by the word *prāṇa*"; rather, its meaning is "the *prāṇa* that exists in the mouth" (*mukhe bhavaḥ*). This is because in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, within the same context, the word *āsanya* is used in place of *mukhya*, as in the passage: "Then they spoke to this *prāṇa* in the mouth" (*athahemamāsanyaṃ prāṇam ūcuḥ*). And since *āsanya* means "that which exists in the mouth" (*āsye bhavaḥ*), the word *āsya* undergoes the substitution *āsanna-* according to the rule *paddannomās* [Pāṇini 6.1.63].

If, however, the meaning of "the principal breath" (*mukhyaḥ prāṇaḥ*) is that it is the principal among the breaths, even so, the status of the breath as a sense-organ (*indriyatva*) is not established. This is because the interpretation is tenable in the sense that this breath is the primary denotation of the word "breath," while the other breaths are the senses, which are its secondary (or figurative) designations rather than primary ones; for it is stated that the eyes and the other organs are to be designated by the very term that denotes the principal breath: "They all became his very form; therefore they are designated by his name. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7)

All of this will become clear in the section concerning the "Combination of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) in the sūtra, "If it be argued that there is a difference because of the word 'otherwise'" (*anyathātvam śabdād iti cet*). Therefore, the eyes and so forth, being distinct from the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), are indeed the sense organs (*indriya*). This is also determined by the separate mention [of them] in the mantra, "From this [Being] the vital breath is born. Although the mind is mentioned separately from the sense organs, its status as a sense organ is accepted in accordance with another scriptural statement: "The sense organs, of which the mind is the sixth."

There is no other scriptural statement here to the effect that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is an organ (*indriya*). Furthermore, there is a distinction between the vital breath and the organs: for while all the organs such as the eye have ceased their activity in deep sleep, the activity of the vital breath is still perceived. This is also confirmed by scripture: "The fires of the vital breath alone remain awake in this city; it breathes 'bhūr-bhūḥ'. Moreover, there is a difference in their functions: knowledge and action are the functions of the organs, whereas the maintenance of the body is the function of the vital breath.

Therefore, the sense organs are indeed the eyes and so forth, distinct from the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). And the common definition for these eleven is their being modifications of the sattvic ego (sāttvikāhaṃkāra).
Summary Verses.

"Prāṇa is also an organ, because it is denoted by the word 'praṇa' like all the others. "Not so; because of its separate mention, the others are organs, while the status of prāṇa is [only] figurative."
Thus ends the section on the sense-faculties.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching. ||17||
The [perception] of meat and so forth is based on the earth; for the other two [elements], it is according to their respective names. ||18||
But on account of its preponderance, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation. ||19||

By demonstrating that Brahman is the creator of each subsequent body from among the preceding bodies in the *khādi* passages, the fact that Brahman is the direct agent in every creation is shown by the sūtra "Because of the scriptural statement of difference. That [position] is not tenable; for in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), the agency belongs solely to Hiraṇyagarbha, according to Śruti and Smṛti.

The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that [the Lord's agency] is already well-known. Alternatively, there is a connection by way of an illustration: just as in the creation of ether and so forth, His status as the direct agent is established even in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*). The scriptural authority is: "Having entered with this living self (*jīva*), let me differentiate names and forms," and: "The naming and the manifestation of beings and their functions."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Smṛti passage beginning with "In the beginning, he created the gods and others from the very words of the Veda" establishes that Hiraṇyagarbha is the one who differentiates names and forms, or rather that it is the Supreme Self having him as its body, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is: it establishes this for Hiraṇyagarbha alone, because of the scriptural statement, "Let me differentiate by means of the individual soul (jīva)."

But if this were so, then in the common worldly expression, "Just as a king considers the enemy army to be encompassed by means of his spy," the act of encompassing the enemy army—which is actually performed by the spy—is figuratively attributed to the king; likewise, here too, the differentiation of name and form (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa), which is performed by the individual soul (jīva), would be figuratively attributed to Brahman. This is not a fault.

Just as in the case of a king and his spy, since there is no difference in essential nature between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara)—being related as part and whole—even here, because the soul is referred to as the agent of the Lord's own selfhood through the phrase "by the living self," it is logically established that the synthesis performed by the soul is primarily the work of the Lord, through the reference to the soul as being the Lord’s own self and his agent.

Nor should it be argued that this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is characterized by association (*sahayoga*), such that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of God (*īśvara*) would also be possible therein; for a case ending denoting a *kāraka* (agent, object, etc. is stronger than a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada-vibhakti*), as the former is independent of connection with other words. Nor can its status as a *kāraka*-case ending be maintained by interpreting it as having the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because in a grammar whose agent is God, the individual soul (*jīva*) lacks the quality of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, even if it were interpreted as having the sense of an instrument, grammar would ultimately result in having the individual soul as its agent.

It is not the case that God is the agent [of the Veda]. For when there is a conscious agent, the assistance rendered by another consciousness through its status as an instrument occurs only by virtue of that other being an agent impelled by the former. On this view, just as a king has a non-primary agency in a compilation produced by his agents, it must be understood that God’s agency in the grammatical treatise produced by the individual soul (jīva) is intended as non-primary. Thus, when the meaning is taken as "instrument," even the suspicion regarding the impossibility of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is dispelled; for such a suspicion would arise only if the meaning were "agent."

Because the agent [of the act of entering] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and because the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) does not terminate in mere entry; furthermore, since it is postulated that the act of creation belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*) alone, the use of the instrumental case for the agent is justified. This is because the rule "when two actions have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* is used for the earlier one" (Pāṇini 3.4.21) is traditionally understood to signify identity of agent, and thus cannot apply to actions with different agents. Moreover, since that suffix is also traditionally understood to denote the agent, the instrumental case would be untenable even if the agent were already expressed by it.

Just as in grammar, the primary agent is indeed the life-force (*jīva*) of that which lacks its own synthesis; only thus does the Smṛti passage, "the name and form of beings," become consistent. For it is not the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the *jīva* Hiraṇyagarbha, who, for the sake of creating the names and forms of gods and others, would depend upon Vedic words for the purpose of remembering the names and forms that occurred in a previous creation. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

The fashioning of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti*)—the differentiation of the names and forms of gods and others—is the creation of the Supreme Lord alone as he performs the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). This is because of the scriptural hearing that the tripartition and the differentiation of names and forms have a single agent, as stated: "That divinity thought: 'Well now, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms; let me make each of them threefold. For the act of tripartition is indeed the work of the Supreme Lord alone.

But this does not refer to Hiraṇyagarbha, who is remembered in the Smṛti as having been born within that egg—as in the passage, "In that egg was Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds"—because the egg itself is to be produced from the triad of fire, water, and food (tejo-vāyu). Therefore, the Lord, who is the agent of the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa), is also the agent of the differentiation of names and forms (nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa). Even the Smṛti tradition regarding Hiraṇyagarbha’s agency is justified because, like a jar or similar objects, his production involves two agents. Now, how is the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the phrase "by the living self" (jīvenātmanā) to be understood?

Understand that this is because the word *jīva* refers to the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as His body. For, when the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* consists merely in two things: first, the priority in time of the action denoted by the root of the *ktvā*-suffix relative to the action conveyed by the verbal suffix whose agent it is; and second, the identity of the agent of those two actions. This is due to parsimony (*lāghava*). It does not include the "agent-power" (*kartṛ-śakti*) itself, which is already obtained through other means.

Even so, since connection with the principal action is more significant, one might argue that only the connection with the act of grammar should be stated for the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as its body. This is true; however, when connection with the principal action is impossible, connection with a subordinate action is indeed appropriate. For example, in the sentence "Having made bricks, he eats," there is an impossibility because the bricks cannot logically be connected as the object of the act of eating.

The distinction here is simply this: that which is indicated by the third case-ending (the instrumental) is unfit for connection with a verb whose meaning is the agent (*kartṛ*). If one were to accept that the suffix *ktvā* expresses merely the identity of the agent and the priority in time, while rejecting its status as denoting the agent-power (*kartṛ-śakti*), then in this case—just as in the example "I shall eat after living"—even in the sentence "Having made bricks, I shall eat," there would necessarily have to be a third case ending, such as "by me" (*mayā*), according to the rule governing the third case prescribed under the heading of "that which is not already expressed" (*anabhihita-adhikāra*). Therefore, it must be accepted that the suffix *ktvā* denotes the agent-power, and only on that basis can the use of the nominative case (*prathamā*) there be justified.

Furthermore, since the agent is expressed here by the suffix *ktvā*, the instrumental case in "by the living self" (*jīvena*) would be improper; rather, the nominative case should have been used. Thus, there is an inconsistency in attempting to justify the instrumental case on the grounds that the agent's power is not expressed. In that case, this instrumental must be explained as being Vedic (chāndasa) with respect to the Supreme Self, who has the individual soul as His body and is the agent of the creation. However, one should not justify this instrumental by accepting the non-difference of the individual soul from the Lord and the fact that the individual soul is the agent of the creation.

Since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been established, it is proven that the "differentiation" (vyākaraṇa), which shares the same agent as the "triplication" (trivṛtkaraṇa), is the work of the Lord alone, who is the agent of the triplication. Although the Śruti records the triplication after the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha and subsequent to the differentiation of names and forms, nevertheless, because the sequence of meaning (arthakrama) is more authoritative than the sequence of textual recitation (pāṭhakrama), the detailed explanation of the fact that the triplication occurs prior [to those events] should be sought in the Commentary (bhāṣya).
In the summary verses:
The Lotus-born [Brahmā] alone is the creator of the names and forms of the grammatical system,
because of the scriptural statement "by means of the individual soul" (jīvena) and because he is remembered in the context of that which is to be created.

Do not say so; for he who made the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is indeed declared to be the agent in the process of differentiation (vyākṛti), whereas the Sustainer (dhātṛ) is not likewise the agent in the production of the cosmic egg from the earth and other elements that have been tripartitely formed.
Therefore, the Lord alone is the agent of both differentiation and tripartition.
But the word "jīvena" (by the living self) is capable of signifying that very [Brahman] in its sense of being the embodied one.
Thus ends the section concerning name and form (the Saṃjñāmūrti-adhikaraṇa).

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled *Caturmatasāra*, composed by Appayadīkṣita— the son of the eminent Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and a jewel in the ocean of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage, and a preeminent teacher of the non-dualistic knowledge (*Advaitavidyā*).
The second chapter is completed.
Salutations to the glorious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Prosperity!
The second chapter.
"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for Smṛti, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis."
And because others are not perceived.

In the first chapter, it was established through reasoning that the Supreme Brahman known as the illustrious Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the entire universe, by demonstrating the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedāntas. Now, the second chapter is commenced in order to consolidate that very conclusion by resolving all possible contradictions. In this regard, in the first topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), the suspicion that the Vedāntas might have another purpose due to conflict with the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is refuted.

Now, how can there be a suspicion that the Śruti has another meaning when it contradicts Smṛti? For it was established in the section of the Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtras, "In case of contradiction, however, it should be disregarded, for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference," that in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Smṛti alone lacks authority.

For in that case, it has been stated that the Smṛti rule, "The Audumbarī post is to be entirely covered," is to be disregarded due to its contradiction with the direct Śruti, "Having touched the Audumbarī, one should sing"; and it has also been stated that when there is no contradiction with a direct Śruti, the Smṛti possesses authority because it leads to the inference of a foundational Śruti. This is true; such is the case indeed when the meaning of the direct Śruti is explicit.

The Vedānta texts concerning the cause of the world, however, do not have their meanings made explicit like the Śruti on touch; rather, they are extremely profound and of various kinds. As it is said: "Even if one knows the meaning of the Veda by oneself, there may still be ignorance regarding it; but when it has been determined by the great-souled sages (ṛṣis), what doubt could there be? Thus, for the sake of providing certainty through supplementary expositions (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), there certainly arises a suspicion that these [Vedānta texts] have other purposes, following the Smṛti of Sāṃkhya composed by great sages such as Kapila. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute that.

Here, a doubt arises as to whether the Brahman’s status as the cause of the world—established in the first chapter—is untenable or tenable. Because of conflicting Smṛtis such as those of the Sāṃkhya and Manu, there is uncertainty: are the Vedāntas to be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, and thus intent upon primordial matter (pradhāna) as the cause in accordance with it; or are they to be supplemented by the Smṛtis of Manu and others, and thus intent upon Brahman as the cause? Since this has not been determined, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are to be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, because that [Smṛti] is otherwise without scope.

This is because the Smṛtis of Manu and others have their scope (sāvakāśatva) regarding the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma), as well as ritual acts such as the Agnihotra. Nor should it be argued that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti must be assumed to be rooted in error due to its contradiction with the many Smṛtis of Manu, Vyāsa, and others; for such an assumption is untenable, since the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad declares the perfection of knowledge of Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, stating: "He who in the beginning sustained with his knowledges the sage Kapila, who was born [in the past] and was being born [again]. Thus, there is no room for such a supposition.

If it is argued that the authority of Manu’s utterances is established in its entirety by the Vedic text, "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine," we say no; for that is not established, as the word "medicine" (bheṣaja) does not signify authoritative validity.

In the Yajurveda, after prescribing a sacrifice for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) with the injunction, "He who desires spiritual luster should offer this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra," and following the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the fruit—"It accomplishes all that constitutes spiritual luster"—the text continues: "They say that by performing this sacrifice, excessive spiritual luster is produced; therefore, the sacrificer is liable to become afflicted with skin disease (*duścarmā*). Thus, it describes the very same result [of the sacrifice] as being [both] the production of excessive spiritual luster and the potential for the sacrificer to become leprous (*citrībhavituṃ*).

Having again proclaimed [the defect] that results in a fault, for the purpose of its removal, there is the injunction: "One should make the two verses seen by Manu the *dhāyyā*s. Regarding how the leucoderma is removed by means of the two verses seen by Manu—namely, the verses beginning with "I praise Agni, your ancient Aṅgiras, the god of the Vasus"—which are to be placed in the form of *dhāyyā*s within the *sāmidhenī*s, the following explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) provides the connection: "Whatever Manu said is indeed a remedy; he thus provides a remedy for him. However, it is not... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].

This establishes the authoritative status of the meanings of the *ṛg* verses such as "Agni is the first among the Vasus," as well as the meanings of the statements in the *Manusmṛti*. If it is argued that the meaning of Manu’s words is contradicted because they function as medicine for leprosy or other diseases, then let them be considered *arthavāda*s (explanatory passages) based on unreal matters. For it is not appropriate to adopt another meaning that does not cohere with the subject at hand merely to establish that an *arthavāda* must be based on a real matter.

Therefore, since it is unestablished that the passage beginning with "tasmād yad vai kiñca" is intended to demonstrate the authority of all *anuvākyās* regarding their respective objects in every instance, it is more appropriate to assume that the statements of the *Manusmṛti* find their scope only within the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), setting aside the portion concerning the doctrine of Brahman as the cause. Consequently, because the Vedāntas must be supplemented by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti—which possesses no other scope—they should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Sāṃkhyasūtras*, the *Haribhāṣya*, the *Harihara-vārtika*, and other such works.

Those [scriptures] that are intent upon primordial matter (pradhāna) as the cause must be interpreted otherwise. Among them, those which explicitly state that the Person alone is the cause should be understood as attributing the primary function of the material cause to the Person, just as one might speak of a queen’s victory through her ministers; thus they are to be interpreted in accordance with the Smṛtis of Manu and others. This is because those many Smṛtis, composed by the most authoritative sages, cannot be set aside.

Nor do those [scriptures] concerning ritual actions possess any independent scope, because even those texts that enjoin rituals—which constitute the worship of the Supreme Person—have their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) solely upon Brahman, the cause of the universe and the Supreme Person who is to be worshipped and who is the substratum of those rituals. For this very reason, when Manu was questioned by the sages regarding the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), he first taught the Supreme Person who is to be worshipped by them, and only thereafter did he instruct them in those duties. "This [universe] existed as darkness, unperceived, without defining characteristics..."

Inconceivable and indescribable, as if entirely asleep, thereupon the Lord Svayambhū—the unmanifest one whose power operates through the great elements and who dispels darkness—became manifest, revealing this world. Desiring to create various beings from his own body, he meditated and first created the waters; into them, he cast his seed. That became a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun. Within it, Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds.

It is clearly evident from such statements as, "The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *Nara*; since they are declared to be his *ayana* (abode), he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*," and "In the Purāṇas, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is worshipped; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction," that the teaching of ritual action (*karman*) is presented solely as being subordinate to and for the purpose of worshipping Him.

Likewise, Yājñavalkya also, having introduced the Lord with the words, "The supreme purification of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is held to arise from the knowledge of the Lord," establishes His status as the cause of the universe through the method of the Puruṣasūkta, just like Manu, stating: "From His mouth, feet, thighs, and sides, the social classes (varṇas) arose in due order."

The ultimate intent [of the scripture] is revealed to be Nārāyaṇa alone—the Lord of Śrī, who is to be propitiated by those whose duties of caste and stage of life (varṇāśramadharma) have been well-described, and who is the subject of the Puruṣasūkta. Likewise, Āpastamba also introduces Nārāyaṇa in the form taught in the Subālopaniṣad—beginning with "All living beings are indeed the city of Him who dwells in the cave, who is unslain and stainless," and "This is the inner Self of all beings, the divine, singular God Nārāyaṇa, free from sin"—and continues: "From that body, everything originates together with its root..."

By stating that "He is eternal and not non-eternal," it is revealed that His intent is to show that He alone is to be propitiated through the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) as described by Himself. In this manner, the statements of other Smṛti-authors may also be cited as examples. Nor should it be argued: "Since there is an equal lack of scope [for both], how can it be determined that the Smṛtis of Manu and others alone are to be used as supplementary support? For Manu and the others are the most authoritative of trustworthy persons (āpta).

The supreme authority of Manu is established by the scriptural statement that his words possess the nature of medicine (*bheṣaja*). To explain: here, the term "nature of medicine" is intended merely in the sense of being a means for the common purpose of alleviating both disease and sin, and not specifically in the sense of being solely for the alleviation of physical disease. Otherwise, the statement "whatever [Manu has spoken]" would result in the absurdity of being entirely devoid of meaning; for among the utterances of the *Manusmṛti*, there is no single statement that propounds a medicine for the sake of curing disease in the manner of medical treatises.

There certainly exists a collection of statements concerning the duties of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) that establish the means for the pacification of committed sins; this is because the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties of the castes and stages of life are causes for the destruction of evil. Now, it might be argued: "Even so, not all the statements in the *Manusmṛti* are applicable to the destruction of sin, since there are also those in the *Manusmṛti* whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), such as those dealing with statecraft (*rājanīti*) and the adjudication of legal disputes (*vyavahāra-pada*); therefore, the use of the word 'whatever' (*yatkiñcit*) in its distributive sense is inconsistent. To this we reply: [this objection does not hold].

For even those [other duties] contribute indirectly to that end by assisting in the performance of actions intended for the destruction of evil; furthermore, since the word "all" (*sarva*) can be restricted when its unrestricted sense is impossible—given that it may refer to the entire collection of injunctions concerning the duties of the castes and stages of life even in the absence of [the destruction of all evil]—it is appropriate that it signifies a restricted "all."

Therefore, regarding the scriptural statement within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, "All indeed desire [the portion] of the Hāriyojana," since it is impossible for the word "all" (sarva) to refer to an unrestricted totality, and since its reference to a totality must be specified by some limitation, it is logical that it refers to the totality delimited by those who are priests (ṛtvij) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Thus, it was determined in the Pūrvatantra that this sentence prescribes the consumption of the Hāriyojana only for the priests.

And thus, by the statement that [the Manu-smṛti] is a medicine, it has been stated that for the words of Manu—which have attained authority—it is impossible for their ultimate purport to terminate merely in the performance of worship, setting aside the one who is to be worshipped as the object of that ultimate purport. For it has been stated therein that for all the words of Manu, which constitute the Dharmaśāstra, it is impossible for their ultimate purport to terminate merely in the performance of worship, setting aside the one who is to be worshipped as the object of that ultimate purport.

In that very context, the authority of all the verses in the form of Dharmaśāstra is obtained; thus, he possesses the status of being the most authoritative (āptatama). Likewise, by the Śruti statement, "Vyāsa Pārāśarya said," the gravity [of his words] is demonstrated through their being spoken by Vyāsa regarding the subject matter he propounded; thus, the authority of everything taught by Vyāsa is obtained, and therefore he possesses the status of being the most authoritative.

In this way, for Yājñavalkya and others as well, their status as the most authoritative (āptatamatva) is established through expressions such as those found in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "Janaka indeed performed the sacrifice with many sacrificial fees"; whereas Kapila possesses merely the status of an authority (āptatvamātra), since passages such as "the seer who was impelled" are satisfied by referring merely to his possession of knowledge regarding a few Vedic texts and the meaning of the Vedas that is relevant to his status as a seer (ṛṣitva).

Likewise, it is well known that the expounders of the Sāṃkhya treatise, such as Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and others, were only three or four in number, whereas the expounders of the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, such as Manu and others, were exceedingly numerous. And it is perfectly clear that the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas are far more voluminous than the Sāṃkhya treatise consisting of the few sūtras composed by Kapila and his followers.

Therefore, because it contradicts the many treatises composed by Manu and others who are most authoritative, the Sāṃkhya system lacks any scope and is ineffective; thus, the Vedāntas are to be supplemented precisely by those Smṛtis of Manu and others which have no other application. Consequently, through their consistent harmony (samanvaya), the status of Brahman as the cause of the world remains unshakable.
The summary verses.

For the sake of ascertaining the true meaning of the flood of Vedānta and the exceedingly profound Sāṃkhya Smṛti, it is proper that the *Upabṛhmaṇa*— which has no other object and finds its scope therein— should be spoken; but no other work, though renowned for its focus on the understanding of Dharma, possesses such scope.
Therefore, that Brahman which is to be known through the Vedāntas is not the cause of the world.
Do not think thus; for even the Smṛtis originating from the mouth of Manu are recognized as having no scope [for contradiction].
Indeed, they intend their application toward Nārāyaṇa when He is to be propitiated by their respective rites.
Therefore, those very [teachings] composed by the most authoritative persons are honored; they alone serve as the supplements (*upabṛhmaṇa*) for them.
As for the Sāṃkhya-smṛti, which is seen to have meanings contrary to those [authoritative teachings], it is based on delusion.
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti.
By this, Yoga is refuted. (Sūtra 3)

Here too, the subject matter, doubt, prima facie argument, established conclusion, and reasons are to be understood as before; for since error is impossible for Hiraṇyagarbha, [the teaching] was not composed by him.

Since this scripture accepts the existence of Īśvara, describes the practice of Yoga as taught in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts, and differs from the Smṛtis of Kapila and others, it is an integral part of Vedānta; therefore, the Vedāntas are to be supplemented by it. Consequently, the doubt raised in this section concerning the "extended application" (*atideśa*) is whether the claim that Brahman is the cause is untenable, because one must accept that Pradhāna, presided over by Īśvara, is the cause according to the method set forth therein.

The resolution of that objection is as follows: since even Hiraṇyagarbha is a *kṣetrajña* (an individual soul), it is possible that the scripture composed by him is rooted in error; because he accepts the non-Brahman *pradhāna* as the cause; because he admits that the Lord is merely the efficient cause; because there is a discrepancy between his object of meditation and that intended by the Vedānta; and because he prescribes a distinct form of meditation defined differently from that [of the Vedānta], the Vedāntas are not to be supplemented by such a contradictory work.
Summary Verses.

[The opponent argues: "In that case, let Yoga be the means of nourishment [for Sāṃkhya], for the Lord (Īśvara) was established therein by the Lotus-born [Brahmā], and Yoga is known from the Śruti as having Him as its object.
Let it not be so; for who here would not have the delusion that those two [Sāṃkhya and Yoga] possess characteristics distinct from the Lord declared by the Śruti and from the Yoga declared from Him?"
Thus ends the section concerning the refutation of Yoga.
Not so, because this [dream experience] has a different character, and its being such [as waking experience] is due to the word [of scripture].
But the designation [of the Self] as the presiding deity is due to distinction and conformity.
But it is indeed seen.
If it be argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because of the existence of the negation and of the persistence [of the material cause].
Because of the consequence that [the individual soul] would likewise [merge into Brahman] at the time of dissolution, [the doctrine of the Self as the size of an atom] is untenable.
But it is not so because of the existence of an illustrative example.
And because of the defects in one's own position.
Also because of the non-establishment of reasoning.
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

The previously stated position—that the [Vedānta] should be supplemented by the Smṛtis of Manu and others—is incorrect, because those [Smṛtis] contradict reason (tarka). Therefore, the connection [of this section] arises from the counter-argument that the supplementation should instead be performed solely by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, which is supported by reason.

If it be asked whether Brahman’s status as the cause is logical or illogical, there arises a doubt based on whether the production of a world that is dissimilar from Brahman—which is sentient—is possible or impossible. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the production of an insentient world from a sentient Brahman is not possible, because they are dissimilar. For the relationship of cause and effect is observed only when there is similarity between them through the specific, characteristic form residing in the cause—for instance, in the case of a jar, a bowl, clay, gold, and so forth, where the effect shares the nature of "clay-ness" or "gold-ness" belonging to its cause.

Furthermore, the unique quality of consciousness belonging to the conscious being is not perceived in its effects; nor can consciousness—which is never unperceived—be postulated as merely unmanifest in objects such as jars (as it is in the case of living beings in deep sleep) on the grounds that the doctrine of Brahman as the cause would otherwise be inexplicable. For since consciousness must necessarily manifest at some time, such a postulation is untenable.

Otherwise, by the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of explaining otherwise), one would have to assume that even the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) possesses a non-manifest solar nature, since it is heard [in scripture] as being the sun; furthermore, there would arise a contradiction with scriptural texts such as "consciousness and unconsciousness," which distinguish between the sentient and the insentient; and finally, if one accepts a causal relationship between the dissimilar and the non-dissimilar, then given their dissimilarity, a difference (*bheda*) necessarily follows, which would contradict the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the identity of cause and effect. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

If it is argued that, although there is a difference between worms, honey, and so forth, a causal relationship is observed between them, and that there is a similarity insofar as the insentient portion alone has honey as its material cause (*prakṛti*), we say no. For if some kind of similarity were to serve as the determinant for a causal relationship, then everything could arise from everything.

The objection that [the effect] would follow as being identical [to the cause] is based on your own intended view that similarity consists in the possession of the unique, specific form residing in the cause. However, that cannot be established here, because the nature of being a honeybee (*mākṣikatva*) is absent in a worm. Thus, the relationship of cause and effect is established even between the world and Brahman, despite their having different characteristics. Nor does this entail the acceptance of actual difference; for even while denying similarity, non-difference is established, just as in the case of a bracelet and gold.

Furthermore, if there were no distinction between the world and Brahman, then since the creation and other processes of the world exist, the states of the world—which are to be abandoned—would also exist in Brahman just as they do in the world. Consequently, there would arise the inconsistency of having both "abandonable" qualities within the one Brahman and, conversely, qualities such as being "free from sin" established by other scriptural passages that are contrary to those abandonable qualities.

Since the non-difference between cause and effect—which is accepted as the established doctrine (siddhānta)—is of the nature that Brahman having the subtle sentient and insentient entities as its body is the cause, while Brahman having the gross sentient and insentient entities as its body is the effect, those [objections] do not apply; for there is the existence of the illustrative example that qualities belonging to a body do not attach to the embodied one, just as childhood, youth, old age, and so forth, have no connection with the Self.

And thus, although it can be said that there is a similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) between cause and effect—since they are insentient (*acetana*) in their aspect as qualifiers consisting of the gross and subtle bodies, yet sentient (*cetana*) in their aspect as the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—nevertheless, by accepting that the aspect of the qualified in the cause must also be the cause for the aspect of the qualifier in the effect, a dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is established. In this regard, the illustration is as follows:

This has been presented: for even when a thing in its state of childhood attains another state such as youth, the causal factor residing in the substantial part (viśeṣyāṃśa) remains the cause even with respect to the qualifying part (viśeṣaṇāṃśa) residing in the effect; this is because a body devoid of the self cannot attain youth and so forth. Thus, it is shown that here too, despite the difference [in appearance], the relationship of cause and effect is logically established.
These are the summary verses.
"How could the insentient universe arise from that which is sentient? This objection is too crude; for if the cause and effect belong to two distinct orders, this objection would find no footing."
Nevertheless, reasoning and counter-reasoning are stated; total similarity is not observed anywhere.
In some way or another, this applies even to the case under discussion, but especially so in the case of insects such as the *krimi* and the honeybee (*mākṣika*).
Thus concludes the section concerning the difference in characteristics.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.

Although there is no sublation of the harmony [of the Vedas] by the mere logic of the Sāṃkhyas who maintain that Pradhāna is the cause, this section is intended to extend the previous reasoning in order to dispel a further doubt: namely, that such sublation might occur through the logic favored by the many followers of the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Jain, and other schools who maintain that atoms are the cause.

Regarding the question of whether the unity of the universe (*samanvaya*) is destroyed by the reasoning of those who maintain that atoms are the cause, there arises a doubt based on the presence of mutual contradictions among them and the resulting uncertainty as to whether they possess the capacity to destroy that unity or not. This constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The capacity to destroy that unity is indeed possible; for example, even though dogs are mutually antagonistic, when they act with a common purpose out of a desire to devour a single boar, all of them succeed in killing the boar even if they do not obtain it.

Thus, atoms are real, void, consisting of consciousness, momentary, and fourfold or singlefold; even though such internal disputes exist, since we observe that only things of small dimensions, such as threads and the like, can be the originators of large-dimensioned effects such as cloth, the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) between Brahman and the world—which possess opposite dimensions—is impossible. Therefore, the refutation of that [atomistic theory] is established by means of the logic favored by all proponents of atomism. This is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however:

Just as the single sun dispels even a vast mass of darkness scattered in various directions, so too does the Veda itself remain awake—dispelling through counter-examples such as the clay lump, the jar, and the bowl, this aforementioned web of reasoning and other similar arguments, beginning with the words, "O dear one, as by a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay [is known]. Therefore, no further effort need be exerted here.
The summary verses.
The doctrine of atoms as the cause, though established here by many disputants through reasoning, is in vain;
exhausted by the strife of arguments over its internal subdivisions, it has no power at the boundary of the revealed scripture.

The doctrine of those who claim that "from the small comes the great" and "the great does not come from the small" has been cast aside by the Śruti through the description of the analogy of the dog and the boar.
Thus concludes the section concerning [theories] not accepted by the learned.
If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the identity with the enjoyer, it would be as in the case of the world.

Since the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*) is a section on extended application (*atideśa*), this present section is connected to it by way of its foundational source, setting that aside. For in that [preceding] section, by the sūtra "But not because of the existence of an analogy" (*na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt*), it was stated—using as an analogy the fact that childhood, youth, and so forth belonging to the body do not apply to the embodied self—that defects residing in the body of Brahman (which consists of the sentient and insentient) do not apply to Brahman itself. That [conclusion] is challenged as being untenable; for if Brahman were the embodied self like the individual soul (*jīva*), there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain produced by that [body]. Thus it is objected.

In the first chapter, by the sūtra "If it be argued that there would be the attainment of experience [of pleasure and pain], no, because of the difference in nature," the possibility of the Supreme Being experiencing pleasure and pain resulting from entering bodies such as ours was refuted; just as a master of a house who has entered another's house does not partake of joy or dejection caused by the completeness or deficiency of that house, so it is with the Supreme Being. Here, however, that [experience] resulting from being the master of the body is refuted.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because of the scriptural statement, "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant," it is impossible to prevent the experience of pleasure and pain caused by that [body] as long as one holds ownership over the body. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Just as one who has built a prison in order to afflict an offender in accordance with his crime, and having entered it himself for that purpose, does not incur the suffering caused by that [offender] despite being independent, so it is for the Supreme Lord as well. Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "Not indeed for one who possesses a body" refer to a body acquired through one's own karma, and not merely to the mere ownership of a body.

This is because the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, after stating the Supreme Lord's lordship over the bodies of earth and so forth in the passage beginning "Whose body is the earth," [continues with the aforementioned statement].

In order to dispel the suspicion that [the inner controller] might experience pleasure and pain produced by those [beings], just as the presiding deities of those respective things do, the text declares immortality in every instance with the words: "This Self is the inner controller, immortal."
These are the summary verses.
If Brahman, whose body consists of consciousness and unconsciousness, were described as the cause,
then this embodied being would possess the status of an enjoyer of pleasure and pain.

Let it not be so; that [agency] is produced by karma and is not produced by the body, therefore it would not belong to the body, just as the power to bestow favor or inflict punishment belongs to the king alone.
Thus ends the section concerning the transformation into the enjoyer.
The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning "origination" and so forth.
And because [the self] is perceived when there is a mental state.
And because of the existence of another.

If it be argued that [the soul] does not exist because of its being designated as non-existent, we say no; for [it exists] by means of another attribute, as is established by the remainder of the passage and by other scriptural texts.
And like cloth.
And just as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth [are not the self].

In the section concerning "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*), it was established against the Sāṃkhya that even though the effect—the world—is different in character from its cause—Brahman—it is nonetheless non-different from it, as stated in the *Guṇasūtra*: "If it be said 'it is non-existent,' no, because [the negation] is a mere denial," and this was demonstrated by the analogy of the earring and gold. Now, [the opponent argues] that non-difference is untenable when there is a difference in character, because difference in character is pervaded by (i.e., entails) actual difference; for this very reason, non-difference is unestablished even in the case of the earring and gold.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having adopted the view of the Vaiśeṣika—who asserts that "in all cases, a difference between cause and effect must necessarily exist because of differences in cognition, distinct terminology, and so forth"—the non-difference [of the world from Brahman] is challenged and then resolved. In this regard, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: if there is non-difference, the status of Brahman as the cause of the world is not possible; for in the world, among things standing in the relation of cause and effect, such as a jar and a lump of clay, it is determined that the causal relationship is pervaded by difference, through differences in cognition, distinct terminology, and so forth.

For neither does the word "lump" arise in the lump of clay, nor does the cognition of the form of a lump arise in the jar; nor is the word "jar" applied to the lump of clay, nor is the word "lump" applied to the jar. Nor does the form of a lump exist in the jar, nor does the form of a broad base and belly exist in the lump of clay. Nor is the fetching of water performed by the lump of clay, nor is the construction of a wall performed by the jar. Nor is there multiplicity in the jar as there is in the threads, nor is there unity in the threads as there is in the jar.

Furthermore, the staff, the wheel, and so forth do not function as causes for the jar in the same way that the lump of clay does; nor does the kneading preceded by the addition of water function as a cause for the jar in the same way that the lump of clay does. Moreover, the lump of clay does not exist at the time when the jar exists, nor does the jar exist at the time when the lump of clay exists. Furthermore, there is no perception of the jar and so forth at the earlier time, nor is there any perception of the lump of clay at the later time. Therefore, due to the difference in cognition, verbal designation, and so forth, a distinction between cause and effect must be admitted.

If it is argued that, just as in a single body there arise different cognitions and designations due to the differences in states such as childhood and youth, or just as in a single substance of clay there arise different cognitions and designations due to the differences in states such as a lump and a jar, we say no; for if these states were impermanent, it would follow that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production] (asatkāryavāda), since it is impossible for impermanent states to be non-different from their cause which exists prior [to them].

Furthermore, this would result in the collapse of the established doctrine that cause and effect are non-different. For if those [states] were also eternal, it would be impossible to establish the distinction between cognition, different words, and so forth, and it would entail the uselessness of the entire collection of causes such as the staff and the wheel. [Objection: But the state of being a jar is unmanifest during the stage when the clay is a lump; it is only when it becomes manifest that it becomes the locus for cognition, different words, and so on, and the collection of causes such as the staff and the wheel serves the purpose of bringing about that manifestation.

And this being the case, it would not follow that by the operation of the staff, wheel, and so forth—intended for the manifestation of the state of a jar residing in a lump of clay—one would also have to manifest the states of the handle, the rim, the neck, the bowl, and so on, just as a lamp brought in to manifest a jar in a room might manifest the handle and other parts within it; for when both blueness and lotus-ness are present, the light of the lamp manifests only the lotus-ness.

If it is argued that—just as we observe a fixed principle such as the manifestation of only "water-ness" (and not "whiteness") when the water of one well remains within another well, and thus the diversity of the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor is established here as well according to observation—it is not so.

Even regarding manifestation (*abhivyakti*), the previously mentioned defects would not fail to apply to the alternative options of its being either eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, what is this manifestation? If it is cognition (*jñāna*), then the conjunction of the staff, the wheel, and other factors would result in being the cause of the cognition of the jar; consequently, in the absence of that [conjunction], the arising of the cognition of the jar would never occur anywhere. If it is the suppression of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), then what is that obscuration suppressed by it? If you say it is the state of a lump existing previously in the clay—no.

If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the state of the jar even after the blow of the hammer that destroys it; for the state of the lump (piṇḍāvasthā), which serves as its veil, would have been concealed at that time. [Objection: But at that time, the state of the potsherds (kapālāvasthā), manifested by the blow of the hammer, is the veil [of the jar]; for it is accepted that any effect-state manifested by its own cause serves as a veil for all other effect-states residing within it.

And this being the case, there is no contingency of the manifestation of the state of a jar occurring at some time within the shards when the causes of the jar are assembled, for that is exactly what we accept. Furthermore, by pulverizing the shards and applying the operations of mixing with water and clay, and kneading, one brings about softness.

If it is argued that this is because the manifestation of a jar is observed upon the conjunction of the rod, the wheel, and other factors; and that one should not suspect that the state of being a cloth is never seen again in the case of the causes of a burnt cloth—since the manifestation of their state as cloth is observed through the gradual transformation of the fruits of the cotton trees grown from the earth where their ashes have fallen, and subsequently—we say: not so.

Likewise, regarding the existence of states such as the jar within states such as the lump of clay, since there is no basis for postulating that they are unperceived at that time or that the perceived states of the lump and so forth act as their concealment, it is logical to establish the states as adventitious according to experience. Otherwise, the distinction between the perception and non-perception of states—whereby only a particular state is ever experienced while other states are not—would be untenable.

For manifestation is not something obtained through the self-choice of experience, whereby one could establish a fixed rule such that there is experience of the state of a lump of clay prior to the conjunction of the staff, wheel, and other factors; of the state of a jar immediately thereafter; and of the state of shards immediately after the falling of the mallet, and so forth.

Nor can the status [of these stages] be established by asserting that the application of water, the softening of the clay, and so forth; the staff, the wheel, and so forth; and the striking with a mallet are the instruments for the experiences of the states of the lump, the jar, and the shards, or for the non-experiences of those other respective states. This is because, even after the conjunctions of the aforementioned respective causes have passed, there persists the experience of the states such as the lump and the non-experience of the states opposed to them.

Therefore, it is logical to accept the established order according to experience: first, the state of the lump alone; in the middle, the state of the jar alone; and thereafter, the state of the shards alone. If it is argued that since states are adventitious, this would entail the doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the effect being non-existent [in the cause]), and thus this [doctrine of manifestation] is postulated as a remedy for that—[we reply: why does that [doctrine of non-existence] not follow if manifestations themselves are adventitious? Furthermore, if manifestations are also eternal, how can the established order you have described be established in any way?

Thus, since those respective manifestations or states are adventitious, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) remains beyond refutation; consequently, the acceptance of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) with respect to the substance alone would be purposeless.

Just as one observes the uncontradicted usage of difference between the agent and the action in such cases as "the pot was made by the potter" (*kulālena ghaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) and "the earring was made by Kalāda" (*kalādena kuṇḍalaṃ kṛtam*), so too one observes the uncontradicted usage of difference between the inherent cause and the effect inhering in it, as in "the pot was made from a lump of clay" (*mṛtpiṇḍena ghaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) and "the earring was made from gold" (*suvarṇena kuṇḍalaṃ kṛtam*). Therefore, it is logical to accept a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) between cause and effect, characterized by a difference in state (*avasthābheda*). If it is argued that the usage of difference is sublated by the usage of non-difference—as in "the pot is clay" (*mṛdghaṭaḥ*) or "the earring is gold" (*suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalam*)—we say no.

Since the properties of "earth-ness" (*mṛttva*) and "gold-ness" (*suvarṇatva*) are universals (*jāti*) residing in both parts and the whole, their usage [as such] is justified; therefore, it is impossible for that [usage] to subvert the conventional usage of difference. For this very reason, where a universal such as "thread-ness" (*tantutva*) resides in the parts but not in the whole cloth and so forth, there is no such conventional usage as "the threads are the cloth."

Therefore, since it is logical that there is indeed a distinction between the substance of cause and effect based on their co-existence—and because in the world one observes a rule of distinction between cause and effect—it would be impossible for Brahman to be the cause of the world if the world were non-different from Brahman; thus, the claim that there is a "harmonious convergence" (*samanvaya*) upon Brahman as the cause of the world does not hold. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

The non-difference from that means the very non-difference of the world from Brahman, the supreme cause; this is established by the words beginning with "originating" (*ārambhaṇa-śabda*) and so forth. Thus, in the *Chāndogya*: having introduced the subject with "There was once Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi; his father said to him," and then, after the father has instructed him, saying, "Śvetaketu, dwell as a religious student (*brahmacarya*); for, my dear, no one in our family has ever returned without having studied the Vedas, lest he become like a kinsman of a Brahmin [in name only]," the text describes his departure to the teacher's house and his return after staying there for twelve years.

Having said, "When he has reached twenty-four years of age, let him return," the father—perceiving the pride rooted in his son's study of the Vedas, desiring to remove that pride, and wishing to arouse in him the desire to know Brahman (brahmajijñāsā)—questioned him in this manner, as it is told: "Are you so conceited? Did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? The meaning is: "by which [instruction], when heard, thought, and known. This is because of another scriptural passage: "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known."

Thus, having kept in mind that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause and that the effect is non-different from its cause, and once it was proposed that through the knowledge of Brahman there is the knowledge of everything, the son—unaware of the intended meaning and thinking, "How can the knowledge of one thing result in the knowledge of another?"—asked, "How indeed, O Venerable One, is the instruction [to be understood]? To which the father spoke a worldly illustration regarding the non-difference of the effect from the cause in order to establish his own proposition; this has been described.

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay might be known"—the meaning is that just as jars, bowls, and so forth, which are produced from a single lump of clay, are not substances distinct from it, they are known through the knowledge of that [lump].

In this context, having raised the objection—based on the Vaiśeṣika method—that the effect is a distinct substance from the cause due to differences in cognition, designation, and so forth, the remainder of the passage, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," is intended to establish the non-difference of the effect from the cause through common worldly experience. Its meaning is as follows: *ārambhaṇam* means that which is grasped, touched, or handled. The letter *ra* is used for *la*, as in the verse "He beheld the center of the stream," because there is no distinction between *ra* and *la*. Here, *ālambha* signifies touching.

For the authors of the *Kośa* state: "The roots *ālabh*, *spr̥ś*, and *hiṃs* [take the accusative]. Here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The word "by speech" (*vācā*) means by the cause that is the practical activity (*vyavahāra*), such as fetching water preceded by the sentence "Fetch water with a jar. By the word "speech," the practical activity itself is also included through the figure of speech known as *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication). The third case ending in "by speech" (*vācā*) denotes the cause, as in the expression "He dwells for the purpose of study" (*adhyayanena hetunā vasati*), where the purpose is intended to function as the cause.
