For the sake of establishing linguistic usage preceded by speech, a specific configuration consisting of modifications such as broad base and large belly is touched upon by means of the substance clay itself, and the name "jar," which is prompted by that [configuration], is applied. According to the rule "The neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter, and optionally takes the singular number," the word *ārambhaṇa*—which resides in both the modification and the name—is treated as neuter and put in the singular.

For the sake of accomplishing specific worldly transactions such as fetching water, the substance of clay itself undergoes different states and acquires different names. Therefore, even things like a jar are truly and authoritatively nothing but clay, and not a separate substance. By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "from the words regarding origination and so forth," scriptures such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth,'" which establish the non-difference between the effect and the cause—the world and Brahman—are included.
And thus, although according to the perspective of a child and an elder...

Cognitions, different words, and so forth, are accounted for by differences in state (*avasthābheda*), just as a jar, a golden ornament, and the like are accounted for by differences in substance (*dravyabheda*). Indeed, the difference in substance alone would provide the ultimate consistency. Nevertheless, since the scripture, citing examples such as clay and the jar to demonstrate the non-difference between cause and effect, shows that there is only a difference in state, one must accept that cognitions, different words, and so forth, are caused solely by differences in state. Nor is it a fault to claim that states are adventitious (*āgantuka*), as this does not entail the fallacy of the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*).

Indeed, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the arising of a substance that already exists; it does not mean, however, that even its various states (*avasthā*) are non-accidental. Nor is it untenable for a substance that already exists to arise. For we do not accept that "arising" means coming into being after having previously been non-existent. Rather, arising is the production of a different state, while destruction is the relinquishing of the previous state. And thus, in the case of jars, bowls, and so forth, which are produced from a single lump of clay, there occurs the attainment of a state of multiplicity through the relinquishing of the state of oneness.

In a cloth produced from densely packed threads, there occurs the attainment of the state of unity through the abandonment of the state of multiplicity. Therefore, in a cloth produced from loosely arranged threads, even when the state of unity belonging to the cloth is attained, there is no abandonment of multiplicity—just as the thread-ness [of the threads] remains; rather, multiplicity persists as delimited by the nature of being threads (tantutva), while unity is attained as delimited by the nature of being cloth (paṭatva). Such specific distinctions should also be understood in accordance with observation.

Now, it has been explained that by the scriptural text, "It is only clay that is real," which means that the jar, the bowl, and so forth are established as being nothing but clay and not as distinct substances, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has also been shown regarding the non-difference of the substance of the effect from its cause. If one asks what that other means of valid cognition is, we reply: it is the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*). For even while the state of the lump of clay exists, the existence of the substance of the jar, the bowl, and so forth is perceived through the perception of recognition.

The recognition is observed that "all this—the jar, the bowl, and so forth—was previously nothing but a lump of clay," meaning that the single mound of clay existing in the forenoon was in the form of these jars, bowls, and the like. Now, one might object that in common worldly usage it is also seen that "all this—the jar, the bowl, and so forth—did not exist in the forenoon. Even in the Śruti, the non-existence of the world prior [to creation] is designated: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat)."

If it is asked how the establishment of the non-difference between cause and effect in both the world and the Veda is proven by direct perception and scripture, it is replied: this designation of "non-existent" refers to that other property of subtlety which is the opposite of the grossness found in things such as the broad base and belly [of a jar]; it does not, however, mean that the effect was entirely non-existent prior [to its production].

Why? Because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) in the Śruti. For in the passage, "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing whatsoever," there is heard a supplementary statement—"That [non-existent] thought, 'May I be,' and so it became"—which establishes that the non-existent possesses a mental volition (*manaskāra*) known as *saṅkalpa*. Even in common worldly usage, it is understood through reasoning that the designation "non-existent" is applied for that very reason; for nowhere does there exist such a thing as "non-existence" apart from the absence of those specific qualities that are its opposites.

Since it is sufficient for the conventional usage of "non-existence" (*abhāva*) to have as its basis simply another established positive entity (*dharma*) that is opposed to the object to be negated—just as in the case of the absence of something to be imagined—it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate non-existence. Furthermore, because there is another word in both common parlance and the Veda that serves as the antithesis to the designation "non-existent" (*asat*), such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*), and "This [world], consisting of jars, bowls, and so forth, in the morning..."

It is understood from such statements as "the clay alone existed" that the designation of non-existence is weaker than the designation of existence—which culminates in the non-difference between cause and effect—due to its lack of supporting reasoning (*yukti*). Indeed, the reasoning previously set forth was that one should not postulate a separate entity called "non-existence" distinct from the properties of a contradictory state of being; just as the threads themselves, apart from their interwoven state, do not constitute a separate composite substance called a "cloth."

For if it were devoid of color and so forth, it would follow that it lacks visibility and other such qualities; whereas if it possessed a different color and so forth, there would follow the perception of a separate color in the whole distinct from the colors of its parts, as well as a doubling of its weight.

Just as there is the state of a cloth from threads that are interwoven, and just as there is the state of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth from the single wind through its various functions within the body, so too the existence of the world in its diverse forms of moving and non-moving things is possible from Brahman alone; therefore, one should determine that by this reasoning as well, the designation of "Being" (sat) possesses greater force than the designation of distinct entities, and thus no real difference between things need be postulated. Furthermore, common usage such as "a ring was made from gold" must be explained solely through the relation of cause and effect produced by a difference in states.

Otherwise, if gold were weighed and given to a goldsmith to be made into an earring, and after he had fashioned the earring, it would have to be returned by him upon weighing again with a double weight due to its increased heaviness. Therefore, because there is no difference between the lump of clay and the jar, bowl, and so forth, by that example, there is non-difference between Brahman and the world, which stand in the relation of material cause and effect.
The Summary Verses.

The diversity of effects from their causes—due to distinctions such as intellect (*buddhi*), word (*śabda*), form (*ākṛti*), fruit (*phala*), enumeration (*gaṇanā*), cause (*hetu*), time (*kāla*), and so forth—is not a permanent difference; rather, that diversity arises from a change of state (*daśābheda*). For indeed, many states, characterized by existence, non-existence, and so on, arise for a single entity through various causes at different times. Thus, this entire world is indeed non-different from Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the originative material cause (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa).
On account of the designation of [the Self] as other [than the Lord], there would follow the defects of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. (21)
Moreover, because of the teaching of distinctions. ||22||
And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is untenable. ||23||

The introductory connection (*saṅgati*) is by way of an objection: if Brahman were the creator of the world without being distinct from it, defects such as His failure to act for the benefit [of others] would follow; and the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is this: the status of Brahman as the cause—characterized by the subtle *cid-acit* (sentient and insentient) manifold—and as the effect—characterized by the gross *cid-acit* manifold—is not established by the example of the lump of clay, the jar, the bowl, and so forth.

It should not be said that non-difference is stated only between Brahman and its effects and causes, and not between Brahman and the world; for since Brahman is the cause of all, its causality must necessarily be affirmed even with respect to the world—which is its own specific effect—consisting of the sentient and the insentient.

Consequently, since non-difference from that [Brahman] must also be asserted for the individual soul (*jīva*), it follows that Brahman—which is omniscient and omnipotent—though perceiving the *jīva* as non-different from itself, creates a world that is not beneficial to it, but rather creates a world that is indeed harmful. Thus, defects such as "failing to act for one's own benefit" would attach to Brahman itself. Therefore, the claim that Brahman creates a world that is non-different from itself is untenable. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Brahman is superior to the individual soul (jīva) and is indeed distinct from it, because of scriptural indications of difference such as: "He whose desires are true and whose resolves are true," "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord," "The Cause, the Lord of the lords of the senses," and "The Illusionist (māyī) creates this universe from this [Cause], while another, bound by illusion, is confined within it. However, the scriptural texts concerning non-difference refer to the state of being non-separate; for the phenomenal world, consisting of the sentient and the insentient, exists as a mode of Brahman that is nonetheless distinct from it.

In the scriptural passage beginning with "sadeva," the subsequent statement "all this was then Being alone" (idaṃ sarvaṃ sadevāsīt) indicates through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) that the world, in its subtle state, is qualified by Brahman denoted by the word "Being. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the description of Brahman’s resolve to become manifold, expressed as: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

By demonstrating that [the world] possesses the status of being a qualification of That (Brahman) during its state of grossness, it is understood that the world never exists as something separate from Brahman; therefore, even the clay, the jar, the bowl, and so forth, serve as examples for non-difference insofar as they consist in non-separateness. This is because it is impossible for anything to ever exist separately from itself, which is non-different from it.

Nor should it be argued that the scriptural texts concerning non-difference, such as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "That thou art," have as their primary object the essential identity [of the self with Brahman], whereas the scriptural texts concerning difference have as their object a figurative difference based on the distinction between various attributes; for if that were so, one would fail to avoid the very defects already mentioned, such as the failure to perform what is beneficial, and because it is impossible for individual souls—whose qualities are utterly fit to be abandoned like stones, wood, or clods of earth—to be identical with Brahman, who consists solely of faultless, auspicious qualities.

Therefore, it is logical that the scriptural passages concerning non-difference, such as those stated in the sūtra beginning with "Because of the subsistence [of the world in Brahman], thus [says] Kāśakṛtsna," have as their object the relationship between a substrate and its mode in which they are not separate.
Summary Verses.

In this way, since individual souls (*jīvas*) are necessarily non-different from Brahman according to such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), one should not perform creation devoid of Him.

To this [the opponent] says: "Not so; the statement does not intend to express that non-difference, because we observe the mention of difference; rather, it is taught as existing within Him. This is the position of Kāśakṛtsna.
Thus ends the section concerning designation by the other.
"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [all-pervading] because we observe its withdrawal [from one body to another], we say no; for it is like milk. (2.3.24)
And also like gods and others in the world. ||25||

Because of the mention of distinctions such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpa*), the scriptural texts concerning non-difference (*ananya*) refer merely to the state of being non-separate. It is not the case that, even though [Brahman] possesses true resolve and all powers, the scriptural texts regarding Brahman’s being the material cause (*upādāna*) and the creator (*sraṣṭṛ*) of the world can be justified if it were accompanied by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For even a capable agent does not produce an effect if devoid of auxiliaries; thus, there is a subordinate connection (*antarasaṅgati*) arising from this objection.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: By the restrictive statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," Brahman is indeed heard in scripture to be devoid of all auxiliary causes prior to creation. How then could it attain the status of being the cause of the universe? Nor can any distinction be made on the basis of its possessing all powers; for even a potter, who possesses the power to produce pots and the like, produces them only by depending upon auxiliary causes.

Thus, if Brahman is also capable of producing all effects, it must produce those various effects only by depending upon auxiliary causes appropriate for each respective effect. For a potter, though he possesses the power to produce a jar, does not produce it without depending on auxiliary causes. One who lacks power does not produce it even when auxiliaries are present; this indeed is the distinction between the powerful and the powerless. Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that Brahman, devoid of auxiliary causes, cannot be the cause. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

Even in the absence of auxiliary causes, Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe and its creatorship are both established, just as milk attains the state of curd, or as gods, sages, and others create the means for their respective enjoyments. Furthermore, in the transformation of milk into curd, neither heating nor churning serve as auxiliary causes; likewise, there is no auxiliary cause whatsoever for Brahman’s status as the material cause of the universe.

Furthermore, for gods and others who have attained sovereignty through the power of yoga and thus possess mastery over the elements (*bhūta-vaśin*), the status of creator is possible by means of elements drawn forth by their own volition. If it is argued that the Lord, being eternally established, does not possess such a power of yoga that brings about mastery over the elements—this is not so. Even without heating or churning, milk indeed becomes curd after a long time; however, there is a need for those two [processes] for the sake of a rapid transformation into curd and for the sake of a specific flavor.

The attainment of lordly power (*aiśvarya*) through the practice of yoga is to be understood from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of the mantras in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts. Furthermore, there is no distinction [between the yogin and Brahman] insofar as even Brahman is a creator by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), as there are indeed such explanatory passages regarding Him.

Moreover, it is observed that everyone causes their own body to act by mere volition; since the entire world is the body of Brahman, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in His presiding over the activity of the world.
The Summary Verses.
How could that which is singular and devoid of auxiliary causes at the outset become the world by way of being its material cause?
And how could it create [the world] through mere volition? Understand this to be like the case of milk and the like, or as with the gods and others.
Thus ends the section concerning the observation of reabsorption (*upasaṃhāradarśana*).
Either there would be the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness. 26.
But on account of scripture, because [the knowledge of Brahman] has its root in the Word. ||27||
And likewise in the self; for indeed, they are manifold. ||28||
And because of the defects in one's own position. ||29||
And she is endowed with all [qualities] through the sight of him. ||30||
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered. ||31||

If, by the analogy of milk, Brahman undergoes the state of becoming the world, then it would follow that Brahman also undergoes the state of becoming the world in its entirety, just as milk becomes curds in its entirety; this constitutes the objection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*). As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): does Brahman transform into the form of the world in its entirety, like milk transforming into the form of curds?

Or does it transform only in certain parts used for various effects, like a lump of clay joined with fire transforming only in one part used for making a seal-ring and so forth? It cannot be the first case, because the entire Brahman would become the world, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that no Brahman remains.

Nor should it be argued that in the position where Brahman qualified by the subtle *cit* and *acit* manifold is the cause, and Brahman qualified by the gross *cit* and *acit* manifold is the effect, there is no consequence of the defect of leaving nothing of Brahman remaining, because Brahman exists in the form of the effect; for it must be stated that Brahman exists even now in its causal form as well. Otherwise, there would follow the futility of those scriptural passages which teach the eternal existence of Brahman as the cause, as well as those which enjoin the knowledge (*vidyā*) that is the means to its direct realization.

Furthermore, since the causality of Brahman, which is the material cause of everything, must also be asserted with respect to its constituent parts characterized as conscious and unconscious, the following objection becomes as unassailable as a diamond coating: if the entire Brahman were to transform into the nature of one effect, there could be no transformation into the nature of other effects, nor could there be any remaining Brahman as the cause. Therefore, the first position is not tenable. Nor is the second position tenable. If it is argued that because it is impossible for a partless entity to undergo transformation in only one part, it must therefore be admitted that Brahman has parts, we say: no.

Because this would entail a contradiction with scriptural passages such as "partless, actionless, and tranquil," which describe [Brahman] as being without parts; therefore, it is not tenable that Brahman is the material cause of the world. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

There is no room for such doubt, because the Śruti itself explicitly teaches that Brahman, though partless, transforms into the form of the world while remaining as before, perfectly complete in itself. Furthermore, a matter established by the Śruti cannot be undermined by fallacious reasoning; for the Śruti declares: "This wisdom is not to be attained through ratiocination. If it be argued that even the Śruti is incapable of teaching something that contradicts other means of valid knowledge—just as in the case of stones floating on water—the answer is no.

Because Brahman is to be known solely through the Word (śabda), it is distinct from that [empirical reality]. For even the Śruti does not teach anything contradictory regarding an object that is accessible to perception and other means of knowledge; however, an object that is to be known exclusively through the Śruti is established precisely by the Śruti. It cannot be sublated by any other means of knowledge incapable of having that as its object. Indeed, the ear, which is incapable of apprehending color, cannot sublate it. Furthermore, in the case of the individual self (jīvātman), agency, enjoyership, and so forth—distinct from the attributes of the non-intelligent—are admitted.

In this way, why should there not be attributes in the Supreme Self that are distinct from the attributes of consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit)? In the world, even fire, water, and so forth are seen to be diverse by virtue of heat, cold, and other qualities; indeed, they are not accepted as being devoid of mutually distinct attributes merely because of the analogy of one with another. Nor is it the case that "the universal (jāti) exists in the individual (vyakti) neither partially—because it is partless—nor by pervading it entirely."

"Because it would follow that [the universal] is absent in other individuals"—thus, by means of the dilemma regarding whether it subsists in its entirety or in part, the subsistence of the universal (*jāti*) in the individual (*vyakti*) is refuted. Furthermore, this same objection applies equally to the Sāṃkhya's own position: how can *pradhāna*, which is partless, be the originator of diverse effects such as the "Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth? If it is argued that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are its constituent parts (*avayava*), we say no.

If one were to admit that those parts exist apart from Pradhāna, it would contradict the established number of twenty-five principles; furthermore, those parts too could not initiate the production of Mahat, Ahaṅkāra, and so forth, because of the dilemma regarding whether they produce them as a whole or by parts. This same difficulty applies to those who maintain atoms and other such causes, for their production of dyads and the like is untenable due to the dilemmas concerning conjunction as a whole or by parts.

Therefore, for one who considers even the postulated *pradhāna* to be beyond the scope of the dilemma regarding whether it exists as a whole or in part, what hope can there be that Brahman—established by scripture—is subject to such a dilemma? Furthermore, because Brahman is endowed with all powers (*sarvaśaktyupetavat*), its transformation into the form of the diverse world is possible even though it is partless, just as it is on the authority of scripture. For Brahman is indeed endowed with all powers, as seen in such scriptural passages as: "His power is declared to be truly manifold."

Even among those possessing limited power—the sentient and insentient entities within the phenomenal world—a manifold and inconceivable variety is observed; how then could this not be the case for the One who possesses all powers? Now, it may be argued that even for those possessing power, the manifestation of that power is seen to depend upon instruments and bodies; therefore, [how can there be power] independently of such things? Even so—

If it is argued that possessing all powers (*sarvaśaktimattva*) is not dependent on study—just as possessing intellectual power (*dhīśaktimattva*) is not a sufficient cause [for omniscience]—the answer to this has already been stated: An entity whose sole authority is the Word (*śabda*) must be accepted exactly as the Word describes it. It cannot be rejected merely because it lacks causes observed in the world. And thus says the Śruti: "He who is handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper; who sees without eyes and hears without ears; for whom there exists no activity nor instrument; and than whom no one equal or superior is seen."

"For His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed; knowledge, strength, and action are inherent. Therefore, it is entirely logical that Brahman, although partless, transforms itself into the form of the universe and remains fully complete in that very state, as established by scripture and supported by the reasoning shown therein.
These are the summary verses.

If Brahman were to undergo transformation in its entirety, then nothing would remain; nor could it do so in part, because it is partless. This same objection applies equally even to the specific position [of the opponent].
Such defects would apply to the Pradhāna, to atoms, and so forth;
but not to Brahman, who is established by hundreds of scriptural texts and endowed with manifold powers.
Thus concludes the section concerning the consequence of the whole [of Brahman] being affected.
Not so, because it possesses a purpose. ||32||
But as in the world, it is mere sport. ||33||
[The Lord's] inequality and cruelty [are not faults], because He takes [other factors] into account; for thus [the scripture] shows. ||34||

If it be argued that [the distinction between soul and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of action, we say no; for it is justified by beginninglessness, and it is both logically established and perceived. ||35||
And because all phenomena arise. ||36||

Even though the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been established by refuting defects such as the over-extension (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) through scripture supported by reasoning, the establishment of its status as the creator (*sraṣṭṛtva*) is not yet possible. This constitutes the transition [of the topic] because of the rule that the activity of an intelligent being must have a purpose. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: Is the creation of the world by Brahman for its own sake or for the sake of others? It cannot be the first, because Brahman has attained all desires and thus lacks any required purpose.

Nor should it be suspected that even for discerning people, the perception of games such as ball-play is seen to be purposeless; for even in those intent on play, there exists a momentary joy arising from it. Furthermore, one should not postulate a similar motive for Brahman even in the creation of the world, because that would contradict the scriptural testimony that [Brahman] has attained all desires. If it is objected: "But the activity of kings who have attained all their desires is also seen in games such as ball-play"—we say: no.

For even those who have attained all desires through the enjoyment of various objects still engage in that [creation] solely for the sake of obtaining the joy of playful sport (*krīḍā*), which they have not yet attained. However, it is impossible to say this regarding Brahman. Furthermore, if Brahman were to immerse living beings in the suffering of *saṃsāra* for its own purpose, it would follow that Brahman is both partial (*vaiṣamya*) and cruel (*nairghṛṇya*). Moreover, its "play" (*līlā*) would be comparable to the play of Aśmaka and Sagara’s sons. By this, the second position—that creation is for the sake of others—is also refuted.

For if creation were for the sake of another (the Supreme Being), He would surely create all beings as happy alone; He would not create some happy and others miserable through partiality and inequality. Furthermore, if He created miserable beings, the charge of cruelty would follow. Nor can it be argued that Brahman brings suffering upon the wicked merely to protect them by exhausting their karma—just as a physician inflicts the pain of burning and cutting on a wound merely to protect the patient.

Just as a physician who is unable to bring about the healing of a wound without first causing pain, burning, and so forth, is considered guilty even though he inflicts that suffering, it is likewise impossible for Brahman—who possesses all powers and is capable of protecting beings without causing them suffering—to inflict such suffering. Nor should it be argued that the faults of partiality and cruelty do not attach to the Creator of this unequal creation because He takes those specific karmas into account.

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," thus it is heard that in the primordial creation, where only Brahman remains, there is an absence of karma; consequently, the objection regarding the contingency of partiality and cruelty due to an unequal creation at that time cannot be avoided. Therefore, it is argued that Brahman's status as the creator of the world is not tenable. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

True. The activity of a discerning person is indeed solely for the sake of a purpose. Here too, there certainly exists a purpose in the form of sport (*līlā*) for Brahman through creation, just as it does for a king or a child through dice-games and the like. For the venerable Parāśara has said: "All this is the sport of Hari; let it be understood that this perishable world is His play, like the activities of a playing child. And this being so, there is no contradiction with the fact that Brahman has attained all desires.

The capacity to obtain whatever one desires—that is, the attainment of all desires—is indeed common to everyone from the universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) downwards; it does not mean, however, that there is the constant attainment of every single desire. Otherwise, due to the unequal creation of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, varying according to differences in time such as cold and heat, the faults of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) would result, in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action. The inequality of the world is rooted in specific actions (*karma*); the Lord is merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta-mātra*) in its production, the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*), just as rain is the common cause for the growth of crops.

This is because it is accepted that the disparity regarding the greater or lesser quantity, such as rice or barley, is produced by the specific differences of the field, the seed, and so forth. As stated by the venerable Parāśara: "He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating those things to be created, since the powers of creation truly belong to the primary material causes (the *pradhāna*). Here, "powers of creation" refers to the actions of those things to be created.

And thus, when Brahmā observes the worldly dealings of his subjects and bestows specific favors according to their appropriate or inappropriate speech—just as a king does—there is no loss of his faultlessness; on the contrary, it would be a loss for him if he were to grant uniform favor to those who speak appropriately or inappropriately while all beings are created identically, just as it would be for a judge of legal cases. Nor should it be argued that because the state of unity was determined prior to creation, the absence of individual souls at that time implies the absence of their actions.

Because both the individual souls (*jīvas*) and the streams of their karma are beginningless (*anādi*), the determination of their oneness is intended to signify the absence of gross forms characterized by names and forms that would justify distinct designations. Therefore, although the souls and their karmas exist as beginningless entities, their state of non-division (*avibhāga*) is logically established. This beginninglessness of the souls and the streams of their creation is found in such scriptural passages as: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and "The Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before."

Since the stream of diverse creations is beginningless, it is likewise determined that the stream of diverse karmas, which serve as their cause, is also beginningless. Therefore, because all attributes necessary for Brahman’s status as the material cause and creator of the world are logically consistent with Brahman, whereas they are inconsistent with Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth—according to the arguments already stated and those yet to be presented—it is established that it is entirely reasonable to hold that Brahman is the fundamental cause of the world.
The Summary Verses.
There is no fruit whatsoever to be attained by one whose desires are fulfilled;
thus does the creative play proceed in the world, for those who are not inconsistent with the truth.
If He were for the sake of others, how could He ever create suffering for anyone?
Furthermore, the avoidance of action depends upon karma, and thus there would be no primordial creation.
This creation of the world by Brahmā is like a game of dice played by a king;
because it depends upon the necessity of karma, there is neither inequality nor cruelty.
And that [subtle body] exists even during the cosmic dissolutions, because the enjoyers of saṃsāra are beginningless;
for the scriptural determination "Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) refers to that state when [the subtle body] is not yet fit for differentiation.
All those factors that can fulfill the requirements of causality are possible in Brahman;
such completeness is lacking in Pradhāna and the other [causal principles].
Thus concludes the section concerning the possession of purpose.

Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled *Caturmatasāra*, composed by Appayadīkṣita— the son of the illustrious Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and a teacher of the glorious Advaita-vidyā, and a Kaustubha-jewel in the ocean of the lotus-like Bādarāyaṇa.
The first quarter.
Salutations to the illustrious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.
And because the origination [of the world] is not possible [through atoms], there is no inference [for the existence of a creator]; and because of [the nature of] activity. 1.1.18.
If it is argued that [the soul's movement] is like that of milk or water, [we reply] that this is also the case there.
And because there is no stability in their distinction, and because they are independent. ||3||
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [it is] not like grass and so forth. ||4||
If it is argued that [the soul] is like a person and a stone, even so [the objection remains]. ||5||
And because the status of being a constituent part (aṅgin) is untenable. ||6||
And otherwise, in the case of inference, there would be an absence of the capacity for knowledge. ||7||
Even if [the existence of the object] were admitted, it would be because of the absence of an object. ||8||
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. ||9||

In the first chapter, the objections raised by the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others—who maintain that the cause of the world is *pradhāna* or atoms—by relying solely on mere logic (*kevalatarka*) against the doctrine that Brahman is the cause of the world, were refuted in the first *pāda*. Furthermore, the suspicion that those arguments might be acceptable due to the venerability of their authors was refuted in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* and the *Yogādhikaraṇa*. Finally, the suspicion regarding their acceptability based on a close examination of the nature of those specific arguments was refuted at the commencement of the *Navilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*.

Thus, although there is a difference in the intermediate subject matter between the first two sections and the eight subsequent sections beginning with the third, they possess a single purpose insofar as they aim to refute the arguments that reject the doctrine of Brahman; for in this pāda, the positions of the Sāṃkhyas and others, which rely on dry logic, are refuted by means of precisely such logic.

Otherwise, for those of dull intellect who establish the causality of *pradhāna* and other such principles, and who recognize that the opposing views are rooted in a mere semblance of reason, their faith in the doctrine of Brahman might falter due to the suspicion that those [opposing views] possess authority. Thus, while the first quarter (*pāda*) was intended for the establishment of one's own position, this quarter is for the purpose of refuting the opposing positions. Because the establishment of one's own position is of primary importance, it was performed first; hence, this follows immediately after it.

Although the establishment of one's own position through the removal of contradictions with scriptural texts concerning the scope of the effect (*kārya*) is also carried out in the third and fourth quarters, nevertheless, there is an intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) between the first and second quarters due to their shared subject matter regarding the cause (*kāraṇa*). Among those, because the Sāṃkhya doctrine possesses a greater degree of plausibility as a candidate for acceptance—due to its acceptance of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) and other principles sanctioned by the Vedas—it is refuted first.

The Sāṃkhyas establish their own doctrine through independent reasoning and interpret Vedic passages in accordance with that doctrine. The interpretation provided by them has been refuted in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* and other sections. Now, their independent reasonings are being refuted; thus, there is no tautology.

This is the system of the Sāṃkhyas: "The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. In this context, the root-nature is the state of equilibrium of the substances whose forms are the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. It is one, non-conscious in itself, intended for the enjoyment and liberation of all conscious beings, eternal, and omnipresent; it is a nature in its own right and is not a modification of anything.

From primordial nature (prakṛti) arises the Great One (mahat); from the Great One, the ego (ahaṅkāra); and from the ego, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these seven are evolvents (prakṛtis) with respect to their own effects and evolutes (vikṛtis) with respect to their own causes.

The sixteenfold group of qualities—consisting of the five great elements beginning with space, the five organs of cognition beginning with the ear, and the five organs of action beginning with speech—is exclusively a modification (*vikṛti*) and not the material cause (*prakṛti*) of anything else. The *puruṣa*, however, because it is unchanging, is not the material cause of anything; because it is eternal, it is not a modification of anything. Being devoid of attributes, having consciousness alone as its essence, all-pervading, and distinct in each body, it is neither an agent nor an enjoyer due to its lack of transformation.

Even though reality is thus constituted, the deluded, through the mere proximity of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, superimpose consciousness upon *prakṛti*. Consequently, due to the association with consciousness and the possession of the power of agency, there arises the state of being a knower. They further superimpose the agency of *prakṛti* itself—which has assumed the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—upon the *puruṣa*. Thus, through this mutual superimposition, experience consists of the conceit "I am the agent" and "I am the enjoyer"; liberation results from the knowledge of reality. Such are the twenty-five principles.

In that system, it is held that liberation results from the knowledge of the reality of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), which are considered to be the fundamental cause of everything. Since their entire doctrine is refuted by the rejection of the inference for the independent *pradhāna*—which is asserted to be the fundamental cause of all—it is this [inference] that is here being refuted. Their inference here is as follows: "Every effect has as its material cause a substance whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because it is permeated by them; as in the case of a jar and so forth, according to the universal pervasion."

In the first inference, substances consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion are established as the causes of effects; they resolve precisely into *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, because they possess that nature. This has been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "They consist of joy, displeasure, and despondency, and have the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint. The meaning of this is as follows: the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* consist respectively of joy, displeasure, and despondency—that is, they consist respectively of pleasure, pain, and delusion—and they have respectively the functions of illumination, activity, and restraint.

Sattva manifests clarity; the quality of rajas impels sattva toward its manifesting function. Since it follows that the light quality of sattva would cause activity everywhere due to its inherent mobility when joined with rajas, the heavy quality of tamas restrains it according to the specific effect required. Nor is the first reason unestablished, for it is well-known in the world that effects are permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion. To illustrate: a jar becomes pleasant for one who acquires it, because the quality of sattva arises in relation to him.

When that which belongs to one person is taken away by another, it becomes of the nature of suffering for the latter due to the emergence of the quality of *rajas*. For one toward whom there arises not even the perception of it through indifference, it becomes of the nature of delusion due to the emergence of the quality of *tamas*; for the verbal root [of *moha*] is *muha*, meaning "to become bewildered. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*) regarding the emergence of the qualities based on the distinction between different *puruṣas*, since their emergence is established by virtue of the specific purpose consisting of the experience of this or that particular *puruṣa*.

For example—just as *sattva* occasionally overcomes *rajas* and *tamas* with respect to something and attains its own tranquil state, so too *rajas* overcomes *sattva* and *tamas* and attains its own fierce state, and *tamas* overcomes *sattva* and *rajas* and attains its own deluded state. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) in the second inference by taking atoms and the like as the cause, because parsimony (*lāghava*) establishes that there is a single cause.

Nor does this lead to the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), such as an insentient entity consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion having Brahman as its material cause; for there is no room for establishing anything other than that which is not of such a nature as the cause of the entire collection of effects. Thus, the following inference is stated as a refutation of the Sāṃkhya inference of such a form: "Pradhāna is not capable of the construction of the world, because, while being insentient, it is not presided over by a conscious being; whatever is so [is like that], just as clay, wood, and the like, which are not presided over by a conscious being."

Nor is there a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it is logically impossible for that which is not presided over by a conscious being (*cetana*) to initiate an effect, and because it is observed everywhere that only that which is presided over by a conscious being engages in the commencement of an effect. Now, one might object: "In your established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished. It should not be argued that the *pradhāna* is established even in our doctrine, as it is established by the scripture (*śruti*) stating, "The Lord of *pradhāna* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Master of the qualities (*guṇa*). For that [scriptural entity] cannot be designated by the word "sūtra" (in the sense of an inference) derived from the root *sū* meaning "to infer," since it lacks the status of being accessible through inference.

If it is argued that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the probandum (*sādhya*), because even in the [Sāṅkhya] final doctrine (*siddhānta*), the capacity for the construction of the world is admitted for the Pradhāna; and that there is a non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason (*hetu*), because in that final doctrine, the existence of superintendence by a conscious being (*cetanādhiṣṭhāna*) is accepted—[we reply: True. However, since one must refute an opponent by means of the opponent's own method, this inference was stated while adopting the thesis and other elements established by the opponent. Alternatively, an inferential refutation in the form of a counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) against the opponent’s inference has been stated: if the Pradhāna were insentient and not superintended by a conscious being, it would be incapable of the construction of the world.

Alternatively, the qualificand portion of the reason (hetu) is construed as a qualifier of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) within the probandum (sādhya). Consequently, the formal structure of the inference is as follows: "Pradhāna is not a producer of effects when unguided by consciousness, because it is insentient, like clay, wood, and so forth, which produce jars, houses, and the like. Nor is there a fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi), since Pradhāna is not accepted as a subject established by inference.

The inference—"the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, together with primordial nature (prakṛti), are effects because they are products, like a jar"—can be accepted in our final position (siddhānta) because there is no contradiction; for independence is not included in the probandum (sādhya), since scripture is required only to establish that these [entities] are dependent upon the Lord. Now, it may be argued that there is no rule that an insentient thing acts only when presided over by a sentient being, for we observe that the milk contained in a cow flows out of its own accord for the sake of the growth of the calf.

If it is argued that just as water released from a cloud flows out of its own accord for the sake of increasing crops, so too the activity of *pradhāna*—though devoid of consciousness—is possible for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of the person (*puruṣa*), we say no. For even in the cases of milk and water, since they are insentient, their activity is impossible in the absence of a conscious controller; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule], because the case of milk and water is equivalent to the subject of the argument (*pakṣa*). By this, [the objection is refuted].

The transformation of grass and other substances consumed by a cow and so forth into milk and the like has also been explained. In that case as well, since the necessity of a conscious presiding agent makes the two cases equal, otherwise—if there were no regulating factor in the form of a specific conscious intention—there would be the undesirable consequence of grass and other substances consumed even by oxen and the like turning into milk. Furthermore, there is no difference in the cooking process when cow-dung and fire come together; for contact with fire alone is the cause of cooking, and that remains unchanged even when it occurs in conjunction with the digestive fire of an ox or similar animal.

In the world, it is observed that a specific result of cooking arises from a specific intention of the cook. Now, one might object: "This inference for the existence of a conscious controller is not a valid motivator; for just as a blind man, though endowed with the power of action, acts through proximity to a lame man endowed with the power of sight, and just as iron moves through proximity to the magnet-stone, so too the activity of *pradhāna* is possible through the mere proximity of the Person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is consciousness. [To this we reply: Even if such examples are adduced, regarding *pradhāna*—

The defect consisting in the impossibility of activity remains as it was. For instance, there is the case of a lame man who lacks the power of locomotion but is being carried by a blind man; there is his own observation of the path and his instruction regarding that path for the sake of the blind carrier. But for the Puruṣa, who is inactive, no such activity exists. Even if there were activity, since the necessity of being presided over by consciousness (cetanādhiṣṭhāna) would still apply, there is no deviation from the rule. Therefore, the inference of the defect is faultless.

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya inference itself is refuted by counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*). If the *pradhāna* undergoes transformation merely through the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of the *puruṣa*, then there would never be a dissolution (*pralaya*) distinct from creation, because the proximity of the eternal *puruṣa* remains unchanged at all times. Therefore, it must be accepted that the specific volitions (*saṅkalpaviśeṣa*) of the presiding Lord (*adhiṣṭhātṛ īśvara*) alone are the regulators of creation and dissolution. Nor should it be argued that merit and demerit (*dharmādharmāu*) themselves are the regulators thereof.

For *dharma* and *adharma*, as established by all the scriptures, consist precisely in the propitiation of the Puruṣa and its opposite; thus, in the absence of their acceptance [by you], they lack any means of coming into being. Furthermore, if one were to admit that the *guṇas* sometimes exist in a state of equilibrium, then—since there would be no basis for the predominance of the *guṇas* and consequently no relationship of primary and subordinate parts (*aṅga-aṅgin*)—there would be no production of the world caused by that [predominance]. Therefore, in the state of dissolution, when the *guṇas* exist in equilibrium, they cannot spontaneously enter a state of disequilibrium due to the absence of any activity of a Puruṣa who acts as their disturber.

Since the relationship of part and whole (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is impossible for those [qualities] that cannot attain [such a state], the creation of the world would never occur at any time. If, upon seeing the world in a state of inequality consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, one infers the triad of qualities (triguṇa) to be existing in a state of inequality according to its effects, then—given that the state of inequality established by the means of cognition apprehending the subject (dharmigrāhakamāna) exists eternally—there would necessarily be eternal creation.

If it should be argued that the triad of qualities (*triguṇa*) is inferred neither to be in a state of imbalance nor in a state of equilibrium—lest there be constant creation or dissolution—but rather, because of the existence of the persistence of two kinds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the root of the beginningless stream of creation and dissolution, it is inferred to possess a dual nature, partaking of both equilibrium and imbalance according to the predominance of the awakening of this or that particular impression; even this is not tenable.

Just as a blind man attains the status of a knower of the path through the proximity of a preeminent guide who points out the way, it has been stated that it is impossible for the *pradhāna* to become a knower through the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyāpatti*) due to its proximity to the inactive *puruṣa*. Furthermore, since such [knowing] is impossible, an insentient entity cannot engage in activity without being presided over by a conscious being. Moreover, if there were some purpose in the postulation of the *pradhāna*, we might somehow accept it; however, there is no purpose whatsoever.

It is held that the purpose of the *puruṣa* (the self) is indeed experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). Experience consists of the perception of pleasure and pain, and is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is a transformation of *pradhāna*. For the *puruṣa*, however, experience is the witnessing of that [intellect], occurring when it has attained a state of apparent identity with it through the reflection of the intellect upon it. Consequently, due to its failure to grasp the distinction from that [intellect], the *puruṣa* possesses a superimposed status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). Liberation, according to the Sāṃkhyas, is the cessation of this superimposition of enjoyership through the discriminative knowledge (*vivekakhyāti*) of that [distinction].

Furthermore, for the Puruṣa, whose nature consists solely of changeless consciousness, neither the false identification with the intellect (buddhi) which undergoes modifications, nor the witnessing of its experiences, nor the failure to perceive the distinction from it, is possible. But surely, by the Sāṃkhyas themselves, through the two activities of being an enjoyer and engaging in the means to liberation—which are impossible for non-conscious entities such as the intellect—the Puruṣa has been established as distinct from the intellect and so forth, and as one who engages in hearing and other such activities, according to the principle: "The Puruṣa exists because there must be an enjoyer, and because there is activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya)."

That the purpose of *prakṛti* is for the experience of the *puruṣa*, and that liberation (*apavarga*) occurs for the *puruṣa* at the very moment that the true nature of *prakṛti* is perceived—both of these points have been explained extensively in various ways: "By means of manifold methods, the helpful *prakṛti* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*, who is unhelpful [in return]; she, possessing qualities, acts for the sake of him who is devoid of qualities, yet her efforts are ultimately fruitless. Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after showing herself to the audience, so does *prakṛti* cease from her activity after manifesting herself to the *puruṣa*."

"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than Prakṛti; she, having been seen by the Puruṣa, ceases to appear to him again. Therefore, according to that system, the Puruṣa indeed possesses the status of an enjoyer of Prakṛti and the agency for performing hearing and other acts for the sake of perceiving her true nature. If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be an impossibility of purpose in that system? [the answer is: then, it is precisely because of the statement of mutually contradictory meanings.

That doctrine is inconsistent. For in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, it is elaborated at length that bondage and liberation belong to *prakṛti* alone, through such statements as: "Prakṛti, which has various substrates, is bound and liberated. Furthermore, by those very people who assert that when the cause of the world is established, it is established as one and only *prakṛti* on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is admitted that *prakṛti* is merely an aggregate of the three *guṇas*, and that there is no such thing as *prakṛti* distinct from them; for this reason as well, their doctrine is self-contradictory.

Having stated that there are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), it was further asserted that the *guṇas* are mutually distinct; this too is contradictory. For if the *guṇas* were distinct, there would be twenty-seven principles. Moreover, this has been shown to be a contradiction in meaning: it is not logical to postulate that pleasure, pain, and delusion inhere in the objects themselves simply because they possess qualities such as being covered by a cataract [or perceived erroneously]. Otherwise, since desire, aversion, and so forth arise in those who perceive silver, snakes, and the like [where none exist], one would have to conclude that the objects themselves also possess those qualities.

Furthermore, since objects are associated with pleasure, pain, and so forth, from what [source] is their cause established? It cannot be established as being due to pleasure, pain, and delusion. If it is argued that this is not so because qualities such as whiteness or "cowness" do not become causes by being inherent in the object—just as clay is the cause of a jar—we say no; for it is not established that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are substances (*dravya*). Indeed, *sattva* and the others are merely the qualities (*guṇa*) residing in substances such as earth, serving as the causes of lightness, illumination, and so on. For this very reason, they are well-known precisely as "qualities. Therefore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent both through mutual contradiction and through contradiction with the nature of its own categories.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world].
Or it is like the "large" and "long" [concepts] derived from the "short" and the "circular. ||10||
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] is non-existent. ||11||

The logical consistency of the analogy is established by the fact that the theory of atoms as the cause, being inferential, is refuted for the same reasons as the theory of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as the cause; namely, that it is untenable. While in the theory of *pradhāna* as the cause, the impossibility of formation arises due to the absence of the superintendence of a conscious agent because *Īśvara* is not admitted, this is not the case in the theory of atoms as the cause, since the Vaiśeṣikas do admit *Īśvara*. For this very reason, the defect of the impossibility of dissolution (*pralaya*) does not apply here either.

Furthermore, there is a connection by way of a counter-example, because it is possible to assert that at that time the Lord’s will in the form of a desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) is absent, since it is conditioned by the specific karma of living beings that brings about creation. This is the process of those who maintain the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇuvādin*): when the world has dissolved and the Lord’s will in the form of a desire to create arises due to the influence of the particular awakening of the karma of living beings, the first motion arises in the immobile, partless atoms. By that motion, two atoms conjoin.

A dyad (dvyaṇuka) is initiated by two atoms (paramāṇu) in conjunction; a triad (tryaṇuka) by three dyads, and so on, in this sequence the entire world arises. In that regard, first of all, the partlessness of atoms is untenable.

Just as two fingers, each delimited by ten spatial points (pradeśa) connected to the ten directions, when joined together, are conjoined with three points each by one great direction (mahādiś) and two intermediate directions (vidiś), thus being united on six sides; in the same way, the threads that constitute a cloth, while being joined together, are conjoined on six sides and, possessing seven sides each that are not so conjoined, [produce] a dimension greater than their own.

It is observed that one begins a cloth [from threads]. In the same way, atoms too must be joined on all six sides; otherwise, there would be no possibility of the magnitude (prathiman) of a dyad (dvyaṇuka)—which possesses a dimension greater than its own spherical measure (pārimaṇḍalya) and is minute and short—or of a triad (tryaṇuka), which is larger and longer than the dyad. Nor should it be argued: "Let there be no magnitude for the dyad from the atoms, but the magnitude of the triad from the dyad will arise due to the multiplicity of its causes"; this is not so.

If that were the case, there would follow the consequence of an absence of distinction between the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) as the size of an atom and the atomicity (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Furthermore, if the conjunction of two atoms were all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), it would entail that the dyad itself must be spherical. Moreover, for one who accepts the conjunction of two atoms as the producer of a dyad, those very atoms must have distinct spatial parts established by that conjunction; for two atoms, while conjoining, cannot both occupy the same location, and thus their distinct parts are thereby established.

For two atoms, even when conjoining, do not join while occupying the same location, because it is contradictory for corporeal entities to occupy the same space. Therefore, one must say that they join while situated in different locations—either by way of east and west, south and north, or above and below.

If that were the case, consider this: with what other atom situated in the same location as it is joined could a given atom be joined, even by one delimited by a different location? Or, if it cannot be so joined, how could there not be a distinction of spatial parts within that [atom]? Reflect upon this yourself.

[Objection: "But even if atoms are partless, it is possible to speak of a distinction of spatial divisions (pradeśabheda) obtained through their delimitation by various directions; from that alone, the conjunction of two atoms will possess spatial limitation (prādeśikatva), and there will be an increase in dimension (parimāṇotkarṣa) in the dyad. [Reply: This is not so—for, since there is no constituent part (aṃśa) in an atom that could establish that a conjunction with a specific direction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), it follows that such a conjunction must be pervasive (vyāpyavṛtti); consequently, it is impossible for that same conjunction to establish the non-pervasive occurrence of a conjunction with another atom.

For it is not the case that, as with the roots and tips of a tree which serve as the delimiters for the presence and absence of conjunction with a monkey, mere existence of some kind of delimiter-distinction can suffice when there is no fixed spatial delimiter.

It may be argued that the conjunction of two atoms is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). However, since all spatial conjunctions (*diksaṃyoga*) are equally pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), there is no determining factor here to establish that one spatial conjunction delimits the conjunction with another atom. Consequently, all spatial conjunctions would likewise result in being the delimitors of that [internal] conjunction. Furthermore, in the absence of a distinction among the delimitors, or even if some distinction were somehow obtained, the lack of a fixed location would render it impossible to establish their non-pervasiveness.

Otherwise, since earth possesses number, "substantiality" (dravyatva) would be its delimiting property (avacchedaka), and since it possesses odor, "earthness" (pṛthivītva) would be another; and because of the existence of such distinct delimiting properties, there would follow the undesirable consequence that number and the other qualities must be treated as non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). Therefore, for the sake of accounting for the conjunction that produces the dyad (dvyaṇuka), a distinction of parts in the form of spatial divisions (pradeśabheda) within atoms must necessarily be admitted. Likewise, for the sake of accounting for the conjunctions of the three dyads that produce the triad (tryaṇuka), that [distinction] must also be admitted.

For that conjunction between the body and the book must be accomplished by means of the conjunction between the hand and the book, just as the conjunction of a dyad with another atom that initiates a second dyad is accomplished; for you yourself have accepted the principle that "from the conjunction of cause and non-cause arises the conjunction of effect and non-effect."

Furthermore, when the conjunction of another atom that initiates it has already been established and remains in an atom that is currently breaking up a dyad (dvyaṇuka), how could there also be a conjunction with another dyad at the time of the production of the triad (tryaṇuka), in the absence of a distinction of spatial location? This is because of the contradiction of corporeal entities occupying the same location. If, however, one does not accept the restriction regarding the contradiction of corporeal atoms occupying the same location despite their corporeality, then a triad in the form of a mass composed of six atoms would be no larger than a single atom.

Regarding this, they say: "Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts; if the six were in the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom. The meaning is as follows: when a central atom is conjoined with six surrounding atoms situated in the directions of east, west, south, north, above, and below, that central atom must possess six parts, because the points of conjunction are distinct. Alternatively, if all these conjunctions occupy the same location, then the entire aggregate of them would result in a mass no larger than a single atom.

This same refutation applies equally to the production of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) from dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Therefore, even those proponents of atoms (*paramāṇuvādin*) who do not wish to accept that atoms have six parts (*ṣaḍaṃśatva*) must nevertheless admit it for the sake of establishing the production of dyads, triads, and so forth, as well as the resulting increase in dimension (*parimāṇātiśaya*). [Objection: But if that is admitted, then by the aforementioned reasoning, those very parts would also possess parts, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And thus, because there would be no difference in being composed of an infinite number of parts, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be equal in dimension.

If you argue that having parts (sāṃśatva) is therefore also unworthy of acceptance, then abandon this very obsession with the doctrine of atoms as a cause—which falls into error on both sides: for if they have parts, there is an infinite regress (anavasthā), and if they are partless (niraṃśatva), the production of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth becomes untenable; instead, be happy. Furthermore, there is no fault in atoms having parts, because even though Mount Meru and a mustard seed are both composed of infinite constituent parts, a difference in their dimensions is possible due to a specific difference in those infinities.

For indeed, there is no gradation of difference between the following: (1) the infinite regions delimited as being prior to the Padma-kalpa and posterior to the Vārāha-kalpa; (2) the infinite individual instances that serve as substrata for universals—both higher and lower—such as "substance-ness" and "earth-ness," which are themselves infinite; and (3) the infinite atoms contained within Mount Meru and Mount Mandara. Nor is there such gradation between the infinite space above the netherworld (pātāla) and the infinite space below the solar orb.

If, however, partlessness is not accepted for the atom—lest its having parts lead to the consequence of impermanence and thereby result in the failure to establish its status as the fundamental cause admitted by you—then the production of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, as well as their magnitude (*prathiman*), would be unavoidable. Therefore, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, the theory of atoms as the cause, being beset by one or another of these refutations—namely, the impermanence of the atom, the impossibility of producing dyads and so forth, or the impossibility of their magnitude—is simply to be rejected.

Furthermore, it must be admitted that during the dissolution (pralaya), when atoms are motionless, a conjunction cannot occur because action—which would produce the conjunction initiating the dyad (dvyaṇuka) at the beginning of creation—is impossible. Now, one might object: "It is accepted that 'the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)'; therefore, a conjunction is possible through action produced by the power of the unseen force. This is not so.

If that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were inherent either in living beings or in atoms, in either case it could not be the cause of that action. For if it were the cause of such action, then since it would exist even during the dissolution (*pralaya*)—having been acquired in a previous cycle—it would follow that actions would arise from it at that time as well, leading to the absurd consequence of the world being constantly created.

Now, on the occasion of commenting upon the collection of Akṣapāda’s sūtras beginning with “The cause [of the world] is God, because we see that human action is fruitful” (NS 4.1.19)—which aims to demonstrate the efficacy of both types of causes for the world: the unseen maturation of karma (*vipākādṛṣṭa*) and the Lord as the cause of action—the author of the *Vārttika* states: “We do not say that God is the cause independently of karma; rather, God favors the karma of the person. What is the meaning of this favor? It is that He brings about exactly what has occurred, for whom it is due, and at whatever time its period of fruition (*pākakāla*) arrives, then and in that very manner.”

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because [the scripture] teaches that [the *adṛṣṭa*] is "employed" (*viniyukta*), we say no; for just as with substances such as *harītakī*, there can be no ripening (*vipāka*) of the *adṛṣṭa*, which is a quality of the self. If it is argued that "ripening" is simply the arrival of the time for the fruit, and that this occurs precisely at the beginning of creation, we say no; for it is unauthoritative to maintain that the time for the fruit of the various *adṛṣṭas* produced by the non-simultaneous performance of ritual acts by infinite living beings is only at the beginning of creation, and that during the dissolution (*pralaya*)—which lasts for two *parārdhas*—there is not even a single moment [in which those fruits could arise].

Now, on the day that is the period of creation, when the various living beings who have been engaged in incessant coming and going have been made to enter a night of equal duration and have been led by the Lord’s will—desiring to grant them rest—to a great deep sleep, even those karmas whose time for fruition has arrived during the dissolution become obstructed in their power.

If it is argued that for this very reason, the fruit prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin—namely, the experience of torment for the duration of a *kalpa* immediately after the fall of that body, followed by the persistence of its marks such as consumption and leprosy in seven subsequent births—does not apply to a man who committed the murder of a Brahmin at a time immediately preceding the dissolution (*pralaya*), because his body has fallen away [at that point], we say no. For in your own view, the eternal will of the Lord exists even during the dissolution.

In my view, although at the time of dissolution there exist the previously established unseen merits and demerits (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings as well as the various wills of the Lord, there is an absence of creation because of the non-existence of those future wills of the Lord which take the form of the creative resolve for that specific time, such as: "May I become many, may I procreate," "I shall make each of these tripartite," and "I shall manifest name and form."

If it is argued: "In that case, at whatever time you maintain that the will of the Lord in the form of such a volition occurs, my desire to produce motion in the atoms will be the eternal will of the Lord conditioned by that very time," it is replied: I do not accept some such time for volition imagined merely by my own fancy; rather, [I rely on the scriptural testimony] beginning with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

The period consisting of a great night (*mahāśarvarī*) of two *parārdhas*—as established by the authority of the Vedas, their exegeses (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth—is accepted here. Nor is it possible for one who seeks to postulate the Lord and His activities such as creation through reasoning alone to maintain that during this time there was the resolve to become manifold, followed by the sequential creation of the elements, then the resolve for the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the tripartition itself, and finally the resolve for the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) and that differentiation, and so on.

It does not enter the path of reason. For the life-story of Rāma and the like, as established in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts, cannot be constructed by means of logical arguments. If the Śruti must be sought as a refuge regarding the Lord’s activities such as creation, which are delimited by specific times, then it is equally proper to seek that very same Śruti as a refuge regarding the Lord himself. Thus, the Lord should be accepted as a mine of infinite auspicious qualities according to the Śruti, performing the sport of worldly activity through various volitions arising at their respective times; however, one should not [reject] those portions within the Śrutis that are not favored by oneself.

Having abandoned [the other qualities], one must admit that [the Lord] possesses only eternal knowledge, desire, and effort, and is merely the agent of the activity of creation as he intends. Furthermore, the God inferred through logic has been refuted in the section on "The Scripture Being the Source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa). By that [section] as well, his status as creator—according to your intended process of producing motion in atoms—is effectively discarded. Therefore, because it accepts the theory of atoms as the cause [of the world] despite their lack of sensory perception, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is inconsistent. Likewise, it is inconsistent because of its acceptance of inherence (samavāya).

For inherence (*samavāya*) is postulated precisely to establish the inseparable connection (*ayutasiddhi*) among parts, qualities, actions, and universals that are themselves inseparably established; in that case, another relation must be required for inherence as well, since it is equally characterized by inseparable establishment. Thus, for each subsequent relation that establishes inseparable establishment, yet another relation would have to be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that inherence is accepted as having an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), like non-existence (*abhāva*) and so forth, then let that same [essential relation] suffice for the whole (*avayavin*) and the others as well.

[Objection: But surely, since the wholes and so forth are infinite, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), one single inherence (*samavāya*) that pervades all of them should be postulated. [Reply: No. For when both one and many are to be postulated, it is the postulation of one that is parsimonious; however, in this case, since many [inherences] are already established, why postulate even one? [Objection: Even if many are established, the property of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) must be postulated among them, and that cannot be postulated as a single entity.

Because a single, uniform relation that conforms to the nature of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth cannot be defined; and because it would otherwise require the postulation of an infinite number of relations, the postulation of a single inherence (*samavāya*) and a single relatedness residing therein is not possible. This is because a single, uniform relation conforming to the nature of the whole and so forth remains undefinable. If it is argued that this is simpler than postulating an infinite number of relations, we say no.

If it is argued that since the status of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) has already been established for wholes (*avayavin*) and so forth with respect to their respective absences (*tattadabhāva*), one need not postulate a relationhood defined by parts (*avayava*) and so on for those [wholes], and thus those [relations] are not to be postulated as infinite—this is not so. For if relationhood differs according to the difference in the relatum (*nirūpaka*), then even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), those [instances of inherence] would have to be postulated as infinite due to that difference, and inherence itself would also have to be postulated; thus, the position of inherence results in a greater complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is argued that, by encompassing parts, qualities, actions, universals, and their possessors through the relation of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*), one may postulate for *samavāya* (inherence) only a single relation defined by inseparable existence, we say no. For if such an encompassing allows for the postulation of a single relation among those very things, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to simply postulate a single relation rather than postulating *samavāya*. Furthermore, even if *samavāya* is accepted for parts and wholes and so forth, the acceptance of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) remains necessary.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the relationship between locus and located could not be established among parts and wholes and so forth, due to the absence of a specific inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" and similar instances must be accounted for by means of two distinct relations of essential nature (*svarūpasambandha*): one being the nature of being a locus as determined by the whole and so forth with respect to the parts and so forth, and the other being the nature of being a located entity as determined by the parts and so forth with respect to the whole and so forth. It is by means of these two relations of essential nature, which serve as the objects [of the cognition], that such a cognition is explained.

If that [inherence] were to be established through inherence itself, then since the inherence of color exists in air, the cognition "color is in air" would result. Therefore, since an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha) is necessary even in cases of inherence, and since the cognition of the relationship between locus and located can be accounted for by that alone, what is the use of inherence?
