By this, the statement in the Kaṇāda-sūtra—"Inherence is that from which [the notion] 'here' arises with respect to cause and effect"—is refuted.

Because the cognition "here" (ihapratyaya) necessarily has as its object two types of relations—namely, the relation between locus and located and the essential nature (svarūpa-sambandha)—the qualified cognition is fully accounted for by that alone. It might be argued: "It is true that in this Sūtra it was stated that the existence of inherence (samavāya) is established by its being the means for accounting for the aforementioned cognition; however, that 'being the means for accounting for it' is not intended here in the sense of being its object, because in his [the opponent's] view, inherence is not perceptible."

But [it may be argued that] whatever cause is established as the common ground for cognitions qualified by the activity of parts and so forth, by virtue of being their cause, is "inherence" (samavāya). This is not so; for since the cognitions qualified by parts and so forth are themselves not uniform, they have no need for a uniform cause, which would lead to the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of inherence to all qualified cognitions.

If it is argued that there is a unifying factor (anugama) consisting in being a qualified perception whose object is a pair of related things from which their distinctness is not very clearly distinguished—a definition that does not over-extend—then let the parts and the whole themselves, as characterized by that lack of very clear distinction, be the cause in those cases; what is the use of postulating *samavāya*? Furthermore, this stated nature of "qualified cognition" is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), as it applies to the qualified cognition of an absence and its locus, and even to the qualified cognition of the two supporting substances in the case of the cognition "the gold is yellow."

[Objection: Surely, since a single cause that is common to all specific perceptual cognitions—such as the cognition of "qualified by a staff" and so forth—is being postulated, and since it must exist everywhere due to its eternity and unity, it is established as *samavāya* (inherence) alone; for even without being an object (*viṣayabhāva*), it can serve as the cause in all those [cognitions]. [Reply: No, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible as the common cause. Indeed, in the case of specific perceptions such as visual ones, the respective conjunctions between the substance and the sense organ are already established as the causes.

Even in the case of the perception of sound, there exists a conjunction between the ear and the mind; let it be precisely these conjunctions that possess the causal status. Furthermore, since "being a qualified cognition" (viśiṣṭajñānatva) is the delimiting property (avacchedaka) of the effectness of the cognition of a qualifier, and "perceptuality" (pratyakṣatva) is the delimiting property of the effectness of the sense organ, [the former]—because it resides in an effectness that already possesses another delimiting property—is established by the force of the facts (arthavaśasampanna), just like "blue-pot-ness. Thus, "qualified perceptuality" is not itself a delimiting property of effectness; consequently, there is no requirement for a common cause delimited by that [qualified perceptuality].

If it is argued that, because the destruction of the threads and so forth entails the destruction of the qualities and parts residing in them, and since the property of "being the destruction of the whole residing therein" is not pervasive across all such cases, nor is the property of "being the destruction of what is related to it" applicable (as it would over-extend to the destruction of grass joined with those threads), therefore an inclusive relation—which, being established, results in *samavāya*—is proven; we say no. For even if *samavāya* were accepted, upon the destruction of the threads...

Because the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of the threads—which possess inherence—cannot be avoided; nor can "being inherent" in the sense of being a substratum (ādheyatva) be introduced as the delimiting property (avacchedaka) when inherence is present, for even so, the aforementioned consequence of the destruction of grass and other things resting on the threads remains unavoidable, since inherence is one and thus the inherence in the threads exists in the grass as well. Furthermore, it is more appropriate to introduce the unburdensome and already established "resting upon that which is inseparably connected" (ayutasiddha-ādheyatva) itself as the delimiting property of the effect.

And this being the case, it does not follow that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of the cloth’s destruction and so forth—which are inseparably established (ayutasiddha) with their substrates; for even on the opponent's view, the consequence of the destruction of universals (jāti) and the like inhering in the threads is equally applicable. If the rule is that "upon the destruction of the threads, the effect inhering in them is destroyed," then let the rule be: "upon the destruction of that [substratum], that which is inseparably established with it and is perishable is destroyed. Nor does anything undesirable result from the destruction of a destruction; for just as the antecedent negation (prāgabhāva) of a jar is destroyed when the jar arises, so too the destruction of that [destruction] is logically possible.

For, by accepting that both the destruction of the jar and [the destruction of its destruction] possess the nature of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and subsequent non-existence (pradhvaṃsa), one can establish the non-reemergence of the prior non-existence; and likewise, by accepting that the series of the jar's destructions possesses the nature of the jar's destruction, it is logically consistent to establish the non-reemergence of the jar.

Thus, since inherence (samavāya) is unestablished, its constituent property—being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva)—is also unestablished; consequently, the inference of dyads and atoms as the inherent causes of triads and dyads cannot proceed. For this reason as well, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is inconsistent. Furthermore, because inherence is admitted to be eternal, it must be admitted that its substrata are also eternal; otherwise, upon the destruction of the related entities, inherence would likewise be subject to destruction, just like conjunction (saṃyoga).

Furthermore, because you would have to assert that even the triad (tryaṇuka) is eternal on the grounds that it is the substratum of inherence (samavāya), the inference of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth as its cause remains unestablished for this reason as well. If it were argued that, due to parsimony (lāghava), the property of being a conjunction (saṃyoga) is the determinant for destruction by the destruction of the related term;

It is not the case that [the relation] lacks the status of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), for thus, by one who follows the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) even in the inference of the root cause of the world, the parsimony of unity must be followed; therefore, since neither Brahman nor Pradhāna is established by that [inference], atoms are not established by it. Nor should it be argued that parsimony is irrelevant here because the production of a single substance from one [cause] is impossible—given that the rule that an effect-substance is produced by the conjunction of its parts is observed in the case of cloth and the like.

Since there is no evidence for the hypothesis that milk begins to produce curd as a single composite whole—because that would violate the rule [of causal continuity]—and because the production of curd is established through the parts of the milk joining one another and subsequently attaining further conjunctions (just as the destruction of the milk is unperceived as a cause), it follows that this is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the milk due to the manifestation of different qualities; for the aphorisms of Akṣapāda, such as "not from the manifestation of other qualities," lack a foundation in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, even while the substance remains, [the change occurs] just as in the case of the atoms of earth.

Because the manifestation of a different quality is logically established; and because, since the causal complex consisting of the weaver’s activity and so forth is identical for both the conjunction of the threads and the cloth, they are produced at the same time, it is not accepted that the cloth is originated by the conjunction of the threads. Nor should it be argued that, since the destruction of the cloth is observed upon the destruction of the conjunction of the threads, and since the destruction of a non-cause cannot entail the destruction of its effect, one must assert a cause-and-effect relationship between the cloth and the conjunction of the threads—for the destruction of both may also be established as simultaneous due to the identity of their respective causal complexes.

Furthermore, if the root cause of the world were to possess color and other qualities, then its eternity and partlessness would be contradicted; for it is observed that things possessing color and other qualities are non-eternal and composite. Thus, because this [position] is refuted by the inference supported by reasoning—"The triad (tryaṇuka) has as its root cause something devoid of color and other qualities, because it is eternal and partless"—the existence of atoms as a cause characterized by color and other qualities is not established.

If it is argued that the reasoning (tarka) is of loose foundation because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*), then what subverting argument against the contrary case has been observed for the two inferences establishing the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*)—namely, "the triad (*tryaṇuka*) is originated by an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it is the originator of something large"—by which my inference would be weak and yours would be strong? Surely, there exists a subverting argument against the contrary case for the inference establishing the triad.

For instance, if magnitude (*mahattva*) is produced, the only operative factor is the mere inferiority (*apakarṣa*) consisting of a sub-class of magnitude; it is not two distinct sub-classes consisting of superiority (*utkarṣa*) and inferiority, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

And so, since the largeness (*mahattva*) of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) is of the nature of a subordinated largeness and is thus produced, it requires a cause. Given that for largeness, only specific numbers, dimensions, and conjunctions residing in the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its own substratum serve as the cause, the status of the triad as an inherent cause must necessarily be accepted. Thus, by the very method stated, there exists a reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) against the counter-example even regarding the pervasion rooted in reasoning: if color and the like were produced, then "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth would be the determining factor (*prayojaka*), because they are inclusive (*anugata*) and parsimonious (*laghu*).

But [this does not apply] to properties such as "being a color residing in an effect" (kāryagatarūpatva), because such properties are not co-present (ananugata) in the color and other qualities of earth-atoms, and because of their heaviness. Furthermore, if one accepts color in atoms, then according to your own view—that colors and other qualities not produced by contact with fire are produced by the color and other qualities residing in the causes of their own substratum—it follows that atoms must be established as having parts (avayava). This is because atoms would necessarily serve as the substrata for the colors and other qualities required for the production of the color of water-atoms and the blackness of earth-atoms. Thus, these atoms cannot be prevented from having parts.

Furthermore, since being composed of parts entails impermanence, you must necessarily accept that when color and other qualities are produced, the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth are the causal factors. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that color and other qualities could not be established in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), which are inferred to be the causes of triads (*tryaṇuka*). For in inferring the possession of color and other qualities in those [dyads], one must indeed rely on a reductio ad absurdum (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) based on the rule that qualities are invariably preceded by the qualities of their cause.

Furthermore, if magnitude (*mahattva*) were produced, it would be logical that a diminution of dimension (*parimāṇāpakarṣa*) is its cause; for this reason, the exclusion of the "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*) residing in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth is established. However, it is not a diminution of magnitude [that causes it], because [magnitude] is a specific form and because length (*dairghya*) is not universally concomitant [with all magnitudes]. Thus, if a diminution of dimension were admitted in the primary cause of the triad (*tryaṇuka*), then, since that [triad] is produced, the primary cause would necessarily possess parts (*sāvayavatva*) in relation to the dimension of its own cause. To avoid this consequence, one must admit that supreme magnitude itself resides in it.

Furthermore, there is no rule that an effect-substance must be produced from constituent substances of smaller dimensions; for we observe that a thread may be produced from long threads twisted into a more solid form, or from broad cloths of lesser length, or from cloths of lesser width. Therefore, the inference for a primal cause of the world is set aside by a stronger counter-argument, just like the inference for [the existence of] color and other qualities.

Likewise, if, in order to avoid [the charge of] impermanence and so forth, it is asserted that atoms are devoid of color and other qualities, then the rule that the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their cause would be unestablished. And if, for the sake of establishing that rule, one accepts that they possess color and other qualities, [then the aforementioned faults remain].

Since it entails the consequence of impermanence and other defects, the atomic theory of causation is flawed in both ways; thus, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is inconsistent. Therefore, although the Sāṃkhya position is contrary to scripture and reason, there is partial acceptance of it by the Vedists in certain respects, such as the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda). However, since no part of the Vaiśeṣika position is accepted, it must be entirely disregarded.
The summary verses.
In the world, it is observed that the production of something vast arises from the conjunction of minute things;
therefore, atoms are the cause, being partless, for the sake of ending the infinite regress.

Since their conjunction occurs through the division of their parts, where would there be a finality? If not, let there be a conjunction even without such parts; how then could there be magnitude in the effect?
And the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the mote (trasareṇu) is inferred by that very [mote] itself;
for there exist many subverting arguments, and inherence itself lacks any means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, because being the fundamental cause of that [space] would entail the consequence of impermanence regarding its possession of form and so forth;
for in the world, it is observed that those things possessing form and the like are non-eternal due to their having parts.
Thus concludes the section on "the large and the long."
Even if it were based on the cause of a composite whole, that [result] would not be attained. ||17||
If it is argued that [the formation of the body] is possible because of mutual causality, we say no, because that is not the cause for the state of being a composite aggregate. ||18||
And because of the cessation of the preceding [moment] upon the arising of the succeeding one. ||19||
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the thesis and simultaneity [of the two]. (20)
The non-attainment of analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation [is established] because there is no interruption. ||21||
Because there is no fault in either case. ||22||
Because there is no distinction from space. ||23||
And because of mindfulness. ||24||
[The self is not non-existent] because it is not seen as non-existent. ||25||
And in this way, success is achieved even for those who remain indifferent. ||26||

The Buddhists are of four types, designated as Mādhyamika, Yogācāra, Sautrāntika, and Vaibhāṣika. All of them are disciples of the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*), who respectively propound the doctrine of universal emptiness, the emptiness of external objects, the inferability of external objects, and the perceptibility of external objects. Regarding this, it is said: "When things are analyzed by the intellect, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is apprehended. Therefore, they are shown to be ineffable and devoid of intrinsic nature."

When the disciples were taught the total emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) by the Guru through such principles as "in whatever way they are investigated, in that very way [they are empty]," those who accepted the Guru’s words exactly as they were and did not raise further objections were the "superior" because they accepted what the Guru said with faith; yet, because they failed to go beyond that into further inquiry, they were the "inferior. Thus, due to this combination of being superior and inferior, they occupied an intermediate position.

The Mādhyamikas are those who, while accepting the emptiness of external objects, raised the objection: "How can consciousness itself be empty? For that would result in the world being blind. They are called Yogācāras because they possess both the practice (*ācāra*) of accepting what was taught by the Master (Maitreya), as defined in their own system, and the yoga (*yoga*) of further inquiry beyond that, as defined in their own system.

The Guru explained to them: "There exists only internal consciousness (*vijñānamātra*); that very [consciousness] appears in the form of blue and so forth, but there is no external blue or the like apart from it. This is because the non-difference between blue and its cognitions is established by the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*); for if they were different, as in the case of a cow and a horse, the rule of their simultaneous perception would not obtain. Thus, this very blue and so forth, which consists of the forms of consciousness, appears as if external due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). When this was taught, [the student asked]: "How can there be the voidness (*śūnyatva*) of external objects in every respect? [For there is] the external..."

Regarding those who have raised the objection: "Since blue and so forth appear [externally], while consciousness appears as internal through the manifestation of 'I' and blue and so forth appear as external through the manifestation of 'this,' when a difference thus manifests, the mere rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*)—being an insufficient reason—is incapable of proving non-difference; moreover, by the very mention of simultaneity, difference is already admitted. To them, we reply: It is true that external blue and so forth exist, but they are not perceived (*pratyakṣa*). For that which has not yet arisen or does not currently exist cannot be perceived, and that which has already arisen is momentary and lacks duration.

"But rather, as it arises, the blue and so forth, having imparted its own form to the cognition, perishes. Therefore, when it is explained that past blue and so forth are inferred by means of the form residing in the cognition,"—this being thus taught, they asked at the end of the discourse: "To what extent will this thread of instruction proceed in accordance with the student's questions? To which the Teacher replied:

Because they asked for the end of the Sūtra, they are the Sautrāntikas; thus, they are called Sautrāntikas. Consequently, the statement that the external world is to be inferred through consciousness is a contradictory assertion. This is because that very consciousness is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of its own object, and since there would be no perception of any object whatsoever, inference could not function due to the absence of a locus for the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Those who were questioned in this manner are the Vaibhāṣikas; to them, the direct perception of the external was also taught.

Thus, having faith in the meaning of the answers to their respective questions exactly as they had heard them, they maintained their various differing views. In that regard, there are four formal treatises (*adhikaraṇas*) intended to refute, in sequence, the four types of Buddhists beginning with the Vaibhāṣikas; thereafter, this present treatise is intended to refute the Kṣapaṇakas.

Following the refutation of the Vaidika, Kāpila, and Kaṇabhuj [schools], those non-Vaidikas are now being rejected; thus, following the refutation of the partial nihilists (*ardhavaināśika*), the total nihilists (*sarvavaināśika*) are being refuted—this constitutes the structural connection (*peṭikā-saṅgati*) with the preceding section. Among the three sections concerning the Vaibhāṣikas and others, certain logicians who accept momentariness are the partial nihilists.

For, due to the imbalance in the moment-by-moment accumulation and depletion of the components of food and drink being digested by the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), the composite body itself also becomes something new every moment through that process of accumulation and depletion.

Although there is no perception of the body's increase or decrease at every moment, nevertheless—just as one perceives the water of a pond due to the falling of rain showers, or the water of a well due to the pumping of a water-wheel—at the end [of life], such a perception occurs; thus, it is logical that there is indeed knowledge of some slight increase or decrease occurring at every instant. This is because, through the assimilation of the components of food into the components of the body, the decrease or increase of the body necessarily follows from the decrease or increase of those [components].

For just as they accept that there is a logical inference of the moon, stars, and so forth reaching slightly different locations every moment—based on the observation of their arrival at many distant places after an interval of time such as a muhūrta—so too do all the Nihilists (Sarvavaināśikas) accept the momentariness of the terrestrial globe due to its increase and decrease caused by inevitable processes such as digging and filling at every moment, and the momentariness of the ocean due to its increase and decrease through contact with river waters and the rising of spray.

The Buddhists, however, accepting the momentariness of the entire phenomenal world, are thoroughgoing nihilists (*sarvavaināśika*). The Buddhists, however, accepting the momentariness of the entire phenomenal world, are thoroughgoing nihilists.

Even among the Buddhists, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas are proponents of atomism; thus, in the first section, both are refuted by means of arguments common to both as well as those specific to the Sautrāntikas, due to their close proximity to the followers of Kaṇāda. In the second section, the Yogācāras are refuted because of their similarity in advocating momentariness. Following that, the Mādhyamikas are refuted due to their shared Buddhist identity. Finally, the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas) are refuted due to their shared non-Vedic character. This is the distinction.

Although the Jainas (*kṣapaṇakas*) are also proponents of the theory of atoms (*paramāṇuvādins*), nevertheless, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas accept four kinds of atoms characterized by the natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. Furthermore, while logicians maintain that atoms possess absolute stability or absolute momentariness, the Jainas, however, are proponents of the uniformity of atoms and maintain the non-absolute nature of stability and so forth. Thus, one should observe a particular affinity between the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, as they share a superior proximity to the logicians.

In this regard, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, who maintain the doctrine of atoms, say as follows: Earth-atoms have the nature of visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility; water-atoms have the nature of visible form, taste, and tangibility; fire-atoms have the nature of visible form and tangibility; and air-atoms have the nature of tangibility. These combine in the form of the primary elements (*bhūta*) consisting of the earth, mountains, oceans, the submarine fire (*vaḍabānala*), and great winds. And from those [elements], such as earth and the rest, there arise the material aggregates (*bhautika-saṃghāta*) consisting of bodies, sense organs, and objects such as jars.

In all cases, a composite (*saṃghāta*) is merely an aggregate of parts; there is no production of a separate substance as a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from those [parts]. For if such a [whole] were produced, one would have to admit that it possesses its own distinct color and other qualities in order for it to be visible and so forth. Furthermore, no color or other quality belonging to a whole is perceived apart from the color and other qualities of the parts. Indeed, in a cloth woven from threads of various colors, there is no other color in the cloth apart from the various colors residing in the threads; nor is there any other taste in a mango fruit apart from the sweet or sour tastes located in the different parts of the fruit—whether it be very ripe or slightly underripe.

We do not perceive any other odor in the betel leaf apart from the fragrant and putrid odors situated in its distinct parts; nor do we perceive any other touch in the plantain petal apart from the hard and soft touches situated in its distinct parts; nor do we perceive any other dimension in the tree apart from the large, small, and smaller dimensions situated in its root, middle, and tip portions.

If it is argued that some maintain there is a distinct color called "variegated" (*citra*) produced in cloths woven from threads of various colors, that has already been refuted by others: "If it is variegated, it cannot be one; if it is one, how can it be variegated? To say that it is both one and variegated is truly most extraordinary! Furthermore, no one accepts that taste and the other qualities exist as non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

Therefore, the external object consists of two types of aggregates: an aggregate of primary elements caused by atoms, and an aggregate of derivative matter caused by those primary elements. This theory is untenable; for if these two types of aggregates caused by atoms and primary elements are accepted, the existence of the world as a single aggregate and the conscious being's practical engagement with it would not be possible. Why?

If atoms (*aṇu*) and primary elements (*bhūta*) were causes without an activity for the purpose of their conjunction, it would follow that the effect would be produced at all times. Therefore, it must be stated that atoms and primary elements possess causality toward the primary elements and their derivatives (*bhautika*) only when they are qualified by an activity that serves as the cause of conjunction. However, this is not possible if they are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because those [atoms] in whom the entry of activity occurs have perished by the time of the moment of conjunction, and those [atoms] in whom the conjunction occurs have not yet arisen at the moment of activity.

Because that which lacks consciousness ceases to exist at the time when cognition arises for it, and that for which cognition arises ceases to exist at the time of the practical activity of avoidance and so forth; and because if one were to admit the conjoining of some [atoms] through the operation of a cause of conjunction while admitting the perception of another through the contact of a sense-organ and so forth, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Nor can it be argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because those atoms which possess activity and are conjoined exist within a single continuum, and because the conscious being who possesses sensory contact and sensation exists within a single continuum; for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness do not admit a stable continuum distinct from the momentary continuum. Now, one might object: even among unstable things, there exists ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of the delusion of stability, and this is the cause of attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, while subjection to attachment and the like is the cause of ignorance; thus, [the cycle of] ignorance, attachment, and so on...

The continuum (*pravāha*) is indeed established by experience; since it would be untenable in the absence of the existence or non-existence of the aggregate consisting of the body, sense organs, objects, and so forth, the establishment of that aggregate implied by it cannot be rejected. If this is argued, we say no. For when the impossibility of the aggregate's existence has been stated due to the absence of a cause, its possibility must be supported by stating such a cause. And ignorance, attachment, and the like are not the cause of the aggregate independently of the operation of atoms and other factors.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that a mother-of-pearl shell, through the ignorance consisting of the delusion of silver and the resulting attachment to silver, would lose its aggregate nature as a shell and instead attain an aggregate nature as silver. Moreover, if one thing were to produce attachment and so forth in another through ignorance, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby the continuity of the stream of ignorance, attachment, and so on, could not be established. It might be argued: "The fault of over-extension—namely, that the action of one thing produces conjunction in another—does not apply to the Buddhist system. For they do not admit that action or conjunction exists within momentary entities such as atoms."

However, the production of one thing situated in another location by something situated in yet another location is the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the cognition of action; likewise, the production of a nearby object by a distant one is the basis for the cognition of conjunction. Consequently, just as in the Nyāya system a cognition of a "tumult" (*kolāhala*) arises when many sounds are combined through a sequence of sound-productions originating from various directions, so too a cognition of the earth, mountains, and so forth arises when many atoms are thus aggregated.

For it is observed that although a single hair is not visible from a distance, when many hairs are gathered together in the form of a braid or the like, that collection becomes visible; nor is there a rule that a collection of invisible things must itself be invisible, for such a reason is not established.

Just as a collection of threads possesses the power to draw [an object] even though each individual thread lacks that power, and just as a collection of atoms possesses the power to attract [an object] even though each individual atom is invisible, so too it is logically established that a collection of atoms is visible despite the invisibility of each individual atom. As they say: "Even though atoms are individually unfit for perception, visibility may arise when they are combined, just as threads possess the power to pull a boat and the like."

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no impossibility of the existence of a composite whole due to the absence of a cause, even so, the relationship of cause and effect is not tenable. This is because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment of the jar, the preceding moment of the jar has already perished; thus, its status as a cause for the subsequent moment of the jar is untenable. In the Buddhist view, time does not exist in reality. A jar or similar object, being inherently fragile and perishing by its own nature even as it arises, serves merely as the basis for the conceptual construction of "moments."

And that [object], such as a jar, is metaphorically designated as "momentary" because it possesses moments (kṣaṇa) as conceptually constructed through its own arising and destruction—just as one might say "the stone statue has a body"—such is their system. Therefore, according to the limits of that doctrine, since the jar itself is the moment, there is the usage in the treatises "the jar is a moment" by way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). [Objection: But surely it is impossible for what has perished to be a cause; for it is said of them in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "The causality of entities is neither through having perished nor through remaining present."

Furthermore, [it acts] by virtue of being real (*bhūtatayā*). And that which is real may be either persisting or destroyed; provided there is the completeness of other auxiliary causes, it performs its own effect without delay. For it is observed that the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced in a seed by watering (*dohada*) is the cause of specific colors and tastes in the flowers, fruits, and so forth that appear at a later time. Therefore, if you argue that because it is destroyed it cannot function as a cause, do not say so.

If, even though it is non-existent at the time of its effect, something could ever be a cause merely by virtue of its prior existence, then everything would arise everywhere and at all times. At the moment of the production of a jar, even a sprout and the like would have to be produced, because seeds and such things that have perished exist within the beginningless flow of time. Nor should one suspect the absence of auxiliary conditions such as the field or its cultivation; for those too, having perished, are no different from [the seed] in their prior existence.

Indeed, the persistence of the substances of a pregnancy-longing (*dohada*) in a subtle form until the production of the effect is well-known from the science of pregnancy-longings (*dohala-śāstra*), such as the *Vṛkṣāyurveda*. It may be argued: "Let there be no causality for that which has long since perished and is devoid of activity; however, let there be causality for that which exists in the preceding moment, whether by its own nature or by way of its own operation. Furthermore, the priority (*pūrvavṛttitva*) of the cause must necessarily be asserted. Since causality is established by that alone, what is the use of its existing at the time of the effect? In common experience, the causality of a seed that has perished with respect to a sprout, of milk with respect to curds, and of a lump of clay with respect to a jar is observed."

If, however, it were required that a cause exist at the time of its effect, then one might argue: "Let the destruction of seeds and the like be the cause of sprouts and the like, and let the destruction of the preceding moment of a jar be the cause of the succeeding moment of the jar. If this is so, and you accept that a cause can exist while the effect is non-existent, then you contradict the Buddhist tenet: "The four conditions—the dominant, the co-operative, the objective, and the immediate—are the causes of mind and mental factors."

For it is said in the *Buddhasūtra*: "Mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes. The dominant cause (*adhipati*) is the sense faculty (*indriya*). For that [faculty] determines that knowledge has as its object only one specific thing among the five, such as form and so forth; and in the world, that which determines is called the dominant cause. The cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) is light and so forth. The objective cause (*ālambana*) is the jar and so forth. The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the prior cognition.

The meaning of the proposition is that it is by depending upon these four kinds of causes that the mind, cognition, mental factors, and [feelings] such as pleasure—which are non-different from them—are produced. This proposition would be undermined, because if they do not exist in the preceding moment, they cannot function as causes; and if they do not exist in the succeeding moment, they cannot be objects of perception which apprehends the present.

Otherwise, in order to establish that the cause possesses the status of being an object, one would have to admit its persistence even at the moment the effect arises; in that case, there would be simultaneity between the contact and the cognition, which stand in the relation of cause and effect. By this, the view that the destruction in the preceding moment is the cause of the succeeding moment is also refuted. For if that were so, it would contradict the thesis regarding [the four types of] causes, such as the sovereign cause (*adhipati-hetu*) and others. Furthermore, the very destruction called "cessation" (*nirodha*), as conceived by the opponent, is impossible. For they imagine it in this way:

In all cases, that which is designated by the term "cessation" (nirodha) is entirely without continuity and without persistence; it is not [merely] what is spoken of. It is of two kinds: gross and subtle. The gross destruction of a jar, perceived by everyone immediately after the falling of a mallet, is "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). "Deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā) refers to the worldly intellect which is opposed to the apprehension of an object's existence and instead grasps its non-existence. Its opposite is "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), which is subtle, incapable of being perceived by worldly means, and established through reasoning as the destruction occurring at every moment.

This total destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*), even in its two forms, is not possible because there is no interruption. For a substance that persists eternally in an uninterrupted manner, the conventional usage of "destruction" and "origination" occurs solely through the relinquishing of a prior state and the assuming of a subsequent state; however, as established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, there is never any total destruction of a substance without residue. Therefore, it is impossible for destruction to function as a cause [of cognition]. As it is said: "Space and the two types of cessation—these three are the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and eternal.
That which is other than these three, being cognizable by the intellect, is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and momentary."

Furthermore, for the Buddhists, it is untenable for the two types of cessation (*nirodha*)—which they accept as eternal, asserting that "the conditioned, being an effect, is impermanent, whereas the unconditioned, such as the triad beginning with space, being non-effects, is eternal"—to function as causes; for if that which persists without interruption were a cause, it would follow that all effects would arise everywhere at all times, since even those factors intended to act as its auxiliaries would be eternal due to the eternity of the two cessations.

Furthermore, the Buddhists maintain that the triad consisting of the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*) is non-substantial (*tuccha*). In that case, how can the world arise from what is non-substantial? If it were to arise from the non-substantial, then because the non-substantial is devoid of all distinctions, it would be impossible to establish a specific causal relationship whereby a particular effect is produced by a particular cause; consequently, the entire world might arise immediately after the moment of a single jar. Moreover, an effect produced from the non-substantial would itself have to be non-substantial, and it could not be perceived as having the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*).

Because the effect conforms to its cause, according to the analogy of gold and its ornaments such as bracelets (*rucaka*) and the like. Furthermore, the Buddhists assert that even space (*ākāśa*) is insubstantial (*tuccha*). How is this tenable? For space is clearly perceived as the locus for the flight of hawks and other birds, as in the cognition, "A hawk flies here; a vulture [flies] there. [Objection: This perception is explained by having the light of the moon or the sun as its object. In thick darkness, the perception, "A firefly flies here," is explained by having the light of the firefly as its object.

The cognition, "The moon is here; the sun is here," is also explained by taking each as having light as its object. Furthermore, the cognition of even that light—which is itself dependent [on them]—as being their substratum is also explained by means of a specific relation of identity (svarūpa-sambandha-viśeṣa). This is because we observe that in the expression "the *tilaka* tree in the forest," the forest, which consists of a collection of trees, is perceived as the substratum of the *tilaka* tree through such a specific relation of identity. Indeed, the fact that the sky is the substratum of a hawk must likewise be accounted for by means of a specific relation of identity alone.

For it is impossible for that [space] to be primarily the substratum of a heavy substance, just as the earth and other such things—which possess a dense, material form—cannot be so. Furthermore, the two cognitions of being a substratum and not being a substratum, expressed as "the bird is here" and "the bird is not here," can be explained in the case of light by means of the delimitation of different parts; however, this is not possible in the case of space, because it is partless (*niravayava*). Nor should it be argued that even in the case of space, the distinction between the various downward portions of the earth serves as the differentiating delimiter (*avacchedaka*).

If it is argued that [the notion of space] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding space because the cognitions "a bird is here" and "a bird is not here" with respect to upper and lower locations lack such [spatial] existence—since it is possible for the cognition of a hawk’s flight and so forth to have light as its object—it is replied: There certainly exists the cognition, "The hawk flies in the eastern part; the vulture in the western part," and so on. In that cognition, a locus (*ādhāra*) consisting of the eastern direction and so forth is perceived. That very [locus] is space (*ākāśa*), because directions are not admitted apart from it.

For it is possible for that very [space] to assume the form of the eastern direction and so forth through the distinction of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor should it be argued that, by connection with those respective adjuncts, light itself should be the eastern part and so on; for even in cognitions such as "the moonlight is in the eastern part" or "darkness is in the western part," the place in the east and so forth is perceived as the locus of the light and other things. If it is then argued that, by the common usage "there is space in the eastern part," there must be a place distinct from ether—which is of the nature of space—that serves as its locus, we say no.

In this context, the word "space" (avakāśa) refers to the absence of obstruction by another corporeal substance, which is the opposite of the state of being occupied by a dense corporeal substance. For this very reason:

In some places, even a prohibition of space is observed, such as: "There is room in the eastern part, but not in the western part, for it is crowded with those eating. For a prohibition of ether (ākāśa) in that context is impossible, because it is omnipresent; and if it were not omnipresent, it would follow that there would be an absence of space even when obstructions are removed. Indeed, ether was not non-existent previously. Thus, the doubt that "space is merely the absence of corporeal substances, which—delimited by various adjuncts—serves as the basis for designations such as 'east' and so on" is also refuted.

This is because that [space] is perceived as being contained within a location; and because even when there is a negation of space in the form of an absence of obstruction—as in the statement, "There is no room in the eastern part; there the twice-born sit closely packed"—there is still the conventional usage of the existence of a location such as the "eastern part. Furthermore, there is no conventional usage of a location such as the "eastern part" as being itself contained within a location, in the same way that space in the form of an absence of obstruction is said to be so contained; for if there were, a location distinct from that [absence] would be established. Indeed, the conventional usage is simply "this is the eastern location," and so forth.

It is not, however, in the form "in this place" or "in that eastern place," and so forth. If it is argued that because of the common worldly cognition "here is space," there must be a location distinct from space itself, we say no. For the worldly cognition of space is established by scripture as being fixed upon a blue substance—which appears like a great downward-facing sapphire bowl surrounding the top of Mount Meru and is distinguished by the particular radiance of its jewels—and thus there is no contradiction in its being perceived as contained within a specific direction.

Since spatial ether (*deśarūpa-ākāśa*)—unlike time—is never admitted to appear independently in any worldly cognition without appearing as an objective entity within cognitions such as "now, here is a jar," it follows that because ether is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), the claim that "ether, the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), and the three kinds of non-existence (*tuccha*) alone are eternal, while everything else that is of the nature of existence is momentary" is incorrect. [Objection: But how can momentariness, which is established by valid means of knowledge, be rejected?

If it is argued that perception, having the present object as its domain, makes known its own object as distinguished from what is not present—namely, from the past (the preceding moment) and the future (the succeeding moment)—just as the perception of a blue jar makes known the jar as distinguished from red ones and so forth; we reply: while the aforementioned cognition of direct recognition (*abhijñā*) grasps the jar’s connection with the present time, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that same jar" also takes as its object its connection with a time that is not present.

Therefore, since the connection of a single entity with both the present and non-present times is established in accordance with that [perception], and since the non-contradiction of these two times is possible through their sequential occurrence, the cognition whose object is the connection with the present time should be understood as excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not as excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), or as excluding connection with another by means of its own delimitation; but it does not do so in every respect. For this very reason, the cognition of blueness in a variegated cloth does not convey the exclusion of the non-blue; rather, it conveys that exclusion only as delimited by a specific location.

Indeed, the non-contradiction between two attributes need not be established solely by means of a difference in their substrates; rather, it may also be established through the failure of a cognition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) to arise. However, once such a cognition does arise, a contradiction imagined merely through one's own fancy does not touch the hearts of those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). If it is objected: "Since memory and perception possess well-established causes, there ought to be two distinct cognitions—one of the nature of memory in the form 'that,' and one of the nature of experience in the form 'this jar'—rather than a single cognition in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)," we say no.

Since those seeking that silver are observed to act toward this object upon hearing "this very silver has been deposited by me," the unity of the cognition [of recognition] is established; and since that is so, it is logical to postulate—on the strength of the effect—that the cause there is the sense organ conjoined with the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as its auxiliary condition (*pratyāsatti*). Now, one might object: even so, recognition is merely of the nature of an error.

If it is argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is nowhere a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is seen to be a false witness even in cases such as trees, shrubs, and creepers—which undergo a continuous succession of the accumulation and depletion of parts—or in mountains and oceans, which are entirely distinct [from moment to moment], or even in bodies affected by childhood and old age, we say no. For the validity of the aforementioned recognition is established by its having as its object the identity of the substance (*dravya*) that possesses the states (*avasthā*), despite the difference between those states.

For recognition does not have the identity of states as its object, such that it would be invalid; rather, its object is precisely the identity of the substance possessing those states. Nor should it be argued that there is no substance at all persisting through multiple states beyond the states that appear and disappear, for it is impossible to reject that [substance] since the validity of the very recognitions cited above is established in relation to it. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to suppose that the mere recognition of a flame, or of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again, is an error based on similarity.

If one were to assume the invalidity of even those cognitions that are not sublated by using as an example a cognition that is sublated, it would follow that the very establishment of a real entity through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be lost. By this [argument], the following Buddhist claim is refuted: "Memory concerns an object previously experienced, while perception concerns a present object. Since these two are absolutely distinct, how can their non-difference be perceived? Due to differences in form, capacity, and so forth, an old man is vastly different from a child; not even a trace of the former's form is perceived in the latter."

Even for the opponent, how could that [entity] be one in the preceding case? "If this distinction belongs to the states and not to the possessor of the states, then only the states are perceived, and nothing further, even in a dream. Now, it may be argued that this entire web of reasons for refuting momentariness does not apply to the Sautrāntika system as it does to the Vaibhāṣika; for instance, the objection regarding the contradiction with recognition—that the object of perception could not be the cause [of that perception]—does not apply there.

For that proposition belongs only to those who maintain the perceptibility of external objects. Furthermore, the statement that the conceptualization of momentariness is sublated by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) does not even proceed; this is because recognition as a perception regarding external objects is unestablished. And thus, the Buddhists' inference of momentariness—namely, "A jar and so forth are momentary because they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), like the body and so forth"—is free from disturbance, since the sublation by recognition remains unestablished.

And here there is a counter-reasoning (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) that refutes [the opponent's position]: it would follow that existence (*sattva*) is annihilated. For existence is nothing other than the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); it does not consist of a genus (*jāti*) or other such forms, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that. Furthermore, this [capacity] is not possible in the case of a permanent entity. To explain: a permanent entity would have to perform its own causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously. In the first case, regarding an effect that occurs at a later time, is it capable now or not?

First of all, one should perform [the action] right now; for one who is incapable at this time does not become capable at another time. However, in the view that [actions occur] simultaneously, because everything that was to be done has been completed right now, one becomes capable at another time. In the view that they occur simultaneously, since everything to be done has been completed right now, its non-existence would follow at another time. But surely, in this inference of momentariness, there exists a powerful counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*).

Indeed, if things were momentary, even the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) intended to subvert your counter-argument would not function; for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the determination of the absence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), and the observation of the frequent coexistence of the probandum and the probans—which are necessary for that [reductio]—require the restriction of their occurrence to a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). Do not say so. For proponents of momentariness do not accept such a restriction to a single substratum for these [logical operations]. As for the fear of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is to be warded off by the fact that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) itself acts as the regulator.

For Caitra, Maitra, and others consist each of a collection of moments of *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) that arise in an uninterrupted continuum, having entered into the state of cause and effect. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in the Sautrāntika position; thus is the view of the Sautrāntikas who respond with further argumentation: "The external objects are inferred by means of the forms (*ākāra*) such as blue and so forth residing in cognition. For the cognition produced by an external object such as blue, which is in contact with the sense organ, itself assumes the form of blue and so forth, just like the object."

That cognition, by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*), takes itself as its object; however, the outward activity of one desiring an object such as "blue" residing within that cognition does not arise from the immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*). Rather, it arises from the inferential cognition (*ānumānikajñāna*) occurring immediately thereafter. For example, for one desiring to catch the wind, the activity at the foot of a tree occurs after seeing the movement of a branch, but not from the visual cognition of the branch's movement itself; rather, it is from the inferential cognition whose object is the movement of the wind, which is inferred from that mark (*liṅga*).

In this regard, the following is the refutation: cognition arises in the moment immediately following the moment of the object that is in contact with the sense organ. In that case, it is not logical for that momentary object to be the cause for the transference of its own attributes [to the cognition]. For we do not observe non-existent things, such as flowers [in the sky], acting as causes for the transference of their own attributes onto crystals and the like. Even if the transference of blue and other qualities were admitted, would the properties residing in that object—such as being in front, proximity, distance, insentience, and so forth—also be transferred, or not?

If [the reflection] were a transference, then there would be no appearance of its contradictory properties, such as internality or the nature of cognition, just as whiteness does not appear when redness is transferred to a crystal. Alternatively, if it does not transfer—as in the case of the forward-facing nature and proximity belonging to the face appearing in a mirror—then, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga), that appearance could not occur. Therefore, since in the doctrine of momentariness the inference of external objects is impossible just like their direct perception, one must necessarily accept their permanence for the sake of establishing worldly transactional activity.

Since all phenomena are momentary, the agent of those worldly or prescribed actions performed for the sake of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired would not be the enjoyer of their fruit; rather, it would follow that someone else entirely is the enjoyer. Consequently, even those who are indifferent would achieve results, and no one at all would engage in actions. If it is argued that engagement occurs due to the delusion of identity with a future enjoyer, this is not so; for one who possesses the certain knowledge of momentariness would never engage in action. Nor is it the case that engagement occurs due to the delusion of identity with a future enjoyer.

For one who possesses the certainty that things are momentary, purposeful activity is untenable. [Objection: But even when there is a perception of difference, we observe engagement in ritual acts due to a desire for a fruit to be experienced by a succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth; likewise, there may be such engagement here as well, since in those cases the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established as the regulating factor. [Reply: In that case, the fruit of all actions performed by a father would accrue to the succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and there would also be the recollection of the fruit of the father’s experience and so on.

Because the relationship of cause and effect exists in that [stream of consciousness] just as it does in one's own stream of cognition (*vijñānasantāna*). Therefore, since the relationship of cause and effect is not a restrictive factor [for establishing identity], for the sake of establishing the distinction between results and so forth, and for the sake of validating recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the stability of the self and other things must indeed be accepted. Furthermore, no counter-argument (*vipakṣabādhakatarka*) against the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) can be applied; for even if a thing is capable [of producing an effect], the sequence of effects is possible due to the sequential occurrence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-samavadhāna*). The detailed refutation of momentariness, beginning with these points, is to be found elsewhere.
Summary Verses.

When the Vaibhāṣika has stated that the two— the momentary existence and the aggregate— cannot account for the arising of contact, cognition, grasping, abandoning, destruction, water, fire, and so forth,
then the one called the Sautrāntika says that these [objects], though non-existent, are inferred from the forms of cognition;
yet he must be enlightened by the statement that the transfer of the form of a perished object is impossible.
Thus ends the section concerning the aggregate.
Not non-existence, because [the world] is perceived. ||27||
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and so forth. ||28||
There is no non-existence, because it is not perceived. ||29||

The refutation stated against the Vaiśeṣika and Sautrāntika positions—namely, that if objects such as blue are momentary, their status as either perceptible or inferable is untenable—does not apply to the Yogācāra position. This is because, since objects such as blue are of the nature of internal consciousness, they are self-luminous; thus, it is possible for those very [consciousnesses] to perceive them. This constitutes the rebuttal. Now, here [we consider] the Yogācāra position: that cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth cannot possess a specific correspondence with their respective objects without being similar in form to those respective objects.

Since [the existence of external objects] is not tenable, one must necessarily admit that cognition possesses a form identical to the object; for by that alone, all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are established. Apart from the blue and other forms belonging to cognition, there is no postulation of an external object. Furthermore, regarding the blue and other such things being forms of consciousness, there is the following inference: "Blue and so forth are non-different from cognition, because they appear [together with it], because they are invariably perceived simultaneously with cognition, and because they are [of the nature of] cognition. Nor should it be argued that the second reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), on the grounds that simultaneity implies difference.

This is because the meaning of that [term] is "being the object of a perception that is pervaded by the perception of knowledge," and because pervasion—in the form of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—exists even when there is non-difference. Nor does non-difference contradict the appearance of difference in the form of the relation between action and its object (the subject-object relationship) in such cognitions as "I know this. For that [appearance] is an error, like the cognition of two moons. As they say: "Because of the rule of simultaneous perception, there is non-difference between difference and the cognition thereof; however, difference is seen through erroneous cognitions, just as the moon is seen as dual despite being non-dual."

If it is asked how the manifestation of external objects such as blue can be an error consisting in the appearance of internal cognition, [we reply that] the appearance of externality is itself an error, just like the appearance of stars and so forth situated above as being on the ground when they are rising. By this, the appearance of duality in the form of agent and object—as in "I know"—is also explained. As they say: "The nature of consciousness, though undivided, appears as if possessed of the distinction between the grasped, the grasper, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted."

If it is asked, "How is it that a single cognition, in reality, manifests as if divided into the forms of agent, object, and action—as in 'I know this'?"—the answer is: "Due to the force of successive latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The non-arising of a cognition of the form of potsherds immediately after the arising of a cognition of the form of a jar is due to the diversity of latent impressions. This is incorrect; for when the perception of external objects such as blue occurs, with the agent appearing as the object of the action, there is no emergence of those inferences claiming the non-difference [of the object] from the cognition while one is awake.

Nor should it be argued: "Even for those who accept external objects such as blue and so forth, the fact that cognitions possess the form of blue and so forth must be admitted as established by experience. Since all worldly transactions are accounted for by this alone, what is the use of postulating an external object? For two forms—of the object and of the cognition—are not perceived. This is because the "form of blue and so forth" of a cognition is simply its conformity with the transactions of desire and so on directed toward specific objects such as blue; it does not possess a primary form of blue and so forth in the same manner as an external object does.

For there would be the consequence that a collection of cognitions apprehending blue, cold, heat, and so forth, would possess multiple mutually contradictory forms. Furthermore, the postulation that cognitions are devoid of external objects on the analogy of dreams is also not tenable; for by means of sublation and non-sublation, even dream-cognitions possess objects existing at that very time. Moreover, the justification for the arising of diverse cognitions based on the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is also untenable, because in the doctrine of momentary destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśavāda*), the depositing of a latent impression is impossible.
The Summary Verses.
For the Yogācāra who asserts that consciousness alone consists of the threefold division [of subject, object, and act of cognition],
the denial of the cognized and the cognizer is refuted by the very fact of apprehension.
Thus ends the section on apprehension.
And because it is impossible in every way.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: immediately after the refutation of the Yogācāra school, which asserts the existence of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*), the doctrine of the Mādhyamikas—who deny even that—is now being refuted. They indeed say: "That consciousness is not accepted by the wise as ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky. Even for cognitions, since they are plagued by the conceptual difficulties of having a nature that is either blue/yellow, cold/hot, or one/many, they are not ultimately real; therefore, their true reality is merely their emptiness (*tucchatva*). This is incorrect.

For one who asserts that emptiness is itself empty, the intention—whether that emptiness is of the nature of existence, of the nature of non-existence, or some other mode—is in every respect impossible in the world.

Since it has been established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*) are merely specific states of a substance that persists eternally, it is impossible to demonstrate that [the effect] is either non-existent, existent alone, non-existent alone, or some other mode; for in all effects, only that which is already existent can be the cause, and there is no production of an effect from what is purely non-existent or from what has attained another mode. By this, it is shown that "insubstantiality" (*tucchatva*) consists either in being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) or in being devoid of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭivinirmukta*).

This is refuted by the statement: "The Madhyamikas do not know reality, which is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is liberated from the four alternatives. For, by not admitting an absence distinct from existence, the assertion that absence is the cause results ultimately in a doctrine of real causality (*satkāraṇavāda*). Furthermore, just like the cognition and term for "existence," the cognitions and terms for the negation of existence and so forth also have as their object things delimited by space and time; therefore, unsubstantiality (*tucchatva*) is not established on that basis.

For even in the case of the cognition and the word "existent" (sattva), they are well-established in common worldly usage as having as their object only that existence which is delimited by space, time, and substance—such that "this exists now," or "this becomes of such a form"; consequently, an unconditioned negation of existence is not established anywhere.
The Summary Verses.
The doctrine of universal emptiness, however, is not tenable in any way,
because the expressions "existent" and "non-existent" refer to a thing and its states, which are themselves dependent upon that thing.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility [of the world] in every respect.
Not [in both], because of the impossibility in one. (31)
And thus, there would be incompleteness of the self. (32)
And even from the perspective of figurative interpretation, there is no lack of contradiction, because of the occurrence of transformation and other such changes. ||33||
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both are eternal, there is no distinction. ||34||

The followers of the Sugata have been refuted; now the Jains are being refuted. They indeed maintain that the world consists of six substances (ṣaḍdravya) called soul (jīva), merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), matter (pudgala), time (kāla), and space (ākāśa), and is devoid of a Lord (nirīśvara). Among these, souls are of three kinds: bound, those who have attained yoga-perfection, and the liberated. Merit is a pervasive, specific substance that is the cause of motion for things possessing movement. Demerit is a pervasive, specific substance that is the cause of stability. Matter consists of atoms, mountains, oceans, and so forth. Time is a specific atomic substance that serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "was," "is," and "will be."

Space is also one; however, it consists of infinite points (*pradeśa*). Furthermore, they provide another summary: "Living beings (*jīva*), non-living matter (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), shedding (*nirjarā*), stoppage (*saṃvara*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). Living beings have already been described. Non-living matter (*ajīva*) refers to the entire collection of things that are objects of experience for living beings. Influx (*āsrava*) is the aggregate of the sense organs, because by means of this, the living being flows toward [objects] in the form of cognitions of pots and so forth. Some, however, say that influx (*āsrava*) is the bondage of karma, because when the living being flows—that is, moves—it follows after everything.

Regarding this, Jinadatta said: "Influx is the bondage of karma; liberation is its release. Bondage is of eight kinds, distinguished by the four destructive (ghāti) karmas and the four non-destructive (aghāti) karmas. Among these, the first group of four consists of sins that have been flowing without beginning and act as obstacles to the qualities of knowledge, vision, bliss, and vigor of the soul, which are destined to manifest at the state of liberation.

The second group of four consists of the body, bodily configuration, the ego-identification with that [body], and the sustenance thereof; these are of the nature of merit (*puṇya*) because they are mixed with merit that serves as the cause for pleasure and so forth. Austerity (*tapas*) is defined etymologically as that by which desire, anger, and the like are completely worn away (*niḥśeṣaṃ jīryati*); it takes the form of practices such as plucking out the hair or ascending heated stones. Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cessation of the senses. Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the manifestation of the soul’s own innate nature. Some, however, maintain that liberation is the continuous upward movement; for it is the inherent nature of one freed from bondage to move upward.

Just as for a parrot released from its cage, or as for a fully ripened castor seed that has burst open, or as for a dried gourd whose coating of thick mud has been worn away by immersion in water; so too, due to the cessation of bondage that has persisted since beginningless time, there is a constant upward movement. They say that the infinite *alokākāśa* (space beyond the world), situated above all worlds, provides the space for this constant upward movement.

Thus they recite: "The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again; but those traveling on the path of the *aloka-ākāśa* (the space beyond the world) do not return even today. Others, however, say that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the state of abiding in the upper region for one whose qualities such as knowledge have become manifest. They apply this entire collection of entities according to the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī-naya*).

"It may be that it exists, it may be that it does not exist, it may be that it both exists and does not exist, it may be inexpressible, it may be that it exists and is inexpressible, it may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible, and it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible. In this regard, there are four modes concerning existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and the inexpressibility consisting in being distinct from both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, by combining existence, non-existence, and both existence and non-existence with indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), three modes are produced; thus, seven modes can be conceived by those who propound such views. All these modes are described by the Jains in relation to all categories of reality (*padārtha*), each of which they accept as being only partially so. Some maintain that the word *syāt* means "somewhat" (*īṣat*); others hold that it means "non-exclusive" (*anaikāntya*). In either case, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions as a substitute for a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

The method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), demonstrated regarding existence in the form "it may be eternal," "it may be non-eternal," and so forth, is equally applicable to properties such as eternity and its opposite; therefore, this Jaina doctrine is also not tenable. For it is impossible for contradictory multiple attributes to coexist in a single entity without a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). [Objection: But is it not accepted that even in a single entity, there is a coexistence of contradictory attributes through a distinction of limiting conditions such as space and time?

But surely, even in a single entity, the coexistence of contradictory attributes is admitted on the basis of differences in limiting conditions such as place and time? It is not that this difference in limiting conditions is admitted merely because it is impossible in that case; rather, it is admitted because there is valid evidence for it.

For this very reason, even though the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) accepts the coexistence of "lump-ness" (piṇḍatva) and "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) through the distinction of temporal adjuncts (kālopādhi), he does not accept the coexistence of "individual-soul-hood" (jīvatva) and "Lord-hood" (īśvaratva) and so forth through any minor adjunct whatsoever, on the grounds that there is no evidence for such coexistence. Thus, it being established that the coexistence of attributes depends solely upon evidence (pramāṇa) and not upon the mere possibility of adjuncts, [the status of] reality (satyatva) and so forth—

If it is argued that since various proponents have established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and so forth, why should these not all coexist? We say no; for while it might be possible for all the means of valid cognition imagined by those various proponents to be valid, because they are mutually contradictory, it is certain that some must be fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*).

Otherwise, since the disputants [accept] the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the defects [they cite] regarding its unreality and so forth would themselves be objects of cognition; consequently, those defects would also have to be superimposed [upon the object], leading to the undesirable consequence that even the proponent of non-exclusivity (*anaikāntya*) would be subject to the very defects alleged by each respective opponent. By this, the statement in the *Syādvādamañjarī*—“Just as other doctrines are envious due to their mutual status as thesis and counter-thesis, so too is not this system, which desires all vehicles without distinction and is thus free from partiality”—is refuted.

For if one were to adopt [the doctrine] without partiality, there would be the undesirable consequence of including even those defects such as non-existence that have been stated by various [opposing] systems, since they too are included among the categories of existence and so forth mentioned in all [systems]. [Objection: In that case, we shall establish the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) precisely without contradicting worldly convention. For everyone agrees that for a single entity, existence and non-existence occur through a difference in time. Therefore, by intending to express each of these in its own respective time, there are the two propositions "it exists" and "it does not exist," intended sequentially.

"This is both existent and non-existent" is the third proposition (*bhaṅga*), intended by the desire to express existence and non-existence simultaneously. "It is indescribable" is the fourth proposition; for it is indeed impossible to describe the simultaneous existence and non-existence of a single thing. When existence and non-existence are taken together with their indescribability, and when existence, non-existence, and both taken sequentially are combined, the remaining three propositions are established. Thus Anantavīrya said: "When there is no desire to express those [specific] modes, the understanding would be 'it exists' (*syād asti*)."

"If the intention is to negate that [existence], the formulation 'it does not exist' (syān nāsti) would occur. When there is a desire for both [existence and non-existence] in succession, the formulation partakes of their combination. When there is a desire to express them simultaneously, it would be 'inexpressible' (avācya) due to incapacity. When the first [existence] is intended as inexpressible, the fifth proposition (bhaṅga) is accepted. When the last [non-existence] is intended as inexpressible, the sixth proposition arises. And when joined with a conjunction [of the two inexpressibles], it is called the seventh proposition."

If it is argued that, therefore, the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) is established through non-contradiction, then if this *saptabhaṅgīnaya* is merely conventional (*pāribhāṣika*), we certainly accept it. This is because ordinary people and investigators do not disagree when existence and non-existence are combined according to differences in place, time, and counter-correlate—such as a jar existing in its own place and not existing in another place, existing at its own time and not existing at another time, and existing in its own nature and not existing in another nature. However, this does not establish the "non-absolutism" (*anaikāntyasiddhi*) of the object as intended by the Jainas.

This is because there is no loss of the restrictive rule that [a thing] exists only at its own time and does not exist at other times, and so forth. If it is argued: "But for those who maintain the non-exclusivity (anaikāntya) of all phenomena, even unity is not established. Therefore, by adopting 'multiplicity' (*anekatva*) as a synonym for 'it may be manifold' (*syād aneka*), the coexistence of existence, non-existence, and so on, becomes logically possible," we say no. For it is impossible to establish—even without contradiction—the very coexistence of unity and multiplicity that was required in the first place.
