Furthermore, if the doctrine of absolute non-universality (*anaikāntyavāda*) were not accepted, it would be impossible to establish one’s own philosophical position that there are six substances, such as the soul (*jīva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth. What more need be said? For those who maintain that everything is non-universal, even the established order of "this is her son," "this is her husband," and "this is her father" could not be established; consequently, the appropriate social conventions regarding motherhood and the like among sons and others would also fail to be fixed. Therefore, this doctrine of non-universality must be rejected by all.

Furthermore, the Jains maintain that the self (ātman) is equal in size to the body; this too is untenable. For if the self, which occupies the entire body of an elephant, were to enter the body of a mosquito, it would follow that it becomes deficient [in size]. Moreover, when entering from the body of a mosquito into the body of an elephant, because it lacks the capacity for transformation sufficient to pervade that [larger] body, it would follow that it could not experience pleasure throughout all its limbs therein.

[Objection: Surely it is accepted that the self undergoes contraction and expansion, attaining successive states—either in the form of contraction or expansion—in accordance with its respective bodies; therefore, there is no fault. [Reply: No, for if that were so, it would follow that the self is subject to modification and the impermanence resulting therefrom. Therefore, even the Jainas must admit that in the state of liberation, the self remains with whatever its final dimension may be, since after that point there is no further body and thus no possibility of a dimension suited to one.

Therefore, since the dimension of the self is likewise eternal—just like the nature of the self as it exists in the state of liberation—it is logical to accept that very [dimension] as the self's natural size, rather than its possessing the capacity for contraction and expansion.
Summary Verses.
The Digambaras should not place their hopes in the system of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī),
for it is impossible for existence, non-existence, and so forth to occur simultaneously in a single thing.
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] in one [substratum].
On account of the inconsistency of the Lord [being the cause]. 35.
And because a substratum is untenable. ||36||
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of experience and so forth. ||37||
If [the self] were finite, it would follow that it is not omniscient. //38//

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is established that the doctrine of the Śaivas is also inconsistent, due to mutual contradictions—such as those between "existent" and "non-existent"—just like the doctrine of the Jainas, and because it contradicts the Vedas. Among the four types of Śaiva systems known as Kāpāla, Kālāmukha, Pāśupata, and Siddhānta-Śaiva, the views of the Kāpālas and the Kālāmukhas have been presented in the commentary. Regarding the Pāśupatas, they say: "The five categories—effect, cause, yoga, ritual injunction, and the end of suffering—must be understood for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its fetters (pāśa)."

In this context, the effects (*kārya*) consist of ten types: the five gross elements beginning with earth, and the five qualities (*guṇa*) beginning with form (*rūpa*). The instruments (*karaṇa*) are thirteenfold: the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the three internal organs consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Sacrifice (*yajña*) consists of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Ritual injunction (*vidhi*) refers to activity directed toward merit (*dharma*) and worldly ends (*artha*); it is twofold by way of vows (*vrata*) and gates (*dvāra*). Vows include the ritual bath in ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), sleeping on ashes (*bhasmaśayana*), offerings (*upahāra*), and the like. The ritual bath in ashes is of two kinds: one is obligatory (*nitya*), to be performed at the three junctions of the day as a substitute for the water-bath.

In cases such as the voiding of feces and urine, sneezing, or spitting, one should perform another occasional rite called the "subsequent bath" (*anusnāna*), which serves as a substitute for purification with water; furthermore, there is the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*). Sleeping on ashes should be performed using ashes obtained by begging from the houses of householders, just as one would beg for food. The offering (*upahāra*) is of six kinds, distinguished by laughter, song, dance, the *huḍukkāra* sound, prostration, and recitation (*japa*). Among these, laughter is loud, boisterous laughter. Song and dance are to be performed according to one's inclination, without regard for the rules of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*).
The *huḍukkāra* is a sound resembling the bellowing of a bull, produced by the contact of the tongue with the palate. In this matter, worldly people...

In that regard, these four [methods] do not exist; rather, they should be employed secretly. Recitation (*japa*) consists of the five Brahma-mantras; salutation (*namaskāra*) is well known. The gates (*dvārāṇi*) are of six kinds, distinguished by: bodily movement (*kāyanam*), trembling (*spandanam*), slow walking (*mandayānam*), affected speech (*śṛṅgāraṇā*), acting like another (*itatkaraṇā*), and speaking like another (*itadbhāṣaṇa*). Bodily movement (*kāyanam*) is the display of the characteristics of one who is asleep while actually being awake. Trembling (*spandanam*) is the shaking of the limbs of the body like one overcome by a wind-disease (*vātavyādhi*). Slow walking (*mandayānam*) is the manner of moving like one whose faculty of the feet is impaired.

*Śṛṅgāraṇa* (amorosity) is that behavior by which one displays amorous gestures toward a woman endowed with beauty and youth, as if one were a lover; it also includes performing actions censured by the world like one devoid of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done, and speaking words that are contradictory, meaningless, and so forth. *Duḥkhānta* (the end of suffering) is twofold: non-essential (*anātmaka*) and essential (*sātmaka*). The non-essential is the absolute cessation of all sufferings. The essential, however, is sovereignty characterized by the power of the faculties of vision and action.

In that regard, although the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) is one, it is figuratively designated as fivefold according to the distinction of its objects: seeing, hearing, thinking, discerning, and omniscience. Knowledge whose objects are all visual and tactile things—whether subtle, concealed, or remote—is "seeing. Knowledge whose object is every sound is "hearing. Knowledge whose object is the entirety of the scriptures is "thinking. Knowledge that is free from doubt regarding both the letter and the meaning is "discerning. Omniscience is well known.

The power of action (kriyā-śakti), though single, is treated as threefold: swiftness like thought (manojava-tva), the capacity to assume any form at will (kāmarūpa-tva), and the state of possessing the quality of being free from instruments (vikaraṇa-dharmitva). Swiftness like thought is the state of moving with unsurpassed speed. The capacity to assume any form at will is the state of presiding over infinite bodies and senses by one's own will, independent of karma. The state of possessing the quality of being free from instruments is the possession of unsurpassed sovereignty even when the body and senses have been withdrawn. As for Paśupati, he is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) who is the efficient cause (nimitta) in every effect.

For living beings, [the Lord] bestows fruits by His own will alone, independent of their karma, because He possesses unsurpassed sovereignty. Nor is karma thus rendered useless; for karma that is favored by the Lord's will is fruitful, while karma not so favored is fruitless—just as agricultural labor is fruitless when not favored by rain—but there is no fault in this, since engagement in actions is justified by the possibility of such favor. Furthermore, the sequence of creation is dependent upon the Lord's will at that particular time, and is not governed by a fixed rule such as "ether first" and so on.

The contradiction between such a Pāśupata doctrine and the Kāpālika and Kālāmukha doctrines is evident. Even though there is a similarity in terms of ritual action (*kriyā*)—such as the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*)—there is a contradiction regarding the nature of the ash to be accepted; for while [the others] hold that any ash whatsoever, like the ash of a corpse, should be smeared on, [the Pāśupatas] maintain that only specific ash is to be taken. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the Veda; for practices such as the *huḍukkāra* sound and so forth are not clearly found in the Vedas or their auxiliary scriptures (*upabṛhmaṇa*).

The practice of "loving dalliance" (śṛṅgāraṇa), the substitution of ash-baths and subsequent baths for water-baths—which thereby precludes the purification of water—and the disregard for the sequential order of abandoning living beings as prescribed by ritual action are all utterly contrary to the Vedic path. Thus, it is established that the three Śaiva systems beginning with Kāpāla are inconsistent due to their mutual contradictions and their opposition to the Vedas. Although Siddhānta Śaivism does not possess such extreme contradiction with the Vedas;

And in the absence of any contradiction with the Vedas, the mutual contradictions among the twenty-eight forms of the Tantras, beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula*, along with their sub-divisions—such as those consisting of the Āgama-siddhānta, Divya-siddhānta, Tantra-siddhānta, and Antaratantra-siddhānta varieties of the Pāñcarātra—can be reconciled by means of the different classes of qualified practitioners (adhikārī) recognized by each respective Tantra, just as the mutual contradictions among the various sub-tantras within the Pāñcarātra are reconciled.

The statement regarding the superiority of the Śiva-āgamas over the Veda found in texts such as the *Kāmika* can be reconciled in the same manner as the statement regarding the superiority of the *Pāñcarātra* over it. Nevertheless, even while accepting the authority of the Veda, the Siddhānta Śaiva Tantras conceal the Veda and establish the Lord through inference alone; this is certainly because, when the Lord is accepted according to the Veda, the causal statements generally designate the causal substance by the name "Nārāyaṇa"—a name unique to Puruṣottama—thereby indicating that He alone is the cause of the world and the Supreme Brahman.

It is concluded that the term "distinction" (*bheda*) is used for the purpose of concealing that [non-difference]. Therefore, we point out the inconsistency in their attempt to establish the Lord through inference alone. For, by observing distinctions such as the potter and the lump of clay in the world, they disregard the non-difference between the efficient cause and the material cause established by Śruti, and instead seek to prove an absolute efficient cause who is the Lord through inference. If that is so, then on the very basis of worldly observation, He must also be admitted to possess a body; for it is only potters and the like who are seen to be agents when they possess bodies.

Nor should it be argued that his body must consist solely of things like magical illusions (*māyā*) because they are objects of superintendence, since it is observed that in the functioning of one's own body there is no dependence on a body other than the one being controlled. For we do not mean merely any body; rather, we mean a body that serves as the locus of experience. Indeed, when one who presides over such a body for the sake of experience does so for the purpose of pleasure or the avoidance of pain, its localized nature is observed.

Furthermore, if one accepts a body as the locus of experience for the sake of accounting for agency, it would follow that [the self] possesses merit and demerit rooted in that [body]; because the body is necessarily impermanent, [the self] would be finite; and since those subject to the cycle of birth and death are observed to be limited in knowledge, [the self] would be non-omniscient. Therefore, for those who seek to establish God through inference, God would not be established in the form they intend.

As for the objection raised in the section on the Scripture being the Source (*Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*)—namely, that if God were established through inference, then the multiplicity of Gods and other such issues would also be established—that too is precisely the same objection as the one here. For it is in this very [present] context that the Sūtrakāra is seen to state the refutation of inference explicitly. In that [previous] context, however, the status of the Supreme Lord as having Scripture as His source was established solely through an investigation into the purport of such scriptural passages as "He is to be known from the Upaniṣads" (*Tattvam aupaniṣadam*). Therefore, there is no tautology with that [previous discussion].

In the Sāṃkhya section [of the *Brahmasūtra*], under the aphorism "And because the arrangement is impossible," the Sāṃkhya—who infers that the world, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, must have a cause of a similar nature according to the analogy of clay and pots—is met with the following consequence: "Then, by that very same example, there must necessarily be a presiding intelligence. However, it was not established therein that an independent inference for God is faultless; therefore, the Lord was not proven there. Consequently, there is no contradiction between the fact that the inference for God was accepted there and is refuted here.
(This is the summary verse.)
The husband's opinion is certainly not to be respected, for it is contradicted by each other even according to scripture;
moreover, the conception of God as a mere instrumental cause makes even His presiding over [the world] inconsistent.
Thus concludes the section concerning Paśupati.
Because origination is impossible. ||39||
And there is no instrument for the agent. 40.
Or, if consciousness and the other [aggregates] exist, there is no negation of that [self]. ||41||
And because of contradiction. ||42||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that the *Pāñcarātra* is likewise unauthoritative because it is a *tantra*—just like the *Pāśupata*—it is now refuted. The *Pāñcarātrikas*, known as the Bhāgavatas, believe that the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman, abides in the form of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) beginning with Vāsudeva. Among these, Vāsudeva possesses the six complete attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). These six attributes are knowledge, strength, sovereignty, power, and splendor.

In this context, his knowledge (*jñāna*) is said to be that which has all things as its object, because it is free from the obscuration of all particularities pertaining to the entire manifold (*prapañca*), whether sentient or insentient. His power (*śakti*) is the state of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the world. His strength (*bala*) is the absence of fatigue for one who creates the world, and the effortless sustaining of the entire universe he has created, like a mole on the skin. His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the state of having unimpeded will. His valor (*vīrya*) is the absence of transformation despite being the material cause of the world, just as milk remains itself even when becoming curd.

*Tejas* is the capacity for the creation of the world without dependence on auxiliary causes and the power to overcome others. From that, through the manifestation of the strength of knowledge (*jñāna*), he appears in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa. Then, through the manifestation of valor and sovereignty (*vīrya-aiśvarya*), he appears in the form of Pradyumna. Then, through the manifestation of power and splendor (*śakti-tejas*), he appears in the form of Aniruddha. And Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others have the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

In this way, by propitiating the Blessed One—who consists of the fourfold manifestation—daily through the fivefold practice beginning with *abhigamana* (approaching) and through vows lasting a hundred years or more, a person is liberated from the afflictions (*kleśas*). Among these, *abhigamana* is the recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, prostrations, and so forth, addressed to the Blessed One in the morning. Following that is *upādāna*, which is the procurement of flowers and other materials for worship. Next is *ijyā*, the actual act of worship. Finally, *svādhyāya* consists of listening to the scriptures of the Blessed One and the Purāṇas and Āgamas that accord with them.

"Therefore, Yoga is the concentration of the mind upon the Blessed One following the evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā). This [definition] is incorrect; such is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). For instance, in the *Pāñcarātra*, the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is traditionally taught: "From Vāsudeva, the individual soul named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born; from Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind named Pradyumna is born; from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) named Aniruddha is born. And it is not possible for an eternal (anādi) soul to have a birth.

Nor should it be said that this [text] asserts that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are the presiding deities (abhimānin) over the individual soul (jīva) and so forth; for if that were the case, such statements as "Saṅkarṣaṇa is the individual soul" would be untenable. For by this [text], the names Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are prescribed for the well-known individual soul, mind, and ego, according to the technical terminology of the Pāñcarātra.

Furthermore, when the *Saṅkarṣaṇa* and other names are mentioned and the prescriptions regarding their forms, weapons, and so forth are established in that scripture, it is proven that these are intended for the purpose of meditation upon those very [names], just as specific colors are prescribed for the letters beginning with "ka. It does not mean, however, that there are deities presiding over the mind who are characterized by such respective forms, weapons, and so on. Moreover, just as the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) is impossible, the production of the instruments such as the mind from the individual soul as their agent is likewise impossible.

Because it is heard in scripture that the mind and all the sense organs are born from the supreme Brahman alone—according to the text, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses"—therefore, the Pāñcarātra system also lacks authority due to its contradiction with the Vedas.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: in the Pāñcarātra, the production of the individual soul (jīva) from Vāsudeva, and of the mind and other faculties from the [other] souls and so forth, is not stated. Rather, what is taught is the manifestation of the emanations (vyūhas) such as Saṅkarṣaṇa, who are the presiding deities over the individual souls and the rest; this is established by the Śruti text: "Being unborn, he is born in many ways."

Furthermore, the verbal root is *janī-prādurbhāve* (to appear or manifest), and not the well-known terms such as "living being" (*jīva*) and so forth for which the names Saṅkarṣaṇa and others have been stated. This is because, in the second chapter, it will be demonstrated that words like "living being," which denote those who are governed, refer to specific manifestations of their respective governors; that words denoting the body extend to the embodied soul; and that words expressing inseparable attributes extend to the substratum possessing those attributes. Moreover, in the Pañcarātra itself, concerning the living being, it is said: "For he is indeed beginningless and endless in the ultimate sense..."
Furthermore, because its [the opponent's] arising is denied by the statement "it is certain," therefore the Pāñcarātra composed by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is indeed the preeminent authority.
Summary Verses.
If it is argued that the Pāñcarātra is not to be accepted because it teaches the origination of the individual soul (jīva), we say no;
for it speaks of the manifestation of the Vyūhas and explicitly denies the birth of the soul.
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility of origination.

Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, the second section of the *Caturmatasāra*, composed by Appayadīkṣita— the son of the illustrious Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and a teacher of the illustrious Advaita-vidyā, and a *kaustubha* [jewel] in the ocean of the lineage of the venerable Bharadvāja.
The third quarter of the second chapter.

It has been stated that the Sāṃkhya and other systems are inconsistent because they are rooted in fallacious reasoning and involve contradictions. Now, in order to refute the objection—which revolves in the mind as a counter-argument—that our own position also suffers from the defect of contradictory scriptural passages regarding whether the ether is produced or not produced, the manner in which the phenomenal world, as the effect of Brahman, constitutes an effect is clarified in the two subsequent sections (pādas).

If this were the case, then the first quarter (pāda), which serves to refute the objections raised by others regarding the proof of the effect-nature of ether and the rest, would follow immediately after that [first quarter]. If it is argued that the commencement of the two quarters concerning the effect follows the two quarters concerning the cause, then there would be no connection at all between this pair of quarters concerning the effect and the chapter as a whole.

If it is argued that the purpose of the second chapter is indeed to resolve the contradictions that obstruct the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with Brahman as the cause of the world—this concordance having been established in the first chapter—it is replied: The concordance of the scriptural texts concerning the cause with respect to Brahman depends upon the concordance of the texts concerning the origin of ether (*viyat*) and the other elements with their own literal meaning. Otherwise, if ether were eternal and if air and the other elements were not produced from ether and so forth, how could Brahman be the cause of ether and the rest?

And how could Brahman be the cause of every effect? Therefore, there follows an inquiry into the concordance of scriptural texts regarding the origination of ether and the other elements; and, as a consequence thereof, an inquiry into the eternality of the individual soul, its nature as a knower, its atomicity, and so forth.

Alternatively, once the lack of authority in the Sāṃkhya and other systems has been established by such sūtras as "And because of contradiction, [the system] is inconsistent," there might arise a doubt regarding the Vedāntas as well: that since they too contain mutually contradictory scriptural passages—such as those concerning the origin and non-origination of ether and so forth, and those concerning the soul's nature as a knower or its identity with knowledge—their authority would not be established beyond doubt due to the suspicion of a lack of authority even regarding their subject matter, namely the cause [of the universe].

One should also consider that the inquiry into the nature of the knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth is directly relevant, as it serves to raise an objection against the concordance of scriptural texts regarding the cause established in the first chapter. Here, first of all, the non-origination of ether (*viyat*) is established: "Ether is not [produced], because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]. (Sūtra 1.1.2)
It exists. ||2||
Because figurative application is impossible and because of the word itself. (Sūtra 3)
And it may belong to one [thing], like the word "Brahman. (Sūtra 4)
There is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction. ||5||
From words. ||6||
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world. ||7||
By this, Mātariśvan is explained. ||8||
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable. ||9||

Regarding the doubt as to whether space (*ākāśa*) is produced or not—based on the presence or absence of scriptural passages capable of establishing its production—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Space is not produced, because there is no scriptural passage capable of establishing its production. In the *Chāndogya*, for instance, there is no such scriptural passage at all regarding it. Even though such a passage exists in the *Taittirīyaka*, the *Atharvaṇa*, and other texts, it is not capable of establishing its production; for from those [texts], space is understood to be eternal due to its being partless and all-pervading. Nor is the second reason (the absence of a scriptural passage) unestablished.

Because it is impossible for its non-existence to be apprehended anywhere, the negation "space does not exist here" is contradicted; for that very place where it is negated is itself of the nature of space. Therefore, the term "originated" (*saṃbhūta*) heard in reference to space in the Taittirīya Śruti—"From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the senses, as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe"—and the term "is born" (*jāyate*) applied to space in the Atharvaṇa, must both be understood in a figurative sense. Nor...

There is no fault whatsoever in the difference of meaning between the two words *sambhūta* and *jāyate*, both of which are connected with the term *śruta*. Indeed, in the Atharva Veda itself it is said: "Brahman is built up by austerity; from that, food is born."

Therefore, since we observe that even in the two scriptural passages, "From that, this Brahman is born—name, form, and food," the word *brahman* appears in both its primary and secondary senses; and because even for one who maintains the production of ether (*viyat*), it must be admitted that in the scriptural passage, "And like the ether, it is all-pervading and eternal," the words "eternal" and "all-pervading"—though mentioned only once—are to be taken in their primary sense in one instance and in a secondary sense in the other. This being the position reached, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Where the priority of fire (*tejas*) is heard, it is precisely there in the *Chāndogya* that the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—proclaimed by means of the illustrations of the lump of clay and so forth—is not abandoned; for this occurs because even space (*ākāśa*), being an effect of Brahman, is non-different from it. Thus, it is determined that the fact of space being an effect of Brahman is also accepted by the *Chāndogya* scripture.

This is understood from such statements as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), which establishes unity prior to creation, and "All this has that as its Self" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7), which demonstrates that everything has Brahman as its Self; and by other such words, it is likewise determined. Thus, when through these words ether is also determined to be a modification of Brahman in a general sense, its specific production in the form of a separation from Brahman is already stated.

Just as in the world, having stated generally that "all these are the sons of Devadatta," by then specifying the birth of some of them from him, it is effectively stated that all of them were born from him; so too, one might ask, how is it that the priority of the creation of fire is heard in the Chāndogya? It is certainly not heard in scripture that fire was created first by Brahman, such that its priority would be established by the Vedic text.

However, since the creation of fire is mentioned first [in the text], its priority is established by the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*). Nor does the authority of position override the scriptural statement "the ether was produced" (*ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*). The reason based on partlessness (*niravayavatva*) as a proof for the eternity of ether is inconclusive; for in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), even that which is partless can be shown to be non-eternal, according to the analogy of pots, bowls, and other objects fashioned from a single lump of clay cited in the scripture.

Nor does the all-pervasiveness of space (viyat) follow from the contradiction of its negation by the statement "there is no space here," for in that case, it is appropriate to understand "space" as referring to an opening characterized by the absence of dense, material objects; this is because even in common usages such as "one should stand here in this space," that [absence] is also cognized through the notion of "here. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the scriptural testimony regarding the immortality of space, namely, 'The wind and the intermediate space—this is immortal'?"—the answer is: it has the same status as the scriptural testimony regarding the immortality of the wind.

For even air, which has a manifest origin, is heard in scripture to possess immortality. What need is there for more? Whatever exists apart from Brahman—whether it be the unmanifest (avyakta), the great (mahat), the ego (ahaṅkāra), fire (tejas), and so forth—all that, like space and air, possesses an origin, in accordance with the promise of the knowledge of all things and other such passages.
The summary verses.
Space is eternal because it is partless and because of the scriptural declaration of its immortality;
furthermore, since light is mentioned first in the account of creation, the scriptural statement regarding its being "born" is figurative.
The indivisibility [of the soul] is ineffective [as a reason for its immortality], just like the immortality of the gods;
the primacy of the word "fire" (tejas) has not been heard [in the text], and the contradiction is resolved by the order of the recitation.
Therefore, space and air possess birth along with the Great Principle (mahat) and the others;
for in this way, the proposition that all things are cognizable becomes logically consistent.
Thus concludes the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa).
From that [ether], fire [is produced]; for thus it says. ||10||
The waters. 11.
The earth. 12.
[The meaning is determined] from the context, the form, and other words. ||13||
But by meditating on Him alone, for that very reason, he [attains Him]. ||14||
But by the reverse order, the sequence as well as rebirth is established. ||15||
If it is argued that the intermediate consciousness and the mind [arise] sequentially because of their respective signs, we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. ||16||
But the designation [of the soul] as being dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative, because it exists only when those [bodies] exist. 17.

It has been determined that everything other than Brahman is the effect of Brahman. Here, this is considered: does the production of fire and the rest arise from each preceding element such as air, their being effects of Brahman occurring only through a succession; or rather, do they arise from the Supreme Self, who possesses each preceding element as His body? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: their production is indeed from each preceding element. For scripture declares: "From air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth."

Now, it is heard in scripture that the creation of fire and the other elements is preceded by reflection: "It [the Self] thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It created fire; that fire thought, and it created water; those waters thought, and they created food. Reflection is not possible for insentient things. Therefore, on the basis of the mark of reflection, the words "fire" and so forth refer to the Supreme Self as possessing those respective bodies. Thus, it is appropriate to state that from the Supreme Self having fire as its body, water arose with that [Self] as its body, and from that [Self] having water as its body, earth arose.

Nor should it be asked how the earth is denoted by the word "food" (*anna*) in the passage, "They created food. This is because the context concerns the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Within this section explaining the forms of the great elements as they are composed of the three [qualities], the form of "food" is mentioned in the statement: "That which is the red color of fire is the color of heat; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food. Furthermore, in the same context, another term denoting the earth is heard in the phrase, "From water, the earth."

If it is argued that, therefore, words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth must be understood as referring to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) who possesses those respective bodies—since in the *Antaryāmī-adhikaraṇa* it was stated that all things have the Supreme Self as their body—it is not so. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of abandoning the direct Vedic statement (*śrutihāni*) by resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for words like "fire" to mean the Supreme Self within those bodies. Nor is it proper to subvert a direct Vedic statement on the basis of the mark of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*). Rather, in accordance with the Vedic statement, it is proper to say that "seeing" itself is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). [As the scripture says: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the senses."

The Atharvaṇa mantra, "Space, wind, light, water, and earth, the supporter of all," is also appropriately explained as having for its purport the fact that [all things] are effects of Brahman, whether directly or through a lineage such as son, grandson, and great-grandson. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The world originates from the Supreme Self (paramātman) who possesses various bodies, as indicated by the mark of [His] prior reflection (īkṣaṇa). Nor is there any contradiction with scripture (śruti), because all words denoting the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings have their primary meaning (mukhyatva) in the Supreme Self who possesses those respective bodies. This is because, in worldly usage such as "the Brāhmaṇa studies" or "the Brāhmaṇa is learned," and in Vedic usage such as "one should initiate the Brāhmaṇa" or "the Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," it is established through linguistic convention (vyutpatti) that words denoting the body extend to the embodied being itself.

This is because it is understood from the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa that all things, moving and unmoving, constitute the body of the Supreme Self, and from the scriptural statement regarding the differentiation of names and forms—preceded by the entry into fire and other elements—"Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"—that [the Self is the body of all]. Nor should it be argued that the scriptural hearing of being the body of all is merely figurative; for after the creation of fire and the rest, the entry is heard specifically for the purpose of differentiating names and forms, as seen in another scriptural passage: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing. Thus it must be said.

Since it is impossible for the omnipresent Lord—who was previously non-existent in any particular place—to enter [the egg] later on, the scriptural texts concerning "entry" are intended to establish His eternal existence as the Controller. Therefore, because words such as "fire" and "water" have their primary meaning in the Supreme Self, it is determined from passages such as "That fire thought" that the Supreme Self alone is the direct creator of the entire phenomenal world. This is likewise determined by the Atharvaṇa mantra beginning with "From this [Self] is born."

For this mantra—according to the principle of son and grandson, that each subsequent effect among the unmanifest, mahat, ahaṃkāra, and so forth, arises from each preceding one—is naturally intended to convey the sequence in which everything arises directly from the Supreme Self alone, by reversing the order [of the effects]. Thus, the sequence consisting of the immediate succession of everything from the Supreme Self is indeed its inherent meaning.

And that [creation] is established as proceeding directly from Brahman, who possesses those respective bodies, because in the passage "from this [Brahman] it is born," directness is the primary and natural sense. If it is argued: "But this mantra has as its purport the sequence beginning with 'the vital breaths and the elements, from among these the eyes and so forth, and the mind are produced,' based on the evidence of the sequential recitation starting from ether and ending with earth; it does not intend to teach the production of everything, including the vital breaths and so on, from the Supreme Self"—we say: no.

The sense organs, the mind, the ether, and so forth are also included among those created directly by the Supreme Self, as indicated by the phrase "from this [Self] it is born," which applies equally to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For there is no specific scriptural statement to the effect that the vital breath alone is born directly, while others—such as the ether and so on—are born from Brahman through a succession, according to the analogy of a grandson and his progenitors. Furthermore, this mantra is not intended to establish a sequence; rather, the sequence regarding the ether and the rest is merely restated here, having been established by other scriptural passages. Elsewhere, what is contradicted by other scriptural passages is not accepted, as the sequence is clearly set forth in the *Subāla Upaniṣad*.
Therefore, the entire world [is created directly by the Supreme Self].
Thus it is established that [the world] arises directly from the Supreme Self alone.
The summary verses.
Fire, water, and earth arise from air, fire, and water respectively;
however, in accordance with scripture, Brahman alone is the ultimate root, like the immutable Puruṣa.
From the meditation taught in the Vedic tradition,
beginning with "That heat meditated," the cause of those [bodies] is indeed Brahman itself, possessing each respective body.
Thus, the statement, "He is born from this," and so forth, is logically consistent;
for, in the absence of any qualification, that [statement] makes known their immediate succession to Brahman alone.
Although words such as "splendor" (tejas) and others are well-known in common usage for other things,
through the study of grammar and the Vedas, they are understood to extend up to Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning fire.
The Self is not [the body], because it is heard [in scripture] to be eternal, and because of those [scriptural passages]. (18)

It is now considered whether the individual soul (jīva) is produced like ether and the other elements, or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is produced. This is because of scriptural statements such as, "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; [and] Prajāpati created the creatures," and because of the promise that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all, as well as the determination of unity prior to creation. Nor is production untenable on the grounds that the non-difference of the soul from Brahman is heard in the text, "That thou art."

For, by the scriptural hearing that "all this is indeed Brahman," there would follow the undesirable consequence that even ether and the other elements are unproduced. Nor should it be suspected that the denial of the soul's production is intended by the passage, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," because that would lead to the denial of the production of air and ether as well—since they are declared to be immortal—and because that [passage] actually refers to the absence of birth and death connected with the production and destruction of the body.

Furthermore, because the intention of this [text] is understood to be exactly the same as that of another scriptural passage which negates death associated with the body's demise—namely, "Verily, it is when devoid of life that this [body] dies; the living self does not die"—the objection regarding the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) is not a valid fault. For in the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), which is accepted by the proponent [of this system], substance is eternal; its destruction is the relinquishing of a previous state, and its origination is the attainment of another state. Thus, since the living self is eternal in its nature as a substance, those two faults do not apply.

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, it would follow that the individual soul (jīva) must be admitted to undergo origination in the form of coming into being after not having existed, just like jars and other such things. Therefore, the soul is produced like ether and the rest. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The individual soul (jīva) is not produced, unlike ether and other elements. This is because its non-production is heard in such passages as, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," and from such Śruti texts as, "Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, this [soul] is not slain when the body is slain," and "The eternal among eternals, the consciousness among conscious beings. Furthermore, since its eternity is established, it is understood that there is no production of it.

Nor should it be said that the Śruti statement, "It is neither born nor does it die," is intended merely to negate birth and death associated with the body's production and destruction; for in that very same passage, by the statement "It is not slain when the body is slain," which speaks of the absence of being slain in relation to the slaying of the body, there is no need to state that [negation] separately, as its meaning is already established.

Furthermore, if one were to admit that the non-sentient (ajīva) transforms into the form of the sentient (jīva) prior [to creation]—just as space previously exists in the form of non-space—the faults of "loss of what was done" (*kṛtahāna*) and "acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) could not be avoided; for merit and demerit, which are necessarily the products of a sentient agent, could not possibly reside in a non-sentient entity. Moreover, the promise of universal cognition and the determination of oneness are both consistent with the view that the sentient being, prior to creation, exists in a subtle state and, during creation, attains the state of a gross effect. How, then, is this different from the doctrine of the *Vidādis*?

Thus—the ether and other elements possess a change in their essential nature (svarūpa), and it is by virtue of that form that they have the status of being effects. However, for the soul (jīva), which is immutable, there is no change in its essential nature; rather, there is merely a change in its attributes (dharma) characterized by the contraction and expansion of the quality called knowledge (jñāna). It is on account of that alone that it has the status of being an effect. This will become clear in the subsequent section (adhikaraṇa).

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other being restricted. 32.

In connection with the inquiry into the origin of the individual soul (*jīva*), its attributes such as being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) are examined by resolving the contradictions with scriptural texts concerning its nature as knowledge; this is for the purpose of establishing the unimpeded authority of those scriptural passages regarding Brahman, the cause of the world. Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that the modification (*vikāra*) of the individual soul consists in a change of its attributes rather than a change in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), because there exists no attribute called "knowledge" apart from its essential nature.

For since knowledge alone is its very nature, the introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṃgati*) should also be understood as arising from this point. Regarding the doubt—whether the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of knowledge, or whether it is indeed insentient (*jaḍa*) with knowledge being adventitious, or whether it is eternally a knower by itself as the substratum of the quality of knowledge—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: "Knowledge performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts."

"One who, dwelling in consciousness, is within consciousness, whose nature is knowledge, and who is utterly pure in the ultimate sense"—from such scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti), one prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the Self is indeed of the nature of knowledge. Another [prima facie] view, however, holds that if the individual soul (jīva) were of the nature of knowledge, then since it is all-pervading, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its perceiving all objects at all times; furthermore, there would be the consequence of the eyes and other organs being useless; and there would also be the consequence of the absence of states such as deep sleep and fainting, which are characterized by a lack of cognition. Therefore, its being of the nature of knowledge is not tenable.

Therefore, even the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), as intended by the Siddhāntin on the grounds of being the substratum of eternal knowledge, is untenable. Rather, it must be accepted—as in the view of the Naiyāyikas and others—that [the Self] possesses knowledge dependent upon instruments such as the eyes. This being the position reached, the Siddhānta states:

Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as, "Now, he who thinks 'let me smell this,' he is the Self; seeing these desires with the mind, he rejoices; the seer sees not death; this person indeed knows," and "For he is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster," it follows that this Self is indeed known. And even if this is so, there is no consequence of its perceiving all objects at all times, because of its atomicity (*aṇutva*), as stated in such scriptures as, "He is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster."

And its atomicity [is established] from the scriptural mention of its departure, going, and returning. For its departure, going, and returning are heard in such passages as: "By that light this Self departs; and all those who depart from this world go to the moon alone; from that world they return again to this world for the sake of action. And these cannot be logically accounted for if it were omnipresent.

If it is argued that the self is not atomic because, after introducing the individual soul (jīva) as connected with the vital breaths in the passage, "This one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," the text later declares, "He indeed is this great unborn Self," and thus its greatness is taught—this is not so. For in that context, it is Brahman, other than the individual soul, that is the subject; even though the individual soul is introduced at the beginning, the Supreme Self is established in the middle by the statement, "He whose Self is known and realized," and the teaching of its greatness is intrinsically connected to that [Supreme Self].

Furthermore, the direct atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is heard in scripture: "This subtle self is to be known by the mind, in which the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has entered fivefold. Also, its state as a minute atom is heard in such passages as: "The soul is to be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold," and "A part of a hundredth part of the tip of an awl. If this is so, one might ask: how can the soul, residing in only one part of the body, experience pleasure and other sensations throughout all its limbs? We reply: it is like sandalwood paste.

Just as a drop of yellow sandalwood paste, though residing in only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation that pervades the entire body, so too the individual soul (jīva), though situated in one place, experiences happiness extending to all its limbs. This is because, according to such scriptural passages as, "This which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart; for this Self is in the heart," it is accepted that the soul also resides in the region of the heart.

In reality, however—the individual soul (jīva), although situated in the heart, pervades the entire body by means of its own quality, knowledge, just as a gem or the sun pervades many places with its rays located in a single spot. Nor should it be doubted that the self is of the very nature of knowledge and does not possess knowledge as a quality; for just as there is a distinction between fragrance and the earth despite fragrance being perceived as a quality of the earth, so too [is the case here].

This is because knowledge—which is experienced as an attribute of the self—is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*). This is shown by the Śruti text, "This person surely knows," which demonstrates that knowledge is an attribute of the knower; and also because of the separate instruction regarding the knower and knowledge in the Śruti text, "For there is no loss of the knower's [knowledge]. How then is there the conventional usage of its being of the nature of knowledge in passages such as, "Knowledge performs the sacrifice"? It is because knowledge is its essential attribute (*sāra*). For knowledge is indeed its essential quality.

And therefore, just as for Brahman—which is pure consciousness (prājña)—knowledge and bliss are its essential attributes, such that there is a designation of knowledge and bliss in the passages, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "Bliss is Brahman," so too here there is a designation of knowledge. Now, one might object: in the phrase "truth, knowledge," by the force of the final acute accent (udātta), the meaning appears to be "the state of possessing knowledge. However, this is not the case, because if the suffix *lyuṭ* were used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), the final acute accent would be impossible.

For instance: in the case of the suffix *ana* (the substitute for *lyuṭ*), by the rule "ādyudāttaśca," the first vowel (*a*) of the suffix receives the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Then, because the suffix marker *lit* is present, by the rule "lit-svareṇa," the radical vowel (*a*) also becomes udātta. Consequently, by the rule "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam," the remaining vowels are assigned the *anudātta* accent; thus, the two *a*s residing in the suffix become *anudātta*. When the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the radical *a* and the initial *a* of the suffix occurs, by the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ," this single substitute becomes udātta. This being so, [the status of] the final *a* of the suffix, which is *anudātta*, [is as follows:]

Furthermore, regarding the vowel *a* of the case-ending, since it is anudātta (unaccented) by the rule "anudāttau suppitau," its replacement by the single substitute [of the preceding and following vowels] according to "ami pūrvaḥ" would also be anudātta by the paribhāṣā "sthānāntaratamaḥ. And for that anudātta, there would be a svarita substitute according to "udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ. For this very reason, the word *tat jñānam* would end in a svarita if it were formed solely with the suffix lyuṭ; as in the Kaṭha recension: "saṃjñānaṃ vijñānaṃ prajñānam."

Therefore, in order to account for the final acute accent (*antodātta*), this word *jñāna* must be explained as being derived from a different suffix *lyuṭ* (ana), or as ending in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). This is because the *arśas* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Such being the case, the final acute accent is logically established.

In the case of the word *arśas-* with the suffix *-ya-* (by Pāṇini 5.2.127), when the final vowel *a* of the base is elided by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), and the suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) becomes acute by the accent of the *cit*-suffix (Pāṇini 6.1.163), then the single substitute for that [acute] vowel of the suffix and the vowel of the case-ending also becomes acute by the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.5). Thus, if one follows this derivation of the word *jñāna*, it would only establish that the self possesses knowledge (*jñānavattva*), not that its very nature is knowledge (*jñānarūpatva*).

If it is argued that, therefore, its nature as knowledge is not perceived by this [word], it is replied: when one resorts to the view that it ends in an *auṇādika* suffix *-na*, then that [nature] also appears. Even though no suffix is prescribed directly for the verbal root *jñā*, because the term "variously" (*bahulam*) is included in the rule "the *uṇādi* suffixes occur variously," these suffixes occur elsewhere as well; thus, its establishment [as knowledge] is achieved. Furthermore, its status as having the sense of a state (*bhāva*) is also justified when it ends in an *auṇādika* suffix.

Since the suffix *man* prescribed by the *arty-ādi* sūtra would result in an udātta accent, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for that [suffix] and the vowel of the case-ending would also necessarily be udātta. Thus, although both derivations of the word *jñāna* are possible here, the author of the Bhāṣya, intending that the sense of "being" (bhāva) is more appropriate—on the grounds of brevity of derivation (*prakriyālāghava*)—by taking it as ending in the Uṇādi suffix *-na*, has cited this as evidence for its nature as knowledge itself. Furthermore, it is designated as such because knowledge persists as long as the self exists.

This is because we observe that even for things like sugar-candy and the like, they are designated by words such as "cow," which denote properties like "cowness" (gotva) that persist as long as the thing's own nature exists. Furthermore, the designation of the individual soul (*jīva*) as "knowledge" is justified by its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). This self-luminosity is relative to itself alone and not dependent on another; even this self-relation consists merely in its being qualified by immediacy (*pratyaktva*) and unity (*ekatva*) as expressed in the notion "I. However, the quality of illuminating both itself and others belongs specifically to the knowledge of attributes (*dharma-jñāna*). Thus, the relationship between the attribute and the substratum, or between knowledge and its object, follows the analogy of light and its source.

As they say: "A lamp is the illuminator of itself, while its radiance is the illuminator of both itself and other things; thus there is this distinction between the two cognitions, even though they share the same nature as property and substratum. Now, one might object: since cognition is absent during states such as deep sleep, how can it be a quality intrinsically connected to the very nature of the self, like the property of being a cow?

We say that it is manifested like virility and so forth: just as in a body composed of the seven constituents (dhātus), the seventh constituent in the form of virility, though always present, is not manifested in childhood or even in youth; likewise, the quality of knowledge, though always present, is not manifested in deep sleep as it is in the waking state. Even then, there is no loss of self-luminosity, which consists in the fitness for being self-manifesting by itself. Indeed, the "I-sense" (ahamartha) continues to be manifest even in deep sleep.

This is because of the retrospective reflection (parāmarśa): "I slept happily. As they say: "When the self-luminous, eternal blissful Person is established [as the substrate], in such cognitions as 'I slept happily,' there is an inferential establishment regarding the temporal and other factors. Just as sweetness and so forth appear in such cases as 'I sang sweetly' or 'I drank wine,' so too here, the happiness shines forth as belonging to that very time. Therefore, in our position—that the quality of knowledge possesses contraction and expansion, while its substratum, the individual soul (jīva), is atomic—there is no defect whatsoever.

However, regarding the position that "the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of consciousness and is all-pervading," there would necessarily follow either the consequence of its being eternally perceived or not perceived, or else a restriction to one or the other. To explain: if the nature of the soul, which is all-pervading consciousness, were the cause of perception alone, then it would be perceived everywhere, just as it is in the region delimited by the body. If, on the other hand, it were the cause of non-perception alone, then it would not be perceived even in the region delimited by the body. If it were the cause of both, [the aforementioned contradiction would persist].

In the third case, constant perception and non-perception would be mutually contradictory. This same defect applies even to the position of the Naiyāyikas and others, who hold that the soul (*jīva*) is omnipresent but possesses knowledge that arises and moves in dependence upon instruments such as the eyes. This point will become clear in the section [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] beginning with "A part [of Brahman], because of various designations" (*aṃśo nānā-vyapadeśāt*).
[The following are] the summary verses:

Some have declared that the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of consciousness, and it is heard that it is so; yet others have said that it possesses the state of being a knower through adventitious cognitions.
Others maintain that it possesses eternal consciousness; thus, here, the middle position of reasoning is established.
For this pervasive soul would otherwise be unable to know [objects] situated at a great distance.

It is not the case that this [self] becomes omniscient merely by virtue of being of the nature of a knower as proclaimed in the Upaniṣads— such as "He knows indeed"— for it is atomic according to the measures of its departure, movement, and so forth; rather,
its pervasion of the body is logical due to its quality of knowledge, which is like the light of a lamp.
The statement that it is "knowledge" is consistent because it possesses the essence of being a quality, and it is also self-luminous.
Thus ends the section concerning knowledge.
There is a creator, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. (33)

And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the grammatical indication. ||35||
There is no fixed rule, just as in the case of perception. ||36||

And because of the absence of meditative concentration. ||38||
And as the carpenter [is] in both ways. ||39||

Following the examination of the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), agency (*kartṛtva*) shall now be examined; since action (*kṛti*) is dependent upon knowledge, there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) based on the relationship of cause and effect. Just as in the case where the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading and identical with the nature of consciousness, the established order of the restriction of perception and so forth would be untenable, so too, if Prakṛti were the agent, because she is common to all, the established order of the restriction of agency would be untenable—this is what is stated here.

And there is a connection with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntasaṅgati*). When the doubt arises as to whether the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is due to the superimposition of agency upon it because Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) alone is the agent, or whether the soul is an agent by its very nature—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the Self is indeed a non-agent. This is because of the scriptural statement in the *Kaṭhavallī*: "If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. Here, "slayer" (*hantā*) means "one who slays. The suffix *-tṛ* (forming *hantṛ*) is an *auṇādika* suffix, as in words such as "living being" (*jantu*).

This is because it has the same meaning as the statement in the Gītā: "He who knows this [Self] as the slayer, and he who thinks this [Self] is slain—both of them do not understand; this [Self] neither slays nor is it slain. Furthermore, the negation of being the agent of killing is an illustration (upalakṣaṇa) for the negation of agency in general. For this very reason, the Lord says in the Gītā: "Actions are performed in every way by the qualities of *prakṛti*; one whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the agent. In the state of being the cause of action and its instrument, *prakṛti* is said to be the cause."

"The person is said to be the cause for being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), superimposing upon itself either the agency residing in primordial nature (prakṛti) or the agency residing in the intellect (buddhi)—which is a specific transformation of nature unique to each individual soul—is designated as the "agent. The scripture also proceeds by taking into account such agency, along with the conventional usage regarding the acquisition of materials and so forth. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

If either the intellect (*buddhi*) or primordial nature (*prakṛti*) were the agent, then scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "one desiring liberation should meditate on Brahman" would be enjoining only the enjoyer who desires fruits such as heaven and liberation; this is according to the maxim: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer. Furthermore, the scripture enjoins the agent by means of generating knowledge. Since neither the insentient intellect nor primordial nature can be made to know, it is logical that the Self alone—because it is the enjoyer and because it is capable of being made to know—is the one enjoined by the scriptures of prescriptions and prohibitions.

Furthermore, the immutable Self cannot even be capable of superimposing the agency belonging to another—the agent—upon itself. Therefore, since superimposition must be understood as having the nature of a quality of that [Self] by way of being a transformation of the knowledge of qualities which stands in the place of the Self's own light, let action (kṛti) likewise be understood as having the nature of a quality of that [Self]. For what purpose, then, is it postulated that the manifestation "I am the agent" is of the nature of an error, and that the scripture has for its object an agency produced by error, even though no sublation is perceived?

If the killer thinks, "I am killing," this [notion] is consistent with the subject matter of the mantra, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," because the preceding mantra, "He is not slain even when the body is slain," has established that the Self, being distinct from the body, is incapable of being killed. Furthermore, the passages prohibiting agency are consistent with other statements of his own: "In this situation, he who perceives the isolated Self as the agent, due to his unrefined intellect, does not see, O dull-witted one. Thus, they share the same meaning.

Furthermore, because we see the teaching regarding its dwelling through appropriation in the passage, "Just as a great king, having taken hold of his subjects, moves about as he pleases in his own kingdom, even so this [Self], having taken hold of these vital breaths, moves about as it pleases in its own body," and because consciousness is designated as the agent in worldly and Vedic activities in the statement, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts," the Self is indeed the agent. Nor does the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) refer to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), for in the case of a reference to the internal organ...

Because in the Śrutis the instrumental case alone is observed; here too, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of a reversal in that designation. Indeed, in other passages such as, "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of [his own] consciousness," the word *vijñāna* (consciousness), referring to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is seen to be designated with the instrumental case. Furthermore, if Prakṛti were the agent, since it is common to all souls, the restriction of actions would also be impossible—just as the restriction of perception and so forth mentioned in the previous section is impossible due to Prakṛti's universality.

And thus, all actions would result in the experience of everyone, because according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, since the selves are all-pervasive (vibhu), there is no distinction in their proximity to everything everywhere. Nor should it be argued that this fault does not apply to the view where the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the agent, on the grounds that internal organs are distinct for each body; for it is impossible to establish a restriction to individual selves regarding those [organs] and their substrates, the bodies, which arise in the presence of all selves.

Furthermore, on the view that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent, since it is impossible for one who is the agent to be a different entity from the enjoyer, the intellect itself would have to be the enjoyer; consequently, the Self would lack the power of being an enjoyer. Thus, there would be a contradiction with their own accepted tenet that "the Person exists because of the state of being an enjoyer. Moreover, if the intellect were the agent, then even the agency in *samādhi*—which is the means to liberation consisting in the realization "I am other than primordial nature" (*prakṛti*)—would have to be attributed to that very intellect.

Furthermore, neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—in its own form nor in the form of the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*)—is capable of concentrating with the thought, "I am the immutable one, distinct from primordial nature. Moreover, if agency were admitted for the Self, it would act when there is a desire and not act otherwise; this restriction is intelligible, just as a carpenter, though equipped with tools such as an axe, acts only when there is a desire and not otherwise. However, if the insentient intellect were the agent, then because of the absence of any cause for restricting its desire for experience and so forth, it would be an agent at all times. Therefore, it is logical that the Self alone is the agent by its very nature.
"He is not the agent of the qualities, for agency is attributed to the all-pervading Lord.
[Reply: "It is not so; because of the meaningfulness of the scriptures and other reasons, he is the agent through his association with the qualities."
Thus ends the section concerning the agent.
But [the self] is from another, because of scripture. ||33||
But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons. (34)

The connection [of this section] is that, having considered agency in general, its specific nature is now considered. Since there is a doubt—arising from the scriptures on injunctions and prohibitions on one hand, and the scripture concerning the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) on the other—as to whether the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) belongs to it independently or is dependent upon the Supreme Self, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the agency of the individual soul is indeed independent. Otherwise, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered utterly useless.

Nor should one suspect that agency is dependent upon the Supreme Self on the basis of such scriptural texts concerning the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) as: "The Teacher has entered within, the Self of all beings; for he alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds, and he indeed makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down."

If that were the case, it would follow that the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions—which function solely for the purpose of inducing or restraining human activity—would become utterly useless; furthermore, it would result in the inconsistency of the scripture concerning the Inner Controller (antaryāmin). For it is not reasonable to suppose that anyone, having himself caused another to perform some undesirable action, would then inflict punishment as its fruit. This being the position reached, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

His agency is dependent upon the Supreme Self, because it is impossible to subvert that [dependence] when the multitude of scriptures concerning the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) remains uncontradicted; moreover, the non-futility of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions can be established without contradicting that [dependence]. This is because the Lord exists in three states: He is indifferent toward the initial activity, but toward subsequent activities He is the permissive witness, causing His own devotees and those who hate Him to perform actions that are respectively desired and undesired by Him.

For instance—the Lord remains indifferent at first, having provided the soul with the instruments of action, such as the body and so forth, while observing, "What will this one do? He then permits the second and subsequent activities in the form of the fruits of whatever merit or demerit that soul performs; this permission for what has already begun to proceed is called *anumati*.

As for the virtuous action (sādhukarma) of those seeking liberation, such as surrender (prapatti) and meditation (upāsana), and the non-virtuous action (asādhukarma) of the tamasic who hate the Lord, such as blaspheming Him—He Himself causes both of these to be performed. The two scriptural passages beginning with "For He indeed... refer specifically to those [two types of people], not to everyone. [This is known from: "To those who are ever steadfast and worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me," and "But them, hating and cruel, the lowest of men in this world, I hurl into births... [and so forth].

And because of the Lord’s own words, "I incessantly cast the inauspicious ones into the very wombs of the Asuras," there is room for the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions elsewhere; thus, some teachers maintain that they are not entirely useless, and they resolve that apparent futility.

Others, however, say: "The scope of the scripture concerning the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) should not be restricted in this manner. For there is no evidence for postulating that the Blessed Lord is indifferent toward or merely a permissive witness regarding the specific actions of individual souls. Furthermore, there is no basis for postulating that the cited statements from the *Gītā* extend to the point of His not being the instigator of other actions. Nor can such a postulation be made merely to avoid rendering the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions purposeless."

Even though God is a cause in all prescribed and prohibited actions—just as time, unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), and the sense organs are causes—the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) remains unimpaired; for it is logically consistent that God’s causality exists just like His will and other attributes. Nor is it the case that...

Thus, it cannot be said that the soul lacks agency—characterized as "the agent being independent" with respect to prescribed and prohibited actions—on the grounds that its independence is lost because the Lord compels it, like a man being dragged by the current of a river. For we observe that even ministers and other subordinates, though appointed by a king who acts as their instigator, exercise independence in their own respective duties as they proceed according to their own will.

Therefore, since it is impossible to justify the non-futility of injunctions and prohibitions without restricting the *Antaryāmi-śāstra*, one should not postulate such a restriction. The detailed exposition supporting both these views is to be found in their respective texts.
The summary verses.
If the agency of embodied beings is described as being dependent on the Lord,
then the futility of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions can be countered by no one.
There is indeed the scriptural testimony that the lotus-eyed Lord is both the ruler and the controller;
it is now explained how He, as the leader, ensures that one does not commit transgressions of injunctions and prohibitions.
Having first bestowed the instruments, the body, and so forth, the Lord remains indifferent while one exerts effort;
afterwards, He sanctions the fruit thereof. Thus, for some, He becomes even the instigator of their action.

Some have asserted that the scriptural texts concerning the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) must be restricted in scope due to the fear that otherwise other [scriptural] passages would be rendered purposeless; this applies particularly to those actions performed by those who hate seekers of liberation.
Just as there is dependence on desire and so forth, there is likewise dependence on the Lord;
yet, by that much alone, the scriptures do not become useless—thus the opponents maintain that [the Lord's power] is unrestricted.
Thus concludes the section concerning dependence on another.
A part [of Brahman], because of various designations and also otherwise; moreover, some record that He is like the fisherman, the wood-cutter, and so forth. (3.2.27)
