The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, if there were a relationship of the impelled and the impeller between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as in the case of a king and his servant, there would be an absolute difference between them; consequently, even the statement that the individual soul is a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman) would have to be regarded as merely figurative.

Is the individual soul (*jīva*) absolutely different from the Supreme? Or is it the Supreme Brahman itself in a state of ignorance? Or is it Brahman limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*)? Or is it a constituent part of the qualified Brahman in the form of its qualification? Due to such conflicting scriptural statements, a doubt arises; therein, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the individual soul is absolutely different [from Brahman], because of the mention of difference in passages such as, "The two—the Knower and the ignorant. Alternatively, the individual soul is Brahman itself when ignorant, because of scriptural texts such as, "That thou art," and "This Self is Brahman."

Brahman itself, as delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of sentient beings, is the individual soul (jīva). This is known precisely from scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). It is not logical to hold that the jīva is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman; for being a "part" does not mean having the nature of a limb or member, like [the parts of] a thread [in a cloth], because Brahman, being partless, cannot be composed of limbs. For this very reason, it is also not a part in the sense of a fragment of stone split by a chisel, since Brahman is incapable of being divided. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

The individual soul (jīva) is indeed a portion (aṃśa) of Brahman, because of the designation of difference and because of the designation of non-difference. For a great many designations of difference are observed, such as being the creator and the created, the controller and the controlled, omniscience and limited knowledge, self-dependence and dependence on another, lordship and subservience; likewise, the designation of non-difference is also seen in such passages as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). Moreover, the followers of the Atharva Veda study in the *Brahmasūkta* that Brahman even possesses forms such as Dāśa and Kitava.

"Brahma’s slaves, Brahma’s servants, and Brahma’s gamblers—I am their [master]; both woman and man are born from Brahma; whether it be a woman or a man, they are Brahma. Therefore, one must accept that the individual soul (jīva) is a specific part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Brahman acting as its attribute. Only when this is so are the scriptural texts concerning both difference and non-difference, as well as the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation, rendered consistent.

However, in the theories that define the Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) as being delimited by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of truth and falsehood respectively, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation becomes untenable, as does the consistency of all the scriptures; this has been elaborated elsewhere. Therefore, it is logical that the individual soul is indeed a part (*aṃśa*) that constitutes a specific portion of the Whole. This is understood from the Vedic mantra: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three immortal feet are in heaven," and from the statement in the *Gītā*: "An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul, exists in the world of the living. Thus it is known.

And thus, just as light is a qualifying part (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) of luminous objects such as gems, or as the body of gods, humans, and so forth is [a qualifying part] of embodied beings, in the very same way, the individual soul (*jīva*) is a qualifying part of the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of being an inseparably established mode (*apṛthaksiddhaprakāra*) and by virtue of being His body. Yet, it is not the case that they are identical. Consequently, the scriptural texts concerning difference are justified by the distinction between the qualifiers, while the scriptural texts concerning non-difference are justified by the unity of the qualified entity.

The individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) and so forth, is not of the same nature as the Supreme (*para*), which is characterized by being the subordinate (*śeṣin*) and so forth; thus, through the analogy of light and its source and by way of the relationship between body and embodied, the established relationship of subordinate and superior between the *jīva* and the Lord is logically consistent. Furthermore, Parāśara and others record the analogy of light and its source and the relationship of body and embodied regarding the *jīva* and the Lord: "Just as the radiance of fire situated in one place spreads abroad, so too is this entire universe the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Brahman."

"O twice-born one, whatever being is created by whomsoever, in the production of that which is created, all of that is indeed the body of Hari. Now, if it is asked: "Since there is no distinction in the fact that all are portions of the Lord, why is the study of the Vedas and so forth permitted for the twice-born, while it is prohibited for the Śūdras? We reply: it is due to the connection with specific bodies.

Just as fire, water, and so forth are fit for ritual action when situated in the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), yet those same elements become unfit for ritual action once they reach a cremation ground, so too the two states of permission and prohibition are logically established for the selves (*ātman*) depending on their state of abiding in various bodies. Although all selves are uniform insofar as they are portions of Brahman (*brahmāṃśatva*), there will be no confusion of experiences because they are distinct from one another and, being atomic (*aṇu*), are separate in each body.

However, the doctrine of the identity of Brahman and the Self necessarily entails the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Supreme (*para*), as well as the identity among all individual souls. Nor can it be argued that this consequence does not arise because of the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); for there is no valid cause to establish the existence of distinct limiting adjuncts that could obscure the essential nature of Brahman, which is an undivided, single-flavored manifestation of pure light. Indeed, a limiting adjunct, even as it enters into Brahman, does not divide Brahman in the way an axe falling upon a block of wood divides that block of wood. If it is argued that the limiting adjuncts themselves are distinct [from one another], [the response follows].

What follows from that? How could the confusion resulting from the identity of the substrata of experiences—which would arise through the distinction of those very substrata—be avoided? If it is argued that, in the theories of Brahman and the individual soul as conditioned by real and unreal adjuncts respectively, there will be a systematic order due to the power of beginningless unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) which cause the adjuncts, we say no.

Since even invisible limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot bring about division and so forth within the indivisible Brahman, this also refutes the objection that the systematic order of experience is maintained through the specific determination of bodies, the performance of volitions, and the causes of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). For there is no cause for restricting to each individual soul those volitions and other factors which arise in the presence of all souls alike. If it is argued that the systematic order of experience may be established by a distinction between the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) of the Self, we say no; for the parts of Brahman that are contained within bodies must themselves be declared to be the substrata of experience.

However, the spatial points contained within those [bodies] are not fixed, because almost all spatial points are included within all moving bodies. Therefore, just as in the theory of an omnipresent self (*sarvagatātmapakṣa*), even in the theory of the identity of the self as conditioned by real limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the regulation of experience (*bhogavyavasthā*) is not possible; thus it is established that, like the atomicity of selves, their distinctness (*bheda*) must also be accepted.
The Summary Verses.

If the individual soul were absolutely different from the Supreme, its movement [into the body] would be merely figurative; if there were absolute non-difference, however, the unavoidable confusion resulting from the multitude of texts on difference would be difficult to avoid.
Therefore, it is appropriate here that the soul is a part of the Supreme; indeed, it must be a portion of a single reality.
This renowned [quality] is a specific part and a particular mode within the distinguished Blessed One.
Thus ends the section concerning the parts (aṃśādhikaraṇa). ||7||

Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, a work on the essence of the four systems composed by Appayya Dīkṣita— the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarāja Adhvarin, who was a jewel of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage and a teacher of the glorious Advaita Vidya.
The fourth quarter of the second chapter.
Likewise, the vital breaths. ||1||
Because a figurative sense is impossible, and because that [figurative sense] was previously rejected. ||2||
Because speech is preceded by that [mind]. ||3||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: after the determination of the soul’s birth, its subsequent bondage, its nature as a knower, and so forth, the manner of the origin of the sense organs—the instruments of the soul—is now clarified. A doubt arises due to conflicting scriptural statements (śruti-vipratipatti) regarding whether the origin of the sense organs is an origination consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*), like that of ether and other elements, or whether it is merely a change in state (*dharma-anyathābhāva*), like that of the soul. Regarding this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: although it was established in the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*) that "everything other than Brahman is subject to origination," nevertheless, concerning the sense organs—

There is no production in the form of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*), as in the case of space (*viyat*) and other elements. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding their persistence even at the time of the beginning of creation: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asat*). Regarding that, they asked: 'What was there then? [The reply is: 'In the beginning, there were indeed the seers (*ṛṣi*); what were those seers? They are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),' for the plural form of the word *prāṇa* refers specifically to the sense organs, as seen in the usage: 'When the [chief] breath departs, all the breaths depart after it. Furthermore, the word *ṛṣi* also refers to them in the passage: 'Of that non-existent, the seven seers were the shores.'"

And because [the usage] is seen [in that sense]. Although the word *prāṇa* is indeed seen used for Brahman, and the word *ṛṣi* is applicable [to Brahman] because of its possession of knowledge, nevertheless, the connection of these two words in their plural forms with it (Brahman) is not tenable. The plural number here cannot be explained—as in the case of "the nooses of Aditi"—as referring to a plurality of parts, because Brahman is partless. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Because it is heard in many restrictive Śrutis that Brahman alone exists at the time of creation and so forth; because the word *prāṇa* has an established conventional usage (*nirūḍhi*) for Him; and because the word *ṛṣi*, in view of the sense organs which are the means of knowledge, naturally applies to Him who possesses knowledge—here, Brahman alone is the *prāṇas*. As for the plural number, it must be interpreted according to the maxim "when there is an improper assumption, it should be understood as being based on a quality," just like the plurality of nooses [in the phrase "the nooses of Varuṇa"], since there exists a basis for the plurality of qualifiers even in the absence of [actual] parts.

Nor should it be argued that even if unity is established, the existence of the sense organs must likewise persist as it does for the individual soul (jīva). For, in order to avoid the fallacies of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), their existence at that time cannot be asserted, since they serve as the substrata for unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) just like the soul; furthermore, the cited scripture has already demonstrated that such existence belongs to Brahman alone.

At the time of the beginning of creation, there was no activity of the sense organs such as speech, because no such activity is observed; for it is heard that the differentiation of names and forms occurs only after the creation of the elements, from which it is understood that prior to that, activities of the sense organs such as the utterance of names were absent; and furthermore, in the mantra "From this [Being] it is born," their birth is heard to be a transformation into a state different from their previous nature, similar to that of ether and the other elements.
The Summary Verses.

If it is argued that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are eternal because they exist from the beginning, we say no, because they are created. The plural usage of the term "prāṇa" with respect to Brahman is to be understood as a metaphorical designation.
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
And because the sevenfold course has been specified. ||4||
But since the hands and other [limbs] remain [in place], it is not thus. ||5||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having established that the sense organs possess origination—just like ether and other elements—their specific number is now being considered. Regarding the doubt arising from conflicting scriptural statements as to whether "the sense organs are seven or eleven," the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is: they are only seven; for it is heard in scripture that in both this world and the next, only seven [organs] proceed along with the individual soul (jīva).

"From that, the seven vital breaths arise; seven are the flames, seven the fuel-sticks, and seven the tongues; these seven worlds exist wherein move the vital breaths, which, dwelling in the cave, are deposited seven by seven. The repetition [of "seven"] is intended to refer to the distinction between different persons. And those moving vital breaths are further specified by a description of their essential nature: "When the five means of knowledge stand still together with the mind..."

"And when the intellect no longer functions, they call that the supreme goal. For here, the seven internal organs—namely the five beginning with the eye, along with the mind and the intellect—are specified. The meaning is that they call "the supreme goal" yoga, which is the means for attaining liberation, the supreme state.

As for the scriptural mentions of numbers exceeding eight—such as "There are eight graspers (graha) and eight over-graspers (atigraha)," "There are indeed seven vital breaths (prāṇa) in the head and two directed downwards," "There are nine vital breaths in a person, with the navel as the tenth," and "There are ten vital breaths in an animal, with the self (ātman) as the eleventh"—these are merely figurative designations of "organ" (indriya) based on their being of some service to the living being, just like the navel. For the navel is not an organ; rather, the organs are only those seven which possess the capacity for movement.

Furthermore, when both fewer and more [organs] are heard of in scripture, it is logical to accept the smaller number because of parsimony (*lāghava*). If it is argued that it is more logical to accept the larger number—since the smaller numbers are included within the larger and thus all are subsumed under it—the answer is no. Since the hands and other limbs also serve as instruments for the experience of that [Self] while it resides in the body—each performing its specific function—it should be understood that there are eleven sense organs: five organs of cognition, five organs of action, and the mind. Therefore, the number of sense organs established by such scriptural and traditional authorities as, "These ten vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, with the self as the eleventh," is indeed fixed. When various numbers are heard in the texts, it is logical to determine the number based on their functional roles.

It is like the restriction of what is to be expressed according to one's capacity when hearing various accounts of past deeds (*avadāna*). As for those who speak of a greater number [of faculties], their intention refers to the different modifications of the mind (*manovṛtti*): the mind assisted by *mahat* performs determination (*adhyavasāya*); the mind assisted by ego (*ahaṅkāra*) performs self-conceit (*abhimāna*); and the mind assisted by prior latent impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) performs reflection (*cintā*). Thus, it is the mind itself, as conditioned by these distinct modifications such as determination and the rest, that is designated by the terms "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ego" (*ahaṅkāra*), and "mind" (*citta*).

However, the mentions of fewer numbers in various places are intended with reference to specific functions, such as movement, which are intended to be expressed in those contexts. The Smṛti passage, "When the five [breaths] come to rest," intends to convey the predominance of the organs of cognition (jñānendriyas) over the organs of action (karmendriyas) during the state of yoga, in that they must be brought under control with effort. The Śruti passage, "There are seven breaths in the head," intends to convey the predominance of the seven based on their location in the head; this is also the intention behind the Śruti regarding the "seven breaths" and the scriptural texts concerning movement.

The scriptural mention of eleven [organs] indeed exists even for the others: "These ten are the vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, with the self as the eleventh; when they depart from this mortal body," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that there are eleven sense organs. [This concludes the] summary verse.

It is not so; there are seven vital breaths (prāṇas) joined [together], because only seven are mentioned as having movement. [If you object that] they would be eleven along with the hands and so forth, we reply: no, because of the distinction in their functions.
Thus concludes the section on the seven destinies.
And they are atomic. 6.

Regarding the doubt as to whether those sense organs are all-pervading (vibhu) or limited (paricchinna), since it is heard in scripture that "all these are indeed equal, all are infinite," and because no specific dimension has been stated for this sense organ such that its measure might be defined, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they must be all-pervading. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

Because their movement is heard to be characterized by going upward and reaching the end, and because the hearing of their infinity—through the supplementary passage, "He who meditates upon these as infinite wins an infinite world"—is understood to be for the purpose of meditation, they are indeed limited. Furthermore, the perception of distant objects is possible due to their possessing rapid speed and other such qualities.
The Summary Verses.

They are infinite because of the scriptural teaching of their infinity; it is not so through the processes of going, coming, and departing. They are subtle, and for them, the fruit of worship is again the hearing of their infinity.
And he is the most excellent. ||7||

Following the investigation into the origin of the sense organs, the origin of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is investigated; this constitutes the logical connection (*saṃgati*), because in the dialogue between the senses and the principal breath recorded by the Chāndogas, the principal breath—having attained preeminence through its dispute with the senses—is understood to possess a nature identical to theirs simply by virtue of the account of that very dispute. Thus, immediately after the inquiry into the origin of the sense organs, the origin of the principal vital breath is considered.

Although the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—just like that of the sense organs—is established by the mantra itself, namely, "From this [Being] is born the *prāṇa*," and thus its production is proven to be like that of ether and the other elements, nevertheless, the origin of the *prāṇa* is considered here for the following reasons: first, to determine through the resolution of scriptural contradictions that the *prāṇa* is distinct from both elemental air and the functions of the senses; second, to establish its relevance to the present discussion on the inquiry into origins; and third, to dispel certain further doubts.

Furthermore, there is this additional doubt: at the time of the beginning of creation, just as the function of the individual soul (jīva) does not exist because it remains in an unmanifest state, so too the functions of the organs such as speech—such as the utterance of names and so forth—do not exist. Therefore, it has been stated that the words "prāṇa" and "ṛṣi," having been observed to be used for Brahman, refer to Brahman.

Regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), in the *Nāsadāsīya Sūkta* which begins with, "There was neither non-existence nor existence then; there was only darkness hidden by darkness in the beginning, without distinctive marks," it is heard that there exists the activity of the unmanifest (*ananākhya*) in the verse, "That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power" (*ānīd avātaṃ svadhayā tadekam*). Nor can it be argued that the word *ānīt* has never been seen used for Brahman. Furthermore, one cannot say that because of the qualification "windless" (*avātam*), the word *ānīt* does not refer to the activity of the unmanifest vital breath, but rather refers to the existence of Brahman.

[Objection: In the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other such passages, because Vāyu and Prāṇa are taught separately, it is possible for Prāṇa to exist even in the absence of Vāyu. [Reply: Its refutation is as follows: since there is no distinct ontological principle (tattvāntara) apart from Vāyu, Prāṇa is indeed a specific form of Vāyu. Therefore, because of the negation of Vāyu in general by the term "without wind" (avātam), it is proper to say that the word *ānīc* refers exclusively to Brahman, as it cannot logically be the function of Prāṇa. Thus, by the etymology "that which is supported by or enjoyed by itself" (*svena dhīyate upabhujyate*), the word *svadhā* denotes Lakṣmī; [the passage thus refers] to the Blessed Lord as qualified by Lakṣmī.

Some say that since the state of persistence of the Supreme Brahman at the time of creation and so forth has already been stated, the sūtra "And because He is the best" (Śreṣṭhaśca) is merely a supplement to the preceding section, intended for subsequent deliberation—just like the sūtra of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā school, "The grinding of the Pūṣan-cake is understood as being for the modified sacrifice"—and not a separate section. Thus ends the section on the minuteness of the best [individual soul].
Nor are [the prāṇas] merely functions of air, because they are taught separately. 8.1.8.
But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. (9)
And because it is not performed, there is no fault; for thus [the scripture] shows. ||10||
The fivefold activity is designated as being like that of the mind. ||11||

Is this principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) merely air, or is it the action consisting of inhalation and exhalation, or rather air that has attained a particular state? In this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because of the scriptural statement, "That which is the *prāṇa* is air," it is merely air, or the action consisting of inhalation and exhalation, since the word *prāṇa* is applied to that [action]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is: it is not merely air, because of its being taught separately in the mantra, "From this [Self] it is born"; and because the word *prāṇa* is not applied to mere air. For this very reason, it is also not the action of inhalation and so forth belonging to that [air].

Just as in the case of the activity of fire, the activity of air also cannot be taught as having a separate origination in the mantra concerning the production of substances which states, "From this it is born"; for although that [activity] may be fit for the word *prāṇa* ending in a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvārtha*), there is no usage of it with a suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛ*) as in "it breathes" (*prāṇiti*), nor with a suffix denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*) as in "one lives by means of this" (*anena jīvati*).

Now, if prāṇa is indeed air that has reached a certain particular state, then would prāṇa, like fire, abandon its nature as air? No, it is said in reply. This [prāṇa] is not a different element like fire; rather, without abandoning its nature as air, it is a specific instrument of the living being (jīva), like the eye and other organs, because it is distinguished by those [organs].

For in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is said: "Then indeed the vital breaths disputed for the sake of superiority, each saying 'I am superior,'" by which, through the description of their quarrel with the eye and the other organs, it is determined that they possess an equal appearance; and because immediately thereafter, by the words of the eye and the others—"You are not the best"—the preeminence of the vital breath is established. Indeed, a mutual dispute over superiority arises among those of the same class when there is a doubt regarding their equal capacity to provide assistance.

Furthermore, the determination of primacy occurs through the observation of a superior degree of service rendered by one [organ] over another. Moreover, the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belongs to the same class as those well-known as the instruments of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established only if it too serves as an instrument for that soul. If it is objected that no specific benefit to the soul is seen from the vital breath in the same way as from the eyes and other organs, we reply that this is not a fault; for scripture itself demonstrates that its service consists in the action of sustaining the body and the senses.

As in the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the speech of the *prāṇa* to the eyes and other organs is: "Do not fall into delusion regarding me; it is I who, having divided myself fivefold and supported this body, hold it together. Now, one might ask: when there is a fivefold division, are the *vyāna* and the others distinct principles from the *prāṇa*? It is said: no.

Because of the scriptural statement, "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind," desire, resolve, and so forth are merely modifications (*vṛtti*) of the single vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), just as prāṇa, apāna, and the others are. By this, the Sāṃkhya position—that *prāṇa* is the common function (*sādhāraṇī vṛtti*) of the senses—is refuted. For they [the Sāṃkhyas] imagine that it is like the movement of a cage causing all the parrots within it to move, or like [a single movement] of all [the senses].

"The common function of all the senses located in the body is *prāṇa*, like the raising up of a snare that has fallen upon a flock of pigeons"—this is not correct. For apart from the perception of objects, which is the specific activity of the senses, we observe that the functions of inhalation and exhalation, as well as the act of sustaining the body by dividing itself fivefold, are the independent activities of the principal *prāṇa*.
The summary verses.
The chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is also merely air, as it was produced from Brahman according to the method stated for the group of sense organs;
nor is it the activity within the body in the form of respiration, because it is taught that it arises together with the material elements.
The statement that it is air is consistent with its being a different state of air;

this occurs because the previous state persists, just as in the case of fire, and not because it is a distinct element. This [air] remains as a constant instrument for those subject to transmigratory existence, along with the eyes and other senses.
Renowned for its supreme service, it sustains this body composed of the subtle instruments and functions through its fivefold activity.
Thus ends the section concerning the functions of air.
And it is atomic. ||12||

The connection [of this section] is that after determining the essential nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), its magnitude is now being defined. Since there is a conflict of scriptural statements regarding whether the vital breath is all-pervasive (vibhu) or limited (paricchinna), a doubt arises; the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is all-pervasive, because of the scriptural hearing: "He is equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe; everything is established in the vital breath, for all this is enveloped by the vital breath."

[Objection: Even though the infinity of the sense organs (*indriya*) is heard [in scripture], their finitude has been established by the evidence of their departure (*utkramaṇa*) and so forth; by that same logic, the finitude of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) would also be proven. What, then, is the purpose of this section? [Reply: It is said: The opponent maintains that the infinity [of the senses] was mentioned as being subordinate to the injunction for meditation (*upāsti*), whereas this [infinity of the *prāṇa*] is not so. Alternatively, the scriptural statement of complete equality—accompanied by the supporting argument that "all this is enveloped by the *prāṇa*"—is more powerful than the evidence of departure and so forth.

Therefore, the opponent's intention is that the form of the departure (*utkramaṇa*) and so forth, which is the means to that [liberation], must be described. Furthermore, the status of being a subordinate element of an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi-śeṣatva*) is equal even in the case of the mark of total similarity, because of the proximity to the injunction for meditation in the passage: "Thus this similarity is in the Veda. Moreover, the statement, "Everything is established in breath; for all this is enveloped by breath," speaks of the fact that the entire body is established in breath and enveloped by breath, but not of the fact that the entire world is enveloped by breath.

The established conclusion is that the pervasiveness of the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed [the meaning], because the use of the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that it expresses a well-known fact; and because, just as with the body, the facts of the vital breath being established in and enveloping the body are well known from common experience, from other Vedic texts, and from tradition.
The Summary Verses.

Because of the traditional teaching that "He is equal to the three worlds," this [Self] is all-pervasive; yet because of its departure [from the body] and other such facts, it is minute. The scriptural statement regarding total equality is a mere eulogy.
Thus concludes the section concerning the minuteness of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
But the presiding over fire and the other elements belongs to Him (the Self), because of the scriptural teaching; as in the case of the possessor of breath, on account of the word.
And its eternity [is established]. ||14||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: immediately after the investigation into the origin, dimension, and other attributes of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the specific manner in which they are presided over by deities such as Agni is now considered. Is the status of deities like Agni as presiding overseers of the vital breaths that which was previously mentioned in the context of the introductory discussion under the sūtra, "But there is designation of the presiding deities, because of distinction and following"?

Regarding the doubt as to whether that [presiding] is dependent on itself or dependent on God, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: although it was stated in the section beginning with "But from the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement" (*parāt tu tacchruteḥ*) that the agency of individual souls (*jīva*) is dependent on God, nevertheless, since fire, the sun, and so forth—whose sovereignty has been granted by God—possess the capacity to grant boons and bestow fruits just like God, they possess independence; therefore, let their presiding be dependent on them alone. This is because the scriptural teaching regarding dependence can be restricted to human beings and others.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

The fact that light and the other elements—such as fire and the sun—possess presiding agency over the eye and the other senses is due solely to the will of the Supreme Lord. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching that He is the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all. Therefore, just as it is logical that the individual soul’s (jīva) presiding over the senses is dependent on another, despite the scriptural statement of its independence—"In this very way, having taken these vital breaths (prāṇas), he moves about at his own pleasure within his own body"—so too is it logical for the presiding deities (abhimānidevatās) to be likewise dependent.

If it be argued that there is a distinction between the deities and humans such as ourselves because the deities possess sovereignty granted by the Supreme Lord, we say no. This is because for all transmigrating beings, the state of being governed by the Lord is eternal; for the scripture states without qualification, "He is the eternal Lord of this world.

Therefore, since they were governed by the Supreme Lord prior to attaining their status as deities, even after that attainment, their subjection to the Lord remains unavoidable—just as ministers remain subject to the king even after their appointment.
The summary verses.
What harm is there if the presiding over the vital breaths (prāṇas) were to belong to deities such as Agni— who are themselves worthy of worship and bestowers of fruits— and be dependent upon them?
Let it not be so; for these—God and the others—possess an eternal connection with those who possess vital breaths, namely, their state of being governed by Him.
Thus ends the section concerning the presiding over light and so forth.
These are the organs, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one. ||15||
Because of the scriptural statement of difference and because of the distinction [between the two]. ||16||

Following the determination of the origin and other characteristics of the sense organs (*indriya*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is now investigated whether all those designated by the term *prāṇa* are sense organs, or whether they are distinct from the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of this investigation? If it is argued that the purpose is simply a specific conventional usage based on an investigation into the definition of what is included in or excluded from the principal vital breath, we say: not so. Indeed, unlike in the Vaiśeṣika system, an investigation into definitions for the sake of mere conventional usage is not stated to be the purpose of this scripture.

This inquiry is indeed for the purpose of dispelling contradictions in the scriptures. To explain: it is beyond dispute that the word *prāṇa* in its plural form is a synonym for the sense organs (*indriya*). Its usage is seen as distinct from its primary sense [the vital breath] in the passage: "When the principal *prāṇa* departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it. By this, it is understood that the sense organs are precisely those beginning with the eye, other than the most excellent one.

Furthermore, because the term *mukhyaprāṇa* (the principal vital breath) is applied to that which is the principal *prāṇa* in the passage, "Now, they meditated upon that very principal *prāṇa* as the Udgītha," it is understood that this [principal *prāṇa*] too is included among the sense organs (*indriya*). For by whatever basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the word *prāṇa* is applied to the eyes and so forth, by that same basis it is applied to the principal one; thus, the principal *prāṇa* becomes the chief among the *prāṇas*, just as a certain individual becomes the chief Brāhmaṇa among the Brāhmaṇas.

Thus, there being a conflict of scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed an organ (*indriya*). This is because among those things denoted by the word *prāṇa*, it is established that this [vital breath] is primary. Nor should one suspect a difference between the vital breath and the organs on the grounds of the statement in the mantra, "From this [Self] it is born," which speaks of the separate origination of the vital breath; for if that were the case, it would follow that the mind (*manas*) is also distinct from them.

Even if the vital breath (prāṇa) were indeed an organ, the mutual rivalry and dispute observed in the world among members of the same class—as heard in the case of the eyes and so forth versus the vital breath—is consistent [only with it being an organ]. Furthermore, when homogeneity based on the internal factor of being an organ is possible, that rivalry cannot be justified by a homogeneity based on the external factor of being an instrument of the individual soul (jīva). Thus, statements such as "the organs are eleven" refer to the organs and so forth, excluding the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).

Just as the statement "there are seven vital breaths" (saptaprāṇāḥ) refers exclusively to the breaths located in the head, and thus does not contradict the mention of the number eleven, so too the meditation on the sense organs enjoined by the passage "He who meditates on these as infinite" must be performed together with the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

The term *mukhya-prāṇa* (the chief vital breath) does not mean "the one that is the principal sense-organ among those denoted by the word *prāṇa*"; rather, its meaning is "the *prāṇa* that exists in the mouth. This is because in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, within the same context, the word *āsanya* is used in place of *mukhya* in the passage, "Then they spoke to this *prāṇa* in the mouth" (*athahemamāsanyaṃ prāṇam ūcuḥ*), and because that term signifies "that which exists in the mouth" (*āsye bhavaḥ*). In that instance, the substitution of *āsya* for *āsana* occurs according to the rule *paddannomās* (Pāṇini 6.1.63).

If, however, the meaning of "the chief vital breath" (*mukhyaḥ prāṇaḥ*) is that it is the chief among the vital breaths (*prāṇānām*), even so, the status of the vital breath as a sense organ (*indriyatvam*) is not obtained. This is because it is logically consistent to interpret the meaning as follows: this [central] vital breath is the primary denotation of the word *prāṇa*, while the other vital breaths are the senses, which are its secondary (or indicated) meanings rather than primary ones; for it is stated that the eyes and so forth are to be indicated by the very term that denotes the chief vital breath, in the passage: "They all became his very form; therefore they are designated by his name. (*ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan tasmādeta etenākhyāyante*).

All of this will become clear in the section concerning the "Combination of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) under the sūtra "If it be said that there is a difference because of the word 'otherwise'" (*anyathātva-śabdād iti cet*). Therefore, the eyes and so forth, being distinct from the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), are indeed the sense organs (*indriya*). This is also determined by the separate mention [of them] in the mantra: "From this [Being], the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born. Although the mind (*manas*) is mentioned separately from the sense organs, its status as a sense organ is accepted in accordance with another scriptural statement: "The sense organs are five, and the mind is the sixth."

There is no other scriptural statement here to the effect that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is an organ (*indriya*). Furthermore, there is a difference in nature between the vital breath and the organs: for even when all the organs such as the eyes have ceased their functions during deep sleep, the activity of the vital breath is still perceived. This is also confirmed by the Śruti: "The fires of the vital breaths alone remain awake in this city; it breathes 'bhūr-bhūḥ'. Moreover, there is a difference in their respective effects: knowledge and action are the effects of the organs, whereas the sustenance of the body is the effect of the vital breath.

Therefore, the sense organs (indriyas) are indeed the eye and the others, excluding the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). And the common definition (lakṣaṇa) of these eleven is their being modifications of the sattvic ego (sāttvikāhaṃkāra).
The Summary Verses.

"Prāṇa is also an organ because it is denoted by the word 'praṇa' like all the others. This is not so; because of its separate mention, it is distinct from the others, while its status as a "prāṇa" is only figurative.
Thus concludes the section on the sense-faculties.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, because of the scriptural teaching. ||17||
The [perception] of meat and so forth is based on the earth; for the other two as well, it is according to their respective names. ||18||
But on account of its preponderance, there is a designation of that; indeed, there is a designation of that. ||19||

By demonstrating that Brahman is the creator of each subsequent body starting from the very first one within the *khādi* [passages], the fact that Brahman is the direct agent in every instance of creation is shown by the sūtra, "Because of the scriptural statement of difference. That [position] is not tenable—because in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), scripture and tradition [state] that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the agent.

The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that [the Lord's authorship] is already well-known; or else, there is a connection by way of an illustration, since His status as the direct agent is established even in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), just as it was in the creation of ether and the other elements. The scriptural authority is: "Entering with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me differentiate names and forms," and: "The naming and the detailed manifestation of beings and their activities..."

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Smṛti passage beginning with "In the beginning, he created the gods and others from the words of the Veda itself" establishes that Hiraṇyagarbha is the one who differentiates names and forms, or rather that the Supreme Self embodied in him is so, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it establishes this for Hiraṇyagarbha alone, because of the scriptural hearing: "By means of the individual soul (jīva), let me differentiate."

[Objection: But if this were so, then in the common worldly statement, "The king considers the enemy's army by means of his spy," the act of ascertaining the enemy's army—performed by the spy—is figuratively attributed to the king; likewise here too, the differentiation of names and forms performed by the individual soul (jīva) would be figuratively attributed to Brahman. [Reply: This is not a fault.

Just as in the case of a king and his spy, because there is no difference in essential nature between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—being related as part and whole—even here, since the phrase "by the self which is the living being" (jīvenātmanā) identifies the living being with the agency and selfhood of the Lord, it is logically established that the synthesis performed by the agent who is the living being is, in its primary sense, the agency of the Lord himself, through that very identification of the living being's agency with the Lord's own agency and selfhood.

Nor should it be argued that this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes association (*sahayoga*), such that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of Īśvara would also be possible therein; for a case ending expressing a *kāraka* (grammatical relation) is stronger than a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada-vibhakti*), as the former is independent of connection with other words. Nor can its status as a *kāraka*-case ending be maintained by taking it to mean "instrument" (*karaṇa*), because in grammar, which has Īśvara as its agent, the individual soul (*jīva*) lacks the quality of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, even if it were taken in the sense of an instrument, grammar would ultimately result in having the individual soul as its agent.

It is not the case that God is the agent [of the act]. For when there is a conscious agent, the assistance rendered by another consciousness through its status as an instrument occurs only by way of being prompted by that agent. On this view, just as in the case of a king’s supervision over an act performed by his servants, the agency of God in the grammatical analysis performed by the individual soul (jīva) must be understood as intended in a non-primary sense. Thus, since the interpretation of the word as having the sense of an "instrument" (karaṇa) is established, even the suspicion regarding the impossibility of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is dispelled; for such a suspicion would arise only if the word were taken to mean "agent" (*kartṛ*).

Because the agent of the act of entering is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the individual soul (*jīva*) does not have agency that culminates in mere entry. Rather, by postulating that the agency belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*) alone, the use of the instrumental case for the agent is justified. This is because the rule "when two actions have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* denotes the prior action" (Pāṇini 3.4.21) is traditionally understood to require identity of agent; thus, it is impossible for it to apply when the agents are different. Furthermore, since that suffix is also traditionally understood to denote the agent, even if the agent is already expressed [by another word], the instrumental case would be untenable.

Just as the life-force (jīva) alone is the primary agent of grammar, which is like the movement of an uncountable [number of elements], so too the Smṛti statement, "the names and forms of beings," becomes consistent only if this is the case. For it is not the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the individual soul Hiraṇyagarbha, who would depend upon Vedic words for the sake of remembering the names and forms that occurred in a previous creation in order to create the names and forms of the gods and other beings. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

The fashioning of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti*)—the differentiation of the names and forms of the gods and others—is the creation of the Supreme Lord alone as he effects the triplication (*trivṛtkurvataḥ*). This is because the scripture declares that the agent of both the triplication and the differentiation of names and forms is the same: "That divinity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms; let me make each of them threefold by means of triplication. Indeed, the act of triplication belongs to the Supreme Lord alone.

But this does not refer to Hiraṇyagarbha, who is recorded in Smṛti as having been born within that egg—as in the passage, "In that egg was Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds"—because the egg itself must be produced from the triply refined (trivṛtkṛta) elements of fire, water, and earth. Therefore, the Lord, who is the agent of the triple refinement, is also the agent of the differentiation of names and forms. As for the Smṛti tradition attributing that agency to Hiraṇyagarbha, it is consistent because, like a jar or similar objects, he possesses a dual agency [being both an effect and an instrument]. How then is the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the phrase "by the living self" (jīvenātmanā) to be understood?

Understand this: the word *jīva* refers to the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as its body. For, when the agent is expressed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* consists merely in two things—due to parsimony (*lāghava*): first, the priority in time of the action denoted by the root of the *-ktvā* suffix relative to the action conveyed by the verbal suffix of which that agent is the performer; and second, the identity of the agent of those two actions. It does not include the "agent-power" (*kartṛ-śakti*) itself, as that is already obtained through other means.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because connection with the principal action is more significant, only connection with the act of grammar should be predicated of the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as its body—this is true; yet, when connection with the principal action is impossible, connection with a subordinate action is indeed appropriate. For example, in the case of the statement, "Having made bricks, he eats," there is an impossibility because the bricks cannot possibly be connected as the object of the act of eating.

The distinction here is simply this: that which is designated by the third case-ending (the instrumental) is unfit for syntactic connection with a verb whose meaning is the agent. If one were to accept that the suffix *ktvā* expresses merely the identity of the agent and the priority in time, while rejecting its denotation of the agent-power (*kartṛ-śakti*), then in cases such as "having made bricks, I shall eat" (*iṣṭakāḥ kṛtvāhaṃ bhokṣye*), there would likewise have to be an instrumental ending—just as in "I shall live" (*jīvena*)—by virtue of the rule governing the third case for what is not already expressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*). Therefore, it must be accepted that the suffix *ktvā* denotes the agent-power, and only on that basis can the use of the nominative case therein be justified.

Furthermore, since the agent is expressed here by the suffix *ktvā*, the instrumental case in "by the living self" (*jīvena*) would be improper; rather, the nominative case should have been used. Thus, there is an inconsistency in attempting to justify the instrumental case on the grounds that the agent's power is not expressed. In that case, this instrumental case must be explained as being Vedic (*chāndasa*), applicable to the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as His body and acts as the creator of the grammar. However, one should not justify this instrumental case by accepting the non-difference of the individual soul from the Lord and the fact that the individual soul is the actual agent of the creation of grammar.

Since the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been established, it is proven that the differentiation (*vyākaraṇa*), which shares the same agent as the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), is the work of the Lord alone, who is the agent of the tripartition. Although the scripture records the tripartition after the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha and subsequent to the differentiation of names and forms, nevertheless—because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the order of textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—the detailed exposition of the fact that the tripartition occurs prior [to those events] should be seen in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*).
These are the summary verses.

The Lotus-born (Brahmā) alone is the creator of the name and form called "grammar," because of the scriptural statement "by means of the living self" (jīvena), and because he is remembered in the context of that which is to be created.

Do not say so; for he who is declared to be the agent of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is indeed the creator (*kartṛ*) in the process of manifestation (*vyākṛti*), but the Sustainer (*dhātṛ*) is not likewise the producer of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) from the elements such as earth that have already been triplicated.
Therefore, the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is the agent of both manifestation and tripartition.
But the word "jīva" (living being) is capable of denoting that very [Self] in its sense of being the embodied one.
Thus ends the section concerning name and form (the Saṃjñāmūrti-adhikaraṇa).

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, titled *Caturmatasāra*, the work of Appayadīkṣita, son of the eminent Raṅgarājādhvarin— who was a performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice and a jewel in the ocean of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage, as well as a teacher of the glorious Advaita-vidyā.
The second chapter is completed.
Salutations to the illustrious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Prosperity!
Salutations to the illustrious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
The Fourth Chapter.
The First Quarter of the Fourth Chapter.

Following the determination of the means [of knowledge], the fruit is now examined in this chapter. For the knower situated in the body, there are four kinds of fruits: the non-clinging and destruction of sin, the departure from the body through the cranial artery (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*), the journey via the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) for one who has departed, and the attainment of Brahman. These fourfold fruits are investigated in sequence by means of the four quarters [of the chapter]. First, certain specific points regarding knowledge that ought to be considered are examined.

In order to demonstrate that the Vidyā, which serves as the means of attainment, possesses the nature of the fruit when it has reached the state of devotion, there is now this investigation concerning the third point to be considered:
"Repetition [is required], because of the instruction more than once" (Sūtra 1.1.3).
And because of an indicative mark. ||2||

Regarding the doubt as to whether the knowledge (vidyā) heard in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is to be practiced only once or is to be repeated many times, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: it is to be practiced only once, because there is no evidence for repetition; because, unlike the act of threshing and so forth, it lacks the character of being a means to a visible result; for even knowledge is established in the sūtra "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (BS 3.2.38) as being like ritual acts such as sacrifices.

If it be argued that repetition is established because, in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, after introducing the subject with the verb "to know" (*vid*) in the passage "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*), the conclusion is made with the verb "to meditate" (*upās*) in "He who knows this" (*ya evaṃ veda*); and because in the Vedāntas, after introducing the subject with the verb "to know" in "He who knows that" (*yas tad veda*), the conclusion is made with the verb "to meditate" in "The deity which one meditates upon" (*yāṃ devatām upāste*), it is understood that the meaning of the root *vid* culminates in meditation (*upāsanā*) involving repetition; therefore, repetition is established—even so, the purpose of the scripture is accomplished by three or four repetitions, not by more.

The opponent’s position—that liberation is accomplished by that [meditation] alone through repeated practice—is refuted. The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: because of the scriptural injunctions, "He is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) and "But then, meditating, he sees Him who is partless" (*tatas tu taṃ paśyati niṣkalaṃ dhyāyamānaḥ*), it is demonstrated that knowledge possesses a manifestation so exceedingly clear that it attains a state identical in form to direct perception (*darśana*). Therefore, in accordance with the Smṛti passage—"A continuous stream of cognition whose essence is that very form, free from desire for anything else, is meditation; this is accomplished by the first six ancillaries (*aṅga*s)," it follows that knowledge must be practiced repeatedly.
In the summary verses:
The knowledge of Brahman, when imparted even once by those seeking liberation, is indeed equal to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices; for it has a visible purpose, unlike the act of threshing.
That [text] is to be repeated many times as its means of worship,
measured by the words occurring in the introduction, the conclusion, and other Vedic branches.
Thus ends the section concerning repetition (āvṛtti-adhikaraṇa). ||1||
They accept [the existence of] a self and cause others to grasp it as well. ||3||

In the section on Knowledge (*vidyā*), it was established—through the presumption (*arthāpatti*) arising from the result consisting of a clearer manifestation—that repetition (*āvṛtti*) is a required quality. Immediately following that, it is now demonstrated—through the presumption arising from the result consisting of dependence upon the Lord even in liberation—that the Lord is not to be meditated upon as one's own self. This is the logical connection (*saṅgati*). In Knowledge, the Lord is not to be meditated upon as one's own self; rather, He is to be meditated upon only as distinct.

"Having realized the individual self and the Impeller as distinct, one becomes beloved by Him and thereby attains immortality"—so says the Śruti. If it be argued that the Lord’s identity with one's own self, as stated in the *Atmayāmin* Brāhmaṇa, exists and is not denied here, [we reply: the contemplation for the sake of liberation must be performed precisely as a distinction, according to the aforementioned Śruti. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is this: by the principle of *tatkratu* (the nature of one's meditation determines one's attainment), even in liberation, contemplation must be performed as one's own self in order to establish the Lord's sovereignty.

In the same way, even the ancient worshippers meditated thus: "O venerable deity, I am indeed you; you are indeed I. Likewise, the scriptures teach [the identity] of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), Brahman, and so forth. Nor is there any contradiction with the meditation on distinctness; for such meditation is appropriate because one's own Self is superior to one's own body, and the Supreme Self is superior even to that.
In the summary verses:
the worship of the Blessed One must be performed by the worshiper as something other [than himself],
because of the scriptural statements such as "I am not" and "the self is distinct," which indicate a state of difference.
Even though the self of the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from the body of Brahman,
it is nonetheless appropriate to say "I am Brahman," just as one says "I am a man."
Thus concludes the section on the meditation on the Self. 2. Not in a symbol, for he [the Self] is not that. 4.
The view of Brahman [arises] from the sense of superiority. ||5||
The worship of the Self as the Lord within the planets has been described; its connection with the meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) also arises from that same doubt.

In passages such as "The mind is Brahman," there arises a doubt as to whether Brahman should be meditated upon as the Self or not; this doubt stems from the two possibilities that Brahman may either be an independent object of worship or a mere qualifying attribute. If the meditation consists of viewing the mind as Brahman, then since Brahman is an independent object of worship, it must be meditated upon as the Self according to the principle established in the preceding section. If, however, the meditation consists of viewing Brahman as the mind, then because the object of worship would not be Brahman, such meditation should not be performed. This is the relationship between the prima facie view and the final conclusion.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Brahman is the object of worship, while the qualification "viewing [it] as the mind" is intended for the mind itself. For it is impossible for the non-conscious mind—which lacks the power to bestow the fruit of action—to be the object of worship. Therefore, the meditation on Brahman within the mind is what is to be enjoined, because Brahman is superior. Indeed, the perception of the superior in that which is inferior leads to prosperity, just as perceiving a king in the king’s servant. Conversely, the perception of the inferior in that which is superior would lead only to misfortune. Consequently, the mind is the object of worship; one should not perform the contemplation of it as being the Self, since even the mind is conscious by virtue of having a presiding deity as its form.
In the *Saṅgrahakārikā*:
"In this way, the cognition of identity [with Brahman] should be cultivated even in the case of symbolic meditations (*pratīkopāsana*).
Do not say so; for he (Brahman) is indeed your own Self, but certainly not with respect to the meditator."
For that [Self] is indeed to be meditated upon as Brahman;
there is no inconsistency here, because a perception of the exalted Brahman yields its fruit even when directed toward a lower [substrate].
Thus ends the section on the Pratīkas. ||3||
And the meditations on the sun and so forth are attributes of the member [of the sacrifice], because it is logical. ||6||

It has been stated that the vision of the superior should be applied to the inferior. Therefore, there arises a connection based on the doubt as to whether the vision of the *udgītha* and so forth should be applied to the sun and so forth. In passages such as, "They meditated upon him who shines yonder as the *udgītha*," a doubt arises because it is not determined which of the two possesses superiority—whether the vision of the *udgītha* etc. is to be enjoined upon the sun etc., or the vision of the sun etc. upon the *udgītha* etc. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the vision of the *udgītha* etc. is to be enjoined upon the sun etc., because [the latter] is productive of fruit by virtue of being an auxiliary to a fruitful ritual action.

Even though the sun and other deities serve as constituent parts of the ritual by virtue of their divine form, because the udgītha and so forth—which are themselves to be accomplished—are more closely connected to the fruit, and because, as in the case of "mind is Brahman," the sun and others mentioned first are perceived as the objects of meditation.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of Āditya and others upon the *udgītha* and other parts of the sacrifice is to be enjoined. This is because it is logically consistent that the deities such as Āditya possess superiority, since ritual acts serve as means to their fruits only by way of propitiating deities like Āditya. Since acts of propitiation have the deity being propitiated as their primary object, it is logical that the act itself is also treated as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through its connection with that goal; therefore, the superiority derived from that [act] is not to be disregarded.

If it is argued that, although the Sun and others are the bestowers of fruits in other rites enjoined by injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman," they do not bestow fruit here because they lack the status of a deity within this context of meditative worship (*upāsanā-prakaraṇa*), and therefore the excellence of the *Udgītha* and so forth is stated here because they possess fruit as being integrated into the fruitful ritual—then even in that case, the meditation on the Sun and others must be prescribed as being upon the *Udgītha* itself; for meditations characterized by the co-mention of a subordinate part (*aṅga*) and a non-subordinate part (*anaṅga*) take the form of superimposing the non-subordinate upon the subordinate part.

Because they have the primary action as their basis for application; even though those [subsidiary actions] have independent fruits, a separate application for them is not postulated, because of the parsimony of application (prayukti-lāghava), whereas in the opposite case there would be the complexity of postulating a different application (prayukti-antara-kalpanā-gaurava).
In the summary verses.
Because they are the primary among their respective classes— such as the Ādityas and so forth—
and because they are the means for attaining results through ritual action, the Udgītha and others are superior.

Therefore, the visualization of the Udgītha and so forth should be applied to the sun and so forth. It is not so; for in this context, it is the deity alone who is the object of worship in the ritual, and that deity is superior.
Thus ends the section concerning the meditation on [the breath] as having the sun and other deities as its essence. ||4||
Because it is possible [for him] while sitting. ||7||
And because of meditation. ||8||
And with reference to immovability. ||9||
And they remember. ||10||
Wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], [the result follows] without distinction. ||11||

The discussion concerning the *ahaṃgraha* (meditation on the Self as "I")—both the primary and the secondary—has been concluded. Now, the discussion continues regarding the subject matter of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) itself. Having already examined whether the *ahaṃgraha* and repetition (*āvṛtti*) are established by the implication of the primary fruit of higher knowledges, we shall now consider whether a specific rule regarding the posture is established by the implication of its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that renders assistance. Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a restrictive rule concerning the posture for higher knowledges, there is no such regulating factor. Nor should it be argued that one-pointedness suitable for meditation is possible only for one who is seated.

For such meditation is possible even for one who remains standing, just as in the case of meditations connected to the limbs [of the sacrifice] performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); for it is observed that the priests, while remaining standing in accordance with the injunctions for their ritual duties, perform meditations based on those respective limbs.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Since meditations (*upāsanā*) upon the Supreme Brahman—which serve to bring about a state of conformity with a vision characterized by an extremely clear manifestation—consist in the nature of *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant recollection) in the form of an uninterrupted stream of memory, they differ from meditations based on the constituent parts of a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*). Considering their commonality in being "unwavering," and because of scriptural indications such as "the earth meditates, as it were; the intermediate space meditates, as it were," and because of the traditional teaching, "Sitting upon a seat, one should apply oneself to yoga for the purification of the self," one should indeed perform meditation while seated.

Because sleep occurs for one who is lying down; because one who is walking or standing requires an effort to support the body; and because even one who is sitting possesses the effort to support the lower half of the body—there is a need to avoid these states. Therefore, one should sit with a support. However, there is no further restriction regarding place or time, since no specific place or time other than that which is conducive to one-pointedness is prescribed. Whatever place and time are favorable to one-pointedness are suitable for meditation; there is no distinction beyond that.

The statement, “In a clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, which is cool due to shelters and the like, agreeable to the mind, not dazzling to the eyes, and situated in a cave or a windless spot, one should practice,” also describes a location conducive to one-pointedness, but it does not restrict [the practitioner] to a specific type of place, because of the supplementary phrase “agreeable to the mind. As stated in the *Saṃgrahakārikā*:
“One should practice yoga while sitting alone, for the sake of generating one-pointedness.”
Because of the great effort required for staying and moving, and because one is overcome by sleep while lying down.
"Only suitability to one's own mind is required with respect to place and time;
[factors such as] stars, forests, or specific lunar days are not required, because it is so heard in the supplementary portion of the scripture.
Thus ends the section concerning the posture of sitting (āsīnādhikaraṇa). 5.
For even there, it is seen until the final departure. ||12||

Just as there is a restriction regarding time such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth, one might think that the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) must be performed only for that duration; however, since no such limitation of time is heard [in scripture], it should be performed on a single day alone, according to the maxim: "When the work is done, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled. It is not to be performed throughout one's entire life. The scriptural passage, "He, indeed, living thus until the end of his life, reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again," speaks of the lifelong performance of ritual actions (*karman*) themselves, not of knowledge (*vidyā*); this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since it is appropriate to establish that the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*)—which has as its fruit the non-return [to this world] for the duration of one's life—is a direct auxiliary (*svarūpopakāra*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), the force of that statement leads to the inference that the performance of knowledge itself is intended to last for the duration of one's life. Furthermore, because of the observation of another scriptural passage stating, "One should meditate on the syllable Om until the end of life," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [knowledge] is to be performed for the duration of one's life.
In the summary verse:
"This worship should be performed on a single day alone;
for by that much, the teaching of worship becomes truly fulfilled."
The practice of meditation should be undertaken daily from its commencement until the dissolution of the body;
for there is an injunction in the Śruti stating "as long as life lasts" and likewise in the Śruti "until the time of death."
Thus ends the section concerning [the meditation] up to the time of departure. ||6||
The non-clinging and destruction of future and past sins, respectively, result from that attainment, because of the designation [of them as such]. ||13||

Thus, the specific details regarding repetition and so forth in the case of knowledge (*vidyā*) have been examined. Now, the connection [of this section] is that the fruit consisting of the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of sin—which constitutes the subject matter of this chapter—is being examined. For it is heard in scripture: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," and "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed. These two—the non-clinging and the destruction of sin—must indeed be the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman.

Regarding the doubt arising from the conflict between the scriptural statement that "karma is not destroyed without being experienced" and the fact that those two [the moon and the lightning] are the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Those two are indeed the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman. For it is understood from scripture that "karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of aeons unless it has been experienced," and thus karma is known to be destroyed solely through experience; consequently, it is impossible to conceive of those two as being the fruits of knowledge. Nor should it be argued that this general scriptural rule refers to karma other than sins which are destroyed by knowledge. [The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) follows: This is not so, because of the contradiction with the specific scriptural teaching regarding the destruction of karma by knowledge. If one were to assume that the general rule excludes sins destroyed by knowledge, then there would be no room for the specific teaching that "all karma is destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, since the fruit of knowledge is liberation, and since the attainment of that fruit is impossible without the exhaustion of all karma, it must be admitted that the exhaustion of all karma occurs through knowledge. Therefore, the general rule is set aside by the specific teaching. Moreover, the mention of "even hundreds of millions of aeons" is intended to emphasize the extreme difficulty of exhausting karma through experience alone; it does not mean that karma is never exhausted otherwise. Thus, the exhaustion of all karma results from the power of knowledge. Consequently, the two mentioned are indeed the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman.
