Since there is no scriptural injunction (vidhi) stating that knowledge has the purpose of preventing the attachment of sin and destroying it, and since there is no reason to assume a restriction [of its scope], one should not imagine such an injunction. This is because knowledge, being enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman, does not depend on any other result; thus, the mention of the prevention of the attachment of sin and the destruction of it can appropriately be understood as a praise of knowledge.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: once knowledge is attained, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of subsequent and prior sins certainly occur, because such is designated in scriptural passages beginning with, "Just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf. Nor should it be argued that this designation is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the knowledge whose fruit is the attainment of Brahman; for that would contradict the scriptural teaching on the exhaustion of karma through its being experienced.

In the absence of the exhaustion of karma without experience [of its results], a body must be assumed for the sake of that experience; moreover, in that very body, the acquisition of further karma is unavoidable. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of no liberation at all, because the scriptures on liberation themselves require the non-adherence (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of sin. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the scriptural teachings on the non-adherence and destruction of sin and those on the exhaustion of unexperienced karma, as they have different scopes. For instance, the scripture concerning the exhaustion of unexperienced karma establishes that karma possesses the capacity to produce its fruit.

In the *Pāpavināśāśleṣa-śāstra*, however, two distinct powers are taught: the power to destroy the capacity of past actions to produce their results, and the power to obstruct the arising of the capacity for future actions to produce their results. There is no suspicion of contradiction therein, as this is logically consistent—just as fire possesses the power of heat while water possesses the power to neutralize it. Furthermore, the statement regarding "non-adherence" (*aśleṣa*) refers exclusively to sins committed through negligence.

This is because scriptures such as "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct... indicate that knowledge, which must be practiced daily until death, is to be accomplished through the renunciation of evil conduct; and also because of the Smṛti: "If a yogi should commit some sin through negligence, he should practice yoga alone and perform no other action."

Now, it must be discerned whether this twofold process—the non-attachment and the destruction of sin—occurs on the very first day of commencing the meditation, or in the middle, or at its conclusion. It is clearly stated that it occurs in the middle, at the time of attaining a state identical in form to the vision [of the Lord], according to the scriptural text: "And his actions perish when He is seen. Objection: Previously, the destruction of karma was said to occur at the time of the fall of the body; how then can a different time be mentioned here? Reply: It is said: Sin is the absence of the Lord's pleasure. Non-attachment and destruction consist in a specific form of His pleasure.

Furthermore, at the time of attaining a state of identity in form with the Vision (darśana), there is supreme joy; and upon its completion, one forms the resolve, "May the Supreme Self forgive my transgression. This section concerns that [joy]. The preceding section concerns the resolve, "May He forgive me upon completion. Thus, there is no contradiction.
In the summary verses:
the description of the non-clinging and destruction of past sins immediately following the arising of knowledge is a mere eulogy;
it is incapable of establishing that [knowledge] is the fruit [of the means], as it is contradicted by the scriptural teaching that karma is not exhausted without being experienced.
Between these two, which possess distinct powers and contradictory natures as established by scripture, one must be invalidated in vain;
for why should even that which possesses unfailing power not arise, provided there is no cause for its obstruction?
Thus ends the section concerning the realization of that [truth]. ||7||
In the same way, there is no connection for the other [karma] either; let it fall away. ||14||

It should not be argued that this refers to actions other than evil ones; for since the injunction regarding knowledge has the purpose of preventing the attachment to and destroying evil deeds, there is no basis for restricting its scope. Nor can such a restriction be imagined, because knowledge—enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman—requires no other fruit, and thus the scriptural mention of the non-attachment to and destruction of evil deeds is appropriately understood as being for the sake of praising knowledge.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: when knowledge (*vidyā*) is attained, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of subsequent and prior sins indeed occur. This is because such a designation is found in scriptural passages beginning with, "Just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf. Nor should it be argued that this designation arises merely from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the fruit of knowledge—which is the attainment of Brahman—and is not intended to apply literally; for that would contradict the scriptural teaching regarding the exhaustion of karma only after its fruits have been experienced (*abhuktakarmakṣaya*).

Since there can be no destruction of karma without its being experienced as enjoyment (*bhoga*), one must take up a body for the sake of that enjoyment; and since the acquisition of further karma is unavoidable even in that body, it would follow that liberation is impossible. Therefore, the scriptures on liberation themselves require the non-adherence (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of sins. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the scriptural teachings on the non-adherence and destruction of sins and those on the exhaustion of unexperienced karma, because they have different scopes. To explain: the scripture concerning the exhaustion of unexperienced karma establishes that karma possesses the capacity to produce its fruit.

In the *Pāpāvināśāśleṣa-śāstra*, however, it is established that there is a power to destroy the capacity of past actions (*prācīna-karman*) to produce their fruits, and a power to obstruct the arising of the capacity of future actions (*āgāmi-karman*) to produce their fruits. Nor is there any suspicion of contradiction therein; for this is logically consistent, just as fire possesses the power of heat while water possesses the power to neutralize it. Furthermore, the statement regarding "non-adherence" (*aśleṣa*) refers only to those sins committed prior to [the rite], and not—

The statement regarding destruction [of sins] does not apply to all types of sin, because scriptural texts such as "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1) indicate that the knowledge which must be practiced daily until death is accomplished through the cessation of evil conduct; and also because of the Smṛti: "If, however, a practitioner should do anything through negligence, he should practice yoga alone and perform no other action. Now, it must be discerned whether this twofold process—non-adherence to and destruction of sin—occurs on the first day of beginning the meditation, in the middle, or at its conclusion.

In the interim, there is the occasion of attaining the same locus as the vision [of Brahman]; this is indeed distinct [from the previous state], according to the Śruti: "And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. Now, an objection is raised: previously, the exhaustion of karma was stated to occur at the time of the body's fall; how then can a different occasion be mentioned here? It is replied: sin consists in the absence of devotion to the Blessed Lord. Its destruction occurs through the removal of that [sin] and the manifestation of its opposite, namely, devotion.

Therefore, at the time when the state of co-locus with the vision [of Brahman] is attained, the Supreme Self, being pleased, forms the resolve, "I shall forgive the transgression of the worshiper upon its completion. This present section (adhikaraṇa) concerns that [state]. The preceding section concerns the resolve, "It is forgiven at the completion [of the vision]. Thus, there is no contradiction.
The summary verses.
The praise concerning the non-clinging and destruction of past sins immediately upon the arising of knowledge is not capable of establishing that [knowledge] is the fruit [of the means],
as it is contradicted by the scriptural injunction that karma is not exhausted without being experienced.
Between these two, which possess distinct powers, there is no contradiction in their being scriptural; thus, the sublation of one is futile.
For even that which possesses unfailing power—why should it not have causes for destruction, birth, or obstruction?
Thus ends the section concerning that attainment.
In the same way, there is no connection for the other [action] either; let it fall away. ||14||

Since there is non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of merit (*puṇya*) just as there is of evil (*pāpa*), the principle of extension (*atideśa*) applies. In this regard, there arises a further doubt that must be resolved by the principle of extension: because the words concerning non-clinging and destruction specifically mention "evil" (*pāpa*), it might be thought that merit does not undergo non-clinging or destruction. Nor can it be argued that because in another scriptural passage—"Neither old age nor death, neither grief, nor good deeds (*sukṛta*), nor evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*); all evils (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from here"—the word "evil" (*pāpman*) is used as a common term for both merit and demerit, the same word denoting "evil" found elsewhere in the Vedāntas is likewise common to both.

It should not be said that [these are undesirable fruits] because there is no difference in their being undesirable for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). For there is no such restrictive rule. This is because even old age, death, and sorrow—which were included under the word "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*)—are mentioned separately in the passage, "He is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow. Likewise, here too, it is appropriate to understand the word "evil" (*pāpa*) as referring to evil in general.

Thus, the removal of further doubt is as follows: although in certain places within the Vedāntas the word *pāpa* (evil) refers merely to evil deeds, here it applies equally to both good and evil deeds. This is because, due to the majesty of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the scriptural statement, "Neither his good deeds nor his evil deeds [remain]; all evils turn away from him," which indicates the cessation of even good deeds. Furthermore, by the same logic that establishes good deeds as having results for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and by the authority of the scriptures intended for those seeking liberation, it is common to both [non-clinging and cessation] through the principle of non-clinging (*aśleṣa*).

But surely, even for the knower, meritorious deeds that have fruits such as rain, food, and so forth are required for the completion of his meditative worship (*upāsana*). How then can there be the destruction of all merits? There is no contradiction, because those merits whose fruits are experienced as subordinate to knowledge persist until the maintenance of the body; it is only at the time of the body's fall that the remaining portion is destroyed.
These are the summary verses.
For indeed, that which is well-performed and ordained by knowledge does not undergo either attachment or dissolution;
therefore, by its own word, it is specifically heard in scripture as being distinct from what is ill-done.

Even that which is prescribed [in the scriptures] must be abandoned from afar by those seeking the experience of the Supreme, for it yields undesirable results for those who possess such knowledge and is thus like a foul-smelling object;
this applies even to terms such as "sin" (pāpman) found within the Upanishads, which refer to both [the individual soul and the Supreme].
Therefore, in this case, its non-adherence to that [object] is certain, along with its dissolution therein.
Whatever merit, such as the fruits of rain and food, is required by the wise,
where that remains after [the attainment of knowledge], there is the dissolution of that [merit] upon the falling away of the body;
thus ends the section on "others."
But the previous [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is their limit. ||15||

Regarding the statement that there is a destruction of good and evil deeds through knowledge, a doubt arises as to whether this occurs without distinction or only in the case of those deeds whose effects have not yet begun, due to the apparent contradiction between two scriptural passages: "All sins are burnt away" and "For him, there is delay only so long. In this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, to avoid contradicting the scripture stating "all," there is the destruction of both merit and demerit without exception; as for the holding of a subsequent body mentioned in the passage "for him, there is delay only so long," that will occur through the persistence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), according to the analogy of the continued spinning of a potter’s wheel even after the stick has been removed. If it is argued that [the body persists] through the persistence of residual impressions...

Even for those whose lifespan is exhausted and who have fallen from their status, the maintenance of the body would follow as a consequence by that [remaining karma]. Therefore, when the maintenance of the body has commenced, there is the destruction of other merits and demerits—leaving aside the *prārabdha* (commenced) good and evil deeds—through the exhaustion [of their fruits]. And thus, it is solely by the power of *prārabdha* that the experience of pleasure and pain is possible even for the wise.
The summary verses.
One should know that there is the dissolution of both merit and demerit without distinction;
for the Śruti declares, "All evils [are destroyed]. Thus it is said.
It is heard as a limit that, having abandoned the task already begun, one remains for a long time in the state of dissolution (*laya*) due to the very effort [to maintain it].
If the maintenance of the body were possible through latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), then that [maintenance] would occur even for those of short life-span and for the ignorant.
Thus concludes the section concerning those whose karma has not yet begun to bear fruit.
But the Agnihotra and other rites are for that very purpose, because they are seen to have that as their effect. ||16||
According to some, however, there is another [type of karma] which belongs to both. ||17||
"For it is by knowledge alone [that one attains this]," so indeed [it is said]. ||18||

In the section concerning the non-clinging of the other as well (*itarasyāpy eṣa asaṃśleṣaḥ*), it was stated that by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no clinging even to good deeds (*sukṛta*). Consequently, since obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites such as the *agnihotra*, as well as the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśrama-dharma*), are equally "good deeds," it would follow that they do not cling [to the self] and thus would not be performed even if one did not wish to. For no one desires what is fruitless. If obligatory and occasional rites were to possess fruits, then the statement regarding their non-clinging would be rendered meaningless; indeed, at that time, the statement regarding non-clinging would be without a subject.

Even if one were to postulate another object for that [repetition], we do not perceive any fruit for them. Nor is the uninterrupted continuation of knowledge until death its fruit; for, just as in the case of ritual action, the uninterrupted continuation of knowledge is established by the mere fact of its being practiced. Nor is the removal of evil deeds that obstruct the continuation of knowledge its fruit.

Because past sins are destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), the learned person cannot subsequently engage in intentional sin; furthermore, it is taught that accidental sin is removed through the practice of yoga. Even if one might argue that the abandonment of obligatory, occasional, and situational duties (*āśrama-dharma*) is improper and thus their performance must somehow be maintained as duties of the stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*) for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), nevertheless, their performance for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*) is not thereby established.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that even by the knower (vidvān), those [duties] must be performed both as duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) and for the sake of knowledge (vidyārthatva), solely for the purpose of the effect that is knowledge.

Because of the instruction regarding that [knowledge]. Now, it may be argued that such an instruction is unestablished, since the scriptural passage beginning with "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*) can reasonably be understood as enjoining [rites] for the sake of knowledge prior to its attainment; and since the scriptural passage beginning with "He, indeed, maintaining this" (*sa khalvedam vartayan*) can reasonably be understood as referring merely to the continued performance of the duties of another stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*). If this is said, we reply: no. For even in the case of these two cited scriptures, since it is possible that they refer to the continuation of rites for the sake of knowledge until the final moment of realization (*antima-pratyaya*), it is improper to assume such a restrictive interpretation [of them as applying only to the pre-knowledge stage]. Nor is this [continuation] fruitless.

As long as knowledge continues, one must perform those classes of actions that are auxiliary to knowledge; for if, in the midst of such performance, one should intentionally abandon them, there would arise a transgression due to acting contrary to the scriptures. When the mind is thus defiled by this transgression, the desire to pursue knowledge might at some point be interrupted, or a taste for performing prohibited acts—which obstructs the final realization—might arise. Therefore, even after the dawning of knowledge, which has a form identical to [the object of] direct perception, the actions conducive to knowledge must be performed throughout one's life.
This applies whether it be the "good deeds" such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice...

If it is asked: "Since all merit prior to the arising of knowledge—and indeed all merit existing at the time of the dawning of knowledge, with the exception of that whose fruit has already begun—is destroyed by knowledge, and even that commenced-fruit merit must be exhausted through experience, then what is the scope for the scriptural statement, 'Friends [partake] of his good deeds'? [The answer follows: It refers to the good deeds performed after the attainment of knowledge, which persist until liberation. Furthermore, it may refer to those good deeds performed before knowledge that were not yet operative at the time of its dawning, or to the residue of commenced-fruit merit that was not fully exhausted prior to the rise of knowledge. Alternatively, it may apply to the case where a person dies while still in the process of attaining knowledge, such that the knowledge has not yet reached its full fruition. In such cases, the good deeds performed during the interval between the initial dawn of knowledge and final liberation are what are meant by "friends partaking of his good deeds. Thus, there is no contradiction.

It is said: The subject matter here consists of those meritorious deeds (*sādhukṛtyā*) performed by the knower for the sake of maintaining the body—such as deeds resulting in rain, food, and so forth—which were performed prior to the arising of knowledge and remain with their fruits unexhausted due to being obstructed by other powerful karmas, as well as the meritorious deeds performed for the purpose of generating that very knowledge.

This is because the possibility of the obstruction of even powerful other karmas by karma devoid of knowledge (*vidyā*) is understood from the scriptural text: "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.1.10). Here, this is considered: In the sūtra, "In the same way for the other as well, there is non-clinging; [it perishes] upon falling" (*Brahma-sūtra* 4.1.14), the destruction of "good deeds" (*sādhukṛtyā*)—which have fruits such as rain and food and remain after their fruits have been enjoyed—at the time of the body's fall is stated. How then can it be said that those [deeds] go to friends?

If it is intended that the destruction of [the fruit] in the case of the wise consists precisely in its non-production of results, then at the time of the arising of knowledge, the destruction of other merits could likewise be stated in the same way; thus, since it is possible to state that all of the wise person's good deeds go to their friends, why is there made a restriction of the phrase "good deeds go to friends" to refer only to those deeds that produce results such as rain and food? Furthermore, [it is said that] "enemies [take] evil deeds."

Having seen the object of the [text] "mityasya kaṃ," the determination of the specific object of the [text] "suhṛdassādhu" is made. If it is argued that its object must be the evil deed to be cultivated after the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), we say no; for in that case as well, there is an equal presence of scriptural statements regarding non-attachment (*aśleṣa*).

If it is determined that the statement regarding non-attachment (*aśleṣa*) in the case of the knower (*vidvas*) has the meaning of merely not producing results, then it can likewise be determined that the statement regarding the non-attachment of "good deeds" (*sādhukṛtyā*) in the case of the knower has the same meaning; thus, the mention of a "departure" (*gati*) for those specific good deeds is not required. Furthermore, even this departure should not be restricted [to mean only the departure of deeds whose fruits are obstructed] by the argument that the "good deed" is one whose fruit is obstructed by the influence of more powerful karma.

For it is possible that even meritorious deeds (*sādhukṛtyā*) may have their fruits obstructed; thus, when one’s obstacles to knowledge are few, yet there is a suspicion that they might be many, the numerous rites performed for the purpose of removing them remain without yielding their fruit—just like auspicious ceremonies (*maṅgala*) performed by a *kārīri* sacrifice, or like those performed by sons and others out of delusion and a desire for the practitioner's prosperity, even though he is free from passion, while the obstacles to the commencement [of knowledge] are more numerous than the number of those rites.

For even the establishment of tanks, groves, and so forth are indeed possible. Furthermore, in the section concerning the attainment of that [Self] (*tadadhigamādhikaraṇa*), while establishing that those two [scriptural passages] and the scriptural passage regarding the non-exhaustion of unexperienced karma have different scopes in order to resolve their apparent contradiction, it was stated that the scripture concerning destruction (*vināśa-śāstra*) teaches the capacity for the destruction of the power to produce results in past karmas for the knower, and the scripture concerning non-clinging (*aśleṣa-śāstra*) teaches the capacity to obstruct the arising of the power to produce results in the knower.

In that regard, both the destruction of one's own nature and the non-attachment to one's own nature have been stated. Since the matter is already understood from that alone, what scope is there for a further question regarding the subject of "good deeds"? Therefore, all of this is untenable.

In this regard—someone might think that even for previously performed good deeds (*sādhukṛtyā*), once they have perished, there is no scope for them to be the subject of the scripture concerning their transfer to a friend. With that intention in mind, the question regarding the scope of the statement on the transfer to a friend is posed. It is precisely with that same intention that it is stated that other good deeds persist even after their destruction, continuing as long as is necessary to sustain the body of the knower (*vidvat-deha-dhāraṇārtha*), while bad deeds whose fruits such as rain and so forth have been exhausted constitute the scope [of the transfer]. In the very same way, even when other merits (*sukṛta*) exist, the statement regarding their being the scope [of the transfer] is made.

This being the case, although the verse "those who hate... [and] do evil deeds" (dviṣantaḥ pāpakṛtyām) should also have been addressed by a question regarding their destination and its answer—since the same logic applies—it is not mentioned here; for it can be inferred through the same reasoning that this verse refers to the evil deed (*duṣkṛta*) committed by the knower through negligence, or due to negligence or lack of opportunity, which consists in the failure to perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) of practicing yoga.

Thus, even though the reality of the subject matter of the scripture concerning the transition of the twenty friends as described in the section on the realization of that [Self] exists, the question and answer proceed in this manner solely in accordance with the doubts of an outsider who has faith in the literal meaning of the scriptural teaching on destruction; in this way, everything is clarified.
These are the summary verses.
If merit does not adhere [to one], then rites such as the Agnihotra need not be performed;
however, for the sake of clarifying knowledge, they must be performed day after day by those who possess wisdom.

As for the action performed by the wise man for the sake of attaining joy, health, and so forth, its fruit is obstructed by a powerful [karma]; the statement regarding his going to heaven refers to that very [obstructed] result.
Thus ends the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites.
Having exhausted the others through enjoyment, he attains [the state]. ||19||

It has been stated that merit and demeritorious actions whose effects have already begun are destroyed only through experience, and not by knowledge. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether there is a rule that these [actions] perish only at the end of the body from which knowledge originated, or whether there is no such rule and they may perish even at the end of another body. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they perish only at the end of the body from which knowledge originated, because of scriptural texts such as, "Having shaken off the body, being perfected in self, I shall attain the world of Brahman," and "For him, the delay is only so long as he is not released [from the body]," which indicate that the destruction of karma is restricted to the mere body.

If the *prārabdha* karma is to be experienced in only one body, it is so; however, if it is to be experienced in multiple bodies, then at the conclusion of those, merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpe*) [are exhausted], and immediately thereafter follows the attainment of Brahman. In the phrase "having shaken off the body" (*dhūtvā śarīram*), the singular number is not intended to be restrictive, as seen in that very same context in the passage "having shaken off evil" (*vidhūya pāpam*). Furthermore, in the scriptural text "for him, only so long," the expression "as long as he is not released" refers specifically to the release from *prārabdha* karma, and not to the release from the body which is the source of knowledge (*vidyā-yoni-śarīra*).

Thus, all karma—whether merit or demerit—that was performed prior to the knowledge of Brahman, whose fruits have not yet been experienced and whose effects have not yet begun, becomes incapable of producing its respective fruits for the knower due to the majesty of that knowledge. Furthermore, all karma performed after the commencement of knowledge, with the exception of those rites intended for the sake of the knowledge itself, becomes incapable of producing any fruit therein. This entire karma, both meritorious and sinful, of the knower is transferred to his friends and enemies.
Prārabdha karma, however, is exhausted by being experienced through one or more bodies; thereafter, there is the attainment of Brahman—thus all is faultless.
These are the summary verses.
In whichever body knowledge is born, liberation must occur at its very end;
for it is taught in the scriptures: "Having shaken off the body," and "until one is liberated."
In whichever body—
whether this one or another— the prārabdha karma reaches its complete exhaustion through the enjoyment of its fruits, liberation occurs at the end of that body.
In the phrase "having shaken off the body," the singular number is not intended to be significant;
furthermore, the liberation from that which has been commenced is proclaimed by the word "vimokṣya."
Thus ends the section concerning the destruction of other [defilements].

Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the second section, titled *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, within the *Caturmatasāra* composed by Appaya Dīkṣita, the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarāja Adhvarin— the performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the preceptor of the illustrious Advaita-vidyā, and a crest-jewel of the ocean of the venerable Bhāradvāja lineage.
Salutations to the illustrious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
The second quarter of the fourth chapter.

In this section, the departure through the cranial vein (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*)—which results in the attainment of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) as the fruit of knowledge—must be contemplated as the cause for the wise person's attainment of Brahman.

Among these, the departure up to the entry into the cranial vein is common to both the wise and the ignorant; therefore, it is considered first, because it must also be contemplated as the commencement of the journey when one contemplates the path beginning with light during meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
Speech [is merged] in the mind, because it is so seen and because of scriptural statement. ||1||
Therefore, all [the subsequent ones] follow. ||2||

In the *Chāndogya*, it is heard: "My dear, when this person departs, his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into fire, and fire into the highest deity. Here, a doubt arises: does the merging of speech into the mind refer to the speech itself, or to the function of speech? Since in the passage, "At that time, my dear, he becomes merged with Being," the word "merging" (*sampatti*) is understood to mean dissolution (*laya*), and since the dissolution of the essential nature of speech into the mind—which is not its material cause—is impossible, [the alternative remains] the dissolution of the function even where there is no material cause.

Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Since mental activity is observed even after the cessation of vocal activity, and because of the scriptural statement, "Speech merges into the mind" (*vāṅmanasi saṃpadyate*), it is the speech itself that dissolves into the mind. There is no reason to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "speech" as referring to its function. However, this dissolution should be understood as figurative (*aupacārika*), consisting in a conjunction of the mind preceded by the cessation of the function of speech.

Even in the view that [the senses] are functions (*vṛtti*), since it is impossible for the function whose material cause is speech to dissolve primarily into the mind, when speech is merged, the other external organs also merge into the mind; this is because of another scriptural passage: "The organs merge into the mind."
The summary verses.
For those seeking liberation, the organ of speech does not merge into the mind when in its unevolved state;
for the scriptural statement "speech [merges] into the mind" must be understood as referring to the function of speech.
Speech alone, along with the other sense organs, merges into this [mind], as indicated by the word "dṛk" (the seer).
However, "merging" here does not mean dissolution, but rather a conjunction characterized by the cessation of their respective functions.
Thus ends the section concerning speech.
That [is] mind; [it is] breath, because of the subsequent [scriptural passage]. ||3||

Regarding the statement "mind [dissolves] into breath," however, the dissolution is indeed primary (mukhya). This is because the scripture states, "Mind, my dear, consists of food; breath consists of water," thereby declaring that mind is a modification of earth—denoted by the word "food"—while breath is a modification of water. Thus, since mind has returned to its own material cause (prakṛti), it is possible for it to undergo a primary dissolution into the waters which have themselves become the material cause of breath; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

The mind has *ahaṅkāra* as its material cause (*prakṛti*), whereas the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) has space (*ākāśa*) as its material cause; thus, there is no relationship of material cause and effect between the two in any way. Therefore, in the scriptural passage beginning with "For [the self] consists of food" (*annamayaṃ hi*), what is intended is merely the nourishment of the mind by food and of the vital air by water. Consequently, the meaning to be understood is simply that the mind, conjoined with all the external senses, merges with the vital air after first ceasing its own functions. For the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the activity of the vital air is observed even after the cessation of the modifications of the mind.
These are the summary verses.
The mind, however, must indeed dissolve into the vital breath (prāṇa), because of their relationship as material cause and its modification, just like the existence of clay and its products;
for the scripture declares that the mind consists of food (annamaya), and likewise, the vital breaths are modifications of water.
Let it not be so; for the nourishment of both egoity and the nature of space comes precisely from food and water;
even there, their connection remains.
Thus ends the section concerning the mind.
That [individual soul] [merges] into the presiding deity, because of such passages as "approaching that. (Sūtra 4)

Does the vital breath (*prāṇa*) merge into the individual soul (*jīva*), or rather into heat (*tejas*)? On this point of doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it merges into heat alone, according to the scriptural text: "Speech [merges] into mind, and mind into breath. The correct conclusion is that the vital breath, conjoined with the external organs and the mind, merges into the individual soul. This is because of the scriptural teaching regarding its approach to the soul: "In this very way, at the time of death, all the vital breaths gather around this self"; and because of the scriptural teaching regarding the departure of the soul together with the vital breath: "As he departs, the vital breath departs after him."

Thinking, "Upon whose departure shall I depart, and upon whose settling shall I settle?", he created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, because there is a merging of the vital breath with the individual soul (*jīva*) and then with fire (*tejas*), there is no contradiction even in the statement, "The vital breath [merges] in fire. For even when the Yamunā reaches the ocean after joining with the Gaṅgā, it is conventionally said that "the Yamunā reached the ocean."
These are the summary verses.

It is not correct to hold, according to the literal text, that "the vital breath (prāṇa) directly attains to heat (tejas)," because at that time, scripture declares its approach to the individual soul (jīva) and so forth.
If, first of all, the living soul merges into the light, it does so accompanied by that [mind];
even so, the scripture is appropriate, just as it is said that the Yamunā enters the ocean.
Thus concludes the section on the Superintendent.
[The Self] exists in all beings, because that is heard [in scripture]. ||5||
For it does not show [the object] as having many [parts]. ||6||

Regarding the soul that has been described as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there arises a doubt: does its merging (*sampatti*) into light (*tejas*) refer to light alone, or to all the elements? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it refers to light alone, according to the literal scriptural statement. However, [the correct conclusion is] that it merges into all the elements, because of the scriptural text concerning the soul’s transition: "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of light," which shows that the migrating soul consists of all the elements. Nor can this be explained away by assuming a gradual transition through light and the other elements.

"Of these, He made each one threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3); and from the Śruti and Smṛti passages such as: "Having become separate and possessing distinct potencies, they were unable to produce creatures without merging together in their entirety; having come together in mutual union, the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg. Since these texts demonstrate that each individual element is incapable of producing an effect on its own, it follows that the word *tejas* (fire/heat) denotes fire as mixed with the other elements. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a "convergence" (*sampatti*) of all the elements within each one.
The summary verses.
That prosperity belongs to the vital breath (prāṇa) together with the individual soul (jīva) within the mere element of fire;
if it is expected to exist in other elements as well, let that too be so in due order.
Thus, because the collection of elements lacks individual capacity, that [capacity] is not possible in a single one; therefore, it resides in all the elements together.
Thus concludes the section on the elements.
From the undertaking of the same path, there is immortality even without having burned away [the body]. ||7||
Even in that state [of deep sleep], it is the Self, because the designation "saṃsāra" (wandering) applies to it. ||8||
And [the self] is subtle because it is perceived by means of those two [the body and the senses]. ||9||
Therefore, it is not by means of crushing. ||10||
And from this very same reasoning, there is heat. ||11||
If it be argued that [the soul is not the agent] because of a prohibition, we say no; for according to some, the distinction from the embodied soul is clearly stated. 12.

Thus, the manner of departure has been described. Now, a doubt arises: is this departure common to both the knower and the ignorant, or does it belong to the ignorant alone? On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it belongs to the ignorant alone, based on the scriptural text: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here. This being the position, it is replied: for the knower as well, the prior departure is the same, because the process begins with the entry into the specific channel, according to the text: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality."

The distinction between the knower and the ignorant is heard of specifically at the time of entering the channels for the purpose of departure: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends up to the crown of the head. Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others, branching out in various directions, serve for departing. By the term "in various directions," the absence of restriction to specific channels is expressed, for another scriptural passage states: "This self departs either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body."

And thus, the mention of immortality (*amṛtatva*) in this very context refers to that state of immortality which exists precisely without having burnt away the connection between the body and the senses, and which consists in the destruction of future sins and the non-clinging of past sins; likewise, the statement "he becomes equal to Brahman" also refers to the attainment of Brahman in the form of an experience of Brahman occurring during the time of meditation. This must necessarily be accepted in this way alone.

Because the transmigratory state, characterized by connection with a body, is designated as extending up until the attainment of Brahman via the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), and because the persistence of the subtle body is understood through the dialogue with the Moon regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*); for it is heard in the scripture that, after introducing the dialogue with the Moon with the words, "All who depart from this world go to the moon," it continues: "This indeed is the door to the heavenly world."

He who answers "That which is the moon" is released; but he who does not answer him is born among those places—whether as a lion, a fish, a wild beast, a man, or some other being—according to his karma and according to his knowledge. When he has arrived there, [the deity] asks him, "Who are you? To that he should reply, and so forth.

Therefore, the scriptural passage, "When all are completely released," does not have as its subject the cessation of bondage consisting of the body and senses; for it must necessarily be understood—according to the principle stated in the sūtra *tadantarapratipattau*—that the subtle body departs with the individual soul (jīva) for the purpose of the conversation with the moon.

Even for one who possesses such knowledge, because the departure of the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) does indeed exist, heat is perceived only in certain places as the fiery flame—which pervades the entire body according to the scripture, "It heats its own body from the feet to the head"—is being withdrawn from those very locations when that body is intent on departing. Now, it may be argued that departure is not possible for the knower.

Because of the denial of departure in the passage: "He who is free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the Self—for him the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. Nor can it be argued that because of the Mādhyandina recension reading "the vital breaths do not depart from him," the genitive in the Kāṇva recension reading "from him" (*tasmāt*)—which is prescribed as a general relation—must be understood in the sense of an ablative (point of departure), as in the expression "he hears from the actor," or that its meaning is that the [breaths] do not become separated while being released. This is not tenable.

In both recensions, the word *tat* (that) refers to the body; for in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka itself, in response to Ārtabhāga’s question—"When this person dies, do the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) depart from him?"—Yājñavalkya replied: "No, they are merged right here; he swells up, becomes bloated, and lies dead. Since this describes the swelling of the body like a leather bag due to the filling of air—a physical property of the body—and since the departure of the vital breaths from the living soul (*jīva*) is not even a possibility [in that context], [the term *tat* must refer to the body].

Furthermore, because its negation is untenable, it must be understood that since there is no departure of the body for the knower, all these matters—the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi*), the dialogue with Candra, and the shaking off of good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*)—are the fruits of specific forms of knowledge intended for the attainment of Satyaloka, and not the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman intended for liberation. If it is argued that the occasional vision of fire at the time of death for a knower of Brahman is possible as being prior to the merging of the subtle body (denoted by the word "light") into the Supreme Deity, it is replied as follows:

In the question of Ārtabhāga, the departure from the body is not prohibited; rather, the prohibition of departure applies specifically to the body [only] because it concerns the ignorant. For it is impossible to prohibit the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) from the body for one who is ignorant. If it is asked how it is determined that this concerns the ignorant, it is from the subsequent context. In the subsequent context...

In the question of Ārtabhāga—"When the speech of this immortal person enters into fire, his breath into the wind, his sight into the sun, his mind into the moon, his hearing into the quarters, his power into the sovereign, his body into the earth, his self into the ether, his hairs into the herbs, his hair of the head into the trees, and his blood and semen are deposited in the waters—where does this person then become?"—it is determined in the subsequent passage that action, consisting of merit and demerit, is the substratum [of the person], based on the secret consultation between Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga.

Because it is established by scripture itself; for it is heard in the scripture: "Having departed, those two deliberated; what they said was: 'Now, as for that which they praised—[one] becomes virtuous by virtuous action and sinful by sinful action. Nor should it be argued that because the preceding statement, "He overcomes death again," declares a fruit consisting of crossing over the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), it is therefore determined that the prohibition of departure pertains to the wise person who has realized the nature of reality (prakṛti).

Having stated the meditation on water as the food of fire in the passage, "Fire, indeed, is death; water is its food," its fruit is declared to be, "He overcomes recurrent death. Therefore, if it is argued that here the conquest of death is merely the conquest of fire and not the crossing of *saṃsāra*—and thus the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from the living soul is not something to be prohibited—we say no. For in the case of the knower, there exists the possibility of doubt based on the statement, "For him, there is delay only so long [as he is not released from the body]," which implies that the separation occurs at the very time of the body's dissolution.

Thus, by way of this contextual connection (*prasakti*), since there is a specific prohibition of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the living self (*jīva*) for the wise person, there arises a doubt regarding the case of the ignorant person as well—namely, that for the ignorant, the departure of the vital breaths from the living self does indeed exist. Therefore, the departure exists even for the wise person. Moreover, his departure through the aperture at the crown of the head (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*) is recorded in the Smṛti: "One among them stands above, having pierced the solar orb."

The meaning is as follows: by the statement, "Having transcended the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), he goes not to the supreme goal," it is indicated that among the specific channels (nāḍīs), that particular one which stands above after piercing the solar orb—among those specific channels connected to the head and extending as far as the solar orb—one reaches the supreme state by means of transcending the world of Brahman. By citing this statement of Yājñavalkya, it is also suggested that in the passage "either from the eye or from the head," the mention of the "head" refers to a channel connected to the head, intended for the case of the ignorant (avidvat).
The summary verses.
There is no departure for the wise, because immortality is heard of in that very state;
and because of the prohibition of such departure in the text, "His vital breaths do not depart."
Do not say so; for them too, this very Vedic revelation exists, though it is concealed by the opening words "āgamyopakra-māt," and thus it is identical to that of others.
In this context, their immortality is heard of as consisting in the destruction of karma;
indeed, it is the attainment of Brahman through the burning away of the bondage of the body, which is the non-contemplation of what is not Brahman.
But neither of those two is primary; for by the path beginning with the flame of Brahman (brahmārcis), one attains a stable state above, and therein alone occurs the shaking off of bondage.
It is by that very [path] that the subtle body, which has that [state] as its limit, [attains] the union with the moon and so forth.
And when he emerged, there was a localized heat from the wise one that caused a shower of sparks.

The prohibition of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) refers not to the body, but rather to the Self under discussion; for this is the answer to the question posed by Artabhāga concerning the subject of Brahman-knowledge, as follows:
and here, the genitive case [in *ātmanaḥ*] signifies the status of the point of departure (*apādāna*) required by the verb "to go."
Moreover, in this matter, the Mādhyandinas clearly prescribe the fifth [case-ending] in their statement.
The denial of the departure of the vital breaths from the soul is described for both the knower and the ignorant;
therefore, they might suspect that even for them there is separation from the body.
Thus ends the section concerning the commencement of rebirth.
Those [qualities] belong to others; for thus it has been said. ||13||

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*), together with its collection of organs, its vital breath, and presiding over the body and senses, becomes united with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) at the time of departure. Having raised the doubt as to whether this same union exists for the knower (*vidvas*), it was refuted [in the previous section]. Now, it is considered whether those subtle elements, enveloping the soul, proceed with the soul toward their own effects according to its karma and its specific state, or whether they become merged in the Supreme Self. But is it not said: "The fire [is merged] in the highest deity"?

This reflection on the meaning of the fourth sentence—namely, "But he [the soul] is of the measure of a thumb..."—is appropriately undertaken immediately after the three preceding sections that deal with the meaning of the three sentences ending with "That [soul], upon departing, enters into breath and heat. This is because the subject matter of the fourth sentence, which concerns the departure (utkrānti), precedes the commencement of the journey. Thus, immediately following the investigation into the manner of departure, it must be established by the section beginning with "And it is the same up to the commencement of the path" (*samānācāsṛtyupakramāt*) that this very departure is common even to the knower (*vidvat*). True.

By the method previously stated, there is a "suggestive connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) because that same [point] exists here as well: it was stated in the previous section that for those who know Brahman, there is a journey preceded by departure; however, this is incorrect, because the scripture—specifically the passage "the fire [merges] into the highest deity"—demonstrates the dissolution of the subtle body (consisting of speech and so forth, together with mind and breath) into the Supreme Brahman, which is the material cause of all, in its very own nature. Since one devoid of body, senses, and so forth cannot have a dialogue with the Moon and the like, a journey via the path of light (*arcirādi-gati*) associated with such [a body] must necessarily refer to another subject. Herein lies the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the intermediate state, since no effect in the form of the experience of pleasure or pain is observed in the absence of the attainment of the Supreme Self, they proceed according to their karma and according to their knowledge, in accordance with that effect which is the experience [of pleasure and pain]. As for the statement "the light [merges] in the Supreme," it merely reiterates the Supreme Self's role as the sustainer common to all things.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) under discussion merge into the Supreme Self (paramātman). For the Śruti declares: "Heat [merges] into the highest deity. This scriptural statement is both authoritative and logical; its fruit is the attainment of rest, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution, which serves as the cause for the specific creation of various worlds—a state accessible only through the realization of the One. Thus, since it is possible for the passage "heat into the highest deity" to convey a previously unknown meaning (apūrvārtha), one should not assume it merely reiterates a general principle common to all things.
These are the summary verses.
Living beings endowed with life go indeed according to their fruit;
due to the absence of fruit, they merge into the Supreme Self within the food.
But the phrase "the splendor of the Supreme" (tejaḥ parasya) restates the Lord's status as the universal substratum for all these [elements] when they depart elsewhere.
To ensure the fulfillment of the statement "Let there not be this [separation] from the Supreme Light," the merging [of the individual self] with That must be accepted,
as it is in the cases of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution.
Thus ends the section on the excellence of others.
There is no division, because of the scriptural statement. ||14||

It might be argued that this merging into the Supreme Self is of the nature of an absorption into its cause, similar to the dissolution of the material world (*prākṛta-pralaya*), because the Supreme Self is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of everything and thus lacks distinctions such as those between Manu and other deities. To this, it is replied: it is merely a state of non-separation consisting of a conjunction that renders further distinct empirical usage impossible. This is because in the passage "Heat [merges] into the Supreme," the verb "merges" (*sampadyate*) is supplied from the preceding context; furthermore, there is no established rule that this term must refer to a specific type of prior creation. Moreover, there is no evidence for a difference in meaning here, as there is no mention of a renewed creation following this, as there is after the material dissolution at the beginning of a great cycle of creation (*mahāsarga*).
The summary verses.
This attainment would indeed be a dissolution, because it reverts to its original nature;
therefore, as before, this [word] should be understood as being connected with the attainment of that [state].
Thus ends the section concerning non-differentiation.

Then, there is the blazing forth of the highest flame; with its door illuminated, [the soul] proceeds by means of the power of knowledge, through the application of mindfulness to the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge], and favored by the one within the heart, by means of one out of a hundred [veins]. ||16||

Thus, the common manner of departure for both the knower and the ignorant has been stated. Now, a specific distinction is declared regarding the commencement of the journey: that for the knower, there is a restriction to departing through the channel at the crown of the head (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*). Here, it cannot be restricted that the knower’s journey proceeds only through the Brahma-channel at the crown while others depart differently; for the channels cannot be distinguished by the individual soul (*jīva*) whose heart is agitated by the distress of the process of departure.

Nor can it be argued that, through the proficiency gained from the practice of such contemplation as "At the time of practicing the vidyā, I shall depart by means of such a channel situated in such a location and thereby attain Brahman," there would arise a recognition of the specific channel for one's own departure; nor can it be said that the skill in discernment would also arise through the pacification of the distress of departure by resting in Brahman.

For even so, it is impossible for one situated within the inner chamber of the heart, which is enveloped in dense darkness, to discern the specific channel for one's own departure among the thousands of channels that are incessant, subtle, and extremely minute.

Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the scriptural text, "By that [path] he goes upward," merely restates the occasional, accidental departure of the knower through the cranial channel (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*) for the purpose of its glorification.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the restriction—that the knower departs exclusively by the cranial channel, which has more than a hundred [other channels], and not by any other—is indeed possible. This is because it is improper to assume that the scriptural text, "By that he goes upward," is a partial restatement (*pākṣika-anuvāda*). Furthermore, it is not the case that the channels are difficult to perceive.

At the time of departure, this Self departs by means of that flash which illumines the tip of this very heart; for there is scriptural testimony regarding the illumination of the tip of the heart, and because the power of knowledge exists, as does the practice of contemplating the path remaining from that knowledge at the time of its performance, and because there is the grace of the Supreme Person propitiated by that knowledge, which serves as the subduer [of obstacles].
The summary verses.
The claim that "the channels (nāḍīs) are difficult to perceive" and thus there is no rule regarding the Brahma-channel for the wise,
and that the statement "it goes upward" merely describes its occasional movement— that is not so.

The rule is established that [the soul] exits through the channel located at the crown of the head, its passage having been opened by the grace of the Blessed One attained through the practice of knowledge.
Thus ends the section concerning the abode.
Following the rays. ||17||

It is heard that one who is free from defects, having departed through the *brahman-artery* and followed the rays of the sun, moves toward its orb: "When he departs from this body, he then ascends upwards by these very rays. Therefore, there arises a doubt as to whether the restriction "by the rays alone" is tenable or not. It is not tenable; for it is impossible for one who dies at night to follow the rays of the sun, and the heat experienced during the nights can also be explained as being of the nature of fire (*āgneya*).

Even if one accepts, according to the principles of astronomy, that the rays of the moon are indeed the rays of the sun entering the lunar orb, they too would be absent during the new moon (darśa) and other such nights. Nor can it be argued that for a wise person who dies at night and departs through the *mūrdhanya-nāḍī*, an upward ascent must be described as waiting for the solar rays until sunrise; for this contradicts the statement regarding speed: "As far as the mind is projected, so far shall one go to the Sun. Therefore, it must be concluded that the passage concerning the rays is merely a contingent restatement (*pākṣikānuvādaka*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: even at night, the knower proceeds following the rays of the sun. For, just as in summer there is an intensity of heat from the solar radiance during the day, one perceives heat in sand and other substances at night; through this perception of heat, it is understood that the sun's rays exist [there], and thus their presence is known even at night. In this way, the scriptural statement regarding the rays also becomes meaningful.
These are the summary verses.
Travel by following the rays is not certain during the nights because of their absence;
however, the scriptural statement "by these very [rays]" merely reiterates the possibility of obtaining them as an alternative.
If this were so, the restriction [of the term] would become meaningless;
therefore, it is certain that they exist even during the nights, as evidenced by the sign of your vision.
Thus concludes the section concerning the following of the rays.
If it be argued that [the soul] does not depart [at death], we say no; for the connection [of the soul with the body] lasts as long as the body exists, and the scripture also demonstrates this.

It is considered whether or not there is attainment of Brahman for the knower who dies at night. [The prima facie view is: There is none at all; for it is said, "Daytime, the bright fortnight, and the northern solstice are praised for those about to die, while the opposite is censured. Since dying at night is thus censured, and since what is censured does not lead to the attainment of the supreme goal of man—this being the position reached, it is replied: Even for the knower who dies at night, the attainment of Brahman certainly occurs. It is not the case that by the censure of dying at night, one attains a censured state of existence.

Since the connection with karma culminates in the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), there is an absence of any cause for bondage. Because past karmas whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed by knowledge, and because future karmas do not adhere [to the soul], and because karma whose effect has already begun lasts until the final body, death at night is observed; in such cases, it must be inferred on the strength of the result that those powerful past evil karmas were facing fruition.
The summary verses.
If death occurs at night, there is no attainment of Brahman at all, for that [attainment] is indeed censured;
do not say so, for how can there be a shaking off of the body when there is a connection with ritual action?
Thus concludes the section on the night.
And for this reason, [the same applies] even during the southern course of the sun. ||19||
These two are remembered by the yogin, and they are indeed objects of memory. ||20||

For one who dies at night, the attainment of Brahman is established by that very same cause as for one who dies during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). This is the specific doubt regarding this section on extended application (*atideśādhikaraṇa*): "It is heard in the *Upaniṣad* of the Taittirīyas: 'He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course (*udayana*), having attained the greatness of the gods, goes to union with the Sun; but he who dies during the southern course, having attained the greatness of the ancestors, reaches union with and the same world as the Moon.'"

Therefore, it is determined that even for the wise man who dies during the southern course of the sun, after reaching the moon and experiencing the enjoyments of the ancestors, there is a return according to the scriptural rule, "having dwelt until the [next] conjunction" (*yāvat-sampātam uṣitvā*). In that regard, at the conclusion of the Puruṣa-vidyā, a distinction in results for those who die during the northern or southern courses is indeed stated specifically for one who possesses the knowledge of Brahman prescribed in the preceding section. True; however, in that context, the attainment of Brahman itself is what is intended to be established, as indicated by the supplementary statement, "he attains the greatness of Brahman."

Therefore, it should be understood that for one who dies during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), there is enjoyment of divine pleasures in the world of the Sun, and for one who dies during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), there is enjoyment among the ancestors; these are intended as points of rest on the path. Otherwise, it would follow as a logical conclusion that even for the knower who dies during the northern course, there would be no attainment of Brahman. Now, regarding those about to die, the knower [is distinguished from] the yogis, concerning whom it is said: "I shall declare that time, O bull of the Bharatas, departing at which they do not return and returning.
"Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course... [and so forth].
Departing from there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun's southern course—
having attained the lunar light during that time, the yogi returns.

"These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be eternal for the world; by one a person goes to non-return, by the other he returns again. Therefore, one who dies during the southern course of the sun does not attain Brahman. If it is argued that this is why Bhīṣma’s waiting for the northern course is mentioned in the Mahābhārata, it is replied: here, no specific time of death is prescribed for those about to die; rather, the two paths known as Devayāna and Pitṛyāṇa, which are to be remembered by those devoted to Yoga, are being taught. For such is the concluding summary: [text follows]... Thus, it is said: "The path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is described as the southern course of the sun, and the path of the gods (devayāna) as the northern course. This refers to the two paths to be meditated upon by practitioners of Yoga, not to a restriction on the time of death for those seeking liberation. Furthermore, even for those who have attained knowledge, the attainment of Brahman occurs at the time of death, regardless of the solstice. As stated in the Smṛti: "Whether at night or by day, whether in the season of rain or in winter, at whatever time the knower of Brahman departs, he attains liberation. Moreover, the Smṛti declares that the departure from the body is the cause of liberation: "When the breaths depart from the body, at that very moment he is liberated. Therefore, there is no dependence on the northern course of the sun. Nor is there any contradiction with the Śruti, for the Śruti speaks of the attainment of Brahman through the path of light and so forth, without specifying the time of death. Furthermore, the Smṛti passage regarding the northern course is intended to encourage the practice of Yoga, not to restrict the time of death for those seeking liberation. As the Smṛti says: "For one who has performed his duties and attained knowledge, there is no fixed time for death; wherever and whenever he may die, he attains the supreme goal. Thus, the Smṛti concerning the northern course is merely an exhortation to the practice of Yoga. Consequently, there is no conflict between the Śruti and the Smṛti. Therefore, the conclusion is that the attainment of Brahman occurs for the knower of Brahman at the very moment of death, irrespective of the solstice. ||| End of Section 10 ||| End of Chapter 4 |||
