"No yogin whatsoever is deluded regarding these two paths; therefore, O Arjuna, remain ever disciplined in yoga at all times. By these two verses, "Fire is light" and "Smoke is night," the paths of the gods (*devayāna*) and the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*) are recognized. However, Bhīṣma’s waiting for the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) was intended to demonstrate that he had attained the power of dying at will through the majesty of his yoga and the grace of his father.
Therefore, it is established that even for a knower who dies during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), there is attainment of Brahman.
These are the summary verses.
Nevertheless, the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) is not [the sole factor] for one who has died, because it is stated that such a person attains union with the Moon (candrasāyujya);
and because it is also stated that Bhīṣma, though a knower of Brahman, waited for the arrival of the northern solstice (udagayana).
It is not so; for him too, it would follow from the very absence of the previously mentioned causes of bondage.
His attainment of union with the Moon occurs after a specific period of time, while his attainment of worship occurs swiftly on the path.
For this very reason, the attainment of Brahman is described for him in the supplementary portion of the text;
Bhīṣma’s waiting for that [attainment] is solely for the purpose of proclaiming his greatness.
Thus ends the section concerning the southern course.

Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the section titled *Nayanamukhamālikā*, within the *Caturmatasāra* composed by Adīkṣita— the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarāja, who was himself the son of the illustrious Viśvajidyājin, the teacher of the non-dualistic science (*Advaitavidyā*), and the Kaustubha-jewel of the ocean of the venerable Bhāradvāja lineage.
Prosperity!
Salutation to the illustrious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
The Third Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya.
By the path beginning with light, because that [attainment] is well-known [from scripture]. ||1||

In this chapter, the path of the wise which results in the attainment of Brahman is investigated. First, in the *Chāndogya*, regarding the Upakośala-vidyā, it is stated: "They go to the light (*arcis*); from the light to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward; from those months to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; from the moon to the lightning. There a person belonging to the Manu-race leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman; by this [path]..."

It is heard in scripture that those being led do not turn back during this human cycle. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, within the teaching on the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), it is said: "From there they pass into the light; from the light into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months into the world of the gods (*devaloka*); from the world of the gods into the sun; from the sun into the lightning. A person who is non-material (*amānava*) comes from the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahmā."

In that very same *Purāṇa*, the path is heard described differently: "When a person departs from this world, he comes to the world of Vāyu. There, it opens up for him like the hole of a chariot wheel; through that, he ascends upward. He comes to the sun; there, it opens up for him like the opening of a door; through that, he ascends upward. He comes to the moon; there, it opens up for him like the hollow of a drum; through that, he ascends upward. He...

"It comes to the world of no-sorrow; there it dwells eternally"—thus it is heard. In the *Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad*, the path is heard as follows: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni, then to the world of Vāyu, then to the world of Varuṇa, then to the world of Āditya, then to the world of Indra, then to the world of Prajāpati, and then to the world of Brahman. Furthermore, regarding that same path in the *Dahara-vidyā*, it is heard: "Then, by these very rays, he ascends upwards."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is it that only one single path beginning with light (*arciḥ*) is taught by these scriptural passages, or is another path also taught? Thus, the question is whether there is an uncertainty regarding the path. For the moment, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule. This is because a distinction [in paths] is perceived through the difference in the stages of the path; furthermore, it is not appropriate to establish non-difference by means of a collective synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*), because that would contradict the specific declaration: "When he departs from this body, then he ascends upwards by these very rays."

This is because it would contradict the statement regarding speed: "As soon as he casts his mind, so quickly does he go to the sun. Furthermore, there is no need for a synthesis of the various stages of the path mentioned in different Vidyās, just as there is no synthesis of the various qualities of Brahman. To this, the following is said: The knower goes by one single path, that beginning with light (arcir-ādi), because that very same path is recognized everywhere. Moreover, the restrictive particle (*eva*) serves as a restatement intended to exclude other possible paths.

For it is impossible for a single statement to have the intention (*tātparya*) both of reaching the rays and of excluding everything else; furthermore, the mention of "swiftness" is appropriate in relation to the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*); and the passage "as far as he might throw his mind" is merely a form of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

Furthermore, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā of both the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads, there is the teaching of the very same path beginning with light (arcis) for those devoted to other forms of knowledge as well, as seen in the passages: "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya 5.10.1), and "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship truth with faith" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2.15). Thus, just as for those possessing the Pañcāgni-vidyā, so too for those established in other sciences, the path of light and so forth is taught.
The summary verses.
Various paths for the wise have been taught here and there in the various sciences,
due to differences in the form and qualities of those sciences, and because of the distinctness of their respective preceding sequences.
This entire path, beginning with light, is [known] through recognition;
even though it exists, all that ignorance is not one, because its qualities are not identical.
Thus concludes the section concerning the path beginning with light (arcirādy-adhikaraṇa).
The air [is merged] from the year, by way of both the non-specific and the specific. ||2||

It has been stated that all the knowers proceed by the single path beginning with light (*arcis*). Regarding that path, the followers of the *Chāndogya* study the world of the gods (*devaloka*) as being between the months and the sun: "From the months to the year; from the year to the sun. The followers of the *Vājasaneyi*, however, study the world of the gods as being between those two: "From the months to the world of the gods; from the world of the gods to the sun. Since the path is one and the same, both [worlds] are to be combined in both places.

Although the scriptural sequence (*śrautakrama*) expressed by the fifth case ending is equal for those two, the year (*saṃvatsara*) must be placed after the month; for it is appropriate that it follows the six months of the northern course (*udagayana*), since we observe that each subsequent stage among the day, the waxing fortnight, and the month represents a longer period of time. Therefore, "the world of the gods" (*devaloka*) is situated above the year.

It is thus determined. And here the Vājasaneyins read of wind before the sun: "When a person departs from this world, he comes to the wind; there the wind makes a space for him like the hole of a chariot wheel, and through that he ascends upward; he comes to the sun. Thus they teach wind prior to the sun.

The Kauṣītakins, however, read of Vāyu as being beyond the light (arcis), which is indicated by the term "the world of fire" (*agniloka*) in the passage: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire; he comes to the world of Vāyu. In that case, although Vāyu is obtained as being after the light according to the order of the text for the Kauṣītakins, it is placed before the sun according to the scriptural sequence indicated by the word "upwards" in the Vājasaneyi text—"By that [path] he ascends upwards; he comes to the sun"—for the scriptural sequence is more authoritative than the order of the text.

Thus, after the year and before reaching the world of Āditya, when the worlds of Vāyu and Devaloka are reached, this is considered: Are the worlds of Vāyu and Devaloka distinct, such that the knower goes to them in whatever order he desires; or are they non-distinct, such that after the year one goes from the world of Vāyu directly to Devaloka? What is the logical conclusion?

Because it is well known that the words "upwards" (*ūrdhva*) and the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) have distinct meanings, both [the wind and the world of the gods] are understood to lie within the interval between the year and Āditya according to the sequence of the scriptural text; and since there is no specific distinction [to the contrary], one proceeds as one pleases. Nor should it be argued that the wind and the world of the gods are not distinct because of the scriptural statement: "He who blows here—he is the cup of the gods."

Since another explanatory passage (arthavāda) is heard stating, "The year is the world of the gods" (*saṃvatsaraḥ svaḥ lokaḥ*), there is the possibility of the conception that the year itself is the world of the gods; thus, one might argue that the year and the world of the gods should be inserted between the month and the sun, because there would otherwise be no determining factor (*vinigama*) as to whether the world of the gods comes before or after Vāyu. This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "After the year, the knower goes to Vāyu."

Regarding the term *devaloka*, although it is stated without qualification as "the world (*loka*) of the gods," it is specifically prescribed in the form of Vāyu by the passage, "He reaches Vāyu. This is because of the scriptural declaration: "Vāyu alone is the world of the gods, he who blows here. Nor can this be taken merely as a figurative designation for that [world], as in the case of the statement "The year is the heavenly world" (*saṃvatsaraḥ svargo lokaḥ*); for since the celestial chariots are supported by the tether of Vāyu, it is logical that Vāyu is included within the dwellings of the gods like a pillar, and thus it is possible for the term to refer to its own primary sense.
The summary verses.
Since both the year and the world of the gods are directly enjoined by scripture as occurring immediately after the months,
the year must come first due to its connection with the months, and the other (the world of the gods) should be placed after it.
In that very context, the wind (māruta) also reaches [the sun] by means of the scriptural statement regarding the "upward path" (ūrdhvapada),
which is more powerful due to its immediate sequence with the "light" (arcis) in the Kauṣītaki recension.
There is no rule determining which of those two comes first or second; therefore, they may be arranged as one pleases.
Or rather, that very [wind] is mentioned here without distinction, for it is measured as "air" (vāyu) according to the Vedic revelation.
Even though it was heard that the celestial abode belongs to Vāyu, it was previously thought to belong to the cloud as well;
yet, because the multitude of palaces is held by the cords of the wind, that [earlier notion] has become true only in name, like a mere praise.
Thus ends the section concerning the air.
He is called Taṭita because of his connection with Varuṇa. ||3||

In the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad], based on the scriptural passage beginning with, "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire (agniloka)," it is well-established that the term *agniloka* is a synonym for *arcis* (flame) and thus occupies the first position. In that context, the placement of Vāyu, who stands immediately after that [flame], is stated to be above the year (*saṃvatsara*).

In that context, since Āditya is mentioned immediately after Varuṇa, his placement above Vāyu—referred to by the term "devaloka"—is established according to the sequence of the *Vājasaneyaka* scripture which states, "from the world of the gods to Āditya," thereby not contradicting the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Regarding Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati, the inquiry arises: are they to be placed above Vāyu or above Vidyut? For now, it is concluded that they should be placed above Vāyu, because there is no other available space elsewhere, and because all stages from Arcis up to Vidyut possess a scriptural sequence (*śrautakrama*), [and thus the next stage] must belong to the non-human person (*amānavapuruṣa*) immediately following that.

Furthermore, because [the text] declares that they lead one to Brahman, and since there is no room for them elsewhere, they cannot be inserted [into the sequence]. To avoid rendering that instruction meaningless, some scriptural order (*śrautakrama*) must necessarily be set aside; thus, according to the order of the reading—"He [reaches] the world of Vāyu, he [reaches] the world of Varuṇa"—Varuṇa must be inserted immediately after Vāyu. This is because, when a conflict arises between two orders, it is more reasonable to set aside the sequential order (*kramabādha*). Thus, once the scriptural order of Vāyu and Āditya has been set aside, Indra and Prajāpati must also be inserted after Varuṇa.

This being the position reached, it is replied: Varuṇa must first be placed above lightning. This is because of their connection; since clouds accompanied by water are seen above lightning, it is appropriate for Varuṇa, the lord of waters, to be situated above that. Indra and Prajāpati are to be placed immediately after him by process of elimination, and also according to the maxim that "interpolated elements are to be placed at the end. There is no contradiction, as the non-human person's role as the guide to Brahman is consistent whether he acts through the mediation of Varuṇa and the others, or in conjunction with them.
The summary verses.
Varuṇa and the others should be placed between Vāyu and Bhānu;
otherwise, in any other arrangement, some scriptural sequence would be contradicted.
Thus, there is a contradiction with the Vedic revelation stating "he leads them," because a location for those who have been instructed must be specified somewhere above.
Therefore, Varuṇa should come after Vāyu because he is mentioned [in that position];
immediately after him [should follow] the other two as well, since the sequence of Vāyu and Āditya has been broken.

Let it not be so; for Varuṇa, whose sequence in the Śruti has been sublated by the lightning, is placed above it due to that connection, while the two remaining [deities] are situated above him according to the order of the text.
For the person of lightning does not, when unmentioned, convey the state of being the one who causes the crossing over;
therefore, there is no doubt regarding the "one who causes the crossing" based on the scriptural statement, "He [leads] them."
Thus concludes the section concerning Varuṇa.
The souls are of a subtle, transportable nature (ātivāhika), because of the indicative mark of that [scriptural passage].
Therefore, that [destruction] occurs by means of lightning alone. ||5||

The sequence of the light and the others has been determined. Now their essential nature is being considered: are the light and the others signs of the path (*mārgacihna*), or stages of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), or perhaps bearers who transport the wise? In this regard, [they are signs] because they are understood from statements that bear the character of worldly sentences teaching path-marks such as forests, rivers, and mountains. Or alternatively, they are stages of enjoyment; these very things are worlds (*loka*).

This is because days, nights, half-months, seasons, and years are described as "worlds" (*loka*) in the passage, "Days and nights... years," and because in the Kauṣītaki recension the word "world" is heard in the phrase, "He comes to the world of Agni. Furthermore, they are not the bearers across; for it is specifically the non-human person (*amānava-puruṣa*) who is heard of as the bearer across, and because after lightning, it is the non-human person who is the bearer across, making it impossible for Varuṇa and the others to be the bearers across.

This being the case, it is said in reply: These [beings], beginning with Light (*arciḥ*), are specific deities appointed by the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) to conduct the wise. This is because we understand that the relationship of "the one who causes to reach" and "the goal to be reached," which is heard in the case of the non-human person (*amānavapuruṣa*) in the passage, "He leads them to Brahman," is the very same relationship that exists in the case of the preceding stages such as Light and the rest; for a relationship indicated in general requires a specific determination.

Nor is it untenable for non-conscious entities to be *ātivāhika* (conveying deities), because the light (*arcis*) and so forth refer to the deities presiding over them. If all these were *ātivāhika*, then how could Indra and the others, who are mentioned after lightning, be established as *ātivāhika*? If you argue that this is because only the non-human person (*amānava-puruṣa*) is heard of there as being *ātivāhika*, do not say so; for in that context, Varuṇa and the others are also included within the category of *ātivāhikas* by virtue of their acting as his assistants.
These are the summary verses.
Those signs of the path, such as the "light" (arciḥ) and others, which are recited for the wise,
may either be understood everywhere through the word "world" (loka) or they may be the planes of enjoyment.
For the capacity to carry [the oblation] beyond is indeed described as belonging to the lightning at the time of its withdrawal;
therefore, that very same connection is established for the preceding stages as well.
Thus ends the section concerning the *ātivāhika* (the conductor).
"The effect [is the destination], according to Bādari, because the going of this [soul] is possible [only there]. (Sūtra 6)
And because it has been specified. ||7||
But that designation [of the Self] is due to its proximity. ||8||
When the task is finished, he should depart from that supervision along with [the supervisor], because there is no further need for distinction. ||9||
And because of the Smṛti. ||10||
But Jaimini [holds] the opposite, because of the primacy [of the literal sense]. ||11||
And because it is so observed [in scripture]. (12) Nor is there an intention directed toward the effect. (13)

Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the soul] is led [to the world of the fathers] because there is no connection with a contrary [desire], since there are defects in both cases; and because of the nature of its resolve (tatkratu). ||14||
And he demonstrates the distinction. ||15||

The logical connection is that the investigation into the nature of the goer follows immediately after the investigation into the nature of the guide. Now, a doubt arises: does this series beginning with light lead those who meditate upon the effected (kārya) Hiraṇyagarbha, or those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman, or those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman, or those who meditate upon the inner self as being identical with Brahman? In this doubt, the conclusion is that it leads those who meditate upon the effected [Brahman]. This is because the attainment of the goal is logically possible only for one who meditates upon the effected Hiraṇyagarbha.

For one who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman as already complete, movement to another place for the sake of attaining It is not possible, because It is eternally attained. This is because the effect of supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*) consists solely in the cessation of ignorance regarding the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, this is evident from the specific qualification in the texts: "The person, having reached [the world], leads them to the worlds of Brahman" and "He enters the assembly hall and the abode of Prajāpati. Here, by the use of the word "worlds" in the plural, it is specified that he leads those who meditate on Hiraṇyagarbha—who is designated by the term "Prajāpati"—residing within the assembly hall of that very Hiraṇyagarbha, specifically in those particular worlds.

"He leads them to Brahman"—in this context, the neuter gender of the word *brahman* is appropriate because it refers to that [Brahman] as being proximate due to its status as the first-born (*prathamaja*) of the Supreme Brahman. For one who has attained Hiraṇyagarbha by means of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), there is the scriptural statement: "Going upwards by that, he attains immortality," and "They do not return to this human whirlpool."

Thus, the statement regarding immortality and non-return is justified as referring to the attainment of the world of the Supreme Brahman—which lies beyond the world of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma)—upon the departure from that world, together with Hiraṇyagarbha, the presiding lord of that world, once his office has been completed. "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedānta, who are self-controlled, whose being is purified by the yoga of renunciation, and who are of pure essence..."

For this is established by the Śruti: "But at the time of the final end, they all, having died, are completely liberated in the world of Brahman," and likewise by the Smṛti: "When the dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]. Alternatively, he leads only those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman.

Because the word *brahman* is used there in its primary sense—as in the phrase, "He seeks these [worlds] for Brahman"—and because scriptural texts such as the Paryaṅka-vidyā demonstrate that even though the Supreme Brahman is omnipresent, the cessation of the bondage of karma and its latent impressions occurs only for the knower who has reached that specific world; and because it is heard in scripture that one who has traveled by the path of light (*arciḥ*) and so forth attains the Supreme Brahman, as stated: "Having risen from this body and having reached the highest light, he appears in his own true form."

Nor should it be suspected that there is an attainment of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman) based on the statement, "having entered the assembly hall and residence of Prajāpati," because this is intended to describe the realization of one who possesses knowledge. For in that very context, the mantra—"shaking off the body, being perfected in self, may I attain the uncreated world of Brahman"—specifies "the uncreated world of Brahman"; and in accordance with that, it is appropriate to understand the word *prajāpati* as referring to the Supreme Person through its etymological derivation (*yoga*).

This being the case, it is said in reply: there is no fixed rule that [the Lord] leads only those who meditate on the effect (*kārya*), or that He leads only those who meditate on the supreme (*para*), for faults arise in both cases. If one holds the position that He leads only those who meditate on the effect, scriptural passages such as "having attained the highest light" (*paraṃ jyotir upasaṃpadya*) would be contradicted. If one holds the position that He leads only those who meditate on the supreme, the scriptural passage "those who know thus" (*tad ya itthaṃ viduḥ*) would be contradicted.

For that Śruti passage, while describing the path beginning with light (arcirādi) for those who meditate on the individual soul (jīva) as being identical with Brahman, does so by way of refutation; it establishes the meditation on the true nature of the soul as dissociated from the body, because for those who know Brahman as fire, the attainment of Brahman would otherwise be impossible. Nor should it be argued that even so, the impossibility [of such attainment] remains the same, because in the section beginning with "But he who meditates on Him as the Self" (Brahma-sūtra 4.1.3), it is stated that the attainment of Brahman is achieved only by one who contemplates Brahman as the very Self of the individual soul.

Even when there is a contemplation of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being of the nature of Brahman, the contemplation of Brahman as the Self with respect to the soul remains unimpaired; for in that case, there is merely a difference in the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, just as in the transition from "the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa" to "the younger brother of Rāma. Therefore, the group beginning with the path of light (*arcirādi*) does not lead those who worship only the individual souls such as Hiraṇyagarbha—which are essentially non-conscious entities (*acidvastu*)—or those who worship [such souls] while viewing them as Brahman.

Rather, it leads only those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman either as the substantive (the object qualified) or as its attribute; for this very reason, scriptural passages such as, "As far as name extends, there he has freedom of movement," demonstrate that for those who meditate on symbols (pratīka) such as name and so forth, there is a specific, limited fruit that does not depend on the journey via the path of light (arcirādi-gati) for the sake of attaining Brahman.

For by this scriptural passage, it is stated that those who take hold of symbols (pratīka) may move about as they desire, up to the point where the name of gods, humans, and so forth still persists; that is, as far as the name "Brahman" extends. By this, it is made known that there is no movement [of the soul] in that case where liberation from the names and forms of gods and others—as established by the scripture stating, "Thus the knower is liberated from name and form"—has been attained.

The mantra, however—"those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta"—does not teach that one who has reached Hiraṇyagarbha by means of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) through the meditation on Hiraṇyagarbha attains Brahman along with him. Rather, it teaches that for one who has reached His world through the meditation on Hiraṇyagarbha and has performed meditation on Brahman right there, the attainment of Brahman occurs at the end of his own body. For this is its meaning:

Those foremost of men who have ascertained the true nature of the meaning of the Vedānta through hearing, reflection, and so forth, who have conquered their senses, and who abide in this world solely in the Supreme Brahman, being established in it, are liberated at the end—that is, at the conclusion—of their final body by means of that very Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Immortal, through His grace alone. Therefore, it is established that [the Lord] leads only those who have no other support.
The summary verses.
This group beginning with light leads those who worship Brahmā;
because it is limited in extent, its being reached by traveling is logically established.
Bādari held this view: that for those who meditate on Brahman as all-pervading, there is no going [to Brahman] because it is already attained here; thus, such a journey would be purposeless.
Jaimini maintains that for those who meditate upon Brahman, that very state is indeed the primary goal;
having gone there, it is to be attained as residing in a specific world.
He leads both those who worship that Brahman and those who [worship] the individual soul (jīva) as being of the nature of Brahman,
away from the faults mentioned previously regarding both sides.
According to the view of Bādari, the scriptural teaching that Brahman is to be reached by way of the path beginning with light would be contradicted.
The sage Arciḥ and others, who were heard of among those who know the five fires, would not be found in the mind of Jaimini.

Those who meditate upon Hiranyagarbha, or those who with their intellect worship the Brahman as the mind and so forth, or even those who worship it as the Absolute without attributes— they lead all these [beings] away from that [state], for they perceive only symbols.
The established method of the Siddhānta is that [the Lord] leads those who meditate upon Him by taking either the attribute (viśeṣaṇa) or the substantive (viśeṣya) as His own self, which is Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the effect (kāryādhikaraṇa).

Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the second section, titled "Closing the Eyes," within the *Caturmatasāra* composed by Appaya Dīkṣita— the son of the illustrious Raṅgarāja Adhvarin, who performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, the preceptor of the science of Non-duality (*Advaitavidyā*), and the unique Kaustubha jewel of the glorious Bhāradvāja lineage.
Salutations to the glorious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
The fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
The path of the wise has been described as having the attainment of Brahman as its fruit. Now, the manner of the sovereign power of those who have attained Brahman is considered:
"Upon attaining [Brahman], there is manifestation [of their true nature] by virtue of their own word. (Sūtra 1.3.1)
[The opponent's view is rejected] because it contradicts his own thesis. ||2||
The self [is the subject], because of the context. ||3||

Regarding the passage, "Having attained the highest light, he emerges in his own form," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Is what is intended here an emergence in a form to be achieved—similar to the forms of gods and so forth—or is it the manifestation of one's natural form? For, by virtue of the words "emerges" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) and "in his own" (*svena*), it is impossible for a [newly acquired] form to be what is "emerged"; furthermore, since such a form is not seen to serve the purpose of the person during states such as deep sleep, it is appropriate that the word "own" (*svena*) merely restates what is already established by the sense—that is, the form belonging to oneself. This is the prima facie position.

For although [the Self] is established by its own nature, it is concealed by ignorance in the form of beginningless karmic bondage; thus, its status as something to be accomplished is possible in the sense of being manifested through the cessation of that [ignorance], as has been demonstrated in the *Avadhūti-vidyā*: "Just as the luster of a gem is not created by the washing away of its impurities, so too knowledge of the Self is not created by the removal of defects."
Just as the space occupied by water is not created by the act of digging a well,
but is merely brought into manifestation— how could there be the arising of that which is non-existent?

Furthermore, according to the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "Likewise, through the destruction of qualities that are to be abandoned, qualities such as perfect knowledge (avabodha) and the rest are manifested; they are not produced, for they are indeed eternal to the Self. Thus, when the bondage of karma is destroyed, there occurs a manifestation in the form of expansion of that which consists of knowledge, bliss, and so forth; it is not a production in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). For if that were the case, since the distinction [of the Self] would be established by itself, the form in which one is perfected would have its own possession established as a matter of course; consequently, the word "by oneself" (*svena*) would have to be understood as referring to something that is not an effect to be accomplished. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In the summary verses.
Some adventitious form accrues [to Brahman] merely in accordance with the words "liberated" and "manifested";
for the state of being the goal of human endeavor exists in its own essential nature alone, as is observed from the example of deep sleep.

For one who has become liberated like one who has passed beyond the three realms, the conceptualization of adventitiousness cannot endure within its own form; this is its qualification. Moreover, its manifestation is indeed logical as the shaking off of bondage.
For at that time, the two hundred [verses] beginning with "taj-jñānānanda" are contracted.
Thus concludes the section concerning the manifestation [of the soul's powers] upon reaching [the Supreme].
Because it is seen as non-differentiated. ||4||

Does this wise one who has attained Brahman experience his own self as distinct from Brahman, or rather as non-distinct from it? A doubt arises due to the scriptural passages concerning equality and supreme equality, as well as the *Tattvamasi* (That thou art) and other such texts. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that he experiences it as indeed distinct; for in the passages, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman" and "The stainless one attains equality," there is mention of the liberated soul's association with and supreme equality to Brahman. Therefore, it is distinct, and not non-distinct, because non-distinction would be utterly contradictory [to these statements].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: [the soul] experiences [itself] as undivided. This is because, through the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, its own self—which has become free from distinctions such as "this" and "that"—is seen as it truly is by itself. For the true nature of one's own self is taught by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) to be a mode of the Supreme Self, insofar as it constitutes His body. Therefore, [the soul] experiences [itself] non-differently, precisely as a mode of that [Supreme Self].

However, the scriptural tradition regarding literature (*sāhitya-śruti*), while establishing either identity of agent or identity of object, does not contradict the relationship of the mode and the possessor of the mode (*prakāra-prakāribhāva*) through supreme equality; for even when there is a relationship of mode and possessor of the mode, supreme equality exists by virtue of qualities such as the experience of the bliss of Brahman. Furthermore, it is not intended that there be equality in every respect with respect to all attributes; for if that were the case, the consequence would be non-difference due to the absence of any distinguishing characteristics.

By this, the position of the opponent—who maintains that because the scriptures speak of "supreme equality" (paramasāmya) in liberation, the scriptural mention of a relationship between the "mode" (prakāra) and the "possessor of the mode" (prakārī) must refer only to the state of bondage—is refuted; for equality in every respect is impossible.

This is just as when the supreme equality of two pieces of gold and stone held on a scale is stated, it is intended only because there is absolute equality regarding the specific aspect under consideration.
The summary verses.
The liberated one experiences himself as distinct from the Supreme Self,

in accordance with scriptural passages concerning the identity and equality [of the individual and the universal], and by virtue of the principle that "one becomes according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).
This being so, there is a difference in nature regarding the relationship between the mode and the possessor of the mode;
however, this is because the attainment of supreme equality occurs in liberation solely through the state of being bound.

Let it not be so; for one experiences one's own self as non-different from Brahman by way of being its mode, since the reality of the meaning established by immeasurable scriptures such as "That thou art" has been directly perceived.
Even for one who has become manifest, there may be enthusiasm for the act of enjoyment;
otherwise, there would be mere equanimity. Therefore, it is that [enthusiasm] which is intended by him.
Thus ends the section concerning non-differentiation.
The suffix *brāhma* is applied after [words denoting] *jāmi*, *nirupya*, *nāla*, and so forth. ||5||
"Because it consists of that [Brahman] even by means of mere consciousness," so says Auḍulomi. (6)
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is no contradiction because of such a presentation [of the matter] after it has been previously heard.

The manifestation of the true nature of one who has attained Brahman has been stated. However, because there is a conflict between scriptural passages as to whether this manifestation occurs in a certain specific form or as mere consciousness (*vijñāna*), the matter is now investigated. On this point, it is first argued that it occurs in the form of mere consciousness.

"Just as a lump of salt has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13). Since this passage declares that the Self consists of pure consciousness alone, the scriptural mention of its being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth refers to its not being a substratum for the qualities of sin and the like belonging to the body and mind. Likewise, the scriptural mention of "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) and "having true resolves" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) refers to the fact that during the state of transmigratory existence, these qualities of having true desires and so on occur only occasionally in some [beings]. This being the position reached, it is replied: This manifestation [of the Self] is characterized by the collection of attributes such as being free from sin, which are heard in the *dahara-vidyā* with respect to Brahman in the passage beginning with "brāhmeṇa" (by the Brahmic [nature]).

The Prajāpati-vidyā is taught with respect to the individual soul (jīva) as well, because that [teaching] is introduced there and because of scriptural statements such as "eating" and so forth being attributed to the liberated one. There is no contradiction with the restrictive determination that "[the self] is a mass of consciousness alone" (prajñānaghana eva). For by this, a denial of any form distinct from consciousness is not being made; rather, it is stated that, apart from the distinction between external and internal, it consists of self-luminous awareness everywhere. This is because it accords with the illustrative examples provided therein.

For it is not the case that in the illustrative example of a piece of rock-salt (*saindhava-śakala*), there is an intention to convey that the salty taste pervades every single part, even while its color, touch, and so forth are excluded. Rather, what is intended there is merely this: that there is no multiplicity of tastes according to the difference in parts, as is the case with a mango fruit (*cūta-phala*) and the like due to the distinction between regions such as the skin and so on.

In this context, in accordance with the two scriptural passages, it is logical that when the bondage of karma—which constitutes the form [of the soul]—is destroyed by knowledge, this manifestation occurs through the emergence of the nature of consciousness blossomed by the collection of qualities beginning with freedom from sin (*apahata-pāpmatva*).
In the *Saṃgraha-kārikā*,
Jaimini states that the manifestation of the liberated one consists of the eight qualities of Brahman;
then Auḍulomi says that it is merely consciousness.
The established conclusion is that, because both types of scriptural testimony are observed, both [self-luminosity and objectivity] are accepted;
for here, self-luminosity consists in being consciousness alone in its entirety.
That [liberation] which is taught for one who is released is the cause of cessation, not of other qualities;
just as, for example, the dissolution of a lump of rock salt results in the disappearance of its density, whiteness, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on external objects.
Because that [creation] is understood from mere volition alone. ||8||
And for this very reason, he has no other superior. 9.

The connection [of the passage] arises from the following doubt: "The restriction 'consisting of pure essence alone' does not exclude other properties such as form, which are established by other means of knowledge; likewise, the restriction 'by mere volition alone' does not exclude other activities well-known in the world."

In the Prajāpati-vidyā, there arises a doubt as to whether the attainment of women and other such things by one who has attained Brahman—as described in the passage beginning with "eating, playing, and rejoicing with women, or with vehicles," and so forth—is accomplished by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone, or whether it requires some other external activity. In resolving this, since the volitions of living beings are well known to require further effort even for the accomplishment of desired objects among those things already established—such as the status of a sovereign ruler—the attainment of women and the like by that [liberated soul] likewise requires another activity.

To this it is replied: for one who is liberated, the attainment of women and other objects is accomplished by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*). This is because of scriptural passages that establish such a restriction, such as: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise; if he becomes desirous of the world of women, by his mere volition women arise," and because there is no other scriptural passage here that contradicts this restriction, just as in the case of the statement, "He is indeed a mass of pure consciousness."

Nor does it follow that even for one who is liberated, there could ever arise—by their own nature—a state of frustrated resolve, as in the case of kings and others, because scripture declares that such a person possesses no other lord, being characterized by freedom from the dominion of karma.
The summary verses.
Furthermore, because the non-fruition of their intentions sometimes depends upon karma,
those who are liberated require other efforts to attain relatives and so forth.
Even for kings, nothing has ever been seen anywhere that is to be accomplished by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone;
for there is no scriptural passage that provides a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) stating "from volition alone."
Therefore, like the Lord of All, their creation arises from mere volition alone.
Thus ends the section on the performance of the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and so forth.
Aśravaṇādi says: "For it has been said thus. (10)
Jaimini [holds that there is] hearing [of the Upanishads], because of the absence of any mention of an alternative. ||11||
Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the ritual] is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice. 12.
In the absence of a body, [the soul's existence] is possible as in the case of the intermediate state (sandhyā). ||13||
In the state of existence, it is like the waking state. ||14||
The entry [of the deity] is like that of a lamp; for thus it is shown. 15.
For [the scripture] has made it clear that [the state of being one with the Self] refers to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or final liberation (sampatti). ||16||

Regarding the doubt as to whether the body and senses of one who is liberated exist or do not exist—or whether they exist or do not exist according to his will—the answer is that they certainly do not exist. For the Śruti says: "For one who possesses a body, there is no cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who exists as bodiless, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant touches him. It is for this very reason that the text immediately speaks of his rising up from the body, beginning with: "This serene being, having risen up from this body... and so forth.

Furthermore, once liberated, there would be no need for the creation of his own body or the creation of parents and others for that purpose. In that case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that he has something other than the experience of Brahman as his goal, and that Brahman’s status as the unsurpassed object of enjoyment would be lost. The scriptural passages such as "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold" are merely explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*), because it is impossible for the atomic individual soul (*jīva*) to simultaneously pervade multiple bodies—such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: by the will of the liberated one, bodies may exist or not exist, in accordance with two scriptural passages (*śruti*). Just as, from the observation of two scriptural texts—"Those desiring prosperity should undertake the twelve-day sacrifice" and "By means of the twelve-day sacrifice, one who desires progeny [should sacrifice]"—it is seen that the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possesses the dual nature of both a *sattra* and an *ahīna*. Now, one might object: how can there be the enjoyment of desires in the disembodied state (*videhāvasthā*), and in the absence of such enjoyment, how can there be a desire for the disembodied state?

If it is argued that if enjoyment were by means of the mind alone, then there would never be any dependence on a body, it is replied as follows: In the absence of a body, there is subtle enjoyment, just as in a dream; when a body exists, there is gross enjoyment, clear as in the waking state. Furthermore, when the liberated one possesses instruments such as a body, there is no fixed rule that those must be created by him alone, even though he possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*).

Sometimes, like one in a dream, He enjoys the rasa of His play through the worlds of the ancestors and so forth created by Himself; sometimes, like one in a waking state, He enjoys the rasa of His play through the instruments of the worlds of the ancestors and so forth, both those created by Himself and those created by the Lord of All. Just as the Lord of All, for the sake of His play, creates the world of the ancestors such as Daśaratha and Vasudeva from Himself and enjoys the play of human attributes and the like with them, so too, for the sake of their own play, He Himself creates the worlds of the ancestors and so forth for the liberated souls—this is the distinction.

Nor does this entail the consequence that the liberated one is intent on anything other than the experience of Brahman; for they do not create the world of fathers and so forth out of a craving for their own enjoyment, but rather—

They create [worlds] precisely as specific manifestations of the glory of Brahman, for the purpose of experiencing the glory of Brahman along with its manifestations. If it is objected that this being so, there would be degrees of excellence and deficiency in the experience of the glory of Brahman when it is experienced by those possessing various manifestations, we reply: this is not a fault. For it is accepted that every liberated soul experiences Brahman as distinguished by all manifestations—both those created by themselves and those created by others, whether past or future. Nor is it impossible for the atomic individual soul (*jīva*) to simultaneously preside over multiple bodies.

This is because, just as there exists a capacity for the expansion of dharma and knowledge sufficient to pervade a single body that brings about the experience of all-encompassing bliss during the state of *saṃsāra*, so too does such an expansion exist during the state of liberation (*mukti*), capable of pervading multiple bodies. For it is heard in scripture that in liberation, through the expansion of dharma and knowledge, there is an infinity characterized by non-limitation: "The individual soul (*jīva*) should be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided a hundredfold; yet it is capable of infinity. Thus, due to the expansion of dharma and knowledge in liberation, its nature is unlimited.

Objection: But does not the scripture state that the liberated one lacks knowledge, saying, "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), he knows nothing external nor internal"? How, then, can his expansion of knowledge and omniscience be maintained? This is not a fault, for that scripture refers to either the state of deep sleep or death; indeed, it is well known that the absence of knowledge occurs only in those two states.

"In deep sleep, he does not indeed know himself at this time, thinking 'I am this,' nor does he know these beings; he has gone to utter destruction. Regarding death, it is said: "Having arisen from these elements, he perishes after them; there is no consciousness after passing away. However, regarding liberation, omniscience is clearly stated: "The all-seeing sees everything; he attains everything in every way. Therefore, it is established that liberated souls exist both with bodies and without bodies according to their own will. These are the summary verses.
Those who have attained liberation possess no bodies, as it is so heard in scripture;
nor is that [existence of a body] established by the statement regarding the creation of fathers and others through mere volition.
If those two [the self and the world] were to exist in dependence upon the body, the father, or other such things,
O Brahmin, it would follow that they are not different from the experience of those very things.
Furthermore, the unsurpassed nature of Brahman as the object of enjoyment would be lost;
for their bodies exist or do not exist according to the diversity of their own volitions.
They do not create those [beings] out of a taste for their own enjoyment, along with the instruments such as fathers and so forth;
rather, having considered their inclusion within the divine play (līlā) of the Blessed One, they create them accordingly.

For it has been observed that even the atoms, which are like lamps of living beings, possess consciousness as their own inherent light, through the playful manifestation of the Creator such as Daśaratha and others.
At that time, they pervade even many bodies created simultaneously;
for it is the established doctrine that consciousnesses, which were previously contracted by the multitudes of karma during bondage,
attain pervasiveness upon the removal of that which causes contraction.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa). ||5||
[The Lord is] exempt from the activity of the world, because of the context and because of His non-proximity [to it]. ||17||

If it is argued that [the Lord's form] is not perceptible because of the scriptural teaching [of His invisibility], we say no; for [the scripture] speaks of Him as residing in the spheres of those who hold office. 18.
And it does not abide in modification, for thus it declares its state. ||19||
And thus, perception and inference are demonstrated. ||20||
And because there is a mark indicating equality only with respect to enjoyment. ||21||
Non-return, on account of the word; non-return, on account of the word. ||22||

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether this sovereignty of the liberated one includes the activity of governing the world, like that of the Lord of All, or whether it excludes it. On the grounds of the scriptural teaching of "supreme equality," the initial position is that it includes the activity of governing the world. Nor should it be argued that because the context of creation, control, and so forth concerns only the Lord of All, and because the liberated ones are not present in those contexts, the activity of creation and so on belongs to Him alone and not to the liberated ones.

In the section concerning the Śyena sacrifice, although the arrow is not proximate to the Śyena itself, because of the statement of similarity—"The rest is the same as the Śyena"—the specific subsidiary parts of that [Śyena] are established in those [liberated souls], just as in the case of arrows released from a bow; for there is a statement of similarity with the Lord regarding their activities such as creation. Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that "moving about at will through these worlds, assuming forms at will," the liberated ones wander through the worlds, and such wandering is for the purpose of the divine play (*līlā*) of governing the objects located in each respective world.

Nor should it be argued that this [creation] exists for the sake of experiencing the fruits pertaining to those respective worlds; for if one who experiences the bliss of Brahman were admitted to wander about out of a desire for other objects, its state of being unsurpassed (*niratiśayatva*) would be compromised. Nor should it be argued that if liberated souls possess the power of creating the world and so forth, there would be a total equality with the Lord of All—which would contradict the Śruti stating, "No one is seen equal to Him, nor superior"—and therefore one must conclude that such equality exists only in some other limited form. This cannot be maintained.

Because of the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning equality (*sāmya*), it is logical to restrict the scriptural texts that deny such equality to the context of those still transmigrating; for this denial refers specifically to the equality of Brahman among transmigrators. Furthermore, just as the text "Who indeed knows whether he exists or not in that world? is interpreted differently due to its conflict with the result understood from the qualifying statement, so too it is more appropriate to interpret the scriptural text on equality otherwise, because it conflicts with the statement regarding the result, namely, "He attains supreme equality."

Based on the scriptural statement, "The Cause alone is to be meditated upon," the meditation on Brahman as characterized by being the cause of the world results—according to the *tatkratu* principle—in the sovereignty of the liberated one, excluding only the acts of creation and so forth. This is because there is a contradiction between [the claim of such sovereignty] and the scriptural texts that define Brahman by its status as the cause of the world, as well as the scriptural texts regarding the unity of the Creator of the world. Therefore, the activity of the entire universe—which is common to the Lord of all—is according to the specific context [of each scripture] and does not apply to the liberated ones who are not currently present [in that role]. Furthermore, even the wandering through all worlds is not for the purpose of exercising control.

However, it is for the purpose of attaining the enjoyments belonging to those respective worlds, as indicated by the qualification, "one who eats desires and possesses a form at will. Nor does the unsurpassed nature of the bliss of Brahman—the object of enjoyment—suffer any diminution when the liberated one wanders through the worlds out of a desire for minor enjoyments, accompanied by the transformations of birth, growth, and so forth. For the experience of enjoyments in various worlds by the liberated one is not intended to be like that of worldly pleasure, as it is for the transmigrating soul; rather, it is because he has entered into the bliss of Brahman which consists of his own sovereign power (*vibhūti*).

The principle of *tatkratu* (the attainment of one's desires according to one's resolve), however, applies to matters other than the unique attributes of the object of meditation. Being the cause of the universe is indeed a unique attribute—just like being the Lord of Lakṣmī—because it is established as such by scriptural and traditional texts, such as: "From this very Self, space was produced," and "In the beginning He created the waters and cast His seed into them. Therefore, the mention of supreme equality refers only to equality in the experience of enjoyment consisting in the realization of the bliss of Brahman along with His divine manifestations (*vibhūti*).

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the scriptural hearing of that alone: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman. Furthermore, how could those who are liberated and possess true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*) aspire to such world-creating activity, which is unique to Brahman? Moreover, it has been established by the second chapter sūtra, "And because of its eternity," that both their state of liberation and their qualities, such as true resolve, remain dependent upon the Lord even in liberation.

Even the power of true resolve (satya-saṃkalpatā) belonging to the liberated is restricted solely to the creation of their own bodies, parents, and other instruments necessary for the service of the Lord; therefore, the activities such as the creation of the universe belong exclusively to the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all.
The summary verses.

Even for those who possess liberation, their sovereignty would be all-pervading, encompassing the entire universe, as well as the state of being equal to the Supreme Brahman, the possession of true resolve, the ability to take any desired form at will, and the power to move through all worlds as a self-ruling lord; yet, even from such descriptions, there is clearly perceived here a dependence upon Him who is the ultimate limit of all things.

Let it not be so; for those [passages] dealing primarily with creation and dissolution found in the context of Brahman are not connected to them (the individual souls) in any way, even when proximity occurs.
Their sole nature consists in the enjoyment of the objects of experience renowned in their respective worlds.
The eloquent discourse on wandering through the world does not at all declare the state of being a father by constraint.
Even those objects of enjoyment that exist within the world of transformation are to be abandoned by the liberated;
yet, as manifestations of Brahman, they become objects of experience, and he experiences them along with their full splendor.
That which is called the "truthfulness of resolve" (satya-saṃkalpatā) of the liberated ones is itself a state of existence dependent upon His will;
and all those other qualities of theirs likewise always attain dependence upon Him.
Thus, even in the state of liberation, insentient matter remains the same, and all individual souls possess the single nature of being subservient [to the Lord].
This concludes the section concerning the exclusion of the world-activities [from the liberated souls]. ||6||

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the second section of the *Nayamayūkhamālikā*, a work on the essence of the four systems composed by Appaya Dīkṣita—the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarājādhvarin, who was a jewel in the ocean of the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage and a teacher of the science of non-duality (*advaitavidyā*).
Thus, salutations to Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
And the chapter is completed.
The *Nayamayūkhamālikā* is completed.
